title: British police link substance release at Don Toliver's concert to robbery attempts
summary: British police say the release of an unknown substance at a Don Toliver concert in Manchester is linked to a group of criminals seeking to rob people at the gig
story: British police say the release of an unknown substance at a Don Toliver concert in Manchester is linked to a group of criminals seeking to rob people at the gig

LONDON -- British police said on Friday that the release of an unknown substance during a concert by rapper Don Toliver in Manchester earlier this week is linked to attempts to commit robberies on the night of the event.

Greater Manchester Police did not provide any evidence and did not identify the substance released at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on Sunday night, which resulted in 89 people requiring medical checks for eye and respiratory irritation. One person was taken to hospital.
The 12,000 people present were evacuated soon after the incident.
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said something similar had occurred at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe and that police are in contact with authorities involved in those investigations.
“So far, we suspect that a small group of organized criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night,” he said.

No arrests have been made, but Harding said detectives are sifting through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV and that police are looking to find more than 100 people at the concert to help with enquiries.

Police were called to the venue around 10 p.m. on Sunday after reports that people had been affected by a substance initially believed to be tear gas. Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.
Co-op Live, which opened in 2024, is about 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in a suicide bombing at an Ariana Grande concert in 2017.
“What happened on Sunday night and the imagery on our TVs and online will bring back painful memories of 2017," Harding said.

Toliver, whose music blends trap and R&B, is nominated in five categories, including best new artist, for this year’s Grammy Awards. He also features on the soundtrack to the new “Grand Theft Auto” game.

title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle winery fight lawsuit that surfaced abuse allegations
summary: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt have settled their long-running legal battles over a French winery
story: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt have settled their long-running legal battles over a French winery

LOS ANGELES -- The long-running legal battles between Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt have come to an end a decade after the A-list celebrity couple split, with the actors settling a dispute over the ownership of a French winery.

The actors said in a joint statement Wednesday that they had reached a settlement of the lawsuit, which transcended business matters when a legal filing from Jolie surfaced abuse allegations against Pitt.
“We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,” the statement provided by representatives for Pitt, 62, and Jolie, 51, said.

Jolie filed for divorce in 2016, citing the “health of the family,” after a private jet flight from Europe. The couple’s use of private judges — an increasingly common move among splitting celebrities in recent years — kept the details of the divorce largely under wraps, even after it was settled at the very end of 2024. But the winery lawsuit became a way for details of their dispute to become public.

Pitt sued Jolie in 2022, saying she had abandoned an agreement that he would buy her half of Chateau Miraval, a French winery they owned together. She instead sold her part to the Tenute del Mondo wine group. Pitt said it was a “vindictive” and “unlawful” move that should not have been made without his consent and ruined a private space that had been a second home.

The descriptions of the abuse alleged on the private flight weren’t public until Jolie filed a cross-complaint in the dispute. Jolie and her attorneys said Pitt had demanded she sign a wide-ranging nondisclosure agreement about him as part of the proposed deal that was an attempt to cover up his abuse of her and the children.

The FBI and child services officials had investigated Pitt’s actions on the flight, centering on the treatment of their eldest son. The FBI released a statement in late 2016 saying it would not investigate further, and the U.S. attorney did not bring charges.

Pitt has denied being abusive but did not defend his behavior on the flight. Pitt said in a 2017 interview with GQ that he had a drinking problem at the time, but had since become sober and was going to therapy. In an interview with Esquire earlier this year, he said he was sober for seven years but had started drinking again “in a more restrained manner.”

A heavily redacted FBI report obtained by The Associated Press in 2022 said an agent provided a probable cause statement to prosecutors on Pitt, but that after discussing the merits, “it was agreed by all parties that criminal charges would not be pursued.” The document said Jolie was “personally conflicted” about supporting charges, and in a later court filing she said she opted not to push for them for the sake of the family.
All six children are now adults; the youngest — twins Knox and Vivienne — turned 18 in July. Many of the Jolie-Pitt children have reportedly since dropped their father's surname.

Publicly, both Pitt and Jolie have been extremely tight-lipped on everything surrounding their split, despite robust promotional tours for various projects — including the Pitt-starrer “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” which also landed in select theaters Wednesday.

Both were among the most elite stars in film when they began dating in 2004, after co-starring as hitman-and-hitwoman spouses in “Mr. & Mrs. Smith.” The star of “Maleficent” and “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider,” Jolie won an Oscar for her performance in 1999’s “Girl, Interrupted.”

Pitt, the star of “Fight Club” and “Inglourious Basterds,” thrived as both actor and producer after the split. He won his own Academy Award for 2019’s “Once Upon a Time ... in Hollywood,” the crowning achievement in an awards season that some in media framed as a redemption and brought major public affection for him.

Jolie kept a less visible profile in the years since the divorce, though she directed several films and appeared in several more while trying to focus on raising the children. She was nominated for an Oscar for her portrayal of the legendary soprano Maria Callas in “Maria” and starred in “Couture,” released this summer.
Sen reported from New York.

title: Venice Biennale visitors award top prizes to Nick Cave and India after jury quit
summary: The Venice Biennale art exhibition has awarded its first visitor-decided prizes to U.S. artist Nick Cave and India for its national pavilion
story: The Venice Biennale art exhibition has awarded its first visitor-decided prizes to U.S. artist Nick Cave and India for its national pavilion

MILAN -- The first Venice Biennale art exhibition prizes decided by visitors and not an international jury  have been awarded to U.S. artist Nick Cave for his contribution to the main curated exhibition and to India for its national pavilion, officials announced Wednesday.

Visitors chose the winners of the world's oldest art exhibition for the first time after the international jury quit before the exhibition opened in May. The resignation was triggered by tensions after jurors indicated they would exclude Israel and Russia from consideration for the coveted Golden Lion awards because their leaders face International Criminal Court arrest warrants.

Without a jury to award the traditional Golden Lions, the Biennale announced that visitors to both venues would be able to vote for the ad-hoc Visitors’ Lions. In response, more than 100 participants including artists and pavilion delegations asked to be withdrawn from consideration for the award in support of the jury’s decision.

Cave, best known for his Soundsuits wearable sculptures, presented a suite of seven works representing the seven stages of grief, including a monumental bronze titled Amalgam (Origin) that overlooked the Arsenale’s harbor, for the main show curated by the late Koyo Kouoh.
The Art Newspaper said that Cave’s work embodied Kouoh’s ambition “to counter tragedy — historic and present-day — with beauty and enchantment.”

Cave, 67, is a Chicago-based artist whose practice spans sculpture, installation, dance and performance, and whose works are held by major museums, including the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the Museum of Modern Art and the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

India’s pavilion in the Arsenale titled “Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home” was curated by Amin Jaffer and examined home as an idea constantly subject to change, according to the official catalogue. It was chosen from 100 national pavilions, the highest number ever.

The Visitors' Lions were announced three days after the Biennale closed its doors, and without the customary public ceremony for the Golden Lions. The Biennale announced on Sunday that 684,628 people had visited the Biennale during its May 9-Nov. 22 run, but it did not say how many cast votes.
The Biennale, in announcing the Visitors' Lions, said the awards highlighted artists who “have received the greatest appreciation from visitors.”
“I can say without hesitation that La Biennale is brimming with ever-renewed energy thanks to the vibrant presence of everyone,” Biennale President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco said in a statement.
The 61st Biennale was one of the most contested in memory, and included protests outside the Russian and Israeli pavilions during the preview days open to journalists and the art world.

The main exhibition, “In Minor Keys,” opened a year after Kouoh’s death, her legacy carried on by five co-curators under a title meant to spotlight the overlooked. It featured more than 100 artists and artistic groups selected by Kouoh.

Austria, whose pavilion organizers had asked to be withdrawn from consideration for the Visitors' Lion, had staged one of the most talked about and critically acclaimed national pavilions of the Biennale.

The pavilion featured Florentina Holzinger’s “Seaworld Venice,” which included a naked human clapper hanging from a bell outside and nude riders on a Jet Ski inside a tank of water that had been flushed from nearby toilets and filtered multiple times.
The Austrian Pavilion said Tuesday that it supported the jury’s decision to quit over the participation of countries whose leaders are charged with crimes against humanity by the ICC.
“We want to leave Venice with a feeling of having helped clear the debris of the past,” the pavilion said in a social media post.

title: Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65
summary: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of Duran Duran, has died at 65
story: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of Duran Duran, has died at 65

Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits included “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex” and “Rio” and were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.
Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

“From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed,” the band said.

On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.
“I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band,” he wrote. “You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.”

The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

The band’s 1981 debut album “Duran Duran” had their first hit single, “Planet Earth,” but it was “Rio” that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: “They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — ‘Tiger Beat’ fashion pinups who rocked arenas.”

The band’s imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as “Girls on Film” and “Union of the Snake” and the moody ballads “The Chauffeur” and “Save a Prayer.” Other hits in the coming years included “The Wild Boys,” “New Moon on Monday” and “Come Undone.” Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song “A View to a Kill” and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people’s walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan, which meant a lot to the band.
“It worked well for us,” drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone. “It was genuine. I don’t think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the No. 1 icon of the early ’80s.”

The band’s success was in large part due to their videos, including their Antigua-set song “Rio,” which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht. For the album “Rio,” they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including “Save a Prayer,” which had John Taylor getting sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV’s need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn’t have.

“A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe,” Le Bon told The Daily Beast in 2012. Andy Taylor agreed: “I don’t think we could have done it without MTV.”

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie “Barbarella.” Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the “Fab Five.” Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a “Live-Wire Guitarist.” (None of the Taylors were related.)

“We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band,” Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.

Duran Duran had the unenviable job of following Led Zeppelin at Live Aid in Philadelphia and performed “A View to a Kill,” “Union of the Snake,” “Save a Prayer” and “The Reflex.” In his book, “Wild Child,” Andy Taylor revealed the band was, as he put it, “falling apart at the seams.”

“Everything should have been perfect, but privately we were screwed and in turmoil. When we came offstage in Philadelphia there were no congratulatory hugs or friendly smiles. It was like we were completely foreign to each other, and it would be the last time we played together for almost two decades.”

The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with “Some Like It Hot” and “Get It On.”

In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album “Notorious,” produced by Nile Rodgers — with hits including the title single and “Skin Trade” — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997's “Medazzaland” and 2000′s “Pop Trash” — but returned for 2004's “Astronaut.”
By 2007, Andy Taylor opted not to participate in the Timbaland-led “Red Carpet Massacre,” an attempt to harness a more youthful rhythmic vibe.
“With Andy not turning up, it couldn’t be a rock record, so that whole album was an attempt to patch over the cracks with Andy missing,” John Taylor told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2011.

Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: “People have wrongly assumed that I didn’t want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band.”

At Duran Duran’s height, they were as famously destructive as any rock band. Andy Taylor revealed in his memoir that he had a six-year cocaine habit and band members trashed hotel rooms, argued with management about money and had high-end shopping sprees.

Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children — Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy — and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them, and they credited his devotion to them in a family statement.

“For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home,” the family statement said.

In 2023, he released the album “Man’s a Wolf to Man,” his first solo release in over 30 years. On the title track, he sang: “Last night/I dreamt someone loved me/And life was not surreal/Someone’s souvenir.”

“Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short,” Le Bon said in a statement Wednesday.

title: French actor Gérard Depardieu to stand trial on rape charge, lawyer says
summary: French actor Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress at his Paris home in 2018
story: French actor Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress at his Paris home in 2018

PARIS -- PARIS (AP) — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France’s most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday’s ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France’s highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge’s August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France’s reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country’s most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for “Cyrano de Bergerac” and a Golden Globe for “Green Card.”
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
“I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered,” he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” (“The Green Shutters”).
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France’s national sex offender database.

“On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did,” Depardieu said.
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women’s rights activists when he said the actor “makes France proud.” Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a “manhunt.”
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men’s freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement’s excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France’s most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from “The Last Metro” and “Jean de Florette” to the popular “Asterix” franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

title: Gordon Ramsay to take the lead in revival of BBC's Top Gear
summary: Gordon Ramsay, the renowned British chef and restaurateur who has forged a successful career on television, will lead the revival of the BBC’s motoring program “Top Gear.”
story: Gordon Ramsay, the renowned British chef and restaurateur who has forged a successful career on television, will lead the revival of the BBC’s motoring program “Top Gear.”

LONDON -- LONDON (AP) — Gordon Ramsay, the renowned British chef and restaurateur who has forged a successful career on television, will lead the revival of the BBC's motoring program “Top Gear,” the British public broadcaster said Wednesday.

Ramsay, whose hit shows on both sides of the Atlantic include “Hell’s Kitchen” and “Ramsay’s Kitchen Nightmares,” said he “can’t wait to get started” on a show that has garnered a keen fan base all around the world with its mix of standard motoring news and often absurd driving challenges.

“Top Gear” has been off air since 2022 when former cricketer Andrew Flintoff was seriously injured during filming. Flintoff was taken to the hospital with facial and rib injuries following the accident at Dunsfold Aerodrome, when he was driving a Morgan Super 3. The car, which did not have a roof, flipped upside down and skidded on the tarmac before coming to a stop.
Filming will take place across the U.K., including at the show’s Dunsfold Aerodrome base southwest of London and around the world next year, for broadcast in 2028.
The 60-year-old Ramsay said his “love affair” began as a child, when he grew up near Silverstone, which hosts the British Grand Prix, one of the most prestigious races in the Formula 1 calendar.

“At its very best, Top Gear has always been about the unexpected — surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos," he said. “That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences."
Ramsay is a keen driving enthusiast, and owns an extensive collection of cars that includes multiple Aston Martins and Ferraris, as well as a Porsche, Land Rover and McLaren Senna.

He has appeared on the program several times, including in 2002 when it was rebooted with Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May at the helm. After those three left following an alleged physical and verbal altercation involving Clarkson, the show was rebooted again, with Flintoff, Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris in the driving seat.
The BBC has said Ramsay’s co-presenting team will be announced in due course.
The BBC has promised the new series will feature “epic adventures, daring tests and spectacular stunts,” bringing fans the “stories, machines and mayhem” they love.

title: After 3 decades, Essence Music Festival bidding farewell to New Orleans
summary: A fixture in New Orleans for over 30 years is leaving the Big Easy
story: A fixture in New Orleans for over 30 years is leaving the Big Easy
The Essence Festival of Culture, a fixture in New Orleans that has celebrated Black American culture for more than 30 years, is leaving the Big Easy.

Festival organizers and Essence Communications, which founded the annual event, announced Tuesday across their social media platforms that Essence Fest will relocate next year. The statement did not give a reason for the decision or mention where the festival was moving to. It mostly expressed gratitude to the city and its residents for helping grow the event over the years.
“You didn't simply host us. You embraced us,” the statement said. “And in doing so, you helped shape one of the most beautiful celebrations of Black culture in the world.”

The multiday festival takes place around the Fourth of July weekend and draws major musical acts. Usher, Megan Thee Stallion and Janet Jackson are among the many performers who have headlined in recent years.

On the same day of the Essence announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on Dec. 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to Black American culture.

“Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country’s top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that 1) realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw,” Moreno said in a social media video. “We need to make sure that there’s widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses.”

The Essence Festival was launched in 1995 as the Essence Music Festival when Essence magazine staged a concert event in New Orleans to mark the publication's 25th anniversary. The magazine was acquired by Time Inc. in the early 2000s before becoming Black-owned again in 2018 when the founder of Sundial Brands purchased it. It's part of Essence Communications, a media company that includes digital and video content.

The festival has also become a political draw with panels focused on politics and voter mobilization. Politicians, both Black and white, who are in the middle of big campaigns have made Essence Fest a stop. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris spoke there in 2024 during the presidential campaign.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, founder and president of National Action Network, has participated in every festival since it began in 1995. The civil rights leader said he was saddened that such a cultural institution was leaving New Orleans but pledged continued support.
“My commitment to ESSENCE is not contingent on its geography," Sharpton said in a statement Wednesday. "Wherever the Festival lands, I will be there.”

According to a report Essence released earlier this month, the festival generated $1.3 billion in economic impact from 2022 through 2025. It also supported 11,000 jobs and led to $179.3 million in tax revenue.

However, local businesses and residents have questioned how much the festival benefits the community. During the festival, a “Clean Zone” ordinance prohibits smaller events in certain areas unless they are authorized.

A legal dispute arose in 2023 when a Black-owned bookstore and coffee shop sought to host an event promoting Black authors during the festival. The business and Essence organizers later resolved the dispute.

A similar incident occurred in 2022 when Spotify and a New Orleans real estate developer wanted to put on an event at a music club. Essence dropped the lawsuit the following year, according to NOLA.com.

title: Resurgent ‘Hunger Games’ goes big at box office, despite 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
summary: "Sunrise on the Reaping” debuted with estimated $120 million in North America.
story: "Sunrise on the Reaping” debuted with estimated $120 million in North America.

NEW YORK -- Fourteen years and six movies in, “The Hunger Games” movie franchise rediscovered its box-office might, as “Sunrise on the Reaping” debuted with $120 million in North American theaters over the weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday.

The sun had seemed to be setting on “The Hunger Games” as a cultural force. After the original blockbuster run of four movies led by Jennifer Lawrence, Lionsgate’s 2023 prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” topped off at $361.8 million worldwide — a decent sum but about half what each of the first four movies grossed.

Yet “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has restored the Suzanne Collins adaptations to blockbuster status. The film, a sequel to “Songbirds and Snakes” and set 25 years before the original series, launched with $225 million worldwide on its opening weekend. Lionsgate produced and distributed the movie, budgeted at about $150 million.

“It’s obviously not common for a film in its sixth installment to completely reverse the trajectory, but it’s awfully satisfying to be a part of it,” said Adam Fogelson, chairman of the Lionsgate Motion Picture Group.

At a time when movie series longevity is far from assured, “Sunrise on the Reaping” managed to notch the year’s fifth $100 million-plus domestic launch — something only accomplished in 2026 by some of the most bankable franchises: Spider-Man (“Spider-Man: Brand New Day”), Toy Story (“Toy Story 5”), Super Mario (“The Super Mario Galaxy Movie”) and whatever Christopher Nolan makes (“The Odyssey”).
And it did it while a significant portion of potential moviegoers were locked at home playing “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

Yet Gen Z again powered a big weekend in theaters. Some 74% of the audience for the “Hunger Games” prequel-sequel were aged 18-34. Several of 2026’s box-office hits — including “Obsession,” “Backrooms” and “You Can See Everything” — have likewise succeeded by packing theaters with the most potent demographic in moviegoing.

While “Sunrise on the Reaping” includes a supporting cast of well-known veteran stars (Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons), the movie largely belongs to a new generation of young actors: Jo Zada, Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang and Whitney Peak. The film, directed by Francis Lawrence, is centered around teenage Haymitch Abernathy (Zada), the role originally played by Woody Harrelson.

Fogelson credits several things to the “Hunger Games” turnaround. “Songbirds and Snakes” was an origin story of a villain, and thus a darker tale. “Sunrise on the Reaping” has the Hunger Games themselves more front and center. It focuses on the backstory of a beloved character in Haymitch. And the cast, a mix of newcomers and veterans, elevated the film.

“It’s consistent with how ‘The Hunger Games’ has always operated. Jennifer Lawrence wasn’t the mega movie star when this franchise started with her,” Fogelson says. “There is no question that part of the incredible resurgence we’ve seen at the box office has been Gen Z and Gen Alpha demonstrating how much they love going to movie theaters.”

Reviews were OK (67% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes), but audience scores were better. “Sunrise on the Reaping” earned an “A-” CinemaScore from moviegoers, a tick up from the “B+” received by “Songbirds and Snakes.”

In its first weekend of wide release, Amazon MGM Studios’ “I Play Rocky” came in second with $9.3 million from 2,477 locations. Peter Farrelly’s comic drama about the making of “Rocky” stars Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone. It has previously played in limited release for two weeks.

The biggest win for “I Play Rocky” — a potential Oscar contender — wasn’t its bottom-line gross, but its CinemaScore: an A+. Such a high mark is rare. (Even “The Odyssey” didn’t score so well.) But Farrelly has managed it before. His best picture-winning 2018 film “Green Book” got the same score.
Ticket sales were down about 10% from the same weekend last year, when “Wicked For Good” came out, according to data firm Rentrak. But they were up 84.9% from last weekend.

From the earliest stage of dating “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Lionsgate analyzed the benefits and risks of going up against “Grand Theft Auto.” Ultimately, the studio believed both could coexist. Some 67% of the audience for the “Hunger Games” film was female.

“Many have speculated as to whether the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ would hurt ‘The Hunger Games’ at the box office this weekend, and I think the marketplace has already spoken,” said Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “Both can do just fine.”

Last week's No. 1 film, “Ebenezer,” starring Johnny Depp, dipped 60% in its second weekend with $7.7 million. The Paramount release has grossed $32.5 million domestically and $45.9 million internationally.

Hollywood will now turn its attention to a Thanksgiving holiday weekend full of intrigue. “Sunrise on the Reaping” will be competing with a variety of new releases: Universal’s “Focker in Law,” the Disney animated film “Hexed,” Netflix’s IMAX release of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” and Neon’s wide release of James Gray’s crime drama “Paper Tiger.”
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” $120 million.
2. “I Play Rocky,” $9.3 million.
3. “Ebenezer,” $7.7 million.
4. “The Cat in the Hat,” $6.9 million.
5. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” $2.7 million.
6. “You Can See Everything,” $2.5 million.
7. “Wild Horse Nine,” $2.5 million.
8. “Ghost Soldier,” $2.4 million.
9. “Wildwood,” $2.3 million.
10. “Ramayana,” $2.1 million.

title: A huge new London Museum tells the city's story from the Romans to Banksy
summary: Britain's capital city is getting a new attraction that bills itself as the world's largest city museum
story: Britain's capital city is getting a new attraction that bills itself as the world's largest city museum
LONDON -- A Roman mosaic, a bloodstained shirt, a bagel filled with barbecued pork, a sewer-clogging chunk of fat.
These are just a few of the objects that help encapsulate Britain’s teeming capital at the London Museum, which bills itself as the world’s largest city museum.

The museum opens Saturday after a yearslong, 437-million-pound ($573-million) refurbishment of Victorian buildings that were once part of the city’s Smithfield meat market. It replaces the notoriously hard-to-find Museum of London, which was located half a mile (800 meters) away and closed in 2022.

The London Museum sits in a much more prominent location, between London’s financial district and the creative Clerkenwell area and next to the wholesale meat market, which is due to move elsewhere by 2030 after more than 800 years on the site.
Museum Director Sharon Ament says change has been the one constant in London for two millennia.

“The great thing about London is it’s always been a mashup,” she said. “A defining feature of London is people coming and going. It started with a load of incomers creating (the Roman city of) Londinium, and it’s been ever thus. And London has always been a place, I think, where you can come and go, be yourself, and take opportunities.”

The museum’s airy ground floor covers the market’s former trading hall, and explores the London of living memory. Exhibits include the gilded State Coach used by the Lord Mayor of London, the former telephone switchboard from Buckingham Palace and a police sentry box decorated with piranhas by the street artist Banksy in 2024.
There are signs from iconic London buildings including an Odeon cinema, the now-closed Walthamstow greyhound-racing stadium and local fried-chicken chain Morley’s.

A temporary exhibition explores London’s food, including the changing face of Brick Lane, a street that has housed generations of immigrants and produced Jewish delis, South Asian curry houses and new fusions such as char siu bagels that reflect the area’s burgeoning population of Chinese students.

On the museum’s vast lower floor, exhibits trace the city’s history from Londinium through the Middle Ages, the devastating Great Fire of 1666, boom-time as the capital of the British Empire and the waves of immigration and social movements, from suffragettes to Black Pride, that transformed London during the 20th and 21st centuries.
Like the city, the museum’s collection is dizzyingly eclectic.

There is a chunk of the Whitechapel Fatberg, an 820-foot-long (250-meter-long) lump of hardened fat, oil, diapers and baby wipes found clogging a sewer in 2017. Elsewhere is the bass guitar smashed by Paul Simonon of The Clash on the cover of the punk band’s album “London Calling.”
Pieces of clothing include the shirt reputedly worn by King Charles I when he was executed in 1649, Queen Victoria’s black mourning dress and Olympic diver Tom Daley’s swim trunks.
One large gallery is devoted to the Cheapside Hoard, a trove of gold and gemstones from a 17th-century jeweler’s workshop discovered by workmen demolishing a building in 1912.
Senior curator Hazel Forsyth calls the hoard “a time capsule of contemporary taste, culture, innovation, craftsmanship” and 17th-century global trade.
“It literally takes you on a voyage of discovery,” she said.

The hoard includes priceless items, such as a tiny watch made from a single Colombian emerald crystal. But there are also some highly accomplished fakes — showing that crime and scams have long been part of city life.
At the back of the exhibition space is one more surprise: a 20-foot (6-meter) window with a view of trains thundering past on London Underground tracks into nearby Farringdon station.
The museum is due to get even bigger, with a set of underground vaults scheduled to open in 2027, followed by expansion into a former poultry market building in 2028.

Like many modern museums, it aims to be a place to eat, drink, hang out and shop as well as to learn. It contains four eating and drinking venues and a gift shop where visitors can buy fridge magnets, hair clips and all manner of other merch adorned with the museum’s mascot: a pigeon.
A museum spokesperson said pigeons were chosen because they are an “unlikely hero of the city”: ubiquitous, sometimes unloved and somewhat misunderstood.
“They’re really smart, they’re actually quite beautiful, and they’re everywhere.”

title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to celebrate a milestone with Blue Hippo, Bluey and Megan Moroney
summary: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade celebrates its 100th anniversary with a special appearance by Blue Hippo, a 30-foot-long inflatable recreated from old photos
story: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade celebrates its 100th anniversary with a special appearance by Blue Hippo, a 30-foot-long inflatable recreated from old photos
NEW YORK -- One of the stars of this year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade should be very easy to spot. Just look in the sky for a gigantic blue hippo with a goofy smile.

Blue Hippo is one of 100 inflatables included in the 100th parade set to float — weather permitting — through Manhattan on Thursday, lovingly reconstructed by hand from old photos and video because the original balloon disappeared in 1931.

The long-lost hippo — also part of the store's holiday window displays this year — will take its rightful place in the show along with such musical celebrities as Megan Moroney,Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, JoJo and Jimmy Fallon & The Roots.

This year will include a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer and Holly Robinson Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus. Nine Broadway shows will be featured as part of a 10-minute medley, replacing the traditional sprinkling of full show numbers.

“It’s all about celebrating the tradition of the parade,” says Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production at Macy’s Studios. “It’s got so much weight behind it, and we’re just trying to inflate it with some air and fly it down the street.”

Forecasters say an impending storm may try to foul the party, with AccuWeather forecasting winds of 12 to 25 mph (19 to 40 kph) and rain later in the day. Under guidelines, large balloons must stay grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 kph). The parade balloons have been grounded only once, in 1971.

Will Coss, vice president and executive producer of Macy’s Studios, wanted each decade represented in this year's parade. Joining Blue Hippo will be balloons of Bluey, Petula Pig, Hello Kitty, Snoopy's alter ego Joe Cool, Mickey Mouse, a Minion riding a banana and Underdog. There will also be a 101-foot-long (31-meter-long) Doodlebug caterpillar snaking along the streets and 1,000 clowns.
“The parade every year is a snapshot. It’s a time capsule of that specific year. And, in this case, this is going to be a representation of our larger history,” he says.
The parade began in 1924 as a way of creating buzz for the holiday windows — which that year had 27 fairy tales acted out with marionettes — at Macy's Herald Square flagship store.

Puppeteer and illustrator Tony Sarg created the windows, as well as the floats and costume characters, and Macy's borrowed animals from the Central Park Zoo for the first parades. In subsequent years, they even brought in tigers and lions.

In 1927, Macy's put an end to the animals after children were getting scared, and Sarg — believed to have been inspired by Indonesian shadow puppets — replaced the real animals with air-filled balloons. The next year, he partnered with the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company to create balloons that could be filled with helium.

“With each year, the balloons got a little bit bigger and more sophisticated. And in many years, they would take a character and then the next year they would repaint the balloon to be another character,” says Darin Johnson, founder and CEO of the American Theater for Puppetry Arts.
A float on Thursday will honor Sarg, the creative force behind the parade through 1941 and a man considered the father of modern American puppetry.

In the parade's early years, the helium-filled balloons weren’t packed up and stored for next year. Instead, they were released into the sky, with an attached envelope promising a finder’s fee for anyone who returned them to Macy’s.
Blue Hippo was among those set loose 95 years ago and unfortunately never returned, a mystery that prompted Kennedy to go digging into newspaper archives to look for clues.

He and his team found footage of the hippo flying past the newly finished Empire State Building in 1931 and read accounts that it was likely missing at sea. All the images they found were black and white, of course. But what was the real color of the balloon?

“What we decided was that, of course, it was the color of the sky because how else do you lose a flying hippo?” he says. His team added age spots for the 2026 version: “It’s had some time out there, and we’re really excited to bring it back.”

Blue Hippo will also honor beloved real hippo Fiona from the Cincinnati Zoo, who died this month after ingesting a knit hat. Handlers walking Blue Hippo will wear purple patches with Fiona’s face inside a heart and the words “Celebrating Fiona.”
Parade balloons begin with a sketch that gets turned into a 3D rendering, then into a physical model thanks to digital printing technology.

Technology is embraced: Converted lawn mowers under the floats have given way to today's self-driving electric vehicles, and the “Harry Potter” float this year will have an animatronic Sorting Hat. But the old ways also persist.

“The art of building a balloon is still very much a sacred art for our Macy’s and Macy’s Studios team. Every piece of fabric is cut and sealed together by hand. Every balloon that you see is assembled, painted, and brought to life by hand,” says Coss, who heads a team of 75 full-time staff members.

The parade has marched every year — except from 1942 to 1944 when the balloons were donated to the World War II effort — and has inspired awe for generations. “These giant balloons turn you into a child,” Kennedy says. “I feel like we’re all kind of kids for a day.”
For the 100th parade, Johnson won't be watching — he'll be in it. He's been asked to be a handler for a recreation of one of the first-ever character balloons, Felix the Cat.
“It will be a dream come true,” he says.
Thursday also marks a milestone anniversary for a newer Thanksgiving TV tradition: the National Dog Show, which is turning 25 this year. NBC broadcasts the canine spectacle right after the parade.

It was something of a lark when the network decided in 2002 to broadcast highlights from the Kennel Club of Philadelphia’s venerable annual canine competition and rebrand it as the National Dog Show. But the ratings stunned NBC executives, so the event became a programming staple.

“It’s been quite a 25-year journey, playing a role in establishing a showcase for dogs that has changed the Thanksgiving Day viewing habits of millions of American families,” said dog expert David Frei, who co-hosts the show with actor John O’Hurley.
Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed to this report.

title: Josh Allen teams up with Oscar-winning director to produce ‘The Buffalo Miracle’ documentary
summary: Bills quarterback Josh Allen and two-time Academy Award-winning director Ben Proudfoot have teamed up to deliver an uplifting documentary titled “The Buffalo Miracle.”
story: Bills quarterback Josh Allen and two-time Academy Award-winning director Ben Proudfoot have teamed up to deliver an uplifting documentary titled “The Buffalo Miracle.”

BUFFALO, N.Y. -- Ben Proudfoot’s first encounter with Josh Allen came in the form of seeing a large cardboard cutout figure of the Bills quarterback erected inside a McDonald’s franchise in suburban Buffalo.

Unassuming as the setting seemed, the fast-food restaurant would serve as the centerpiece for a documentary the two-time Academy Award-winning director was filming to highlight the unlikely heroes and communal spirt that emerged during a deadly two-day blizzard which paralyzed the region over Christmas weekend in 2022.
“I said, ‘Who’s that?’” Proudfoot recalled with a laugh. “And they said, ‘That’s Josh Allen. He’s our hero.'"
Store manager Kristin Kosha chuckled at the memory.
“I thought he was trying to get a rise out of me,” Kosha said. “But no, he genuinely didn’t know.”
Little did Proudfoot realize he'd soon get the opportunity to meet Allen.

By sheer coincidence, Allen had just launched his production company, Out of Pocket Studios, and was searching for the ideal initial project to back when Proudfoot's film crossed his desk. With Allen as executive producer, they teamed up in making “The Buffalo Miracle,” a 37-minute documentary premiering on HBO on Tuesday night.

“I think it speaks volumes that the story he chose to inaugurate his company with is about the goodness of the people of Buffalo,” Proudfoot said. “He could do anything. He decided to make a film about the heroism of everyday folks from Buffalo."
For Allen, who grew up on a farm in central California, the film serves as a holiday love letter to his adopted blue-collar home.

“Who knows the reason that I started Out of Pocket,” he said. “Maybe it was for this exact moment to push this film forward and for the world to see because of what I think Buffalo and western New York stand for, the grittiness, the care for one another. We’re called the ‘City of Good Neighbors,’ and this totally encapsulates that.”
Tragic as the blizzard was with Erie County's death toll reaching 47, the film captures those braving the harrowing conditions and opening their doors to save others.

Kosha and assistant Jeffrey Spengler defied McDonald's policy in keeping their restaurant open. They eventually sheltered and fed some 50 people — and one pet dog — during a two-day storm that ended on Christmas morning, brought near-hurricane-force winds and dumped more than 4 feet (1.2 meters) of snow.

It’s a story of Amherst police officers Thomas Brown and Derek Westbrook navigating treacherous whiteout conditions to rescue those who were stranded in cars and in homes without power by transporting them to McDonald’s and other shelters.

And it’s a story that, as survivor Paache’ Spikes-Redding says in the film, is about people and community and even sports, with those gathered at the McDonald’s uplifted by the Bills' AFC East-clinching win at Chicago on Christmas Eve.

“Race, religion and politics, they might divide us. Sports brings us together,” Spikes-Redding says in the documentary. “What was the odds that we all ended up here and what was the reason, people from all walks of life.”
With their car stranded, Spikes-Redding, her son and then-fiancé broke into a closed restaurant and gathered around a gas stove to stay warm before being rescued by Brown.

It’s a story of rekindling friendships, with Westbrook rescuing Jimmy Bessing, who has Down syndrome and was living on his own when the power went out in his apartment. They recognized each other immediately as former high school classmates and took a selfie before trudging back to Westbrook's truck.

And it’s a story about giving back. Immigrants Tan and Lili Zhao were among those who sheltered at McDonald’s. They own a beauty salon and one of the closing scenes shows Kosha and Spengler — “Heroes," the Zhao's called them — enjoying a relaxing spa treatment.

“It’s been absolutely surreal. We never thought what we did would reach the audience that it has. And we most certainly didn’t do it for that reason at all,” Kosha said. “But it’s nice to see a little act of kindness and taking care of your neighbor could hopefully pass on a nice message.”
This is the community Allen has grown to cherish, and a city he watched rally from other difficult moments that year.

That May, 10 Black people were killed in a hate-motivated mass shooting at a Buffalo supermarket. A week after the storm, Bills safety Damar Hamlin had a near-death experience when he went into cardiac arrest and needed to be resuscitated on the field during a game in Cincinnati.
“It’s a fantastic story and it’s very special to me,” Allen said of the film. “If you’re not brought to tears at the end of this, I just don’t know what to tell you.”
Proudfoot is from Halifax, Nova Scotia, and now lives in California, and this is the America he’s grown to know and sought to emphasize.

“What was reaffirmed for me really in hearing about this story is that there are callings greater than your job, greater than your political affiliation, greater than your race, ethnic identity, religion,” Proudfoot said. “It brought out the best in people. And so I think that speaks to the people of Buffalo, it speaks to humanity, it speaks to America.”
His one regret is Spikes-Redding not being alive to see the finished product. Shortly after filming completed, she was killed in a hit-and-run accident.

“It’s hard to make sense of how somebody like that would be taken away from her family,” Proudfoot said. “So I’m happy that she lives on. She’s really the star of the show. And she had the last word.”
In the final scene before the closing credits, a smiling Spikes-Redding appears on screen and playfully says: “Merry Christmas to all. And to all a good night.”

title: Tom Jackson, Broncos star and ESPN 'Sunday NFL Countdown' analyst, dead at 75
summary: Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as an ESPN broadcaster, has died at 75
story: Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as an ESPN broadcaster, has died at 75

Tom Jackson, a fiery cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as a beloved broadcaster on ESPN, has died, his family and the network announced Sunday. He was 75.

Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wishes that his death not be announced until the start of the network's “Sunday NFL Countdown” show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman. A cause of death was not given.

“Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom’s was frequent and unmistakable,” Berman said. “Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too.”
Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years over two stints after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was an inspirational leader of Denver’s first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team's second Super Bowl appearance. He was a first-team All-Pro in 1977 and a second-team All-Pro the following season; he also was a three-time Pro Bowler.

The Broncos held a moment of silence and showed a video tribute to Jackson before their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. After the Broncos won 38-24, coach Sean Payton said the team would give a game ball to Jackson's family.
Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “NFL Primetime.”

Before the internet, and before NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, “NFL Primetime” was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interaction between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other’s sentences.

“I can remember coming from games and waiting in a rush to get home, to watch ‘Primetime’ because all I wanted to know was, what were you and Tom Jackson gonna say about one, the team?” ESPN analyst and Hall of Fame wide receiver Randy Moss said to Berman.

NBC's “Football Night in America” paid tribute to Jackson Sunday night. Host Maria Taylor said: “Before there was a ‘Football Night in America’, there was ‘NFL Primetime,’ where TJ and Chris Berman set the standard for an NFL highlight show. It’s a standard that we look to every single Sunday.”

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, who was in Mexico City for Sunday night's game between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings, said Jackson was “an outstanding player whose toughness and leadership helped define an era of Broncos football. He brought credibility, passion and humor to everything he did, and generations of fans came to know him through his work at ESPN.”

Jackson briefly returned to ESPN in 2019 and reunited with Berman to do an online version of “NFL Primetime.” He was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

“In my lifetime there was Howard Cosell doing ‘Monday Night Football’ halftime highlights and then there were Boomer and TJ doing ‘Sunday NFL Countdown.’ I am not here as a colleague but as one of million who watched, learned from and idolized the two of you,” ESPN host Mike Greenberg said during Sunday’s show.
ESPN’s studio crew wore orange ties in honor of Jackson during the three-hour show.
Berman said Jackson was the last of seven people interviewed for the studio analyst job and that the last person rarely gets the job. But Jackson nailed the interview.

“Tom Jackson was one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN’s history. He brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans. Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make ‘NFL Primetime’ an iconic part of our football weekends,” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. “Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. ... His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure.”
ESPN’s NFL studio in Bristol, Connecticut, is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. It is the only named studio on ESPN’s campus.

“The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history,” the Broncos said in a statement.

“An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country.”
Jackson is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and daughters Taylor and Morgan.
AP Pro Football Writer Arnie Stapleton in Denver contributed to this report.

title: Amy Poehler returns to TV with 'Dig' — just in time for Thanksgiving
summary: Amy Poehler returns to TV comedy for the first time in over 10 years with new show, “Dig” which is set on an archaeological excavation in Greece
story: Amy Poehler returns to TV comedy for the first time in over 10 years with new show, “Dig” which is set on an archaeological excavation in Greece
Amy Poehler’s back on television and that’s a big deal.

Despite the fact that she’s never been away — whether it’s charming guestson her “Good Hang” podcast, presenting at awards shows or starring in movies — it’s been 11 years since she's starred in a TV series.

As the irrepressible Leslie Knope on “Parks and Recreation,” Poehler corralled a team of office workers to do good for the community and each other, picking up six Emmy nominations and building a beloved fan base.
Now “Parks and Rec” fans can rejoice that she’s reunited with co-creator Mike Schur to lead the cast of “Dig,” their new show set on an archaeological excavation in Greece.
“The big deal is Amy deciding to act again, honestly,” says Schur, with Season 1 arriving in full on Monday.
“If you survey a thousand people and say, ‘What do you think of Amy Poehler?’ — 999 of them swoon and laugh. So just her being back on TV is a delight.”
Poehler admits it’s significant.
“I’m at a point in my life, and lucky to be, where the only way I see my friends is by working with them. And I have the most talented and funniest friends.”
And while her cynical “Dig” character Elise is very different from the positivity of Leslie Knope, the show does have the same vibe as “Parks and Rec,” according to co-star Geraldine Viswanathan.

“You just feel like these people are your friends and they’re so distinctive," says Viswanathan. "It’s a very unlikely group of people who kind of are thrown together in this workplace comedy and actually have a lot to learn from each other.”

Based on Kate Myers' novel “Excavations," the show follows a summer expedition to discover history in the Greek dirt, bringing together people from different generations, all soul searching while looking for rare artifacts in the ground.
The show, which also stars Hugh Laurie, Antonia Thomas, and Fina Strazza, premieres on Peacock in the U.S. on Monday.

Poehler spoke about the show, how a meeting of her “Dig” and “Parks and Recreation” characters might go, and navigating family gatherings with The Associated Press. The conversation has been edited for clarity and brevity.

POEHLER: Archaeologist is kind of like the fake job you think you want to have when you’re 10 years old. I did not think that I had any interest in it until I started studying and learning about it and then realizing, oh, this is such an amazing metaphor for who gets to tell their story, what do you have hidden, what stuff do you wanna dig up?
Now I’m obsessed, and all I do is read stories about when people find things on the beach and discoveries that have changed the way we think about science and nature and dinosaurs.

POEHLER: We were only there a short amount of time, a few weeks, but boy, I had never been to Athens. I absolutely loved it. The people, the Greek people are so fun, kind. They’re my kind of people because I enjoy direct people. Little bossy and direct, but kind.

POEHLER: It is because exactly that, 11 years later, getting to be back on set with Mike and getting to work with his amazing talented wife, J.J. Philbin, who’s an incredible writer, worked on “Only Murders” and was at “SNL” with us. That reunion is as important to me almost as the work.
POEHLER: Leslie would be a little intimidated by Elise, because Elise would think Leslie was a lot.

I think they would respect each other, but they have very, very different energies. And it was nice to play somebody who was kind of still and quiet, and people projected stuff on her rather than a person who just constantly projected stuff out.

POEHLER: I’m so bad at this. Kayvan (Novak), who plays my love interest, he’s really that tall. He is so tall and that is all his real hair, beard and hair. He has the hair of a horse. He’s incredible.
I think that the dirt would be that in the very beginning when we were all pretending to not like each other, we actually did.

POEHLER: You just have to have a sense of humor about yourself. If you can take life and what you believe in seriously, but not yourself seriously. When we all start to take ourselves seriously, we get into trouble. And then also just lock yourself in the bathroom. Just go in the bathroom and lock the door and play on your phone. Or you volunteer to go do an errand and then pretend your car broke down and just lie in the back seat and never come back.

title: Miley Cyrus marries rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate Palm Springs wedding
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
story: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
Pop culture icon Miley Cyrus married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate weekend wedding in Palm Springs, California, according to a post on the singer’s Instagram account.

The post said Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, were wed on Saturday. Photographs show the couple embracing in front of a white backdrop with a palm tree characteristic of the Palm Springs desert in the background, a large dog lying at their feet. In one photo, the couple kisses standing in an aisle of white roses.

The “Party in the U.S.A.” singer wore a long-sleeve silk Saint Laurent gown by Anthony Vaccarello and elegant white silk kitten heels, according to a statement from Saint Laurent. The dress had a low back, and she wore flowers in her hair, which was pulled back into an updo.
Morando wore dark, square shades. His single-breasted tuxedo was also made by the French luxury fashion brand.

The pair have been together since 2021, meeting after they were set up on a blind date, according to an interview Cyrus gave Vogue in 2023. Morando proposed to her while the couple were in Japan late last year, he said in a separate interview with Wonderland Magazine.
“I could feel my heart pounding” before popping the question, Morando said for a profile in the magazine.
Morando is the drummer of the rock band Liily.

title: What to stream on Thanksgiving week: 'Dig,' Jennifer Lopez and 'Way of the Warrior Kid'
summary: Amy Poehler's new series “Dig” and Jennifer Lopez’s concert show are among the new streaming releases this week
story: Amy Poehler's new series “Dig” and Jennifer Lopez’s concert show are among the new streaming releases this week
The Amy Poehler-led series “Dig” and a new concert show from Jennifer Lopez are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this Thanksgiving week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: “The Mosquito Bowl,” “Blade Runner 2099” and a new project from Peter Gabriel.

— In “The Mosquito Bowl” (Wednesday on Netflix), Peter Berg directs a World War II drama about four college football stars who enlist in the Marines after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Based on a true story, the movie matches two passions – football and war films – for Berg, the filmmaker of “Friday Night Lights” and “Lone Survivor.” The cast includes Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis.

– “The Magic Faraway Tree” (Friday on HBO Max) adapts Enid Blyton’s classic children’s book series. Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield star as parents of a family that relocates to the English countryside. There, their three children discover a magical tree full of enchanting fairies with branches that lead to fantastical lands.

– In “Way of the Warrior Kid” (Wednesday on Apple TV), a bullied middle school kid named Marc (Jude Hill) experiences a life-changing summer with his uncle, Jake (Chris Pratt), a recuperating Navy SEAL. Jake’s teachings, dubbed “Operation Warrior Kid,” go beyond hand-to-hand combat. With Linda Cardellini.
— AP Film Writer Jake Coyle

— Struggling to think of what to watch with your loved ones this Thanksgiving holiday? Strain no more. On Thursday, “The JLO Show: Live in Las Vegas” will premiere on CBS and stream on Paramount+. It’s a concert spectacular, capturing Jennifer Lopez’s “Up All Night Live in Las Vegas” residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace. It’s all the hits, at home.

— On Friday, Peter Gabriel will release “o(backslash)i,” a companion record to his 2023 release “i/o.” The album's 13 new tracks bring the joint project to a total of 25. “This record has been more of a marathon than a sprint,” he said in a press statement about the prolific work.
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie star in “Dig,” a summer-in-Greece comedy about archaeologists and the college students working beside them. All 10 episodes arrive Monday on Peacock. The series reteams Poehler with “Parks and Recreation” co-creator Mike Schur. Writer J.J. Philbin, who is also married to Schur, joins as co-showrunner.

— A three-part docuseries on the Karen Read story arrives Monday on Netflix. “The Trials of Karen Read” examines the death of Boston police officer John O’Keefe. Jurors and members of O’Keefe’s family speak on camera in the three-part series, which revisits both trials.

— In Prime Video’s “Clashing Through the Snow,” rivals up for the same publishing job end up sharing a rental car after a snowstorm strands them. It stars Chris Briney (“The Summer I Turned Pretty") and Michelle Randolph (“Landman”) with Lukas Gage, Julia Fox and Paris Hilton. It streams Monday on Prime Video.

— Set 50 years after “Blade Runner 2049,” a new sci-fi limited series called “Blade Runner 2099” comes to Prime Video on Wednesday. It stars Michelle Yeoh as the replicant Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Blade Runner Cora in a Los Angeles remade by someone other than humans. All eight episodes drop at once.

— Instead of watching football on Thanksgiving, you could go full camp and binge “The Hunting Wives” Season 2. The series, loosely based on a novel of the same name, stars Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman as Sophie and Margo, whose friendship in an East Texas town turns messy and murderous. The series was originally intended for Starz but ultimately landed at Netflix, where it became a breakout hit and even got its own “SNL” sketch. In Season 2, Sophie and Margo go from friends to foes. WNBA star Angel Reese also joins the cast. A third season has already been ordered.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— If you’re looking for something to download to your laptop after Thanksgiving dinner, check out “Appulse.” It combines two types of arcade classics: pinball and space shooters like “Asteroids.” The gimmick here is that the pinball itself is a spaceship with guns, and whenever you fire them the recoil sends you in the opposite direction. Meanwhile, enemies are landing, so you need to shoot or ram them to conquer the leaderboard. French indie developer Le Rado promises multiple tables and the ability to upgrade your craft as you bounce your way through. Pull the plunger Thursday on PC.
— Lou Kesten

title: Sierra Leone sees steep decline in maternal mortality, but barriers to care persist
summary: Fatmata Kamara's experience in Sierra Leone highlights both progress and challenges in maternal healthcare
story: Fatmata Kamara's experience in Sierra Leone highlights both progress and challenges in maternal healthcare

FREETOWN, Sierra Leone -- During her first two pregnancies, Fatmata Kamara could not afford ultrasound scans at a hospital in Sierra Leone’s capital, Freetown. By her third, she was receiving scans and medication and spending less time waiting to see a doctor.
But care that the government says should be free still came at a cost. Kamara said she spent 1,000 leones ($44) on medication and unofficial fees during her latest pregnancy.

“This pregnancy was different because of the attention I received at the hospital,” said the 28-year-old trader who gave birth to her third child last month at a health center in Freetown’s Mabela neighborhood. The services were "far better" than in the past, she said.
Kamara’s experience reflects both the progress and persistent challenges in Sierra Leone, which has recorded one of Africa's steepest declines in maternal mortality.
The country's maternal mortality ratio fell by nearly 80% from more than 1,600 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 354 in 2023, according to the latest available U.N. estimates.

The World Health Organization attributes Sierra Leone’s declining maternal mortality rate partly to expanded health services, the introduction of free maternal health care in 2010 and the training of more skilled birth attendants.

Despite the progress, unofficial fees, mistrust and poor infrastructure continue to hinder access to maternity care. A 300-day government campaign is also underway to advance the fight against preventable maternal and child deaths. ___

This story is part of a series on maternal mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, which has the world’s fastest-growing population and accounts for 70% of global maternal deaths. Around 180,000 maternal deaths are estimated to occur every year across the continent, along with the deaths of about 1 million newborns.

Launched by Sierra Leone's Health Minister Austin Demby in March 2026, “300 Days of Activism for Triple Zero” is a nationwide government initiative supported by the U.N. Population Fund and other development partners. It seeks to eliminate preventable maternal and child deaths and reach children who have missed routine vaccinations. The initiative combines efforts to encourage earlier treatment with improvements in supplies, staff training and community outreach.

Authorities have touted the campaign as successful. In its Oct. 30 update, the Health Ministry reported that maternal deaths fell 31.3% and child deaths fell 12.7% compared with the same period in 2025, citing data from hospitals. It also said more than 10,000 previously unvaccinated children had received vaccines.

The campaign’s effort to improve medicine supplies also addresses a problem Kamara’s family faced when her first daughter fell ill. The 2-year-old was staying with a relative outside Freetown when she was diagnosed with malaria at a hospital, Kamara said. But the family could not immediately obtain the prescribed medication, and the child died within three days of becoming ill.
“When I arrived, my child’s feet were all yellow. Her body was all pale,” Kamara recalled.

Kamara lives in Susan’s Bay, an impoverished neighborhood in central Freetown. Reaching the Princess Christian Maternity Hospital where she had an ultrasound sometimes required up to an hour's ride on a tricycle, depending on traffic, at a round-trip cost of 10 leones, about 44 cents.

Money is tight for the trader, whose husband is a moto-taxi driver. Their household of seven includes the couple, their two surviving children and relatives of her husband. Their first daughter died at age 2.

Before she stopped trading during her pregnancy, she sold seasonal fruit — mangoes, avocados, watermelon — to help support the family. She said she made 50 to 100 leones ($2 to $4) a day and sometimes nothing at all. It is from that money she had to pay for a scan and delivery at a health center, although both facilities said the services should have been free.
Kamara had attended eight prenatal visits when she spoke to The Associated Press during her pregnancy. Nurses in Mabela advised her to get an ultrasound after seven months.
But she remained wary of the hospital. She said mistrust and demands for money had contributed to her decision to deliver her second child at home.
Dr. Amadu Sesay, the hospital’s medical superintendent, said all available services for pregnant women and lactating mothers were free, and staff had been reminded of the policy in an official memo.
“The hospital doesn’t take such complaints lightly,” he said.

The health ministry acknowledged the harm caused by unofficial fees in a statement last month, saying "no patient should be denied, delayed or humiliated while seeking essential care because they cannot make an unofficial payment.”

Umu Fye, the midwife in charge of the antenatal unit at the Princess Christian Maternity Hospital, said it used to record a “really high number of (pregnancy-related) deaths” because it was the main referral facility in the city. Training now allows midwives to assess fetal heart rates and babies’ positions themselves, and three ultrasound machines were installed at the hospital in 2025, she said.
“There have been a lot of changes,” Fye said.

Dr. Francis Moses, the ministry official leading the campaign, said efforts include improving supplies of medicines and equipment, encouraging earlier treatment, expanding midwifery training and reaching local leaders.

But even reaching a hospital can be a challenge. Moses described a pregnant woman in the northern district of Falaba who died after the ambulance taking her to a hospital became stuck on a rough road. A second ambulance also got stuck. It was the third maternal death in similar circumstances this year, he said.

Victor Lansanah Koroma, who heads the advocacy group Health Alert, said too much emphasis falls on women’s delays in seeking help rather than the obstacles they encounter. A lack of transport, medicines and equipment can prevent treatment or discourage women from seeking it, he said.
Even inside hospitals, some surgeries have been performed by flashlight due to electricity cuts, Moses said.

Officials say the campaign received no dedicated funding and relied on existing government resources and support from partners even as donor funding dwindled. Earlier this month, the Chinese government and UNICEF donated medical supplies and equipment to Sierra Leone’s Health Ministry to support such initiatives.

For Fye, who has witnessed preventable deaths at the maternity hospital, the concern is whether improvements will last. She said more training is needed and worried about resources beyond the campaign.

For Kamara, the financial strain continued through delivery. Her family spent more than 500 leones ($22) on supplies the health center required them to bring, including soap and disinfectant, and were asked by nurses to pay another $22 as a tip, which they negotiated to a smaller amount.
Her husband was happy she had delivered safely. But Kamara worried about their other bills and told the nurses such costs were why women avoided health facilities.
She knew giving birth at the health center was safer, but she also had to consider what she could afford.
“If I give birth at home, I wouldn’t spend more than 300 (leones),” she said.
Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal.
