title: Generic HIV prevention drug arrives in Zambia
summary: The first shipments of a generic version of a twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV have arrived in Zambia and additional shipments are expected soon in Uganda
story: The first shipments of a generic version of a twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV have arrived in Zambia and additional shipments are expected soon in Uganda
The first shipments of a generic version of a twice-a-year HIV-prevention shot arrived on Wednesday in Zambia, and additional deliveries are expected in Uganda in the coming days.

The medication is called lenacapavir and is expected to cost $40 a year per person. It will eventually be available in 120 countries. The injectable form of pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, is nearly 100% effective at preventing an HIV infection and much more convenient than daily preventive pills that are available now.

“With demand for the injection far outstripping supply, the arrival of generics marks a major step towards making this breakthrough prevention option more widely available and affordable in low- and middle-income countries,” said Tenu Avafia, deputy executive director of Unitaid, a global health agency.

The medications are part of a shipment by the Global Fund, a worldwide partnership to defeat AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria. After going through a clearance process in Zambia, the medications are expected to be used within the next three weeks.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the generic shot earlier this month. It can’t be sold in the United States because Gilead Sciences' brand-name version, Yeztugo, is still protected by a patent. The approval of the generic medication is considered “tentative,” the FDA’s designation for generics while the original drug remains under a patent.

Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable greater production of lenacapavir. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America. Gilead officials said the company signed the licenses eight months before regulatory approval to ensure an early generic supply, and collaborated closely with generic manufacturers and global health partners.

The FDA-approved generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid and its partners, which sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
“Access is a priority because we know that breakthroughs like lenacapavir only matter when they reach the people who need them most,” Daniel O’Day, Gilead’s chairman and CEO, said in a press release.
According to the World Health Organization, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.

“We have an unprecedented opportunity to reach millions more people at risk of HIV,” Peter Sands, executive director of the Global Fund, said in a press release. “This is how we bring the goal of ending AIDS within reach.”

title: Test results from samples taken after Iowa lead detonation are expected soon, EPA says
summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency says test results from samples taken after Wednesday's controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa could come in Friday
story: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency says test results from samples taken after Wednesday's controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa could come in Friday

LITTLE ROCK, Ark. -- Test results from sampling done following the U.S. Army's detonation of a stockpile of lead azide in Iowa are expected to start coming in as early as Friday, according to the U.S. Environmental and Protection Agency.

EPA personnel and contractors took over 1,500 samples of air, water, soil and dust before the detonation of the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives. After the detonation, they took hundreds of samples including from homes, parks and drinking water, the EPA said in a Thursday statement.
Samples were sent to labs for testing, the EPA said.

“The Trump EPA will continue its presence on the ground for as long as needed to ensure the proper environmental monitoring is taking place following the successful controlled detonation,” the agency said.
The EPA said there continued to be “zero” airborne lead detected in the region since Wednesday’s controlled detonation.
In addition to lead exposure, the EPA also is testing for other compounds that could have been released in the explosion.
“The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation,” the EPA said.
The Army has said detonating the stockpile was the safest option because it was degrading and might explode uncontrollably as the weather got colder.

Turbay is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Ebola outbreak in Congo reaches 12,000 cases; violence forces responders to evacuate
summary: The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data shows
story: The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data shows

BUNIA, Congo -- The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo’s Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

title: Democrats supporting abortion rights won in the midterms, but changes unlikely soon
summary: Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government jobs
story: Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government jobs

Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.
That’s because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws — those that ban abortion at six weeks or all stages of pregnancy.

And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.

Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy — with some exceptions — and four more do so after about the first six weeks.

In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states — Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — already allow abortion through until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.
Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states’ constitutions to create a right to abortion.

Voters in a dozen states already have passed similar amendments, including two — Nevada and Virginia — this year. Voters in November also kept such protections in Missouri but defeated an initiative to add them to state law in Idaho.

In Georgia, where Democrats gained the House and the governor's office, abortion is banned in most cases after fetal cardiac activity can be detected — around six weeks into pregnancy and before many women realize they’re pregnant.
Josh McLaurin, the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor, is optimistic that one Republican state senator would be willing to join Democrats to repeal that law.
The measure could get at least a vote in the Senate, he said, because Republicans will have a 29-27 majority and may not take a “hyper-partisan approach” to block it.

McLaurin said that voters see the ban as a healthcare issue, especially after a state review board in 2024 found that two women died in Georgia after doctors were hesitant to perform abortions that could have saved their lives.
Still, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms acknowledged that a GOP-held state Senate could be an obstacle.
“If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we’re going to take that opportunity," Bottoms said at a news conference. “And it may not be this session.”

After winning the attorney general election in Texas, Democrat Nathan Johnson said he would not sue out-of-state medical providers who prescribe abortion pills via telehealth and ship them to patients in the state as the outgoing attorney general, Republican Ken Paxton, has done. Paxton dropped his suits in November.

Those pills often come from states that seek to protect medical professionals who prescribe them through telehealth and ship them to patients in places with bans. That practice is why the number of abortions has been higher since the fall of Roe. It's also the heart of the current abortion legal battles.
Johnson could also withdraw Texas from a lawsuit challenging federal policy on the abortion pill mifepristone and decide not to defend the state's abortion restrictions against lawsuits.
“It is deeply gutting that now we don’t have Texas to be fighting with the pro-life side on this,” said Kelsey Pritchard, spokesperson for SBA Pro-Life America.

Pritchard and other anti-abortion activists are pushing the Trump administration to make mifepristone harder to get by persuading the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is studying the drug, to bar filling prescriptions through the mail or at pharmacies. The FDA has said it'll have more information by March.
They're also counting on remaining Republican state attorneys general to keep up the fight.

Ohio lawmakers this month passed legislation to bar telehealth prescriptions for mifepristone sent into the state and to reimpose a 24-hour waiting period before obtaining an abortion. It’s not clear whether outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine will sign them into law — or how courts would rule on legal challenges. Voters passed a constitutional amendment protecting abortion access in 2023.

Ingrid Duran, state legislative director at the National Right to Life Committee, said her group will keep pushing measures that Democrats sometimes support — such as supporting ways for women to anonymously and safely give up newborns for adoption. And, she said, it will encourage anti-abortion bills that may not have much of a chance of passing now as a way to build for the future.
“We're not going to give up just because it's going to be more challenging,” she said.

Some congressional Democrats are planning to push forward a measure that would bar states from banning abortion before viability and rescind restrictions that some states have — such as requiring multiple doctor’s visits or ultrasounds.
With a Trump veto expected if it reaches him, the effort would be aimed largely at forcing him to reject a policy that has public opinion on its side.
About 6 in 10 U.S. voters said abortion should be legal in all or most cases, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters in all 50 states.
Associated Press journalists Scott Bauer, Kate Brumback, Marc Levy, Amelia Thomson-DeVeaux and Anna Wilder contributed to this article.

title: A converted shipping container became an unexpected source of mental health help in South Africa
summary: In a South African township, a sensory room in a repurposed shipping container was initially designed for young children but has since become a mental health haven for teenagers and adults
story: In a South African township, a sensory room in a repurposed shipping container was initially designed for young children but has since become a mental health haven for teenagers and adults

JOHANNESBURG -- Sisanda Hani enters a former shipping container at a community center in South Africa, slips off her shoes and plunges into a sea of blue plastic balls. The 40-year-old mother of a teenager with ADHD and epilepsy lets the balls envelop her and screams.
For Hani, that howl is a release.

The shipping container is now a “sensory room” opened in April by youth-focused non-profit Afrika Tikkun in Orange Farm, a low-income township south of Johannesburg. Initially designed for young children with developmental conditions, it surprisingly also became a place of relief for parents and caregivers in a neighborhood where professional therapy is hard to find.
“We had a lot of stress,” Hani told The Associated Press. “No one was asking us how we were doing.”

The room is an assortment of sights and textures. Fairy lights thread through beaded curtains. Foil fish, tiny mirrors, a hammock and a burlap cushion fill the underwater world, with shapes resembling amoebas and coral covering a wall. Outside are balancing logs, sand and water pits, and a swing.
Locals helped design it, making sensory items from recycled materials in workshops led by Afrika Tikkun and its partner, Sensory-Space.

Hani was among those who helped. Caring for her 19-year-old son makes it difficult for the single mother to hold down a job. Even temporary work can be interrupted by a call about a seizure, sending her rushing home. Encounters with people who do not understand his conditions add to her stress.

She initially thought the room was only for children. A social worker encouraged her and other mothers to try it, and she says now she leaves feeling less burdened and better able to talk calmly to her son instead of shouting. She says he also becomes calmer and more playful during visits.
“We bottle it inside, but when you come here, everything comes out,” she said.

Afrika Tikkun describes the space as South Africa’s first community sensory facility. Program participants and their parents can book free sessions. Its usage records list 450 school-going children aged 6 to 18, 67 young adults and 56 parents and caregivers.

Tegan White, an occupational therapist with the program, says the room’s textures, lights, sounds and movement help users explore sensations and regulate their responses. The ball pit, for example, provides full-body contact that can help users sense where their limbs are.
For adults under stress, it offers somewhere to settle without having to explain their feelings.
“It doesn’t require words. Maybe you aren’t ready to talk,” White said.
The room provides sensory activities beyond her appointments, but she stresses that it complements professional care.
“Therapy is absolutely essential. Having access to ongoing intervention is important,” she said.
Annelize Kruger, an independent occupational therapy lecturer at the University of the Free State, says sensory rooms can help children and adults manage distress, although research remains limited.
“Our sensory needs do not disappear as we get older,” she said.

She distinguishes time spent exploring a sensory room from clinical sensory integration therapy, which involves individually tailored activities guided by an occupational therapist. Guidance can help users identify calming strategies to use beyond the room, Kruger said.

But professional care remains difficult to obtain for many in South Africa. In 2023, then-Health Minister Joe Phaahla said fewer than 30% of people with mental health problems in Africa's biggest economy received treatment. The government’s 2023–2030 mental health policy acknowledges staff shortages and uneven services across provinces.
And across Africa, mental health services remain underfunded and fragmented, particularly in underserved communities, according to the World Health Organization.

At the center, teenagers ask to return simply to sit and relax, says disability inclusion manager Bridget Gumede. Some children have shared troubles at school and home, prompting referrals to social workers. Staff admit up to five people at a time for sessions lasting less than 30 minutes.
“I didn’t know that it can do this much,” she said, adding they now need a bigger space.

The container and its sensory contents cost about $4,700 to $5,300, said Lana Roy, who leads Afrika Tikkun’s Disability Inclusion program. The organization has opened another sensory space in Cape Town and hopes to expand further.
Dee Blackie, the designer of the sensory space, says they invite adults to do something they may have left behind: play.
“So it doesn’t matter if you say, well, playing is not for me. When you get into the space, you immediately start playing,” she said.
For Njabulo Ntombela, 19, that play offers relief from worries about finding work and continuing her education. She says she's afraid she will be unable to support her family.

She visits the sensory room once or twice a month when she feels overwhelmed. Before discovering the room, she said she would withdraw and spend the day without speaking to anyone. Afterward, she feels more comfortable approaching others and asking for help.
The ball pit also gives her a chance to experience play she says she missed growing up.
"When I’m here, I feel like I’m back to 7 years old,” she said.

title: CDC director draws doubts from employees and ire from legislators
summary: Dr. Erica Schwartz, head of the CDC, is facing scrutiny from House Democrats and calls for her resignation
story: Dr. Erica Schwartz, head of the CDC, is facing scrutiny from House Democrats and calls for her resignation

NEW YORK -- Three months into her tenure as head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Erica Schwartz is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency.
What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say.

Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history.
She reports to U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year.
“She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor.

In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC — including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals.
“I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. “Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people.”

Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization’s declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century.
“I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately,” said U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, a Colorado Democrat.
When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her “a STAR!” on social media.

She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies.
Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors.

Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president’s agenda.
Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations and retirements.

At her nomination hearing, Schwartz pledged “radical transparency” to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy.
“I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments,” she testified.

Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about 1 in 6 Americans said they believed that “vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps and rubella cause autism” — even though dozens of studies have determined there’s no causal link. Roughly another 1 in 5 said they didn’t know whether it was true.

Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first “all hands” staff meeting, during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn’t hesitate to disagree with Kennedy — but only privately.
Some say that’s when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade.

“I don’t have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines,” one CDC health scientist told the AP. “If we’re talking about radical transparency,” it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.
Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: “I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line.”

Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz’s salary — even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors.

So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations — including for measles, the flu and COVID-19.
Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated.
But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated.

“I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration,” said Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “I don’t think we have seen that yet.”
Kennedy continues to back Schwartz. The Health and Human Services Department issued a statement in response to Associated Press queries, quoting Kennedy as saying she had his full support.

“Dr. Schwartz brings the judgment to make hard decisions and the courage to see them through. She is reforming CDC and sharpening its focus on its core mission: protecting Americans from disease,” the statement said.
Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles.

Kennedy has challenged health officials’ accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting.
Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death.
Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy.

“As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports,” according to a statement from Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado and Yvette Clarke of New York.
“We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required,” they added.

The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.
Schwartz argued that she was “fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't.”

The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what’s going on within the agency.

Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it’s still too early to judge her.
Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP.
Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled “Esther: The Woman Who Didn’t Know Her Place.”

DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval.

Asked about it, Schwartz said: “There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day.” She also said DeBerry is on “terminal leave” and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail.
None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards.

Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC’s main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows.
(The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as “Officer Stone” during a recent health summit appearance.)

Dr. Tom Frieden, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don’t recall seeing that before.
“It feels like they’re afraid of us,” one health scientist said.

Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said.
A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership.

Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children’s medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs.
The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email.
HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive.
At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, “and I’m trying to earn that trust every day.”
She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency’s leadership and develop a “strategic hiring plan” for 2027.
CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues.
“I think everyone is just exhausted,” one health scientist said. “There’s just a sense that we can’t go on like this anymore.”

title: Experts debunk Thanksgiving food myths, from turkey 'coma' to risky leftovers
summary: Experts say turkey was likely on the table at the first Thanksgiving in 1621, but there's no word on whether anyone took a nap afterward
story: Experts say turkey was likely on the table at the first Thanksgiving in 1621, but there's no word on whether anyone took a nap afterward
CONCORD, N.H. -- Was turkey on the table at the first Thanksgiving? Probably. Did anyone take a nap afterward? Unclear.
Among the many myths associated with Thanksgiving is the notion that today's traditional menu harkens back to what the Pilgrims and Wampanoag people actually ate in November 1621.

While no oral history has been passed down by the Native people, Pilgrim Edward Winslow briefly described the three-day feast in a letter to a friend, said Malka Benjamin, director of colonial interpretation and training at the Plimoth Patuxet Museums in Plymouth, Massachusetts.

According to Winslow’s letter — the only surviving record of the celebration — the Wampanoag leader Massasoit provided five deer, while the Pilgrims killed enough fowl in one day to feed the entire colony for nearly a week. He didn’t mention turkey specifically, but it frequently shows up in other firsthand accounts of the time period, Benjamin said.
“I feel very confident saying that it’s highly likely there was turkey on the table, in addition to duck and goose and other kinds of birds,” she said.

The menu also probably featured seafood, she said, along with squash and nasaump, a porridge-like Wampanoag dish made with ground corn and berries. Potatoes? Nope. And while cranberries were available, there was no sugar to turn them into sauce.
Here are some other more modern myths about Thanksgiving food and what experts have to say about them:

Unless you’ve been asleep for the last few decades, you’ve probably heard that tryptophan in turkey makes you sleepy. While the amino acid does spur the creation of feel-good brain chemicals like serotonin and melatonin, there’s not enough of it in turkey to make you nod off, said Kimberly Dong, associate professor of public health at Tufts University School of Medicine. Chicken and beef have similar levels; cheddar cheese has even more.

“What’s happening is that people are eating a lot of carbohydrate-rich foods that are really quickly absorbed into the bloodstream,” she said. That causes a spike in blood glucose levels followed by a rapid drop. It’s that roller coaster that contributes to fatigue, she said, not the “turkey coma.”

Overeating in general also makes you sleepy because blood gets diverted to the gastrointestinal tract to deal with digestion, leaving muscles tired, said Susan Roberts, a professor and nutrition scientist at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth.
“I’m not one of these punitive nutritionists. I think if you have overeaten and you do feel tired, fine, take a nap,” she said. “Enjoy it.”

That said, both Dong and Roberts take issue with the idea that overeating is a given. Skipping breakfast on Thanksgiving might sound smart, but trying to “save” calories for a big dinner usually backfires, Dong said, “because you are so ravenous by the time the food is served.”

Instead, she recommends eating a light breakfast and staying hydrated early in the day. Roberts, meanwhile, suggests a multi-day strategy: eating high fiber foods for two days before Thanksgiving to keep hunger in check.

The experts disagree when it comes to leftovers, however. Dong says setting aside leftovers can counteract the “this is my one chance to eat this” mentality that leads to heaping helpings. But Roberts says hosts should pare back from the start, and that guests who feel they can’t decline leftovers should throw most, if not all, of them away at home.
Willpower doesn’t work when a plate of food is in front of you, she said, because the sights and smells activate the body to receive a big meal.

“A better place to use your willpower is before it ever comes in the house, when you’re still full from the Thanksgiving meal,” she said. “You can throw half or three-quarters of it away now and it’s easy, but if you put it in the fridge, it becomes a whole different matter.”

If you do end up with leftovers, be careful, says Anne Suelzer, a registered dietitian and licensed dietitian with Health Loft. Properly stored leftovers will be safe for three or four days, but don’t rely on your senses to judge.
“The bacteria that make you sick usually don’t change how food looks or smells,” she said.
Leftovers should be refrigerated within two hours, and the clock starts when the food comes out of the oven, not when you’re done eating.
“It helps to start packing things up while people are still at the table,” she said.

title: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back
summary: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted
story: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted

People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer’s disease.

But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer’s, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.

Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won’t even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble.

“The community will look like, ’Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they’re gonna leave us hanging,'” said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years.

Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation’s long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation’s medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow.

The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city’s Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer’s and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La’Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study’s field coordinator.

Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
As Blair said, "You start forgetting things and you start to wonder, do you have Alzheimer’s? You wonder, do you have dementia?”

Then the study, which had been near completion in its fifth and final year, was stripped of funding last year by the National Institutes of Health, on the grounds that it was “not science,” according to the study’s researchers, despite a rigorous review and vetting from a community advisory board.
“It wasn’t a Black study or a DEI study,” Wagner said. “It was something that was happening that was real.”

Similar terminations happened all over the country. Negar Fani, a neuropsychologist at Emory University in Atlanta, was two years into a five-year, $2.9 million project on how daily experiences of racial discrimination affect the brain and body of Black Americans when NIH terminated it in July.
While Fani tries to find the roughly $2.3 million she needs to complete the study, she and her team were left to try to explain the situation to participants who feel abandoned.
“It takes a lot to restore trust with the Black community, who has experienced so many different betrayals,” she said.
Like the Pittsburgh study's funding, Fani’s grant had been terminated for being “not scientific” and “subjective” — after the study had been approved and had enrolled 66 of the 220 people it needed.
“It’s simply brain science research,” she said.

In Pittsburgh, study lead researcher Andrea Rosso is one of numerous scientists in a recently filed lawsuit against NIH and its parent Department of Health and Human Services, one of a growing body of legal actions as the administration continues to hunt for and halt medical grants with descriptions that include the words “disparities,” “minority” and “racial.”

Ann Cohen, a director of Pittsburgh’s Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, also is part of that lawsuit after her separate, complementary study of Alzheimer’s risk also was halted -- after spending $5.2 million over three years. She, too, has a troubling ethics question: What to do with blood samples collected from the participants?
“You lose trust a hell of a lot faster than you build it,” she said.

A spokesperson for HHS said “Massive amounts of DEI grants have failed to translate into better health outcomes for minority populations. Following President Trump’s directives, NIH is shifting money into rigorous research that will help Americans — including minority populations — live longer, healthier lives.”
This year, the NIH has awarded 2,000 fewer grants for multiyear studies worth a total of $200 million compared with 2025, according to an Association of American Medical Colleges report.

“It’s unprecedented. Many of the decisions are based on political biases and based on what politicians think is valuable rather than peer review processes, evidence-based decisions about where to invest our research dollars,” said Jill Rosenthal, the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress.
“We’re wasting resources, we’re wasting the opportunity to identify cures for diseases,” she said.

Researchers in Pittsburgh are especially concerned that promises made to the community will remain unfulfilled. The study, 15 years in the making, would’ve helped identify participants at a higher risk for Alzheimer’s — and for potential doctor’s visits and care.
Now, Wagner said, the findings are “stuck on a shelf,” and worse, over a decade of trust built with study participants has been breached.
Blair, the study participant, said reinstating trust within their communities will be an uphill battle. “It’s going to take years to reestablish something that was moving pretty good,” he said.

title: UN warns hunger will deepen in the Middle East
summary: The United Nations warns that hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with Sudan and Yemen facing the gravest risks
story: The United Nations warns that hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with Sudan and Yemen facing the gravest risks

CAIRO -- Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-torn Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the gravest risk, the United Nations’ food agencies warned Friday. The agencies pointed to conflict, soaring fuel costs linked to war in the Middle East and steep cuts in aid.
The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program's Hunger Hotspots report covers December through May 2026.

It places Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. All five have appeared on the list repeatedly since 2022. The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, though 67% of Gaza’s population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report warned that the gains were fragile.

In Sudan, a risk of famine is expected to persist through January in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan, the report said. Nearly 19.5 million people, or 41% of the population, faced crisis-level hunger or worse in the latest nationwide analysis. In two displacement camps in South Darfur’s Eastern Jebel Marra, acute malnutrition rates exceeded the threshold for famine.

Sorghum prices in Sudan more than doubled in a year, driven by the fighting and by higher fuel costs tied to the Middle East conflict. Diesel prices have also more than doubled from a year earlier because of the Middle East conflict, according to the report.

Drought linked to El Niño — a natural warming of Pacific Ocean water that disrupts weather worldwide — has added to the strain, affecting up to 55% of cropland in Sennar state and 70% in Gedaref, two of Sudan’s main farming states.
FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol told The Associated Press that El Niño-linked drought poses a major threat to Sudan on top of the war, compounding the conflict’s toll on food production.
In Yemen, the report said, hunger is likely to worsen as fighting that resumed in July spreads across multiple fronts.
The country has been at war since 2014, when the Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year.

The encirclement of the southwestern city of Taiz has created siegelike conditions there, and more than 300,000 people have been displaced since the escalation began, mostly in Taiz, Lahj and Aden provinces. In government-held areas, 1.8 million people face emergency levels of hunger, up from 1.6 million in the previous analysis.

No recent assessment exists for areas held by the Houthis, which have become harder for aid groups to reach as the conflict has intensified. The last nationwide projection, which ran through February, found 18.3 million people, more than half the population, in crisis or worse.

Bechdol said the main obstacles to reaching Yemenis in need were political rather than geographic. She noted that staff from other U.N. agencies had been detained. The Houthis still hold 73 U.N. staffers, including eight from the U.N. human rights office.

Yemen relies heavily on imported food and fuel, and the report warned that attacks on Red Sea shipping threaten that lifeline. Shipping is now disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea. Gulf fertilizer shipments remain largely halted.

Aid has fallen sharply as major donors have pulled back funding. Food and nutrition assistance to the five countries at the highest level of concern dropped by about 62% between 2022 and 2025, and by 79% in Yemen. Shifts among donor governments in recent years have taken billions of dollars out of humanitarian and development funding, leaving agencies unable to reach as many people as before, Bechdol said.

The predictability of funding matters as much as the amount, Bechdol said, because aid for farmers must arrive during the planting and harvest periods. With El Niño forecasts in hand, she said, agencies should be prepositioning seeds and protecting livestock before disaster strikes, rather than responding to one crisis after another.
“When that window is lost, you don’t get it back,” she said. “We’re funding losses and we’re funding damage.”

title: Zapatistas begin a 'Tour for Life' from Chiapas to Mexico City to meet with families of disappeared
summary: More than 1,500 members of Mexico’s Zapatista movement will travel from the southern state of Chiapas to Mexico City to meet with families of the disappeared and join forces to address the issue of the more than 130,000 people missing across the country
story: More than 1,500 members of Mexico’s Zapatista movement will travel from the southern state of Chiapas to Mexico City to meet with families of the disappeared and join forces to address the issue of the more than 130,000 people missing across the country

SAN CRISTÓBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico -- More than 1,500 members of Mexico's Zapatista movement will begin a “Tour for Life” this Saturday, traveling from the southern state of Chiapas to Mexico City to meet with families of the disappeared and join forces in addressing the issue of the more than 130,000 people missing across the country.

The Zapatista Army of National Liberation, the guerrilla group known as the EZLN that rose up against the Mexican state in 1994, never laid down its arms but for decades has chosen social activism and the self-governance of its territories as a way to continue fighting for Indigenous peoples and human rights.

Members of the movement will depart San Cristóbal de las Casas in Chiapas in 35 buses and in Mexico City they will provide “thousands of ears” to listen to and embrace those searching for their relatives, according to a statement by one of its spokespeople, Subcomandante Moisés.
Some people with missing relatives were in San Cristóbal de las Casas to meet with the Zapatistas before the trip and they described their situations.

Adriana Pérez said she lost track of her brother in San Cristóbal de las Casas six years ago while he was on his way from home to work. Liliana Pérez, who is not related, said she has two missing sons and complained that the Mexican army never helped her search for them, even though the eldest was an active-duty soldier in Chiapas. Guadalupe Morales explained how her brother disappeared in 2015, while he was harvesting grapes in the northern state of Sonora and decided to cross the border into the United States.

“It was a warm embrace for our souls to be heard because so often the government wants to silence our voices,” said Yoslín Chavarría, who has been searching for her father since 2023 and was holding a handcrafted Zapatista doll. “This is an opportunity for our missing people to be heard in different parts of the country.”
For 32 years, the Zapatistas have raised their voices for the rights of Indigenous peoples, for human rights in general and to remind the world that they remain active.

In 2001, they traveled across Mexico in a massive caravan. Five years later, they embarked on another tour calling for a different way of doing politics. In 2018, they nominated their own independent candidate for the presidential election. More recently, they set out on a symbolic journey to “invade” Europe, their way of commemorating the route taken in the opposite direction by the Spanish conquistadors 500 years earlier.

While the Zapatistas have previously supported the cause of Mexico's disappeared, this time around they are issuing a broader call that has been heeded by hundreds of people in 27 of the country's 32 states.

The Zapatistas will be in Mexico City until January and plan to join a demonstration there on Dec. 19, when the U.N.’s newly declared International Day of Recognition for Women Searching for Missing Persons will be celebrated.

Fernando Vargas, the father of an engineering student who went missing two years ago in the mountains south of Mexico's capital, traveled to Chiapas to accompany the Zapatistas along the entire route.
“We hope to unite our struggles — those of the Indigenous peoples and those of the families searching for their loved ones,” he said.

The Zapatistas’ uprising in 1994 exposed the racism, marginalization and neglect that affect millions of people in Mexico. The agreements they reached with the government in 1996 led to a major constitutional reform five years later, which recognized the basic rights of Indigenous peoples, such as the right to decide on their forms of organization and the right to respect for their culture, although many of these achievements have yet to be realized in parts of the country.
“We would like to initiate a similar process because our problem is one of absolute impunity and zero efficiency on the part of the authorities,” said Vargas.
Verza reported from Mexico City.

title: Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir Putin
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir Putin

KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe’s future financial commitments to Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelenskyy was “insulting his counterpart,” showing that the Ukrainian leader “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement.”

Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian.”

Moscow’s invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Trump resumed relations.

At the same time, Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia’s ballistic missiles and that SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication, isn’t working properly.

Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia’s invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new $49 billion loan for Ukraine’s economic and military needs next year.
Elections in the EU over the next 12 months could amplify the influence of parties reluctant to send more money to Ukraine and may fray the continent’s support.
A bus pulled up at Ukraine’s northern border on Friday, and an 8-year-old boy ran out of it.
“Mom!” he shouted into the crowd. His mother, Alina Sydorenko, was there to reunite with him after nearly five years apart.
She hugged him tight as he kept saying, “Mother, mother.”
The boy was one of nine Ukrainian children returned Friday from Russia and Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.
“I want to show him everything that he missed and was taken away from him,” Sydorenko said.
Some of the children had lost their parents, who died in occupied territory. Relatives met them off the bus.

Zelenskyy announced the latest Bring Kids Back UA operation on social media, thanking U.S. first lady Melania Trump for her role in mediating wartime reunifications, which so far have brought 43 children home, the White House said on Wednesday.
Ukraine has so far managed to bring home 2,875 children, according to Zelenskyy.
“We remember each and every one of them. We are doing everything we can to find them and return them to their families,” he said.
Ukraine is determined to keep fighting for its independence, Kyiv officials say, and has launched daring attacks against Russian assets.
A recent strike on a Russian navy vessel docked at a port in Libya, however, raised alarm in Europe and Washington that the war could spread and engulf other countries.

In an apparent attempt to defuse tensions, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he held a phone call with Libyan Foreign Minister Al-Taher Al-Baour, informing him that Ukraine had no intentions of drawing Libya into the war.
Sybiha said in comments posted on X late Thursday that he reaffirmed Kyiv’s support for Libya’s sovereignty and efforts to reunify the country.
The grinding aerial bombardment between Russia and Ukraine has escalated recently.
Russia launched close to 300 aerial attacks a week through Nov. 20 on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, or ACLED, that tracks violence.
Zelenskyy warned Thursday that a major Russian attack is looming.

Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 110 of 155 Russian drones launched overnight Friday, including 51 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to the Ukrainian air force. Hits were recorded at 27 locations across Ukraine, it said.

The attacks targeted railway infrastructure, energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings across nine Ukrainian regions, killing at least one person and wounding at least six, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its forces overnight intercepted 318 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and illegally annexed Crimea.
Residents of St. Petersburg reported explosions in eight districts of the city, the Russian online news outlet Astra said.
Also, 70 apartments in a multi-story building were damaged in a drone attack on the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in Russia’s Krasnodar region, local officials said Friday.
Officials reported that Ukraine’s attacks killed at least two people and wounded six others.
Morton reported from London. Associated Press writers Hanna Arhirova in northern Ukraine and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed to this story.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
summary: European Council President António Costa says European Union leaders have failed to agree on the 2028-2034 budget
story: European Council President António Costa says European Union leaders have failed to agree on the 2028-2034 budget

BRUSSELS -- After struggling to chaperone Europe’s leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. “We didn’t reach an agreement,” he said.

Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.

The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world’s biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.

Costa said “some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts.”
It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.
In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.

In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.
Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.
“This is a negotiation process,” he said. “It’s normal that the member states try to defend their own national interests.”

“For me, it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December,” Costa said. He insisted that a new budget must be in place by Jan. 1, 2028. “In order to do this, we need to reach a final agreement by the end of this year," he said.
French President Emmanuel Macron said elections in his country in April, which hard right figurehead Marine Le Pen is favorite to win, mean that he is not willing to negotiate further in 2027.

“I won’t be politically and democratically in a position after December 31 to be able to relaunch a discussion on the budget and to conclude it,” he said, as it will be “a period much too close to the presidential elections.”
Spain has elections this weekend. Voters head to the polls in Italy and Poland next year.

Macron said he’s willing to sign up to “a good agreement” at the next summit on Dec. 17-18. But he said Europe is making “a strategic error” if it narrows its ambitions, and that “France will not accept more cuts.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz noted that two days have been set aside for the next budget talks but that “it could be longer. I want to be home by Christmas.”
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, a newcomer to EU budget haggling, said he had seen “zero results” and that a deal by “Christmas looks unlikely."
If the leaders continue to clutch their purse strings, money will have to be found elsewhere, but not just for the bloc’s traditional policies and future ambitions.

Funds are also needed to pay down debt on the 850-billion-euro ($932 billion) loan that was agreed after the last long-term budget negotiations to dig Europe out of its worst-ever recession, sparked by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Costa has proposed an EU-wide tax on digital services. It would be drawn from online advertising and money that companies make from user data, and could amount to 5 billion euros ($5.5 billion) a year.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin voiced “strong opposition” to the levy. “Europe is reducing competitiveness and we feel, in principle, a digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages,” he said.
But European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that inside the room the tax had “gathered broad support, and I see good prospects for a solid package of new own resources.”
The EU already raises its “own resources” through customs duties and value added tax, and the commission is exploring ways to find more through the carbon emissions trading system and a tobacco duty.

Recent budget proposals foresee a 100 billion-euro ($110 billion) envelope for Ukraine over seven years. The leaders must also decide on a new 45 billion-euro ($49.4 billion) loan to help meet Kyiv’s economic and military needs next year.

A big issue is whether to deduct the interest that European countries pay on that loan from the budget envelope, or put more in to cover it. Ukraine will only reimburse the loan once Russia pays war reparation costs.

A year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion) to cover most of Ukraine’s needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are draining resources.

Costa said 24 of the 27 member countries support the loan plan, with Bulgaria insisting that its share should only pay for economic needs. Costa must find a way to get the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia on board by next month.

title: UK charity honoring WWII veteran who raised millions during pandemic to be disbanded
summary: Capt. Tom Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020.
story: Capt. Tom Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020.

LONDON -- A charity set up by the family of a British World War II veteran who raised tens of millions of pounds by walking laps of his garden during the coronavirus pandemic has applied to be disbanded, two years after the country's charity watchdog found “repeated” financial misconduct.

An application to have the charitable company created in honor of Capt. Tom Moore removed appeared Friday on the register of Companies House, the official U.K. government executive agency that maintains the public register of British companies, including charitable ones.

Moore, who died in 2021 at 100 years old, raised almost 39 million pounds ($49 million) through his daily walks, inspiring people across the U.K. who followed his exploits in daily TV updates during the early weeks of the pandemic. All of the money he raised was donated to Britain’s National Health Service.
Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020 during an outdoor investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle, in recognition of his huge charity efforts.

Following the success of his fundraising, his family established the Captain Tom Foundation to continue his fundraising efforts. However, the charity was soon embroiled in controversy and Britain’s charity regulator concluded in November 2024 that Moore's daughter and son-in-law personally benefited from the charity.

The Charity Commission for England and Wales slammed them in a damning report that found they made almost 1.5 million pounds ($1.9 million) from activities linked to the charity, including a book deal and an 18,000-pound fee to attend an awards ceremony.
It also barred Moore’s daughter, Hannah Ingram-Moore, from serving as a trustee for any charity for 10 years and her husband, Colin, for a period of eight years.
The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission’s inquiry.
The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Moore's name at the request of his family last year.

title: At least 9 reported killed across Ukraine, while Russia downs near-record number of drones
summary: At least nine civilians across Ukraine were reported killed on Saturday, while Russia said it downed a near-record number of Ukrainian drones during the night
story: At least nine civilians across Ukraine were reported killed on Saturday, while Russia said it downed a near-record number of Ukrainian drones during the night
KYIV, Ukraine -- At least nine civilians across Ukraine were reported killed in drone attacks on Saturday, while Russia said it had downed a near-record number of Ukrainian drones during the night.

Seven people were killed and seven others wounded in a Russian attack on an enterprise in Nizhyn, in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, the State Emergency Service reported on Saturday. It said the rescue operations there finished on Saturday following the attack the previous day.

In Russian-occupied Ukraine, two people died and two others were wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a hospital vehicle in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, Kremlin-installed authorities there said on Saturday.

“A drone attacked an official vehicle belonging to the Vasylivka Central District Hospital. As a result of the strike, a nurse and a driver were killed. Two others sustained injuries of moderate severity,” the Russian-installed local health ministry said. It added the hospital’s chief physician was among those hurt. The hospital is near the front line.
Zaporizhzhia is one of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow has formally annexed and tried to fully occupy.

Elsewhere, Russia's Defense Ministry said on Saturday morning that its forces shot down 1,246 Ukrainian drones during the night — one of the highest numbers reported since the start of the war. It did not say how many were launched or how many reached their targets.

Over eight hours overnight, 123 Ukrainian drones were shot down on the approach to Moscow, mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported on Saturday morning. He said a total of 462 drones had approached the wider Moscow region since Friday evening, adding a “majority” had been suppressed.
Gov. Yury Slyusar on Saturday said that over 50 drones were shot down over Russia’s southern Rostov region during the night, including over the city of Novoshakhtinsk — home to a major oil refinery.

He did not immediately specify what was hit, or whether there was damage. But several Russian and Ukrainian news channels on Telegram claimed that some of the drones struck the refinery in Novoshakhtinsk, some 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and caused a large-scale fire.

In Russia's Samara region further east, Ukrainian drones attacked “industrial facilities” overnight, Gov. Vladislav Fedorishchev reported on Saturday. He did not specify the target, but said the attack had been “repelled” and caused no deaths or injuries. He did not immediately comment on any damage.

Hours earlier, Ukrainian and Russian Telegram channels claimed that drones struck the junction of four oil pipelines in the region. The “Samara” production and dispatch station, which they said was targeted for a second time this month, is part of a transport network operated by Russia’s state-owned oil giant Transneft.
In Russia’s southern Bryansk region bordering Ukraine, nine people were injured after a drone struck a company bus, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk reported on Saturday morning.

He said the bus belonged to Miratorg, a Russian producer of marbled beef, pork and other meat products. According to Kovalchuk, six Miratorg employees and three other locals were briefly hospitalized with shrapnel wounds.
Ukrainian air defense forces destroyed or suppressed 141 out of 162 Russian drones launched overnight, Ukraine’s Air Force said on Saturday.

As well as the deaths and injuries in Nizhyn, three people were injured overnight into Saturday in a Russian attack on the city of Bila Tserkva near Kyiv, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
A fire broke out at a garage cooperative, damaging six garages. The blast wave also shattered windows in six nearby apartment buildings, the service said.

title: UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
summary: The U.N. peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon is preparing to end a 50-year mission as tensions between Israel and Hezbollah remain high
story: The U.N. peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon is preparing to end a 50-year mission as tensions between Israel and Hezbollah remain high

NAQOURA, Lebanon -- Among the few buildings still standing in the Lebanese border town of Naqoura are an abandoned hotel occupied by Israeli soldiers, its walls draped with anti-drone netting, and the compound housing the headquarters of the U.N. peacekeeping force.
The roads passing through the once-idyllic seaside town, now largely reduced to rubble, are empty except for the occasional military patrol or convoy of peacekeepers escorting civilians or supplies.
The end of the nearly 50-year mandate of the UNIFIL peacekeeping force is looming in just over a month, and still there is no plan for what comes after it.

The peacekeepers' impending exit, in parallel with an ongoing occupation by Israeli forces and a debate over the disarmament of the Hezbollah militant group, leaves the future of southern Lebanon in limbo.

Lebanon wants the U.N. force to stay. But the U.N. Security Council voted last year to terminate UNIFIL’s mandate at the end of 2026, bowing to demands from the United States and its close ally Israel.

Israel says the mission was a failure, citing Hezbollah’s military buildup over the years. The peacekeepers say they helped preserve calm for 17 years before Hamas’ 2023 attack on southern Israel ignited a regional conflict.

“My mandate is not to disarm Hezbollah,” UNIFIL’s commander, Maj. Gen. Diodato Abagnara, told The Associated Press in an interview. “My mandate is to support the Lebanese Armed Forces, to create the best conditions for the Lebanese Armed Forces to take full control here in the south. It’s not to fight against Hezbollah.”
UNIFIL is set to begin a gradual drawdown of its 7,500 peacekeepers on Jan. 1. Whatever comes after that, he said, “It’s very important to avoid a security vacuum in the south.”

UNIFIL wasn’t able to stop Hezbollah from launching missiles or Israel from carrying out airstrikes in two recent wars. But many residents of southern Lebanon say they still feel safer with its presence.

Mohammed Aoun was late to start harvesting his olive groves this year in the village of Halta, just outside of the Israeli-occupied area. On the first day of harvest earlier this month, as a UNIFIL patrol stopped at the orchard, an Israeli drone was buzzing overhead. The thud of a distant airstrike echoed through the valley.
Aoun said he was hesitant to start picking, but he had already lost out on the previous two years’ harvests. He is apprehensive about the impending departure of UNIFIL forces.

“Of course we feel more secure when we see patrols coming and going; it’s a sort of protection,” he said. “Their presence is important with regards to the security situation. We don’t know what will happen after they leave.”

The U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon was created in 1978 after Israel invaded southern Lebanon to fight Palestinian militants. Israel invaded again in 1982 and didn't withdraw until 2000. During that period, Hezbollah, backed by Iran, emerged as a guerrilla force.

After a monthlong war between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006, UNIFIL was tasked with monitoring violations of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the fighting. When a ceasefire ended another Israel-Hezbollah war in 2024, UNIFIL was part of the mechanism overseeing its implementation.
The Lebanese army was to take over security in southern Lebanon after the U.N. force's exit.

But then another war broke out between Israel and Hezbollah in March, linked to the wider Iran war. Israel now occupies large swaths of southern Lebanon, where its soldiers have emptied and demolished dozens of villages.

About 11,000 people remain in a handful of mostly Christian villages in the occupied area, Abagnara said. They depend on UNIFIL to escort the convoys that keep them connected with the rest of the country.
An agreement between Lebanon and Israel for Israeli forces to withdraw in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah has floundered, and negotiations between the two countries have stalled.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said in a statement Wednesday that “Israel continues to engage in hostile acts in the south” and his government and France — a Security Council member with close ties to Lebanon — both want an extension of UNIFIL's mandate. Any alternative force should continue to operate under the 1701 framework, with some possible amendments, he said.

On Friday, Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told the AP that a proposal is in the works to let UNIFIL continue some of its functions during the drawdown period after its mandate ends, as the Security Council debates what should replace it. But it's not clear if Washington will accept the plan.

U.S. officials have expressed willingness for some sort of international force to remain, but not in its current form. They have suggested that it could be a civilian force or private defense contractor.
Israel wants its military to coordinate directly with the Lebanese army to remove what remains of Hezbollah’s weapons.
Israel’s ambassador to the U.N., Danny Danon, said earlier this month that Hezbollah had "exploited UNIFIL’s presence."
“We do not rely on any international force," he said. "We trust only our own soldiers.”
Lebanon opposes the idea of a civilian contractor and has rejected direct military coordination with Israel.

France is working on a Security Council resolution that would authorize a new international force, a U.N. diplomat said. A Western diplomat said there are also discussions of slowing down UNIFIL's withdrawal and maintaining certain missions to avoid a “power vacuum.”
They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly.
In January, the Lebanese army announced that it had finished removing Hezbollah weapons caches from the border area south of the Litani River.
Hezbollah did not actively oppose the effort but has refused to give up its weapons elsewhere in the country and threatened to fight any attempt to forcibly disarm it.

The Lebanese army has been cautious about any move that might provoke a civil conflict. A Lebanese security official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said the army’s current policy is to stop weapons shipments from moving around the country — a change from the past, when Hezbollah freely transported arms — but not to raid the militant group’s storage sites.

Hezbollah supporters in the past accused UNIFIL of spying for Israel and sometimes attacked peacekeepers. Now the group says it would accept UNIFIL or another U.N.-mandated force, but not a private security contractor or a force seen as supporting Israel's occupation.
Associated Press writer Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations contributed to this report.

title: Clashes erupt in Albania's capital as protesters call for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign
summary: Police in Albania have clashed with protesters during a demonstration by thousands who are demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation
story: Police in Albania have clashed with protesters during a demonstration by thousands who are demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation

TIRANA, Albania -- Clashes broke out Saturday between police and protesters in the Albanian capital, Tirana, as thousands of people called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, the latest in a long series of anti-government protests.
The protest began peacefully, but small groups of masked demonstrators broke away and began smashing the windows of ministry buildings along the march route.

Police used tear gas and water cannons to push back protesters throwing rocks and Molotov cocktails and using wooden sticks to try to smash street cameras and windows on government buildings. Clouds of tear gas billowed through the area as protesters spread out across several streets.

Albanians traveled to Tirana from across the country and abroad for the rally, which coincided with the 114th anniversary of the country's declaration of independence, a day normally marked by celebrations and a public holiday. Police were deployed along the main roads leading in and out of the capital, conducting vehicle checks.

“I came here specifically for the protest,” said Arian Lleshi, a 33-year-old who traveled to Tirana from the United Kingdom. “Why? Because we have been suffering for far too long. We have spread ourselves across Europe and around the world, and it is almost as if we are citizens without a state. We are like stateless citizens.”

The political parties that have been around in Albania since the fall of communism in the 1990s “no longer represent anyone,” Lleshi said. “They need to make way for a new generation of intellectuals and people who have a greater stake in the country’s future.”

Saturday’s protest was part of a series of demonstrations that began in late May, initially sparked by opposition to a major luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast that is linked to an investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

The protests became known as the Flamingo movement and were later followed by student demonstrations in September, many of which turned violent, with students calling for better education and living standards. The demonstrators' demands have since broadened to include calls for Rama's resignation.
Protesters chanted “Resignation!” as they gathered in Tirana’s main Skanderbeg Square.
“We have come out to demand our rights. We have had enough. Life has become very difficult. We are calling for a change to the entire system,” student Juna Vasili said.

Resident Suzana Gjeta, a retiree, said that she was demonstrating both on behalf of young people and those like herself “who are living on just 120 euros a month. We hope this system will go, that Edi Rama will go, and that this corruption will end,” she said.
Associated Pres writer Elena Becatoros in Athens, Greece, contributed to this report.
