title: Mexico files formal complaint to US over DEA tip line
summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum says the country is filing a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officials
story: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum says the country is filing a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officials

MEXICO CITY -- MEXICO CITY (AP) — Mexico filed a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officials, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday, escalating a fight over a move she called interference in its internal affairs.
“We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” she said in her daily news briefing.

The protest comes as U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is pressuring Mexico to intensify its fight against cartels. It's made a public offer to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out.

DEA chief Terry Cole announced on his X account Wednesday that the agency was opening an anonymous tip line to receive information about members and associates of designated terrorist organizations, corrupt officials who support them, criminal networks and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism in Sinaloa.

The northern state is the stronghold of one of Mexico's most powerful cartels, the Sinaloa Cartel, which Washington designated a terrorist organization along with five other Mexican criminal groups. Cole said the agency also plans to open a tip line for the state of Jalisco.

Sheinbaum once again urged Washington to address drug use and combat drug traffickers within its own territory. She also reaffirmed that Mexico would continue working to confront cartels and prevent drugs from reaching the U.S.

“The United States has a responsibility to its people to address drug use, as well as to arrest members of the drug cartels operating in the United States,” Sheinbaum said, insisting that “we cannot have this view that the responsibility lies with Mexico.”

The dispute broke out just days after Mexico captured a major drug kingpin with help from the United States, which flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to pinpoint the location of the capo.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro," was an important ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction who was on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. Both governments celebrated his arrest.
The United States requested the extradition of “El Chapo Isidro,” but Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said this week that “he will be tried in this country.”

title: UN rapporteur Albanese in limbo at airport after being denied entry to Costa Rica
summary: Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, is stranded at Costa Rica’s main airport awaiting for a court to decide whether she could enter the country after immigration authorities blocked h...
story: Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, is stranded at Costa Rica’s main airport awaiting for a court to decide whether she could enter the country after immigration authorities blocked h...

SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica -- Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, was stranded in an airport terminal on Friday after being denied entry to Costa Rica.
Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”
She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.

Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on Thursday, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.

Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinizing human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.

She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of U.S. and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”
Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.

After she was denied entry, a habeas corpus petition was filed on her behalf with the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber. The court issued an interim order allowing her to remain in the country and gave immigration authorities 24 hours to explain why they had denied her entry.

While the petition is pending, Albanese remains in a room at the airport. From there, she joined the university’s honorary doctorate ceremony by video call. One of her assistants, who was allowed into the country, accepted the degree on her behalf.
In her speech, Albanese said the decision to deny her entry could be related to the sanctions.

“I am deeply outraged that the Costa Rican government has spread false information linking me to terrorism. Defending human rights is not terrorism, and the government will answer for these insinuations, as it should in a country governed by the rule of law,” Albanese said.

Costa Rica's right-wing government is among a number of governments in the region that have sought to cozy up to the Trump administration, accepting third-country deportees from the U.S. in a move that provoked heavy criticism, and has built a Bukele-style mega-prison as part of its vow to crack down on crime.

Albanese criticized what she described as the Costa Rican government’s complicity in Israeli policies of oppression against Palestinians, citing its signing of a free-trade agreement with Israel that awaits legislative ratification.
Costa Rican President Laura Fernández has not commented on the issue, but her minister of the presidency, former President Rodrigo Chaves, addressed the court’s intervention on social media.

“Yet another usurpation by an increasingly arbitrary judiciary, one that usurps the powers of the other two branches of government and now protects foreigners flagged by international alerts for ties to TERRORIST ACTS!” Chaves wrote about the habeas corpus petition that halted Albanese’s expulsion.
Costa Rica’s ombudsman’s office criticized immigration authorities for “automatically” denying Albanese entry without assessing her case, her official status or her immunity as a U.N. rapporteur.
U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also said he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to deny her entry.

title: Prosecutors ask for 25 years for man who sold products used by 93 to kill themselves
summary: Prosecutors sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who sold products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves
story: Prosecutors sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who sold products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves

NEWMARKET, Ontario -- Ontario prosecutors on Friday sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides after selling products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves.
Kenneth Law, 61, apologized to victims’ families from the prisoner’s box, saying that his actions were “categorically wrong” and promising never to repeat them.

Prosecutors argued that Law was motivated by money. His lawyers sought a 12-year sentence, describing him as a misguided believer in the right to die rather than a “mercenary predator.” A sentencing decision is expected in February.
Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of counseling or aiding suicide involving people in Ontario. The judge is also considering the deaths of 79 people in the United Kingdom.

At a hearing in September, families of people who died after buying lethal products from Law described their lives shattered by grief. Police said Law sold sodium nitrite, a substance commonly used to cure meats that can be deadly if ingested.

EDITOR’S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. The U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org. In the U.K., the Samaritans can be reached at 116 123 or www.samaritans.org.
Prosecutor Katie Doherty said 93 people, including 12 teenagers, died after using Law’s products.

“These were vulnerable people ... What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death,” she said. Doherty rejected suggestions that Law acted altruistically, saying he sold to anyone who paid upfront.
The former chef shipped products to more than 40 countries over nearly 2 1/2 years, knowing customers were likely to use them to kill themselves, according to an agreed statement of facts.
Defense lawyer Matthew Gourlay argued that Law did not cause customers’ struggles or their decisions to kill themselves. “In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone,” he said.
Aiding suicide carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in Canada. Prosecutors requested 12 1/2 years on each count, with two terms served back to back and the others at the same time.
Credit for time in custody would reduce the proposed term to about 19 years and eight months. The defense sought additional credit for harsh detention conditions.

Prosecutors acknowledged Law’s guilty plea spared families a trial and that he had no prior criminal record. Law has been detained since May 2023. Prosecutors are expected to withdraw 14 first-degree murder charges after sentencing.

Authorities in the United States, Italy, Australia and New Zealand also have investigated the case. A prosecutor had said that it involves some 431 packages of lethal substances that were sent to the U.S.

title: Argentina loses bid to halt oil drilling off nearby UK-held Falkland Islands
summary: An international tribunal has rejected Argentina's bid to block oil drilling off the U.K.-held Falkland Islands
story: An international tribunal has rejected Argentina's bid to block oil drilling off the U.K.-held Falkland Islands
LONDON -- Argentina’s bid to temporarily block oil drilling off the nearby U.K.-held Falkland Islands was rejected Saturday by an international tribunal that rules on maritime disputes.

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea voted 18-3 against Argentina's request to halt drilling at the Sea Lion offshore oil project in Falkland Islands waters, around 300 miles (480 kilometers) east of Argentina’s southeastern coast.

The judges, at a special hearing in Hamburg, Germany, found that Argentina’s claims couldn't be decided without ruling on the rival claims to sovereignty over the islands in the South Atlantic, a question that they said falls outside the scope of the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty governing the world’s oceans.

The dispute over the planned drilling revived bitter memories of the 74-day war that the two countries fought over the islands in 1982. Argentina’s military junta invaded the archipelago, which Argentina calls the Islas Malvinas and which has been under British rule since 1833. The conflict saw 649 Argentine troops, 255 British troops and three islanders killed.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves welcomed the decision and urged Argentina to end its wider economic pressure.

“This outcome is a vindication of the U.K.’s robust legal defense and strategy,” they said in a joint statement. “The U.K. has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders.”
In a 2013 referendum, more than 99% of the roughly 3,500 islanders voted to remain British, a result Argentina rejects.

Argentina respects the court’s decision, but disagrees with it, the office of President Javier Milei said. The Argentine government sought to portray the ruling as a partial win, arguing that by tying the case to sovereignty, the court had effectively recognized the existence of a dispute that the United Kingdom has long refused to negotiate on.
“This decision is not the last word,” Milei's office said.
Argentina will move quickly to form a separate arbitration panel that will hear the full case and ask it for measures to protect the country’s rights, it said.

Argentina wanted work on the $2.1 billion project frozen until the panel rules on the full dispute. It argued that every barrel of oil extracted would be lost to Argentina for good, causing irreparable harm to its claim over the area’s natural resources.

The U.K. countered that Argentina’s challenge was, at its core, a claim to sovereignty. Under the U.N. treaty, rights over the sea and seabed belong to whichever country owns the nearby coast, so the court couldn't rule on the case without wading into that question. The judges agreed, finding that even Argentina’s environmental concerns about the project hinged on it.
Milei vowed Saturday to keep punishing companies working on the oil project, which he has called a “clear and present danger” to Argentina’s claims over the islands.

His government announced new sanctions proceedings on Friday against five individuals or companies involved, warning that “those who participate in the illegitimate exploitation of our resources will have to face the consequences.”

The hard line marks a turnabout for the libertarian. Milei is an admirer of Margaret Thatcher, who was U.K. prime minister during the war over the Falklands. He took office in 2023 striking a conciliatory tone on the islands and seeking warmer commercial ties with Britain.

But his tone has sharpened as his popularity slips and the economy stalls a year before his reelection bid. He has also appeared encouraged by signals from his close ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, that Washington could rethink its neutrality in the dispute.

Following the ruling, Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum are expected to push ahead with the plan under licenses granted by the Falkland Islands government and backed by the U.K. The decision is likely to come as a relief for Falkland islanders, who have long dreamed of oil transforming their lives and their fishing-dependent economy.
The U.K. has said drilling at the field about 220 kilometers (140 miles) north of the islands won't commence until March, with extraction expected to begin a year later.

Saturday’s ruling was only preliminary, marking the beginning of what could be a lengthy legal battle. The court urged both countries to quickly set up the arbitration panel, which could still rule in Argentina’s favor.

Argentina’s pressure on the project goes beyond the courtroom in Germany. At home, it has filed criminal complaints against Israeli company Navitas, the project’s operator, and other firms. The government says it has also sent aggressive warning letters to 180 companies and individuals in 30 countries with ties to oil activity around the islands.

With one of the world’s largest shale reserves, Argentina has a far bigger oil industry, giving companies that work in both places good reason to steer clear of Sea Lion. Last month, Navitas said that it was replacing two contractors that had pulled out over Argentina’s threats.
Isabel DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina.

title: South Korea lets a North Korean fisherman resettle in South and returns six others
summary: Seoul says that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South
story: Seoul says that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South
SEOUL, South Korea -- Seoul said Friday that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South.
South Korea's Unification Ministry said it let the six others return to North Korea aboard their boat across the Koreas’ eastern maritime border Friday morning.
The North Koreans were rescued by South Korea's navy and coast guard in international waters near South Korea's eastern Ulleung Island on Nov. 3.

It's not uncommon for North Korean fishing boats to be found adrift south of the Koreas' eastern and western sea boundaries. South Korea typically returns North Korean fishermen if they want to go home and are not suspected of espionage. But South Korea lets them resettle in the South if they so choose.

North Korea has yet to comment on the fisherman who opted to remain in South Korea. Pyongyang is highly sensitive about defections and often accuses Seoul of enticing its citizens to defect, something the South denies.

The two Koreas remain split along one of the world's most heavily fortified borders since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice. Citizens from the two countries are not allowed to exchange phone calls, letters and emails with each other.

More than 34,000 North Koreans have fled to South Korea for economic and political reasons since the war's end, mostly in the last three decades. Animosities between the Koreas have deepened in recent years, with North Korea terminating ties with South Korea and focusing on expanding its nuclear program.

title: Death toll in Pakistan building collapse rises to 8 with about 10 missing
summary: The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan has risen to eight
story: The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan has risen to eight
KARACHI, Pakistan -- The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan rose to eight Friday after rescuers recovered four more bodies, officials said.

Rescuers are still searching for about 10 people believed trapped beneath the rubble of the building, which collapsed Wednesday in Karachi’s Baloch Colony neighborhood, police official Raja Sarwar said.
Relatives of those still missing were in tears as they prayed for their safety.

On Friday, helmeted rescuers carried a body wrapped in a white covering on a stretcher across a mound of shattered concrete and tangled steel bars. Others were trying to reach into gaps in the wreckage in a congested residential area.
Sarwar said crews were carefully removing debris in hopes of finding survivors.

Building collapses are common across Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced and builders frequently use substandard materials or disregard safety regulations to cut costs. Last month, the roof of a private school collapsed in the northwestern city of Peshawar, killing 34 children and a teacher.

title: What to know about North Korean move to shut down Swiss diplomatic office
summary: North Korea has shut down a Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang and expelled its head, signaling a more assertive foreign policy
story: North Korea has shut down a Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang and expelled its head, signaling a more assertive foreign policy

SEOUL, South Korea -- In shutting down a month-old Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang and expelling its head, North Korea has signaled it will set its own terms as it pursues a more assertive foreign policy. But experts say the move could potentially risk the loss of many European nations as alternative diplomatic partners.
The Swiss drew the anger of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un after they imposed sanctions on a youth camp over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

Just a few days earlier, in a more upbeat diplomatic moment, Kim received credentials from 10 newly appointed ambassadors, including envoys from ally Russia and longtime diplomatic partner Sweden, in the first such event of his 15-year rule.

Kim used the meeting with ambassadors to defend his nuclear arms buildup and call for the world to respect North Korea’s sovereignty, a standard Pyongyang later accused Switzerland of failing to meet by sanctioning the camp.
Here's a look at the closure of the Swiss office in Pyongyang and what it says about North Korea’s foreign policy.

North Korea’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Sylvain Astier, head of the Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, declared him persona non grata and handed him a notice demanding the office’s closure and his departure from the country within 48 hours.

In a statement provided to The Associated Press on Thursday, Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said it regrets the North Korean decision and was arranging for Astier to return to the Swiss embassy in Beijing. It said diplomatic relations will be maintained through the Swiss embassy in Beijing and the North Korean embassy in Bern and that Switzerland will continue to pursue dialogue through these channels.

Kim Jong Un’s powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, earlier condemned Switzerland for imposing sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the North’s eastern coastal city of Wonsan. She called the Swiss steps an “open hostile act” that violated the North’s sovereignty, but didn’t directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated with pro-Russian propaganda.
North Korea is one of Russia’s allies and has sent thousands of troops to fight in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Switzerland earlier this month added the Songdowon camp to its sanctions over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the camp, freezing its assets and banning financial transactions with it. The measures were seen as largely symbolic, given North Korea’s limited financial ties with Europe.
North Korea said in August it downgraded the level of diplomatic relations with the U.K. to that of chargé d’affaires in response to its sanctioning of the Songdowon camp.

Switzerland, which established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974, has been one of the few Western countries to maintain talks with Pyongyang. Switzerland previously operated a humanitarian-focused cooperation office in Pyongyang, which closed when North Korea sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was among the few countries allowed to open a new diplomatic office after North Korea reopened.

Kim Jong Un and his sister spent several of their teenage years at Swiss schools in the 1990s, and that may have deepened the sense of betrayal when Switzerland sanctioned the Songdowon camp, said Koh Yu-hwan, former president of South Korea’s Institute of National Unification.

But more importantly, North Korea is sending a broader warning that it could cut off diplomatic access to any country that expands sanctions or pursues policies it considers hostile, effectively putting pressure on the North's remaining Western contacts like Sweden, Koh said.

While Russia and China have blocked recent efforts to tighten U.N. sanctions over North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, the United States and its European and Asian allies have imposed their own sanctions over illicit activities Pyongyang uses to fund its weapons programs, including information-technology worker fraud and cryptocurrency theft.

Kim Jong Un's diplomatic clout on the global stage has been bolstered in recent years as he's aligned with Russia and has taken steps to strengthen cooperation with China, North Korea's economic lifeline.
Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Seoul’s Ewha University, said North Korea is benefiting enough from its ties with Moscow that it’s willing to make an example of Switzerland.
“By ordering the Swiss office closed just weeks after it opened, the Kim regime wants to show other states it intends to reengage only from a position of strength and on its own terms,” he said.
However, the strategy carries some risk, warned Moon Seong Mook, an analyst at the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.
“Kim Jong Un may win Russia’s favor, but I think this could further deepen North Korea’s isolation from the international community,” he said.

Park Won Gon, a professor at Ewha University, said the North’s move could have long-term consequences, risking the loss of Europe as an alternative partner while further increasing its dependence on China. About 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China in 2025.
“For European countries, this move will only reinforce the perception that North Korea cannot be trusted,” Park said.

Kim's advancing nuclear arsenal and deepened cooperation with Russia have bolstered his international standing, and he has steadfastly insisted that he will not engage in talks with the United States unless Washington drops its demand for denuclearization.

As Pyongyang increasingly believes it has the leverage to deal directly with Washington, rather than through intermediaries, European countries such as Switzerland or Asian U.S. allies such as South Korea — which Kim in recent years declared as his most hostile enemy — have likely significantly less value to the North.
“They think they no longer need to make compromises with individual countries ... as they portray their status as a nuclear-armed state on an equal footing with the United States," Koh said.

title: Pakistan set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under trilateral defense pact
summary: Officials say Pakistan is set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three
story: Officials say Pakistan is set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan is set to host talks Friday with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three, two security officials said.

The talks in Islamabad will focus on developments in the Middle East, including ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels, the officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the meeting publicly.
They said delegations from Turkey and Saudi Arabia have started arriving in the capital.

Meanwhile, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan formally approved the three-nation agreement, completing Turkey’s ratification process for the defense pact, according to Turkey’s Official Gazette on Friday.

Earlier this month, legislators approved the agreement by 279 votes to 119 in Turkey’s 699-seat parliament, despite objections from opposition parties who had argued that the agreement could embroil Turkey in regional wars and put Turkish soldiers in harm’s way.

Turkish officials have said Ankara is considering sending military assistance to Saudi Arabia but insist that the Mecca agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops would be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.

Pakistan has said that the agreement is purely defensive in nature and it is not against anyone, including Iran, and that the trilateral alliance reflects a shared desire to strengthen strategic security cooperation.

Senior diplomats as well as defense and military officials from the three countries are expected to discuss ways to deter threats, expand military cooperation, share intelligence and strengthen defense industry ties, the officials said. Pakistan's Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif, Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will attend the meeting.
Asif has said that Pakistan will use “whatever means are available” to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks from the Houthis.

However, Pakistan is still making efforts with help from countries in the Middle East, including Qatar, to urge the United States and Iran to return to the negotiation table to end the conflict in the region and beyond through talks. Pakistan in June had brokered an interim deal between the two sides.

Friday's meeting of the Strategic, Political and Defense Committee falls under the Joint Mecca Defense Agreement, which was signed in August in the Saudi holy city of Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

Pakistan’s government has not released details ahead of the meeting, but authorities have declared a local holiday in Islamabad to limit public movement as part of security measures for the gathering. Islamabad traffic police have announced road diversions and advised motorists to use alternative routes to accommodate the movement of foreign delegations.

During a previous meeting in Riyadh, the three sides had vowed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.

According to the agreement, the group’s secretariat has been established in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will also attend Friday’s meeting. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, after which they would need to provide three months' notice before leaving.
Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey.

title: Armed group kills 13 soldiers in western Niger attack, defense ministry says
summary: Armed men killed 13 members of Niger’s National Guard and wounded 20 others in an attack on an outpost in western Niger, the country’s defense ministry said
story: Armed men killed 13 members of Niger’s National Guard and wounded 20 others in an attack on an outpost in western Niger, the country’s defense ministry said
NIAMEY, Niger -- Armed men killed 13 members of Niger’s National Guard and wounded 20 others in an attack on an outpost in western Niger, the defense ministry said.

The attack took place Thursday in Sanam, in the Tillaberi region, the ministry said in a statement read on state television the same day. Several attackers were also killed and their equipment was destroyed, the statement said.
The ministry said a large group of heavily armed men carried out the assault and that troops were pursuing them. Several of the wounded were in serious condition, it said.
Niger and its neighbors Mali and Burkina Faso have for many years battled a jihadi insurgency linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group.

Analysts say Niger’s security crisis has worsened since the military toppled the country’s government in July 2023. Following the coup, the new junta turned to Russia as its security partner and ended its military cooperation with the United States and France.
Despite its promise to restore peace in trouble spots, the junta has faced growing questions about its ability to improve security amid more frequent attacks.
In August, disgruntled soldiers staged a mutiny against the junta. Loyalist forces, aided by Russian troops, put it down.

title: Taiwan awaits local election results as China watches
summary: Vote counting is underway across Taiwan's 22 cities and counties after local elections on Saturday
story: Vote counting is underway across Taiwan's 22 cities and counties after local elections on Saturday

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Vote counting was underway across Taiwan 's 22 cities and counties Saturday after polls closed in local elections that will test whether the ruling party can gain ground in races for mayors and council members.

Unlike presidential elections, when relations with China and Beijing’s pressure on the self-ruled island are major issues, Saturday’s vote focused more on local concerns, including social welfare benefits and other livelihood issues.

But China, which claims Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out force to annex it, has not been entirely absent from the debate. Taiwanese authorities have accused Beijing of attempting to sow distrust in the island’s electoral system, allegations that Chinese authorities have rejected.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense reported about 33 sorties by Chinese warplanes, including bombers and fighter jets, toward the island between Friday and Saturday.
Results are normally announced the same day. Winners will serve four-year terms.

Voters also cast ballots in a referendum to overturn a policy that banned nuclear power. The proposal calls for using nuclear energy to boost the economy. Supporters say additional energy sources are needed to meet the artificial intelligence industry’s growing demand for electricity.

The elections featured candidates mostly from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party or the opposition Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT. Traditionally, the KMT has performed well in local elections. In 2022, the DPP won in only five of 22 localities.
Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te has campaigned for DPP candidates, appearing Thursday night to support his party’s mayoral candidate in Taoyuan City.
The capital, Taipei, is traditionally a KMT stronghold, but the DPP’s mayoral candidate Puma Shen has mounted a strong challenge to incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an.
Thousands of people at a DPP rally quietly watched the tallying of votes on large screens. When Shen appeared to narrow the gap with Chiang, the crowd cheered.
Other notable races were in New Taipei City and Kaohsiung. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayor is from the DPP.
A third party, the Taiwan People’s Party, ran in some smaller races and supported Shen in the Taipei race.
Across Taipei, colorful banners promoting each candidate blanketed the otherwise dull brown and gray building surfaces.
Chang Li-fen said the economy was her foremost concern, but declined to say whom she had voted for.

“If the Taiwan economy is good, only then will people be able to live well,” she said. “In France and in Italy, people are protesting because of energy costs, which raised the cost of living, so I think the economy is most important.”
Candidates held rallies Friday in a last-minute bid for votes.
Shen traveled in a motorcade across the city, stopping for 15 minutes at a time to greet the crowds of supporters.
Chiang held a night rally with other KMT city council members, with supporters waving balloons, flags and light-up sticks to cheer him on.

title: Houthis report 11 killed, including children, in an airstrike, and other Mideast news
summary: Houthi rebels say an airstrike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including children
story: Houthi rebels say an airstrike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including children
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels report that an air strike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including children.

Meanwhile, top officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are holding a meeting of their defense pact that is expected to discuss Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. And a senior Hamas official says the son of the group's leader was targeted by an Israeli strike but survived.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.

The Houthi-run health ministry said Friday that a strike on a densely populated area in southwestern Yemen killed at least 11 people, including children, the latest attack in the fight between the Iran-backed rebel group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.

Ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said on X that an airstrike hit a cinema building in Turbah city in Taiz province early Friday morning, killing people including children who sold ice cream in the area and had been living in part of the building. Al-Asbahi didn’t provide details of how many children were killed and said the death toll was preliminary as rescuers are trying to pull out more bodies from under the rubble.
He blamed the strike on Saudi Arabia. The AP couldn’t independently verify his claims and the Saudi coalition made no public comment about this incident.

Footage aired by Houthi-controlled al-Masirah TV showed a destroyed building and people digging through the rubble to recover the bodies of several children. The AP couldn’t independently verify the footage.
Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas’ decision-making political bureau, said Friday that the only surviving son of the group's leader escaped a targeted Israeli strike.
Naim made the claim in a post on X, adding that Khalil al-Hayya’s son was targeted alongside his family, and the family of his brother who was killed in an Israeli strike earlier this year.

The strike that allegedly targeted al-Hayya’s son on Friday was carried out on a residential apartment in Gaza City, wounding six people, including one critically, according to health officials at Shifa hospital.
Hamas condemned the strike, accusing Israel of repeated ceasefire violations in the war-battered territory. Israel’s military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Friday’s alleged targeting comes months after al-Hayya lost another son, Azzam, in an Israeli strike on Gaza. Israeli strikes have killed several top Hamas leaders and their family members throughout the war.

Despite a ceasefire agreement reached with Hamas last year, Israel has continued to carry out attacks against Gaza, where the Health Ministry has reported more than 1,700 killed since the ceasefire took effect.

Top diplomats and defense and military officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are meeting in Islamabad to discuss developments in the Middle East, including ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The meeting is being held under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three.
The Joint Mecca Defense Agreement was signed in August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
Meanwhile, Erdogan formally approved the three-nation agreement, completing Turkey’s ratification process.

Earlier this month, legislators approved the agreement in the 600-seat parliament, despite objections from opposition parties who had argued that the agreement could embroil Turkey in regional wars and put Turkish soldiers in harm’s way.
Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey; Ahmed from Islamabad; and Khaled from Cairo. Toqa Ezzidin also contributed from Cairo.

title: Lula’s choice of Bradesco banker as Brazil’s finance minister lifts markets
summary: Brazilian markets have rallied after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva confirmed that veteran banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco would lead his finance ministry in 2027, a move seen as a commitment to fiscal discipline
story: Brazilian markets have rallied after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva confirmed that veteran banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco would lead his finance ministry in 2027, a move seen as a commitment to fiscal discipline

RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian markets rallied on Friday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva confirmed that he had chosen a veteran banker to lead the finance ministry in 2027, a move seen as a sign of his commitment to fiscal discipline.

Brazil’s currency, the real, and its stock market had tumbled after Lula’s surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro in last month’s presidential election. Investors had been counting on a win by Bolsonaro, who had pledged to slash spending.

But the announcement late Thursday that Bradesco chief Luiz Carlos Trabuco had accepted Lula’s invitation to oversee the country’s finances during his upcoming fourth term, which begins Jan. 5, triggered a sharp rebound.
The real strengthened from 5.88 to the dollar on Wednesday to 5.53 on Friday morning, while stocks surged between Thursday evening and Friday morning.

The currency had already begun strengthening after Brazil’s lower house approved a government plan earlier this week to control spending and increase revenue. Although many investors considered the plan too timid, they viewed it as a step in the right direction.

The package has drawn criticism from some of Lula’s supporters, who accuse his government of bowing to market pressure. They see the measures as a threat to health, education and welfare spending, as well as to his campaign promises.

Lula on Friday appeared to defend the plan as he thanked students in the city of Niteroi, across the bay from Rio de Janeiro, for spontaneously taking to the streets after Bolsonaro bested the incumbent in the first round of the election. The students are largely credited with kicking off a mass mobilization calling on people to vote for Lula that contributed to securing his win in the second round.
“We need to grow, and to grow, we cannot waste money. We will have to spend money wisely,” Lula said, speaking from a stage.
One student held a sign saying “With Lula, against fiscal adjustment.”

Ahead of the runoff, Lula unveiled costly initiatives, including a 15% increase in payments under his flagship welfare program, Bolsa Família, or Family Grant. That measure alone will cost 5.8 billion reais ($1 billion) this year and about 22 billion reais ($3.7 billion) next year, according to Brazilian government figures.

Other measures introduced by Lula’s administration include subsidized credit and debt-relief programs for small businesses and low-income earners, as well as temporary federal fuel tax cuts. The government has also proposed free public transportation on weekends, while Congress has passed legislation shortening the workweek without cutting pay.

Last week, students and left-wing activists protested against the fiscal package on São Paulo’s Brigadeiro Faria Lima Avenue, home to many banks and brokerages, and in Rio de Janeiro’s historic Candelária Square.

Monica de Bolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said that both the hard left and market actors had likely forgotten that Lula — who governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010 before taking office again in 2023 — has consistently shown himself to be what she called a pragmatist.
“Lula hasn't changed. He’s not very ideological when it comes to running the economy,” de Bolle said. “The rally is really a correction of the market's views and expectations.”
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
summary: Canada’s Supreme Court upheld most of a Quebec law banning schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work, affirming the province’s use of a constitutional power to override c...
story: Canada’s Supreme Court upheld most of a Quebec law banning schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work, affirming the province’s use of a constitutional power to override c...

OTTAWA, Ontario -- Canada’s Supreme Court on Friday upheld most of a Quebec law banning public schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work, affirming the province’s constitutional power to override certain rights.
The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, prohibits religious symbols including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses for workers covered by the ban.

The court upheld Quebec’s use of the “notwithstanding clause,” which allows lawmakers to override certain protections in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Canada’s equivalent of the U.S. Bill of Rights. Those include religious freedom and equality rights. Lawmakers must renew the override every five years to keep it in effect.
The justices affirmed that lawmakers can invoke the clause before courts determine whether a law violates those rights.
The court upheld a finding that members of Quebec’s legislature cannot be required to perform their duties with their faces uncovered.
Quebec says the law ensures the separation of religion and government. Opponents say it discriminates against religious minorities, particularly Muslim women wearing headscarves.

“In the 21st century, entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are,” said Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims.
France, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands have full or partial bans on face coverings, including veils worn by some Muslim women.
Quebec’s embrace of secularism grew out of its rejection of the Roman Catholic Church’s once-dominant influence.
The ruling has implications across Canada, where other provinces have used the override to shield laws restricting transgender rights and ordering striking employees back to work.
Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board, which challenged the law, pledged to keep pressing for political change.
“This isn’t the end of the road. This is the end of the legal road,” Ortona said. “We respect the decision of the court, but the advocacy continues.”

title: Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90
summary: An explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan's Kunar province Saturday killed seven people and wounded over 90
story: An explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan's Kunar province Saturday killed seven people and wounded over 90

KABUL, Afghanistan -- An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed seven people and wounded more than 90, the province’s culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.
Up to 15 of the wounded remain in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.
Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.
Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.
In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

title: UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
summary: Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children
story: Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children

LONDON -- Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children.

Andy Burnham made the announcement Tuesday night on the BBC’s “Newsnight” program, saying the panel’s chairman would be “relentless in his pursuit of the facts.” An estimated 22,000 British military personnel witnessed Cold War-era nuclear weapons tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans from 1952 to 1967.
“Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish,” Burnham said in a statement.

Veterans claim Britain’s Ministry of Defense intentionally hid data from blood and urine samples that would demonstrate how they were unwittingly used as test subjects to investigate the impact of nuclear explosions on humans.

Former Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood said in September that he had “inadvertently misled” Parliament in 2018 when he told lawmakers the ministry had been unable to locate any information about such blood testing. He later learned that blood samples were taken throughout the military, although veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses related to radiation exposure were unable to access them.
“This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed,” Ellwood wrote in the Guardian.

Britain has no dedicated compensation program for nuclear veterans, unlike the United States. France, which conducted tests in the South Pacific and in Algeria, has also established a compensation program.

The U.K.’s first atmospheric atomic test took place on Oct. 3, 1952, with the detonation of a plutonium implosion device in the Montebello Islands off Western Australia. The blast made Britain the world’s third nuclear-armed nation, after the United States and the then-Soviet Union.
The U.K. eventually set off dozens of nuclear explosions in Australia and ocean territories in the Pacific, including Kiritimati, formerly known as Christmas Island.

Veterans’ groups say military personnel, many of them conscripts, were exposed to nuclear fallout when they were ordered to fly through mushroom clouds or watch the explosions without protective clothing.
Campaigners are convinced there is a link between the tests and health problems that they, and sometimes their children, suffered later in life.

Burnham said the inquiry would be chaired by Bishop James Jones, who previously led the inquiry into the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, when 97 people were killed in the crush of fans at a match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest.
The panel will release an interim report by next October, the 75th anniversary of the first U.K. nuclear weapons test, Burnham said.
Alan Owen, who co-founded the campaign group LABRATS, described Burnham’s announcement as a “fantastic step forward.’’
Owen, whose father participated in a test on Christmas Island in 1962, said it had taken a lot of work “over many, many years” to reach this point.
“The campaigners have been fighting since 1984,” he said. “We’re just the next lot of campaigners that have come through to get it over the line.”

title: EU leaders seek to agree on a budget deal and a new loan for Ukraine
summary: European Union leaders are struggling to agree on a long-term budget and more money for Ukraine in the shape of a new $49 billion loan
story: European Union leaders are struggling to agree on a long-term budget and more money for Ukraine in the shape of a new $49 billion loan

BRUSSELS -- European Union leaders struggled on Thursday to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree a new $49 billion loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.

At a summit in Brussels, some leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget. Most want extra funds for important new priorities, and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.

“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time there is a series of tasks we must fulfill reliably.”
“The priorities must be a flourishing economy, the internal market must be able to develop its full potential, and we need better defense,” he told reporters.

The new joint spending package is a statement of the EU’s ambitions in the world. It’s small compared to national budgets and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies.
The 2028-2034 plan could amount to between 1% and 1.2% of gross national income, but it appears increasingly likely that the leaders might well miss an end-of-year goal to agree on it.
Germany is one of an important group of so-called net contributors that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, along with Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden, among others.

“The budget needs to be modernized and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said as he arrived for the summit. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”

A large group of countries, led by France and Italy and dubbed the “friends of cohesion,” staunchly defends funds that protect farmers and pay for infrastructure projects in relatively poor member countries, to help bring them up to EU standards.
Agriculture and cohesion policy each make up about a third of the budget.

“Cohesion is about the same level of life in different regions,” said Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, a billionaire. “We don’t have any highway to Austria, unfortunately, and we have to build our hospitals.”

European Council President António Costa, who is chairing a summit that could run into Friday, called on the leaders to approach the debate with an “open mind, a constructive approach and the sense of compromise.”

He said that an agreement is needed “by the end of this year, and for this, we need to reach unanimity.” Costa wants to secure agreement on the budget’s size, how to distribute funds between its priorities, and on ways to raise money from elsewhere.

Last week, he suggested an EU-wide tax on digital services. It would be drawn from online advertising and money that companies make from user data and could amount to 5 billion euros ($5.5 billion) a year.
Failure to reach an agreement now would not be a disaster. The leaders will meet again on Dec. 18-19.

Ukraine is a big part of the budget puzzle. The spending package foresees a 100-billion-euro ($110-billion) envelope for the government in Kyiv over seven years. The leaders must also decide on the new loan, and whether the costs of servicing it should be drawn from the budget.
Earlier this month, Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if there were no “collective commitment” made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception.”

Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. Merz repeated his warning on Thursday and said that “we will talk about this in depth in one-on-one talks.”
But Babiš insisted that the “financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately,” and that the priority for Europe must be the “life of our citizens.”

Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion) to cover most of the Ukrainian government’s needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.
The commission again plans to raise money for the loans on capital markets, with 20 billion euros ($22 billion) earmarked for the economy and 25 billion euros ($27 billion) for the armed forces.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU's plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv “less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war.”

title: Spain's former central bank head chosen as next European Central Bank president
summary: Eurozone leaders have chosen a new president of the European Central Bank
story: Eurozone leaders have chosen a new president of the European Central Bank

BRUSSELS -- European leaders have chosen the former head of Spain’s central bank, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank as the key EU institution confronts inflation driven by the war in Iran and worries about high government debt and borrowing costs in Europe.
Leaders from the 21 European member countries that use the euro also filled two other top posts at the ECB, which decides borrowing costs for the 359 million people in the eurozone.
European Council President António Costa said on X that the body agreed on the three appointments at a summit in Brussels.
De Cos’ nomination still must pass review by the European Parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but those steps are formalities.

The appointment puts an experienced central banker with a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus in charge at a time when several European governments are struggling with heavy debt loads and rising borrowing costs. De Cos, 55, served on the ECB rate-setting council from 2018 to 2024 through his post as head of the Spanish central bank.
A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.
De Cos won out over another main contender for the post, former Netherlands central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favors higher rates to ward off inflation.

In 2020, De Cos joined the council majority under Lagarde in backing 1.85 trillion euros ($2 trillion) in pandemic stimulus to keep rates low and support the economy during widespread closures and travel restrictions. De Cos praised the massive pandemic stimulus in a speech that year, saying it “has been clearly successful in curbing financial market deterioration in all euro area countries” as well as lowering borrowing costs for eurozone governments and corporations.

Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner said that “especially against the backdrop of rising government debt in numerous countries ... many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president.” France in particular is struggling with high debt and burdensome interest costs. However, with inflation at 4%, above the bank’s target of 2%, the bank could still raise rates at its Dec. 17 meeting presided over by Lagarde.

In some circumstances the ECB can intervene to lower borrowing costs for governments hit by market turmoil it views as unjustified, but analysts say the central bank is unlikely to bail out French politicians who can’t agree on how to reduce their deficit.
De Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, an international organization of central banks in Basel, Switzerland.

Lagarde, 70, said Oct. 30 that she would resign on Feb. 7, nine months before the end of her eight-year term. She has said she decided to resign early to be able to speak more freely about matters not related to monetary policy, but her resignation also enables EU leaders to choose a successor while pro-EU French President Emmanuel Macron is still in office and guards against the possibility that right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen might win the election and influence the choice.

The eurozone leaders also filled two upcoming vacancies on the bank’s six-member executive board, which runs the bank’s day-to-day operations. They chose German economist Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, to replace Philip Lane, whose term ends in May. Lane held the influential post of chief economist, proposing rate moves for the full governing council to consider and decide upon.
They also chose Laurence Boone, head of corporate and investment banking in France for Spanish bank Santander, for a seat being vacated by Germany’s Isabel Schnabel, who is resigning in January.

The ECB sets interest benchmarks for the 21 countries that use the euro, influencing borrowing rates throughout the economy: everything from overnight loans between banks to credit cards, home mortgages and government bonds.
Lower rates can spur a slumping economy, while higher ones restrain inflation when it’s above the bank’s target of 2% annually.

The bank’s ability to act swiftly — in contrast to the often drawn-out negotiations among the 27 European Union national governments — has given it a leading role in combating Europe-wide crises such as the pandemic and the peak period of the eurozone’s debt crisis in 2010-12.
The president leads meetings of the bank’s rate-setting council at its headquarters in Frankfurt.

Lagarde is regarded as having steered a pragmatic middle course based on building consensus among the national bank heads who sit on the rate-setting council. She resisted being pigeonholed as a hawk or a dove, saying she was an “owl,” the bird associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology.
She congratulated De Cos on Thursday, praising his “intellect, warmth and good humour” in a note posted online.
“If he is confirmed, I know these qualities will serve him well as ECB President,” she said.
McHugh reported from Frankfurt, Germany.

title: Asian shares mostly rise ahead of Wall Street's reopening after the Thanksgiving holiday
summary: Asian shares are mostly higher, following a market holiday on Wall Street for Thanksgiving
story: Asian shares are mostly higher, following a market holiday on Wall Street for Thanksgiving
TOKYO -- Asian shares were mostly higher in early Friday trading, following a market holiday on Wall Street for Thanksgiving.

Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 added 0.7% to 57,919.30 in morning trading. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.4% to 8,800.50. South Korea's Kospi surged 2.2% to 4,812.65. Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged up 0.4% to 22,310.11, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.1% to 3,473.40.
Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence has been pushing benchmarks higher, despite some profit-taking that has kept those gains in check.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron and Advantest Corp. stocks dropped in morning trading but quickly recovered the declines, underlining the continuing appeal of issues in computer chips and AI.
Investors are also closely watching for the possible damage to the region from U.S. tariff hikes planned on China, Japan, the European Union and other trading partners.
U.S. markets will reopen later Friday for a holiday-shortened session.

In energy trading, oil prices have been volatile lately because of uncertainty over tensions in the Middle East. Benchmark U.S. crude rose 2.09% to $85.43 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, slipped 0.29% to $96.29 a barrel.
In currency trading, the U.S. dollar inched up to 159.25 Japanese yen from 159.23 yen. The euro cost $1.0967, down from $1.0975.
AP Business Writer Chan Ho-Him contributed to this report.

title: Norwegian budget airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy after halting flights
summary: A Norwegian budget airline has filed for bankruptcy after halting flights and ticket sales
story: A Norwegian budget airline has filed for bankruptcy after halting flights and ticket sales

ARENDAL, Norway -- Norwegian budget airline Norse Atlantic Airways filed for bankruptcy Friday, a day after halting flights and ticket sales. The airline, which was founded in 2021, offered cheap flights from Europe to Asia, South Africa and the United States.

The airline's board of directors decided to file a bankruptcy petition after it "concluded that there is no longer a basis for continued operations,” parent company Norse Atlantic ASA said in a statement.

The decision to enter an insolvency process came almost seven months after U.S. budget carrier Spirit Airlines ceased operations during bankruptcy proceedings and went out of business. Higher jet fuel costs during the U.S. war with Iran have put significant financial stress on smaller airlines that weren't in strong shape at the beginning of the year.
“Despite extensive efforts, the company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs,” Norse Atlantic ASA said.

CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement that the company hoped to find a solution that would allow it and another airline subsidiary, Norse Atlantic U.K., to keep operating. All of the U.K. airline's flights were canceled Friday.

The Norse Atlantic website told passengers with tickets for canceled flights not to go to the airport unless they had already booked with another airline. The website advised customers to contact travel agents, travel insurance companies and credit card issuers about alternative travel arrangements and refunds.

“We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home,” the website said, adding that customer service is no longer available by phone, email, chatbot or on social media.
Airline industry bosses have warned travelers about rising jet fuel costs.
The CEO of Ryanair, Europe's biggest carrier, said earlier this month he expects European airfares to go up by as much as 20% next year as the Middle East conflict continues.

title: Republicans rethink tariffs, giving Democrats an opening to challenge Trump
summary: Democrats are looking to blunt some of President Donald Trump's tariffs as they take control of Congress
story: Democrats are looking to blunt some of President Donald Trump's tariffs as they take control of Congress
WASHINGTON -- Democrats hoping to blunt President Donald Trump's tariffs when they retake control of Congress may find partners in an unlikely place: among his fellow Republicans.

After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda. The administration proposed new tariffs on Wednesday targeting China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
Whether Republicans actually buck Trump on tariffs could signal if election losses and the president's lame duck status shake what has been nearly lockstep fealty to him.

In interviews with more than a half dozen congressional Republicans since the election, most said they were open to reviewing tariffs, at least on a case-by-case basis. They expressed a desire for predictability and said Congress could reclaim its constitutional authority over tariffs. They were reluctant, however, to broadly curb the president's own tariff powers and acknowledged Trump could veto any repeal legislation.
But for Democrats eager to score some early bipartisan wins, the mere willingness of Republicans to revisit some tariffs could create an opening.

“A rethink is indeed in order,” said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. “I’ll be a bipartisan voice for making sure we have the most consumer friendly tariff approaches and I think there will be a whole lot of receptivity within the administration to my approach.”
Rep. Michael Guest, R-Miss., said “there may be some areas that I would agree with the Democrats.”

“I would personally be opposed to just a blanket restriction on the president’s ability to impose tariffs,” he said. “But I would be willing to look at it on a case-by-case basis based on what the Democrats may bring forward.”

Trump has made tariffs a defining feature of his second term, calling himself “Mr. Tariff” as he imposed broad levies on imports from allies and adversaries alike. He insists tariffs will revive American manufacturing and strengthen the U.S. economy, though there is scant evidence they have accomplished those goals. Tariffs often increase costs for consumers in the form of a tax.
His aggressive approach marks a sharp departure from the free-trade orthodoxy long embraced by Republicans before Trump moved the party in a more protectionist direction.
If Democrats and Republicans were to unite on the issue, tariffs on Canada could emerge as an early test. Previous repeal efforts won support from a handful of Republicans.

Democrats, including incoming Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden of Oregon, have already identified the Canada tariffs as a top target. And after the levies spurred retribution from Canada, adding to the GOP's election challenges this year, there could be an incentive for more Republicans to join the effort.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who is up for reelection in 2028 and was not among the Republicans who backed the Canada repeal legislation, said he distinguished the Canadian tariffs from levies on other countries like China, which he supports.
“Tariffs with respect to Canada don't make sense to me,” he said.

Young, who also backs some tariffs on China and faces reelection in 2028, made several social media posts in the days after the election saying voters were “rightly focused on the cost of living.” He said one reason for high costs was a tariff structure that is “overly broad, and as a result, it is negatively affecting too many American factory floors, farms, small businesses, and family budgets.”
In the interview, he said tariffs should be “predictable” and focused on goals such as “reshoring strategic goods or applying leverage on trading partners to liberalize their own markets.”

When asked about the Canadian levies, he said he was open to different approaches. But he said he preferred that the administration consult with Congress as part of negotiations to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the regional trade pact known as USMCA.
“The USMCA process seems to work if Congress is actively involved and not patted on the head,” he said.

Republicans are taking an increasingly assertive posture toward the administration. Since the election, Republicans have expressed skepticism about a sudden $50 billion request for the nation's air travel system after air traffic was briefly shuttered. They've pressed for more details about widespread tech outages and criticized Trump's intervention in returning Jensen Huang to the helm of Nvidia.
That bullishness could extend to tariffs.

“Congress has, over a period of years, recognized that Congress, by itself, has a real difficult time making a tariff and then authorizing and enacting it,” said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota. “So they’ve given authorities to the executive branch over a period of years. Some of that has cascaded.”
“There’s nothing wrong,” he added, “with Congress taking a second look at whether or not those authorities should be withdrawn, modified, at least reconsidered, or limited.”
Still, reversal of the tariffs is far from guaranteed. For one, Republicans are still sorting through the lessons of this year's elections.
Rep. Steve Womack, an Arkansas Republican who said he would consider tariff repeals on a case-by-case basis, said he thought the levies “have played a role in some of the affordability issues.”
“I have producers in my district that lament the fact that they’re paying higher for goods that can’t be sourced domestically,” he said.
But Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., expressed concern the party may overcorrect.

“I bet a lot of my Republican colleagues will be happy to join Democrats and get rid of a bunch of them, which makes me just a little nervous that it’s going to be a dramatic pendulum swing,” he said.

White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said “this administration is committed to rebuilding the American communities left behind by previous administrations and will continue fighting to lower costs, expand opportunity, and make life more affordable for hardworking American families.”
Republican voters appeared mixed on the issue.

About half of voters who backed the Republican candidate in their local U.S. House race said Trump's tariff policies had helped the national economy, according to The AP Voter Poll. About 3 in 10 said they hurt the U.S. economy, and about one-quarter said those policies didn’t make a difference.
When it came to their local economy, fewer saw a benefit.

About 3 in 10 said Trump’s tariff policies helped the economy in their area, and roughly one-quarter said it had hurt it. About 4 in 10 said those policies hadn’t impacted the economy in their local area.
Democrats, meanwhile, are contemplating a more sweeping challenge to Trump’s trade policies.
Wyden said that if Democrats were successful in winning Republican support to repeal Canadian tariffs, “we'll have some momentum for going after other tariffs.”
His counterpart in the House, incoming Ways and Means Committee Chairman Richard Neal, said rescinding tariffs on Canada “might be a good starting point.”
“But I think taking up the tariffs discussion in totality is really important, largely because the way they've been used in a punitive manner,” he said.
But no hurdle is as formidable as Trump's veto, which would require support from 67 senators to overturn, a steep challenge even with Democrats poised to enjoy a 56-seat majority.
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., a fervent tariff opponent, said he would back repeals but they would have to be attached to must-pass pieces of legislation for them to have any hope.
“On its own, he'll just veto it,” he said.

title: How moneymaxxing can help you manage your finances
summary: A new social media trend called moneymaxxing is encouraging people to focus on their finances
story: A new social media trend called moneymaxxing is encouraging people to focus on their finances

NEW YORK -- Social media trends can often be bad for your budget. But a new one called moneymaxxing is inspiring people to focus on their finances, learn how they’re spending their money and improve their financial habits.

“Maxxing” is used on social media to refer to someone going all out for a goal. The best-known version is looksmaxxing, which focuses on improving your physical appearance. Moneymaxxing focuses on making the most of your money from getting a side gig to paying off high-interest debt or saving for a trip.

“I think what moneymaxxing is getting at is being responsible with your money and trying to maximize what it is that you have,” said Bennett Pardue, financial adviser at New Canaan Group with Equitable Advisors.

Moneymaxxing has joined other popular budgeting trends such as loud budgeting, which encourages being vocal about your money goals, or the no-buy year in encouraging people to embrace responsible management of their finances. This month, Dictionary.com named maxxing their word of the year due to its popularity in internet culture.
Could moneymaxxing help you get your finances on track? Here are some expert recommendations:

The first step toward reaching your moneymaxxing goals is to track your income and expenses. It’s crucial to know where all of your money is going in order to know how you can maximize your spending, said Myranda Fabian, a certified financial planner with Plante Moran Financial Advisors.

“Take some time to review a month or two of transactions, identify one meaningful opportunity, whether that’s to pay off high-interest rate debt or direct some of your paychecks to the emergency reserve, and then start to automate one positive change,” Fabian said.

Rather than reviewing your expenses in one sitting, which can be overwhelming, Fabian recommends that you divide your review into small tasks. You can start by setting aside 45 minutes one weekend to check your income and how much savings you have. Another day, you can review your expenses and debt. Dividing your money review can help it feel less daunting, Fabian said.
Tracking your finances looks different for everyone; some might prefer using apps while others like keeping it simple by writing down their expenses on paper.

Melanie Ho, 27, recently decided to take a leap of faith and leave her job as a speech therapy assistant to pursue content creation full-time. But to make it sustainable, she needed to make it profitable. Moneymaxxing became a challenge to earn more money.
She likes the simplicity of a spreadsheet, so for her, the best way to keep her budget up to date is to use Google Sheets.

If your income isn't changing, saving on some items can be the best path to achieve your financial goals. Rather than focusing on small expenses, Pardue recommends that you focus on reducing larger expenses. An example could be comparing auto insurance prices to find the best deal.
Big expenses "can really move the needle for you; don’t trip over dollars to get pennies,” Pardue said.
Ho lives in a small studio apartment in Los Angeles. While she could afford to move to a new apartment, she's decided to stay where she is and save on rent so she can prioritize other expenses.

As you cut expenses, it’s important to not completely deprive yourself of spending money on things that bring you enjoyment, recommended Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. Being too extreme when it comes to cutting expenses can make your journey unsustainable.
A key element of moneymaxxing is to lower your debt. Fabian recommends you list your debt from highest interest rate to lowest and prioritize tackling high-interest debt.

“When it comes to paying down the debt, make sure you’re doing the minimum payments, but to the extent you can add more and wipe out that double-digit interest rate debt, I think that would be really powerful,” Fabian said.

Saving on unnecessary expenses and directing your money to prioritize paying down high-interest debt can set you in a better financial position. However, you want to make sure you have a plan to avoid acquiring more debt in the future, Pardue said.

Having a financial goal in mind while you make changes to your finances can help you stay on target. However, it's important to set attainable goals, recommended Jesse Mecham, founder of YNAB, a budgeting app. Setting goals that are realistic in relation to your lifestyle and budget can be the best way to approach moneymaxxing.
“It doesn’t have to be an all out sprint," Mecham said. “Maybe it can just be a doable pace.”
Ho's current goal is to save money to travel more. Ho has separate funds for specific financial goals in a high-yield savings account, including one for travel and one for rent.
While not specifically a part of the moneymaxxing trend, Mecham encourages people who are participating in this trend to take a curious approach to planning their finances.
“I wish so bad that people could be money curious. Like, what is my view of money? What is my relationship with money? How do I feel when saving this money?” Mecham said.
