title: Global stocks are mixed as AI shares tumble after a retreat on Wall Street
summary: World stocks are mixed Wednesday after another wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence hit Wall Street
story: World stocks are mixed Wednesday after another wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence hit Wall Street
HONG KONG -- World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street.
U.S. futures slipped and oil prices also fell.
Relief over Nvidia’s decision to restore Jensen Huang as its CEO has been tempered by questions over the chipmaker's corporate governance and President Donald Trump’s influence.
In early European trading, Germany’s DAX was up 0.1% to 25,046.66. In Paris, the CAC 40 rose 1% to 8,120.72, while Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.5% to 10,515.74.
The future for the S&P 500 was 0.8% lower, while the future for the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%.
In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 5% as AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. sank 3.6%. Chip designer Mediatek plunged 10%.
In South Korea, the Kospi lost 6.2% to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9%. SK Hynix plummeted 11.1%.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8% to 57,011.62. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8% and semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.2%.
The Hang Seng in Hong Kong slipped 1.1% to 21,966.01. The Shanghai Composite index declined 2% to 3,476.47, falling to its lowest level in more than a year.
The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners. China recorded a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged 0.4% lower to 8,692.40. The consumer price index in October rose to 4.9% from a year earlier, topping expectations. That could put pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates.
India’s Sensex rose 1.5%.

On Tuesday, stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower after a surge the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy.
The S&P 500 fell 0.5% to its eighth loss in the last nine days. The Nasdaq composite shed 1.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.9%.
They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month.

The surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO, announced Monday, does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry. But it does not settle deeper concerns such as whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to justify massive investments in data centers.

High interest rates are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised the possibility of more regulation for AI, potentially slowing construction of data centers.
Nvidia fell 5.9% a day after soaring 31.5% to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts.

And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5% to drop below $83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as $115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype.

Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed 2.4% to $88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between $72 and $114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Early Wednesday, Brent was down 1.5% to $87.43 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped 1.8% to $80.56 per barrel.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.42 Japanese yen from 159.26 yen. The euro slid to $1.0944 from $1.0966.

title: China and other US trading partners hit back at Trump's new tariff plans
summary: China, Japan, and other U.S. trading partners have protested planned tariff hikes by President Donald Trump's administration
story: China, Japan, and other U.S. trading partners have protested planned tariff hikes by President Donald Trump's administration
HONG KONG -- China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by the Trump administration and hit back Thursday at allegations they have excess manufacturing capacity.

The new tariffs, which are likely to take effect early next year, were announced Wednesday. They are intended to help reinstate tariffs for most of the economies after the Supreme Court ruling in February struck down most of U.S. President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs implemented last year.

The new import duties followed a monthslong Section 301 probe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he determined that practices of the 14 economies relating to excess capacity and production in manufacturing are “unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.”

China, one of the biggest trading partners of the U.S., is facing a 20% tariff. It slammed the notion of “overcapacity” as a “false premise.” The tariffs could double to 40% if the U.S. finds China not engaging adequately.

“China opposes its use as a pretext for political maneuvering,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said at a regular press briefing. “Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests.”
Beijing will take “necessary measures to defend its legitimate rights and interests,” he added.

The U.S. and China have extended by two months a trade truce that’s set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. The two countries also have agreed on tariff cuts on reciprocal lists of non-sensitive products worth about $60 billion in total.
Japan faces new U.S. tariffs of up to 15%. The Japanese government said it protested to Washington.
“Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a regular news conference Thursday.
“It is regrettable that the United States announced the proposed measures targeting Japan, and we have conveyed our position to the U.S. side.”
Singapore, due to be hit by an up to 20% tariff rate, said it was “very disappointed” with the U.S. proposal.
“Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidize manufacturing for export,” its Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said in a statement.

Malaysia said it “does not have excess capacity in its manufacturing sectors that distorts or disrupts global markets,” adding that it will continue to engage and consult with the United States. Vietnam, facing tariffs of up to 35%, said it's working with the U.S. on a trade deal.
Analysts say the 14 economies targeted by the Trump administration together account for roughly half of the global economy.

The latest U.S. tariffs are not as alarming as they look, said Stephen Brown, a chief economist with Capital Economics, as they are essentially broadly replacing, rather than adding to, earlier announced U.S. tariffs related to forced labor allegations announced in July.
Still, the new tariffs will likely help push prices higher and may “keep core goods inflation firm into next year,” he said in a commentary.
In Thailand, government spokesperson Lalida Persvivatana said Thursday that the latest U.S. proposal, capping tariffs at 18%, was more favorable than expected.

“The government will continue to pursue negotiations to secure competitive tariff levels and additional exemptions for Thai products, with the main goal of protecting Thailand’s export markets,” Persvivatana added.

The 27-nation European Union, which could be hit by a potential 15% tariff rate by the U.S., rejected “the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and pointed to the lack of joint action by the EU and the U.S.

Associated Press journalists Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Mari Yamaguchi and Mayuko Ono in Tokyo, Aniruddha Ghosal in Hanoi, Vietnam, Jintamas Saksornchai in Bangkok and Lorne Cook and Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report.

title: As Google threatens to cut schools' search access, Los Angeles blocks AI features
summary: Los Angeles school officials have disabled AI-generated summaries in Google searches on school-issued devices
story: Los Angeles school officials have disabled AI-generated summaries in Google searches on school-issued devices

School districts are taking steps to block Google's artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America's classrooms.

In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes Los Angeles Unified the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.

The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.
The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee on Friday, Nov. 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.
“It was the talk of the playground,” Lee said.

Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America’s classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google’s suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework and communication among students and teachers.

But concerns about AI's impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country’s two largest school districts — New York and LA — announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it's not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.

LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are “age-appropriate and safe.” It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.

Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.

“We’re thrilled LAUSD did this,” said Lee. “AI is seeping into everything. It’s dangerous. It’s hurting learning. And it’s a corporate overreach into public schools. It’s Big Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone’s consent.”
Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports.
Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cellphones and screentime and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.

The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That's when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and LA schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.

Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.
Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.

While the blog post does not explicitly say search can’t be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” If schools ban AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The integration of AI in search isn't new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.

Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company's leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features “without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole.”

“The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we’re punishing schools for not using AI,” the petition said. “Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products.”

Google says it hears parents' and teachers' concerns about students using AI to “shortcut learning” and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want — the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024 — is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students’ access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.

Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot “guided learning” tool that walks students “step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers.”
“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” the company said in a statement.

Currently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk users through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.

LA schools had already disabled Google’s AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.

“We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite,” Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google’s products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district’s priorities.
“We have choices,” Kelanic said. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.”

title: Judge declines to issue a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda
summary: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Donald Trump
story: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Donald Trump

NEW YORK -- A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., said the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown a likelihood to prevail in the case. It had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president’s campaign message just weeks before November’s midterm elections. Her ruling comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.
In her ruling, she noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away.

“But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone,” she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.
“At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded,” AliKhan wrote.

Democrats sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads that were paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. In court papers, the DNC challenged at least 11 government-created ads that either aired on TV or appeared on Trump administration social media feeds.

Some of the ads glorified the president with highlight reels of scenic speeches, promoted his tax cuts and emphasized support for law enforcement. One of them repurposed a clip that had been used by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, showing him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.”

A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, said in a statement that the organization was “disappointed” by the judge’s decision, adding that the DNC “will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration’s attempts to undermine our democracy.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites.
But in her latest ruling, AliKhan declined to issue a preliminary injunction against the ads.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don’t try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued.

Ahead of the ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed.

title: Necessities join gifts in Black Friday shopping carts as AI and higher costs steer spending
summary: Black Friday comes with a few twists this year
story: Black Friday comes with a few twists this year

NEW YORK -- Stocking up on discounted shampoo while grabbing a flat-screen TV and several Lego sets for under the tree. Making a holiday list, comparing style options and delivery dates, and finding the best price with help from artificial intelligence.

Black Friday, the retail industry's version of the Super Bowl, comes with a few twists this year. Brands and stores have promoted steep discounts online and in stores all month, making the day once considered the holiday shopping season's unofficial kickoff seem more like the fourth quarter of a football game.

AI-powered shopping tools and cost concerns fueled by the U.S. war with Iran also are influencing how, where, when and on what consumers are spending, according to industry analysts. When Black Friday deals are available, basics like T-shirts, toiletries and pet supplies are going into shopping carts along with gift items, analysts said.

“Usually, when you think of holiday shopping, it’s premium handbags and jewelry and those types of items, but we’re fast seeing shoppers also use this season to stock up on the essentials,” said Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at technology company Adobe.

Black Friday still has enough die-hard traditionalists to make it the biggest day of the year for retail foot traffic, according to Sensormatic Solutions, which tracks activity at physical stores. Retailers large and small view the occasion as an opportunity to improve their year-end footing and to attract new customers.
“Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping,” Grant Gustafson, Sensormatic's head of retail consulting and analytics, said.

This year's holiday shopping takes place in a U.S. economic environment marked by lackluster consumer confidence, high inflation and shoppers who have kept spending regardless. Foot traffic data show Americans are visiting stores less often this season, and their purchases appear more intentional than impulse-driven, Gustafson said.
Here are some of the emerging trends for Black Friday and holiday shopping overall in 2026:

Analysts and economists closely scrutinize retail spending on the five days that begin with Thanksgiving Day and end on Cyber Monday for clues about consumers’ financial staying power and retailers’ prospects during the crucial holiday period and into the new year.
The good news for retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as U.S. gasoline prices continued a steady decline.

Online sales have beaten expectations so far this holiday season, according to Adobe Digital Insights, a research and market intelligence program that Pandya leads. U.S. consumers spent $82.5 billion online from Nov. 1 to Nov. 22, 9.1% more than during the same three weeks last year.

Adobe predicted that U.S. online sales for the holiday shopping season that runs through Dec. 31 would grow by 6.7% and total $275.1 billion. The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half of the 4.1% sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast U.S. shoppers collectively spending $1.01 trillion.
U.S. retailers have broadly held the line on prices instead of making big increases across the board, and offered solid discounts that persuaded customers to shop earlier, industry analysts said.

Technology company Salesforce, which tracks digital spending at a range of retailers, including grocery stores, said November discounts are 8% bigger than last year. The seasonal promotions pushed average selling prices of physical merchandise 1% below last November's prices, Salesforce said.

Caila Schwartz, a retail and consumer insights leader at Salesforce, said the discounts encouraged shoppers to add 2% more items in their online carts from Oct. 1 through Nov. 18 compared with the same period a year ago.
“In the last several years, a lot of the (sales) gains have been from higher prices,” she said. “This is not what we are seeing this year.”
While retailers offered discounts earlier this year, with some starting before Halloween, Adobe's Pandya said the best prices still are likely to land on Thanksgiving and Black Friday.
For example, discounts on TVs are expected to average 23% on Friday compared with 11% during the first 22 days of the month.

Self-gifting is an established holiday shopping trend. Black Friday's expansion to a multiweek event also has some consumers filling their cupboards with toiletries and clothes they would typically buy at another time, according to analysts.

Online sales of personal hygiene products were 40% higher from Nov. 1 through Nov. 22 compared to the October average, according to Adobe's data. Sales of household cleaning products spiked 33% and clothing basics by 27% during the same time frame, Adobe said.

The deepest holiday discounts are expected on clothing, home goods, and health and beauty, Salesforce said. The company said it expected health and beauty products to average 33% off between Tuesday and next Monday.
“It's not just a moment where shoppers are buying gifts,” Schwartz said. “They’re also buying things that they need, and so that’s going to help drive up a lot of the spend.”
Consumers are using AI-assisted tools to help them compare products and prices, particularly as inflation and paying more for gasoline has made them more attuned to price tags, Pandya said.
A belief that e-commerce sites will offer “the best value possible” has contributed to shoppers doing more of their holiday period spending online instead of in stores, he said.
Traffic to online retail sites from links in AI-powered tools more than doubled this month compared with November 2025, Adobe said.

Walmart CEO John Furner told analysts during an earnings call this month that customers who employed Sparky, the retailer's AI shopping assistant, spent 40% more per order on average than shoppers who did not use the tool.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told analysts last month that U.S. shoppers using its AI assistant Alexa spend 50% more than those who don’t.

title: Average US 30-year mortgage rate eases to 7.21%, not far from 2026 high
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month
The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. fell to 7.21% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Wednesday. One year ago, it was at 6.23%.
The weekly average rate has been above 7% since late September. As recently as Oct. 15, it was at 7.4%, its highest level in nearly three years.

Elevated mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power at a time when affordability challenges continue to sideline many aspiring homeowners.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also eased this week. That average rate fell to 6.54% from 6.66% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.51%.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.

That yield was at 4.81% at midday on the bond market Wednesday. It's eased in recent days, falling below 5%, amid a flight to safety by many investors amid a stock market swoon fueled by a sharp pullback in artificial intelligence stocks. When demand for U.S. government bonds rises, that tends to pull their yield lower.
Mortgage rates have been climbing overall since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher.

In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. Going by the latest average rate, a home shopper financing a $400,000 home loan is now paying roughly $325 more a month than when the rate was just below 6%.
Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average.

The upward march in mortgage rates this year has weighed on home sales, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged.

Data pointing to accelerating inflation have raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The central bank kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September.
“The debate is not whether the Fed hikes in December, but how aggressively it moves,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com.
While the Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately influence rates on home loans.

title: Martha Ford, former Lions owner with link to auto giants, dies at 101
summary: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died
story: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died
Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry's most iconic families and later took over the NFL's Detroit Lions, has died. She was 101.
The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given.
Ford was a granddaughter of tire magnate Harvey Firestone, and her husband, William Clay Ford Sr., was Henry Ford's grandson. He also owned the Lions for a half-century before his death in 2014.

Martha Ford then took over his controlling interest in the team, keeping it within the family. Although she seldom spoke to reporters or commented publicly on the direction of the franchise, her influence was felt. She was in charge of the team from 2014 until 2020, when she turned the Lions over to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp.

The Lions made the playoffs in 2014, but lost seven of their first eight games the following season. In November 2015, the team fired its president and general manager in a midseason shakeup. When she announced the changes, Ford told fans the franchise intended to “identify and hire the very best leadership in order to produce a consistently, winning football team.”
The Lions played better down the stretch that season, and after hiring Bob Quinn as their new general manager, they returned to the playoffs a year later.

“Martha was special," NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement. "She cared so deeply about her family, the players, their fans, and the city of Detroit. She was committed to making the Lions - and the game of football - better. Martha and her husband, William Clay Ford, led the franchise with dignity and integrity. We will miss her kindness and sweet sense of humor. We extend our deepest condolences to her children, the entire Ford family, and the Lions’ organization.”
Born Sept. 16, 1925, in Akron, Ohio, Martha Parke Firestone graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the next year.

Their wedding received a huge amount of coverage — looking back in 2014, the Akron Beacon Journal described it as “Akron’s royal wedding” — and the marriage joined two families that already had a long history.

Harvey Firestone, the founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., was a close friend of Ford Motor Co. founder Henry Ford. Ford chose Firestone to supply the tires for the first Model T in 1906. The two men often went on long camping trips together, sometimes accompanied by their friend Thomas Edison.

Martha and William Clay Ford had three daughters and a son. Their son, William Clay Ford Jr., is the current executive chairman of Ford Motor Co.. In 2001, Bridgestone/Firestone and Ford severed their nearly 100-year relationship because of a dispute over a series of deadly tire failures on the Ford Explorer.
Sheila Ford Hamp is the Lions’ principal owner and chairman.

William Clay Ford’s first full season leading the Lions was in 1964, seven years after they won an NFL title. Since that 1957 championship, the franchise has won playoff games in 1992 and 2023 and has not played in the Super Bowl.

Although Martha Ford kept a low profile, the shakeup in the middle of the 2015 season was a sign that she was more than willing to bring about change in an effort to reverse the team’s fortunes. Then-coach Jim Caldwell said she was very much a presence within the organization.

“I think visible ownership is great, and Mrs. Ford does it extremely well,” Caldwell said in 2015. “She’s there before games and she’s there after games, and I think guys enjoy that part of it. She comes to practice and things of that nature, so it’s been fun.”
Even at 101, she attended games, including a win over the Minnesota Vikings earlier this month.

Martha Ford also made an impact in the Detroit community. She was an officer on the board for Detroit Lions Charities and on the board of the Henry Ford Health System. Martha and William Clay Ford were credited with helping establish the Maplegrove Center, a substance abuse treatment facility in West Bloomfield.
In 2017, Forbes estimated Martha Ford’s net worth at more than $1.4 billion. She survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren, and 17 great-grandchildren.
See AP’s full NFL coverage here

title: Puerto Rico's Supreme Court cancels a key power contract and many wonder what's next
summary: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy, following a contentious legal fight with the private power company
story: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy, following a contentious legal fight with the private power company

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a contentious legal fight with the private power company.

The 5-4 ruling of more than 200 pages, made public on Wednesday, plunges the island into further uncertainty as many wonder who will take over from Luma while power outages persist across the U.S. territory and crews continue to repair the grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.
Puerto Rico’s government had sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Gov. Jenniffer González to cancel the contract.

The court awarded one year for officials to figure out their next steps. González said her administration would seek a new company and that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority.

She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions" and “unnecessary outages,” asserting they have enough money to provide proper service as she accused them of lacking diligence and driving the cost of electricity in the U.S. territory to a record high.
“You have seen the substations on fire,” she said. “They have not yet been able to explain why.”
As the governor spoke, a federal control board that oversees the island's finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of service.

“The Puerto Rican government's decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there's no “clear plan or successor company in place.”
González rejected those concerns: “There will be no chaos."
Puerto Rico's Association of Industries said it was worried that the ruling could erode the confidence of private investors, while dissenting judges voiced their concerns in sharply worded decisions.
Judge Rafael L. Martínez Torres warned that “collateral consequences” of ending the contract “had to be considered, given their potential monumental impact.”

Judge Ángel Colón Pérez asserted that the ruling in favor of the cancellation stemmed from “an excessive eagerness to satisfy a capricious request from the leader currently in power," an apparent reference to the governor.
One judge referenced and rejected recent allegations that Supreme Court judges were pressured or swayed.

"We do not bow to external pressures, we do not yield to intimidation, nor do we allow smear campaigns to influence the exercise of our judicial function," wrote Judge Roberto Feliberti Cintrón, who was part of the majority vote. “Our obligation is to the Law, Justice, the People, and our conscience.”
Luma also commented on the allegations.

"In light of the serious allegations that have been raised publicly regarding attempts to influence the Court, we reiterate our call for an immediate, rigorous, and transparent investigation,” it said.

Puerto Rico’s government had awarded a multimillion-dollar contract to Luma, which took over the transmission and distribution of power on the island in June 2021. It inherited infrastructure that was crumbling after decades of neglect and mismanagement under Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority.
The company said in a statement Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives.”

“We remain concerned about the potential impact of this decision on ongoing efforts to strengthen and modernize Puerto Rico’s electric grid,” Luma said. “This matter goes beyond a contractual dispute. It has significant implications for the provision of an essential electric service, public safety, and Puerto Rico’s energy future.”
Luma is a consortium made up of Calgary, Alberta-based Atco and Quanta Services Inc. of Houston.

When the lawsuit was filed in December 2025, González said Luma had nearly $11 billion in federal funds at its disposal to rebuild the grid, but that it has only been able to recover some $550 million in reimbursements from the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency.

When the lawsuit was filed, she said, “Despite the operator’s expectations and representations, the electrical system has not improved with the speed, consistency or effectiveness that Puerto Rico deserves and that LUMA promised and lied to us about.”

Puerto Rico’s government has two main agreements with Luma: one for operation and maintenance, and a supplemental deal that was needed because the state-owned Electric Power Authority had not yet completed a debt restructuring process. The island's power company remains mired in that process.
Both deals were set to expire in November 2022, prompting the government to extend the supplemental agreement via an extension letter.
González has said that the letter granted LUMA indefinite control, and that the extension granted was “in violation of the law and the principles of sound public administration.”
The ongoing outages have also been blamed on Genera PR, a private company that oversees the generation of power on the island.

title: After 3 decades, Essence Music Festival bidding farewell to New Orleans
summary: A fixture in New Orleans for over 30 years is leaving the Big Easy
story: A fixture in New Orleans for over 30 years is leaving the Big Easy
The Essence Festival of Culture, a fixture in New Orleans that has celebrated Black American culture for more than 30 years, is leaving the Big Easy.

Festival organizers and Essence Communications, which founded the annual event, announced Tuesday across their social media platforms that Essence Fest will relocate next year. The statement did not give a reason for the decision or mention where the festival was moving to. It mostly expressed gratitude to the city and its residents for helping grow the event over the years.
“You didn't simply host us. You embraced us,” the statement said. “And in doing so, you helped shape one of the most beautiful celebrations of Black culture in the world.”

The multiday festival takes place around the Fourth of July weekend and draws major musical acts. Usher, Megan Thee Stallion and Janet Jackson are among the many performers who have headlined in recent years.

On the same day of the Essence announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on Dec. 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to Black American culture.

“Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country’s top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that 1) realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw,” Moreno said in a social media video. “We need to make sure that there’s widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses.”

The Essence Festival was launched in 1995 as the Essence Music Festival when Essence magazine staged a concert event in New Orleans to mark the publication's 25th anniversary. The magazine was acquired by Time Inc. in the early 2000s before becoming Black-owned again in 2018 when the founder of Sundial Brands purchased it. It's part of Essence Communications, a media company that includes digital and video content.

The festival has also become a political draw with panels focused on politics and voter mobilization. Politicians, both Black and white, who are in the middle of big campaigns have made Essence Fest a stop. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris spoke there in 2024 during the presidential campaign.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, founder and president of National Action Network, has participated in every festival since it began in 1995. The civil rights leader said he was saddened that such a cultural institution was leaving New Orleans but pledged continued support.
“My commitment to ESSENCE is not contingent on its geography," Sharpton said in a statement Wednesday. "Wherever the Festival lands, I will be there.”

According to a report Essence released earlier this month, the festival generated $1.3 billion in economic impact from 2022 through 2025. It also supported 11,000 jobs and led to $179.3 million in tax revenue.

However, local businesses and residents have questioned how much the festival benefits the community. During the festival, a “Clean Zone” ordinance prohibits smaller events in certain areas unless they are authorized.

A legal dispute arose in 2023 when a Black-owned bookstore and coffee shop sought to host an event promoting Black authors during the festival. The business and Essence organizers later resolved the dispute.

A similar incident occurred in 2022 when Spotify and a New Orleans real estate developer wanted to put on an event at a music club. Essence dropped the lawsuit the following year, according to NOLA.com.

title: Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
summary: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs
story: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs

MADRID -- Spain's economy has been growing faster than most of its European peers, but many Spaniards haven't felt the benefits. Discontent, particularly around soaring housing costs, is widespread and bound to be a decisive force in Sunday's national election.

On the campaign trail, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has had to tread a careful line between boasting about Spain's enviable growth rates while acknowledging voters' frustration over the rising cost of living.

The progressive Spanish leader called an early election for Nov. 29 after weeks of nationwide protests over living conditions, hoping to capitalize on their anger. While Sánchez has warned voters that a right-wing government would not make their lives more affordable, his conservative opponents have slammed his government for doing too little.
These five charts illustrate the disconnect between Spain's economic growth under Sánchez and the financial pressures many voters face.

House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.

Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.
Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.

Academics and policymakers trace the origins of the problem to the 2008 financial crash. Home construction plummeted following a building boom that helped fuel the country's housing bubble. Large-scale investors began buying property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation years later.
Both Sánchez and his main opponent, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, have promised to enact measures if elected to financially help first-time home buyers.

That's the share of Spaniards aged 18 to 34 who were still living with their parents in 2025, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute. Almost half of those between 26 and 34 cited an inability to pay rent or buy a home as the reason why.
Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas.
Analysts say the rental supply in these areas has diminished due to a combination of factors, including population growth driven by immigration and tourism.
In cities and holiday hot spots, short-term and tourist accommodations on platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com have proliferated, reducing the available rental stock.

That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidized or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy.
In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month.

“You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.”
That was the last time Spanish real wages peaked when adjusted for inflation.

Spain’s economy has substantially outgrown the eurozone average since Sánchez took office in 2018, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. The Spanish economy is expected to expand by an estimated 2.6% this year, more than double the eurozone's projected growth of 1.2%, according to the EU.
Even so, real wages have barely budged.

Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labor force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions.

“What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.”
Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation.
That's how much the cost of food increased between 2015 and 2025. While housing has become the focus of public discontent in Spain, other costs have also increased while Sánchez has been in office.
To soften the impact of price rises, his government has at various times reduced value-added taxes (VAT) on food, subsidized energy and provided financial assistance.
Analysts say cost increases around food and energy were driven partly by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“Since the war in Ukraine began, we have experienced significant spikes in inflation, and at many points, the rate of inflation has outpaced wage growth,” Aznar said. “Consequently, even if wages rise, if inflation increases by a greater margin, the worker loses purchasing power.”

Conservative opposition leader Feijóo has made the rising cost of living a key campaign issue, promising to lower personal income tax within his first year in office, and criticizing Sánchez for often highlighting Spain's GDP growth.
Talavera said rising costs have left many Spaniards who were employed in 2018 feeling poorer now because their money simply doesn't go as far.
“In economic terms, that is the main story.”

title: How major US stock indexes fared Wednesday 11/25/2026
summary: Stocks on Wall Street recovered most of their steep early losses as a pullback in AI stocks eased
story: Stocks on Wall Street recovered most of their steep early losses as a pullback in AI stocks eased
Stocks on Wall Street recovered most of their steep early losses as a pullback in AI stocks eased.
The S&P 500 index fell 0.3% after being down as much as 3.2% earlier Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 164 points, or 0.3%. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.6%.

The market pared its losses even as a report raised more worries about high inflation and as President Donald Trump plans to escalate the U.S. trade war with major trading partners. AI stocks retreated for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Treasury yields fell in the bond market.
On Wednesday:
The S&P 500 fell 18.31 points, or 0.3%, to 7,182.78.
