title: Morgan Rielly scores twice as Maple Leafs defeat Bruins, who lose David Pastrnak to injury
summary: Morgan Rielly scored his first two goals of the season, including the 100th of his career, to lead the Toronto Maple Leafs to a 3-1 victory over the Boston Bruins
story: Morgan Rielly scored his first two goals of the season, including the 100th of his career, to lead the Toronto Maple Leafs to a 3-1 victory over the Boston Bruins
BOSTON -- Morgan Rielly scored his first two goals of the season, including the 100th of his career, to lead the Toronto Maple Leafs to a 3-1 victory over the Boston Bruins on Friday.

Rielly’s second goal came off a faceoff that Toronto won in Boston's zone and broke a 1-1 tie with 2:04 left in the second period. Colton Sissons added an insurance goal in the third and Anthony Stolarz made 26 saves for the Maple Leafs, who won their second in a row after dropping nine straight.

The Bruins, who have lost five of their last six home games, played the final two-plus periods without captain David Pastrnak. He appeared to suffer a non-contact injury in Boston's zone and left the bench with six minutes remaining in the first period. Before the start of the second, the Bruins announced that Pastrnak had a lower-body injury. The 30-year-old star leads Boston in goals (11), assists (21) and points (32).
Casey Mittelstadt scored the lone goal for the Bruins and Jeremy Swayman made 15 saves.
Boston managed one shot on a 5-on-3 power-play chance that covered 1:58 with the Bruins down 2-1 in early minutes of the third period.

Pastrnak’s exit came after Mittelstadt converted on the power play to give Boston a 1-0 lead. Toronto tied it before the end of the first period when Rielly’s wrist shot from the point eluded Swayman as the goalie contended with traffic in front of his crease.

It was also a costly game for the Maple Leafs. Veteran defenseman Chris Tanev required help off the ice after a collision with Bruins forward Mark Kastelic three minutes into the second period. He was ruled out with a lower-body injury. The 36-year-old Tanev is six games away from appearing in the 900th of his 17-year NHL career.
Maple Leafs: Travel to Pittsburgh on Saturday night for the final game of a three-game road trip.
Bruins: Host Vancouver on Sunday in the fourth game of a six-game homestand.

title: QB Brock Purdy to miss the 49ers' game vs. the Seahawks. Mac Jones will start in his place
summary: San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy will miss Sunday’s game against the Seattle Seahawks with a sprained ankle and Mac Jones will start in his place
story: San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy will miss Sunday’s game against the Seattle Seahawks with a sprained ankle and Mac Jones will start in his place

SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy will miss Sunday's game against the Seattle Seahawks with a sprained ankle and Mac Jones will start in his place.

Purdy missed all three practices this week after getting hurt in the second quarter of last week's win against the Minnesota Vikings. Coach Kyle Shanahan was initially hopeful Purdy could play this week because he avoided a high ankle sprain, but he didn't make enough progress and was ruled out Friday.

“Any time it’s not a high ankle sprain you get pretty relieved,” Shanahan said. “But it was more mid than low, which is a little bit worse. I kind of had a feeling just the way it was by the time Wednesday came around. It didn’t heal up as fast as we wanted so we had to shut him down.”
Shanahan said it was too soon to know whether Purdy would be able to play next week against the New York Giants but he was optimistic. For now, the Niners will go ahead with Jones.

“It’s obviously a challenge when you’re getting thrown in toward the end of the year, but it’s a challenge that I’ve done before in my career,” Jones said. “I played the first eight games before, I played the last eight games and I played all 16. So I’m definitely up for the challenge and looking forward to it.”

Purdy stayed in the game after he was hurt against the Vikings and had a stellar performance. He threw for 255 yards and three touchdowns against one of the top defenses in the league to win NFC Offensive Player of the Week.
Purdy leads the NFL with a 118.2 passer rating and 9.0 yards per pass attempt to go with his 23 touchdown passes and only five interceptions.

Jones started eight games last season when Purdy was sidelined by turf toe and helped San Francisco post a 5-3 record during that time with a 97.4 passer rating, 13 touchdown passes and six interceptions.
The 49ers kept Jones as the backup this season despite some interest in a trade from other teams just for this scenario.

“Mac’s been awesome,” Shanahan said. “He’s had a great week. We went through this a lot with him last year so everyone’s got a ton of confidence in Mac. Mac’s had a hell of a camp and he’s the same guy every day. So it’s been a good week with Mac.”

Receiver Jordan Watkins (groin) was also ruled out for Sunday. Receiver Mike Evans (Achilles tendinitis), linebacker Dre Greenlaw (neck), defensive back Siran Neal (knee, foot), cornerback Upton Stout (shoulder) and offensive lineman Austen Pleasants (knee) are questionable.
Pleasants returned to practice this week for the first time since getting hurt in the preseason and would need to be activated from injured reserve on Saturday to be eligible to play.

title: Sony's dog robot can't do chores but offers companionship
summary: The people at Sony don’t use words like “product” or “reboot” when they talk about Aibo, the Japanese electronics and entertainment company’s robotic dog
story: The people at Sony don’t use words like “product” or “reboot” when they talk about Aibo, the Japanese electronics and entertainment company’s robotic dog
TOKYO -- The people at Sony don’t use words like “product” or “reboot” when they talk about Aibo, the Japanese electronics and entertainment company’s robotic dog.

Aibo robots, which first went on sale in 1999, are all sold out and no longer in production. But some owners who had to part with their Aibo have donated the robots to Tokyo-based Sony Group Corp. for an “adoption program," where they get treated to repairs and upgrades.
Those robot pets now have new homes in hospitals and other facilities, bringing solace and smiles to patients and staff.
Sony does not disclose the pricing or the number of Aibo robots that have been sold.

Packed with sensors, digital cameras and an intelligence of sorts, Aibo has been programmed to remember its name, the owner’s face and its surroundings — details of everyday life that make for a disarming illusion of a personality.

The robot barks, cocks its head, moves its ears, waddles toward you, acts happy when petted and goes to “sleep” — in short it simulates a puppy, except this one can take snapshots and monitors its own mechanical dysfunctions.
“The owners feel as though they are sending off what has become to them like their own child,” said Sony official Yoshiyuki Katsuno, who oversees the program.
Aibo gets people talking to each other, and can offer tired souls a perk to pick themselves up and keep going, according to Katsuno.
“We hope to spread the emotional healing and human interaction that Aibo has to offer,” he said.
At the St. Marianna University School of Medicine in Kawasaki, on the outskirts of Tokyo, a nurse had to do some looking to find a wandering Aibo during a recent visit.
But Aibo has helped with the long waits for visiting patients and succeeded in persuading reluctant children to get examined, says Dr. Manabu Komori of the department of otolaryngology.
That field involves diagnosing and treating sicknesses related to the ear, nose and throat, with many child patients.
“It helps motivate the kids,” Komori said. “Going to a hospital is basically not very pleasant.”

The hospital also uses real dogs to help patients feel better, though the animals require care and food and can be temperamental. That means a robot dog offers some advantages, although Komori was careful not to say they were better than real dogs.

Cuteness is seen as desirable in Japanese culture, where being “kawaii,” or “cute,” is not a sign of weakness or inferiority, but an endearing trait that encourages harmony and communication — both valued in Japanese society.

And so, if the need is for a soulmate, it’s better to have that cute look, be it a dog, cat or even a duck, said Jerry Wang, Executive Chairman of FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem, a U.S. company that offers more foreboding-looking four-legged patrol robots.
“If you want some emotional attachment, you want a cute shape,” he said.

title: Pakistani leader and army chief speak to first astronaut aboard Chinese craft
summary: Pakistan’s prime minister and army chief have spoken with the country’s first astronaut, aboard China’s space station, hailing his flight as a national achievement and a milestone in Islamabad’s close ties with Beijing
story: Pakistan’s prime minister and army chief have spoken with the country’s first astronaut, aboard China’s space station, hailing his flight as a national achievement and a milestone in Islamabad’s close ties with Beijing

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s prime minister and army chief spoke Saturday with the country’s first astronaut, who is aboard China’s space station, hailing his flight as a national achievement and a milestone in Islamabad’s close ties with longtime ally Beijing.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif made his remarks days after Muhammad Zeeshan Ali flew alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi on the craft that blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China.

Ali is the first foreign astronaut in the history of China’s crewed space program and his flight was part of an agreement signed between Pakistan and China in February 2025. The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during the mission.

Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spoke with Ali by video link from the headquarters of Pakistan’s space agency. "Zeeshan (Ali), it is a great day for all of us sitting here and 240 million people of Pakistan,” Sharif said in his televised remarks, as Ali stood aboard the station with a Pakistani flag on his chest.
“I extend my warmest felicitations to you on becoming the first Pakistani astronaut to orbit the Earth,” he said.
A Pakistani adventurer, Namira Salim, paid for a ticket to fly on Virgin Galactic's commercial flight in 2023, but was only in space for a matter of minutes.

Sharif said the Chinese mission opened opportunities for Pakistan’s young people in science and technology and expressed hope it would pave the way for more Pakistanis to travel to space. He thanked Chinese President Xi Jinping for making Pakistan’s participation possible and noted that the mission coincided with the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the countries.

Sharif said Ali’s journey demonstrated Pakistan’s belief that outer space should be used for peaceful purposes and the benefit of humanity. “The experiments you are conducting alongside your talented Chinese brothers are not just for Pakistan; they will enrich the collective scientific knowledge of the international community,” he said.
Sharif told Ali that the entire Pakistani nation was eagerly awaiting his safe return home. The mission is due to last up to 10 days.
Munir also congratulated Ali, saying “We are really proud of you and proud of the armed forces that one of us has gone into space and achieved this great accomplishment.”

title: As Google threatens to cut schools' search access, Los Angeles blocks AI features
summary: Los Angeles school officials have disabled AI-generated summaries in Google searches on school-issued devices
story: Los Angeles school officials have disabled AI-generated summaries in Google searches on school-issued devices

School districts are taking steps to block Google's artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America's classrooms.

In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes Los Angeles Unified the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.

The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.
The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee on Friday, Nov. 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.
“It was the talk of the playground,” Lee said.

Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America’s classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google’s suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework and communication among students and teachers.

But concerns about AI's impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country’s two largest school districts — New York and LA — announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it's not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.

LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are “age-appropriate and safe.” It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.

Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.

“We’re thrilled LAUSD did this,” said Lee. “AI is seeping into everything. It’s dangerous. It’s hurting learning. And it’s a corporate overreach into public schools. It’s Big Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone’s consent.”
Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports.
Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cellphones and screentime and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.

The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That's when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and LA schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.

Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.
Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.

While the blog post does not explicitly say search can’t be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” If schools ban AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The integration of AI in search isn't new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.

Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company's leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features “without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole.”

“The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we’re punishing schools for not using AI,” the petition said. “Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products.”

Google says it hears parents' and teachers' concerns about students using AI to “shortcut learning” and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want — the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024 — is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students’ access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.

Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot “guided learning” tool that walks students “step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers.”
“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” the company said in a statement.

Currently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk users through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.

LA schools had already disabled Google’s AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.

“We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite,” Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google’s products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district’s priorities.
“We have choices,” Kelanic said. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.”

title: Judge declines to issue a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda
summary: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Donald Trump
story: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Donald Trump

NEW YORK -- A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., said the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown a likelihood to prevail in the case. It had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president’s campaign message just weeks before November’s midterm elections. Her ruling comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.
In her ruling, she noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away.

“But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone,” she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.
“At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded,” AliKhan wrote.

Democrats sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads that were paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. In court papers, the DNC challenged at least 11 government-created ads that either aired on TV or appeared on Trump administration social media feeds.

Some of the ads glorified the president with highlight reels of scenic speeches, promoted his tax cuts and emphasized support for law enforcement. One of them repurposed a clip that had been used by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, showing him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.”

A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, said in a statement that the organization was “disappointed” by the judge’s decision, adding that the DNC “will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration’s attempts to undermine our democracy.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites.
But in her latest ruling, AliKhan declined to issue a preliminary injunction against the ads.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don’t try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued.

Ahead of the ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed.

title: Pakistan congratulates China on flight that carried a Pakistani astronaut to space station
summary: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has congratulated China on the successful launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission
story: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has congratulated China on the successful launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday congratulated China on the successful launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission  that took a Pakistani astronaut to the Tiangong space station, making him the first foreign crew member to reach it.

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, flew alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, on the craft that blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday. They later entered the space station and took group photos with three other astronauts from the Shenzhou 23 mission.

Sharif expressed Pakistan’s gratitude to China for providing the opportunity to participate in the mission, according to a statement after a meeting with Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong at the prime minister’s office in Islamabad.
He said that the mission represented the journey of 240 million Pakistanis and embodied the dreams and aspirations of the Islamic nation’s youth and scientific community.

The mission marked the first joint flight by Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China’s crewed space program. It's part of an agreement signed by Pakistan and China in February 2025. The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during the mission.

title: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying 2 Chinese and 1 Pakistani astronaut
summary: China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts, sending the first foreign crew member to its space station
story: China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts, sending the first foreign crew member to its space station
JIUQUAN, China -- China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, flew alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit. They later entered the space station and took group photos with three other astronauts from the Shenzhou 23 mission.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China’s crewed space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
In Pakistan, shouts of “God is great!” and “Long live Pakistan-China friendship!” rang out as the spacecraft carrying Ali climbed toward space.

Many families living thousands of kilometers from the launch site shared the milestone for their country’s space program through television broadcasts. In restaurants, customers followed the images on television, joining the celebrations with cries celebrating Pakistan’s friendship with China. Scientists at the headquarters of Pakistan’s space agency also watched the launch.

Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari and Chinese President Xi Jinping exchanged letters congratulating each other, hailing the Pakistani astronaut’s inclusion in China’s space mission as a milestone in bilateral ties, according to a statement from Zardari’s office.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that Xi described China's space station as a “boat” for peace, friendship and cooperation, and that China is willing to uphold the peaceful use of outer space with other countries and deepen cooperation.

Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif congratulated the nation on the launch, describing Ali’s mission as a source of national pride and an inspiration for Pakistani youth. “This is not just one astronaut’s journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis,” he wrote on X. Sharif thanked China for including the Pakistani astronaut in the mission, saying the flight reflected close ties between the two countries and extended their cooperation into space.

Pakistan's Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, Ahsan Iqbal, told reporters at the center that he hoped this would be the beginning of greater cooperation in the future. He also thanked Xi, the Chinese leadership, scientists and engineers.
When asked if Pakistan could send astronauts independently, he said: “Certainly that day will come.”
Iqbal said Ali carried not merely his name but the Pakistani flag on his shoulders and uniform, lifting the hopes, prayers and technological aspirations of Pakistanis into orbit.
“The sky is no longer our limit, it is our launching pad,” he said in a statement, describing the mission as an inspiration for young Pakistanis hoping to pursue careers in science and technology.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.

The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, China’s official Xinhua News Agency reported earlier. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.

While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and has become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides’ efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali’s Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
“It’s like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights,” he said in Mandarin.

Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The United States is widely seen as China’s main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.
Leung reported from Hong Kong. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Jiuquan and Munir Ahmed in Islamabad contributed to this report.

title: The return of the wolf divides the densely populated Netherlands
summary: The return of wolves to the Netherlands was once hailed as a conservation success story
story: The return of wolves to the Netherlands was once hailed as a conservation success story

DE HOGE VELUWE NATIONAL PARK, Netherlands -- DE HOGE VELUWE NATIONAL PARK, Netherlands (AP) — The return of wolves to the Netherlands some two centuries after they were hunted to extinction was seen as a fairy tale comeback and a conservation success story.

But the initial joy when a pair of wolves first bred in the Netherlands in 2019 soured as the return of the apex predator led to deadly attacks on livestock and unwanted encounters with humans that have fed into existing tensions in Dutch society.

Wolf numbers are growing across Europe, and the population in the Netherlands — estimated at fewer than 150 divided into about 15 packs — is tiny compared to those in many other European Union countries where wolves have been established for far longer.

Even so, the densely populated nation of 18 million people with an influential, multibillion-dollar agricultural industry is the backdrop for a particularly prickly debate about just how well the wolf, a protected animal across the EU, can coexist with people and livestock.

While packs often remain in their own territories, lone wolves can drift around the country. Tracking data gathered by researchers at the respected Wageningen University and Research institute showed a single wolf covered just over 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) in three months, swimming over a major river twice and crossing several highways.
The Dutch government announced this week that it intends to allow some wolves to be culled, citing the need to prevent attacks on people and animals.

When Robertjan Feijen first began raising sheep in the rural northeast of the Netherlands about a decade ago, wild wolves were a distant memory. His sheep grazed on other farmers’ fields and pastures that are submerged during the winter to create speed skating ovals.
Things changed fast.
Since wolves returned to the Netherlands, the farmer has lost around 250-300 sheep in more than 50 wolf attacks.

The worst feeling for Feijen is if he has helped deliver a lamb and then sees that animal maimed or, worse still, “you see it lying dead, completely ripped open and then looking around you, it’s a battlefield with dead animals in ditches,” he said. “It’s indescribable.”

Researchers at Wageningen reported wolves killed more than 3,300 animals last year in the Netherlands, almost all of them sheep, and farmers were paid nearly 1.5 million euros ($1.6 million) for their livestock losses.

Farmers can also get subsidies for protective measures like electric fences. But Feijen said the government support doesn’t come close to covering his losses. He feels forced now to keep many of his sheep in his barn.

Photographer Liesbeth van Asselt has lived near the forests and heathlands that border the central town of Epe all of her 62 years and loves to walk the paths that crisscross shady groves of pine and oak.
But such outings are no longer a source of carefree relaxation.

Even though reports of wolves attacking dogs are rare, when Van Asselt walks with her dog, Raico, she wears a red whistle around her neck to scare off wolves that sometimes walk down the sandy roads near her garden.
“I think we can have an amount of wolves in the Netherlands, but not in between our houses, walking in our streets and in our gardens,” Van Asselt said.

Long seen as a bastion of tolerance, the Netherlands has been roiled in recent years by protesting farmers angry at government plans to rein in nitrogen emissions; by black-clad demonstrators seeking to prevent towns opening asylum-seeker centers; and by people demanding action on climate change.

The debate about wolves opened up one more fault line. In December, when animal welfare activists held a symbolic funeral procession for the only Dutch wolf to have been shot in an officially sanctioned hunt, they were threatened by villagers. Activists said one opponent drove his car at them. Police intervened but made no arrests.
The wolf in question, nicknamed Bram by some locals, had menaced joggers and cyclists and was blamed for biting a child in a forest close to the university city of Utrecht.
Maarten Jacobs, a polarization expert at Wageningen, said wolves are being exploited by agitators seeking to deepen rifts in society.
“So there was existing polarization, and polarization needs fuel to keep the conflict going," he said. “And then the wolf arrived, and that’s perfect new fuel.”

At De Hoge Veluwe National Park, a tourist destination in the central Netherlands, the return of the wolf is having a potentially devastating effect on the protected landscape of inland drifting sands.

Head of operations at the park, Jakob Leidekker, points to countless Scots pine saplings sticking out of a sandy plain. Wild sheep introduced from Cyprus and Corsica called mouflons used to graze on the young shoots before they could mature.
“All the mouflons are gone now because they were killed by wolves,” Leidekker said. “And what you see now is that all these pines are getting up."

The park is home to the Kröller-Müller Museum and its jaw-dropping collection of Vincent van Gogh paintings and other artworks. Some 570,000 people visited the park last year, many of them riding through forests and sand dunes on a fleet of white bicycles. Visitors are now handed a pamphlet explaining what to do if they encounter a wolf.
At least one wolf attacked a jogger and approached visitors. The park sought permission to use paintball guns to scare it off. By the time it was granted, the wolf was gone.
While farmers and others lament the return of the wolf, conservation and animal welfare groups have welcomed it.

Nature organization Natuurmonumenten said it considers the animal “an enrichment to nature, but at the same time attaches great importance to cooperation between parties so that we can coexist with this animal with minimal conflict.”

While wolves are a threat to De Hoge Veluwe's protected landscape, experts say they generally have a positive impact on the environment by keeping large animals like deer on the move, ensuring they don’t overgraze areas.
“There’s a very nice saying in Eastern Europe,” said Hugh Jansman, an animal ecologist at Wageningen. “Where the wolf lives, the forest thrives.”
Wolves are thriving in Europe. The European Commission estimated the population across the continent almost doubled in 10 years to some 20,300 animals in 2023 with breeding packs in 23 countries.

But spurred by anger in communities where wolves prey on livestock, the EU last year relaxed the status of wolves from “strictly protected” to “protected” to give “more flexibility to member states to manage the populations of wolves.”

The Dutch move to allow for some culling will have to be hammered out with provincial governments. But State Secretary for Agriculture, Fisheries and Nature Silvio Erkens called it "an important step because there are now too many serious incidents with wolves.”
Some flout the protections anyway.
A report from the EcoJust consultancy estimates at least 41 wolves have been illegally killed in the Netherlands since their return.
Despite the competition for space in the Netherlands, Jansman says wolves have clearly demonstrated that they have a place in the Dutch landscape.
“I think the biggest challenge is, as humans, are we willing to share this landscape with a predator, the wolf?”
Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed.

title: Australia passes online safety law, putting Big Tech at risk of multibillion-dollar fines
summary: Australia’s Parliament has passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms
story: Australia’s Parliament has passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms
MELBOURNE, Australia -- Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.
The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.
The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.
The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.
The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied."
Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.”
“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy."
The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

“Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23.
“My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added.

The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.
U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”
“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

title: Social media firms not liable for the 2022 Buffalo mass shooting, New York's top court says
summary: New York state's top court says Facebook, YouTube and other social media giants aren’t liable for the racist mass shooting at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York, in 2022
story: New York state's top court says Facebook, YouTube and other social media giants aren’t liable for the racist mass shooting at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York, in 2022

NEW YORK -- Facebook, YouTube and other social media giants aren't liable for the racist mass shooting at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York, the state's highest court ruled this week in lawsuits over the 2022 attack.
In a 4-3 decision Monday, the Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's decision to dismiss claims against the tech firms from survivors and victims' relatives.
The lawsuits accused the companies of offering platforms engineered to promote extreme content and encourage compulsive use and of helping to radicalize shooter Payton Gendron.

Gendron, who is white, absorbed racist conspiracy theories online before he killed 10 Black people and wounded three others at the Tops Friendly Market. The 23-year-old is serving a life sentence after pleading guilty to state-level murder charges.
He told a court in 2023 that he “believed what I read online and acted out of hate.”

The Albany-based Court of Appeals said the four lawsuits “fail to establish that the shooter’s actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants’ decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.”

Three judges disagreed, saying the survivors and families had built enough of a case for it to go forward. Gendron described himself in his diary as an online “addict” whose “mental health has seriously degraded,” the dissenters noted in an opinion by Judge Jenny Rivera.

The ruling affected Facebook and Instagram owner Meta; Google and YouTube parent Alphabet; and Reddit. Under different reasoning, the decision also upheld the dismissal of claims against other messaging and social media apps as well as Amazon, which owns Twitch, the service that Gendron used to livestream the rampage.
Matthew Bergman, who represents victim Heyward Patterson's family and estate in one of the cases, said Tuesday they were assessing their legal options after the ruling.
“The families affected by the tragic May 2022 Buffalo grocery store attack deserve accountability when dangerous product design choices contribute to real-world harm,” Bergman said in a statement.
Messages seeking comment were sent to lawyers for the other plaintiffs and for the companies.
Jury selection is ongoing for Gendron's federal hate crime trial, which carries the possibility of a death sentence if he is convicted. He has pleaded not guilty in that case.

The people he killed ranged in age from 32 to 86. In addition to Patterson, they were Celestine Chaney, Geraldine Talley, Katherine Massey, Pearl Young, Andre Mackneil, Ruth Whitfield, Roberta Drury, Margus Morrison and Aaron Salter.

title: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut
summary: China has unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft, set to launch this week
story: China has unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft, set to launch this week
JIUQUAN, China -- China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft ahead of this week’s launch, with a Pakistani set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will fly alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, the China Manned Space Agency announced, according to the official Xinhua news agency. The spacecraft is scheduled to launch Wednesday morning from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China.

Speaking at a news conference, Ali, a former air force pilot, thanked the Chinese government for helping him realize his dream. In Mandarin, he cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
“It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights,” he said in Mandarin.

Speaking in English, Ali said the mission “is not a finish line” but a long path. He said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit: Look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.

The launch would mark the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China’s manned space program. It is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
“Tomorrow, Pakistan will look to the skies with anticipation, pride and deep gratitude,” he wrote on X.

He praised Chinese President Xi Jinping, saying his “visionary leadership and steadfast commitment to Pakistan-China friendship have taken our All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership to unprecedented heights.”

Sharif also credited Pakistani scientists, the armed forces and national institutions, saying their efforts reflected the country’s growing capabilities and determination to advance space exploration and science.
“Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space,” he said.

Ali will undertake a short mission as a payload specialist, state broadcaster CCTV reported. In orbit, he will primarily conduct experiments under the China-Pakistan partnership, alongside daily operations.
He is expected to carry out four scientific projects in biotechnology and materials science, including an experiment involving photosynthetic microorganisms, CCTV said.
Ali will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, the broadcaster added.
While Ali and Wu will be making their first spaceflights, Tang has flown on two previous missions. He is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, CCTV said.
Tang told reporters that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides’ efforts were paying off.

“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation of the language,” he said, adding that he and Wu had also stepped up their English studies.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The United States is widely seen as China’s main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.
Leung reported from Hong Kong. Associated Press video journalist Wu Jia contributed to this report in Jiuquan.

title: Scientists discover quasar formed within 630 million years of the Big Bang
summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet
story: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

The quasar formed within 630 million years of the universe-forming Big Bang, a German-led team reported Tuesday. That's considered a very early development in the 13.8 billion-year history of the cosmos, and it smashes previous records.

“This time the leap in cosmic time is huge!” the European Southern Observatory’s Julien Wolf, who led the study, said in an email. “The previous two records each took us back by about 15 million years or less. This one takes us back by nearly 40 million years, the biggest advance in nearly a decade!”

Wolf and his team spotted the quasar while digging through millions of observations made by the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Launched in 2023, Euclid is surveying galaxies in an effort to shed light on the dark matter and dark energy that fill so much of the universe and keep it expanding.

Finding a quasar so early in the universe is rare, according to Wolf. What makes this one even rarer, he said, is the massive size of its black hole, despite being such a relatively slow eater of everything around it. Scientists are seeing it as it was 13.1 billion years ago — when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Wolf nicknamed the quasar Dun Aonghasa after the prehistoric stone fort in Ireland's Aran Islands. His wife and daughter are Irish, and he was awestruck when they visited the fort — a frontier holding “the promise of a vast horizon still to explore,” just like this quasar.

His team's findings were corroborated by the Hubble and Webb space telescopes as well as other observatories on and off Earth. Thanks to Webb, scientists learned that the black hole powering this quasar is equivalent in mass to 360 million of our suns, an astounding amount so early in time. The final results appear in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

“Dun Aonghasa gives us a new deadline” for the early universe, Wolf said. “About 630 million years after the Big Bang, its black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun. But how?”
Their prowling of the cosmic dawn continues.
“Honestly, the record could fall again in a few months or it could stand for years,” Wolf said.

summary: The 100th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will take place Saturday morning.
