title: WWE star Bronson Reed dies at 38 due to 'medical complications'
summary: Jermaine Haley, the WWE star known as Bronson Reed, has died at 38 due to "medical complications," the company announced on Friday.
story: He last performed at the Crown Jewel event in Saudi Arabia on Nov. 7.
Jermaine Haley, the World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) star known as Bronson Reed, has died at 38 due to "medical complications," the company announced on Friday.
"Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague," the WWE said in a statement shared on X.
"Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine's entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as all his friends, co-workers and fans," the statement added.
He last performed at the Crown Jewel event in Saudi Arabia on Nov. 7, where he was thrown off the stage while sparring with fellow WWE star Oba Femi.
ABC News has reached out to the WWE and a spokesperson for Haley for further comment.
Haley is from Black Forest, Australia, and made his WWE debut in 2019. In 2024, he won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.

title: Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90
summary: An explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan's Kunar province Saturday killed seven people and wounded over 90
story: An explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan's Kunar province Saturday killed seven people and wounded over 90

KABUL, Afghanistan -- An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed seven people and wounded more than 90, the province’s culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.
Up to 15 of the wounded remain in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.
Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.
Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.
In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

title: Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir Putin
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir Putin

KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe’s future financial commitments to Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelenskyy was “insulting his counterpart,” showing that the Ukrainian leader “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement.”

Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian.”

Moscow’s invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Trump resumed relations.

At the same time, Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia’s ballistic missiles and that SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication, isn’t working properly.

Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia’s invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new $49 billion loan for Ukraine’s economic and military needs next year.
Elections in the EU over the next 12 months could amplify the influence of parties reluctant to send more money to Ukraine and may fray the continent’s support.
A bus pulled up at Ukraine’s northern border on Friday, and an 8-year-old boy ran out of it.
“Mom!” he shouted into the crowd. His mother, Alina Sydorenko, was there to reunite with him after nearly five years apart.
She hugged him tight as he kept saying, “Mother, mother.”
The boy was one of nine Ukrainian children returned Friday from Russia and Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.
“I want to show him everything that he missed and was taken away from him,” Sydorenko said.
Some of the children had lost their parents, who died in occupied territory. Relatives met them off the bus.

Zelenskyy announced the latest Bring Kids Back UA operation on social media, thanking U.S. first lady Melania Trump for her role in mediating wartime reunifications, which so far have brought 43 children home, the White House said on Wednesday.
Ukraine has so far managed to bring home 2,875 children, according to Zelenskyy.
“We remember each and every one of them. We are doing everything we can to find them and return them to their families,” he said.
Ukraine is determined to keep fighting for its independence, Kyiv officials say, and has launched daring attacks against Russian assets.
A recent strike on a Russian navy vessel docked at a port in Libya, however, raised alarm in Europe and Washington that the war could spread and engulf other countries.

In an apparent attempt to defuse tensions, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he held a phone call with Libyan Foreign Minister Al-Taher Al-Baour, informing him that Ukraine had no intentions of drawing Libya into the war.
Sybiha said in comments posted on X late Thursday that he reaffirmed Kyiv’s support for Libya’s sovereignty and efforts to reunify the country.
The grinding aerial bombardment between Russia and Ukraine has escalated recently.
Russia launched close to 300 aerial attacks a week through Nov. 20 on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, or ACLED, that tracks violence.
Zelenskyy warned Thursday that a major Russian attack is looming.

Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 110 of 155 Russian drones launched overnight Friday, including 51 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to the Ukrainian air force. Hits were recorded at 27 locations across Ukraine, it said.

The attacks targeted railway infrastructure, energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings across nine Ukrainian regions, killing at least one person and wounding at least six, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its forces overnight intercepted 318 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and illegally annexed Crimea.
Residents of St. Petersburg reported explosions in eight districts of the city, the Russian online news outlet Astra said.
Also, 70 apartments in a multi-story building were damaged in a drone attack on the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in Russia’s Krasnodar region, local officials said Friday.
Officials reported that Ukraine’s attacks killed at least two people and wounded six others.
Morton reported from London. Associated Press writers Hanna Arhirova in northern Ukraine and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed to this story.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: NY Senate leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, first woman in the role, dies at 76
summary: New York state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins has died
story: New York state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins has died

NEW YORK -- New York state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, the first woman to lead the chamber, died Friday, her office said. She was 76. Her rise opened doors in a state where top decision-makers had long been dubbed “three men in a room.”

A senator since 2006, Stewart-Cousins had just been reelected by her constituents on Nov. 3, and her fellow Democrats chose mid-month to retain her as their leader. Mike Murphy, a spokesperson for the Senate's Democratic majority, announced her death Friday but didn't give the cause or location.

“She was a groundbreaking leader who shattered one of New York's highest glass ceilings,” he said. Gov. Kathy Hochul, a fellow Democrat, said in a statement that she was heartbroken by the death of a legislator she admired “more than she could have ever known.”
“She never forgot where she came from, who she was fighting for or the doors she could open for those coming behind her,” the governor said.

She had led Senate Democrats since 2012. After her party won control of the chamber, she became majority leader in 2019 — the first woman and first Black woman to hold the post — and promised to “give New Yorkers the progressive leadership they have been demanding.” Her ascension also shook up the state's clubby politics, in which the budget and other key bills were routinely hammered out by the so-called “three men in a room” — the governor and the Senate and Assembly leaders.
“I have not been in the room,” Stewart-Cousins told The Associated Press at the time. “So that will be a difference right there.”

Stewart-Cousins used her role to advance some liberal priorities that were going nowhere when Republicans controlled the Senate, such as legalizing marijuana and strengthening gun control laws. She also led an effort to secure voter approval of a state constitutional amendment that supporters billed as protecting abortion rights.

Stewart-Cousins also prioritized passing voting rights laws and a slate of police accountability measures that gained momentum after the 2020 police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis. She called it “a moment of reckoning" and commended the advocacy of Valerie Bell and Gwen Carr, whose sons — Sean Bell and Eric Garner — were killed by New York City police.

“Andrea used her authority in the state Senate to help turn what those mothers had fought for into law,” the Rev. Al Sharpton recalled in a statement Friday. Stunned by her death, the civil rights activist noted that the senator was a guest on “PoliticsNation,” his show on MS NOW, just last week.

In a notable moment in 2021, she became the first senior New York Democrat to call for three-term Democratic Gov. Andrew Cuomo to resign amid mounting sexual harassment allegations and a separate controversy over his administration's count of COVID-19 deaths among nursing home residents. Cuomo, who denied the allegations, initially insisted he wouldn't and shouldn't step down, but he ultimately did.
Cuomo said Friday that while they “did not agree on everything,” he was proud of legislation they worked together to pass.
“She stood up for her members and fought for what she believed was right, without hesitation and always with dignity, grace and class,” Cuomo said in a statement.

A resident of Yonkers, a city just north of the New York City border, Stewart-Cousins was a teacher, sales and marketing professional, and Yonkers city official and Westchester County legislator before she was elected to the state Senate in 2006.
Her husband, Thomas Cousins, died in 2007. Survivors include their children, Kevin, Steven and Candice, and her brother, Robert Stewart Jr.

title: Sales for Biden memoir fall far short of books by Obama, Clinton
summary: Former President Joe Biden’s memoir “Promise Me, America” has sold around 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana, a firm which tracks the physical book sales market
story: Former President Joe Biden’s memoir “Promise Me, America” has sold around 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana, a firm which tracks the physical book sales market

Former President Joe Biden’s “Promise Me, America” sold around 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana. It sold well enough to top The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list, but didn’t approach the level of memoirs by such predecessors as Barack Obama and Bill Clinton.
Circana tracks around 85 percent of the physical books market.

“Promise Me, America,” published last week, received lukewarm reviews. Critics found the book mostly unrevealing about Biden’s time in office and about his decision in 2024 not to run again amid widespread concern about his age and health. A New York Times review was headlined “Reflecting on 2024, Joe Biden Finds No Faults of His Own.”
Sales may also have suffered from the 84-year-old Biden’s limited promotion for the book; he is battling stage 4 prostate cancer.

By comparison, Obama’s “A Promised Land” sold more than 800,000 copies within 24 hours of going on sale in 2020 and topped 1 million by the end of the week. Clinton’s "My Life,” released in 2004, topped 1 million sales within the first two weeks.

Books by and about the Bidens have in general attracted less interest than books about other presidential families. Former first lady Jill Biden’s “View from the East Wing,” published in June, has sold around 46,000 copies according to Circana. By comparison, White House memoirs by Michelle Obama and Hillary Clinton were both million sellers within a month of their release.
The book's publisher, Little, Brown and Company, released a statement saying they were “immensely proud” of it topping the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list.

title: Republicans rethink tariffs, giving Democrats an opening to challenge Trump
summary: Democrats are looking to blunt some of President Donald Trump's tariffs as they take control of Congress
story: Democrats are looking to blunt some of President Donald Trump's tariffs as they take control of Congress
WASHINGTON -- Democrats hoping to blunt President Donald Trump's tariffs when they retake control of Congress may find partners in an unlikely place: among his fellow Republicans.

After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda. The administration proposed new tariffs on Wednesday targeting China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
Whether Republicans actually buck Trump on tariffs could signal if election losses and the president's lame duck status shake what has been nearly lockstep fealty to him.

In interviews with more than a half dozen congressional Republicans since the election, most said they were open to reviewing tariffs, at least on a case-by-case basis. They expressed a desire for predictability and said Congress could reclaim its constitutional authority over tariffs. They were reluctant, however, to broadly curb the president's own tariff powers and acknowledged Trump could veto any repeal legislation.
But for Democrats eager to score some early bipartisan wins, the mere willingness of Republicans to revisit some tariffs could create an opening.

“A rethink is indeed in order,” said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. “I’ll be a bipartisan voice for making sure we have the most consumer friendly tariff approaches and I think there will be a whole lot of receptivity within the administration to my approach.”
Rep. Michael Guest, R-Miss., said “there may be some areas that I would agree with the Democrats.”

“I would personally be opposed to just a blanket restriction on the president’s ability to impose tariffs,” he said. “But I would be willing to look at it on a case-by-case basis based on what the Democrats may bring forward.”

Trump has made tariffs a defining feature of his second term, calling himself “Mr. Tariff” as he imposed broad levies on imports from allies and adversaries alike. He insists tariffs will revive American manufacturing and strengthen the U.S. economy, though there is scant evidence they have accomplished those goals. Tariffs often increase costs for consumers in the form of a tax.
His aggressive approach marks a sharp departure from the free-trade orthodoxy long embraced by Republicans before Trump moved the party in a more protectionist direction.
If Democrats and Republicans were to unite on the issue, tariffs on Canada could emerge as an early test. Previous repeal efforts won support from a handful of Republicans.

Democrats, including incoming Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden of Oregon, have already identified the Canada tariffs as a top target. And after the levies spurred retribution from Canada, adding to the GOP's election challenges this year, there could be an incentive for more Republicans to join the effort.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who is up for reelection in 2028 and was not among the Republicans who backed the Canada repeal legislation, said he distinguished the Canadian tariffs from levies on other countries like China, which he supports.
“Tariffs with respect to Canada don't make sense to me,” he said.

Young, who also backs some tariffs on China and faces reelection in 2028, made several social media posts in the days after the election saying voters were “rightly focused on the cost of living.” He said one reason for high costs was a tariff structure that is “overly broad, and as a result, it is negatively affecting too many American factory floors, farms, small businesses, and family budgets.”
In the interview, he said tariffs should be “predictable” and focused on goals such as “reshoring strategic goods or applying leverage on trading partners to liberalize their own markets.”

When asked about the Canadian levies, he said he was open to different approaches. But he said he preferred that the administration consult with Congress as part of negotiations to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the regional trade pact known as USMCA.
“The USMCA process seems to work if Congress is actively involved and not patted on the head,” he said.

Republicans are taking an increasingly assertive posture toward the administration. Since the election, Republicans have expressed skepticism about a sudden $50 billion request for the nation's air travel system after air traffic was briefly shuttered. They've pressed for more details about widespread tech outages and criticized Trump's intervention in returning Jensen Huang to the helm of Nvidia.
That bullishness could extend to tariffs.

“Congress has, over a period of years, recognized that Congress, by itself, has a real difficult time making a tariff and then authorizing and enacting it,” said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota. “So they’ve given authorities to the executive branch over a period of years. Some of that has cascaded.”
“There’s nothing wrong,” he added, “with Congress taking a second look at whether or not those authorities should be withdrawn, modified, at least reconsidered, or limited.”
Still, reversal of the tariffs is far from guaranteed. For one, Republicans are still sorting through the lessons of this year's elections.
Rep. Steve Womack, an Arkansas Republican who said he would consider tariff repeals on a case-by-case basis, said he thought the levies “have played a role in some of the affordability issues.”
“I have producers in my district that lament the fact that they’re paying higher for goods that can’t be sourced domestically,” he said.
But Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., expressed concern the party may overcorrect.

“I bet a lot of my Republican colleagues will be happy to join Democrats and get rid of a bunch of them, which makes me just a little nervous that it’s going to be a dramatic pendulum swing,” he said.

White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said “this administration is committed to rebuilding the American communities left behind by previous administrations and will continue fighting to lower costs, expand opportunity, and make life more affordable for hardworking American families.”
Republican voters appeared mixed on the issue.

About half of voters who backed the Republican candidate in their local U.S. House race said Trump's tariff policies had helped the national economy, according to The AP Voter Poll. About 3 in 10 said they hurt the U.S. economy, and about one-quarter said those policies didn’t make a difference.
When it came to their local economy, fewer saw a benefit.

About 3 in 10 said Trump’s tariff policies helped the economy in their area, and roughly one-quarter said it had hurt it. About 4 in 10 said those policies hadn’t impacted the economy in their local area.
Democrats, meanwhile, are contemplating a more sweeping challenge to Trump’s trade policies.
Wyden said that if Democrats were successful in winning Republican support to repeal Canadian tariffs, “we'll have some momentum for going after other tariffs.”
His counterpart in the House, incoming Ways and Means Committee Chairman Richard Neal, said rescinding tariffs on Canada “might be a good starting point.”
“But I think taking up the tariffs discussion in totality is really important, largely because the way they've been used in a punitive manner,” he said.
But no hurdle is as formidable as Trump's veto, which would require support from 67 senators to overturn, a steep challenge even with Democrats poised to enjoy a 56-seat majority.
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., a fervent tariff opponent, said he would back repeals but they would have to be attached to must-pass pieces of legislation for them to have any hope.
“On its own, he'll just veto it,” he said.

title: Trump admin proposes new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners
summary: A senior admin official said the countries were informed of proposed tariffs.
story: A senior admin official said the countries were informed of proposed tariffs.
The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and some European Union countries, marking the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

"We're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them. And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries. We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on CNBC Wednesday morning.

President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his economic policy, but has suffered significant defeats in court -- including the Supreme Court's move earlier this year to invalidate most of the global tariffs his administration imposed. Tariffs were also a key issue in the midterm elections, during which Republicans suffered major losses as Democrats took back control of both chambers of Congress.

The administration says the new levies would be enforced under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, where the U.S. is permitted to respond accordingly if it determines that other countries are participating in unfair trade practices that harm the U.S.

The USTR conducted a series of investigations into countries’ trade practices, announcing on Wednesday that they have determined "the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce." The USTR said its investigations into Norway and Mexico are ongoing.
These proposed tariffs will replace Trump's other levies that the Supreme Court invalidated in their ruling.

A senior administration official clarified that these tariffs are not "blanket" tariffs and that they are "targeted" to each specific country. They are also not expected to stack on top of existing duties, except for China.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tariff on China, but threatened to double it to 40% if China does not abide by the agreed-upon trade truce as talks continue, according to a senior administration official. The new tariffs would be added on top of preexisting 25% forced tech transfer tariffs.
Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun reacted to the news of the proposed tariffs in a press conference on Wednesday.

"Our position on handling China-U.S. economic and trade issues is consistent and clear. Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests. Relevant issues should be resolved through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit," Jiakun said.
This comes just a week after Trump visited China for a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

China is among the several countries that have objected to tariffs under the Trump administration. A senior administration official said all of the countries have been informed of these new proposed tariffs, including China, and added that they do not expect retaliatory action.

There is no immediate impact of this announcement as a public comment period would be required to first take place, with the administration eyeing January as the earliest target date to fulfill such requirements.

"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now," Greer said on CNBC.
Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden said in a statement that the proposed tariffs are "not the solution."

"Only weeks after Americans overwhelmingly voted against his high tariffs and higher prices agenda, he’s back with another round. This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses," Wyden, a Democrat, said.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's top Democrat, blasted the proposed tariffs.

"The bad actor here is China, and instead of addressing the problem, Trump continues to let them dictate the terms while alienating our allies and passing the costs onto American families, with little benefit for American workers," he wrote in a social media post on Wednesday.
Separately, the U.S. is also considering modifying Brazil tariffs by increasing taxes on sugar and aircraft products.
"Today’s proposed modification would provide greater leverage to obtain the elimination of Brazil’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices," Greer said in a statement on Wednesday.

Greer's statement argued that imposing an "additional, specific tariff” on Brazil sugar imports as well as a 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports “is intended to help bring Brazil to the table" over what the U.S. perceives to be trade practice violations.
That action also would not be immediate, as the USTR says it will hold a hearing about Brazil's proposed tariff changes on Jan. 14.

title: They want to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan die but the Army won’t let them
summary: Julia Wilson was nine months pregnant when she found herself caught in gunfire at Fort Hood in 2009. 'It's crazy how quickly things run through your brain," she said.
story: The Army is limiting witnesses to victims' survivors and those who were wounded.

Julia Wilson was nine months pregnant when she found herself caught in the gunfire at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. She had just returned from lunch and was shutting off her truck when she heard gunshots and watched a soldier nearby collapse after being struck by a bullet.

A civilian human resources employee at the base, Wilson repeatedly sounded her truck alarm, hoping to distract the gunman from shooting her colleagues, and called 911. As she ducked across the seats of her truck, she counted at least a dozen bullets flying in her direction.
"'I'm never going to see the face of my child. I'm never gonna hold him' -- it's crazy how quickly things run through your brain," she told ABC News.
She and her baby were unharmed.

Now, 17 years later, Wilson wants to witness the execution of the man who could have killed her. But the Pentagon has denied her request to attend the Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 31 others. Nidal is set to die by firing squad at the same Army base where he carried out the attack.

Wilson is among multiple survivors of the massacre who say the Pentagon has denied their requests to witness Hasan's execution, despite assurances that victims and their families would be permitted to attend. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at one time said it would be livestreamed, though that plan was overturned by President Donald Trump.

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, who was then an Army major, opened fire inside a medical processing building at Fort Hood in a rampage he described as a jihad in protest of U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Dozens of other soldiers and civilian employees, including Wilson, Dr. Kathy Platoni and Dr. C. Alan Hopewell, were caught in the attack.

All three had hoped to attend the execution, saying they wanted to be there for the friends and colleagues they lost and that watching the Army carry out Nidal's sentence might bring them some measure of relief after 17 years.

Though none were struck by gunfire, all three witnessed the attack firsthand and said they continue to live with its psychological toll. They say that they are appealing the Army's decision to Department of Defense officials and raising the issue with lawmakers.
The Defense Department did not respond to ABC News' questions about who is allowed to attend.

Wilson called the Army's decision an "institutional betrayal," arguing that its interpretation of its rules effectively dismisses the trauma experienced by those who survived the shooting but weren't hit by gunfire.

The Army's rules on who can witness an execution are relatively broad. They outline that prison staff, the condemned prisoner's attorney and family, and victims of the crimes that led to the death sentence may attend. Hasan was convicted of numerous charges of murder, premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

But the regulations also give the Army discretion to invite additional witnesses, including victims who might not meet the narrower definition of victims. Army rules also require the presence of at least two journalists, effectively as third-party witnesses, a common practice in civilian executions.
Army officials cited security concerns and limited space at the execution site in restricting attendance, correspondence reviewed by ABC News shows.
"The fact that I don't meet the category doesn't change the reality of what I experienced with my unborn child," Wilson said. "I continue to hear the screaming and smell the blood."

Platoni, a retired Army colonel and former chief psychologist for the Army Reserve, was undergoing routine medical processing ahead of a deployment to Afghanistan in an adjacent building when Hasan opened fire. She said she had never met Hasan but would have been his supervisor in Afghanistan.

Military bases can be heavily guarded at their gates while remaining relatively open once someone is inside, particularly someone in uniform. Troops carrying out ordinary duties outside combat zones do not carry weapons. Security falls largely to military and civilian police, who patrol installations.

Platoni, who tended to the wounded in the aftermath of the attack, argued that the Army is applying an unnecessarily narrow interpretation of its own regulations, which authorize victims of offenses punishable by death, including attempted offenses, to witness an execution.
"I've never been this angry in my life that they're doing this to us and telling us we weren't victims because we didn't take a bullet to the brain," she said.
Hopewell, then an Army major who oversaw the outpatient psychiatry clinic at Fort Hood and was Hasan's supervisor, was inside the facility when Hasan tried to force his way in during the shooting.
Armed with an FN-5.7 pistol equipped with a laser sight and a 20-round magazine and carrying a .357 Magnum revolver as a backup, Hasan moved through the halls, shouting for doors to be opened.
Hopewell and his colleagues had barricaded themselves inside a room just before Hasan reached them. Unable to force his way in, he screamed in frustration, Hopewell recalled.
"I was about two feet away from him when he was trying to smash into my clinic to kill me," Hopewell said. "You can't go through something like this and have it not affect you."

Hopewell said he was initially ambivalent about witnessing Hasan's final moments. But Sgt. Kimberly Munley, who was shot three times, asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution. Hopewell had received communications from Army officials inviting him to attend but they subsequently rescinded that invitation.
"Since I was one of the senior officers, I feel it's my duty to represent the families and the victims and my clinic staff," Hopewell said.

For Platoni, attending the execution is not just about watching Hasan die but also supporting the people who survived his attack and the families who lost loved ones. Five soldiers in her unit were killed in the shooting and she still wears a hero bracelet that bears their names to commemorate them.

"It would mean that I could be there to support my fellow soldiers that were wounded and did survive. It would mean that I might be able to, as I did during the court martial, be there to support the families, and I want to witness this so that I know he's gone from the Earth," she said. "So I want to see justice served in some way. But all we've encountered is injustices, one after the other."
All three survivors say they have struggled with post-traumatic stress disorder since the shooting.

Wilson described years of living with a heightened sense of danger, even in otherwise ordinary situations. She said that she has grappled with depression and struggled to hold down a job due to difficulty with concentrating.
"You're constantly looking over your shoulder. You're constantly scanning for threats," Wilson said.

The decision to exclude them from Hasan's execution has compounded a longstanding frustration among the three survivors, who say the Pentagon has repeatedly failed to support those whose lives were upended by the massacre.
For Wilson, witnessing the execution would offer a "smithereen of closure and justice," after 17 years. She said she wants Hasan to see her one final time and recognize that she survived his attack.

"I need him to read from my eyes that you tried to victimize me, but I survived you, and you have destroyed my life and many other people's lives," she said. "And maybe, just maybe, with you ending here -- maybe my life might be able to start somewhat again."

title: Melania Trump reunites seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children with families
summary: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families
story: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families

WASHINGTON -- First lady Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families, bringing the total number of kids in these wartime reunifications to 43, the White House announced Wednesday.

It's the latest example of the first lady taking modest yet tangible interventions to address Russia's war in Ukraine, which started nearly five years ago. Her husband, President Donald Trump, had vowed to broker a quick end to the conflict but has said it's been harder than he expected.

“Children in this region of the world, like children everywhere, cannot possibly understand why geography and government have put them into the horrors of war," the first lady said in a statement shared first with The Associated Press.
“As adults, it is our moral imperative to elevate our children above the divisions that power war in order to restore the simple joys of life, immediately," she said.

Melania Trump said the reunification of these nine children with their families took place with the “full cooperation” of Russian and Ukrainian leaders. No additional information about the children was made available.
The first lady has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
The work began in August 2025, when she had the Republican president hand-deliver a letter that called for peace in Ukraine to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a summit in Alaska.

After a year, she had helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives after they had been separated because of the war, and she has said she has a “direct channel” with the leaders of the warring countries.

Then in October, she helped negotiate a six-day ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Earlier this month, she hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House to mark that milestone.

The local ceasefire in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. During the pause in the war, some 800 people were able to leave the city while food, water and other humanitarian aid were delivered to help those who stayed.
Follow the AP's coverage of first lady Melania Trump at https://apnews.com/hub/melania-trump.

title: Treasury's financial crimes agency says it's investigating 'cybersecurity incident'
summary: The agency handles sensitive information and reports about financial crimes.
story: The agency handles sensitive information and reports about financial crimes.

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is "investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," and has taken some systems offline as a precaution, according to an alert posted on its site.
The agency handles sensitive information and reports about financial crimes including money laundering, trafficking and terrorism financing.
The agency posted an alert on the site where banks and financial institutions can report suspicious activities.
"As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline," the alert read. "The BSA E-Filing website remains operational; however, some services may be temporarily unavailable."
ABC News has reached out for comment.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization'
summary: A D.C. magistrate judge has issued a scathing written order ripping the Trump administration for what he described as the blatant "weaponization" of law enforcement.
story: Judge Zia Faruqui blasted charges that were brought in the Hunter Biden probe.

The D.C. magistrate judge who earlier this month dismissed a criminal case against two former FBI agents accused of lying to Congress about past investigations of Hunter Biden issued a scathing written order Tuesday again ripping the Trump administration for what he described as the blatant "weaponization" of federal law enforcement powers.

"For years, the administration has treated the weaponization of law enforcement like a horror movie villain coming for them. Now the threat is finally real," Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said. "Only the call is coming from inside the house -- the White House."

In a hearing two days before the midterm elections, Faruqui ruled that the criminal complaint prosecutors brought against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides failed to establish probable cause that they purposely misled Congress -- an unusual move given the low evidentiary bar required.

"What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," Faruqui said in the hearing, which he used to summarize testimony about the high-level interventions by senior DOJ officials and FBI Director Kash Patel in pushing for the case.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In Tuesday's written ruling summarizing his decision, Faruqui described the case as just one among a series of politicized prosecutions brought by the D.C. U.S. attorney's office during the second Trump administration.

"This case is not a one-off mistake. This court has seen a line of botched, politicized cases where the government has rushed to charge cases, only to have them fall apart," Judge Faruqui wrote. "The Department of Justice still lists 'Independence and Impartiality' first among its values, stating it 'work[s] each day to earn the public's trust by following the facts and the law wherever they may lead, without prejudice or improper influence.' This prosecution is a betrayal of these values."

"The slapdash prosecution of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides in response to a public command from the President demonstrates a lack of independence and impartiality from the political desires of the Administration," Faruqui said. "Moreover, the rampant errors and misstatements stemming from the slapdash nature of this investigation and prosecution further undercuts public confidence in the work of the Department of Justice."

"If a high-profile case like this is so poorly executed, what can the public expect in the run-of-the-mill case with far less resources and oversight? The erosion of public confidence in the Department of Justice further harms public safety," the judge wrote.

title: On Greece's most glamorous island, faith and tradition endure with a celebration of its women
summary: The Greek island of Mykonos honored its matriarchal heritage with a celebration of St. Catherine, considered a symbol of courage and wisdom for generations of its women
story: The Greek island of Mykonos honored its matriarchal heritage with a celebration of St. Catherine, considered a symbol of courage and wisdom for generations of its women
MYKONOS, Greece -- Long before the cruise ships arrived, Mykonos was run by its poor and iron-willed women. On Wednesday, the Greek island honored them on the feast day of St. Catherine.

Mykonos, now a playground for wealthy travelers, hasn’t forgotten its hardscrabble origins when men left to join fishing crews or work in commercial shipping while women managed its modest and traditionally Orthodox Christian society.
More than 17 centuries after her death, St. Catherine of Alexandria is celebrated here as a bond with that past.

“She represents us as women,” said Anna Athymariti, head of the Mykonos Women’s Cultural and Folklore Association. Founded in 1979, the group chose St. Catherine as its patron in recognition of her courage and wisdom.
“Mykonos has traditionally been considered a matriarchal society,” Athymariti said.

On Wednesday, she joined Father Petros Marangos, parish priest at the Metropolitan Church of Megali Panagia. They led a procession that carried the saint’s flower-adorned icon along Mykonos’ celebrated waterfront.
It passed bars and hotels, iconic Greek island whitewashed homes and Mykonos’ famous windmills. Along the way, women handed out chocolates to residents and visitors.
Katerina Xydaki, who shares the saint’s name, also gave out sweets. Relics of her maternal grandfather are kept in the island’s Church of St. Catherine.
“St. Catherine is the patron saint of my family, of me personally and of our community,” Xydaki said.

Mykonos was first put on the travel map nearly a century ago as a stopping point for Delos, the nearby and uninhabited island that is the mythological birthplace of Apollo and one of Greece’s most important archaeological sites.
Mykonian women sold visitors home-woven textiles and offered up their homes as guest houses. A vacation business was born.

Decades later, the island has been reshaped by luxury tourism. Private yachts, cruises and charter flights deliver affluent visitors, focused on the main town’s hedonistic nightlife and high-end consumption.
According to Christian tradition, Catherine was a young and learned noblewoman in Roman Egypt, tortured and killed for embracing Christianity.
The Orthodox Church venerates Catherine as “all-wise,” the patron saint of scholars, philosophers, students and unmarried women.
“She read Homer and Virgil, studied medicine and explored every field of knowledge available in that era,” said Father Petros, who has served at the church for 35 years.
Beyond its packed beaches and resorts, Marangos said, another Mykonos endures, emerging in the cooler months when the crowds have gone.
“Mykonos is an island rich in tradition,” he said, “and its people continue to uphold that tradition with great love and respect.”
For Athymariti, St. Catherine’s example remains as relevant as ever.
“We take St. Catherine as our example,” she said. “So that we, too, can stand strong in our families and in life.”
Gatopoulos reported from Athens, Greece. Associated Press journalists Theodora Tongas in Athens and Thanassis Stavrakis in Mykonos contributed.
