title: Airline glitches, storms could make for a messy Thanksgiving travel week
summary: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday
story: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday

Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.
No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
On top of all that, there's concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

First there was the Federal Aviation Administration's network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.
“Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said.
As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed.
Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper.

Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s mid-section, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day and reach Maine by Friday, he said.

The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).
The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.
“This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”

Rainy and windy weather also was expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday, and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.
Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state and northwestern Pennsylvania.

“Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Sales for Biden memoir fall far short of books by Obama, Clinton
summary: Former President Joe Biden’s memoir “Promise Me, America” has sold around 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana, a firm which tracks the physical book sales market
story: Former President Joe Biden’s memoir “Promise Me, America” has sold around 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana, a firm which tracks the physical book sales market

Former President Joe Biden’s “Promise Me, America” sold around 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana. It sold well enough to top The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list, but didn’t approach the level of memoirs by such predecessors as Barack Obama and Bill Clinton.
Circana tracks around 85 percent of the physical books market.

“Promise Me, America,” published last week, received lukewarm reviews. Critics found the book mostly unrevealing about Biden’s time in office and about his decision in 2024 not to run again amid widespread concern about his age and health. A New York Times review was headlined “Reflecting on 2024, Joe Biden Finds No Faults of His Own.”
Sales may also have suffered from the 84-year-old Biden’s limited promotion for the book; he is battling stage 4 prostate cancer.

By comparison, Obama’s “A Promised Land” sold more than 800,000 copies within 24 hours of going on sale in 2020 and topped 1 million by the end of the week. Clinton’s "My Life,” released in 2004, topped 1 million sales within the first two weeks.

Books by and about the Bidens have in general attracted less interest than books about other presidential families. Former first lady Jill Biden’s “View from the East Wing,” published in June, has sold around 46,000 copies according to Circana. By comparison, White House memoirs by Michelle Obama and Hillary Clinton were both million sellers within a month of their release.
The book's publisher, Little, Brown and Company, released a statement saying they were “immensely proud” of it topping the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list.

title: USC marching band benched for UCLA game after vandalism prank, officials say
summary: The University of Southern California’s marching band will not perform during this weekend’s rivalry game against UCLA
story: The University of Southern California’s marching band will not perform during this weekend’s rivalry game against UCLA

LOS ANGELES -- The University of Southern California’s marching band will not take the field during Saturday’s rivalry game against the University of California, Los Angeles, after several band members vandalized part of the UCLA campus, USC officials said.
The students removed letters this week from a sign at UCLA’s Wasserman Football Center so it read “Ass Football Center,” according a photograph published by the Daily Bruin, UCLA’s student newspaper.

In an email to students Wednesday, USC President Beong-Soo Kim said the band would skip its traditional pregame and halftime performances at the Rose Bowl on Saturday “out of respect for UCLA, and to provide time to reflect on the collective responsibility we share to uphold our university’s values.”
Kim said any student found responsible for the vandalism “will be subject to discipline under university policy.”

“This conduct runs contrary to USC’s values and is unacceptable,” Kim said. “We want to express our deepest apologies to the entire UCLA community. Our rivalry is one of the great traditions in college athletics, and it has always rested on mutual respect. What happened on UCLA’s campus last night has no place in this tradition.”

USC and UCLA have a decades-old tradition of playing pranks on each other before their football games. Among the most infamous pranks: In 1958, UCLA fans paid a helicopter pilot to drop manure on USC’s iconic Tommy Trojan statue, though he missed the target. In 1989, USC fans released 20,000 crickets painted in the school's cardinal and gold colors into UCLA's Young Research Library.

The game will be closely watched by college football fans beyond Los Angeles. No. 10 UCLA (10-1, 7-1 Big Ten, No. 9 CFP) would advance to the Big Ten championship game with a win. A victory in the conference title game would give the Bruins an automatic berth in the College Football Playoff.
No. 15 USC (8-3, 5-3 Big Ten, No. 15 CFP) will be playing to keep its slim playoff hopes alive.

title: Asian shares mostly rise ahead of Wall Street's reopening after the Thanksgiving holiday
summary: Asian shares are mostly higher, following a market holiday on Wall Street for Thanksgiving
story: Asian shares are mostly higher, following a market holiday on Wall Street for Thanksgiving
TOKYO -- Asian shares were mostly higher in early Friday trading, following a market holiday on Wall Street for Thanksgiving.

Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 added 0.7% to 57,919.30 in morning trading. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.4% to 8,800.50. South Korea's Kospi surged 2.2% to 4,812.65. Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged up 0.4% to 22,310.11, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.1% to 3,473.40.
Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence has been pushing benchmarks higher, despite some profit-taking that has kept those gains in check.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron and Advantest Corp. stocks dropped in morning trading but quickly recovered the declines, underlining the continuing appeal of issues in computer chips and AI.
Investors are also closely watching for the possible damage to the region from U.S. tariff hikes planned on China, Japan, the European Union and other trading partners.
U.S. markets will reopen later Friday for a holiday-shortened session.

In energy trading, oil prices have been volatile lately because of uncertainty over tensions in the Middle East. Benchmark U.S. crude rose 2.09% to $85.43 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, slipped 0.29% to $96.29 a barrel.
In currency trading, the U.S. dollar inched up to 159.25 Japanese yen from 159.23 yen. The euro cost $1.0967, down from $1.0975.
AP Business Writer Chan Ho-Him contributed to this report.

title: Black Friday shoppers undeterred by inflation and bad weather
summary: Shoppers have flocked from Thanksgiving meals to Black Friday deals, braving weather challenges across the U.S. Black Friday remains the busiest day for physical stores, despite the rise of e-commerce and early online discounts
story: Shoppers have flocked from Thanksgiving meals to Black Friday deals, braving weather challenges across the U.S. Black Friday remains the busiest day for physical stores, despite the rise of e-commerce and early online discounts

NEW YORK -- Shoppers migrated from Thanksgiving meals to Black Friday deals as predictably as geese heading south for winter, with some pursuing discounts with help from artificial intelligence tools and others venturing to malls despite bad weather that unleashed flooding and delayed the Macy’s parade in New York.

Black Friday, the U.S. retail industry’s version of the Super Bowl, produces more foot traffic at stores than any other day despite competition from e-commerce and brands rolling out steep holiday discounts online weeks in advance, according to retail technology company Sensormatic Solutions.
Enough die-hard traditionalists still prefer hitting the shops as soon as they can after Thanksgiving that a line formed outside at Macy’s Herald Square in Manhattan before sunrise.

Aime Becker and her spouse, Tabatha Ferguson, browsed the clothing racks and planned to buy holiday ornaments commemorating the 100th anniversary of the department store's Thanksgiving Day parade, which was rescheduled for Saturday.

The Illinois couple spent $4,000 to visit New York, which they considered a treat as higher costs for basic necessities crimp their overall budget. They said they buy groceries at Walmart, and B&D grocers — short for bent-and-dent — that sell discounted products with damaged packaging or nearing their best-by dates.
Food prices are “astronomical,” said Becker, a retired veteran. “We have no savings, like there’s nothing to save because it’s all gone.”
Analysts and economists scrutinize retail spending on the five days from Thanksgiving Day through Monday for clues about commercial prospects heading into the new year.

The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half the 4.1% sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast U.S. shoppers collectively spending $1.01 trillion.
The good news for U.S. retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as gasoline prices, pushed up by the war with Iran, continued a steady decline.

“We have been incredibly surprised at how resilient the shopper has been through the political climate, through the macro and economic environment,” said Kurt Ivey, senior vice president of marketing and communications at shopping center operator Macerich.
Macerich's more than three dozen malls across the country had anywhere from 2% to 4% more visitors in their initial operating hours than they saw last Black Friday, Ivey said.
Target reported that hundreds of customers lined up before 6 a.m. at many stores, and some showed up as early as 8 p.m. the night before. The first 100 visitors received gift cards.

Online, consumers spent a record $7.1 billion on Thanksgiving, a 10.4% increase from last year, according to Adobe Digital Insights. For Black Friday, Adobe reported that shoppers spent $9.7 billion online as of 6:30 p.m. EST, representing a 12.8% increase from last year. When the final tally is in, the data firm expects online spending will range from $13 billion to $13.4 billion, surpassing its forecast of $12.9 billion.
AI-powered shopping drove twice as much traffic to retail sites as it did last year, according to Adobe.
Chatbots also drove some traffic to malls.
Kara Teising, 48, said AI-generated tips and a desire for time with family inspired her to venture out to Lenox Square in Atlanta with her two teens and her mother.
“I did ChatGPT to kind of look and see which mall had the biggest concentration of stores that my kids would be into, and so that’s how we chose the Lenox Square Mall,” Teising said.
Black Friday's evolution into a multiweek event has encouraged people to stock up on shampoo, T-shirts and other everyday items while checking off their holiday lists, retail analysts said.

Atlanta resident Anna Butler, a retired schoolteacher, bought a couple of pairs of Levi’s jeans and corduroy pants on sale at the flagship Macy’s in Manhattan after she and five friends decided to venture there from a hotel across the street early Friday. Butler said she feels financially secure due to retirement and Social Security benefits.
“The economy is not good, but I am comfortable,” she said.

To lure shoppers out Friday, Walmart focused on specials reserved for its physical stores, including a sampler set from the popular NeeDoh brand, said Julie Barber, chief merchandising officer at Walmart U.S.’s division. But people also used the sale to scoop up items like $5 pillows and discounted crockpots.

Roughly 15,000 shoppers showed up during the first hour after the 7 a.m. opening of Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota, an 8.5% increase from last year, according to Jill Renslow, chief business development and marketing officer.

The first 1,000 customers received goodie bags with $100 worth of giveaways, Renslow said, adding that many shoppers are starting their holiday shopping earlier “and getting those discounts throughout.”
After promoting weeks of solid discounts, many U.S. retailers reserved more substantial deals for Black Friday, said Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at Adobe.

Michael Brown, a partner at management consulting firm Kearney, said after visiting several shopping centers in New York's Westchester County that he observed the most customers at stores offering at least 50% off.

“Because of the inflation right now, you couldn’t soft-pedal the discounts and increase them as the season went through,” Brown said. “So I think coming out big, out of the gates, really gave you an advantage today.”
Saturated by online deals, some shoppers were unimpressed by the discounts in stores.

“I just saw a jacket in Pink for $149 and I was like, I can get that like on Amazon for 20, so it’s just like, it’s a little frustrating,” said Stella Pagani, who was shopping with her mom at Louisiana’s Lakeside Shopping Center, known for offering champagne to Black Friday shoppers who spend more than $50 at any store.
Many said they didn't miss the mayhem of Black Fridays past.

“I don’t think we need people punching each other over a new air fryer,” said Brandon Montalvo, who traveled from Arkansas to Chicago for Thanksgiving and was scouring the Magnificent Mile shopping district for deals on holiday knickknacks.
This story has been updated to correct that shopper Anna Butler bought several pairs of jeans and corduroy pants, not six pairs of jeans.
AP reporters Wyatte Grantham-Philips in Chicago, Emilie Megnien in Atlanta and Stephen Smith in Metairie, Louisiana, contributed.

title: Pizza Hut cofounder Dan Carney dies, nearly seven decades after launching business
summary: Dan Carney, who co-founded Pizza Hut with his brother nearly seven decades ago, has died
story: Dan Carney, who co-founded Pizza Hut with his brother nearly seven decades ago, has died
Dan Carney, who cofounded Pizza Hut with his brother nearly seven decades ago, has died. He was 95.
Wichita State University, Carney's alma mater, announced his death earlier this month. The school said he died on Nov. 13.

Carney and his younger brother, Frank, launched the first Pizza Hut in Wichita, Kansas, back in 1958. They were both students, according to the university, and used a $600 loan from their mother to open one small restaurant at the time.
“The sign out front only had room for eight letters and, just like that, Pizza Hut was born,” Pizza Hut's website notes.

Their business quickly found success, and franchised locations grew Pizza Hut's reach. Pizza Hut’s familiar red roof debuted in 1969 and by 1971 it was the top pizza chain in the world by sales. The company's website boasted nearly 20,000 locations worldwide as of the end of last year.
The International Pizza Hut Franchise Holder’s Association credited Carney with much of the company's mission.

“Dan believed in doing things the right way, taking care of guests, looking out for people and giving back to the community. Those values helped build Pizza Hut into the brand it is today, and they are just as important to us now,” the association said in a statement sent to The Associated Press. "We’re grateful for what he and Frank started, and we’re proud to carry that legacy forward.”

In addition to cofounding Pizza Hut, Carney also spent much of his life doing philanthropy and advocacy. He served as board chairman of the Cerebral Palsy Research Foundation for 50 years. The CPRF said it was “deeply saddened” by his passing, and called Carney a “devoted champion” of its mission.
Wichita State added that Carney was a decades-long supporter of the university, including through scholarship support for students and helping open the on-campus Pizza Hut museum.
“Pizza Hut is known worldwide, but Dan’s legacy at this university is just as lasting,” Wichita State President Rick Muma said in a statement.
Carney's younger brother and Pizza Hut co-founder, Frank, died in 2020.

Pizza Hut is now headquartered in Texas. Amid growing competition, it has had several different owners over the years. PepsiCo acquired Pizza Hut in 1977 but spun off its restaurant division — which became Yum Brands — in 1997. Just earlier this year, private equity firm LongRange Capital bought Pizza Hut for about $1.5 billion, excluding the mainland China business.

title: The Supreme Court will decide whether assault weapons bans violate the Second Amendment
summary: There's an important gun case set for arguments before the Supreme Court
story: There's an important gun case set for arguments before the Supreme Court

WASHINGTON -- Nicole Hockley was still in a fog of grief when she carried a photo of her 6-year-old son Dylan to the Connecticut Capitol. The image of his bright blue eyes and sweep of brown hair was marked with the year he was born and the year he was killed by shots from an AR-15-style rifle.

She was part of a wave of people who helped persuade the state to expand its ban on firearms like the one used to massacre 20 children, including Dylan, and six staff members at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012.
More than a decade later, she remains convinced that the assault weapons ban has helped prevent more mass school shootings.
“This isn’t just about laws. This is about people, and this is about ensuring that people are protected,” said Hockley, who co-founded the group Sandy Hook Promise.

She is heading to Washington next week, along with other families and survivors of deadly mass shootings. The conservative-majority Supreme Court will hear arguments Wednesday over whether state and local assault weapons bans violate the Second Amendment's right “to keep and bear arms," putting the justices at the center of one of the most bitterly contested issues in firearms law.

Gun rights advocates backed by the Trump administration say it is unconstitutional to ban the nation’s most widely owned rifle, which is involved in a relatively small portion of overall gun violence.

“This is the biggest and most pernicious problem we have in the gun control space,” said Bill Sack, senior director of legal operations at the Second Amendment Foundation. “We all view this as the Super Bowl of gun rights for the time being.”

About a dozen states have similar laws banning weapons such as the AR-15. They cover major cities including New York, Los Angeles and Chicago, where a county-level ban is also before the high court next week. A federal law restricting their sale and manufacture expired in 2004.

The guns have since increased sharply in popularity as they became widely available at lower prices. Gun retailer surveys show sales of AR-15-type weapons are second only to semiautomatic handguns, according to court documents.

They also have been used in several high-profile mass shootings, including at an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, a country music festival in Las Vegas and an Independence Day parade in Highland Park, Illinois.

Sheila Gutman was one of dozens of people wounded on July 4, 2022, when a gunman fired 83 rounds into the parade crowd in less than a minute, killing seven. A single round created a wound the size of a baseball on her foot.
She still walks with a limp and suffers from near-constant nerve pain, despite weeks in the hospital and 17 surgeries. “I had no idea the damage it could do,” she said.

Several of the nation's deadliest mass shootings have involved semiautomatic rifles, said James Alan Fox, a Northeastern University criminology professor who maintains a mass killing database in a partnership with The Associated Press and USA Today.

Such attacks have killed nearly twice as many people on average as other mass shootings. “Assault weapons don’t change the likelihood of committing the crime but they do impact the level of carnage,” he said.
But the majority of mass shootings, particularly those away from public places, do not involve semiautomatic rifles, Fox said. Handguns are more prevalent in gun violence overall and mass shootings.

With all that in mind, Adam Winkler, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, questioned how much of an effect the Supreme Court’s eventual decision will have on gun violence more broadly. “I don’t think it’s going to have a big impact on public safety either way,” he said.
But the ruling could have a major impact on other gun laws.
The Supreme Court’s conservative majority issued a landmark decision in 2022 expanding gun rights, ruling that firearm restrictions must be rooted in the nation’s history.

That opinion unleashed a flood of challenges to gun laws across the country, though the Supreme Court has upheld some regulations since then. Lower court judges, meanwhile, have expressed confusion about exactly what the court’s new test means and how to apply it.

The assault weapons case could be another milestone. A key legal issue at the heart of the case is whether the widespread ownership of semiautomatic rifles means they cannot be subject to a blanket ban.

The administration argues that while bans on especially dangerous weapons such as machine guns have been upheld, there's no historical basis for similar restrictions on weapons “in common use” by law-abiding citizens.
Americans own an estimated 40 million AR-15-type rifles, according to a 2026 survey cited by challengers, making them more common than Ford F-Series pickup trucks.
“We’ve agreed, as a society, that certain policy choices are off the table in terms of trying to address a problem,” said Sack, of the Second Amendment Foundation.

Defenders of the laws in Connecticut and Illinois say the guns were originally designed as “weapons of war” and remain especially dangerous. Semiautomatic rifles today fire one round for each squeeze of the trigger, but their high-velocity rounds cause “catastrophic damage” to the human body, Connecticut’s attorneys said.
Just because the rifles have been sold to millions of people does not mean they cannot be subject to state regulations passed by democratically elected lawmakers, attorneys argue.
“Once it becomes clear that a new weapon poses an unacceptable threat to human life, legislatures should be able to act,” lawyers for Cook County, Illinois, wrote.
The Supreme Court’s decision is expected around the end of June.

title: Postponed Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day parade gets a do-over with 100 balloons and 1,000 clowns
summary: Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade is taking place a few days later than the holiday after being postponed due to bad weather
story: Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade is taking place a few days later than the holiday after being postponed due to bad weather
NEW YORK -- What's 48 hours? Macy's milestone 100th Thanksgiving Day parade is getting a do-over, long after most of the turkey leftovers have been repurposed into sandwiches.

The parade is set to step off Saturday morning with the same balloons and floats, 1,000 clowns and most of the original celebrities — plus the addition of LL Cool J and Gloria Gaynor — that were promised on Thursday, until bad weather postponed the annual kickoff of the holiday season.

“I’m pleased to say that we will deliver the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade that we’ve been planning for the last couple of years,” Will Coss, vice president and executive producer of Macy’s Studios, told The Associated Press late Friday.

A powerful storm forced the first-ever postponement of the holiday tradition. Some marching bands from afar scrambled to raise tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars to extend their stays in New York.

The original celebrity lineup included such stars as Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, JoJo and Jimmy Fallon & The Roots. There was also scheduled to be a tribute to Dolly Parton, led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer and Holly Robinson Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus. Gaynor, behind the timeless song “I Will Survive,” and actor-rapper LL Cool J have now been added.
NBC will broadcast the parade and stream it on Peacock from 8:30 a.m. to noon Eastern, followed by a rebroadcast of this year’s National Dog Show, a post-parade TV tradition marking its 25th year.

The parade follows a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) route that starts on Manhattan's Upper West Side before it finishes in Herald Square in front of the Macy's flagship store. It will feature its classic favorites, including Snoopy, Spider-Man and Buzz Lightyear, as well as some new ones, such as: Bluey, Earl the Squirrel and Hello Kitty Big Apple.

The weather Saturday morning should be dry, with “a little bit of wind in the morning,” but nothing like Thursday, National Weather Service meteorologist Matt Wunsch said Friday. He added that sustained winds are expected to be around 10 to 15 mph (16 to 24 kph) and gusts perhaps 25 mph (40 kph) or so.
Those speeds would be below the city’s decades-old threshold for grounding the parade’s large balloons.

The Thanksgiving storm scrambled planning for the parade that was over two and a half years in the making. Coss said one of the organizers' biggest hurdles was deflating the entire balloon complement, packing it up, bringing it to the studio and then re-prepping for Saturday.

title: EPA says no rise in contamination after Army detonates lead azide stockpile in Iowa
summary: Initial laboratory results indicate the controlled detonation of five tons of dangerous lead azide in southeastern Iowa has not caused a rise in the heavy metal in the bodies of water that supply drinking water to the area, the U.S. environmental agenc...
story: Initial laboratory results indicate the controlled detonation of five tons of dangerous lead azide in southeastern Iowa has not caused a rise in the heavy metal in the bodies of water that supply drinking water to the area, the U.S. environmental agenc...

Initial laboratory results indicate the controlled detonation of five tons of dangerous lead azide in southeastern Iowa has not caused a rise in the heavy metal in the bodies of water that supply drinking water to the area, the U.S. environmental agency said Saturday.
Test results from sampling done following the U.S. Army’s detonation of an aging stockpile of lead azide in Iowa were released by the Environmental Protection Agency.

The EPA said about 300 people spent Thursday in the field sampling schools, playgrounds, churches and homes across the region. More than 1,500 samples were taken of air, water, soil and dust before the detonation and hundreds of samples, including from homes, parks and drinking water, afterward.

“The EPA monitored for the presence of airborne lead for 30 consecutive hours after the controlled detonation using the Xact air monitoring systems. We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water samples … return and get validated,” the EPA said in a post on X.

Lead is a heavy metal that’s especially dangerous to children and pregnant women. The Army has said the safest option was to detonate the stockpile right away because it was degrading and might explode uncontrollably at any time as the weather got colder.
But the detonation has spurred widespread concerns about potential environmental contamination as well as questions about how and when the federal government communicated its plans.
Residents and some elected officials have criticized the Army for not being more transparent and providing more notice when it first determined the stockpile was unstable.

Residents in the tiny town of Middletown, where the Army stockpile was held, knew of the plans, but few others did — and the warnings largely failed to register with elected officials and the broader public until days before the planned detonation.

title: New Mexico authorities search for pregnant woman who escaped during prison transport
summary: New Mexico authorities say a pregnant woman serving prison time for vehicle thefts escaped by stealing a corrections transport vehicle
story: New Mexico authorities say a pregnant woman serving prison time for vehicle thefts escaped by stealing a corrections transport vehicle
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. -- A pregnant woman serving time in connection with vehicle thefts escaped by stealing a corrections transport vehicle, New Mexico authorities said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, fled Wednesday while being transported from a prenatal appointment in Albuquerque back to Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants, authorities said.
Taylor was sentenced to six years in prison after pleading guilty to four counts stemming from a series of vehicle thefts dating to 2024, according to court records.
She escaped while three correctional officers accompanying her were stopped at a Whataburger.

Taylor was not restrained during the drive because of her pregnancy, said Brittany Roembach, a spokesperson for the department. Taylor climbed from the back seat into the driver’s seat and drove away while an officer was standing nearby the vehicle, Roembach said.
A second inmate exited the vehicle after Taylor took control and is still in custody.

Police found the vehicle 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) away about an hour later, but Taylor was not inside. Her orange prison jumpsuit and a transport cellphone issued by the Corrections Department were found in the same area Wednesday afternoon.
The New Mexico Corrections Department is investigating how Taylor escaped, Roembach said.
Several law enforcement agencies searching for Taylor said she has ties to the Houston area as well as Albuquerque. They asked anyone who sees her to call 911.

title: King tides, strong waves destroy part of Pacifica pier as officials warn of flooding
summary: King tides combined with powerful waves have destroyed part of a pier in Northern California
story: King tides combined with powerful waves have destroyed part of a pier in Northern California

SAN FRANCISCO -- SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — King tides combined with powerful waves destroyed part of a pier in Northern California on Wednesday, and officials warned more beachfront homes are at risk of flooding.

A video showed a massive wave tearing down a portion of the pier in the city of Pacifica and slamming it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped, 1,140 feet-long (350 meters-long) pier in the summer after finding cracks in the structure.
Beachfront homes in the city south of San Francisco began flooding this week as king tides, the highest tides of the year, arrived in the area.

North of San Francisco, Marin County officials issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront properties in Stinson Beach, saying large waves expected through the afternoon could send water and debris into roads and homes. The warning was lifted later Wednesday but authorities advised people to stay away from the beach as large waves continue to pound the area.

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Pacific Coast and bay shorelines along San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay through 4 p.m. Wednesday. It also issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area for Wednesday, when breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 meters), about two to three stories high, could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.
“Rising tides will bring water and waves farther up the beach than normal, restricting escape from beaches and coastal area,” the weather service said.

King tides occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.
High tides have already flooded several communities this week along California’s coast.

In the Bay Area, some homes and streets in the coastal Marin County cities of Mill Valley, Larkspur, Sausalito and Corte Madera flooded. Farther north, in Humboldt County near the Oregon border, the sheriff’s office ordered evacuations in a small coastal community where most of the buildings flooded.

title: China and other US trading partners hit back at Trump's new tariff plans
summary: China, Japan, and other U.S. trading partners have protested planned tariff hikes by President Donald Trump's administration
story: China, Japan, and other U.S. trading partners have protested planned tariff hikes by President Donald Trump's administration
HONG KONG -- China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by the Trump administration and hit back Thursday at allegations they have excess manufacturing capacity.

The new tariffs, which are likely to take effect early next year, were announced Wednesday. They are intended to help reinstate tariffs for most of the economies after the Supreme Court ruling in February struck down most of U.S. President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs implemented last year.

The new import duties followed a monthslong Section 301 probe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he determined that practices of the 14 economies relating to excess capacity and production in manufacturing are “unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.”

China, one of the biggest trading partners of the U.S., is facing a 20% tariff. It slammed the notion of “overcapacity” as a “false premise.” The tariffs could double to 40% if the U.S. finds China not engaging adequately.

“China opposes its use as a pretext for political maneuvering,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said at a regular press briefing. “Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests.”
Beijing will take “necessary measures to defend its legitimate rights and interests,” he added.

The U.S. and China have extended by two months a trade truce that’s set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. The two countries also have agreed on tariff cuts on reciprocal lists of non-sensitive products worth about $60 billion in total.
Japan faces new U.S. tariffs of up to 15%. The Japanese government said it protested to Washington.
“Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a regular news conference Thursday.
“It is regrettable that the United States announced the proposed measures targeting Japan, and we have conveyed our position to the U.S. side.”
Singapore, due to be hit by an up to 20% tariff rate, said it was “very disappointed” with the U.S. proposal.
“Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidize manufacturing for export,” its Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said in a statement.

Malaysia said it “does not have excess capacity in its manufacturing sectors that distorts or disrupts global markets,” adding that it will continue to engage and consult with the United States. Vietnam, facing tariffs of up to 35%, said it's working with the U.S. on a trade deal.
Analysts say the 14 economies targeted by the Trump administration together account for roughly half of the global economy.

The latest U.S. tariffs are not as alarming as they look, said Stephen Brown, a chief economist with Capital Economics, as they are essentially broadly replacing, rather than adding to, earlier announced U.S. tariffs related to forced labor allegations announced in July.
Still, the new tariffs will likely help push prices higher and may “keep core goods inflation firm into next year,” he said in a commentary.
In Thailand, government spokesperson Lalida Persvivatana said Thursday that the latest U.S. proposal, capping tariffs at 18%, was more favorable than expected.

“The government will continue to pursue negotiations to secure competitive tariff levels and additional exemptions for Thai products, with the main goal of protecting Thailand’s export markets,” Persvivatana added.

The 27-nation European Union, which could be hit by a potential 15% tariff rate by the U.S., rejected “the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and pointed to the lack of joint action by the EU and the U.S.

Associated Press journalists Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Mari Yamaguchi and Mayuko Ono in Tokyo, Aniruddha Ghosal in Hanoi, Vietnam, Jintamas Saksornchai in Bangkok and Lorne Cook and Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report.

title: Trump heads to Arizona next week for a high-stakes expansion of TSMC's computer chip factories
summary: President Donald Trump plans to visit Arizona next week to speak at the groundbreaking of a new computer chip foundry for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. The company has been expanding aggressively in the Phoenix area, manufacturing chips for ma...
story: President Donald Trump plans to visit Arizona next week to speak at the groundbreaking of a new computer chip foundry for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. The company has been expanding aggressively in the Phoenix area, manufacturing chips for ma...

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. -- President Donald Trump, who has staked his economic policy on growth in the artificial intelligence sector, will travel to Arizona on Dec. 4 to speak at the groundbreaking for a new Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. computer chip foundry, according to both the White House and the Taiwan-based company.

The trip will come at the end of a week where AI comes under the microscope in Washington in the aftermath of Trump intervening to get his ally Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. Huang is slated to testify at a Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3 and will face questions about how his company has been selling its chips abroad — and his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Beijing has denied it.

TSMC has expanded aggressively in the Phoenix, Arizona, area, using its U.S. facilities to manufacture chips for tech companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, and Qualcomm. Trump is attending the start of construction on the fifth phase of TSMC's expansion in Arizona.
TSMC in July announced plans to spend another $100 billion on expanding its manufacturing capacity in the United States, bringing its total pledged investment in American chipmaking to $265 billion.

The size of the investment has grown as the development of artificial intelligence has stimulated demand for more computer chips, at the same time as Taiwan's dominance in chipmaking has led countries including the U.S. to address supply chain vulnerabilities by producing more domestically.

While Trump has sought to promote the investments as a function of his tariffs, the company began construction in Arizona during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden. The bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law by Biden, also helped to provide some financial support for the project.

The White House said the expansion would enable the creation of 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the wider community. The site currently accounts for more than 12,000 construction jobs.

title: FedEx airplane overruns runway at Miami airport, temporarily closing all but 1 runway
summary: Officials say a FedEx airplane has overrun a runway at the Miami International Airport
story: Officials say a FedEx airplane has overrun a runway at the Miami International Airport
A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before Thanksgiving, according to officials.

There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m., the airport reported. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground.
By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays.
The FAA, which is investigating, said the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis.
FedEx said the plane had “an issue upon landing” and that it is coordinating with investigating officials.
“We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries,” the company said in a statement.

FedEx had just started flying MD-11s again in May to deliver packages after that type of plane crashed in Kentucky last year as it was taking off. The UPS plane's left engine flew off and three pilots along with 12 people on the ground were killed. The FAA had approved Boeing’s proposed fix for the MD-11s “after extensive review.”
The airport recommended that passengers scheduled to fly Wednesday night should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before traveling to the airport.
“We appreciate our passengers’ patience as we work to safely resume normal operations,” the airport said in a statement.

The runway this FedEx plane landed on Wednesday is different than the one the Amazon cargo plane overran in September. But three of Miami’s runways converge at the west end, so the FedEx plane ended up close to where the Amazon plane careened across a road and struck a van filled with a plane cleaning crew.

The incident also comes less than two weeks after a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at the Miami airport. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the incident Wednesday. The National Transportation Safety Board said it had no information about the situation.
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk contributed.

title: Melania Trump reunites seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children with families
summary: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families
story: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families

WASHINGTON -- First lady Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families, bringing the total number of kids in these wartime reunifications to 43, the White House announced Wednesday.

It's the latest example of the first lady taking modest yet tangible interventions to address Russia's war in Ukraine, which started nearly five years ago. Her husband, President Donald Trump, had vowed to broker a quick end to the conflict but has said it's been harder than he expected.

“Children in this region of the world, like children everywhere, cannot possibly understand why geography and government have put them into the horrors of war," the first lady said in a statement shared first with The Associated Press.
“As adults, it is our moral imperative to elevate our children above the divisions that power war in order to restore the simple joys of life, immediately," she said.

Melania Trump said the reunification of these nine children with their families took place with the “full cooperation” of Russian and Ukrainian leaders. No additional information about the children was made available.
The first lady has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
The work began in August 2025, when she had the Republican president hand-deliver a letter that called for peace in Ukraine to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a summit in Alaska.

After a year, she had helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives after they had been separated because of the war, and she has said she has a “direct channel” with the leaders of the warring countries.

Then in October, she helped negotiate a six-day ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Earlier this month, she hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House to mark that milestone.

The local ceasefire in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. During the pause in the war, some 800 people were able to leave the city while food, water and other humanitarian aid were delivered to help those who stayed.
Follow the AP's coverage of first lady Melania Trump at https://apnews.com/hub/melania-trump.

title: As GLP-1 use grows, patients and doctors rethink Thanksgiving dinner
summary: Thanksgiving can be a challenge for those on weight loss medications like GLP-1s, but it doesn't have to derail progress
story: Thanksgiving can be a challenge for those on weight loss medications like GLP-1s, but it doesn't have to derail progress

WASHINGTON -- For many people, Thanksgiving can feel like a competitive eating event. But for Kim Dillard Davis, one of millions of American adults who take prescribed weight loss medications known as GLP-1s, it is a day like any other.

The 54-year-old Raleigh, North Carolina-based digital creator and wellness coach has lost around 80 pounds since 2023 using GLP-1s. Thanksgiving on a GLP-1 means she doesn't participate in the part of the holiday associated with indulgence.

“I can’t sit down and eat the amount of calories that I once could. I’ll still be able to sample everything, but I just can’t overdo it,” said Dillard Davis, who said she plans to be on the drug for life so long as her insurance is covering it.

More and more Americans are using GLP-1s, and as the medications become more popular, they could be changing some Americans’ approach to food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving, altering how they eat, what they enjoy about food and scrambling some social interactions surrounding food.

The jump in popularity comes as President Donald Trump's second administration has made expanding access to GLP-1s part of its health policy, arguing that the drugs, if made more affordable, could help combat rising obesity rates and other related chronic illnesses, eventually lowering broader healthcare costs.

While GLP-1s will likely cause major shifts in ways that are hard to predict, Ashley Gearhardt, a psychology professor at the University of Michigan, suggests the over-indulgence associated with the holiday could diminish over time.
“I anticipate that flavors and tastes that have been culturally linked with Thanksgiving will continue to be important. There just may be fewer turkey comas at the end of the day," she said.

Some people who use GLP-1s feel full faster and stay full longer, meaning they tend to eat smaller portions. The drugs have been reported to change how people think about food, reducing cravings and emotional eating but also diminishing the sensory pleasure people get from food. Some users also avoid eating rich or heavy foods, because the drugs can cause nausea or bloating.
Doctors say people who are just starting their weight loss journey this year with the drugs should be particularly mindful of potential side effects.

“Thanksgiving doesn’t have to be off-limits,” said John Horlander, a Louisville, Kentucky, gastroenterologist. “The key is moderation, smaller portions, avoiding excessive fatty foods, staying hydrated and recognizing warning signs.
"A little prevention can go a long way toward keeping someone out of the emergency room over the holiday.”

The Trump administration has framed its steps toward increasing access to and bringing down costs for GLP-1s as “a historic opportunity to reverse the obesity epidemic.” More than 100 million American adults are obese, according to the latest Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data.
In 2025, Trump, a Republican, signed a deal with drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to expand coverage and reduce prices for the popular weight loss drugs Zepbound and Wegovy.

And coverage of the drugs for obesity was expanded to Medicare patients this year when the federal government began offering a selection of the brand name medications to certain Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries for $50 a month through a new trial called Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. The program is scheduled to sunset after Dec. 31, 2027.

A June analysis by healthcare research nonprofit KFF found that 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries could be eligible for the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, based on claims data from 2023. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services does not provide projections of how many people will start taking GLP-1s as a result of the Trump administration’s actions. The agency wants to expand access to GLP-1 treatments, said a spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak publicly and talked to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Those policy changes come as the share of people on GLP-1 medications for weight loss has risen in the past few years — 11% of U.S. adults said they currently take the drugs for weight loss purposes, according to a Gallup poll conducted in May and June 2026. The poll found that 15% of Americans report having used the medicine for weight loss, an increase of 9 percentage points from two years ago.

That means Americans, even if they aren't taking the drugs, could find more people on the medication who are sitting across from them at the Thanksgiving table. That could change how people talk about eating.
Gearhardt said that dinner guests should be mindful about not pushing loved ones to eat or commenting on appearances.
“We all have a tendency to kind of monitor and police each other’s eating behavior," said Gearhardt, who studies food marketing and how addictive processes shape eating behaviors and mental health.

Commenting on how little or how much someone is eating “usually isn’t a great relationship strengthener,” she said. GLP-1 users might be especially sensitive, she said, because Thanksgiving can evoke feelings of grief over losing the intense reward sensation of highly processed foods.
Dillard Davis advised family members not to ask, “Is that all you’re going to eat?”
“Leave that phrase off the table. We’ve spent our whole lives overeating. Let us eat small portions and be happy,” she said.
Babak Orandi, an obesity medicine specialist at NYU Langone Health, said, “There’s a social aspect of eating, especially around the holidays. We don’t want to lose that.”
Patients, Orandi said, should focus “a little bit less on weight loss and a little bit more on weight loss maintenance” during the holidays, so as to not lose the enjoyment of eating.

For Dillard Davis, Thanksgiving has changed in other ways. Because of the reduced appetite brought on by the medication and to avoid large quantities of leftovers at home, her family has spent the last four years celebrating Thanksgiving at restaurants.
But as someone who has been on a weight loss journey since she was 8 years old, she has learned to accept the changes.
“We still have to eat," she said. "Just don’t worry about it so much.”

title: US plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
summary: President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
story: President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.

The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.

The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
Like China, Vietnam also faces a 20% rate, pending finalization of trade talks, the USTR said on Wednesday. The tariffs for other trading partners range from 10% to 18%.

The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.

Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.

China has pushed back consistently on U.S. tariffs. On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. “The so-called overcapacity is a false narrative, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”

The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.

The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
AP writer Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: What is lead azide? A look at the chemical being detonated at an Iowa Army base
summary: The U.S. Army has detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide at an Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
story: The U.S. Army has detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide at an Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
The U.S. Army has detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday.
Here's what to know about lead azide, and why local officials and scientists have some concerns about potential health and environmental effects from the explosion.
Lead azide, which typically appears as a white or colorless crystalline powder or needlelike crystals, is a highly sensitive chemical compound containing lead and nitrogen.
The compound is used as an initiating explosive in munitions, and historically has been used in detonators to set off other explosives, such as TNT.
It is sensitive to shock, heat, impact and friction, and may explode when dry. With temperature changes and time, lead azide can form unstable, larger crystals that are even more sensitive.
The decades-old lead azide supply in Iowa was crystallizing, posing the risk of spontaneous detonation.
Broken down, lead is a toxic heavy metal that can harm the brain, nervous system, kidneys, heart and other organs. Lead exposure also causes developmental damage.

As lead exposure can pose both immediate risks and longer health and environmental hazards, officials and researchers are questioning the levels of lead that might be in the air and nearby land and water sources, impacting residents, crops, cattle and wildlife after the detonation.
The military stopped using lead azide in the 1980s because of its hazards.
The Army says safety preparations ahead of Wednesday's detonation included barriers around the blast zone to reduce the spread of the resulting plume, along with ballistic gels to absorb lead dust.
Alexa St. John is an Associated Press climate reporter. Follow her on X: @alexa_stjohn. Reach her at ast.john@ap.org.
