title: Vance is set to serve up turkey to Air Force troops at an Ohio base pitched as Space Academy home
summary: Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children are planning to visit Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio
story: Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children are planning to visit Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio

DAYTON, Ohio -- DAYTON, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children are visiting Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, where they plan to serve a Thanksgiving meal to troops on Wednesday and join them for lunch.

The family plans to spend the holiday in the state, Vance's office said. The base in southwest Ohio is about 60 miles (97 kilometers) from their home in Cincinnati and close to where Vance was born. In tow for the trip: Ewan, 9; Vivek, 6; Mirabel, 4; and four-month-old Alec.

The visit comes just days after Ohio’s congressional delegation, led by Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, a friend and former Senate colleague of Vance, made a push for the Trump administration to locate the U.S. Space Academy close to the technologically advanced Wright-Patterson complex.

"What West Point is to the Army and Annapolis is to the Navy, Wright Field should be to the United States Space Force,” Moreno wrote in a letter co-signed by GOP Sen. Jon Husted and all 15 of Ohio’s U.S. representatives.

title: US travelers facing long airport lines, bad weather in the run up to Thanksgiving
summary: Thanksgiving travel is in full swing, with airline and road traffic ramping up across the U.S. But travelers in many spots are facing weather challenges, including rain on the East Coast, snow in the nation's mid-section and coastal flooding in the West
story: Thanksgiving travel is in full swing, with airline and road traffic ramping up across the U.S. But travelers in many spots are facing weather challenges, including rain on the East Coast, snow in the nation's mid-section and coastal flooding in the West

Airline and road traffic are ramping up even more on the eve of Thanksgiving on one of the busiest travel days in the U.S., with rain storms expected on the East Coast, snow in the nation's mid-section, coastal flooding in the West and lingering worries about technology failures.

Travelers at some airports took to social media to report long security-check lines on Wednesday morning. Some of the longest wait times were 81 minutes at Miami International Airport and around 40 minutes at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey and Portland International Airport in Oregon, according to the Transportation Security Administration.
The TSA expected to screen about 17.6 million passengers between Tuesday and Monday.

Terri Zimmerman said she waited in the security line at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport for nearly an hour early Wednesday morning before boarding a flight to Tallahassee to see relatives for the holiday.

“I was just surprised when we walked in to see that kind of line,” said Zimmerman, 71, a retiree from Deerfield Beach, Florida. "It was 5 a.m. in the morning. I thought we’d be like the first flight out and there wouldn’t be anybody there, but the place was packed.”
Zimmerman and scores of other South Florida travelers trudged through heavy rains that sparked concerns about more flooding in the Sunshine State.

AAA projected that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80 kilometers) between Tuesday and Monday, including nearly 73 million on the roads and nearly 6 million in the air. Another 2.6 million people were expected to take buses, trains and cruises.
The flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 31 flight cancelations and more than 1,100 delays in the U.S. on Wednesday morning.

For Tracy VanLeuven Miller, an early morning flight out of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to Atlanta did the trick Wednesday. It was the first time she had ever flown to see family for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. She sailed through baggage check and the TSA in less than 10 minutes, adding online, “Now I’m ready for a Mimosa!”

“As a military spouse (now retired), my family always traveled by car due to affordability,” she told The Associated Press via social media. “I decided to try air travel this year after a long, grueling road trip last year from northern Virginia to Atlanta. Since I’m traveling solo this year, I decided to fly, using points to absorb some of the crazy expensive plane ticket.”
For people on the road, bad weather was shaping up to be a challenge in parts of the country.

A major storm developing along the Eastern Seaboard could bring heavy rain, coastal flooding, high winds and power outages to the Carolinas on Wednesday and the northern Mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving, the National Weather Service said. Wind gusts could hit 50 mph (80 kph) along the Interstate 95 corridor. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.
Heavy rain was falling Wednesday morning in parts of Florida, the Carolinas, Mississippi and western Washington state.
Winter storm warnings and watches were posted for parts of Missouri and Illinois, with up to 9 inches (23 centimeters) of snow expected in the St. Louis area.
And king tides were continuing on the West Coast, with coastal flood warnings issued from Southern California to the San Francisco area to the Oregon and Washington coasts.

Travelers were also hoping to avoid new tech and system failures like the ones that upended airlines this month, including the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years caused by a Federal Aviation Administration network malfunction. Within the past week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

title: What's closed on Thanksgiving and when stores reopen on Black Friday
summary: Thanksgiving is for diet busters
story: Thanksgiving is for diet busters
Thanksgiving is for diet busters. Black Friday is for doorbusters.
Most big U.S. retailers will be closed on Thanksgiving Day. But they plan to open early the following day, Black Friday, as the holiday gift-buying season shifts into high gear.
Here are the holiday schedules for selected services and stores on Thursday and Friday:
Federal government offices, post offices and courts are closed on Thanksgiving but open the following day.

The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are closed Thursday. Both reopen on Friday for a shortened trading day, wrapping up at 1 p.m. EST. Banks, including Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, said local branches will be closed on Thanksgiving but ATMs and mobile banking will be available. Banks reopen on Friday.

Standard FedEx and UPS pickup and delivery services will not be available on Thanksgiving, although some critical services will be offered at certain locations. Both FedEx and UPS will operate as usual on Friday.

Check local grocery store listings online. Many major supermarket chains, including Kroger, Albertsons, Safeway and Sprouts, have reduced Thanksgiving Day hours. Whole Foods also will be open but individual locations may close early. All Trader Joe’s, Aldi and Publix stores will be closed. Hy-Vee will be open from 8 a.m. to 11 a.m. only for customers picking up premade holiday meals.
Walmart will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will open at 6 a.m. on Friday.
Target will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will open at 6 a.m. on Friday.
Dollar General stores in most states will be open on Thanksgiving from 7 a.m. – 8 p.m.
Costco will be closed on Thanksgiving but will reopen on Friday. Executive members get in starting at 9 a.m. Doors open to other members at 10 a.m.
Best Buy will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will open at 6 a.m. on Friday.
Macy’s will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will be open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. on Friday.
Kohl’s will be closed on Thanksgiving but will be open from 5 a.m. to midnight on Friday.

Walgreens said its nearly 8,000 stores will be open on Thanksgiving, with pharmacies operating in about half. Most locations will be open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and 24-hour locations will remain open around the clock.

title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
summary: The Trump administration has given SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space
story: The Trump administration has given SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk’s rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million “orbital compute modules” (forming a data center constellation called “Starmind”) would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing “the full power of the sun.”

“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move “opens a bold new frontier.”

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least “one authorized space station” by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.
Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers “a fantasy."
“It’s not going to happen,” he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun’s energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are “basic physical limits” to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.
He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

“You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions,” said Becker, noting such crashes could create “a cloud of debris” in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a “substantial number” of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites “serves the public interest” — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.
The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and “the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.”

“The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that “these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky.”
Becker echoed that sentiment. “It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye,” he said.
Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press’ requests for further comment Wednesday.

title: Inflation remains uncomfortably high despite a retreat in gas prices as challenges mount for the Fed
summary: A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas prices cooled in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington
story: A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas prices cooled in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington
WASHINGTON -- A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas prices cooled in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington.

The Commerce Department said Wednesday that consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September. On a monthly basis, consumer prices climbed 0.3% from September to October, down from a 0.6% increase the previous month.

The stubbornly elevated price figures come as the economy is expanding at a healthy pace, driven by strong consumer spending and surging business investment as large tech firms splurge on building out AI infrastructure. Consumer spending has been resilient even as persistent inflation raises the costs of many necessities and has soured most Americans on the economy. Yet much of the spending is driven by upper-income households, and there are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending.

Gas prices rose just 0.8% last month, according to the department, after surging 9.2% in September. Food prices, however, jumped 0.4% from September to October, the biggest monthly increase since April.

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core inflation accelerated to 3.3% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.1% in September. On a monthly basis, core prices rose 0.3% for the third month in a row.

The yearly core figure is now at its highest level in three years and above the Fed's target of 2%, which will likely intensify concerns among Fed officials that inflation is getting worse and further rate hikes are necessary.

Also Wednesday, the government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3% annual rate, the fastest in three years.
Consumer spending jumped 4.2% in the third quarter, while business investment soared 16.1%, lifted by big gains in spending on equipment and intellectual property products such as software.

“Taken together, the data reinforce the Fed’s latest assessment that growth in economic activity is ‘strong,’ meaning more must be done to bring inflation down,” Bradley Saunders, an economist at Capital Economics, a consulting firm, wrote.

The Fed combats inflation by lifting its key interest rate, which over time can raise borrowing costs for cars, homes and credit cards. By discouraging borrowing and spending, the Fed seeks to cool the economy and inflation.

Many officials have signaled that they support raising the Fed's short-term rate, and economists expect an increase at its next policy meeting Dec. 8-9. Solid economic growth and still-high inflation suggest that the Fed's key rate isn't yet high enough to cool price increases.
In October, the government also reported that incomes jumped 0.7%, before adjusting for inflation, a healthy gain after prices rose faster than incomes in the previous month.

In another report, the number of people applying for unemployment benefits dropped 13,000 to just 189,000, a very low figure by historical standards and evidence that layoffs are low and companies are mostly holding onto their workers.

title: A timeline of key events in Kilmar Ábrego García's fight with the Trump administration
summary: Kilmar Ábrego García has been a focal point in the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies
story: Kilmar Ábrego García has been a focal point in the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies

Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it. His complicated legal fight after that galvanized both sides of the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies.

In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries. A criminal case in Tennessee, where the government accused him of human smuggling, was dismissed after a judge found evidence of “vindictive prosecution” by the Justice Department. Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Here is a timeline of key events:
Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.
Ábrego García is arrested outside a Maryland hardware store. Police accuse him of being a gang member and turn him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family. He is given a work permit and placed under federal supervision.
Ábrego García is detained by ICE in Maryland while driving home with his 5-year-old son.
Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.
The U.S. Supreme Court says the Trump administration must work to bring Ábrego García back.
In defiance of Trump, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland meets with Ábrego García at a hotel in El Salvador, helping to establish hope and momentum for Ábrego García’s family.
Ábrego García is returned to the U.S. and charged with human smuggling, based on a Tennessee traffic stop from 2022.
ICE announces plans to remove him to a series of African countries, but is blocked by an injunction from a Maryland federal judge.

Ábrego García leaves the Tennessee jail, where he has been since June, to return to his family in Maryland and await trial. Within minutes of his release, ICE sends notice that they intend to deport him to Uganda.
Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.
A federal judge in Maryland orders ICE to immediately release Ábrego García.
A Maryland federal judge rules ICE cannot re-detain Ábrego García.
A federal judge in Tennessee dismisses the human smuggling case against Ábrego García after finding evidence that the government engaged in “ vindictive prosecution."
The Justice Department tells a federal appeals court that the federal judge in Tennessee erred in his scathing May ruling in the criminal case against Ábrego García.

Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport. According to an unsealed Nov. 20 order, a federal judge said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.” The judge, in turn, set Nov. 24 as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.
Ábrego García lands at Madrid’s international airport. He doesn't speak to reporters but raises a fist as he enters a van.

title: Judge halts order for Georgia's Fulton County to give 2020 election records to state election board
summary: A judge has paused an order for Georgia's Fulton County to hand over digital copies of ballots and other records from the 2020 election to the State Election Board
story: A judge has paused an order for Georgia's Fulton County to hand over digital copies of ballots and other records from the 2020 election to the State Election Board

ATLANTA -- A judge on Wednesday put on hold an order instructing Georgia's Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of ballots and other records from the 2020 election that were seized by the FBI earlier this year to the State Election Board.

Fulton County Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe on Tuesday had ordered county election officials to deliver the records to the board by 5 p.m. Wednesday. But after county election officials filed a notice of appeal, she granted the county's request to halt her order while the appeal is pending.

The FBI served a search warrant at the Fulton County elections hub on Jan. 28 seeking records related to the 2020 election, leaving with hundreds of boxes containing ballots and other records. The county unsuccessfully sought to have a judge order the return of the records, but the federal government did provide the county with what it said was a digital copy of the records that were taken.

A majority of the State Election Board aligned with President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to reopen a case alleging wrongdoing by Fulton County during the 2020 election. The board in November 2024 served subpoenas on the county seeking records related to that election.

The overwhelmingly Democratic county, which includes most of the city of Atlanta, has been a target of Trump and his allies since he narrowly lost the presidential election in Georgia to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. Trump has insisted without evidence that widespread voter fraud in the county cost him victory in the state. Multiple courts and state and federal officials have found no evidence of fraud that would have altered the outcome.

County election officials asked a judge to quash the subpoenas from the State Election Board. Fulton County Superior Court Judge Robert McBurney in December 2025 declined, finding that the board's inquiries “fell squarely within the SEB’s authority.” He ruled that the state board would have to bear the costs of producing the records it was seeking, and a hearing on that matter was pending when the FBI seized the county’s records. As a result of the seizure, McBurney put the case on hold.
Ellerbe, who took over the case this year, held a hearing on the matter in October before issuing her order Tuesday.

title: FACT FOCUS: Maps online falsely claim to show the path of fallout from Iowa lead azide detonation
summary: Maps falsely claiming to show the projected fallout from the Army's controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa have spread on social media
story: Maps falsely claiming to show the projected fallout from the Army's controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa have spread on social media
Maps falsely claiming to show the projected fallout of a controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday spread widely on social media in advance of the blast.

One showed lead dust spreading throughout the Midwest and Southeast. Another had it reaching Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan and Ohio. In a third, the contamination enveloped the entire East Coast and in another it expanded in all directions, moving as far south as New Orleans and north toward Montana.

But none of these maps are accurate. The U.S. Army, which conducted the blast, released updated maps early Wednesday morning that include a much more contained area. They predicted that winds would blow the plume, potentially containing toxic lead dust, southwest from the detonation site at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and into nearby Missouri.
Here's a closer look at the facts.
CLAIM: Toxic lead dust from a controlled detonation of lead azide will spread far beyond Iowa and Missouri, according to maps of the projected fallout.

THE FACTS: This is false. Official maps published by the U.S. Army projected the plume heading from southwest Iowa as far as northern Missouri. In some cases, social media users misrepresented maps that showed unrelated data.

Those in charge of the detonation called it a success. All of the lead azide was successfully destroyed, said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who led the Army operation. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency air monitors detected no lead in the air around the ammunition plant in Middletown, about 200 miles (300 kilometers) west of Chicago.

Still, it’s unclear yet whether the plume carried any toxic lead toward the homes and farms in its path. Lead is a heavy metal that’s not safe at any level and is especially dangerous to children and pregnant women. Government agencies plan to do more testing in the days and weeks ahead. Independent researchers also intend to do extensive environmental testing on water sources, farms, homes and playgrounds.

One map misrepresented on social media shows the Midwest with colored bands expanding from an orange center on the border of Missouri and Illinois. It has nothing to do with the lead azide detonation. The map, which was created with the College of DuPage's weather prediction modeling tool, shows snowfall accumulation predicted for Friday. It is labeled as such in the top-left corner.

On another map, skinny blue lines cover states in many different regions. But the lines represent Mississippi River tributaries, not the path of the plume. A map published by the EPA shows a similar tributary structure, as does one from the conservation nonprofit American Rivers.

The Army took steps to mitigate the spread of the plume. The hazardous materials were surrounded by concrete and sand barriers two stories high. Additional “blast barriers” were set up around the two bunkers where the 68 barrels of lead azide were detonated. Ballistic gels, foams and more than 100,000 gallons (380,000 liters) of water were intended to absorb the lead dust. A video of the site released by the Army before the detonation showed a bunker encased by an earth berm and sand-filled blocks.

Following two loud booms around 9 a.m. local time, a pair of wispy white plumes rolled high in the air before quickly dissipating, according to an Associated Press report. The Army attributed the smoke to the foam.

Environmental groups had filed a lawsuit to halt the detonation, but a court ruling on Monday put it back on track. A federal appeals court found the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.
Find AP Fact Checks here: https://apnews.com/APFactCheck.

title: High school band raises $350K to stay for Macy's Thanksgiving parade
summary: Other marching bands from around the U.S. are also raising funds to cover the cost of staying in New York City after the parade was rescheduled for Saturday.
story: One high school marching band from Texas says it has raised $350,000 to cover the cost of its 500-member group remaining in New York City after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was rescheduled until Saturday due to a potentially historic storm hitting the region on Thursday.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School in Texas, told CBS News about raising the funds required to cover the extended trip.

"I started scrambling through that," Demkovich said. "Can we find a hotel to stay in? Can we get our transportation back? How, at the last second on a holiday weekend, how astronomical are the prices going to be?"

Other marching bands that traveled to New York from across the country are also raising money to cover the cost of their extended stays. For many of the high school musicians, the parade is a once-in-a-lifetime chance to perform for millions of spectators along the route and watching at home, and the postponement has made the trip significantly more expensive.
"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Demkovich added.
In just the span of a few hours, the Pearland community came together to raise hundreds of thousands of dollars.
"They organized a fundraiser, they went on news stations, they broadcasted it, they posted it to get the word across," Pearland High School senior and band member Deborah James told CBS News.

By Thursday, the band had raised enough money to pay for two extra nights at a hotel and to charter buses back to Texas after the parade on Saturday. One logistical challenge: They'll have to relocate from the Marriott Marquis in Times Square, which is booked for the weekend, to a hotel near the Meadowlands Sports Complex in New Jersey.
And they'll travel home by bus on Saturday because flights are booked until late Monday or Tuesday, Demkovich said. The donations also cover extra meals for the ensemble.
"We are going to make sure you stay there," Kevin Cole, Pearland's former mayor, said of the band. "We are going to make sure you get to perform."

The parade's delay also scrambled plans for tourists and family members who had traveled to New York to see the parade on Thursday. Among them was the Sims family, who traveled from Florida to see their daughter perform as part of the Great American Marching Band.
"We came up to see her. It's our first time in New York City," Dustin Sims told CBS New York. "We've had a great week, but now we gotta decide whether we're gonna stay another day or not."
Outpouring of support

Demkovich told CBS News that the group's fundraising push quickly spread across social media, soliciting contributions from Pearland businesses with a history of charitable giving and from strangers alike.

Several Texas businesses, including Gringo's Mexican Kitchen in Pearland and Houston's Mattress Mack and CenterPoint Energy, opened their wallets by making generous donations through a fundraising link on the marching band's website.

Eight other marching bands are scheduled to perform on Saturday. The Dobyns-Bennett High School Band from Kingsport, Tennessee, also issued a plea on social media, calling on its community to help defray the cost of the band staying in New York through Saturday.

"While we are grateful that our students will still have the opportunity to perform in this historic 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade during the Dobyns-Bennett Band's own centennial year, this unexpected change presents significant logistical and financial challenges for our program," the group said in a post on social media on Wednesday.

"Extending our stay in New York City means additional expenses that were never anticipated in our original trip budget, including extended charter bus rentals, additional nights of hotel accommodations, and meal stipends for our students," the group added.

By Thursday morning, the Dobyns-Bennett Band said it had met its undisclosed fundraising goal and that the band would be staying in New York through Saturday to perform in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
"We have secured the necessary funding for the band to stay the extra night and to pay for the extended bus contract to get the kids home on Saturday!" the group said in the post.

title: French actor Gérard Depardieu to stand trial on rape charge
summary: A lawyer representing French actor Gérard Depardieu says he has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a young actress at his Paris home in 2018.
story: French actor Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping an actress at his Paris home in 2018, one of his lawyers told The Associated Press on Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Defense lawyer Delphine Meillet wrote in a message to the AP that the 77-year-old actor would face trial over only one of the two alleged rapes reported by actress Charlotte Arnould.
Depardieu, who has denied the rape allegations, had challenged an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send him to trial.
The Paris Court of Appeal upheld that decision Thursday in relation to one of the two alleged rapes.
"He disputes the decision," Meillet told AP, without specifying whether Depardieu would file a further appeal.

Arnould first lodged a complaint in 2018, when she was 22. The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
For half a century, Depardieu was a towering figure in French cinema.

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, he became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

Earlier this month, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology.
"I was found guilty," Depardieu said in a written statement on Nov. 16, adding that he accepted the sentence.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters"). The case was widely seen as a test of the French film industry's response to the #MeToo movement.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said in his statement.

Depardieu's behavior toward women came under renewed scrutiny in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.
French President Emmanuel Macron drew criticism from women's rights activists at the time when he defended Depardieu, saying the actor "makes France proud."
Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in France over the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to pursue women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.
Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.
His career spanned hundreds of films, including "The Last Metro," "Jean de Florette" and the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

title: Andy Taylor, longtime Duran Duran guitarist, dies at 65
summary: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died at age 65 following a battle with prostate cancer.
story: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran — whose huge pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf," "The Reflex" and "Rio" — and who were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.

Taylor died following a "courageous battle with prostate cancer," his family and the band said in a joint statement posted to social media. He died Monday at his home surrounded by friends and family.
"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his family said.

On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote at the time. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."
His family said Wednesday that Taylor "faced the last few years with so much courage and determination until the very end, never losing his love of life."

The two-time Grammy Award winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," the band said in Wednesday's statement. "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music."

The band's 1981 debut album "Duran Duran" had their first hit single, "Planet Earth," but it was "Rio" that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: "They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — 'Tiger Beat' fashion pinups who rocked arenas."

The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as "Girls on Film" and "Union of the Snake" and the moody ballads "The Chauffeur" and "Save a Prayer." Other hits in the coming years included "The Wild Boys," "New Moon on Monday" and "Come Undone." Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song "A View to a Kill" and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band was all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics.

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie "Barbarella." Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the "Fab Five." Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a "Live-Wire Guitarist." None of the Taylors were related.

"We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band," Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.

The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with "Some Like It Hot" and "Get It On."

In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album "Notorious," produced by Nile Rodgers — with hits including the title single and "Skin Trade" — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997's "Medazzaland" and 2000's "Pop Trash" — but returned for 2004's "Astronaut."

Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: "People have wrongly assumed that I didn't want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band."

Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children — Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy — and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them.

title: Beloved drive-thru worker on making a year's salary on last day of work
summary: When Sighle Williams decided to retire from Mac's Drive Thru after 37 years, she never could have expected the send-off she received, which is the focus of a new Netflix documentary.
story: Sighle Williams keeps it simple.
"I just like to treat people the way I like to be treated," she told "CBS Mornings."

So when Williams, who'd spent her 37-year career making people smile at Mac's Drive Thru in Gainesville, Florida, was approached about having a documentary made about her last day, she was excited but a bit skeptical.
That short film, called "One Last Order," premieres on Netflix Tuesday and has already garnered awards from the Aspen Shortfest, Nantucket Film Festival, Miami Film Festival and more.

The movie documents Williams' final day on the job, but it also shows the side of Williams that her beloved customers didn't see, like how she raised five girls — her sister and niece's children — as her own. The film shares how she lived in a house for a while with no running water or electricity.
"I just did what I needed to do, I knew I needed to make sure they were straight, and I needed to make sure I went to work," she said.
When she went to work, she made everyone feel like she was glad to see them. She remembered people's orders.

On her last day at Mac's, her boss decided that every dollar made would go back into Williams' pocket as a retirement bonus. Community members lined up around the block and waited for up to four hours to say goodbye and give Williams one final order.
The whole thing made her feel on "top of the world," she told "CBS Mornings."

"I didn't even eat all day, I didn't go to the restroom all day," Williams said, "I was just so -- I wanted to acknowledge everybody and thank everybody for coming out, you know, sharing the love with me on my last day."
She ended up making a year's salary on that final day, but won't reveal how much she made.
"I don't want nobody to feel no type of way because, you know, I'm hamburgers and fries," she said.
Now that she's been retired for a couple of years, Williams has some time for herself.
"I'm traveling, I'm ready to go," she said. "With the film fests, I've been going to different places and enjoying myself."
When asked about where her drive comes from, she said, "Just be kind. Just be patient and, you know, don't take everything so serious."

title: Don Toliver concert in U.K. evacuated due to mystery substance
summary: Some 12,000 fans of American rapper Don Toliver had to evacuate his concert in Manchester, England, after a noxious substance spread through the arena.
story: More than 12,000 people were evacuated from an arena in northern England Sunday night after the crowd at American rapper Don Toliver's concert suddenly started screaming, choking and coughing when a powerful smell spread through the venue.
Police said the Co-op Live arena in Manchester was evacuated at about 10 p.m. (5 p.m. Eastern).
There's been speculation online that the mysterious substance that spread through the air in the arena was tear gas, but authorities have not confirmed that.
Don Toliver, who is set to end a world tour with a Tuesday night show in London, left the stage in Manchester and police declared it a major incident.
One person was hospitalized and dozens were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms according to the local ambulance service.
The arena was being fully decontaminated as a precaution, the emergency medical service said.
Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News newspaper that he was in the audience standing section when he "started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy."

He said the lights came on as Toliver left the stage, but that everyone remained in the venue for almost an hour before an announcement asking people to make their way out was heard over the loudspeaker.
"We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about," Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker told reporters.
The venue opened in 2024 and is only about 2 miles from the Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in 2017 by a suicide bomber who blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert.

title: Tony Shalhoub on food, family, and his book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave"
summary: For the award-winning star of "Monk," food had always been an integral part of family. And now he's teamed with daughter Josie Adams to write a food memoir: "We Thought They'd Never Leave," the story of their family reunions - and their recipes.
story: He was a detective with a quirk in "Monk," and played an alien opposite the "Men in Black." But if you really want to feel the soul of Tony Shalhoub, this character might be it: the stubborn chef Primo in "Big Night," his 1996 film with Stanley Tucci about food, family and … even more food.

Shalhoub is himself an investor in a New York City restaurant, Massara, where he invited us last week to break bread with his daughter, Josie Adams. The act of breaking bread, he said, is very important: "It's part of the family tradition, really. Having bread at the center of the table, it's how we were formed."
He's even made a TV series, "Tony Shalhoub Breaking Bread," about different types of bread from different places.

For him and his family, the passion for food can be traced back to a time when there wasn't any. Shalhoub's father, Joseph, was born in war-torn Lebanon. Orphaned at a young age, he faced hunger and food shortages as a child. "A lot of his early memories were about that hunger," he said, "so that ties into our current family situation and our appreciation for and devotion to preparing food and feeding each other."
The Shalhoubs settled in Green Bay, Wisconsin, and by the time Tony came along in 1953, there were a lot of mouths to feed; he was one of ten children.

The family was close, and stayed that way. Every summer, the entire extended Shalhoub clan – more than 50 in all – gathers in Wisconsin for a reunion. It's a week of big, homecooked meals and intense family bonding. And when the party's over, everyone gets a traditional Shalhoub family send-off: "At the end of the week," Tony said, "as people are loading up their cars, everyone else who's remaining gathers in a line in the drive and raises their hands," and a chorus cries out: "We thought they'd never leave!"
"We Thought They'd Never Leave" became the title of a book Shalhoub co-wrote with Josie, the story of their family and its recipes.

She actually started it during the pandemic, when both of her parents (Tony and actor Brooke Adams) were sick with COVID, and she feared that their memories and recipes would be lost forever. So, she gave them both journals to write it all down. "My dad was like, 'Do you think we're going to die? Why are you giving us this right now?'" Josie said. "He's like, 'I'm better now!' So I said, 'OK, well, will you maybe work on this cookbook with me? I'd like to do the family cookbook for real.' And he said yes."

Shalhoub and his wife raised two daughters in Los Angeles as he navigated the feast-or-famine life of a Hollywood actor. But for every Emmy-winning success like "Monk," there were lesser roles. "Sometimes there were jobs that I did that were just for the money," he said. "Do I regret doing those jobs? Not really. I mean, maybe one or two, but sometimes you just got to eat."
In 2016 he said he wanted to take a break from screen acting, move to New York, and just do live theater. He won a Tony Award for best lead actor in a musical for "The Band's Visit."
But then he got a job offer that was irresistible. As family patriarch Abe Weissman in "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel," Shalhoub won his fifth Emmy.

In real life, Shalhoub has been married to Brooke Adams for 34 years, and he actually does a lot of the cooking at home. Josie said, "Yeah, you cook for Mom a lot. Every morning my dad wakes up before my mom and makes her a cappuccino and brings it to her in bed. Every single morning."
"Except when I'm not there!" he laughed.
And that's the Shalhoub family's love language: cooking and serving each other, whether it's one loved one, or a crowd of 50.

Josie said, "It's really easy to send a text and say, 'I love you, thinking about you.' But it's a lot harder to do something for someone else. And that's what this whole reunion is about: getting together and showing the people that you love, that you love them."

title: Kwame Onwuachi's culinary journey
summary: The New York Times named the award-winning chef's Tatiana the best restaurant in the city two years in a row. Kwame Onwuachi discusses his Afro-Caribbean menu, and his path to becoming one of today's brightest culinary stars.
story: New York City's famed Lincoln Center is a dream destination for ballerinas, baritones, and one award-winning chef. As a youngster, Kwame Onwuachi sat on the steps in the plaza, taking a break from selling candy on the subway. "I never thought that one day ... I would have my sister's name on the side of the building," he said.

Onwuachi's restaurant Tatiana, located right on the renowned plaza, is one of the hardest reservations to book. The New York Times named Tatiana the best restaurant in New York City two years in a row; Time magazine put Onwuachi on their list of Most Influential People; and the James Beard Foundation gave him the Rising Star Award.

For Onuwuachi, now 37, he's just cooking what he knows. Asked to characterize the food he makes, he replied, "I would say Afro-Caribbean. The technical term is African people who came through the Caribbean. You're going to see a couple different things from these different regions, but they're all tied together. Jambalaya and joloff rice, gumbo and okra stew, right? Barbecue and suya. Like, these things are connected."
Onwuachi's love of food started early. He grew up in the Bronx. His mother was a caterer, his father an architect.

Asked his first memory of food, Onwuachi said, "Oh man, I remember very, very vividly being on my grandmother's hip, and her putting this piece of bread, this thin bread with, like, this electric, almost like a muted electric green sauce into my mouth. And it was curry goat with roti. And I remember the explosion of flavors. It was very vivid."

As a teenager, he found himself working a variety of jobs, but always had an appetite for the kitchen. He enrolled at the Culinary Institute of America in Hyde Park, New York. On a return visit, he said, "It's always feels good to be back here. So many memories, so many, like, defining moments for me, like truly becoming like a leader – that happened here."

He's a star there now, mentoring students at the school that gave him direction and purpose, when he was one of the few Black students in his class. "I think there was two of us in my class," he said. Asked how it made him feel, he said, "I'm a chef, for God sakes! I took it out on the lobsters.

"I focused on my studies at the end of the day," he said. "It's reflective of the industry, too, in the fine dining sense. There's not a lot of people of color in that. I didn't focus on this, but I knew I wanted to use my platform to help amplify my culture."

Onwuachi has a lot on his plate. Over the past decade, he's been everywhere from bookshelves to competing on shows like "Top Chef." He now has three restaurants, including Dogon in Washington, D.C., and his latest, Maroon, which opened last April on the Las Vegas Strip.

For Kwame Onuwachi, success never gets stale. And we witnessed him receive Maroon's first big review last month, when the Los Angeles Times called his restaurant "the best steakhouse in Las Vegas, and beyond."
But the chef says he's cooking up more than just food.
"I think if a dish tells a story, it has a soul," Onuwachi said. "You're not just cooking for perfect seasoning, you're cooking to share something with someone."

title: Brits are having less sex, but watching a lot of porn, survey finds
summary: A third of Brits aged 16 to 24 have never had sex, a landmark survey finds, though most acknowledge sexting and watching pornography.
story: London — One-third of Brits between the ages of 16 and 24 have never had sex, according to a large-scale, periodic survey that has studied the prevalence of sexting and pornography use for the first time.

The decline in youth sexual activity is part of a wider trend of British people having less sex compared to previous generations, all revealed in the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), a survey of nearly 7,000 Britons between 2022 and 2024, which was published Tuesday in The Lancet medical journal.

Adults aged 45 and below are having sex twice a month on average, down from four times a month in 1990-91, and three in 2010-12, according to the survey. The proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds who said they had never had sex rose from 18% to 38% among women and 18% to 28% among men, compared to the previous Natsal study.
The latest survey was the first time participants had been asked about their online activity.

Half of the women respondents between 16 and 24 said they had watched pornography   in the past year, while 86% of young men said they had. Half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phone in the past year.

"There has been an emerging shift towards less sexual experience among young people," wrote the authors of the study. "Sexual lifestyles now commonly incorporate online behaviors such as sexting and pornography, especially for young people."

One of the researchers on the project, Prof. Wendy Macdowall at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told CBS News partner BBC News that while it may be tempting to link the online activity with the decline in sexual activity, there are several other reasons for the drop, "especially among young people."

Similar declines among young people have been observed "in other high-income countries," the study states, and while "these changes are not yet well understood," it added, the shifts have coincided with rising rates of mental health conditions and declines in alcohol consumption, and "later attainment of traditional markers of adulthood," as well as "increasingly online lives."

Respondents reported an increase in masturbation across all age groups and genders, as well as sexting and pornography use, according to the survey's authors, but while that "might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behavior … masturbation and pornography use were lower among those reporting never having had sex, challenging the notion these behaviors simply substitute one another."
The study did not ask participants about any use of artificial intelligence in sexuality.

"When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi," Soazig Clifton, a researcher on the Natsal project from University College London, told the BBC. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behavior and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."
The study also revealed that the average number of sexual partners over a lifetime for people in the U.K. is five, and that same-sex intercourse has increased among both men and women.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: OpenAI countersues Apple over allegations of stealing trade secrets
summary: OpenAI alleged in a lawsuit Friday that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing trade secrets.
story: OpenAI on Friday responded to Apple's June lawsuit accusing the company of stealing trade secrets by countersuing.

The ChatGPT maker alleged that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing proprietary information. Apple created "a situation in which it can accuse virtually any departing employee, and their new employer, of 'stealing' purported Apple trade secrets," the suit, filed in the Northern District of California, claims.

In a statement provided to CBS News Friday, an Apple spokesperson said that the case "is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information. OpenAI's counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple's confidential information."

Apple's complaint in June accused OpenAI and two of its employees, Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan and Chang Liu, a technical staffer at the company, of stealing Apple's proprietary information to help OpenAI develop its own hardware. Both formerly worked at Apple.

OpenAI claims in its countersuit Friday that Apple's employment practices are designed to set a trap for a departing employee and their future employer — "a trap that can be sprung whenever Apple sees an opportunity to slow down a potential competitor."

Tech analysts expect OpenAI to make a foray into hardware design, putting it in more direct competition with Apple. In July 2025, OpenAI acquired the AI device startup of former Apple star designer Jony Ive, io Products Inc.

title: How Nestlé chefs are making meals to target GLP-1 users
summary: Major chains and food companies are trying new products targeted at GLP-1 users, estimated at about 11% of the U.S. population.
story: As millions of Americans take GLP-1 drugs for weight loss, food and beverage companies are working hard to keep up with their changing tastes.

Nearly every major chain is trying new products targeted at GLP-1 users, estimated at about 11% of the U.S. population — or around 30 million people. Starbucks and Dunkin' are selling protein drinks, Chipotle offers a high-protein menu and McDonald's is exploring smaller meal sizes.
And it's not just restaurants. Companies like Conagra, General Mills and Kraft have all developed GLP-1-friendly foods. Even processed snacks like Doritos now feature protein-packed options.
At Nestlé's test kitchen near Cleveland, Ohio, chefs are working on new recipes targeting GLP-1 users. "CBS Mornings" took an exclusive look at their efforts.

Anna Kim, the senior chef of culinary innovation, creates frozen meals for Nestlé's Vital Pursuit line, which is marketed specifically to GLP-1 users. She said proteins like beef and chicken are popular, along with vegetables such as potatoes, tomatoes and broccoli.
One of the latest creations is a cheddar cheese smashburger bowl, with 30 grams of protein and 8 grams of fiber.
"Consumers are eating more nutrient-dense meals in smaller portions, so every bite matters more," Kim said.

Jenn Barnes, Nestlé's vice president of marketing, said the shift toward GLP-1s is the biggest she has seen in her career. The drugs have "democratized health," she said. She isn't concerned about data that shows GLP-1 users eating less, she said.
"I see it as an opportunity to meet people where they're at, as they're continuing to evolve their eating," Barnes said.

While Nestlé is courting GLP-1 users, data shows the majority of those who buy the healthier Vital Pursuit meals are actually not on GLP-1s, showing that even people who don't use the drugs are looking for healthier food.

The healthier meals do come at a cost. Kim said that any time a dish is made with higher-quality ingredients, there's a price increase. The Vital Pursuit meals cost about $5 each, while Lean Cuisine, another Nestlé line, runs closer to $3 apiece, but has less fiber and protein.

Maeve Webster, the founder of Menu Matters, said that Nestlé is far from the only manufacturer to be thinking about healthier options. Menu Matters tracks food trends for national manufacturers and restaurant chains.
"There's no doubt that GLP-1s are absolutely part of the innovation process for many, if not most, manufacturers," Webster said.
Soon, trends may change so fast that major companies can't keep up, she said.
"We're going to reach a point where trends are moving so quickly that large manufacturers (and) chain restaurants simply can't keep on top of it," Webster said.

title: Allstate roiled by tech outage over Thanksgiving week
summary: The insurer's systems are out of commission during the busiest road travel period of the year, leaving customers unable to access roadside assistance.
story: Allstate has joined the growing list of companies bedeviled by a technology disruption in recent weeks, leaving some customers unable to file claims or seek roadside assistance during Thanksgiving week.

The Northbrook, Illinois-based insurer said in a statement on Wednesday that some of its services had been restricted after customers reported being unable to access them on social media and on Downdetector, which tracks web outages.

"Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims," the company said. "To the extent service interruptions impact a customer's ability to make a payment, they won't lose coverage or be charged late fees."
People seeking roadside assistance on Allstate's website encountered an error message through Friday.
In a statement on its website, Allstate added that customers may reach the insurer through multiple channels, including by phone.

Allstate offers a range of policies, including home, life and auto insurance. Its consumer-facing tech problems during one of the busiest times of year for road travel follow disruptions at other major U.S. airlines, banks, software providers and government agencies.
Microsoft, which suffered a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, said a technical issue caused the disruption and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio also said at the time that the tech outages were distinct from one another. The incidents were caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems, they said.

"In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio said. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

title: Fake online stores may fool AI shopping bots on Black Friday
summary: AI bots are accidentally steering shoppers toward websites and online shops created by scammers using AI.
story: Scammers are using AI to churn out convincing copies of real online stores, and this Black Friday, the AI agents that many shoppers will rely on often can't tell the difference.
These fake sites pose a risk to the millions of Americans who are tasking their AI agents with making online purchases and transacting on their behalf.

"Artificial intelligence just makes building websites so much easier. You can upload anything into HTML and build a website very, very easily," Harrison Tang, co-founder of Spokeo, a data aggregator, told CBS News.

AI is enabling scammers to build what Tang described as convincing dupes of legitimate online stores in only hours, including copies of a brand's logo, marketing language and product images and descriptions.

"AI just makes creating these look-alike fake stores a lot easier, so there is a proliferation of them," Tang explained. "Platforms will try to catch them by not directing users there, but there are so many of them popping up all the time that they are hard to keep up with."
Research from Microsoft shows that criminals can use AI to set up fraudulent e-commerce sites in mere minutes rather than the days or weeks that were once required.

Spokeo identified copycat sites of dozens of popular brands, including UGG, L.L. Bean, Converse and Stella McCartney. As of Nov. 15, it had identified 65 distinct online stores that mimicked the legitimate sites of 60 brand names, according to its online shopping scam study.
The discrepancies between the authentic stores and the scam websites are subtle and require close examination.

The first place to look for proof of fraud, according to Tang, is in the online store's web address. For example, a fake Converse store uses the web address converseshop.us.com, whereas the real store's address is converse.com. The .us domain name is the top-level domain for the U.S. and is reserved for U.S. residents, but is commonly used for phishing attempts, according to Tang.
"It looks like an official website, but it's not, so if you don't pay close attention, it's easy to get tricked," he said.
AI agents need to get savvy
Bots aren't as well trained as some humans are at spotting phony websites, which can dupe even discerning shoppers because of how realistic they look.
Recent research from Podqi, a firm that monitors for intellectual property infringement, on AI search risks shows that AI engines can inadvertently direct shoppers to scammy stores.

The group asked popular AI tools, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Perplexity, questions about where to buy particular brands online. More than 18% of the AI bots' answers drew on a fake, infringing or invalid website.

For example, when asked where to buy clothing from Stussy, a streetwear brand, Perplexity referred to us-stussy.com, which it mistakenly identified as the brand's official website and "the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items." The web address us-stussy.com directs shoppers to a fake store. The real store's address is stussy.com.
Other brands with duplicate online stores include Figs, a medical scrubs maker; sock company Bombas; and dairy brand Fairlife.

title: Here's how GLP-1 drugs are changing people's shopping habits
summary: More than 60 million Americans could be using the drugs by 2030, double the number that currently use them, according to a new forecast.
story: The millions of Americans who use GLP-1 drugs to lose weight are reshaping consumer spending and buying patterns, forcing businesses to rethink their offerings.

The medications could make the population at large healthier and increase worker longevity, thereby driving productivity gains. More than 60 million Americans are expected to start using the drugs by 2030, more than double the number that currently takes them, according to an estimate from Oxford Economics, an economic advisory firm.
Their user base is already large enough to drive noticeable spending pullbacks on some goods and services while boosting others, according to research from the firm.

"GLP-1s are no longer a niche story for the U.S. economy," Oxford Economics U.S. economist Grace Zwemmer wrote in a report. "Faster adoption and broader access will continue to drive a reallocation of consumer spending away from food and toward apparel."
The drugs could boost labor supply if workers are healthier and can remain on the job for longer, she noted.
Shopping baskets start to look different

Spending on food, both at home and at bars and restaurants, stands to take the biggest hit, according to Zwemmer. Oxford Economics estimates that households using GLP-1 reduce food spending by about $500 a year on average.

A study from Cornell University and Numerator found that GLP-1 users cut grocery spending by roughly 5% within months of starting the drug. The most noticeable cuts were in the savory snacks and sweet bakery goods aisles, although GLP-1 users bought more yogurt and fresh produce.

The medication leads users to spend about $200 more a year on clothing, according to the Oxford Economics report. Separate research shows that GLP-1 users tend to overhaul their wardrobes to accommodate their slimmed-down figures. They favor smaller sizes and, in some cases, body-hugging styles versus baggier alternatives, according to Impact Analytics, a retail forecasting firm.

"As long as adoption continues to rise, new starters will have demand for new clothes," Zwemmer wrote in the report. "For now, that translates to an additional $200 in spending on apparel per year per user. Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 [million] users entering 2027, this would translate to an $8 [billion] uplift in apparel spending next year."

title: What stores are open on Black Friday? Here are the hours.
summary: Many retailers open their doors early on Black Friday, but the stock market will have shorter hours. Here's what to know.
story: The turkey's been carved, the pie's been gobbled up and the family squabbles have been (mostly) settled. Now comes Black Friday, the unofficial kickoff to the holiday shopping season.
While many stores open early to jump-start their holiday sales, some services may have limited hours on the Friday after Thanksgiving.
Read on for a snapshot of which stores are open and their hours, as well as any services that may operate differently on Black Friday.
Black Friday store hours
Some stores extend their hours on Black Friday, with many consumers planning to kick off their holiday shopping.

title: High school band raises $350K to stay for Macy's Thanksgiving parade
summary: Other marching bands from around the U.S. are also raising funds to cover the cost of staying in New York City after the parade was rescheduled for Saturday.
story: One high school marching band from Texas says it has raised $350,000 to cover the cost of its 500-member group remaining in New York City after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was rescheduled until Saturday due to a potentially historic storm hitting the region on Thursday.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School in Texas, told CBS News about raising the funds required to cover the extended trip.

"I started scrambling through that," Demkovich said. "Can we find a hotel to stay in? Can we get our transportation back? How, at the last second on a holiday weekend, how astronomical are the prices going to be?"

Other marching bands that traveled to New York from across the country are also raising money to cover the cost of their extended stays. For many of the high school musicians, the parade is a once-in-a-lifetime chance to perform for millions of spectators along the route and watching at home, and the postponement has made the trip significantly more expensive.
"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Demkovich added.
In just the span of a few hours, the Pearland community came together to raise hundreds of thousands of dollars.
"They organized a fundraiser, they went on news stations, they broadcasted it, they posted it to get the word across," Pearland High School senior and band member Deborah James told CBS News.

By Thursday, the band had raised enough money to pay for two extra nights at a hotel and to charter buses back to Texas after the parade on Saturday. One logistical challenge: They'll have to relocate from the Marriott Marquis in Times Square, which is booked for the weekend, to a hotel near the Meadowlands Sports Complex in New Jersey.
And they'll travel home by bus on Saturday because flights are booked until late Monday or Tuesday, Demkovich said. The donations also cover extra meals for the ensemble.
"We are going to make sure you stay there," Kevin Cole, Pearland's former mayor, said of the band. "We are going to make sure you get to perform."

The parade's delay also scrambled plans for tourists and family members who had traveled to New York to see the parade on Thursday. Among them was the Sims family, who traveled from Florida to see their daughter perform as part of the Great American Marching Band.
"We came up to see her. It's our first time in New York City," Dustin Sims told CBS New York. "We've had a great week, but now we gotta decide whether we're gonna stay another day or not."
Outpouring of support

Demkovich told CBS News that the group's fundraising push quickly spread across social media, soliciting contributions from Pearland businesses with a history of charitable giving and from strangers alike.

Several Texas businesses, including Gringo's Mexican Kitchen in Pearland and Houston's Mattress Mack and CenterPoint Energy, opened their wallets by making generous donations through a fundraising link on the marching band's website.

Eight other marching bands are scheduled to perform on Saturday. The Dobyns-Bennett High School Band from Kingsport, Tennessee, also issued a plea on social media, calling on its community to help defray the cost of the band staying in New York through Saturday.

"While we are grateful that our students will still have the opportunity to perform in this historic 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade during the Dobyns-Bennett Band's own centennial year, this unexpected change presents significant logistical and financial challenges for our program," the group said in a post on social media on Wednesday.

"Extending our stay in New York City means additional expenses that were never anticipated in our original trip budget, including extended charter bus rentals, additional nights of hotel accommodations, and meal stipends for our students," the group added.

By Thursday morning, the Dobyns-Bennett Band said it had met its undisclosed fundraising goal and that the band would be staying in New York through Saturday to perform in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
"We have secured the necessary funding for the band to stay the extra night and to pay for the extended bus contract to get the kids home on Saturday!" the group said in the post.
