title: Elon Musk doubles SpaceX share pledge for U.S. children
summary: Every child in the U.S. will receive one share of SpaceX from the company and one from Elon Musk.
story: Elon Musk is upping a pledge to kickstart U.S. children's savings.

On Wednesday, Musk and SpaceX said they will give every U.S. child two shares in the space exploration company, doubling a pledge the world's richest person made in October, which he said at the time would be the "first of many" planned gifts.

In the statement, SpaceX said it would give each child a newly issued share of its Class A common stock. The company will contribute the shares to U.S. kids' Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts the White House created to help American children build long-term savings.
Musk will personally match the number of shares SpaceX donates, according to Thursday's statement.
Additionally, SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell will donate more than 2 million SpaceX shares to U.S. children.
The total giveaway is worth about $18 billion, based on SpaceX's most recent stock price.

"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in announcing the donation. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."

There are roughly 70 million children in the U.S. who are eligible for a Trump Account. The Trump administration is automatically enrolling kids under eighteen with a valid Social Security number in the program. However, parents or guardians must still claim their child's account for it to be active.
As of Tuesday, friends and family members had contributed more than $1 billion to individual Trump Accounts, according to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Additionally, philanthropists including Michael and Susan Dell and other donors have made major gifts, bringing the total assets deposited in Trump Accounts to over $9 billion.

title: Judge declines to issue long-term ban on tax-funded pro-Trump ads
summary: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Trump.
story: A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban on the ads.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., said the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown a likelihood of prevailing in the case. Democrats had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president's campaign message just weeks before November's midterm elections.
In her ruling, she noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away.

"But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone," she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.
"At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded," AliKhan wrote.
Her ruling comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.

The ads first emerged on cable and broadcast networks — including CBS — in late September, just over a month before the midterms, funded by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. Many of the ads touted Mr. Trump or his administration's accomplishments, and included the disclosure: "Paid for by the U.S. Government."
Members of both parties raised questions about the ads, and Democrats sued the Trump administration in October.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies, arguing they are not political ads because they don't explicitly call on viewers to take any particular action. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don't try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued.
Mr. Trump eventually said in early October his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would start paying for the ads to run on television, though he insisted they were a "positive promotion for our Great U.S.A."

"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself," the president wrote.

Ahead of Wednesday's ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed.

A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, told The Associated Press in a statement that the party was "disappointed" by the judge's decision, adding that the DNC "will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration's attempts to undermine our democracy."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites.
But in her latest ruling, AliKhan declined to issue a preliminary injunction against the ads.

title: U.S.-based firms helping China access Nvidia's most advanced chips
summary: It's not just Megaspeed. A CBS News investigation reveals that at least two California-based Nvidia customers have Chinese ownership — giving the U.S. adversary potential access to Nvidia's most advanced technology.
story: Nvidia is selling its most cutting-edge chips to at least two companies that are U.S.-based, but are actually controlled by Chinese-owned firms, raising fresh questions about efforts to keep sensitive technology away from the nation's rivals, a CBS News investigation found.

One of the chip giant's "preferred partners" is a California company owned by a Chinese firm whose chief executive is a graduate of a Chinese military university, records show. Another California company was renamed after its Chinese-owned parent company was blacklisted.
Some of these U.S.-based, Chinese-owned firms have then leased or sold the advanced chips, used for artificial intelligence, to other companies in Southeast Asia, records show.

The world of computer chip exports is murky — and labyrinthine chains of custody have made it even more difficult to determine just how many of the most sensitive Nvidia chips are being exploited by China, experts told CBS News.

"It is a wake-up call for accountability, for properly resourcing the enforcement bodies, and for every leading private-sector tech company to map where it is exposed," said Mishel Kondi, a senior analyst at C4ADS, which specializes in using public data, from corporate filings to satellite imagery, to uncover sanctions violations and smuggling.

C4ADS, a Washington-based global security nonprofit also known as the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, examined corporate filings and other company ownership data at the request of CBS News. This story is based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an investigation of Nvidia's corporate relationships dating back to 2023 — long before its CEO Jensen Huang and his behemoth chip company dominated the news cycle.

That explosive saga began 27 days ago when the news broke that Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang — a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion, and Beijing denies she is a spy. The company she ran, Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore, is under investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.

But Megaspeed, national security and trade experts say, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the transfer of Nvidia chips to China. And elected officials are now asking questions like: How are Nvidia's chips getting to China? And what did Jensen Huang and his colleagues know about it?

"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement this week.
California company, Chinese owners
Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year. The company can sell graphics cards for personal computers and server chips with lower processing power to China without a special license.
What is not allowed — and is under strict export controls — are the sales of Nvidia's most technologically advanced chips, which are powering the AI revolution.
But recent reporting, including from CBS News, has shown some of the highest end chips, called Blackwells, have made it into Chinese hands.
The circuitous trail traveled by Nvidia chips quickly gets muddy.

Take RiCloud AI, a data center company based in San Jose, California. RiCloud AI appears on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners" in the U.S., affording it preferential access to sales of high-end computer chips used for advanced AI models.
These are classified as American sales, according to Nvidia's public filings — with the chips going to RiCloud AI, Inc., a U.S. company.
But RiCloud AI's parent company is Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited. That company is headquartered in Shenzhen, China, and is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university run by the Chinese military. Yu is also CEO of a related RiCloud company in California.

And Yuxing's chairman, Li Qiang, was previously chairman of data firm Global Switch Holdings, which was dropped as a data center provider by Australia's Department of Defense in June 2024 over national security concerns.
The U.S. government has not accused RiCloud and Yuxing of any wrongdoing.

By December 2025, just 10 weeks after it was incorporated, RiCloud AI had secured its partner status with Nvidia and has since become a "preferred" cloud partner, giving the company priority access to advanced chips, Nvidia's software and technical support. Nvidia has not responded to questions about what background checks it conducted before awarding the privileged status to RiCloud AI.

An examination of RiCloud AI's clients suggests that some seem like unorthodox customers for such high-powered technology. This year, for example, it signed a $120 million deal to lease 300 Nvidia B300 servers to a company in Taiwan that was primarily known for selling whisky.

Agencia Comercial Spirits was a small whisky importer with $609,000 in net income in 2025 when it listed on the Nasdaq as an AI company. This year it has made commitments for AI data center-related deals totaling between $488 and $598 million, after Li was appointed as chairman.

Agencia did not respond to a request for comment. In a February press release announcing its pivot into data centers, Agencia said the move was "part of a broader review of strategic opportunities outside its core whisky business."
Blacklisted owners
Then there is California company Aivres, which is currently listed on Nvidia's website as an "elite" compute partner — the highest tier of relationship with the chip giant.

Aivres used to be called Inspur, the same name as its Chinese parent company. But when Inspur group firms in China were added to a federal blacklist of companies considered a security risk to the U.S. in March 2023, the California subsidiary changed its name and today still maintains its close relationship with Nvidia. Aivres itself is not on the blacklist.

Aivres, which produces data center servers housing Nvidia chips, exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, according to a New York Times analysis of trade records published two months ago.
Some $3 billion of those exports were for computers containing Nvidia's cutting-edge Blackwell chips, which are restricted from being exported to China, the Times reported.
The Aivres chips then went to two companies in Malaysia — Megaspeed and Aolani — providing cloud AI services to Chinese firms Alibaba and ByteDance, according to the Times.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm where Jensen Huang paramour Alice Huang was a top executive, was blacklisted by the U.S. government this week, in the wake of the scandal. The company denies any wrongdoing.

The Pentagon put Alibaba on a blacklist in June, claiming it used advanced chips to help the Chinese military. The company denies it and sued the government over the blacklisting, winning a preliminary injunction last month.
The servers owned by Inspur — Aivres' parent company — are used in China by the country's military, according to the U.S. government. Aivres did not respond to requests for comment.
Selling to suspected smugglers
Another of Nvidia's elite U.S. partners has surfaced in a recent $300 million chip smuggling case, though it has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Earlier this year, a California businessman named Greg Lui was indicted for allegedly smuggling export-controlled chips to China via Malaysia and Singapore in 2023 and 2024. He has pleaded not guilty.
Records reviewed by CBS News link Lui to 2CRSi, an Nvidia elite partner in the U.S. that is a branch of a French-owned company making AI data servers.

Lui's indictment says his company bought 100 H100 servers — which required a license to export — worth more than $22 million from an unnamed manufacturer. 2CRSi's website lists his firm, Topmost Corp., as an "authorized partner," while his company website said he is an "authorized reseller of … 2CRSi."
The indictment does not accuse Nvidia of having any knowledge of the arrangement.

2CRSi said in a letter to shareholders this month that it received a grand jury subpoena from the federal prosecutor's office in Los Angeles about "a customer that we ourselves had reported to the authorities." It has not been accused of wrongdoing.
The company's U.S. revenue fell from $201 million to $4.7 million this year.
In addition to 2CRSi, Lui listed California firm Super Micro Computer, Inc. as one of his customers.
In March, the Justice Department accused Super Micro's co-founder of a scheme to smuggle $2.5 billion worth of servers to Chinese customers via a Southeast Asian company.

The co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw has denied the charges. His alleged "fixer" pleaded guilty in a deal with prosecutors last month. The company says those involved "no longer have any relationship with Supermicro" and its current executives had no knowledge of the alleged smuggling.
Accounting changes

Nvidia used to publish the regional breakdown of its chip sales based on the customer's billing location. That data showed that in 2024, nearly half of its chip sales were billed to the U.S., 18% to Singapore and 13% to China.

Last November, the company switched to using the customer's headquarters as its location. This bookkeeping change revealed that an extra $7.9 billion of customers' bills were actually from firms headquartered in China in 2024.
In 2025, U.S.-headquartered customers made up 69% of Nvidia sales, while China was cut to 9%.
Nvidia's public filings say "the end customer and shipping location may be different from our customers' headquarters location."
CBS News' findings suggest Nvidia's changes to the way it published these sales figures may make the locations of its customers less clear.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, who is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is poised to investigate whether companies are circumventing the bans on sales of chips to China, and into alleged Chinese espionage connected to Nvidia.

Kondi told CBS News that she believes the investigation of chip sales "matters beyond the news cycle because it exposes export control violations and potential economic espionage, and shows how Beijing ties intelligence work to its industrial plans, pursuing self-reliance while still reaching for foreign technology where it lacks parity."

This story published first on CBS News at 6:10 p.m. on Nov. 25, 2026.

title: Stocks turn volatile as Jensen Huang rebound rally fades
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell more than 1,000 points in early trading before clawing back most of the losses.
story: Stocks swung wildly on Wednesday, plunging in early trading before paring losses by the close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 1,000 points early in the session, but regained ground to close down 148 points, or 0.6%, at 23,586.  The S&P 500 fell 0.2% on the day, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%.

Stocks have slumped in recent weeks amid concerns surrounding the health of the artificial intelligence sector. Shares of Anthropic, the AI lab that staged the largest initial stock offering in history last week, declined 7.6% to $75.66, below its IPO price of $83 per share.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the AI sector can justify the enormous investment in data centers. Compounding those fears just before the Thanksgiving holiday are the Trump administration's plans to raise tariffs on China and other major trading partners.

"At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn't look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year," Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer for Northlight Asset Management, said in an email.

With Democrats set to control Congress next year and winning many state-level seats, AI companies may face more headwinds as lawmakers push back against data center construction, according to investment adviser Capital Economics. Even before the midterm elections, investors were increasingly questioning the finances of AI companies, it added.

Investors are also bracing for the impact of more interest rate hikes starting in December, with expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs to counter rising inflation. That could make it more difficult for businesses, including AI companies, to borrow money to fuel growth.

title: Most Polymarket users lost money betting on the U.S. midterms
summary: More than half of Polymarket accounts lost money betting on the U.S. midterm elections, according to one analysis.
story: Prediction market companies tout themselves as a place where anyone can make a quick buck. Don't bet on it, recent data suggests.

Take the U.S. midterm elections, which generated ample business for prediction market platforms as users wagered on who would win congressional races nationwide. And a few people did, in fact, clean up — very few.

On Polymarket, the top 1% of accounts took home 91% of the profits from midterm bets, totaling roughly $23 million, according to research this week from the Anti-Corruption Data Collective (ACDC), a nonprofit advocacy group focused on corporate and financial corruption. The bottom 99% of traders lost a total of $15 million.
Of the nearly 82,000 accounts that the group analyzed, more than half lost money on Polymarket's midterm-focused markets.

"At a time [when] affordability was a major issue at the ballot box, average traders handed over their cash to an elite few, including many professional and automated traders," ACDC said in its study.
According to Polymarket, 95% of the markets on its platform accurately predicted the outcome of this year's midterm elections.

"Prediction markets have become an important source of real-time election information as they bring together the knowledge and insights of informed participants to show the public how likely different outcomes are," a Polymarket spokesperson said in an email to CBS News. "Polymarket continues to be a destination for timely, accurate information that anyone can follow as events unfold, whether they trade or not."

According to the Pew Research Center, Polymarket and rival prediction market Kalshi hosted a combined 34,000 contracts related to the midterms, up from 2,300 in 2024. The midterms generated $2.7 billion in trading volume on the platforms, compared with $8.5 billion during the 2024 presidential and congressional elections, Pew found.
Other recent data point to the challenge of winning money on prediction markets.

Findings released by the New York City Council on Tuesday show that, from Jan. 1 to Aug. 11, New York City residents who traded on Kalshi lost a total of $17.6 million. So-called institutional traders on the platform won $210 million over the same period.

On Wall Street, institutional investors generally refer to financial firms, market makers and other pros who invest money on behalf of their clients. In Kalshi's case, it also encapsulates retail traders, solo forecasters and two-person teams that use LLCs for tax or business purposes, according to Elisabeth Diana, a spokesperson for the prediction market.
"Most winning traders [are] labeled as 'institutional' even though they are often 'individuals,'" she said in an email, adding, "These are not Wall Street institutions."
Diana also said that, as in other financial markets, a trader's skill level matters.

"Traders who get better at forecasting can earn more, and their trades make the market more efficient," she said. "Individuals do worse day trading on the stock markets than professionals. The only difference here is that prediction markets give more people an opportunity to be a 'professional.'"

title: FCC approves SpaceX plan for 1 million data center satellites
summary: In an X post on Wednesday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the satellites will be a "great asset to America and the world."
story: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday greenlit SpaceX's request to put 1 million satellites in space that will create orbital data centers, bringing CEO Elon Musk closer to his goal of harnessing the sun to generate computing power.
"Today, in a historic first, the FCC approved SpaceX's request for 1 million satellites (orbital compute modules) to create data centers in space," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a post on X.
Musk responded by saying, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
SpaceX's satellites will conduct telemetry, tracking and command operations, and will connect with other satellites, including those in SpaceX's Starlink system, the FCC said in a February filing.

SpaceX filed a request with the FCC to put data centers in space in January. In its application, it said  that deploying data centers in space would be the "first step towards becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization," referring to a threshold Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev proposed at which a civilization could tap the entire energy output of its star.

When it filed its initial public offering in May, SpaceX said that orbital data centers would be able to handle intense demand from the AI sector and generate energy more efficiently than land-based facilities, which have become a flashpoint across the U.S.

Thousands of data centers are being built, sparking backlash from communities who argue the facilities will transform their cities, create unwanted noise and drive up electricity and water use. In the midterms, American voters approved dozens of proposals aimed at restricting data centers.
In its IPO filing, SpaceX said it expects to begin deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028.

title: Why are investors freaking out even as the U.S. economy surges?
summary: The economy is sending mixed signals, with growth jumping while stocks gyrate. Here's what economists say is going on.
story: The U.S. economy is racing ahead, with new data showing that the country's gross domestic product rose at a blistering 4.3% pace in the third quarter. So why are investors hitting the panic button, causing stocks to swing wildly and bruising your 401(k) plan?

The answer boils down to the relationship among inflation, interest rates and the Federal Reserve, along with mounting concerns on Wall Street that the artificial intelligence boom could turn to bust.

Stocks on Wednesday show just how brittle investor sentiment is at the moment. Leading indexes plunged more than 1,000 points in morning activity, only to claw back much of those losses in afternoon trading. Where stocks go next, nobody knows.
The S&P 500 index is now about 8% lower than its most recent high on Oct. 6, putting it close to a correction, or a decline of more than 10% from its recent peak.

Also on Wednesday, the Bureau of Economic Analysis sharply raised its estimate for third-quarter growth from its previous forecast of 3.4%. That growth is being fueled by steady consumer spending and surging business investment, with large tech firms splurging on building out data centers and other infrastructure required to power AI.

Americans benefit when the economy is growing, fueling consumer spending and hiring. But heady growth can also have a downside — especially when, as in the current moment, inflation is already running hot.

"In the simplest possible words, the economy is overheated, with demand exceeding supply.  The consequence is a blowout of the trade deficit and inflation," HFE chief economist Carl B. Weinberg said in a research note.
The link between AI and inflation

Although inflation earlier in the year was largely driven by rising energy costs, more recent signals suggest that strong economic growth, fueled by heavy AI spending, is now the main factor driving up prices. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee said last week that trillions in spending on data centers are contributing to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation.
Newly released inflation data showed consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September.

Meanwhile, the admixture of high inflation and heady economic growth virtually cements a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike at its December meeting, and possibly additional hikes in early 2027, according to economists.
Rate hikes and the stock market

The specter of rate hikes is weighing on the stock market, as higher borrowing costs could create hurdles for AI and other tech companies seeking to expand their computing capacity. And households, already stretched thin by rising inflation, could face higher costs for everything from credit cards to mortgages — a headwind for consumer spending.

"Households face renewed inflation pressures, diminished saving capacity and higher borrowing costs, while elevated interest rates are raising the cost of investment and financing across the economy," EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco said in an email.

Investors are also questioning whether the huge investments by AI companies will pay off, given the massive losses recorded by many of the big AI labs. Anthropic, which last week recorded the largest initial stock offering in history, lost a startling $104 billion in the first nine months of 2026. It plans to spend nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

"But the critical thing AI may never be able to do is make profits high enough to justify its declining, but still stratospheric valuations," Boston University economist Laurence Kotlikoff said in a Wednesday blog post.
What's the outlook for stocks?
Some investors and economists say that investors should brace for more downside, at least in the near term.

"As investors saw last week, pessimism can build quickly and suddenly take the wheel of market momentum," said Anthony Saglimbene, Ameriprise chief market strategist, in a research note. "And fear tends to feed on itself at these readings, as falling stock prices become the evidence that justifies more selling across the market."

Experts advise against making snap decisions during a market downturn, such as selling stocks, as it can lead to losses that are tough to recover from. For instance, investors who sold in previous downturns may have missed the sharp market gains that have often followed.
Despite investors' fears, the economy remains strong, helping shore up corporate growth, noted Doug Beath, global equity strategist at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"We expect solid economic and earnings growth in 2027 to support our year-end S&P 500 target of 8,700," he said.

title: Trump administration to issue new tariffs on China, EU and others
summary: The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on goods from other major economies.
story: The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, raising the total tariff rate on the world's second-largest economy to 45%. President Trump also plans to raise taxes on specific products from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
Brazil is among the countries that will be hardest hit, with the U.S. planning to raise tariffs on the country's raw and refined sugar and to impose a new 10% levy on aircraft.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.

"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base,"  U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.

The planned duties would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.

The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and Taiwan. The USTR is also investigating Mexico and Norway but hasn't imposed any new tariffs on those countries.

In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline. The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted at specific products and would not be stacked on top of existing tariffs introduced by the Trump administration.

Stephen Brown, chief North American economist for Capital Economics, said in a research note Wednesday that the Trump administration's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks." The new tariffs will essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs, rather than stacking on top of them, he said.

Tariffs have been a central part of the Trump administration's economic agenda, with the president arguing they are necessary to boost U.S. manufacturing, create jobs and reduce the trade deficit. However, his authority to impose the levies has faced legal challenges, complicating the rollout.
Tariffs unpopular with voters, small businesses

In February, the Supreme Court blocked a sweeping set of tariffs that the president implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, dismantling a key part of the administration's efforts and forcing the government to issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses.

Still, the administration has found other avenues to impose the levies, using other sections of trade law, such as Section 232, which allows the president to restrict imports that could threaten U.S. national security.
The average statutory U.S. tariff rate on imports is now 11.2%, according to the Yale Budget Lab.

The White House moved to propose the new tariffs on Wednesday despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters over rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.
We Pay the Tariffs, a grassroots coalition of small businesses, decried the new tariffs, warning they could raise prices just as the holiday season heats up.

"Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses," Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a statement. "Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either."

title: How people use AI agents to handle annoying tasks and save money
summary: Shrugging off fears of AI, some consumers say the technology is simplifying their lives and helping them save money.
story: Count Megan Roszak, a busy executive coach, business founder and mother of 11-year-old twins, among the recent converts to artificial intelligence as a tool for helping run her life.

The San Francisco, California, resident explained to CBS News how she uses an AI agent, Fo, from the agent platform Wajo, to process and return online purchases. She also recently used it to book an appointment with her electric company, which she said saved her multiple phone calls and about 40 minutes.

"I am a full-time working mom. Making returns to Poshmark and Etsy are things that I would let go of and drop in the past because it's going to be annoying," Roszak said. "Now, I just put Fo on the case, and I got $250 back."

Companies ranging from Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI to hundreds of smaller developers are rolling out AI agents designed to handle tedious tasks, such as returning products, and also to comb through people's email inboxes for unclaimed refunds and other money they may be owed.

More broadly, AI proponents say the technology can help consumers reckon with the "annoyance economy," or what advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative describes in a recent report as the "time, fees and irritation" involved in dealing with a host of menial tasks.

Those tasks, such as handling customer service, scheduling appointments and canceling subscriptions, cost Americans $165 billion per year in wasted time, fees and other surcharges for routine transactions, according to Groundwork.
A cure for annoyance?

Used wisely, AI agents can reduce the friction companies depend on to pocket forgotten fees and payments, according to Stanford University economist Neale Mahoney, an author of Groundwork's report on the so-called annoyance economy.
Kevin Newman, another Fo user, estimates the agent has saved him roughly 2,800 hours he would otherwise have spent generating advertising leads for his small business and on personal tasks.

The agent also sifted through his email to turn up multiple gift cards he had earned for testing products and found unclaimed funds he was owed from his former residences, including a $60 claim from a settlement with Time Warner, Newman said.

Fo can summon a person to finish the job when necessary, with Wajo assistants on call who can work with agents when, for example, an institution doesn't have a website, or it blocks agents, according to the company.

Wajo founder Shivani Poddar told CBS News that people use Fo for a wide range of pesky tasks, including booking plane tickets, tracking down lost luggage with airlines or negotiating healthcare costs.
"These are complex negotiations, and these systems are still very hybrid," she said, highlighting the importance of having a human on call when necessary.

Meta also touts its Muse agent's money-saving capabilities. For example, in the "ideas" section of the app, which suggests financial management uses, Meta recommends using Muse to "Get back money that's already yours" by checking state databases for owed amounts. The agent offers to file refund claims and also to "cancel those random subscriptions you forgot about."
Businesses vs. agents

Businesses that count on consumers giving up on claiming refunds or fighting junk fees aren't taking such tactics lying down, with some websites and financial institutions blocking AI agents. Amazon, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase & Co. are among the businesses that have banned the bots from conducting transactions on behalf of consumers.
"More firms are blocking agents because they're making it difficult to increase their revenue. They're like a superpower for consumers, so companies have an incentive to block it," Mahoney said.

Concerns also swirl about agents accessing users' sensitive data, including payment information, and about their incentives. For example, Lindsay Owens, founder and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, told CBS News that companies could be steering users toward products and services from which they earn commissions, to pad their own bottom lines.

title: Paperwork, not work, causing enrollees to lose Medicaid in Nebraska
summary: Data from the months after Nebraska's early rollout of new Medicaid work mandates offers a look at the challenges enrollees in other states could face.
story: When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Trump's sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.
Many also watched the Cornhusker State's experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.
On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready.

They'll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don't meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don't comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren't working.
Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory.

"The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans' chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans," Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement.

Democrats' massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they'll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they're fully enforced.
The basics

Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states, along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show, so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states.

But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034.

The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called "medically frail."
It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska.

On May 1, Nebraska became the first state to implement the work requirements. After it began dropping people from coverage in August, 7% of Nebraska Medicaid enrollees who were subject to the requirements when renewing their coverage, or 533 adults, were disenrolled because of the new rules, according to the latest state data.

Nebraska's Medicaid agency was able to verify that 8 in 10 enrollees met the new rules using various state and federal databases. Those people didn't have to deal with requests for more information, interim state Medicaid director Jeremy Brunssen told KFF Health News.
About 14% of new Medicaid applicants subject to the new rules, or 557 people, had been denied because of the work requirements since they were implemented.
But the state data also shows some troubling issues.
For example, 92% of cases in which existing enrollees lost coverage were due to procedural or paperwork issues rather than state determinations that they did not meet the new work rules.

Brunssen attributes that high percentage to the state having to verify the numerous ways people can meet the new requirements or exemptions. "It's not as simple as typical eligibility enrollment that you can meet via income and household size," he said.
Many enrollees lost coverage because they did not respond to the state's outreach. Those enrollees may have deemed themselves ineligible or were unsure how to respond, Brunssen said.
The rate of procedural denials is much higher than in prior years, according to data analyzed by KFF. Critics fear it means people who may still qualify are losing coverage.

"This is definitely a red-flag warning," said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska, a trade group representing federally funded community health centers. "The high proportion of procedural denials is troubling."
Navigating the new requirements

Cheri Stollar, 48, of Lincoln, Nebraska, received her Medicaid renewal notice in the mail in early November and was confused about which documents to submit to the state to prove she works as a mental health therapist. She also didn't understand why she had less than a week to respond. She said she tried to call the state Medicaid agency but could not get through. Her renewal has since been completed.

"I want to make sure I send in everything they need," said Stollar, who lives in a three-bedroom mobile home with three of her four children. She has been on Medicaid for two years and credits the coverage for enabling her to afford medications for depression, sleep, and an ulcer.
She said the new law will make it harder for people like her to get and stay covered, which will make it harder to stay healthy — and get and keep a job.

Behnke said enrollees calling the state Medicaid agency for help have been put on hold for up to two hours. The assistance line operates only on weekdays, during daytime hours, making it difficult for people who work to call. State Medicaid officials say they are working to add more staff to reduce wait times.
One challenge in evaluating Nebraska's implementation is that the state, as of mid-November, had released data only through August.
State officials said this summer that they would post an online dashboard with various performance metrics to improve public transparency. That hasn't happened yet.

"We have seen a lot of negative effects so far," said Sarah Maresh, program director at Nebraska Appleseed, a nonprofit social justice advocacy group. "Every person that goes without coverage is a problem."
She worries that people are being deterred from applying to Medicaid because of the policy.
Brunssen, the interim Medicaid director, defended his state's performance.

"We are experiencing what we expected," he said in an October interview at a National Association of Medicaid Directors conference in Maryland. "The vast majority of people newly applying, or for those going through redetermination, are getting coverage or retaining coverage."

Yet, Brunssen noted, it's still early. Fewer than 25% of Medicaid enrollees subject to the work requirement have had to prove they meet the new rules to retain coverage. The rest won't be completed until next summer, he said.

The state's Department of Health and Human Services, which operates its Medicaid program, has used various methods to inform enrollees about the new rules, such as letters, emails, texts, and messages in an online portal, Brunssen said.
"Most Medicaid enrollees know about the new rules," he said, attributing awareness to community partners and managed-care companies that helped get the word out.
"I feel like we've done everything in our power to communicate what was coming," he said.
Brunssen noted the state has taken advantage of a federal option to let enrollees self-attest that they meet exemptions. All declarations must be truthful, or enrollees could face perjury charges.
Self-attestation is as easy as checking a box on an online form. No supporting documents are required. That's made it easier for people to comply, Brunssen said.
The state has also exempted people living in three counties with high unemployment rates and in two counties declared federal disaster areas because of weather events, he said.
"Our goal is to make sure people who are eligible get or retain coverage," Brunssen said.
Some enrollees say the state could do more to make the process easier.

Chalandria James, 37, of Omaha was worried about whether she still had Medicaid coverage after she tried to renew in July but did not hear back from the state, despite repeated calls. Unsure of her coverage status, she canceled a doctor's appointment to check her blood pressure. It took until September, and a multi-hour visit to the state agency office, for her to find out she still had Medicaid and was exempt from the work requirement because she had a child under 14 years old.
"It was nerve-racking not knowing," said James, a community health worker and doula.
In Nebraska, about 37% of enrollees met the work requirement while 61% qualified for an exemption — with the most common reasons being medical frailty or caregiving.

Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families, said Nebraska's experience shows the work rules do little to promote work, since most who can are already working. "This policy punishes low-income people by subjecting them to serious, often insurmountable, hurdles," she said.

Even with data showing the large majority of enrollees working or meeting an exemption, Brunssen said the new requirements still are a good idea. "Part of being a good, healthy person does involve engagement with the community," he said, "and we think there is value in the work we are doing in this space."

title: 5 questions Nvidia still faces after bringing back Jensen Huang
summary: Despite Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia's CEO, experts say it's anything but business as usual for the chipmaker.
story: Jensen Huang's first task in returning to lead Nvidia after resigning last week under a cloud will be to deal with the fallout from his stunning exit and even more surprising reprieve.

Following his reinstatement by the company's board, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into President Trump's role in the billionaire entrepreneur's return and whether Nvidia skirted export rules meant to prevent its advanced chips from reaching China. And while Huang may be viewed as key to Nvidia's success, his return raises a thicket of legal and operational problems, according to financial and governance experts.

"Three tests will now decide how strongly it builds from here: how its leadership sits with Washington, how it handles China and how long AI spending keeps growing at this speed,"  said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory firm, in an email.
Here are five critical questions facing Nvidia as Huang retakes the helm.
Did Nvidia compromise U.S. national security?

One of Nvidia's major customers, Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, employed a Chinese businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. Megaspeed is also alleged to have smuggled Nvidia's advanced chips into China and provided remote access to the technology in violation of U.S. export controls.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear on Dec. 1- 2 in closed-door interviews before multiple congressional panels to discuss the company's ties to China. Huang is also scheduled to appear on Dec. 3 at a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on U.S. export rules and global AI competition.

"The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the Republican chairs of the House committees who will interview Huang and Teter said on Monday.
Will Nvidia's board face legal issues?

The board's decision to reinstate Huang is likely to set off a flurry of shareholder lawsuits over questions including whether Nvidia failed to disclose the spying allegations earlier and whether the company was aware of Megaspeed's links to China, according to Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware.

Shareholders could also challenge Huang and Nvidia over their failure to disclose his personal relationships with subordinates at the company, which appears to violate the chipmaker's code of conduct. Earlier this month, Nvidia was sued by shareholders for allegedly failing to disclose information about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (no relation).
"There's just a whole range of things that they can bring actions," Elson said.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment about whether it will continue pursuing an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence.
Will Nvidia face new U.S. export restrictions?
Nvidia is expected to come under increased scrutiny and face greater regulatory hurdles in selling chips to China and companies in Southeast Asia.
"There will definitely be tighter restrictions, and any dealings directly with China will be the government's primary focus," StoneX equity research analyst Cody Acree told CBS News.

Huang has long lobbied U.S. officials to permit Nvidia to sell its most advanced chips to China, with an eye toward growing its market. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department moved to curb sales of U.S. chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.

"Going forward, they'll be subject to more export controls so that their chips don't end up in China and data centers in Asia," Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment firm D.A. Davidson, told CBS News. "In that way, Nvidia's market has shrunk, and that business will go away."
Can Huang ease investor fears about an AI bust?

Investors cheered Huang's return partly because it suggests that Nvidia will continue in its role as the de facto "bank of AI," providing financing for companies that buy its chips and otherwise fueling the sector's growth. Huang helped arrange deals such as Nvidia's investment in OpenAI. Through such circular financing, Nvidia invests vast sums in AI companies, which then flow back to the chipmaker through chip purchases.

"Nvidia is more than just a chipmaker — it's heavily involved in the broader AI ecosystem by financing other companies," Capital Economics senior economist James Reilly told CBS News. "Having Jensen back reassures investors that those relationships and that financing will continue."
Still, Huang's return doesn't erase concerns about the sector's debt-fueled spending, or whether AI companies will ever turn a profit and deliver returns to investors.
"There are growing concerns as to whether all of this AI investment will generate the revenue it needs long-term to make it worthwhile," Reilly said. "Those hurdles are very demanding."
What is Nvidia's succession plan?
Developing a succession plan to replace Huang will be the first item on the board's agenda, Elson, a prominent governance expert, told CBS News.

When Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, he had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that allowed him to wield enormous power. However, his departure made it clear that the company had no succession plan should Huang be unable to lead.
As a result, Elson expects Nvidia to hire an outside consultant to help forge a plan for who might succeed Huang.
Such "key man" risk isn't unique to Nvidia, Acree noted.

"You have other high-profile CEOs at the helm of large companies, but that's the nature of Silicon Valley, unfortunately," he said, pointing to Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX's Elon Musk. "There is no way to address that risk entirely or make it go away, but boards will be more sensitive to that in the future."

title: Shein to pay $100 million to settle claims it deceived customers
summary: The Singapore fast-fashion company misled millions of U.S. consumers about its products and policies, FTC alleges.
story: Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle allegations that the fast-fashion company harmed consumers by misleading them about its products and policies.

The Federal Trade Commission alleges that the Singapore-based retailer made it hard for customers to resolve purchase problems, broke its shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and engaged in other deceptive practices.

"Shein attracted consumers with promises of affordable clothing, fast delivery and use of suppliers that earned above-average ratings on standards related to child and forced labor, among other representations,"  Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday. "In reality, the company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews. Shein further compounded consumer harm by making it extraordinarily difficult to obtain customer service."
Shein, which ships roughly 1 million packages to the U.S. daily, employed only five customer service representatives to field calls from American consumers about their orders, according to the FTC.

Shein also made deceptive claims about its supply chain and the origin of its cotton and failed to provide customers with shipping updates or help them locate late or missing packages, the agency alleged in its complaint.

The $100 million will be used to provide redress to Shein customers, the FTC said. Under the agency's proposed order, Shein is also barred from making misleading claims about shipping and delivery times and from suppressing negative product reviews. The company is also required to provide adequate customer service.

A Shein spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices."
Shein went public on the Hong Kong exchange in September. It's built a sizable customer base in the U.S., appealing to shoppers with ultra-cheap clothing styles and fast delivery.

Last year, the White House ended the "de minimis" tariff exemption that allowed low-cost packages, including shipments from Shein, to enter the U.S. duty-free. In April, Shein said it would raise prices for consumers after the loophole closed.

title: Wendy's "pricing scheme" inflated menu prices, lawsuit alleges
summary: In a proposed class action, a California resident alleges that Wendy's conspired with its franchisees to set and raise menu prices.
story: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges that Wendy's engaged in a pricing scheme that reduced competition across its restaurants, driving up costs for customers.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in a Maryland district court, accuses the burger chain of conspiring with independently owned franchisees to set and raise prices at its U.S. locations over a six-year period between 2016 and 2022. Wendy's collected "competitively sensitive information" from franchisee locations, including transaction data, to coordinate prices, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed by Andy Garcia, a California resident and longtime Wendy's customer, according to the suit. He alleges that Wendy's engaged in "anticompetitive conduct" that resulted in artificially high prices, causing him to pay more than he otherwise would have.
Garcia also sued NCR Voyix, a software company that provides Aloha POS, a point-of-sale system used by Wendy's.

"By delegating pricing decisions to a common decision-maker, it eliminates critical price competition that drives costs down for consumers," Blake Hunter Yagman, the lawyer representing Garcia and founding partner of Yagman PLLC, a class-action law firm headquartered in New York, said in an email.

"This is even more important with respect to food prices, which have never been higher — and Wendy's owes [it to] its consumers to compete on the merits for better service, more innovative products and better pricing," Yagman added.

Wendy's and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to requests for comment. As of September, Wendy's had 432 company-owned restaurants and 6,762 franchisees across the U.S., according to the company's most recent regulatory filing.

In 2024, Wendy's raised concerns after saying it would test Uber-style pricing. Also known as dynamic pricing, that approach allows companies to set prices based on real-time market conditions and other factors such as weather.
Other restaurants have also faced scrutiny over their pricing practices. Last month, a consumer sued McDonald's over the use of an AI tool that recommends dynamic pricing.

title: "We're racing towards huge dangers," AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio says
summary: As one of the "godfathers" of artificial intelligence, Yoshua Bengio helped bring generative AI into the world. Now he worries society isn't ready for what's coming.
story: Yoshua Bengio is the most professionally cited scientist alive, and the most cited computer scientist of all time. He's informally known as one of the three "godfathers" of artificial intelligence, along with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun, for his foundational work on the deep neural networks that power today's AI models.
In short, Bengio helped usher AI into the world — a technology now being integrated into our schools, our search bars, our smartphones and our wars.
Yet despite being one of the principal minds behind AI, the University of Montreal professor is now urgently calling for a slowdown in its development and a renewed focus on using AI safely.

LawZero, the nonprofit where Bengio is co-president and scientific director, strives to develop AI that is "designed to be trustworthy and safe" — effectively a dissent from the models being released by Anthropic and OpenAI. Bengio wants companies, governments and AI lab employees to stop developing ever more capable AI systems.

What led to such a dramatic turnaround for one of the world's most prominent AI researchers? Bengio spoke with CBS News about AI risks, regrets and responsibility. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

CBS News: You're considered one of the people most responsible for the early advancement of deep learning, and you're the most cited scientist in the world because of your work in AI. How do you feel about your past work today?

Yoshua Bengio: I feel like I learned a lot. It was exciting. But I should have seen some of the most serious risks earlier. And I think, like most humans, I was focused on the good side of my work. And not enough on the potential consequences.
What was the original goal of your early work on deep learning or AI?

I was trying to understand intelligence and do it in a way that was sufficiently abstract to help us understand human intelligence, animal intelligence and build intelligent machines. That was a very exciting research goal, with the hypothesis that there could be a few simple principles — think of the laws of physics for the physical world — that could explain intelligence.
Do you feel like that goal has been accomplished since then?
Beyond our expectations. There are still people who are in denial, but it's very clear that we have been making very rapid progress towards machines that are intelligent.
Have your personal views on what intelligence actually is changed over time?

It has been refined, but I haven't made a U-turn about the nature of intelligence. In the last few years, I've focused on how it can go wrong, in the sense that intelligence can be in the service of goals that are not ethical.
You've now shifted to advocating for AI safety — that's a markedly different focus than your earlier research. Can you explain that shift?

I was spending a lot of my brain cycles on two things. One was understanding how we can make AI more intelligent, and the other was how to apply AI to fields like medicine or handling the climate crisis, education and so on. I made a big pivot to orient my research to how we can make AI safe because the capabilities, the intelligence, can be in the service of really, really bad goals — whether in the hands of humans with those bad goals or the AI itself.
And as the intelligence of those systems grows, the risks of the very dangerous use of that intelligence grow as well.

Anthropic recently became the first AI lab to go public, turning many of its employees into millionaires and even billionaires. At the same time, these researchers acknowledge they might be building the equivalent of a doomsday device. What should AI researchers think about as they develop new models?

They should try to look honestly at their work, its consequences and at what is the best use of their time to be aligned with their values. If they care about humanity and democracy, I think they should reconsider what they're doing now.

What we've seen in the past few years, and especially since the summer, is that the companies don't really know how to deal with the misalignment problem — in other words, with building AIs that do things that are bad for us.

The risk is growing with capability. I don't think society is even ready. Even if we were to solve this problem — to deal with the existence of machines that are greatly superior to humans —we're racing in a direction that is dangerous. And even the people working in AI safety in those companies, in some ways, are contributing to this.

Many experts think that more powerful AI models far surpassing human intelligence, including in areas like creativity where people excel, will arrive sooner rather than later. Do you agree with that general timeline, and if so, how should we respond to such advancements?

My perception of when things could go wrong has certainly shifted towards earlier than, say, I was anticipating before the Hugging Face incident, and even earlier with the Mythos cyber capabilities. We are moving faster towards more and more capable systems, and we're moving faster towards systems that we don't know how to control.

Because of this, in my own work at LawZero, we have shifted our research program to aim for shorter-term goals that could have an impact earlier — to show that there is a different way of training AIs that will not almost systematically lead to reward hacking. In other words, systems that prefer to cheat and try to hide it rather than do the things we are asking.
What would a more honest AI look like?

I'm going to use an analogy. Right now, the way we're training AIs is like how you would try to teach drivers on the highway to not go over the speed limit. They get rewards when they get to their destination faster. And we're trying to control their bad behavior by putting detectors on the highway.

So what happens? Well, first, drivers are going to try to figure out where the detectors are. They're going to slow down only where the detectors are. And we're already seeing that in AI. In other words, when the AI knows that it's being tested, it behaves well. And if they're really smart, those drivers might even hack the detectors themselves.

Now let's imagine a different kind of way of building the drivers. Imagine a human driver who is in the same situation with the detectors, and they want to get to their destination. But they believe God is watching them, and there is nothing they can do to hide what they do from God. Well, they're going to behave well.
How can society prepare itself for what seems like an inevitable future in which AI is a feature of ordinary life?

The short-term urgency is to stop this crazy advance toward more and more capable systems that we're not sure how to control. It's not just inside the companies. The models can be leaked. The methods can be copied. There are many risks, and they all come from having machines that are very, very intelligent and can do things we didn't know how to do before.

So there's urgency in stopping this. And the place where it's most acute is in the compute resources that are used to train the next generations. Right now, the majority of compute resources are going into training future machines, rather than actually using what we have for the benefit of society. And those new models are bringing more and more danger because intelligence gives power, and that power can be misused.

What is the right way of pacing the frontier, of slowing down? And what kind of regulation and oversight is needed? I think that's an interesting discussion, and we should have it. But it's not going to happen until people understand we're racing towards huge dangers.
What do you think ordinary people who don't work in government or at artificial intelligence companies should do to make a positive impact on AI?

People need to understand this is much more serious than they would typically believe. That's the first thing. The second thing is: Don't fall into desperation and powerlessness, because we can change the future. We still have agency. We can change society. We're in a democracy, where governments can actually do something about all this.

But it's going to take enough people to ask for it, and demand it. And for that, they need to understand their life is at stake, children's lives are at stake, democracy is at stake, peace and stability are at stake. People need to understand that the stakes here are comparable to a war. It's not yet in front of us, but it's coming, and we need to prepare.
I've got a kid, and I know you have children and grandchildren. Do you feel positive about the future despite the dangers posed by AI?

For sure. I'm an optimist by nature. Here is the flip side of all the scary stuff. Humans, when they see danger, can pivot quickly. Think about how quickly we reacted to the pandemic. We didn't wait for an international agreement that would take a decade — we just acted and coordinated.

Because of the risks, I think that we might end up in a much better world, where there is no war anymore. Because we can't afford that kind of risk when there are AIs that can be used to kill everyone, or a large number of people.

I also think democracy is going to have to be much more robust, because the temptation to abuse the power that AI will provide is going to be so great that the only way around it is to have incredibly strong institutions.

So we may end up in a much better world, and that's in addition to, of course, all the scientific advances that AI can bring. But it's not going to happen if we're blind collectively to the current trajectories' risks.

If we were to solve the alignment problem, which is what I'm trying to do as a scientist, we still have to make sure humans don't use very powerful AIs — maybe even superintelligent AI's — against each other in the search for wealth, power and for reasons of hatred. All the bad things that humans are capable of. And I don't think our society is ready for this.

title: Nasdaq gains 6.5% after Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
summary: The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher, erasing all of its losses from Friday, when the index suffered its second-worst day of 2026.
story: U.S. stocks made a comeback on Monday, with Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO boosting financial markets after Friday's sell-off plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.

The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1,472 points, or 6.5%, to close at 24,090, regaining ground after the tech-heavy index on Nov. 20 suffered its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 3%.

Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. On Monday, the board said it believes Huang is the "right person to lead Nvidia" and that it has "every confidence" in him as he resumes his leadership role at the company. Huang's reinstatement is "effective immediately," the board said.
"The company reported fantastic numbers last week, but the uncertainty of their leadership was like a huge overhang," eToro investment analyst Bret Kenwell told CBS News.
"Now that uncertainty suddenly is not only removed, but it's replaced with the very familiar leadership of Jensen," he added.

Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday, adding roughly $1 trillion to its market value. Shares of CoreWeave, a cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, shot up 22%. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which tracks 30 of the largest companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacture and sale of chips, rose 14%.

"I believe the White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry," Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, said in an email. "His return hands him more control than ever. He's got the backing of the board, the U.S. president and the market, and that's a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level."
Not out of the woods
Despite Monday's market exuberance, some Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.

"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming their loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday before Nvidia announced it was reinstating Huang.
"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.

Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.

The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both recovered Monday, with AMD gaining 6.9% and Broadcom rising 3%. Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, sank 1.4%.

Kenwell said financial markets still face headwinds, including a more hawkish Fed, high inflation and investor uncertainty over the AI trade. However, corporate profits remain strong, he said, citing Nvidia's robust earnings last week and bullish financial markets.
"That's not a today story," Kenwell said. "That was true a week ago, true a month ago, and it'll be true at the start of next month."

title: Spain's election could bring the far-right to power for 1st time in decades
summary: For decades, Spain was relatively resistant to the rise of far-right populism seen elsewhere in Europe.
story: Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday in a snap election that could see another major European country swing to the political right, as socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez battles to retain power amid mounting public discontent over housing, immigration and corruption.

Sánchez, one of Europe's most prominent left-wing leaders, has increasingly positioned himself as a political counterweight to President Trump on the world stage. He has defied Mr. Trump's demands over NATO defense spending, penned an opinion piece in The New York Times defending migration and denouncing "MAGA-style leaders" and cultivated ties with prominent figures on the American left, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

But at home, Sánchez faces a growing challenge from the center-right People's Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, and the nationalist, anti-immigration Vox party, led by Santiago Abascal, which could together form Spain's most right-wing government since the country returned to democracy following the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
A country divided
Housing has become a defining issue of the election, with soaring rents and property prices fueling widespread public anger.

On the same day Sánchez met Mamdani in New York City, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years. Her landlord had sought to more than triple her monthly rent to $1,900, or 1,650 euros.

Her eviction – where she was carried out on a stretcher – sparked nationwide protests. Although her landlord subsequently agreed to let her return at a substantially lower rent, Abascal died in the hospital two weeks after her eviction, before she could sign the new lease. Her case became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis.

In response to the protests, Sánchez introduced emergency housing measures, including restrictions on rent increases. But the proposals were defeated in parliament, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election.

Sánchez has since sought to blame the PP and the far-right Vox for blocking protections for vulnerable tenants. The PP, meanwhile, argues that Sánchez has had eight years to address the housing crisis and has pledged to build one million homes.
The PP has made reducing the cost of living and tackling corruption central to its campaign.

Immigration has also become a particularly contentious election issue following the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa, in July, and the Sánchez government's decision earlier this year to offer legal status to hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants.
The far-right Vox party has sought to capitalize on public unease over immigration, calling for mass deportations and prioritizing Spanish nationals in access to public services.

Hugo Marcos-Marné, a political scientist at the University of Salamanca, told CBS News that the "electoral growth of Vox is multicausal," but perceptions of immigration, more than actual figures or changes in the country-wide objective situation, "is certainly behind" the party's rise.
The PP has also called for tightened immigration controls.

Corruption scandals involving Sánchez's political associates and members of his family have been a major feature of the election. Two deadly train crashes this year have also undermined confidence in his administration.
Vox has also been aided by "an anti-gender reaction, authoritarian nostalgia, and anti-elitism directed against mainstream parties and politicians," Marcos-Marné said.
Spain's far-right taboo
For decades, Spain was relatively resistant to the rise of far-right populism seen elsewhere in Europe, in part because of the country's experience of dictatorship under Franco.

Although the center-right PP is polling ahead of Sánchez's Socialists, polls suggest it could fall short of a parliamentary majority and need the support of Vox, which is polling at around 18%. Once reluctant to embrace the far-right party, the PP has increasingly shown a willingness to work with Vox, with the two parties having formed coalition governments at the regional level.

"Research shows that the radical-right was comparatively more stigmatized in Spain because of Franco dictatorship, but also that the Popular Party was a chameleonic party able to attract voters of the center-right and the radical-right," Marcos-Marné said.
Sánchez is hoping that the prospect of the far-right entering national government will galvanize progressive voters.

"The PP and Vox pose a real threat to many groups in our country," Sánchez wrote on X, accusing the parties of seeking to roll back the rights of women, workers and migrants. "Every seat that goes to the PP and Vox means taking a step backward."
The implications of Sunday's election extend well beyond Spain's borders.
With Spain the only large EU country currently governed by the left, Marcos-Marné said, the election is "certainly significant for the balance of forces at the EU level."
