title: Iowa detonation did not increase levels of lead in water, EPA says
summary: The EPA conducted sampling at more than 130 structures in Iowa, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches.
story: The Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday the controlled detonation of a stockpile of degrading explosives in Iowa did not result in an increase of lead in water bodies that serve as a source of drinking water.

"EPA found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake," the agency said in a press release.
"EPA sampled 35 drinking water sources across Iowa, Illinois, and Missouri before the controlled detonation to set a baseline," it added.

The EPA said it collected more than 1,632 air, water, soil and dust samples ahead of Wednesday's destruction of the lead azide stockpile, followed by 1,607 samples after the detonation, the agency said. Samples were sent to multiple EPA and private labs for testing.
"The agency is expecting to start receiving lab results on post-detonation sampling as early as tomorrow," the EPA said in a news release.

The EPA said it collected samples at more than 180 structures, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches, as well as at parks, nearby farms, drinking water sources and the Mississippi River watershed.
The EPA said Friday that it had completed 88% of post-detonation sampling at homes that were sampled pre-detonation, and expected to finish the remainder Friday.
As of Thursday, no airborne lead had been detected throughout the region, the EPA said.
The agency said it is also testing for other compounds that may have been released during the detonation.
"The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation," it said in Thursday's news release.

The Army on Wednesday detonated 5 tons of deteriorating explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant located in the small community of Middletown, citing the risk of an unplanned explosion. Local residents and environmental groups had sought to block the detonation over concerns that a plume of toxic lead dust could threaten public health and agriculture.

The Middletown plant housed about 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. The EPA said the lead azide had degraded over the last 20 years it had been in storage. It had undergone a recrystallization process that increased "the material's sensitivity to friction and shock" and made it more susceptible to the "risk of unintentional detonation," the EPA said.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily halted the detonation last week while it considered whether to impose a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups challenging the plan had failed to show they were likely to succeed.

The chaotic lead-up to the detonation reached the White House, prompting questions within the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
President Trump praised the detonation as having "exceeded expectations."

title: U.S. Air Force cloud platform breached by hackers, report says
summary: The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month.
story: The U.S. Air Force's cloud computing platform was breached in a cyberattack, multiple sources told Reuters on Friday.
The hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, according to Reuters, potentially exposing sensitive military and personnel information.
The breach was discovered at some point in the last month during system upgrades, sources told the outlet.

In a statement provided to CBS News, an Air Force spokesperson did not confirm or deny the breach, saying that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems."
"Ensuring the security, resilience and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority," the Air Force spokesperson said.

In a follow-up statement, the Defense Department said that its systems "are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world," adding that it "will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications."

When reached by CBS News, Leidos, the tech company which has served as the main contractor operating Cloud One since May, declined to comment specifically on the hack, deferring to the Air Force. A Leidos spokesperson noted that earlier this year, it announced a $454.9 million contract to modernize and secure the Air Force's cloud operations.

The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month, including at the National Security Agency, the CIA, the FBI, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the Federal Aviation Administration, the latter of which prompted a nationwide ground stop that triggered chaos for tens of thousands of travelers at U.S. airports.
In the FBI breach reported last week, hackers accessed a large database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to access criminal records.

The NSA's network outage was linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News. The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline during the ordeal, the sources said.

The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence, meanwhile, suffered an intrusion of an internal network that gathers intelligence from publicly available information, such as social media.
An ODNI official told CBS News in a statement Tuesday that there were "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems" from that breach.

All this comes as White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired from his position last week. Sources told CBS News that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, and that he had told people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.

title: Sen. Deb Fischer's husband died by suicide, her office says
summary: "His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him," Sen. Deb Fischer said of her late husband, Bruce.
story: Washington — Nebraska Sen. Deb Fischer's husband, Bruce Fischer, died by suicide, a spokesperson for her office said Friday.
On Monday, the Republican senator's office announced that he had died Sunday, "peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors."

But on Friday, a spokeperson for Fischer's office said in a statement on X, "Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home. Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life. The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning."

Fischer's office said no further details would be provided at this time. When the senator announced her husband's death earlier this week, she referred to him as "my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family." They were married for 54 years.

According to her Senate profile, Fischer met her husband, a cattle rancher, while she was a student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. After they married, the two moved to the family ranch outside of Valentine, Nebraska, where they raised their three sons.

"His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him," Fischer said of her late husband, adding that she "will cherish the decades we spend building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills."
Fischer, 75, has represented Nebraska in the Senate since 2013.
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental health crisis, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing or texting "988."

title: Zelenskyy: Trump calling Putin a friend like calling Hitler a friend
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy described President Trump calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" as "strange" because the Russian leader is "an aggressor and a killer."
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe's future financial commitments to Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with CBS News partner BBC News Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Mr. Trump calling Putin "my friend" at a recent summit in China as "strange" because the Russian leader is "an aggressor and a killer."
"He can't be a friend," Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to Adolf Hitler being viewed as a friend during World War II.

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
In the BBC interview, Zelenskyy called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the U.S. to show both "power and respect."
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor ... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he told the BBC.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Mr. Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend ... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin. You know ... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

Zelenskyy's comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a "grandmaster" of politics and weeks after Kushner's partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a "humanitarian."

Moscow's invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Mr. Trump resumed relations.

At the same time, Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia's ballistic missiles and that SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication, isn't working properly.

Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia's invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new $49 billion loan for Ukraine's economic and military needs next year.
Elections in the EU over the next 12 months could amplify the influence of parties reluctant to send more money to Ukraine and may fray the continent's support.
Ukraine looks to allay concerns over Libya strike
Ukraine is determined to keep fighting for its independence, Kyiv officials say, and has launched daring attacks against Russian assets.
A recent strike on a Russian navy vessel docked at a port in Libya, however, raised alarm in Europe and Washington that the war could spread and engulf other countries.

In an apparent attempt to defuse tensions, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he held a phone call with Libyan Foreign Minister Al-Taher Al-Baour, informing him that Ukraine had no intentions of drawing Libya into the war.
Sybiha said in comments posted on social media late Thursday that he reaffirmed Kyiv's support for Libya's sovereignty and efforts to reunify the country.
Russia launched nearly 300 aerial attacks a week this month
The grinding aerial bombardment between Russia and Ukraine has escalated recently.
Russia launched close to 300 aerial attacks a week through Nov. 20 on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, or ACLED, that tracks violence.
Zelenskyy warned Thursday that a major Russian attack is looming.

Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 110 of 155 Russian drones launched overnight Friday, including 51 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to the Ukrainian air force. Hits were recorded at 27 locations across Ukraine, it said.

The attacks targeted railway infrastructure, energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings across nine Ukrainian regions, killing at least one person and wounding at least six, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.

Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line.
On Wednesday, a senior military adviser to Zelenskyy said Ukraine used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its forces overnight intercepted 318 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and illegally annexed Crimea.
Residents of St. Petersburg reported explosions in eight districts of the city, the Russian online news outlet Astra said.
Officials reported that Ukraine's attacks killed at least two people and wounded six others.

Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.

title: Trump to visit maker of semiconductor chips, including Nvidia's
summary: President Trump will visit the Phoenix TSMC facility, one of the largest manufacturers of advanced chips, including Nvidia's.
story: A White House official said Thursday that President Trump is planning to visit the groundbreaking of a Phoenix facility for a manufacturer of semiconductor chips, including for Nvidia, a trip that comes as the company is under increasing scrutiny for the president's involvement in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO after he had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

On Dec. 4, Mr. Trump will tour and deliver remarks at the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company facility in Phoenix, Arizona, a White House official confirmed Thursday. The Taiwan-based company has been expanding in Arizona since 2020, according to the company's website, and next week's visit will be to the latest expansion of its facilities.
A TSMC spokesperson also confirmed to CBS News in a statement that the president was expected to attend the groundbreaking.
The White House official said the new expansion is expected to fund more than 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the surrounding community.
It's unclear whether Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs or the state's Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego would attend the event next week.

The planned visit comes amid scrutiny of Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, with its high-powered chips emerging as integral to the race for AI dominance between the U.S. and China. Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang earlier this month resigned after the news broke of his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed and who U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it.

Mr. Trump advocated for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, with an official saying earlier this week that reinstating him would "preserve America's technological edge over China, strengthen our national security" and ensure the future of AI will be built in the U.S. Sources also told CBS News that Mr. Trump was privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.
Nvidia's board reinstated Huang on Monday, and Mr. Trump touted his return in a social media post shortly afterward.

title: Trump claims "fake economic numbers" were released before election
summary: President Trump demanded an investigation into the Commerce Department's recent revising of the GDP, which happens routinely.
story: President Trump is spending Thanksgiving in Florida, where he had a policy meeting early Thursday morning and then headed to his golf club nearby.

He and first lady Melania Trump, who are staying at Mar-a-Lago, called U.S. service members on Thursday evening, including members of a unit that was involved in Operation Epic Fury, saying Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon."

On Thursday morning, Mr. Trump posted a holiday message on social media, wishing a happy Thanksgiving to the "American patriots who have worked so hard to make our country great!" He continued in the lengthy post to wish a happy Thanksgiving to several others with whom he has grievances, including the Commerce Department, immigrants, "the radical far left" and more.

Mr. Trump claimed that before the midterm elections where Republicans suffered heavy losses, there were "fake Economic Numbers" released. Mr. Trump cited the Commerce Department on Wednesday revising the gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3% on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%. The Commerce Department regularly updates its monthly economic data to improve its accuracy, including not just the GDP but also the monthly employment data.
Although he did not present any evidence, the president demanded an investigation.

Mr. Trump also wished a happy holiday to "all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left, those that are looking to change our Court System to that of Sharia, those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work."
The president continued his post with messages about the Somali community, deported immigrants and those who he believes do not appreciate the White House ballroom he is constructing.

Overnight, Mr. Trump praised the Army's controlled detonation of about five tons of degraded lead azide in Iowa, blaming former President Barack Obama for the situation and writing that no "carcinogens were released into beautiful Iowa air." Although Mr. Trump and other administration officials have praised the detonation, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday that prior to it, there was a chaotic lead-up inside the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner.

On Wednesday night, Mr. Trump met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and the pair issued a joint statement describing the meeting as "very impactful" and focused on Russia, Ukraine and Iran. The statement said they discussed "the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."

Mr. Trump earlier in the week continued the annual tradition of pardoning turkeys, sending turkeys named Freedom and Feathers to live on a farm in Texas. Melania Trump, meanwhile, welcomed the official White House Christmas tree on Monday.

Kristin  Brown
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: ICE detains man after he picked up $1 million lottery winnings
summary: The Massachusetts State Lottery posted on social media last week a photo of Ariel Velasquez-Morales, who won $1 million from a scratch-off ticket purchased in Boston.
story: Immigration officials detained a man in Massachusetts this week days after he won $1 million from a scratch-off lottery ticket, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Wednesday.

The Massachusetts State Lottery posted on social media last week a photo of Ariel Velasquez-Morales, who won $1 million from a scratch-off ticket purchased in Boston. A few days later, ICE reposted the smiling photo of Velasquez-Morales and said he had been detained.
According to a statement from ICE, Velasquez-Morales entered the U.S. illegally from El Salvador in 2013, and an immigration judge in 2014 ordered his removal.
ICE said Velasquez-Morales is being detained pending removal from the country. It's unclear where he is being held.

ICE's Boston office also posted the photo of Velasquez-Morales and wrote, "Welcome to the ERO Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!" Enforcement and Removal Operations, or ERO, is a branch of ICE.
ICE said Velasquez-Morales opted to take the lump sum of $650,000, and it's unclear if he will be able to keep the winnings.
It's unclear if Velasquez-Morales has legal representation.

The news comes the same week that Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who had unwittingly become the face of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, left the U.S. for Spain. Abrego Garcia entered the country illegally in 2011, but a court order had barred him from being returned to his home country of El Salvador. Despite that, he was mistakenly deported in March 2025 to El Salvador's notorious CECOT prison, and a judge ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.

Trump administration officials had fought against allowing Abrego Garcia to return to the U.S. and immediately arrested him on criminal charges when he did return. For over a year, Abrego Garcia and the Trump administration fought over his removal, with the administration seeking to deport him to various African countries while Abrego Garcia said he would voluntarily leave for Costa Rica.

Speaking from Spain on Wednesday, Abrego Garcia said, "The government did not decide where my story continues." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, however, said Wednesday that he is "delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain."

title: Trump owned millions in Nvidia stock as he pressed for Jensen Huang's reinstatement
summary: President Trump holds tens of millions in Nvidia shares, giving him a personal stake in the company's stock market roller coaster ride of the past two weeks, financial disclosure documents show.
story: President Trump holds tens of millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, giving him a personal stake in the company's stock market roller coaster ride over the past two weeks, financial disclosure documents show.

Mr. Trump stood to lose large sums with CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt departure, and stood to profit handsomely after he successfully pressed the chip developer's board to reinstate Huang. Nvidia stock surged more than 30% when Huang returned to the company on Monday, reversing a weekslong slide.

Huang resigned two weeks ago over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China, and another alleged affair with a subordinate. Mr. Trump said Monday he personally spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced them" to rehire Huang, offering an "assurance" that there was no national security threat.

Mr. Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock in his investment accounts as of the end of 2025, according to financial disclosures filed with the Office of Government Ethics. He bought or sold the company's stock in more than 100 transactions that were worth between $27 million and nearly $98 million between January 2025 and September 2026.

The value of the president's Nvidia shares increased anywhere from $1.3 million to $14.8 million on Monday, before paring back some of those gains when Nvidia's share price ticked down Tuesday. The range is so large because it isn't clear how many shares of Nvidia the president currently owns, but it can be roughly estimated based on his sales and purchases this year.

"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions," a White House spokesman told CBS News Tuesday, adding that his investments mirror indexes like the Schwab 1000. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."

In addition to the president, several of his appointees to positions in the State, Commerce and Treasury departments as well as the IRS reported millions in Nvidia stock in their investment portfolios. Many have since sold their holdings.

Forbes estimates Mr. Trump's net worth at more than $6 billion, making Nvidia a small part of his total wealth. And Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable public companies, at more than $3.7 trillion, so many investors hold shares in the tech giant.
Still, some ethics experts questioned Mr. Trump's large stake in Nvidia, especially after he intervened to boost the company's fortunes.

"This goes beyond a conflict of interest," said Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "He is squarely, explicitly using his power as president to benefit himself financially. He has prioritized his finances over the security of the nation."

Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit government watchdog, told CBS News that Mr. Trump's "continued ownership of stock in this company is the clearest example of how the president's personal financial interest makes everything he does suspect."

Mr. Trump's personal investments have drawn controversy in the past, including his stakes in publicly traded energy companies, firms that have business with the government and his family's cryptocurrency firm. He has denied any conflict of interest.

Some critics called for legal reforms to prohibit the president and members of Congress from buying and selling stocks while they hold office. Elected officials are generally allowed to trade individual stocks, though lawmakers from both parties have called for the practice to be banned.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and former chief ethics attorney for the White House between 2005 and 2007, said he has long argued for changes to the federal conflict of interest law that prohibits government employees from participating in matters that result in their personal enrichment while in office. That current law does not apply to the president, vice president or members of Congress, he said.
"We need a prohibition on this right away," he said, adding that the new Congress may take up the cause in January.
Painter called Mr. Trump's intervention with the Nvidia board "a huge conflict of interest" and overreach of government power.
"It's not the job of the government to call up and say who the CEO of a company should be," he told CBS News.

The president has defended his decision to intervene, saying on CNBC that "we have to protect our geniuses" and arguing that Nvidia — as the world's leading designer of advanced chips — plays a key role in maintaining the U.S.' lead over China in AI technology.

Mr. Trump has also frequently pointed to the performance of the stock market as a barometer of his success as president. Shortly after Huang was reinstated, Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal the "response from the market has been very positive," and "that really shows the decision was right."
Beyond Mr. Trump, numerous political appointees held Nvidia stock. Some divested themselves of their holdings after they were appointed to government positions, federal filings show.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin owned between $250,000 and $500,000 in Nvidia stock in March 2026, and sold $500,000 to $1 million in shares of the tech company in June of this year, his financial disclosures show.
"As Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin acts to ensure full compliance with all ethics and conflict of interest rules," said a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

In the Commerce Department, where Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing scrutiny over whether he has done enough to crack down on highly sensitive AI chip sales to China, a number of senior advisers last year reported selling large positions in Nvidia.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm that was previously run by Lutnick and is now controlled by his sons, reported holding roughly 1 million shares of Nvidia for its clients as of Sept. 30, worth around $228 million at the time. Those shares were worth just over $150 million at Tuesday's price. None of Lutnick's personal financial disclosures filed by the federal government mention Nvidia holdings or transactions.
In the State Department, some of Mr. Trump's diplomatic appointees had Nvidia holdings.

Charles Kushner, the U.S. ambassador to France and father of Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, reported Nvidia holdings totaling between $1.5 million and $6 million, according to public disclosures filed January 2025.

U.S. Ambassador to Costa Rica Melinda Hildebrand reported Nvidia holdings between $5 million and $25 million, her April 2025  disclosures show. The Texas billionaire, who was a major Trump campaign fundraiser, sold the stock in November of that same year, filings show.

Warren Stephens, another major Trump donor and ambassador to the United Kingdom, reported Nvidia holdings between $750,000 and $1.5 million, according to his January 2025  disclosures. He sold those shares in July and August 2025, a few months after he was sworn in as ambassador.

In the Treasury Department, when she was nominated to be under secretary for International Affairs, Erin Browne held Nvidia shares totaling between $250,000 and $500,000, her disclosures from January show. Browne sold the stock before her confirmation in August, filings show.

Todd Newnam, who was appointed chief financial officer of the IRS in January, holds between $115,000 and $250,000 in Nvidia stock, according to his financial disclosure, filed in April of last year. Newnam, a former CEO of a tech company, was part of the Department of Government Efficiency team that sought to streamline government spending and cut the federal workforce.

"All OGE (Office of Government Ethics) 278 filers are required to disclose any equity positions they hold and are advised of their recusal obligations in accordance with the ethics rules," an IRS spokesperson said Tuesday, referring to the financial disclosure required by members of the executive branch of the federal government.

Many other officials could be indirectly exposed to Nvidia stock if they invested in mutual funds or similar assets. For example, Vice President JD Vance reported $1 million to $5 million in a fund that tracks the S&P 500 — and Nvidia is one of that index's largest components.

title: Judge temporarily blocks FCC from reviewing ABC's licenses
summary: A federal judge blocked the FCC from moving forward with an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses, a move the network argues is an attempt by the Trump administration to punish speech it does not like.
story: A federal judge blocked the Federal Communications Commission from moving forward with an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses Wednesday, a move the network argues is an attempt by the Trump administration to punish speech it does not like.

In a 45-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan found ABC is likely to succeed in showing the FCC's license review was retaliatory. Her preliminary injunction bars the FCC from "taking any continuing or further action against [ABC] in relation to the early license renewal proceedings" while the network's lawsuit against the agency works its way through the courts.

The judge pointed to at least 11 different examples of President Trump publicly urging the FCC to strip ABC of its licenses in recent years — an action the president argues is necessary because the network's news coverage or late-night shows are unfair to him.
AliKhan also said FCC Chair Brendan Carr — who frequently echoes Mr. Trump's criticism of media outlets — "has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders."

"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," the judge wrote.

She said the question of whether ABC's interest in a preliminary injunction outweighed the federal government's interests was "not a close case." She did not agree to ABC's request for a broader ban on "taking any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten Plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion."
An ABC News spokesperson said: "Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration."

An FCC spokesperson called the decision to grant ABC's motion "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear," and said the agency "looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter."

Earlier this year, the FCC ordered ABC to file early license renewal applications for the eight local television stations it owns and operates, saying it was investigating "possible violations" of the Communications Act of 1934 and the agency's prohibition on unlawful discrimination. The licenses originally weren't scheduled for renewal until 2028 to 2031.
ABC sued over the move, calling it "blatant retaliation" in violation of the First Amendment and arguing the FCC's investigation into discrimination was a pretext.

"Each day, Plaintiffs (and every other broadcaster observing the Commission's actions) face a choice between exercising independent editorial judgment or risking the loss of valuable broadcast licenses—precisely the type of choice that chills protected First Amendment activity and cannot be remedied after the fact," the network and Disney wrote in a filing.

At one point during a court hearing last month, Disney attorney Beth Wilkinson invoked the French Revolution, saying the FCC's review was forcing the company to sit with its "head on a guillotine" while it awaits a decision about the licenses.

The FCC has denied that it is seeking to punish ABC for its speech. Government lawyers say the agency has been investigating the broadcaster since last year over its compliance with anti-employment discrimination rules, alleging its responses to requests for information have been insufficient, leading the FCC to push for early license renewal.

"The commission decided to look for information that it needed by calling for early renewal of plaintiffs' broadcast license," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remme said in last month's court hearing before AliKhan.

AliKhan appeared skeptical of the government's arguments in Wednesday's ruling. At one point, she noted that the FCC took action shortly after late-night ABC host Jimmy Kimmel joked that first lady Melania Trump had "the glow of an expectant widow."
She said "it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings."

The Trump administration has often tangled with ABC and other outlets. Last year, following another controversial joke by Kimmel, Carr did not rule out punishing the network, saying on a podcast: "We can do this the easy way or the hard way."

More broadly, Carr has suggested networks could lose their licenses for coverage of the Iran war, and Mr. Trump called for licenses to be revoked when some networks opted out of carrying a primetime speech in July. The FCC has also warned daytime and late-night talk shows that they must provide equal time to political candidates — a rule that historically hasn't applied to them. Separately, the administration has sought to restrict some outlets' access to the White House.

title: A look at the probes involving Nvidia, Jensen Huang and Megaspeed
summary: The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president and CEO of Nvidia sent shockwaves through the political and business world, and has fueled scrutiny by Congress.
story: Washington — Revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset have put the leading AI company under a microscope, as lawmakers and states question whether Nvidia skirted federal export rules that aim to stop its most advanced chips from going to China.

While Huang initially resigned his post amid scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, Nvidia's board of directors announced Monday that it reinstated Huang as president and CEO.

News of Huang's return to Nvidia sent shockwaves through the business and political worlds, even as President Trump said he had spoken to the board and "convinced them" to bring Huang back. The president told CNBC in an interview that his administration gave Nvidia "assurances" that Huang is not a threat to national security.

The company, meanwhile, said it received "input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."
Still, investigations by at least one state and Congress are unlikely to be derailed by Huang's dramatic return to Nvidia.
California Department of Justice

California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia last week following revelations of Huang's affair with the woman who is alleged to have ties to China's Ministry of State Security.

Bonta, a Democrat, said the state's Department of Justice is seeking information from Nvidia about whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether the company misled investors and the public.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," he said in a statement. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law."
Bonta said the information his office receives from Nvidia will help determine whether the company broke state law.
Congressional probes

Numerous congressional committees were readying investigations into Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy, and his reinstatement as CEO did not diminish lawmakers' appetite for more information about Huang's actions and whether his company's chips were diverted to China.

Huang is set to answer questions behind closed doors from lawmakers on three House panels, the Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select Committee, on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, will appear before the committees on Dec. 2.
The Senate Banking Committee will then hold a public hearing with Huang on Dec. 3.

Democrats, who will take control of the House and Senate in January, say they intend to launch investigations into Nvidia and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose agency oversees government export controls on sensitive technology.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to serve as House speaker in the next Congress, denounced the decision by Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible."

"Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," he said in a statement Monday.
Senate Democrats have also pledged to act.

"Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X. "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is poised to take the helm of the Senate Banking Committee in January, said Nvidia officials and the Trump administration will have to answer questions from lawmakers.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," she said in a statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."
House and Senate Democrats have also demanded that the president and his administration provide information about their role in Huang's reinstatement.

"President Trump has acknowledged personally intervening on Huang's behalf, and Nvidia has acknowledged that it received 'input from senior levels of the United States government' in reaching its decision," a group of five Democratic senators said in a joint statement. "The American people deserve to know why the president intervened in this extraordinary manner, whether serious counterintelligence or national security concerns were disregarded, and whose interests this intervention was intended to serve."
The senators are: Warren, Chris Coons of Delaware, Ron Wyden of Oregon, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Maria Cantwell of Washington.
Justice Department

The Justice Department and Commerce Department said in a joint statement earlier this month that the federal government had been investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based computing company that is a Nvidia client, since 2024.
The Commerce Department sought records from Nvidia in May 2025 about direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed and placed the Singaporean company on its "no sell" list that June.

Agents with the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, working with Singaporean law enforcement, conducted an on-site, in-person check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang, the Commerce and Justice Departments said in their statement. After that action, the Justice Department took the lead in the criminal probe into Megaspeed.

Nvidia has received a subpoena as a witness from the Department of Justice in relation to its investigation into Megaspeed and export controls, a source directly familiar with the situation told CBS News.
Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025. China has denied allegations that she is a spy.

Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this month that the FBI was "looking into" Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who is of no relation. A Justice Department official said Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche spoke with Mr. Trump about Jensen Huang and Nvidia over the weekend, and said "the DOJ has no evidence of any wrongdoing" by either Huang or his company.

At a press conference Tuesday, the attorney general said the Justice Department did not have any information showing Huang committed criminal acts, and if he had, Blanche "would have certainly told the president."

Reporters pressed Blanche on how he and the Justice Department had made that determination if there was no investigation into Alice Huang or potential violations of federal export control laws by Nvidia. He dodged questions on the topic. Still, the attorney general referred to Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen."
Blanche said that "looking into it" does not mean there was an investigation into the Nvidia CEO and his alleged mistress, or the company itself.
The attorney general also said there was a "collective consensus" to conclude there was no national security risk posed by Huang.
Securities and Exchange Commission

The Securities and Exchange Commission is conducting its own civil investigation into Nvidia, the Wall Street Journal reported last week. Among the matters that the SEC will look into is whether the company's disclosures misled investors, sources told the Journal.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 11 that Nvidia altered its reporting methods for international chip sales and stopped reporting revenue tied to Singapore on financial disclosures last year.
Reuters said Friday that the SEC is examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. It's unclear when the agency began its investigation.
The SEC declined to comment.

Huang resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12, and the board said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO. During an earnings call on Nov. 17, Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Kress, too, told CNBC on Nov. 17 that the "board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen."
Less than a week later, on Nov. 23, the board reinstated him.
Internal Nvidia probe

After the New York Times reported that Huang was the target of a potential Chinese intelligence operation, Nvidia's board announced earlier this month that it would be launching an independent investigation into the allegations and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to help with the probe.
After announcing that Huang would return to Nvidia as president and CEO, the board said the investigation "will proceed to conclusion."
"Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it," the board said.

Jo Ling  Kent, 
                                                  
                                  Sophia  Vlahakis, 
                                                  
                                  Jacob  Rosen and 
                                                  
                                  Nicole  Sganga
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Judge declines to issue long-term ban on tax-funded pro-Trump ads
summary: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Trump.
story: A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban on the ads.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., said the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown a likelihood of prevailing in the case. Democrats had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president's campaign message just weeks before November's midterm elections.
In her ruling, she noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away.

"But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone," she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.
"At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded," AliKhan wrote.
Her ruling comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.

The ads first emerged on cable and broadcast networks — including CBS — in late September, just over a month before the midterms, funded by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. Many of the ads touted Mr. Trump or his administration's accomplishments, and included the disclosure: "Paid for by the U.S. Government."
Members of both parties raised questions about the ads, and Democrats sued the Trump administration in October.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies, arguing they are not political ads because they don't explicitly call on viewers to take any particular action. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don't try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued.
Mr. Trump eventually said in early October his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would start paying for the ads to run on television, though he insisted they were a "positive promotion for our Great U.S.A."

"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself," the president wrote.

Ahead of Wednesday's ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed.

A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, told The Associated Press in a statement that the party was "disappointed" by the judge's decision, adding that the DNC "will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration's attempts to undermine our democracy."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites.
But in her latest ruling, AliKhan declined to issue a preliminary injunction against the ads.

title: U.S.-based firms helping China access Nvidia's most advanced chips
summary: It's not just Megaspeed. A CBS News investigation reveals that at least two California-based Nvidia customers have Chinese ownership — giving the U.S. adversary potential access to Nvidia's most advanced technology.
story: Nvidia is selling its most cutting-edge chips to at least two companies that are U.S.-based, but are actually controlled by Chinese-owned firms, raising fresh questions about efforts to keep sensitive technology away from the nation's rivals, a CBS News investigation found.

One of the chip giant's "preferred partners" is a California company owned by a Chinese firm whose chief executive is a graduate of a Chinese military university, records show. Another California company was renamed after its Chinese-owned parent company was blacklisted.
Some of these U.S.-based, Chinese-owned firms have then leased or sold the advanced chips, used for artificial intelligence, to other companies in Southeast Asia, records show.

The world of computer chip exports is murky — and labyrinthine chains of custody have made it even more difficult to determine just how many of the most sensitive Nvidia chips are being exploited by China, experts told CBS News.

"It is a wake-up call for accountability, for properly resourcing the enforcement bodies, and for every leading private-sector tech company to map where it is exposed," said Mishel Kondi, a senior analyst at C4ADS, which specializes in using public data, from corporate filings to satellite imagery, to uncover sanctions violations and smuggling.

C4ADS, a Washington-based global security nonprofit also known as the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, examined corporate filings and other company ownership data at the request of CBS News. This story is based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an investigation of Nvidia's corporate relationships dating back to 2023 — long before its CEO Jensen Huang and his behemoth chip company dominated the news cycle.

That explosive saga began 27 days ago when the news broke that Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang — a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion, and Beijing denies she is a spy. The company she ran, Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore, is under investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.

But Megaspeed, national security and trade experts say, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the transfer of Nvidia chips to China. And elected officials are now asking questions like: How are Nvidia's chips getting to China? And what did Jensen Huang and his colleagues know about it?

"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement this week.
California company, Chinese owners
Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year. The company can sell graphics cards for personal computers and server chips with lower processing power to China without a special license.
What is not allowed — and is under strict export controls — are the sales of Nvidia's most technologically advanced chips, which are powering the AI revolution.
But recent reporting, including from CBS News, has shown some of the highest end chips, called Blackwells, have made it into Chinese hands.
The circuitous trail traveled by Nvidia chips quickly gets muddy.

Take RiCloud AI, a data center company based in San Jose, California. RiCloud AI appears on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners" in the U.S., affording it preferential access to sales of high-end computer chips used for advanced AI models.
These are classified as American sales, according to Nvidia's public filings — with the chips going to RiCloud AI, Inc., a U.S. company.
But RiCloud AI's parent company is Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited. That company is headquartered in Shenzhen, China, and is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university run by the Chinese military. Yu is also CEO of a related RiCloud company in California.

And Yuxing's chairman, Li Qiang, was previously chairman of data firm Global Switch Holdings, which was dropped as a data center provider by Australia's Department of Defense in June 2024 over national security concerns.
The U.S. government has not accused RiCloud and Yuxing of any wrongdoing.

By December 2025, just 10 weeks after it was incorporated, RiCloud AI had secured its partner status with Nvidia and has since become a "preferred" cloud partner, giving the company priority access to advanced chips, Nvidia's software and technical support. Nvidia has not responded to questions about what background checks it conducted before awarding the privileged status to RiCloud AI.

An examination of RiCloud AI's clients suggests that some seem like unorthodox customers for such high-powered technology. This year, for example, it signed a $120 million deal to lease 300 Nvidia B300 servers to a company in Taiwan that was primarily known for selling whisky.

Agencia Comercial Spirits was a small whisky importer with $609,000 in net income in 2025 when it listed on the Nasdaq as an AI company. This year it has made commitments for AI data center-related deals totaling between $488 and $598 million, after Li was appointed as chairman.

Agencia did not respond to a request for comment. In a February press release announcing its pivot into data centers, Agencia said the move was "part of a broader review of strategic opportunities outside its core whisky business."
Blacklisted owners
Then there is California company Aivres, which is currently listed on Nvidia's website as an "elite" compute partner — the highest tier of relationship with the chip giant.

Aivres used to be called Inspur, the same name as its Chinese parent company. But when Inspur group firms in China were added to a federal blacklist of companies considered a security risk to the U.S. in March 2023, the California subsidiary changed its name and today still maintains its close relationship with Nvidia. Aivres itself is not on the blacklist.

Aivres, which produces data center servers housing Nvidia chips, exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, according to a New York Times analysis of trade records published two months ago.
Some $3 billion of those exports were for computers containing Nvidia's cutting-edge Blackwell chips, which are restricted from being exported to China, the Times reported.
The Aivres chips then went to two companies in Malaysia — Megaspeed and Aolani — providing cloud AI services to Chinese firms Alibaba and ByteDance, according to the Times.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm where Jensen Huang paramour Alice Huang was a top executive, was blacklisted by the U.S. government this week, in the wake of the scandal. The company denies any wrongdoing.

The Pentagon put Alibaba on a blacklist in June, claiming it used advanced chips to help the Chinese military. The company denies it and sued the government over the blacklisting, winning a preliminary injunction last month.
The servers owned by Inspur — Aivres' parent company — are used in China by the country's military, according to the U.S. government. Aivres did not respond to requests for comment.
Selling to suspected smugglers
Another of Nvidia's elite U.S. partners has surfaced in a recent $300 million chip smuggling case, though it has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Earlier this year, a California businessman named Greg Lui was indicted for allegedly smuggling export-controlled chips to China via Malaysia and Singapore in 2023 and 2024. He has pleaded not guilty.
Records reviewed by CBS News link Lui to 2CRSi, an Nvidia elite partner in the U.S. that is a branch of a French-owned company making AI data servers.

Lui's indictment says his company bought 100 H100 servers — which required a license to export — worth more than $22 million from an unnamed manufacturer. 2CRSi's website lists his firm, Topmost Corp., as an "authorized partner," while his company website said he is an "authorized reseller of … 2CRSi."
The indictment does not accuse Nvidia of having any knowledge of the arrangement.

2CRSi said in a letter to shareholders this month that it received a grand jury subpoena from the federal prosecutor's office in Los Angeles about "a customer that we ourselves had reported to the authorities." It has not been accused of wrongdoing.
The company's U.S. revenue fell from $201 million to $4.7 million this year.
In addition to 2CRSi, Lui listed California firm Super Micro Computer, Inc. as one of his customers.
In March, the Justice Department accused Super Micro's co-founder of a scheme to smuggle $2.5 billion worth of servers to Chinese customers via a Southeast Asian company.

The co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw has denied the charges. His alleged "fixer" pleaded guilty in a deal with prosecutors last month. The company says those involved "no longer have any relationship with Supermicro" and its current executives had no knowledge of the alleged smuggling.
Accounting changes

Nvidia used to publish the regional breakdown of its chip sales based on the customer's billing location. That data showed that in 2024, nearly half of its chip sales were billed to the U.S., 18% to Singapore and 13% to China.

Last November, the company switched to using the customer's headquarters as its location. This bookkeeping change revealed that an extra $7.9 billion of customers' bills were actually from firms headquartered in China in 2024.
In 2025, U.S.-headquartered customers made up 69% of Nvidia sales, while China was cut to 9%.
Nvidia's public filings say "the end customer and shipping location may be different from our customers' headquarters location."
CBS News' findings suggest Nvidia's changes to the way it published these sales figures may make the locations of its customers less clear.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, who is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is poised to investigate whether companies are circumventing the bans on sales of chips to China, and into alleged Chinese espionage connected to Nvidia.

Kondi told CBS News that she believes the investigation of chip sales "matters beyond the news cycle because it exposes export control violations and potential economic espionage, and shows how Beijing ties intelligence work to its industrial plans, pursuing self-reliance while still reaching for foreign technology where it lacks parity."

title: Blindsided by Iowa detonation, White House scrambled, sources say
summary: White House officials have expressed frustration in internal conversations that they had to scramble to deal with the crisis.
story: Washington — The chaotic lead-up to Wednesday's detonation of barrels of chemicals at a U.S. Army munitions plant in Iowa that raised contamination fears has prompted questions inside the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

President Trump and other administration officials praised the controlled detonation of about 5 tons of degraded lead azide at the plant in Middletown as having "exceeded expectations," saying maximum mitigation efforts were successfully achieved.
"Great job by the Army, and others, in Iowa!!! President DJT," Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social about five hours after the blast took place.

But White House officials have expressed frustration in internal conversations that they had to scramble to deal with the crisis. The situation rapidly became a national news story, with complaints from Iowa residents that they had not received sufficient notice about the potential dangers.

The Army had known since spring that the lead azide at the plant posed a threat to the public and to the environment, but then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll failed to raise the issue to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or to other senior administration officials, according to several U.S. officials who requested anonymity to speak about a controversial topic.
A separate source familiar with the discussions surrounding the ammunition said the Army notified Hegseth's office early on. The notification never reached Hegseth directly, other officials said.
The process of coordinating the response was triggered before Driscoll left the administration, two sources said. Driscoll resigned in September amid tensions with Hegseth.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle learned of the stored chemicals and the risks in September, officials told CBS News, but didn't brief superiors. There have been discussions about quietly moving Telle out of the acting role in coming weeks, several sources said.

Administration leaders at the most senior levels were taken by surprise when they learned Thursday about the extent of the problem as they flew home from China after Mr. Trump's Asia trip, one U.S. official said. That forced White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to launch an intensive response from Air Force One, involving hours of phone calls, a dozen agencies and nearly every member of the Cabinet.

Mr. Trump and other White House officials in post-blast conversations Wednesday were relieved about the results of the detonation and the steps taken from Thursday on to handle the crisis. But Mr. Trump was furious about how the Army had handled the matter in the months before that, three of the sources said.
The president's plans to golf Wednesday in West Palm Beach were dashed by rain, and he watched the television coverage of events in Iowa closely, sources told CBS News.
There have also been internal administration conversations about the role in this by Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's chief of staff, the sources said.

Other officials defended the administration action, saying the dozens of lower-level career officials who knew about the impending danger from the lead azide for months appropriately discussed how to handle it.
CBS News reached out to the White House for comment. The Pentagon referred questions to the Army, which has not yet responded to a request for comment.
In March, the Army officially notified the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that 68 barrels of potentially unstable chemicals were discovered during a routine inspection at the Iowa plant.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday that the administration became aware about six months ago "that it was impossible to move it — it was impossible to effectively neutralize it without causing significant danger to the surrounding community." Vance said the administration examined other options.

But other U.S. officials said the conclusion was reached only about two months ago that a controlled detonation would be the only safe way to get rid of the chemicals. A private contractor retained by the Pentagon looked into potential disposal processes, two of the sources said.

Miller worked on the problem over the weekend before the blast, calling various officials, including Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand on Monday, two sources said. The administration sought to keep the response – and the public blame – bipartisan, one of the sources said.
Miller thanked Sand and outgoing Gov. Kim Reynolds "for their cooperation and engagement" shortly after the detonation.

Sand and Mr. Trump have exchanged some verbal blows. The Democratic governor-elect said on social media Wednesday the "lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," and called for "immediate transparency." Mr. Trump responded by writing that Sand had "hurt and delayed the process" and should stop trying to "nitpick and issue phony complaints."

Earlier in the week, Mr. Trump said the detonation wouldn't move forward unless Sand and an appeals court approved, but warned he would hold Sand responsible "for any and all death or destruction" if he blocked the operation. Sand, who did not have authority over the detonation, responded that the Trump administration should make the decision based on the information available.

A federal appeals court on Monday cleared the way for the detonation amid challenges from environmental groups and elected officials about the operation's potential risks to public health. The military ultimately went forward with a controlled blast of the material, rather than letting it further degrade.
Maps released Tuesday by the Army noted that the dust cloud may travel as far as 100 miles, but the most potent effects would likely be felt within 30 square miles of the munitions plant.

Fifteen minutes after the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitoring stations in the area. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA.
The Army said it had taken steps to barricade the concrete bunkers holding the munitions and absorb the toxic dust, including with aqueous foam, which is used to extinguish fuel fires.
This story published first on CBS News at 4:27 p.m. on Nov. 25, 2026.

title: China may have surveilled Alice Huang amid affair with Nvidia CEO
summary: China's Ministry of State Security may have been surveilling Alice Huang and sought information from her after her affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began, U.S. officials told congressional staffers.
story: China's Ministry of State Security may have been surveilling Alice Huang and sought information from her after her affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began, U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers Tuesday, according to people familiar with the briefing.

While there are still gaps in what U.S. intelligence agencies know, there is no indication to date that Alice Huang was specifically tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or that she passed information of significant value to the Chinese intelligence service.

But she was known to U.S. intelligence agencies to have been in contact with an MSS officer starting at least in spring 2025, multiple sources said, and her contacts with the agency raised counterintelligence concerns among U.S. intelligence officials. China's intelligence services rely not only on trained officers and formally recruited assets but also on citizens who are obliged under Chinese law to provide assistance when called upon.
Congressional staffers were also told that Kang Wei, believed to be Alice Huang's husband, had more extensive ties to the MSS, people familiar with the briefing said.
The New York Times was first to report on the briefing.

The two-hour briefing for House and Senate Intelligence Committee staffers, which included senior analysts from across the U.S. intelligence community, came two days after President Trump intervened to secure Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, despite national security concerns raised by some of his senior advisers.
Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under U.S. investigation for potentially diverting sensitive American technology to China.

Concerns about Alice Huang were laid out in a classified memo drafted this spring by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio that summarized U.S. intelligence, including intercepted communications involving the former Megaspeed executive. It was intended to ensure senior administration officials involved in relevant policy decisions were aware of the potential counterintelligence risks posed by her interactions with Jensen Huang.

Among those who received the memo were Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and senior White House staff. Rubio also briefed the president on intelligence.
The memo was not provided during Tuesday's briefing, despite requests from both congressional intelligence committees to see it.
China has denied allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.

Shortly after the existence of the memo came to light earlier this month, Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an extramarital affair. He later resigned as Nvidia CEO, but after less than two weeks, the company's board of directors reinstated him.

The reinstatement came after Trump administration officials offered Nvidia assurances that Jensen Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation and that the government had no legal issues with him, CBS News reported earlier Wednesday. The assurances did not extend to Alice Huang.

Two criminal investigations involving potential violations of U.S. export controls by Megaspeed and another buyer of Nvidia chips, Super Micro Computer, remain ongoing. The FBI has been investigating both cases for more than a year, with the Justice Department's National Security Division leading the Megaspeed investigation. Megaspeed has denied any violations of U.S. export control laws and says Alice Huang left the company last year.
Jensen Huang is expected on Capitol Hill next week for a closed-door session with House lawmakers and public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee.

title: Vance says Nvidia's Huang isn't under investigation, doesn't need a pardon
summary: Vice President JD Vance said he was assured Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang isn't under federal investigation.
story: Washington — Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday said he doesn't think Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang needs a presidential pardon, as he said the Justice Department and national security officials informed him that Huang isn't under federal investigation.

Speaking to reporters after serving Thanksgiving dinner at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base near Dayton, Ohio, the vice president was asked about his involvement in Huang's reinstatement and the assurances he received that Huang isn't a national security risk. CBS News has reported that President Trump and Vance spoke repeatedly with Huang, Nvidia board members and their legal counsel.

"Well, number one, we were told that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters Wednesday. "And frankly, I think we have to, in our country, remember that we don't try people in the court of public opinion. ... But most importantly, at just I think a personal level, we received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation, and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence."

Asked who gave him those assurances, Vance said he spoke with "multiple people in the United States government," including Attorney General Todd Blanche. Asked if he thinks Huang needs a pardon, the vice president said he doesn't. In an interview with the New York Post, the president said a pardon is "always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary."
But Vance told reporters, "I don't think he needs a pardon at all."

"I haven't seen any evidence, again, that he committed a crime," Vance continued. "And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him. And again, I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation."

Vance said "ultimately, it was the board's decision to bring Jensen Huang back." Nvidia's board reinstated Huang after President Trump urged them to do so. The president himself said he "convinced" the board to reinstate the ousted CEO.
Mr. Trump owned millions of dollars in Nvidia stock as he pushed for Huang's reinstatement amid tanking stock prices.
