title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. and arrives in Spain
summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year, left the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.
story: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, left the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, his team and the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.

Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid early Wednesday morning, alongside his wife, an American citizen, and his lawyer, a representative for the family told CBS News. Video of his departure from the U.S. showed his ICE ankle monitor being removed.
CBS News was first to report Abrego Garcia's plans earlier Tuesday.
Abrego Garcia, whose case became an early flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration's deportation crackdown, flew to Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday night.
"I can now breathe freedom," he said during a virtual press conference on Wednesday.
Abrego Garcia, speaking from Spain, said he and his family, not the U.S. government, will decide their "next steps."
"The government did not decide where my story continues," he said. "My family and I decide our future."

Abrego Garcia traveled out of the U.S. with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez, his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and representatives from We Are CASA, the U.S. advocacy group that has been helping him and his family.

Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia entered Spain with his Salvadoran passport and has a pathway to becoming a lawful permanent resident of the U.S., though that would require a waiver from the State Department that is unlikely to be granted by the current administration.
Still, he said the Trump administration did not succeed in its efforts to deport him to Liberia, as it sought to do.

"Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines," Sandoval-Moshenberg added. "Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus. And there's really no other way to see this other than, you know, Mr. Abrego Garcia's decision to hold strong throughout the last two years."
Trump administration officials touted Abrego Garcia's departure.

"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said. He reiterated the Trump administration's allegation that Abrego Garcia belongs to a gang — which his legal team has denied — and said he now "cannot terrorize innocent Americans."

In a social media post late Tuesday night, the Department of Homeland Security wrote: "To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives. He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."

The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country's CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the U.S. last year to face criminal charges.

Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal.

But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, DHS said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa.

Abrego Garcia's departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly canceled. The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued.

But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis' orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia's "prompt removal." The Justice Department said in March that the government was "ready, willing, and able" to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa.
In an order Wednesday, Xinis officially closed Abrego Garcia's case and dissolved the injunctions that she had previously imposed after "having received confirmation" that he had left the U.S.

The judge also directed a separate order issued Friday to be unsealed. That order, now publicly available, stated that Abrego Garcia would leave the U.S. by Tuesday and directed the Trump administration to "take all steps within their control to ensure [Abrego Garcia's] unimpeded departure and transit from the United States — to include the lifting of any detainer, lookout, alert, hold, or other records — that would cause Petitioner to be detained, questioned, or denied boarding on any aircraft."

The judge also directed the Trump administration to remove Abrego Garcia's GPS ankle monitor before boarding the plane taking him out of the country, and reiterated that the Department of Homeland Security could not interfere with his travel to the airport and departure from the U.S.

Abrego Garcia's case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an "error." Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT.

But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs.

In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.

The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and in May, a federal judge in Tennessee dismissed the criminal charges on the grounds that his prosecution was vindictive.
The Justice Department has appealed that decision, and arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit are scheduled for February.
This story published first on CBS News at 5:06 p.m. on Nov. 24, 2026.

title: Trump administration to issue new tariffs on China, EU and others
summary: The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on goods from other major economies.
story: The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, raising the total tariff rate on the world's second-largest economy to 45%. President Trump also plans to raise taxes on specific products from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
Brazil is among the countries that will be hardest hit, with the U.S. planning to raise tariffs on the country's raw and refined sugar and to impose a new 10% levy on aircraft.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.

"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base,"  U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.

The planned duties would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.

The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and Taiwan. The USTR is also investigating Mexico and Norway but hasn't imposed any new tariffs on those countries.

In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline. The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted at specific products and would not be stacked on top of existing tariffs introduced by the Trump administration.

Stephen Brown, chief North American economist for Capital Economics, said in a research note Wednesday that the Trump administration's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks." The new tariffs will essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs, rather than stacking on top of them, he said.

Tariffs have been a central part of the Trump administration's economic agenda, with the president arguing they are necessary to boost U.S. manufacturing, create jobs and reduce the trade deficit. However, his authority to impose the levies has faced legal challenges, complicating the rollout.
Tariffs unpopular with voters, small businesses

In February, the Supreme Court blocked a sweeping set of tariffs that the president implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, dismantling a key part of the administration's efforts and forcing the government to issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses.

Still, the administration has found other avenues to impose the levies, using other sections of trade law, such as Section 232, which allows the president to restrict imports that could threaten U.S. national security.
The average statutory U.S. tariff rate on imports is now 11.2%, according to the Yale Budget Lab.

The White House moved to propose the new tariffs on Wednesday despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters over rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.
We Pay the Tariffs, a grassroots coalition of small businesses, decried the new tariffs, warning they could raise prices just as the holiday season heats up.

"Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses," Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a statement. "Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either."

title: Army wants to resume training flights near site of collision
summary: An Army helicopter on a training mission collided with an American Airlines passenger jet on approach at DCA, killing all aboard both aircraft, in January 2025.
story: The U.S. Army is planning to resume helicopter training flights near Washington, D.C.'s Reagan National Airport less than two years after a deadly midair collision that killed 67 people, including 3 Army pilots.
The helicopter flights could resume as early as Tuesday, Dec. 1, according to National Transportation Safety Board chairwoman Jennifer Homendy, though the Army has not said what its timeline is.
The FAA said in a statement that it has not received a formal request to resume military helicopter flights around the airport and agency approval is required before any training flights can restart.
The agency formally suspended training flights in the crowded airspace in  May 2025 after two passenger jets were forced to abort landings when a Blackhawk helicopter came too close to the airport.
At the time, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the helicopter traffic on the Pentagon.
"No more helicopter rides for VIPs or unnecessary training in a congested DCA airspace full of civilians," Duffy wrote on social media. "Take a taxi or Uber."

That incident happened just four months after an Army helicopter on a training mission collided with an American Airlines passenger jet on approach at DCA, killing all aboard both aircraft, in January 2025. After a yearlong review, the NTSB said there were years of unheeded warnings about helicopter traffic in the skies near DCA as well as other dangers that were ignored ahead of the January 2025 collision.

"Resuming Army helicopter training in crowded DCA airspace is exactly the wrong direction we should be headed," said Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington in a statement. "The FAA should not authorize the resumption of these training flights until critical safety measures are implemented and a thorough safety risk assessment has been completed."

Cantwell and Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas have been working together on legislation in the wake of the midair collision to add new safety features to aircraft that would alert other aircraft in its vicinity.

Cruz announced last week that a deal was reached in principle between the House and Senate to adopt a requirement to have a  feature that shows nearby air traffic with visual and audible alerts,  Cruz said he intends to get it passed before the new Congress is sworn in in January.

title: Inside Trump's effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO
summary: Jensen Huang's comeback as Nvidia CEO came after a weekend of strategizing by Trump administration officials, who offered assurances to the company.
story: President Trump made it clear to advisers on Friday: He wanted Jensen Huang back at Nvidia.

It had been less than two weeks since the computing giant's CEO and founder had resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose firm had allegedly funneled Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia's share price spiraled, imperiling a company whose semiconductors and financing deals have helped power the U.S. artificial intelligence boom.
The president had been on the phone with various Wall Street and Silicon Valley titans. The main takeaway from those conversations: The U.S. needs a strong Nvidia.
Mr. Trump was also privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.

Nvidia's board chair told investors on Tuesday of last week that the company did not intend to reinstate Huang. But before the end of the week, the board was privately signaling to the White House that it was serious about bringing him back. Board members just wanted to examine it from all angles first.

Huang's surprise comeback as CEO on Monday came after Trump and his team spent the weekend working on making it happen, in part by offering the Nvidia board a range of legal assurances about Huang. After the deal was done and the tech giant's shares surged, Mr. Trump publicly celebrated it, telling CNBC that he "convinced them" to rehire him.
CBS News spoke with U.S. officials and others directly familiar with the negotiations about how the deal came together.
Two days of assurances

Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance spoke repeatedly with Huang, Nvidia board members and their legal counsel. Huang privately shared with the White House that he felt the board wanted to bring him back, but would need to be assured that the U.S. government didn't think he was a national security risk.

In phone calls, board members were told Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation, that the government had no legal issues with him, and that the administration wouldn't view his return to Nvidia's helm as a problem.

But what about Alice Huang, they wanted to know. She's the woman with whom Huang had an affair, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed. The White House made it clear their assurances didn't extend to her.

Megaspeed has been accused of transferring the high-tech Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence to China, which the company denies. The company was put on a U.S. trade blacklist this week, and it has been investigated by the Justice and Commerce departments.

Trump, Vance and board members hashed over the next steps. The board wanted to know what Mr. Trump would say publicly. They wanted Attorney General Todd Blanche himself to confirm Huang wasn't under investigation. The attorney general was comfortable with this.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton had conducted a deep dive into U.S. intelligence related to Alice Huang and her interactions with Jensen Huang. The information was circulated to Trump and senior officials.
Mr. Trump later told CNBC that Huang was "exonerated" after a "pretty good investigation."

Clayton, who previously led the Securities and Exchange Commission, helped connect Nvidia board members to administration officials for backdoor discussions, according to the sources, though he was not involved in the discussions surrounding Huang's reinstatement this weekend.
Clayton was also consulted by the president and others in the administration for his expertise in corporate governance matters.
On Sunday, Jensen Huang met with the board for hours.
Afterward, board members called the White House.
Earlier, Mr. Trump had discussed the prospect of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, though Lutnick was not involved in the weekend strategizing.

Lutnick's Commerce Department is responsible for enforcing export controls on advanced semiconductor chips — and since the Nvidia scandal erupted, he has been accused of not doing enough to prevent their diversion to China.

Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent openly suggested the Commerce Department had failed to act, saying other government agencies had supported putting Alice Huang's company Megaspeed on a trade blacklist "for months," but "Commerce has the pen."
Billionaire Elon Musk spoke with Mr. Trump about export controls and told Trump officials that the people he knew in the tech and business communities were steadfastly behind Huang.
Two senior national security officials were not involved in the effort to reinstate Huang: CIA director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio.

Earlier this year, Rubio had prepared a classified memorandum, based on U.S. intelligence that included intercepts of Alice Huang's conversations, warning Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was known to be in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security.
Rubio also briefed Mr. Trump on the intelligence aboard Air Force One in May, before Jensen Huang joined the presidential delegation en route to China during a stop in Alaska.

Allies of both Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS News on Monday that both men had expressed private concern about aspects of Huang's return but have so far not weighed breaking with Mr. Trump publicly over it. Some of their supporters, the sources said, have voiced their alarm about Rubio and Bessent standing by Mr. Trump on this decision.
Rubio was particularly angry when the news of Huang's reinstatement broke on Monday morning.

On Sunday, as Vance continued to press the Nvidia board, Bessent was asked in an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" about his previous comment that Nvidia's board should go "outside" to find new leadership. He responded, "Well, Jensen is on the outside now."

Late Sunday night, the board shared with Mr. Trump and the vice president that Nvidia would announce before the markets opened Monday that Jensen Huang was being reinstated as president, CEO and board director.
"We were told, 'This is going to happen,'" one official told CBS News.

The language the two sides had gone over — that Mr. Trump's post on Truth Social would hail the decision and say Nvidia should cooperate with continued probes into Megaspeed and chip exports — was finalized. The White House told board members they could reveal publicly that they had been given assurances by the U.S. government that Jensen Huang did not pose a national security risk.

Nvidia is likely to continue to draw scrutiny as the FBI and Justice Department's National Security Division examine potential export control violations involving Megaspeed and another company, Super Micro Computer.
Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns about Jensen Huang's return. He is scheduled to appear before House and Senate panels next week.

title: Paperwork, not work, causing enrollees to lose Medicaid in Nebraska
summary: Data from the months after Nebraska's early rollout of new Medicaid work mandates offers a look at the challenges enrollees in other states could face.
story: When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Trump's sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.
Many also watched the Cornhusker State's experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.
On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready.

They'll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don't meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don't comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren't working.
Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory.

"The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans' chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans," Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement.

Democrats' massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they'll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they're fully enforced.
The basics

Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states, along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show, so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states.

But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034.

The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called "medically frail."
It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska.

On May 1, Nebraska became the first state to implement the work requirements. After it began dropping people from coverage in August, 7% of Nebraska Medicaid enrollees who were subject to the requirements when renewing their coverage, or 533 adults, were disenrolled because of the new rules, according to the latest state data.

Nebraska's Medicaid agency was able to verify that 8 in 10 enrollees met the new rules using various state and federal databases. Those people didn't have to deal with requests for more information, interim state Medicaid director Jeremy Brunssen told KFF Health News.
About 14% of new Medicaid applicants subject to the new rules, or 557 people, had been denied because of the work requirements since they were implemented.
But the state data also shows some troubling issues.
For example, 92% of cases in which existing enrollees lost coverage were due to procedural or paperwork issues rather than state determinations that they did not meet the new work rules.

Brunssen attributes that high percentage to the state having to verify the numerous ways people can meet the new requirements or exemptions. "It's not as simple as typical eligibility enrollment that you can meet via income and household size," he said.
Many enrollees lost coverage because they did not respond to the state's outreach. Those enrollees may have deemed themselves ineligible or were unsure how to respond, Brunssen said.
The rate of procedural denials is much higher than in prior years, according to data analyzed by KFF. Critics fear it means people who may still qualify are losing coverage.

"This is definitely a red-flag warning," said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska, a trade group representing federally funded community health centers. "The high proportion of procedural denials is troubling."
Navigating the new requirements

Cheri Stollar, 48, of Lincoln, Nebraska, received her Medicaid renewal notice in the mail in early November and was confused about which documents to submit to the state to prove she works as a mental health therapist. She also didn't understand why she had less than a week to respond. She said she tried to call the state Medicaid agency but could not get through. Her renewal has since been completed.

"I want to make sure I send in everything they need," said Stollar, who lives in a three-bedroom mobile home with three of her four children. She has been on Medicaid for two years and credits the coverage for enabling her to afford medications for depression, sleep, and an ulcer.
She said the new law will make it harder for people like her to get and stay covered, which will make it harder to stay healthy — and get and keep a job.

Behnke said enrollees calling the state Medicaid agency for help have been put on hold for up to two hours. The assistance line operates only on weekdays, during daytime hours, making it difficult for people who work to call. State Medicaid officials say they are working to add more staff to reduce wait times.
One challenge in evaluating Nebraska's implementation is that the state, as of mid-November, had released data only through August.
State officials said this summer that they would post an online dashboard with various performance metrics to improve public transparency. That hasn't happened yet.

"We have seen a lot of negative effects so far," said Sarah Maresh, program director at Nebraska Appleseed, a nonprofit social justice advocacy group. "Every person that goes without coverage is a problem."
She worries that people are being deterred from applying to Medicaid because of the policy.
Brunssen, the interim Medicaid director, defended his state's performance.

"We are experiencing what we expected," he said in an October interview at a National Association of Medicaid Directors conference in Maryland. "The vast majority of people newly applying, or for those going through redetermination, are getting coverage or retaining coverage."

Yet, Brunssen noted, it's still early. Fewer than 25% of Medicaid enrollees subject to the work requirement have had to prove they meet the new rules to retain coverage. The rest won't be completed until next summer, he said.

The state's Department of Health and Human Services, which operates its Medicaid program, has used various methods to inform enrollees about the new rules, such as letters, emails, texts, and messages in an online portal, Brunssen said.
"Most Medicaid enrollees know about the new rules," he said, attributing awareness to community partners and managed-care companies that helped get the word out.
"I feel like we've done everything in our power to communicate what was coming," he said.
Brunssen noted the state has taken advantage of a federal option to let enrollees self-attest that they meet exemptions. All declarations must be truthful, or enrollees could face perjury charges.
Self-attestation is as easy as checking a box on an online form. No supporting documents are required. That's made it easier for people to comply, Brunssen said.
The state has also exempted people living in three counties with high unemployment rates and in two counties declared federal disaster areas because of weather events, he said.
"Our goal is to make sure people who are eligible get or retain coverage," Brunssen said.
Some enrollees say the state could do more to make the process easier.

Chalandria James, 37, of Omaha was worried about whether she still had Medicaid coverage after she tried to renew in July but did not hear back from the state, despite repeated calls. Unsure of her coverage status, she canceled a doctor's appointment to check her blood pressure. It took until September, and a multi-hour visit to the state agency office, for her to find out she still had Medicaid and was exempt from the work requirement because she had a child under 14 years old.
"It was nerve-racking not knowing," said James, a community health worker and doula.
In Nebraska, about 37% of enrollees met the work requirement while 61% qualified for an exemption — with the most common reasons being medical frailty or caregiving.

Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families, said Nebraska's experience shows the work rules do little to promote work, since most who can are already working. "This policy punishes low-income people by subjecting them to serious, often insurmountable, hurdles," she said.

Even with data showing the large majority of enrollees working or meeting an exemption, Brunssen said the new requirements still are a good idea. "Part of being a good, healthy person does involve engagement with the community," he said, "and we think there is value in the work we are doing in this space."

title: Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa Wednesday morning
summary: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa.
story: The Army is set to detonate 5 tons of explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a back-and-forth that has played out between politicians and in court.

The detonation will take place at 9 a.m. Central time, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said Tuesday at a press conference. Telle said the unstable explosives become more dangerous as temperatures drop, and the weather forecast for Wednesday is "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."
The government has argued the detonation — which could send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area — is necessary because the lead azide could spontaneously explode.

"There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said Tuesday.

In a social media post late Tuesday night, Telle said that federal authorities had constructed "earth berms, large sand-filled blocks" and what he described as a "water wall" filled with 100,000 gallons of water, all designed to "mitigate the effects of the blast."

"After the detonation, residents near the plant may see dark smoke," Telle wrote. "That smoke comes from explosives like C4 and diesel fuel, which are being used to direct the blast safely downward. Both are standard materials the Army burns every day."
Telle said that air quality would "be monitored throughout the operation and well into the day."

A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives. The court's ruling came after environmental groups challenged the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency and argued the EPA hadn't given enough notice to residents.
Following the ruling, the Army noted Monday night that current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds "has given her support to go forward."

"It is the unanimous judgement of our people — the Army, Navy, EPA, ATF, FBI, DARPA, DoE, CDC, HHS, FEMA and every other agency involved — that the Army should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation, which will occur this Wednesday morning, as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions," Telle said on X.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week to give itself time to issue a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups that challenged the plan had failed to show they are likely to succeed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," the ruling said. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

President Trump said earlier Monday the government would not carry out the detonation until the appeals court ruled and unless Democratic Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Mr. Trump added that government experts felt detonating the material was the best option.

"If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," the president said on social media.

Sand, whose input was not required and who is not yet in office, said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

The government has argued that even if the appeals court had stayed its EPA permit, the Army has the legal right to move forward without a permit to "respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion."

The Army has stored the lead azide in earthen-covered containers for decades at its ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town located near the Mississippi River in southeastern Iowa. The EPA has said the government discovered earlier this year that the material deteriorated over time, risking explosion if it is moved or disturbed.
The Pentagon asked the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Lincoln Laboratory to study the detonation plan, officials told CBS News.
In a statement posted to Facebook Tuesday night, the laboratory agreed that the detonation plan is better than the possibility of a sudden, unexpected explosion.

"Lincoln Laboratory has performed a review of the Army's planned lead azide detonation at the request of the DoW," the laboratory said. "Based on the Army's documentation, we concurred that conducting the detonation under the planned controlled conditions is preferable to accepting the risks associated with a potential unplanned detonation."

As part of an earlier detonation plan that had been previously slated for Friday, the Army asked some Middletown residents to temporarily evacuate their homes for six hours, and said people could expect loud noises, vibrations and a dust plume.

Environmental groups and Iowa and Illinois politicians from both parties criticized the plan, arguing the detonation could lead to widespread lead contamination in both states and pressing the EPA and Army to consider other options.

The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council asked the federal appeals court to step in and review the EPA's permit last week. The environmental groups said the EPA failed to fully assess the risks of the detonation or consider alternatives, and argued the Army was operating on an "extraordinarily rushed timeline" that prevented residents from getting enough notice.

On Monday, a panel of three appellate judges sided with the federal government. The court found that the EPA "adequately incorporated safeguards" to mitigate the risks, including barriers and plans for environmental monitoring, and the Army considered a range of alternatives.

title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still has security clearance, sources say
summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche did not say whether federal investigators interviewed Jensen Huang — who was rehired as CEO on Monday — or examined his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang still holds a security clearance, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Huang has drawn weeks of scrutiny, following reports that he had an affair with a businesswoman and alleged Chinese intelligence asset whose company is suspected of transferring advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive two weeks ago, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday following direct appeals from President Trump, who said he offered the board an "assurance" that Huang did not pose a national security threat.
Revoking Huang's clearance was discussed, sources said.

Huang never received a defensive security briefing from the administration after he was alerted about businesswoman Alice Huang's alleged ties to China, a source directly familiar with the matter said. Such briefings, also called counterintelligence briefings, help people with a U.S. government security clearance recognize threats.
It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances.

Earlier Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters he wasn't sure whether Huang still held a security clearance. He did not offer any specific findings on Huang, and didn't say whether federal investigators interviewed Huang or examined his relationship with an alleged spy.

Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information.
An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance.

In an interview on CNBC Monday, Mr. Trump broadly defended Huang, saying a "very thorough investigation" found he "did nothing wrong," aside from "bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents."
Asked what Blanche had told him about the situation, Mr. Trump said: "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was exonerated."

The Justice Department has overseen a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, after the Commerce Department looked into whether Megaspeed had violated export control rules, both agencies confirmed last week. The status of that probe is unclear.

Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime.

"To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this … that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said.

Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings.
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
Blanche also described Nvidia as "a good corporate citizen," saying he had no reason to suggest the company was obstructing a federal investigation.

Asked whether Huang's reported relationship with someone allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence presented a national security risk, Blanche said officials must rely on actual intelligence assessments rather than news accounts.

"I don't deal in leaks or in the public reporting that's in some newspaper," Blanche said. "We have to deal with actual facts and what the intelligence community has actually said, which is not something that we should be sharing with the media. And so my personal view of that question is completely irrelevant."
This story published first on CBS News at 6:57 p.m. on Nov. 24, 2026.

title: Newly found farthest quasar from Earth is also oldest known to man
summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.
story: Cape Canaveral, Fla. — Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

The quasar formed within 630 million years of the universe-forming Big Bang, a German-led team reported Tuesday. That's considered a very early development in the 13.8-billion-year history of the cosmos, and it smashes previous records.

"This time the leap in cosmic time is huge!" the European Southern Observatory's Julien Wolf, who led the study, said in an email. "The previous two records each took us back by about 15 million years or less. This one takes us back by nearly 40 million years, the biggest advance in nearly a decade!"

Wolf and his team spotted the quasar while digging through millions of observations made by the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Launched in 2023, Euclid is surveying galaxies in an effort to shed light on the dark matter and dark energy that fill so much of the universe and keep it expanding.

Finding a quasar so early in the universe is rare, according to Wolf. What makes this one even rarer, he said, is the massive size of its black hole, despite being such a relatively slow eater of everything around it. Scientists are seeing it as it was 13.1 billion years ago - when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Wolf nicknamed the quasar Dun Aonghasa after the prehistoric stone fort in Ireland's Aran Islands. His wife and daughter are Irish, and he was awestruck when they visited the fort - a frontier holding "the promise of a vast horizon still to explore," just like this quasar.

His team's findings were corroborated by the Hubble and Webb space telescopes as well as other observatories on and off Earth. Thanks to Webb, scientists learned that the black hole powering this quasar is equivalent in mass to 360 million of our suns, an astounding amount so early in time. The final results appear in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

"Dun Aonghasa gives us a new deadline" for the early universe, Wolf said. "About 630 million years after the Big Bang, its black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun. But how?"
Their prowling of the cosmic dawn continues.
"Honestly, the record could fall again in a few months or it could stand for years," Wolf said.

title: Canadian astronaut's wife gives birth with husband aboard ISS
summary: The wife of Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who is currently aboard the International Space Station, gave birth to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
story: The wife of a Canadian astronaut who is currently aboard the International Space Station gave birth Tuesday to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
Heather Kutryk, the wife of astronaut Joshua Kutryk, gave birth to a girl, the Canadian Space Agency said in a news release.
"Heather and baby are both doing well," the agency said, adding that Joshua Kutryk was able to share in the experience from the space station.

"Joshua is currently living out a childhood dream aboard the International Space Station," the couple said in a statement. "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives."
The couple's two other children are ages 7 and 5.
Joshua Kutryk traveled to the space station on Oct. 1 from Florida aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule as part of Crew 13, accompanied by two NASA astronauts and a Russian cosmonaut.
In an interview just prior to his departure, he told CBS News that it would be tough to miss the birth, but that he would "try to take the positive things out of it."

"Physically, of course, I won't be here, but as hard as that will be, it also lends itself to what I hope will be a very unique and enriching life experience that we'll look on fondly," Joshua Kutryk said.

In the history of space travel, Joshua Kutryk is just the fourth astronaut to miss the birth of a child. A former military test pilot, this was Kutryk's first spaceflight. He is the 17th Canadian to fly in space.

"We have an enormous support network, and we feel just happy and joyful to be doing this," he said in that interview. "This is a hard job. There's a lot of good things about it, there's some bad things. One of those bad things is that it's very unpredictable, and you can't predict when things like launches are going to happen."
Crew 13 does not yet have a confirmed date for its return to Earth.

Kutryk told CBS News: "We think it's exceptionally important, and I hope that my new child looks at it as such, as making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

title: Spacecraft enters Mercury's orbit after 8-year journey despite glitch
summary: BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018.
story: A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet.
BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury.

On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release.

As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes.

But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver.

"Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement.
The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing.

Despite the error and the incomplete maneuver, ESA scientists were eventually able to confirm that BepiColombo had locked onto Mercury's orbit. It took six hours from the time the maneuver started to confirm that it had been successful, the ESA said.

Over the next few weeks, the spacecraft will continue to make small thruster burns to gradually adjust its orbit around Mercury. Each movement will be adapted by BepiColombo's flight dynamics team using the spacecraft's actual trajectory. This will allow BepiColombo to enter the "optimum point" in orbit. The ESA compared it to "braking a car at just the right moment" to find the "sweet spot." Conducting multiple maneuvers also allows the craft to maximize its fuel supplies.

On Dec. 9, BepiColombo will release two science orbiters. The ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO, will spend another few months navigating to find the right spot in Mercury's orbit. It is expected to enter its final orbit in March 2027 and begin science operations in April.
The scientific operations will study Mercury's interior, surface and the space around the planet, Geraint Jones, ESA's BepiColombo lead project scientist, said.

The second science orbiter is the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, or Mio. Mio's studies will include Mercury's magnetosphere, interplanetary dust and electric fields, according to the ESA.

title: Allstate roiled by tech outage over Thanksgiving week
summary: The insurer's systems are out of commission during the busiest road travel period of the year, leaving customers unable to access roadside assistance.
story: Allstate has joined the growing list of companies bedeviled by a technology disruption in recent weeks, leaving some customers unable to file claims or seek roadside assistance during Thanksgiving week.

The Northbrook, Illinois-based insurer said in a statement on Wednesday that some of its services had been restricted after customers reported being unable to access them on social media and on Downdetector, which tracks web outages.

"Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims," the company said. "To the extent service interruptions impact a customer's ability to make a payment, they won't lose coverage or be charged late fees."
People seeking roadside assistance on Allstate's website encountered an error message through Friday.
In a statement on its website, Allstate added that customers may reach the insurer through multiple channels, including by phone.

Allstate offers a range of policies, including home, life and auto insurance. Its consumer-facing tech problems during one of the busiest times of year for road travel follow disruptions at other major U.S. airlines, banks, software providers and government agencies.
Microsoft, which suffered a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, said a technical issue caused the disruption and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio also said at the time that the tech outages were distinct from one another. The incidents were caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems, they said.

"In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio said. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

title: Fake online stores may fool AI shopping bots on Black Friday
summary: AI bots are accidentally steering shoppers toward websites and online shops created by scammers using AI.
story: Scammers are using AI to churn out convincing copies of real online stores, and this Black Friday, the AI agents that many shoppers will rely on often can't tell the difference.
These fake sites pose a risk to the millions of Americans who are tasking their AI agents with making online purchases and transacting on their behalf.

"Artificial intelligence just makes building websites so much easier. You can upload anything into HTML and build a website very, very easily," Harrison Tang, co-founder of Spokeo, a data aggregator, told CBS News.

AI is enabling scammers to build what Tang described as convincing dupes of legitimate online stores in only hours, including copies of a brand's logo, marketing language and product images and descriptions.

"AI just makes creating these look-alike fake stores a lot easier, so there is a proliferation of them," Tang explained. "Platforms will try to catch them by not directing users there, but there are so many of them popping up all the time that they are hard to keep up with."
Research from Microsoft shows that criminals can use AI to set up fraudulent e-commerce sites in mere minutes rather than the days or weeks that were once required.

Spokeo identified copycat sites of dozens of popular brands, including UGG, L.L. Bean, Converse and Stella McCartney. As of Nov. 15, it had identified 65 distinct online stores that mimicked the legitimate sites of 60 brand names, according to its online shopping scam study.
The discrepancies between the authentic stores and the scam websites are subtle and require close examination.

The first place to look for proof of fraud, according to Tang, is in the online store's web address. For example, a fake Converse store uses the web address converseshop.us.com, whereas the real store's address is converse.com. The .us domain name is the top-level domain for the U.S. and is reserved for U.S. residents, but is commonly used for phishing attempts, according to Tang.
"It looks like an official website, but it's not, so if you don't pay close attention, it's easy to get tricked," he said.
AI agents need to get savvy
Bots aren't as well trained as some humans are at spotting phony websites, which can dupe even discerning shoppers because of how realistic they look.
Recent research from Podqi, a firm that monitors for intellectual property infringement, on AI search risks shows that AI engines can inadvertently direct shoppers to scammy stores.

The group asked popular AI tools, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Perplexity, questions about where to buy particular brands online. More than 18% of the AI bots' answers drew on a fake, infringing or invalid website.

For example, when asked where to buy clothing from Stussy, a streetwear brand, Perplexity referred to us-stussy.com, which it mistakenly identified as the brand's official website and "the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items." The web address us-stussy.com directs shoppers to a fake store. The real store's address is stussy.com.
Other brands with duplicate online stores include Figs, a medical scrubs maker; sock company Bombas; and dairy brand Fairlife.
Here are other tip-offs that a site is phony and should be avoided, according to Spokeo:
Look-alike web addresses, but with misspellings Site lacks a corporate phone number or addressPrices are too good to be trueThird-party warnings on ScamAdviser or from the BBB

title: How people use AI agents to handle annoying tasks and save money
summary: Shrugging off fears of AI, some consumers say the technology is simplifying their lives and helping them save money.
story: Count Megan Roszak, a busy executive coach, business founder and mother of 11-year-old twins, among the recent converts to artificial intelligence as a tool for helping run her life.

The San Francisco, California, resident explained to CBS News how she uses an AI agent, Fo, from the agent platform Wajo, to process and return online purchases. She also recently used it to book an appointment with her electric company, which she said saved her multiple phone calls and about 40 minutes.

"I am a full-time working mom. Making returns to Poshmark and Etsy are things that I would let go of and drop in the past because it's going to be annoying," Roszak said. "Now, I just put Fo on the case, and I got $250 back."

Companies ranging from Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI to hundreds of smaller developers are rolling out AI agents designed to handle tedious tasks, such as returning products, and also to comb through people's email inboxes for unclaimed refunds and other money they may be owed.

More broadly, AI proponents say the technology can help consumers reckon with the "annoyance economy," or what advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative describes in a recent report as the "time, fees and irritation" involved in dealing with a host of menial tasks.

Those tasks, such as handling customer service, scheduling appointments and canceling subscriptions, cost Americans $165 billion per year in wasted time, fees and other surcharges for routine transactions, according to Groundwork.
A cure for annoyance?

Used wisely, AI agents can reduce the friction companies depend on to pocket forgotten fees and payments, according to Stanford University economist Neale Mahoney, an author of Groundwork's report on the so-called annoyance economy.
Kevin Newman, another Fo user, estimates the agent has saved him roughly 2,800 hours he would otherwise have spent generating advertising leads for his small business and on personal tasks.

The agent also sifted through his email to turn up multiple gift cards he had earned for testing products and found unclaimed funds he was owed from his former residences, including a $60 claim from a settlement with Time Warner, Newman said.

Fo can summon a person to finish the job when necessary, with Wajo assistants on call who can work with agents when, for example, an institution doesn't have a website, or it blocks agents, according to the company.

Wajo founder Shivani Poddar told CBS News that people use Fo for a wide range of pesky tasks, including booking plane tickets, tracking down lost luggage with airlines or negotiating healthcare costs.
"These are complex negotiations, and these systems are still very hybrid," she said, highlighting the importance of having a human on call when necessary.

Meta also touts its Muse agent's money-saving capabilities. For example, in the "ideas" section of the app, which suggests financial management uses, Meta recommends using Muse to "Get back money that's already yours" by checking state databases for owed amounts. The agent offers to file refund claims and also to "cancel those random subscriptions you forgot about."
Businesses vs. agents

Businesses that count on consumers giving up on claiming refunds or fighting junk fees aren't taking such tactics lying down, with some websites and financial institutions blocking AI agents. Amazon, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase & Co. are among the businesses that have banned the bots from conducting transactions on behalf of consumers.
"More firms are blocking agents because they're making it difficult to increase their revenue. They're like a superpower for consumers, so companies have an incentive to block it," Mahoney said.

Concerns also swirl about agents accessing users' sensitive data, including payment information, and about their incentives. For example, Lindsay Owens, founder and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, told CBS News that companies could be steering users toward products and services from which they earn commissions, to pad their own bottom lines.

title: Brits are having less sex, but watching a lot of porn, survey finds
summary: A third of Brits aged 16 to 24 have never had sex, a landmark survey finds, though most acknowledge sexting and watching pornography.
story: London — One-third of Brits between the ages of 16 and 24 have never had sex, according to a large-scale, periodic survey that has studied the prevalence of sexting and pornography use for the first time.

The decline in youth sexual activity is part of a wider trend of British people having less sex compared to previous generations, all revealed in the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), a survey of nearly 7,000 Britons between 2022 and 2024, which was published Tuesday in The Lancet medical journal.

Adults aged 45 and below are having sex twice a month on average, down from four times a month in 1990-91, and three in 2010-12, according to the survey. The proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds who said they had never had sex rose from 18% to 38% among women and 18% to 28% among men, compared to the previous Natsal study.
The latest survey was the first time participants had been asked about their online activity.

Half of the women respondents between 16 and 24 said they had watched pornography   in the past year, while 86% of young men said they had. Half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phone in the past year.

"There has been an emerging shift towards less sexual experience among young people," wrote the authors of the study. "Sexual lifestyles now commonly incorporate online behaviors such as sexting and pornography, especially for young people."

One of the researchers on the project, Prof. Wendy Macdowall at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told CBS News partner BBC News that while it may be tempting to link the online activity with the decline in sexual activity, there are several other reasons for the drop, "especially among young people."

Similar declines among young people have been observed "in other high-income countries," the study states, and while "these changes are not yet well understood," it added, the shifts have coincided with rising rates of mental health conditions and declines in alcohol consumption, and "later attainment of traditional markers of adulthood," as well as "increasingly online lives."

Respondents reported an increase in masturbation across all age groups and genders, as well as sexting and pornography use, according to the survey's authors, but while that "might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behavior … masturbation and pornography use were lower among those reporting never having had sex, challenging the notion these behaviors simply substitute one another."
The study did not ask participants about any use of artificial intelligence in sexuality.

"When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi," Soazig Clifton, a researcher on the Natsal project from University College London, told the BBC. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behavior and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."
The study also revealed that the average number of sexual partners over a lifetime for people in the U.K. is five, and that same-sex intercourse has increased among both men and women.

title: 5 questions Nvidia still faces after bringing back Jensen Huang
summary: Despite Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia's CEO, experts say it's anything but business as usual for the chipmaker.
story: Jensen Huang's first task in returning to lead Nvidia after resigning last week under a cloud will be to deal with the fallout from his stunning exit and even more surprising reprieve.

Following his reinstatement by the company's board, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into President Trump's role in the billionaire entrepreneur's return and whether Nvidia skirted export rules meant to prevent its advanced chips from reaching China. And while Huang may be viewed as key to Nvidia's success, his return raises a thicket of legal and operational problems, according to financial and governance experts.

"Three tests will now decide how strongly it builds from here: how its leadership sits with Washington, how it handles China and how long AI spending keeps growing at this speed,"  said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory firm, in an email.
Here are five critical questions facing Nvidia as Huang retakes the helm.
Did Nvidia compromise U.S. national security?

One of Nvidia's major customers, Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, employed a Chinese businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. Megaspeed is also alleged to have smuggled Nvidia's advanced chips into China and provided remote access to the technology in violation of U.S. export controls.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear on Dec. 1- 2 in closed-door interviews before multiple congressional panels to discuss the company's ties to China. Huang is also scheduled to appear on Dec. 3 at a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on U.S. export rules and global AI competition.

"The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the Republican chairs of the House committees who will interview Huang and Teter said on Monday.
Will Nvidia's board face legal issues?

The board's decision to reinstate Huang is likely to set off a flurry of shareholder lawsuits over questions including whether Nvidia failed to disclose the spying allegations earlier and whether the company was aware of Megaspeed's links to China, according to Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware.

Shareholders could also challenge Huang and Nvidia over their failure to disclose his personal relationships with subordinates at the company, which appears to violate the chipmaker's code of conduct. Earlier this month, Nvidia was sued by shareholders for allegedly failing to disclose information about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (no relation).
"There's just a whole range of things that they can bring actions," Elson said.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment about whether it will continue pursuing an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence.
Will Nvidia face new U.S. export restrictions?
Nvidia is expected to come under increased scrutiny and face greater regulatory hurdles in selling chips to China and companies in Southeast Asia.
"There will definitely be tighter restrictions, and any dealings directly with China will be the government's primary focus," StoneX equity research analyst Cody Acree told CBS News.

Huang has long lobbied U.S. officials to permit Nvidia to sell its most advanced chips to China, with an eye toward growing its market. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department moved to curb sales of U.S. chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.

"Going forward, they'll be subject to more export controls so that their chips don't end up in China and data centers in Asia," Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment firm D.A. Davidson, told CBS News. "In that way, Nvidia's market has shrunk, and that business will go away."
Can Huang ease investor fears about an AI bust?

Investors cheered Huang's return partly because it suggests that Nvidia will continue in its role as the de facto "bank of AI," providing financing for companies that buy its chips and otherwise fueling the sector's growth. Huang helped arrange deals such as Nvidia's investment in OpenAI. Through such circular financing, Nvidia invests vast sums in AI companies, which then flow back to the chipmaker through chip purchases.

"Nvidia is more than just a chipmaker — it's heavily involved in the broader AI ecosystem by financing other companies," Capital Economics senior economist James Reilly told CBS News. "Having Jensen back reassures investors that those relationships and that financing will continue."
Still, Huang's return doesn't erase concerns about the sector's debt-fueled spending, or whether AI companies will ever turn a profit and deliver returns to investors.
"There are growing concerns as to whether all of this AI investment will generate the revenue it needs long-term to make it worthwhile," Reilly said. "Those hurdles are very demanding."
What is Nvidia's succession plan?
Developing a succession plan to replace Huang will be the first item on the board's agenda, Elson, a prominent governance expert, told CBS News.

When Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, he had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that allowed him to wield enormous power. However, his departure made it clear that the company had no succession plan should Huang be unable to lead.
As a result, Elson expects Nvidia to hire an outside consultant to help forge a plan for who might succeed Huang.
Such "key man" risk isn't unique to Nvidia, Acree noted.

"You have other high-profile CEOs at the helm of large companies, but that's the nature of Silicon Valley, unfortunately," he said, pointing to Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX's Elon Musk. "There is no way to address that risk entirely or make it go away, but boards will be more sensitive to that in the future."

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."
