title: How Huang's resignation and return unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday, Nov. 23, that it is reinstating Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's CEO. The move marks an abrupt shift from board members' position only last week that they had no plans to rehire the billionaire entrepreneur at the company he co-founded more than 30 years ago.

Huang's departure from Nvidia on Nov. 12 capped a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation, and the board's decision to rehire him:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to The Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to The New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, with interim CEO Colette Kress hosting the call following Huang's resignation. Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Nvidia reverses course on Huang's exit, announcing his reinstatement as CEO effective immediately. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company said in a statement.

title: Trump, tech CEOs cheer Huang's return, but lawmakers question board
summary: President Trump and prominent tech figures applauded Huang's reinstatement as CEO, though some lawmakers criticized the move as "reckless."
story: President Trump and high-profile business leaders applauded Nvidia's shock move to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after the billionaire entrepreneur's resignation from the chipmaker.
In a post on social media platform Truth Social on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered the board's move, calling it "an absolutely GREAT decision" that would benefit the U.S. economy.

Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken to Nvidia's board members to encourage them to reinstate Huang. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he is certainly a genius," he told the media outlet.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, another prominent supporter of Huang's, said in a post on X that "The mistake has been corrected," referring to the Nvidia co-founder's Nov. 12 resignation following revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair and apologized to his family. Huang also had a relationship with a subordinate at Nvidia, the New York Times reported last week, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company.

Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones on Monday announced that Huang's "reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." Last week, during a quarterly earnings call discussing Nvidia's latest financial results, Jones said the board had no intention of rehiring him.
Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, in which Nvidia has pledged to invest up to $100 billion, issued a one-word post on X on Monday. "Jensen!" he wrote.
For their part, investors also seem heartened by Huang's return. Nvidia's stock soared $39.80 per share, or 32%, on Monday, quickly adding more than $1 trillion to the company's market value.
Lawmakers keep heat on Nvidia

Not everyone cheered Huang's return to the world's most valuable AI chipmaker. In a statement, Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "reckless." The Massachusetts Democrat also pressed Nvidia's board to offer more details on its decision to rehire Huang.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

Lawmakers have moved to strengthen controls around U.S. exports to restrict China from gaining remote access to the most powerful chips and chipmaking equipment. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to close a loophole to protect sensitive American technology.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Sen. Charles Schumer, a Democrat from New York, said in a social media post. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."

Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, also expressed concern on social media about Nvidia's decision to restore Huang, questioning the board's conclusion that rehiring him posed no national security risk.

In addition to existing license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the rule adds new license requirements for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. The department said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

Despite Huang's resumption of his duties at Nvidia, the House Intelligence Committee plans to carry on with a closed-door hearing with the executive next week, sources told CBS News. Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter were also expected to appear before other congressional panels in early December to answer questions about the company's export practices, among other issues.
Huang has long lobbied for the federal government to allow Nvidia to sell its most powerful AI chips to China.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" sometime after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
Anthropic increases stock price amid high demand

In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each. The initial public offering raised around $81 billion and valued Anthropic at $1.5 trillion, making it the largest public offering in history. Elon Musk's SpaceX raised $75 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic is selling 956.3 million shares, although only 7.4% will be available for public trading (up to 9.8% including Class A shares held by nonfounder employees), according to Renaissance.

The company plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
summary: Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion, catapulting it past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion​ when it went public in June.
story: Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
"Seminal" moment
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

title: Afghan women in U.S. fear returning to Taliban rule
summary: The threat of imminent deportation may have subsided, but some Afghan women who fled Taliban rule still face anxiety and legal limbo in America.
story: Ever since the Trump administration announced earlier this month that it planned to deport nearly 200 Afghans through Pakistan back to their Taliban-controlled homeland, some in the Afghan community in America have been watching and waiting in fear.

A federal judge temporarily blocked a planned Nov. 3 flight, but many Afghans still feel stuck in limbo. The deportations could lead to some who helped the U.S. in the war in Afghanistan being persecuted by the Taliban, advocates and others fear.

Frequent changes to immigration policies have placed immense strain on the Afghan community, said Naheed Samadi Bahram, U.S. country director for Women for Afghan Women, a U.S.-based humanitarian organization advocating for Afghan women's rights.

"It also brings a lot of stress and anxiety to the community members who are unsure of their future in the United States," Bahram said. "They don't know if they are being deported or sent back to Afghanistan, where the only thing they will be faced with will be death or threats."
Bahram added it is especially tough on the women "who are really the backbone of the family."
There were reports of at least three women on the canceled flight, said Shawn VanDiver, president and founder of #AfghanEvac, an advocacy group supporting Afghan allies who were resettled in the U.S.

Two Jane Does are listed as plaintiffs in a court case filed Nov. 2 by nonprofit Project Rousseau in the U.S. Southern District of New York, which asked a federal judge for an emergency order to stop the planned removals.
If returned to Afghanistan, women "will face the consequences more than anyone in the family," Bahram said.

Women in Afghanistan have been barred from most jobs, university, secondary school and political life since the Taliban returned to power. Early and forced marriage remains common, with nearly 30% of Afghan girls under 18 married, according to U.N. Women. Additionally, the risk of violence against women and girls has increased, the organization said.
A devastating choice

For Shaima, a 56-year-old mother of four, just the thought of returning to Afghanistan is unimaginable. She asked to be identified only by her first name for safety reasons. Her husband, she said, worked alongside the U.S. government for more than five years during the war in Afghanistan and believed his association put their family in danger.

Yet Shaima, who said she worked as a doctor in her home country, was initially reluctant to leave behind her home, parents and extended family. After the Taliban seized power in 2021 and its rulers banned formal education for all girls beyond sixth grade, her thoughts gradually shifted.
She had a daughter to consider, and it wasn't the life she wanted for her.
"First, she can't continue education. Second, they can't go to work and she should be married and stay at home. But she don't like this," Shaima told CBS News.
Shaima said she knew she had to leave for her family's safety and children's future, leaving her elderly parents behind — an agonizing decision.
"Should I select my parents or my children, and it's very difficult," Shaima said. Shaima immigrated to New York City in 2024 with her children and husband.

The Afghan population in the United States has expanded dramatically in recent years, quadrupling between 2010 and 2024, according to the Migration Policy Institute. The vast majority immigrated after 2021 — roughly 180,000 Afghans — when the U.S. ended its two-decade war in Afghanistan and the Taliban regained control.

Upon arriving in the U.S., adjusting to life presented steep challenges. The Migration Policy Institute found that nearly 40% of Afghan immigrants lived in poverty in 2022, compared to 14% for overall immigrant populations. Shaima says her family faced significant hurdles accessing education and employment.
An unknown future
"Living in New York is very difficult," Shaima said.

Anxiety heightened after reports of potential deportations began circulating, especially since her family has not yet secured permanent residency, she said. She explained that her family applied for green cards about nine months after arriving, but the process abruptly stalled.

The Department of Homeland Security ended Temporary Protected Status for Afghans in July 2025, with then-Secretary Kristi Noem saying, "Afghanistan has had an improved security situation, and its stabilizing economy no longer prevents them from returning to their home country."
"Now all the time we are afraid. My husband wants to go to buy some grocery but we are afraid because we don't have green card," Shaima said.
In a Nov. 2 statement, Taliban officials expressed "deep concern" over reports that the U.S. intended to deport Afghan refugees through Pakistan.
"The Afghan side is ready to engage constructively on this matter," the statement said.

The U.S. government has not publicly announced new dates for deportation flights, and on Nov. 17, a federal judge in New York's Southern District granted a preliminary injunction to stop the deportations as the case is considered.
However, "the government has not given up," VanDiver said.
Since Oct. 14, his organization has received reports of at least 76 Afghans being detained, he said.
VanDiver said on social media Wednesday that deportation flights are scheduled for next week. He didn't provide further details or immediately reply to CBS News for clarification.
CBS News reached out to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment on possible future deportation flights.

There may be legislative options ahead to ease the pressure on Afghans in the U.S., VanDiver said. Congressional representatives introduced a bipartisan bill in July 2026 to extend Temporary Protected Status for at least 9,000 Afghans, and in November filed a discharge petition to force a floor vote on the measure.
Meanwhile, Shaima continues building a life in New York for her family, drawing strength from the fact that her children are safe.
Her daughter now has the opportunity to pursue an education. Despite ongoing uncertainty, Shaima reminds her children not to lose faith.
"I say our journey is very difficult … but we hope," Shaima said.

COVER STORY: What's in a name? How a trade war became a war of wordsIn the midst of the Trump administration's trade war with its northern neighbor, President Trump announced that he was declaring the name of Lake Ontario – a 7,300-square-mile body of water between the United States and Canada – to be "Lake America," an executive action that has been applauded by some Trump allies and derided by critics as legally dubious or silly. But who really gets to decide what geographic areas are called? "Sunday Morning" national correspondent Robert Costa gets the lay of the land on what a map should say.

title: Power being slowly restored as heavy Thanksgiving storm eases
summary: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers.
story: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some places stayed on guard for high-tide flooding following a round of holiday storms.

The storms snarled travel and downed trees and power lines. The heavy weather led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, preparations were underway to hold Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.

Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.
Another storm system in the Northwest brought rain along coastal Oregon. More snow was forecast in the Cascade Range and in mountain passes in Montana and Wyoming.
There were just under 3,700 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday night, with another 162 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.
The number of power outages, which peaked Thursday at more than 900,000 customers, fell to just under 200,000 by Saturday morning, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us.
Bad weather in the East is taking its time to go

Conditions were expected to improve Friday across the entire eastern U.S., "but this huge system will take some time to weaken," the National Weather Service said on its website. Coastal flood warnings were posted from New Jersey to Virginia.
"A lot of standing water, tree branches, siding ripped off of houses and buildings," homeowner Chris Rizzo told CBS New York.

In Hampton, Virginia, the storm toppled a beloved landmark at Grandview Beach: a weathered, leafless tree known as the "Grieving Tree" or the "Shell Tree." Visitors regularly decorated its branches with seashells, and it became a popular subject for photographers.
After surviving many storms, the tree "may have finally met its match," local meteorologist Ricky Matthews wrote on Facebook, sharing a photograph.
Roofs in Ocean City and Rockville collapsed. In Norfolk, Virginia, crews rescued 39 people and two dogs, City Councilman Tommy Smigiel posted.

In Baltimore, the storm brought a record 3.04 inches of rain to BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport on Thursday, while high tide in Annapolis reached 4.48 feet that night, a level officials said was among the 10 highest on record.
Part of a fishing pier collapsed in Virginia Beach, Virginia, closing a 3-mile section of beach, including the boardwalk, "due to dangerous conditions," the city said.

Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey, scrambled to pump out saltwater Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community's history. More than 1,100 people participated in a charity run, and Santa Claus was scheduled to arrive on a fire truck by evening to light the Christmas tree.
Conditions were a "million times better than they were 24 hours ago," borough business administrator Scott Wahl said.

Cheryl McKenna of Ocean City, New Jersey, said water flooded her garage and surrounded her property, keeping her family inside for six hours on the holiday. She said flooding has become more frequent since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

"Our family has been here for 36 years," McKenna said. "But honestly, we're thinking, is this the right place for us to be? We're now retired, and we want to stay down here, but how often can we continue to do this."

Another round of rain and strong winds are expected to hit the East Coast by Sunday evening, potentially disrupting the Monday morning commute. Up to 2 inches of rain and wind gusts of 65 mph are possible in some areas, according to CBS News meteorologist Nikki Nolan.
Parts of South and Midwest see snow, while California contends with coastal flooding

Part of Tennessee was under a winter storm warning for up to an inch of snow Friday, after rain turned into light snow on Thanksgiving. Conditions were calmer for the Midwest, compared with Thanksgiving, when as much as 15 inches of snow fell in eastern Missouri.
The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, was empty when the roof caved in early Thursday.

Snow is expected to begin falling Saturday from Montana to Colorado, with accumulations of up to 10 to 18 inches in some areas, according to Nolan. The storm will then move into the Midwest and Gulf Coast on Sunday, bringing rain to cities including Chicago, St. Louis, Nashville and New Orleans.

Waves driven by high tides caused flooding along the Pacific Coast and continued to affect train service Friday. Buses were pressed into service as Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner canceled or shortened more than a dozen trains between San Diego and Los Angeles.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.

Heavy snow was expected in parts of Montana and Wyoming. A renewed surge of moisture associated with an atmospheric river across the Pacific Northwest moved toward the northern Rockies, the weather service said.

title: Iowa detonation did not increase levels of lead in water, EPA says
summary: The EPA conducted sampling at more than 130 structures in Iowa, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches.
story: The Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday the controlled detonation of a stockpile of degrading explosives in Iowa did not result in an increase of lead in water bodies that serve as a source of drinking water.

"EPA found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake," the agency said in a press release.
"EPA sampled 35 drinking water sources across Iowa, Illinois, and Missouri before the controlled detonation to set a baseline," it added.

The EPA said it collected more than 1,632 air, water, soil and dust samples ahead of Wednesday's destruction of the lead azide stockpile, followed by 1,607 samples after the detonation, the agency said. Samples were sent to multiple EPA and private labs for testing.
"The agency is expecting to start receiving lab results on post-detonation sampling as early as tomorrow," the EPA said in a news release.

The EPA said it collected samples at more than 180 structures, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches, as well as at parks, nearby farms, drinking water sources and the Mississippi River watershed.
The EPA said Friday that it had completed 88% of post-detonation sampling at homes that were sampled pre-detonation, and expected to finish the remainder Friday.
As of Thursday, no airborne lead had been detected throughout the region, the EPA said.
The agency said it is also testing for other compounds that may have been released during the detonation.
"The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation," it said in Thursday's news release.

The Army on Wednesday detonated 5 tons of deteriorating explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant located in the small community of Middletown, citing the risk of an unplanned explosion. Local residents and environmental groups had sought to block the detonation over concerns that a plume of toxic lead dust could threaten public health and agriculture.

The Middletown plant housed about 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. The EPA said the lead azide had degraded over the last 20 years it had been in storage. It had undergone a recrystallization process that increased "the material's sensitivity to friction and shock" and made it more susceptible to the "risk of unintentional detonation," the EPA said.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily halted the detonation last week while it considered whether to impose a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups challenging the plan had failed to show they were likely to succeed.

The chaotic lead-up to the detonation reached the White House, prompting questions within the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
President Trump praised the detonation as having "exceeded expectations."

title: U.S. Air Force cloud platform breached by hackers, report says
summary: The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month.
story: The U.S. Air Force's cloud computing platform was breached in a cyberattack, multiple sources told Reuters on Friday.
The hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, according to Reuters, potentially exposing sensitive military and personnel information.
The breach was discovered at some point in the last month during system upgrades, sources told the outlet.

In a statement provided to CBS News, an Air Force spokesperson did not confirm or deny the breach, saying that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems."
"Ensuring the security, resilience and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority," the Air Force spokesperson said.

In a follow-up statement, the Defense Department said that its systems "are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world," adding that it "will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications."

When reached by CBS News, Leidos, the tech company which has served as the main contractor operating Cloud One since May, declined to comment specifically on the hack, deferring to the Air Force. A Leidos spokesperson noted that earlier this year, it announced a $454.9 million contract to modernize and secure the Air Force's cloud operations.

The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month, including at the National Security Agency, the CIA, the FBI, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the Federal Aviation Administration, the latter of which prompted a nationwide ground stop that triggered chaos for tens of thousands of travelers at U.S. airports.
In the FBI breach reported last week, hackers accessed a large database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to access criminal records.

The NSA's network outage was linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News. The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline during the ordeal, the sources said.

The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence, meanwhile, suffered an intrusion of an internal network that gathers intelligence from publicly available information, such as social media.
An ODNI official told CBS News in a statement Tuesday that there were "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems" from that breach.

All this comes as White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired from his position last week. Sources told CBS News that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, and that he had told people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.

title: 2 American Airlines jets clip wings on tarmac of Reagan Airport
summary: There were no injuries when the wingtips of two American Airlines jets made contact Friday evening on the tarmac of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport outside Washington, D.C.
story: There were no injuries when the wingtips of two American Airlines jets made contact Friday evening on the tarmac of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport outside Washington, D.C., officials said.

American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 a little after 5 p.m. local time while both aircraft were taxiing for departure, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
In a separate statement provided to CBS News, American Airlines said that both planes returned to their gates and were "removed from service for inspection by our maintenance team."
Both the FAA and American Airlines said no injuries were reported.

The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority said in a statement that its fire and rescue personnel responded to both planes. The airports authority said there were no disruptions to any other flights.
Flight 638 was bound for Dallas, while Flight 2152 was headed to Chicago. The airline said passengers would be placed on new planes and depart for their destinations later Friday night.
Earlier this month, two passengers suffered minor injuries when the wingtip of a Copa Airlines jet struck the nose of a UPS cargo plane on the tarmac of Miami International Airport.
And in early October, the left wingtip of a Delta Air Lines plane clipped the tail of an Air Canada aircraft on the tarmac of Los Angeles International Airport. There were no injuries.
Reagan Airport has three runways, one of which is considered the busiest in the nation, and it operates with a tightly restricted airspace due to its location near the White House and Capitol Hill.

In January 2025, an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided in midair with an American Airlines plane that was approaching to land at Reagan Airport. All 64 people aboard the American Airlines flight were killed, along with the three soldiers aboard the chopper.

title: OpenAI countersues Apple over allegations of stealing trade secrets
summary: OpenAI alleged in a lawsuit Friday that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing trade secrets.
story: OpenAI on Friday responded to Apple's June lawsuit accusing the company of stealing trade secrets by countersuing.

The ChatGPT maker alleged that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing proprietary information. Apple created "a situation in which it can accuse virtually any departing employee, and their new employer, of 'stealing' purported Apple trade secrets," the suit, filed in the Northern District of California, claims.

In a statement provided to CBS News Friday, an Apple spokesperson said that the case "is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information. OpenAI's counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple's confidential information."

Apple's complaint in June accused OpenAI and two of its employees, Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan and Chang Liu, a technical staffer at the company, of stealing Apple's proprietary information to help OpenAI develop its own hardware. Both formerly worked at Apple.

OpenAI claims in its countersuit Friday that Apple's employment practices are designed to set a trap for a departing employee and their future employer — "a trap that can be sprung whenever Apple sees an opportunity to slow down a potential competitor."

Tech analysts expect OpenAI to make a foray into hardware design, putting it in more direct competition with Apple. In July 2025, OpenAI acquired the AI device startup of former Apple star designer Jony Ive, io Products Inc.

title: Powerful Thanksgiving storm causes flooding, power outages
summary: The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of customers.
story: A Thanksgiving storm brought foul weather to the East Coast and Midwest on Thursday, causing major power outages, disrupting holiday travel and prompting the historic postponement of New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

More than 440,000 customers were without power Friday afternoon across the Midwest and Northeast, according to the utility tracking website PowerOutage.us. Of those, more than 109,000 customers were without electricity in Pennsylvania, along with more than 68,000 in New Jersey and 54,000 in Maryland. The outages reached more than 800,000 customers at the height of the storm Thursday night.

There were 2,286 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday afternoon, with another 137 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. That nearly equals the 2,500 flights to or from U.S. destinations delayed on Thursday, though more than 460 were canceled, according to FlightAware.

The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency, declared by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Wednesday night, as were parts of New York, following a declaration from Gov. Kathy Hochul. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.
Stormy weather creates havoc in New York City

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning that two people had to be rescued from their cars because of flooding. He cautioned people not to attempt to walk, bike or drive through flooded areas.
"We want to remind everyone to stay safe and there is no destination worth your safety," Mamdani said.

The New York City Emergency Management agency reported that the city received 1.5 to 2 inches of rain on Thanksgiving, with some parts seeing up to 3 inches. High tides brought flooding to the city's coastal areas, including portions of Staten Island and Long Island.

Central Park saw wind gusts higher than 30 mph, the agency said, while LaGuardia Airport recorded winds of 56 mph. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, with no injuries were reported.
Macy's postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade's massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers.
A high school marching band from Pearland, Texas, near Houston, said it raised a staggering $350,000 to allow its 500 members to stay in New York City for two extra nights.

"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band for Pearland High School, told CBS News on Thursday.

Visitors who had traveled to New York to attend the parade were forced to make last-minute changes to their travel plans. Amanda Anderson, a Florida-based makeup artist who was hired to do makeup for parade performers, told CBS News New York she was able to rebook her flights so she could stay an extra day.

"I was in Macy's, actually, when I found out, and I look up and there was like three girls crying already," Anderson said when she learned the parade had been postponed. "People were sitting down, very somber. It was an experience."
Major roadways flooded, holiday travel disrupted

The storm flooded coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey as the high tide rolled in Thursday morning. Roads were closed and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, Borough of Avalon Business Administrator Scott J. Wahl said.
"Not quite Hurricane Sandy," Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south of New Jersey's Atlantic coast.
Floodwaters washed debris over the road next to the shore, and a few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.

Lance Miller, 54, said floods in his neighborhood of Ocean City, a small coastal town in New Jersey, are about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest grocery store would probably "destroy your car."
"I wouldn't do that, I'm a car guy," said Miller. "You're gonna have a good foot of water that you'd have to drive through."

Miller, who had his Thanksgiving Day meal preparations set, said he would be staying indoors and have dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends in the area were "not so lucky" and had flooding inside their homes.
"So they're dealing with cleanup, you know," he said.
The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted a video on Facebook of water pouring through the city's streets on a gray day even before heavy rains started.
A firefighter there said the tide was coming in ferociously and it was still an hour before its peak. Water closed in on steps to houses, and businesses had sandbags piled in front of their doors.
A stretch of U.S. Route 30, a major artery that goes into Atlantic City, was shuttered in both directions due to heavy flooding, the Absecon Police Department reported.
"Please stay off the roads until conditions improve," Absecon police said. "Do not attempt to drive through flooded roadways or around barricades."
Chester County Hospital in West Chester, Pennsylvania, sustained a partial power outage on Thursday afternoon, but power was restored before patients had to be transported to other facilities.

Residents of the Pennsylvania community of Springfield Township north of Philadelphia were asked to temporarily evacuate out of caution after a tree fell on a propane tank, local officials said. That evacuation advisory was later lifted.

The storm prompted the temporary closure of some coastal highways and bridges. The nearly 18-mile Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel over the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes again and covered the two-lane highway.
North Carolina was particularly hard-hit by heavy rain. Emerald Isle, in the state's Outer Banks, received 9.16 inches of rain. Atlantic Beach, North Carolina, saw 9.06 inches.

In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, which are in the Washington metropolitan area, were asked to conserve water by the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission      because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. The water conservation request, which applied to all 1.9 million WSSC customers, was due to the risk that power outages posed to the agency's two water filtration plants.
Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St. Louis recording 7.3 inches of snowfall. French Village, Missouri, received 15 inches of show while Ste. Genevieve recorded 14 inches.
The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 a.m., according to the city.
The rain isn't quite over yet for the Northeast. More storms are expected Sunday night into Monday morning for New York City, Philadelphia and Boston.

title: Pregnant inmate escapes in prison SUV after stop at Whataburger
summary: Rebecca Taylor, who was not restrained because of her pregnancy, slid into the front seat of the transport vehicle and drove away.
story: A pregnant prisoner is on the run in New Mexico after escaping in a corrections department SUV following a prenatal doctor appointment on Wednesday.

Rebecca Taylor, 26, who was not restrained at the time because of her pregnancy, managed to slide into the front seat of the Dodge Journey transport vehicle and drive away as she was returning to Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants from the appointment in Albuquerque, according to the corrections department.
Taylor escaped while the correctional officers accompanying her had stopped at a Whataburger, according to The Associated Press.
The Dodge Journey was later located via GPS, but Taylor was no longer in the vehicle, corrections officials said. Her prison jumpsuit was found near the vehicle, the AP reported.
Taylor is serving time after pleading guilty to four offenses related to the theft of a vehicle, vehicle burglary and receiving a stolen car, according to court records.

She is from Cleveland, Texas, which is located outside of Houston, where she also has ties, according to authorities. Officials said they were following up on leads she may have taken public transportation and were checking Greyhound buses and Amtrak trains.
The U.S. Marshals Service is offering a $5,000 reward for information leading to her arrest.
Taylor is about 5-foot-7 and 180 pounds and has blue eyes and red hair. Authorities are asking anyone who sees her to call 911.
All prison facilities in New Mexico were put on lockdown in the wake of the escape as a precaution. That lockdown was lifted at 6 a.m. on Friday.

title: Sen. Deb Fischer's husband died by suicide, her office says
summary: "His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him," Sen. Deb Fischer said of her late husband, Bruce.
story: Washington — Nebraska Sen. Deb Fischer's husband, Bruce Fischer, died by suicide, a spokesperson for her office said Friday.
On Monday, the Republican senator's office announced that he had died Sunday, "peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors."

But on Friday, a spokeperson for Fischer's office said in a statement on X, "Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home. Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life. The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning."

Fischer's office said no further details would be provided at this time. When the senator announced her husband's death earlier this week, she referred to him as "my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family." They were married for 54 years.

According to her Senate profile, Fischer met her husband, a cattle rancher, while she was a student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. After they married, the two moved to the family ranch outside of Valentine, Nebraska, where they raised their three sons.

"His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him," Fischer said of her late husband, adding that she "will cherish the decades we spend building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills."
Fischer, 75, has represented Nebraska in the Senate since 2013.
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental health crisis, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing or texting "988."

title: Allstate roiled by tech outage over Thanksgiving week
summary: The insurer's systems are out of commission during the busiest road travel period of the year, leaving customers unable to access roadside assistance.
story: Allstate has joined the growing list of companies bedeviled by a technology disruption in recent weeks, leaving some customers unable to file claims or seek roadside assistance during Thanksgiving week.

The Northbrook, Illinois-based insurer said in a statement on Wednesday that some of its services had been restricted after customers reported being unable to access them on social media and on Downdetector, which tracks web outages.

"Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims," the company said. "To the extent service interruptions impact a customer's ability to make a payment, they won't lose coverage or be charged late fees."
People seeking roadside assistance on Allstate's website encountered an error message through Friday.
In a statement on its website, Allstate added that customers may reach the insurer through multiple channels, including by phone.

Allstate offers a range of policies, including home, life and auto insurance. Its consumer-facing tech problems during one of the busiest times of year for road travel follow disruptions at other major U.S. airlines, banks, software providers and government agencies.
Microsoft, which suffered a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, said a technical issue caused the disruption and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio also said at the time that the tech outages were distinct from one another. The incidents were caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems, they said.

"In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio said. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

title: Fake online stores may fool AI shopping bots on Black Friday
summary: AI bots are accidentally steering shoppers toward websites and online shops created by scammers using AI.
story: Scammers are using AI to churn out convincing copies of real online stores, and this Black Friday, the AI agents that many shoppers will rely on often can't tell the difference.
These fake sites pose a risk to the millions of Americans who are tasking their AI agents with making online purchases and transacting on their behalf.

"Artificial intelligence just makes building websites so much easier. You can upload anything into HTML and build a website very, very easily," Harrison Tang, co-founder of Spokeo, a data aggregator, told CBS News.

AI is enabling scammers to build what Tang described as convincing dupes of legitimate online stores in only hours, including copies of a brand's logo, marketing language and product images and descriptions.

"AI just makes creating these look-alike fake stores a lot easier, so there is a proliferation of them," Tang explained. "Platforms will try to catch them by not directing users there, but there are so many of them popping up all the time that they are hard to keep up with."
Research from Microsoft shows that criminals can use AI to set up fraudulent e-commerce sites in mere minutes rather than the days or weeks that were once required.

Spokeo identified copycat sites of dozens of popular brands, including UGG, L.L. Bean, Converse and Stella McCartney. As of Nov. 15, it had identified 65 distinct online stores that mimicked the legitimate sites of 60 brand names, according to its online shopping scam study.
The discrepancies between the authentic stores and the scam websites are subtle and require close examination.

The first place to look for proof of fraud, according to Tang, is in the online store's web address. For example, a fake Converse store uses the web address converseshop.us.com, whereas the real store's address is converse.com. The .us domain name is the top-level domain for the U.S. and is reserved for U.S. residents, but is commonly used for phishing attempts, according to Tang.
"It looks like an official website, but it's not, so if you don't pay close attention, it's easy to get tricked," he said.
AI agents need to get savvy
Bots aren't as well trained as some humans are at spotting phony websites, which can dupe even discerning shoppers because of how realistic they look.
Recent research from Podqi, a firm that monitors for intellectual property infringement, on AI search risks shows that AI engines can inadvertently direct shoppers to scammy stores.

The group asked popular AI tools, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Perplexity, questions about where to buy particular brands online. More than 18% of the AI bots' answers drew on a fake, infringing or invalid website.

For example, when asked where to buy clothing from Stussy, a streetwear brand, Perplexity referred to us-stussy.com, which it mistakenly identified as the brand's official website and "the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items." The web address us-stussy.com directs shoppers to a fake store. The real store's address is stussy.com.
Other brands with duplicate online stores include Figs, a medical scrubs maker; sock company Bombas; and dairy brand Fairlife.
Here are other tip-offs that a site is phony and should be avoided, according to Spokeo:

title: Mother dies after walking into plane propeller at Alaska airport
summary: Christina Blake, 38, drove a car onto the taxiway of Big Lake Airport, then got out of the vehicle and walked toward a stopped plane.
story: A woman has died after walking into the propeller of an airplane at Alaska's Big Lake Airport, officials said.

Christina Blake, 38, was driving a car on the airport's taxiway when a Taylorcraft F19 plane landed at the airport and began moving from the runway to the taxiway, according to a preliminary investigation by the Alaska Department of Public Safety. The plane stopped and waited for Blake's vehicle to move off the taxiway.
Instead, Blake got out of the car, approached the running aircraft, and "walked into the airplane's propeller while it was stationary," the Alaska Department of Public Safety said.
The Anchorage Daily News reported that the pilot shut off the engine to try to stop the propeller as Blake walked toward it, and that Blake gestured at the pilot.

State troopers, EMS and fire department resources were called to the scene, and lifesaving efforts were administered, but Blake was pronounced dead at the scene, the department said. Her family was notified and her body has been sent to the state medical examiner's office for an autopsy.

The Anchorage Daily News reported that authorities do not believe the incident was intentional. Alaska Department of Public Safety interim Deputy Commissioner Austin McDaniel told CBS affiliate KTUU that Blake's death appears to have been accidental.

Alaska State Troopers and the medical examiner's office will review the incident to determine Blake's cause and manner of death, McDaniel told KTUU. That will include determining if any laws were broken, McDaniel said.
The National Transportation Safety Board has been notified, KTUU reported, and will also review the incident.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the pilot was uninjured and that no passengers were aboard the plane.

Sheri Stewart, Blake's half-sister, told the New York Post that Blake had schizophrenia and had used drugs and alcohol in the past. Stewart, a 50-year-old U.S. Navy veteran who lives in Oregon, told the Post that Blake had previously been arrested for trying to direct traffic.
"I could totally see her thinking she was directing the airplane," Stewart told the Post.

Blake's aunt Laura Blake told the Post that Blake was on mental health medications and that whether she was taking them "made a difference in her behavior." Stewart told the Post that the family believed Blake was off her medication at the time of the incident.
Blake is survived by two daughters, Stewart said.
"I think this was a tragic accident due to my sister's mental health," Stewart told the Post. "My sister was really a beautiful person, but she just couldn't get a hold of it."

title: Here's how GLP-1 drugs are changing people's shopping habits
summary: More than 60 million Americans could be using the drugs by 2030, double the number that currently use them, according to a new forecast.
story: The millions of Americans who use GLP-1 drugs to lose weight are reshaping consumer spending and buying patterns, forcing businesses to rethink their offerings.

The medications could make the population at large healthier and increase worker longevity, thereby driving productivity gains. More than 60 million Americans are expected to start using the drugs by 2030, more than double the number that currently takes them, according to an estimate from Oxford Economics, an economic advisory firm.
Their user base is already large enough to drive noticeable spending pullbacks on some goods and services while boosting others, according to research from the firm.

"GLP-1s are no longer a niche story for the U.S. economy," Oxford Economics U.S. economist Grace Zwemmer wrote in a report. "Faster adoption and broader access will continue to drive a reallocation of consumer spending away from food and toward apparel."
The drugs could boost labor supply if workers are healthier and can remain on the job for longer, she noted.
Shopping baskets start to look different

Spending on food, both at home and at bars and restaurants, stands to take the biggest hit, according to Zwemmer. Oxford Economics estimates that households using GLP-1 reduce food spending by about $500 a year on average.

A study from Cornell University and Numerator found that GLP-1 users cut grocery spending by roughly 5% within months of starting the drug. The most noticeable cuts were in the savory snacks and sweet bakery goods aisles, although GLP-1 users bought more yogurt and fresh produce.

The medication leads users to spend about $200 more a year on clothing, according to the Oxford Economics report. Separate research shows that GLP-1 users tend to overhaul their wardrobes to accommodate their slimmed-down figures. They favor smaller sizes and, in some cases, body-hugging styles versus baggier alternatives, according to Impact Analytics, a retail forecasting firm.

"As long as adoption continues to rise, new starters will have demand for new clothes," Zwemmer wrote in the report. "For now, that translates to an additional $200 in spending on apparel per year per user. Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 [million] users entering 2027, this would translate to an $8 [billion] uplift in apparel spending next year."

title: Rocker the coonhound nabs Best in Show at 2026 National Dog Show
summary: The black and tan coonhound defeated six other outstanding dogs to claim the 2026 National Dog Show's top honor.
story: Rocker, a black and tan coonhound, took home the top honors Thursday as Best in Show during the 2026 National Dog Show in Philadelphia.
The coonhound defeated six other outstanding dogs to claim the show's top honor, the National Dog Show said in a statement to CBS News.

"There were seven outstanding examples of their different breeds. I mean, it's a tough decision," said Lorraine Bisso, a show judge from Louisiana. She praised Rocker's physical appearance and his athletic ability in the show ring.
"He has beautiful feet. He has a lovely forechest — which is necessary, because he's going to run for 25 miles. Tail is up. I mean, this is a hunting hound," Bisso said.
"He's just a beautiful dog," she added.
A Lhasa apso named Kissy nabbed reserve Best in Show.

The show, which is put on by the American Kennel Club in Philadelphia, took place on Nov. 14 and 15 but was televised on Thanksgiving. There are more than 190 AKC-registered breeds assigned to one of seven groups representing characteristics and functions they were originally bred for, according to the show. There is the toy group, terrier group, working group, sporting group, hound group, non-sporting group and herding group.

Rocker won the hound group competition before advancing to the Best in Show round. Although Rocker has been crowned Best in Show 15 times, his California-based handler Mandy Clevenger was surprised by his win this year.
"I just didn't expect it. It was great. What was a wonderful win," she said.
Clevenger, who has handled Rocker since he started his show career at 6 months old, said the dog was energized by the crowd and "loves all the people," and he "loves all the commotion."
Rocker is expected to be among the contenders at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show early next year in New York City.
The other 2026 National Dog Show group winners were:

title: Stocks turn volatile as Jensen Huang rebound rally fades
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell more than 1,000 points in early trading before clawing back most of the losses.
story: Stocks swung wildly on Wednesday, plunging in early trading before paring losses by the close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 1,000 points early in the session, but regained ground to close down 148 points, or 0.6%, at 23,586.  The S&P 500 fell 0.2% on the day, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%.

Stocks have slumped in recent weeks amid concerns surrounding the health of the artificial intelligence sector. Shares of Anthropic, the AI lab that staged the largest initial stock offering in history last week, declined 7.6% to $75.66, below its IPO price of $83 per share.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the AI sector can justify the enormous investment in data centers. Compounding those fears just before the Thanksgiving holiday are the Trump administration's plans to raise tariffs on China and other major trading partners.

"At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn't look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year," Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer for Northlight Asset Management, said in an email.

With Democrats set to control Congress next year and winning many state-level seats, AI companies may face more headwinds as lawmakers push back against data center construction, according to investment adviser Capital Economics. Even before the midterm elections, investors were increasingly questioning the finances of AI companies, it added.

Investors are also bracing for the impact of more interest rate hikes starting in December, with expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs to counter rising inflation. That could make it more difficult for businesses, including AI companies, to borrow money to fuel growth.

title: Argentina's bid to halt oil drilling off Falkland Islands rejected
summary: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea voted against Argentina's request to halt drilling at an offshore oil project in Falkland Islands waters.
story: Argentina's bid to temporarily block oil drilling off the nearby U.K.-held Falkland Islands was rejected Saturday by an international tribunal that rules on maritime disputes.

At a special hearing in Hamburg, Germany, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea voted 18-3 against Argentina's request to halt drilling at the Sea Lion offshore oil project in Falkland Islands waters, around 300 miles east of Argentina's southeastern coast.

The dispute over the planned drilling revived memories of the bitter war the two countries fought 44 years ago over the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and which have been a British overseas territory since 1833.

In a joint statement, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves welcomed the decision and urged Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders, who number around 3,500 people, to "determine their own future" and end its wider economic pressure.

"This outcome is a vindication of the U.K.'s robust legal defence and strategy," they said. "The U.K. has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders."

In its decision on Saturday, the judges ruled there did not appear to be any basis for believing Argentina had jurisdiction, as the tribunal is unable to make decisions based on questions of sovereignty, Agence France-Presse news agency reported.
Buenos Aires had argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.

Argentina respects the court's decision, but disagrees with it, the office of President Javier Milei said. The Argentine government sought to portray the ruling as a partial win, arguing that by tying the case to sovereignty, the court had effectively recognized the existence of a dispute that the United Kingdom has long refused to negotiate on.
"This decision is not the last word," Milei's office said.
Argentina will move quickly to form a separate arbitration panel that will hear the full case and ask it for measures to protect the country's rights, it said.
Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno also sounded triumphant, hailing the ruling as "a historic step" and vowing to press on "with more determination than ever."

Milei has vowed to penalize companies working on oil production around the islands and argued that the joint U.K.-Israeli operation is a "clear and present danger" to his country's claims over the islands.
Milei has doubled down on his country's claim over the islands since President Trump said he was open to reviewing Washington's stance on the territory.
The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain British.
But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by Britain after 1833.
Following Saturday's ruling, Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum are expected to push ahead with the plan under licenses granted by the Falkland Islands government and backed by Britain.
The decision came as a relief to the people of the Falklands, who have long dreamed of oil transforming their lives and their fishing-dependent economy.

"This is a good day for the Falkland Islands," the islands' Legislative Assembly said in a statement. "Sea Lion will transform our economy and give future generations a more secure and self-reliant Falklands."

The U.K. has said drilling at the field about 140 miles north of the islands won't commence until March 2027, with extraction expected to begin a year later. Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.
