title: Afghan women in U.S. fear returning to Taliban rule
summary: The threat of imminent deportation may have subsided, but some Afghan women who fled Taliban rule still face anxiety and legal limbo in America.
story: Ever since the Trump administration announced earlier this month that it planned to deport nearly 200 Afghans through Pakistan back to their Taliban-controlled homeland, some in the Afghan community in America have been watching and waiting in fear.

A federal judge temporarily blocked a planned Nov. 3 flight, but many Afghans still feel stuck in limbo. The deportations could lead to some who helped the U.S. in the war in Afghanistan being persecuted by the Taliban, advocates and others fear.

Frequent changes to immigration policies have placed immense strain on the Afghan community, said Naheed Samadi Bahram, U.S. country director for Women for Afghan Women, a U.S.-based humanitarian organization advocating for Afghan women's rights.

"It also brings a lot of stress and anxiety to the community members who are unsure of their future in the United States," Bahram said. "They don't know if they are being deported or sent back to Afghanistan, where the only thing they will be faced with will be death or threats."
Bahram added it is especially tough on the women "who are really the backbone of the family."
There were reports of at least three women on the canceled flight, said Shawn VanDiver, president and founder of #AfghanEvac, an advocacy group supporting Afghan allies who were resettled in the U.S.

Two Jane Does are listed as plaintiffs in a court case filed Nov. 2 by nonprofit Project Rousseau in the U.S. Southern District of New York, which asked a federal judge for an emergency order to stop the planned removals.
If returned to Afghanistan, women "will face the consequences more than anyone in the family," Bahram said.

Women in Afghanistan have been barred from most jobs, university, secondary school and political life since the Taliban returned to power. Early and forced marriage remains common, with nearly 30% of Afghan girls under 18 married, according to U.N. Women. Additionally, the risk of violence against women and girls has increased, the organization said.
A devastating choice

For Shaima, a 56-year-old mother of four, just the thought of returning to Afghanistan is unimaginable. She asked to be identified only by her first name for safety reasons. Her husband, she said, worked alongside the U.S. government for more than five years during the war in Afghanistan and believed his association put their family in danger.

Yet Shaima, who said she worked as a doctor in her home country, was initially reluctant to leave behind her home, parents and extended family. After the Taliban seized power in 2021 and its rulers banned formal education for all girls beyond sixth grade, her thoughts gradually shifted.
She had a daughter to consider, and it wasn't the life she wanted for her.
"First, she can't continue education. Second, they can't go to work and she should be married and stay at home. But she don't like this," Shaima told CBS News.
Shaima said she knew she had to leave for her family's safety and children's future, leaving her elderly parents behind — an agonizing decision.
"Should I select my parents or my children, and it's very difficult," Shaima said. Shaima immigrated to New York City in 2024 with her children and husband.

The Afghan population in the United States has expanded dramatically in recent years, quadrupling between 2010 and 2024, according to the Migration Policy Institute. The vast majority immigrated after 2021 — roughly 180,000 Afghans — when the U.S. ended its two-decade war in Afghanistan and the Taliban regained control.

Upon arriving in the U.S., adjusting to life presented steep challenges. The Migration Policy Institute found that nearly 40% of Afghan immigrants lived in poverty in 2022, compared to 14% for overall immigrant populations. Shaima says her family faced significant hurdles accessing education and employment.
An unknown future
"Living in New York is very difficult," Shaima said.

Anxiety heightened after reports of potential deportations began circulating, especially since her family has not yet secured permanent residency, she said. She explained that her family applied for green cards about nine months after arriving, but the process abruptly stalled.

The Department of Homeland Security ended Temporary Protected Status for Afghans in July 2025, with then-Secretary Kristi Noem saying, "Afghanistan has had an improved security situation, and its stabilizing economy no longer prevents them from returning to their home country."
"Now all the time we are afraid. My husband wants to go to buy some grocery but we are afraid because we don't have green card," Shaima said.
In a Nov. 2 statement, Taliban officials expressed "deep concern" over reports that the U.S. intended to deport Afghan refugees through Pakistan.
"The Afghan side is ready to engage constructively on this matter," the statement said.

The U.S. government has not publicly announced new dates for deportation flights, and on Nov. 17, a federal judge in New York's Southern District granted a preliminary injunction to stop the deportations as the case is considered.
However, "the government has not given up," VanDiver said.
Since Oct. 14, his organization has received reports of at least 76 Afghans being detained, he said.
VanDiver said on social media Wednesday that deportation flights are scheduled for next week. He didn't provide further details or immediately reply to CBS News for clarification.
CBS News reached out to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment on possible future deportation flights.

There may be legislative options ahead to ease the pressure on Afghans in the U.S., VanDiver said. Congressional representatives introduced a bipartisan bill in July 2026 to extend Temporary Protected Status for at least 9,000 Afghans, and in November filed a discharge petition to force a floor vote on the measure.
Meanwhile, Shaima continues building a life in New York for her family, drawing strength from the fact that her children are safe.
Her daughter now has the opportunity to pursue an education. Despite ongoing uncertainty, Shaima reminds her children not to lose faith.
"I say our journey is very difficult … but we hope," Shaima said.

title: Charity honoring veteran who raised millions with walks to be disbanded
summary: Capt. Tom Moore raised almost $49 million with daily walks in his yard during the early days of the coronavirus pandemic.
story: A charity set up by the family of a British World War II veteran who raised tens of millions by walking laps of his garden during the coronavirus pandemic has applied to be disbanded, two years after the country's charity watchdog found "repeated" financial misconduct.

An application to have the charitable company created in honor of Capt. Tom Moore removed appeared Friday on the register of Companies House, the official U.K. government executive agency that maintains the public register of British companies, including charitable ones.

Moore, who died in 2021 at 100 years old, raised almost 39 million pounds, or $49 million, through his daily walks in his yard, inspiring people across the U.K. who followed his exploits in daily TV updates during the early weeks of the pandemic. All of the money he raised was donated to Britain's National Health Service.
"That's a lot of dollars — isn't it?" Moore told CBS News in 2021.

Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020 during an outdoor investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle, in recognition of his huge charity efforts. He also received about 125,000 cards from the public for his 100th birthday and participated in a charity music single that saw him become the oldest British No. 1 artist ever.

Following the success of his fundraising, his family established the Captain Tom Foundation to continue his fundraising efforts. However, the charity was soon embroiled in controversy and Britain's charity regulator concluded in November 2024 that Moore's daughter and son-in-law personally benefited from the charity.

The Charity Commission for England and Wales slammed them in a damning report that found they made almost 1.5 million pounds, or $1.9 million, from activities linked to the charity, including a book deal and an 18,000-pound fee to attend an awards ceremony.
It also barred Moore's daughter, Hannah Ingram-Moore, from serving as a trustee for any charity for 10 years and her husband, Colin, for a period of eight years.
The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission's inquiry.
The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Moore's name at the request of his family last year.

title: Gaza strike kills 2 MSF guards whom Israel claims were Hamas fighters
summary: The IDF accused the two men killed of being terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.
story: Doctors Without Borders, also known by their French acronym MSF, said Friday night two of its staff who worked as guards were killed in an Israeli strike on a clinic in Gaza. The Israeli military accused the men of being Hamas fighters.
"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen," the humanitarian organization said in a post on X. "This is a direct hit on MSF," it added.
In the statement, MSF also said its premises are marked with logos and its locations are communicated to the Israeli military.
"We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability," the statement said.
In response, the Israeli Defense Forces named the two men killed as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, and claimed they were terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.

"While also serving as terrorists, the two worked as security guards at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF). This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," the IDF said in a statement released on Friday.

The Israeli military also disputed the claim that MSF facilities were targeted in the attack, claiming that no damage was caused to medical infrastructure. It added that it had used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to minimize "the expected harm to civilians."
MSF say the deaths bring the total number of their workers killed in Gaza to 17.
Mourners gathered Saturday for the two men's funeral prayers. Ahmad Abu Haseira, a relative of one of the killed men, said they were unarmed and wore MSF uniforms at the time of the attack.
A local MSF employee, Ahmad Shehada, said the two were making their rounds to check the clinic's facilities when a missile struck.

title: Spain's election could bring the far-right to power for 1st time in decades
summary: For decades, Spain was relatively resistant to the rise of far-right populism seen elsewhere in Europe.
story: Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday in a snap election that could see another major European country swing to the political right, as socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez battles to retain power amid mounting public discontent over housing, immigration and corruption.

Sánchez, one of Europe's most prominent left-wing leaders, has increasingly positioned himself as a political counterweight to President Trump on the world stage. He has defied Mr. Trump's demands over NATO defense spending, penned an opinion piece in The New York Times defending migration and denouncing "MAGA-style leaders" and cultivated ties with prominent figures on the American left, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

But at home, Sánchez faces a growing challenge from the center-right People's Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, and the nationalist, anti-immigration Vox party, led by Santiago Abascal, which could together form Spain's most right-wing government since the country returned to democracy following the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
A country divided
Housing has become a defining issue of the election, with soaring rents and property prices fueling widespread public anger.

On the same day Sánchez met Mamdani in New York City, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years. Her landlord had sought to more than triple her monthly rent to $1,900, or 1,650 euros.

Her eviction – where she was carried out on a stretcher – sparked nationwide protests. Although her landlord subsequently agreed to let her return at a substantially lower rent, Abascal died in the hospital two weeks after her eviction, before she could sign the new lease. Her case became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis.

In response to the protests, Sánchez introduced emergency housing measures, including restrictions on rent increases. But the proposals were defeated in parliament, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election.

Sánchez has since sought to blame the PP and the far-right Vox for blocking protections for vulnerable tenants. The PP, meanwhile, argues that Sánchez has had eight years to address the housing crisis and has pledged to build one million homes.
The PP has made reducing the cost of living and tackling corruption central to its campaign.

Immigration has also become a particularly contentious election issue following the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa, in July, and the Sánchez government's decision earlier this year to offer legal status to hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants.
The far-right Vox party has sought to capitalize on public unease over immigration, calling for mass deportations and prioritizing Spanish nationals in access to public services.

Hugo Marcos-Marné, a political scientist at the University of Salamanca, told CBS News that the "electoral growth of Vox is multicausal," but perceptions of immigration, more than actual figures or changes in the country-wide objective situation, "is certainly behind" the party's rise.
The PP has also called for tightened immigration controls.

Corruption scandals involving Sánchez's political associates and members of his family have been a major feature of the election. Two deadly train crashes this year have also undermined confidence in his administration.
Vox has also been aided by "an anti-gender reaction, authoritarian nostalgia, and anti-elitism directed against mainstream parties and politicians," Marcos-Marné said.
Spain's far-right taboo
For decades, Spain was relatively resistant to the rise of far-right populism seen elsewhere in Europe, in part because of the country's experience of dictatorship under Franco.

Although the center-right PP is polling ahead of Sánchez's Socialists, polls suggest it could fall short of a parliamentary majority and need the support of Vox, which is polling at around 18%. Once reluctant to embrace the far-right party, the PP has increasingly shown a willingness to work with Vox, with the two parties having formed coalition governments at the regional level.

"Research shows that the radical-right was comparatively more stigmatized in Spain because of Franco dictatorship, but also that the Popular Party was a chameleonic party able to attract voters of the center-right and the radical-right," Marcos-Marné said.
Sánchez is hoping that the prospect of the far-right entering national government will galvanize progressive voters.

"The PP and Vox pose a real threat to many groups in our country," Sánchez wrote on X, accusing the parties of seeking to roll back the rights of women, workers and migrants. "Every seat that goes to the PP and Vox means taking a step backward."
The implications of Sunday's election extend well beyond Spain's borders.
With Spain the only large EU country currently governed by the left, Marcos-Marné said, the election is "certainly significant for the balance of forces at the EU level."

title: 25-year sentence sought for former chef who aided 14 suicides
summary: Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally.
story: Canadian prosecutors on Friday requested a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold poison to help people die by  suicide, stressing his victims were largely young and experiencing mental distress.
Former chef Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally through a series of online forums.
Prosecutors had also charged him with murder but, citing a lack of evidence, agreed to withdraw the more serious accusations in exchange for Law pleading guilty to lesser offenses.

That decision drew widespread condemnation, notably from friends and family of victims who believed Law was directly responsible for killing their loved ones, but prosecutors maintained they would still seek a stiff penalty.
"An appropriate global sentence to impose in this matter is 25 years less (time already served)," Crown prosecutor Katie Doherty told the court.
Courts often use comparable cases in determining sentencing, but Doherty noted there is "no case even remotely similar to Mr Law's conduct."
The Canadian public was shocked when the breadth of Law's operation was revealed following his arrest.

He sold poison to people in at least 41 countries, including China, France, and Brazil. He sold 330 packages to people in the United Kingdom, according to an agreed statement of facts signed by the defense and prosecution. There, 79 deaths are linked to him, according to Canadian prosecutors.

He admitted to entering suicide chat forums under an alias, identifying people considering ending their lives and then directing them to one of his online shops where he sold lethal concentrations of the meat preservative sodium nitrite.
In 2023, Canadian police released photos of the sodium nitrite, adding that a joint operation led by 11 police agencies from across Ontario were investigating the case.
"Investigators are asking members of the community to be alert of any packaging or label identifying sodium nitrite," Constable Sarah Patten said at the time.
Law, who was born in 1965, sold poison to people who were "just starting off their lives" and "battling mental illness," Doherty said.
That is "a very significant aggravating factor in this case," Doherty said.
The judge is expected to make a final sentencing decision over the coming weeks.
Prosecutors in the U.K. decided not to charge Law despite investigating him for dozens of deaths.
The Crown Prosecution Service and the National Crime Agency said they had decided Law "should be sentenced for the full extent of his offending within a single sentencing process in Canada."
In a letter to bereaved families, the organizations said it had been a "difficult decision."
"No outcome in any court can remove the pain victims and their families have suffered," they said.

title: U.S. opens hotline for tips about cartels, angering Mexico
summary: President Claudia Sheinbaum blasted the DEA after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of interference.
story: Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders. President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday the country's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson.
"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," she said in her daily news briefing.

Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs.

"The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups."
"It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added.
Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?"

Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism.
"Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.
U.S. steps up pressure on Mexico

The United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, "but without subordination."

On Nov. 20, Mexican military forces captured drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "El Chapo Isidro," a key ally of a Sinaloa cartel faction. The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

The military operation o capture him tsparked panic in the region, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks. In clashes with security forces, 16 cartel suspects were killed, officials said, and four soldiers also died.
Mexico requested Washington's support for the operation, and the United States sent a drone to help gather information about the drug lord's whereabouts.
The U.S. has requested Meza Flores' extradition, but Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said he will be tried in Mexico.
Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.
Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.

The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Although cooperation between the two countries went smoothly in that operation, tensions arose between Mexico and Washington in late April after federal prosecutors in New York made public a drug trafficking indictment against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya, a member of Mexico's governing party. He and nine other officials were accused of collaborating with a faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which the Trump administration has designated a foreign terrorist organization.

Amid the controversy, Rocha Moya took an indefinite leave of absence, and his bank accounts in Mexico were frozen. But Mexican authorities refused to carry out the U.S. request to arrest him. Former Sinaloa Security Secretary Gerardo Mérida Sánchez surrendered to U.S. authorities in May.
DEA accused of "walking" fentanyl

DEA whistleblowers in June revealed to the AP how agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized. At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a "weapon of mass destruction."

That denial, however, was further contradicted by new AP findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history.

The AP based its tally on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage showing dealers moving large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states.

The Mexican president in her comments Thursday called the DEA's decision to permit fentanyl to hit the streets the "Fast and Furious of Fentanyl," a reference to the 2011 gun-walking scandal in which straw buyers smuggled some 2,000 assault weapons into Mexico with the intent of tracing the firearms to cartel leaders.

"What is the United States doing in the United States?" Sheinbaum asked. "We have a prosecutor's office here, and the Security Ministry works here. So they should pay close attention to the other side of the border."
The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Cole said a channel for submitting tips about the state of Jalisco would be made public Thursday. The state is a stronghold of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known by its Spanish initials CJNG, which Washington also designated a terrorist organization.
Meanwhile, a veteran DEA agent also told CBS News last month the agency has contributed to the problem by allowing fentanyl pills to reach the streets.

"For three years, I've told my DEA managers that we're allowing dangerous amounts of fentanyl to hit the street, and we're doing nothing to stop it, and they didn't listen to me," DEA Special Agent David Howell told CBS News in his first television interview.

title: Zelenskyy: Trump calling Putin a friend like calling Hitler a friend
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy described President Trump calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" as "strange" because the Russian leader is "an aggressor and a killer."
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe's future financial commitments to Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with CBS News partner BBC News Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Mr. Trump calling Putin "my friend" at a recent summit in China as "strange" because the Russian leader is "an aggressor and a killer."
"He can't be a friend," Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to Adolf Hitler being viewed as a friend during World War II.

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
In the BBC interview, Zelenskyy called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the U.S. to show both "power and respect."
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor ... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he told the BBC.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Mr. Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend ... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin. You know ... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

Zelenskyy's comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a "grandmaster" of politics and weeks after Kushner's partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a "humanitarian."

Moscow's invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Mr. Trump resumed relations.

At the same time, Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia's ballistic missiles and that SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication, isn't working properly.

Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia's invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new $49 billion loan for Ukraine's economic and military needs next year.
Elections in the EU over the next 12 months could amplify the influence of parties reluctant to send more money to Ukraine and may fray the continent's support.
Ukraine looks to allay concerns over Libya strike
Ukraine is determined to keep fighting for its independence, Kyiv officials say, and has launched daring attacks against Russian assets.
A recent strike on a Russian navy vessel docked at a port in Libya, however, raised alarm in Europe and Washington that the war could spread and engulf other countries.

In an apparent attempt to defuse tensions, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he held a phone call with Libyan Foreign Minister Al-Taher Al-Baour, informing him that Ukraine had no intentions of drawing Libya into the war.
Sybiha said in comments posted on social media late Thursday that he reaffirmed Kyiv's support for Libya's sovereignty and efforts to reunify the country.
Russia launched nearly 300 aerial attacks a week this month
The grinding aerial bombardment between Russia and Ukraine has escalated recently.
Russia launched close to 300 aerial attacks a week through Nov. 20 on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, or ACLED, that tracks violence.
Zelenskyy warned Thursday that a major Russian attack is looming.

Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 110 of 155 Russian drones launched overnight Friday, including 51 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to the Ukrainian air force. Hits were recorded at 27 locations across Ukraine, it said.

The attacks targeted railway infrastructure, energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings across nine Ukrainian regions, killing at least one person and wounding at least six, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.

Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line.
On Wednesday, a senior military adviser to Zelenskyy said Ukraine used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its forces overnight intercepted 318 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and illegally annexed Crimea.
Residents of St. Petersburg reported explosions in eight districts of the city, the Russian online news outlet Astra said.
Officials reported that Ukraine's attacks killed at least two people and wounded six others.

Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.

title: Iranian women are facing not just lashings, but "honor killings"
summary: Singer Parastoo Ahmadi's 74 lashes for daring to sing without her hair covered is not a unique case in Iran. Other women are being killed, some by their own families.
story: Helia Fattahi told her parents she was pregnant. She was not married. They allegedly killed her.

Iranian police arrested both parents after the killing on Nov. 21 in Sanandaj, a city in the mountains of western Iran. According to local media, they confessed, citing the shame they believed their daughter had brought upon the family.
The provincial police chief, however, described the motive in more prosaic terms, calling it "family disputes," and the parents have not been charged with any crimes.
Two days later, in the holy city of Qom, another Iranian woman was violently punished for a different act of defiance.
Parastoo Ahmadi, a celebrated singer, and four members of her production team each received 74 lashes over a concert she had performed nearly two years earlier without wearing a headscarf.
One woman had defied the conventions of her family. The other had defied the laws of the state.

Both cases, along with a spate of killings of young women across Iran in recent weeks, illuminate the sharp and still fragile limits to the modest freedoms Iranian women have secured since a popular uprising shook the Islamic Republic four years ago.
At the heart of that struggle are questions about who gets to decide how Iranian women live — what they wear, whom they love, and whether they can marry who they choose.

The protests first erupted in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died in police custody after being arrested for wearing her headscarf improperly. Her family told CBS News she was tortured in custody.
Women discarded their hair coverings, challenged the authority of Iran's morality police, and asserted freedoms that had long been denied to them as they chanted "Women, Life, Freedom."
Still many women walk around in public in Iranian cities with their hair uncovered, but the changes visible on the streets tell only part of the story.
Fereshteh, 27, lives with her partner in what Iranians call a "white marriage," an arrangement in which couples live together without being legally married.
Her family accepts the union. She considers herself fortunate.

One of her friends was not so lucky. After her relationship was revealed, Fereshteh told CBS News her friend was beaten by relatives and threatened with death by her father and brothers. She later fled to Europe to seek asylum.

Fereshteh, who spoke with CBS News online using technology to circumvent Iran's internet restrictions, said the dangers like those her friend faced are particularly acute in smaller towns and rural communities.
In recent days, reports from northern Iran have painted a grim picture of what can happen when young women seek to make their own choices about marriage.

In Gilan province, Sadaf Haghbin, 23, was fatally shot by her former boyfriend at her birthday party. Her refusal to marry him was a possible motive, according to the Iranian news outlet Khabar Online.

In northwest Iran, Zahra Jeddi, 16, was killed by a man she had been religiously married to as a child and whom she was trying to leave, according to Hengaw, a Kurdish human rights organization based in Norway.
Hengaw has documented at least 159 femicides across 27 Iranian provinces over the past year alone. At least 23 were identified by the organization as so-called honor killings.
The figures offer only a partial picture of violence that often goes unreported.
Honor killings are hardly unique to Iran, nor did they originate with the Islamic Republic.

But in Iran, the authority that families exercise over women is, in some circumstances, reinforced by provisions in the country's penal code that can spare their killers the harshest punishments for murder.

Under Article 301 of Iranian law, a father or paternal grandfather who kills his child or grandchild is exempt from qisas, the Islamic principle of retribution under which convicted murderers can be sentenced to death.
Other perpetrators can escape that punishment if they are forgiven by the victim's legal heirs, who, in cases of honor killings, may belong to the same family as the killer.
An Iranian lawyer familiar with such cases told CBS News the problem lies as much in the attitudes of judges as in the letter of the law.

The lawyer, 44, who asked to be identified by the pseudonym Neyazi for fear of repercussions, said judges frequently show leniency toward men accused of killing female relatives in the name of family honor.
The latitude afforded to some men who kill female relatives stands in contrast to the penalties the state can impose on women for appearing in public without a headscarf.

When Ahmadi performed her concert in December 2024, she challenged two of the Islamic Republic's restrictions on women: rules governing how they dress, and rules limiting their ability to sing in public.

Her corporal punishment this week has drawn international attention at a time when Iranian authorities appeared to have relaxed enforcement of some restrictions on women amid the pressures of war with the U.S.
But the laws remain in place.

Women who go unveiled are still vulnerable to prosecution, surveillance, and even the confiscation of their personal vehicles. Businesses that serve women risk being shuttered, according to Human Rights Watch.

Inside Iran, a longstanding debate about the state's responsibility to protect women, particularly those whose lives are known to be in danger, has been revived. The reformist newspaper Shargh, in an article published this month, questioned the failure of public institutions to intervene in such cases.
Few episodes have illustrated the consequences of that failure as starkly as the killing of Romina Ashrafi, a 14-year-old girl whose death in 2020 horrified many Iranians.

Romina had run away from her home in Gilan province with her 35-year-old boyfriend after her father objected to their marriage. Police found the pair and returned Romina to her family, despite her telling officers that she feared for her life, according to reports of what happened.
Her father subsequently killed her in her bedroom, decapitating her with a sickle, according to the local news outlet Gilkhabar. He confessed to the killing and was sentenced to nine years in prison.

Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani has indicated that legislation intended to boost criminal penalties for murder and physical violence against women could be submitted to Iran's parliament.
It is known as the Romina Bill.
In the six years since her death, Iranian women have taken to the streets, defied the morality police and forced the easing of restrictions on the compulsory hijab.
But the legislation bearing Romina's name has yet to become law.

title: Murder suspect crashes into elephant while fleeing police
summary: Witnesses told police the elephant appeared to be unharmed and retreated back into the jungle.
story: A Sri Lankan man suspected of fatally stabbing a woman was arrested on Friday after he crashed his scooter into a wild elephant as he attempted to escape, police said.
The 49-year-old man is accused of stabbing the woman in her home in the northern district of Anuradhapura, a police official told AFP.
However, his attempted escape ended when his scooter crashed into the elephant as it emerged from the jungle onto the road a short distance away, the official said.
Witnesses told police the elephant appeared to be unharmed and retreated back into the jungle.
The man was arrested and was receiving treatment for unspecified injuries under armed guard in hospital. Police also said they had recovered the suspected murder weapon.
Encounters between humans and elephants are relatively common in Sri Lanka, where expanding settlements and farms often overlap with animal habitats.
The island recorded about 400 elephant and 150 human deaths annually over the past five years, according to official figures.
Sri Lanka is home to an estimated 7,000 wild elephants and considers the animals a national treasure that are protected by law.
However, residents in remote villages sometimes attack elephants that destroy their crops.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, "the Sri Lanka elephant is protected under the Sri Lankan law and killing one carries the death penalty."

Conservationists and veterinarians have previously warned that plastic waste in a landfill in eastern Sri Lanka was killing elephants in the region. In 2020, drone footage captured more than a dozen hungry elephants scouring for food in the landfill.

Elephants in the country are also sometimes injured or killed by trains.  Last year, a Sri Lankan express train killed an elephant and was derailed.  The incident happened three months after seven elephants were fatally struck on the same route, marking the country's worst wildlife railway accident.
At the time, wildlife officials said that 139 elephants had been killed by trains over the past 17 years, since authorities began collecting such data.

India, which has a wild elephant population more than twice as large as Sri Lanka, also deals with regular train-pachyderm collisions. India has lost about 200 elephants over the last decade to train accidents alone, and that's in addition to the high number of deaths from poaching and accidental electrocutions.

title: Germany arrests 2 Iraqis allegedly tied to Iran-linked terror group
summary: German police arrested two Iraqi men alleged to be members of an Iran-linked terrorist organization​ that is said to have targeted U.S., Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe.
story: Berlin — German authorities on Thursday arrested two Iraqi men on suspicion of terrorism. The suspects are alleged to be members of an Iran-linked terrorist organization that is said to have targeted U.S., Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe.
The men, who were arrested in Cologne and Heidelberg by the Federal Criminal Police Office, are Iraqi nationals Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., according to the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office.

The investigation centers on alleged links to Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, a shadowy group that emerged to claim a series of sabotage, arson and violent attacks targeting Jewish institutions in Europe not long after the start of the U.S. war with Iran. The U.S. government has labeled HAYI a front for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah in Iraq. Britain has designated HAYI as a terrorist organization.

According to investigators, Mostafa Al-R. is alleged to have maintained contact with Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is currently facing criminal charges in the United States. Al-Saadi is considered a central figure within the alleged terrorist network.

As early as late 2025, Al-Saadi, Mostafa Al-R. and other individuals allegedly founded an independent group whose goal was to carry out terrorist attacks in Germany and other European countries, according to prosecutors. Ameer J. is also a member of this group, they said.

The group planned to target synagogues in Cologne and another European city, prosecutors alleged, saying unknown perpetrators traveled to the locations in March 2026 on behalf of the organization. The plans were not implemented for unknown reasons.
HAYI is also linked to attacks on Jewish institutions in the United Kingdom, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution said.

The suspects are accused of membership in a domestic terrorist organization under Section 129a of Germany's Criminal Code. The investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice had already issued the corresponding arrest warrants on Nov. 18.
Along with the arrests, extensive searches took place in Baden-Württemberg, Hesse and North Rhine-Westphalia. A total of 17 locations were searched.
More than 250 officers from the Federal Criminal Police Office, the Federal Police and the participating state police forces took part in the cross-state operation.
In Hürth, the investigative measures targeted another suspect, prosecutors said.

The proceedings were initiated based on information from the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution. The two detainees are scheduled to be brought to the presiding investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe on Thursday. The judge will decide on their pretrial detention.
The Federal Prosecutor's Office did not disclose further details regarding the length of the two Iraqis' stay in Germany, their immigration status or any other nationalities they may hold.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Could the Black Sea pull the U.S. into war in Europe?
summary: The Russia-Ukraine war is spilling into the Black Sea, where violent incidents have surged, running right up to NATO's doorstep.
story: Constanța, Romania – Out on the Black Sea, the Romanian Navy is always on the lookout for the deadly debris of a war it isn't fighting.

It's a front of the Russia-Ukraine war that most people rarely see. It runs right up to NATO's doorstep and sometimes crosses into its waters — threatening to pull the alliance, and therefore the United States, into the war.
Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships are surging in the Black Sea, NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell told CBS News.
"In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea. This year alone, we're talking four to five hundred," he said.

The roughly tenfold increase threatens a major artery of global grain and fuel shipments and has made the waterway deadlier than the Strait of Hormuz, a flashpoint in the U.S.-Iran war, with both sides trying to enforce blockades on the chokepoint to exert economic pressure on the other.

Twenty-five sailors have been killed in the strait this year, according to the International Maritime Organization, while at least 40 have been killed in the Black Sea in the same period, according to the International Transport Workers' Federation.
"I would say the Black Sea is just as important, and then depending on who you talk to, some might argue could perhaps even be more important … in terms of global trade," said O'Donnell.
Any imbalance in the flow of fuel and food "can have global implications that can impact America just as much as it can any of the nations here," he said.
And this maritime front stretches beyond the Black Sea.
Over the weekend, Ukraine said it struck an advanced Russian warship and a cargo ship that then drifted, on fire, into the waters of NATO member Finland.
On Sunday, Ukraine said it sank a Russian warship docked in Libya.
Three of the six countries bordering the Black Sea are NATO members — Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey.
But as Romanian Navy Captain Mihai Iordache explains, defending those borders is nothing like defending them on land.
"We do not have a fence into the Black Sea to state this is our border, that is the other border," he said.
The Romanian Navy is deploying highly specialized divers and drones, scouring the depths for unexploded weapons.
All this comes as the pressure on NATO is mounting. On Friday, Poland accused Russia of "intentional provocation" as Russian cruise missiles landed in the country's southeast.
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.
Asked whether the alliance will defend itself if necessary, O'Donnell told CBS News: "I would say that there should be no doubt on NATO's willingness and ability to act."
On the Black Sea, Captain Iordache warns the Romanian Navy is already stretched thin.
"We don't have enough people, personnel, equipment to deal with all the commercial ships and all the drones that we have," he told CBS News during an embed.

"Four years ago, we were ready for one drifting mine, and right now we are ready for tens of drifting drones," he said. "So I presume we'll be ready in the future, who knows what the future will bring."
"Could be hotter, could be colder, who knows. Let's hope for peace."

title: French actor Gérard Depardieu to stand trial on rape charge
summary: A lawyer representing French actor Gérard Depardieu says he has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a young actress at his Paris home in 2018.
story: French actor Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping an actress at his Paris home in 2018, one of his lawyers told The Associated Press on Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Defense lawyer Delphine Meillet wrote in a message to the AP that the 77-year-old actor would face trial over only one of the two alleged rapes reported by actress Charlotte Arnould.
Depardieu, who has denied the rape allegations, had challenged an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send him to trial.
The Paris Court of Appeal upheld that decision Thursday in relation to one of the two alleged rapes.
"He disputes the decision," Meillet told AP, without specifying whether Depardieu would file a further appeal.

Arnould first lodged a complaint in 2018, when she was 22. The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
For half a century, Depardieu was a towering figure in French cinema.

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, he became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

Earlier this month, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology.
"I was found guilty," Depardieu said in a written statement on Nov. 16, adding that he accepted the sentence.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters"). The case was widely seen as a test of the French film industry's response to the #MeToo movement.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said in his statement.

Depardieu's behavior toward women came under renewed scrutiny in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.
French President Emmanuel Macron drew criticism from women's rights activists at the time when he defended Depardieu, saying the actor "makes France proud."
Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in France over the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to pursue women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.
Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.
His career spanned hundreds of films, including "The Last Metro," "Jean de Florette" and the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

title: Ukraine says it downed a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser
summary: Ukraine has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone for the first time, a senior adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.
story: Ukraine has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time, a senior military adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday, marking a potentially significant development in the country's effort to defend cities from Russia's daily aerial attacks.

The interception was carried out using the Blysk laser air defense system, which was developed and manufactured by Ukrainian defense technology firm Carmine Sky. Technology for laser air defense systems is being developed as part of the wider Private Air Defense program, Zelenskyy's adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov   said in a statement.
About 100 companies across Ukraine have joined the government-backed private air defense initiative.

Russia started deploying jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine earlier this year. The weapons travel faster, making them harder to intercept than the more common propeller-driven attack drones.

In June, Ukraine was only intercepting about 57% of the jet-powered drones, reflecting a significant vulnerability as Ukrainian forces had been shooting down about 90% of the conventional Russian attack drones.

Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.
The laser interception reported by Beskrestnov   this week gives some insight into Ukraine's mounting efforts to adapt both its offenses and defenses as Russia's weapons and tactics evolve.

Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line.
Ukraine started testing laser air defense systems over the summer. According to Beskrestnov, the Blysk system was used to protect critical infrastructure, though he declined to give more specifics.
He said a number of Ukrainian companies, including Carmine Sky, are working to develop laser technology, but he cautioned that "it is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser."
"Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities," he said.

title: Fuel tanker explosion kills 31 on Egyptian highway
summary: A massive fire killed 31 people in Egypt after a speeding driver allegedly crashed into a fuel tanker truck.
story: Cairo — A massive fire on an Egyptian highway killed 31 people and injured 21 others after a car slammed into a fuel tanker truck at high speed, Egypt's Public Prosecution office said Thursday.
The driver has been arrested, according to the statement. At least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, were destroyed in the fire.
The prosecutor said the suspect admitted causing the accident while driving around 70 miles per hour on a major highway in the Al-Warraq district of Giza, which is part of the Greater Cairo area.

The driver said he was changing lanes and overtaking vehicles when the front-left side of his car struck the rear-right side of the tanker, according to the prosecutor's statement, "causing the steering wheel to slip from his hands and his car to veer off course."
When the car hit the truck, one of the truck's tires exploded, causing it to overturn and slam into a concrete barrier.
Gasoline then leaked from the tanker and caught on fire. Images of the blaze on social media showed multiple vehicles on fire as flames and smoke billowed into the night sky.
The prosecutor said the suspect was being questioned to establish the circumstances of the accident and assess any criminal responsibility.
"It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire," Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic behind the accident, told The Associated Press. "It was a shocking scene."
Sameer told the AP he saw at least eight bodies being removed from charred vehicles.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi expressed his condolences to the victims of the crash.
In a statement on X, Egypt's health ministry said 39 ambulances took part in the rescue operation.

While fatal traffic accidents are common in Egypt, the sheer scale of the incident has prompted calls for greater accountability. Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road traffic accidents across Egypt, according to official data.

title: Andy Taylor, longtime Duran Duran guitarist, dies at 65
summary: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died at age 65 following a battle with prostate cancer.
story: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran — whose huge pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf," "The Reflex" and "Rio" — and who were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.

Taylor died following a "courageous battle with prostate cancer," his family and the band said in a joint statement posted to social media. He died Monday at his home surrounded by friends and family.
"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his family said.

On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote at the time. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."
His family said Wednesday that Taylor "faced the last few years with so much courage and determination until the very end, never losing his love of life."

The two-time Grammy Award winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," the band said in Wednesday's statement. "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music."

The band's 1981 debut album "Duran Duran" had their first hit single, "Planet Earth," but it was "Rio" that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: "They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — 'Tiger Beat' fashion pinups who rocked arenas."

The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as "Girls on Film" and "Union of the Snake" and the moody ballads "The Chauffeur" and "Save a Prayer." Other hits in the coming years included "The Wild Boys," "New Moon on Monday" and "Come Undone." Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song "A View to a Kill" and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band was all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics.

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie "Barbarella." Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the "Fab Five." Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a "Live-Wire Guitarist." None of the Taylors were related.

"We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band," Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.

The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with "Some Like It Hot" and "Get It On."

In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album "Notorious," produced by Nile Rodgers — with hits including the title single and "Skin Trade" — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997's "Medazzaland" and 2000's "Pop Trash" — but returned for 2004's "Astronaut."

Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: "People have wrongly assumed that I didn't want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band."

Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children — Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy — and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them.

title: Titanic postcard sent days before doomed voyage sells for pricey sum
summary: A postcard from Jack Phillips, the Titanic's chief radio officer, was postmarked April 6, 1912, four days before the ill-fated ship set sail.
story: A rare postcard from a Titanic crew member that features the famed ocean liner and was sent less than a week before its doomed voyage in 1912 sold at auction for over $41,000, according to a U.K. auction house.

The postcard from Jack Phillips, the Titanic's chief radio officer, was postmarked April 6, 1912, four days before the ill-fated ship set sail on its maiden voyage across the Atlantic from Southampton, England, for New York City.
Phillips, who turned 25 on the ship, sent the postcard to his sister, Elsie Phillips, according to auction house Henry Aldridge and Son Ltd.
"Thanks very much for your letter. Having glorious weather, went to Cowes yesterday. Will write later before we sail. Love all, Jack," Phillips wrote on the back of the postcard.
The front features a picture of the Titanic at Southampton in southern England. The auction house said the postcard was in "very good to fine condition, with some light soiling and toning."
According to the auction house, the postcard sold for 32,000 British pounds, or around $41,800. With taxes and fees, the final cost was 40,000 pounds, or around $52,300.
During the trans-Atlantic crossing, on the night of April 14, 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg and eventually sank, killing over 1,500 people.
As the Titanic was filling with water, Phillips stayed at his post and tried to get other ships to come to the rescue of the ocean liner's approximately 2,200 passengers and crew.
According to the auction house, Phillips abandoned ship when the water reached his station, and he ultimately died from exposure to the severe cold on an overturned collapsible lifeboat.
The ship's junior wireless officer, Harold Bride, hailed Phillips for his efforts, calling him "the man who saved us all," according to the auction house.

Bride and Phillips, who also handled messages for passengers, received multiple iceberg warnings from other ships during the voyage and sent most of them along to the bridge. On the night the Titanic struck the iceberg, one warning about an ice field from another ship, the Mesaba, didn't make it to the bridge.

title: High-quality medieval armor discovered in shipwreck that sank in 1495
summary: The ship, known as "Griffin" or "Gribshunden," was the warship of Denmark's 15th-century leader King Hans.
story: Maritime archaeologists have found pieces of high-quality medieval armor found among the wreckage of a 500-year-old Danish warship, an international team of researchers revealed on Tuesday.

The ship, known as "Griffin" or "Gribshunden," was the warship of Denmark's 15th-century leader King Hans. The ship was also used for diplomatic expeditions. In 1495, there was an explosion that led to the ship catching fire and sinking while anchored north of Sweden's Stora Ekö Island. The wreck was discovered in the 1970s.

In the decades since, the ship has been the subject of frequent study. The latest discovery of the chain mail armor was made by team of experts from the United Kingdom's University of Southampton and Swedish institutions Södertörn University and Stockholm University, who have been conducting joint expeditions of the wreck since 2019.

The team's archaeologists and hydrographic survey specialists were using advanced robotic survey technology and 3-D photogrammetric imaging to make detailed archaeological records of the wreckage when they found the armor fragments, according to a news release from the University of Southampton.

The chain mail armor is made of copper-alloy, the university said. It was found while documenting an ammunition-tool chest just below the ship's forecastle, which was an elevated fighting platform at the front of the vessel.

Military gear may have been stored in the area, said Dr. Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, a visiting fellow at the University of Southampton's Centre for Maritime Archaeology, in the news release. German mercenaries, known as Landsknechts, were aboard the ship when it sank in 1495, Pacheco-Ruiz said.
"It was truly an amazing find!" Pacheco-Ruiz said in the news release.

Rolf Fabricius Warming, a Southampton alumnus and current Ph.D. researcher at Stockholm University, said that this kind of armor could be used for "extended periods," aided by repairs or being reused by other soldiers. The fragments "may represent older military equipment that was still active," he said.

Analyzing the manufacturing and composition of the armor pieces may reveal more about the origin of the armor, Warming said. Other weaponry-related artifacts aboard the ship were also sampled to undergo further analysis. The researchers will also study the structural elements of the forecastle and other features of the ship to determine how weapons and equipment were stored on the ship, and how military personnel lived and worked while aboard the vessel.

Also undergoing analysis are lead objects found during earlier research expeditions. Those items may be related to molds used to manufacture ammunition, the university said. Samples of lead and other materials were taken from the tool chest for further study.
The wreck is "partly disintegrated," but its remaining pieces "very well preserved."

"The ship is an important piece of the puzzle in the 'military revolution at sea' in the Early Modern Period, in which the primary tactics shifted from hand-to-hand combat to  heavy naval artillery fire," Warming said in 2024, adding that the ship is comparable to other preserved wrecks including the Mars and the Vasa, which has been on display in Stockholm, Sweden since the 1960s after being salvaged from the ocean floor.

title: Princess Diana regretted explosive affair confession, feared it would hurt William and Harry: author
summary: Royal biographer Ingrid Seward says Princess Diana regretted speaking of James Hewitt, fearing the confession would wound Prince William and Prince Harry.
story: Ingrid Seward, author of "Catherine & Diana," discusses the one public admission Princess Diana instantly regretted, knowing the resulting gossip would upset Prince William and Prince Harry.
Princess Diana regretted publicly admitting her affair with James Hewitt, fearing her confession would hurt the two people she loved most: Prince William and Prince Harry.
The late Princess of Wales privately admitted that she wished she had kept quiet about the former cavalry officer, royal biographer Ingrid Seward told Fox News Digital.

Seward, who was among the last journalists to interview Diana before her death in 1997, revisits the royal's turbulent life in her forthcoming book, "Catherine & Diana." The book examines how Diana and Kate Middleton navigated life in the royal spotlight and the lessons that shaped their journeys.
PRINCESS DIANA FEARED PRINCE HARRY WOULD ‘WITHER’ IN PRINCE WILLIAM’S SHADOW: EXPERT
Princess Diana regretted speaking out about her affair with James Heweitt, author Ingrid Seward told Fox News Digital. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"She said to me that she wished she hadn't spoken about James Hewitt because she knew it would upset both William and Harry and that James Hewitt had been extremely good to them both," Seward told Fox News Digital.

"And I think he really embraced who those two young boys were," Seward said. "He used to ride with Harry a lot. Harry's a very good rider. And I think they both rather hero-worshipped Hewitt. He was very handsome. He was a brilliant polo player. He was a brilliant rider. He was very athletic. And I think Diana just wished she hadn't mentioned it."
James Hewitt stands at the Royal Berkshire Polo Club near Windsor, United Kingdom, date unknown. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace for comment. A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace each told Fox News Digital that they do not comment on books.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
Ingrid Seward has written a new book titled "Catherine & Diana: The Inside Story of How the Princess of Wales Shaped the Modern Monarchy." (Orion Books)

Diana and Hewitt reportedly began their romance after meeting at a 1986 cocktail party hosted by her lady-in-waiting. Hewitt offered to help the princess overcome her fear of horseback riding, and their relationship eventually developed into a five-year affair.
Princess Diana and Charles with their children at V.J. Day commemorations in 1995. (Terry Fincher/Getty Images)

According to reports, Hewitt had an affectionate relationship with Diana's sons and taught them to ride horses. Hewitt's relationship with Diana reportedly ended after his deployment to the Middle East.

Diana's affair with Hewitt became a public scandal in 1994 following the publication of Anna Pasternak's book, "Princess in Love," which detailed their relationship. Hewitt cooperated with the author, a move that reportedly devastated Diana.
Princess Diana is seen here with James Hewitt. (Ron Dadswell/Shutterstock )

A year later, during her 1995 interview with Martin Bashir for the BBC program "Panorama," Diana publicly acknowledged the affair for the first time. A 2021 independent investigation found that Bashir used deceptive methods to secure the interview.

James Hewitt presents his book "Love and War" during an interview with Daphne Barak Oct. 25, 1999, in New York City. Hewitt, former lover of Princess Diana for over five years, wrote about his time with Diana as well as his life in the book.  (Evan Agostini/Liaison)

"William was very upset about the 'Panorama' interview," Seward said. "He was actually at Eton College. He went into his headmaster's study and watched the interview there. Diana had told him about it, but she hadn't really told him very much about it, and he was really, really angry with her."
Prince William stands at Eton College in Eton, United Kingdom, wearing a waistcoat as a member of the elite society group called "Pop." (Tim Graham/Photo Library via Getty Images)
The public revelation of the affair fueled years of speculation. Because Hewitt and Harry both have red hair and freckles, tabloids repeatedly suggested that Hewitt was Harry's biological father.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
James Hewitt is a former British Army cavalry officer who had a five-year affair with Princess Diana while she was married to then-Prince Charles. (Yui Mok - PA Images)
In 2002, Hewitt addressed speculation that he was Harry's biological father.
Ingrid Seward told Fox News Digital it's easy to see that King Charles (seen here in his younger years) is the biological father of Prince Harry. (Getty Images)

"I have been aware for a while that the issue of Harry's paternity has been a major talking point," Hewitt said, according to People magazine. "There really is no possibility whatsoever that I am Harry's father. I can understand the interest, but Harry was already walking by the time my relationship with Diana began."
James Hewitt at his London home, date unknown. (PA Images via Getty Images)
Harry was born in 1984, two years before Diana and Hewitt reportedly began their relationship.

Prince Charles (red shirt, number 3) and Major James Hewitt (white shirt, number 2) compete during a polo match at Windsor on July 16, 1991. Hewitt's team won 4-1. Princess Beatrice, the two-year-old daughter of the Duchess of York and Prince Andrew, presented the polo prizes. (Getty Images)
Seward said she has always dismissed the paternity rumor.

"Anyone who ever said anything to me, I said, 'This is ridiculous,'" Seward said. "I've sat with Harry and I've sat with Prince Charles and there is absolutely no way. I said, 'You are crazy. Just because Hewitt's got red hair?' Harry has the facial structure of his father, not of his mother."
Prince Harry walks to his car as he leaves the Royal Courts of Justice in London, Wednesday, April 9, 2025. (AP Photo/Alberto Pezzali)

In 2023, while suing Mirror Group Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mirror, over unlawful information-gathering practices, Harry cited a 2002 article titled "Plot to Rob the DNA of Harry" in a written statement. The article speculated that the prince was Hewitt's son.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, gives a thumbs up as he leaves after giving evidence at the Mirror Group Phone hacking trial at the Rolls Building at High Court on June 7, 2023, in London, England. P (Carl Court/Getty Images)
"Numerous newspapers had reported a rumor that my biological father was James Hewitt, a man my mother had a relationship with after I was born," Harry wrote.

"At the time, when I was 18 years old and had lost my mother just six years earlier, stories such as this felt very damaging and very real to me," Harry wrote. "They were hurtful, mean and cruel. I was always left questioning the motives behind the stories. Were the newspapers keen to put doubt into the minds of the public, so I might be ousted from the royal family?"
Martin Bashir interviews Princess Diana in Kensington Palace for the television program "Panorama." (Photo by Pool Photograph)
In his 2023 memoir, "Spare," Prince Harry described how his father, King Charles III, once joked about the paternity rumor.
Prince Harry's book "Spare" is displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)

"Pa liked telling stories, and this was one of the best in his repertoire," Harry wrote. "He’d always end with a burst of philosophizing … 'Who knows if I’m really the Prince of Wales? Who knows if I’m even your real father?'"

"He'd laugh and laugh, though it was a remarkably unfunny joke, given the rumor circulating just then that my actual father was one of Mummy's former lovers: Major James Hewitt," Harry wrote. "One cause of this rumor was Major Hewitt's flaming ginger hair, but another cause was sadism."

In 2024, Diana's hairdresser, Richard Dalton, dismissed the paternity rumor in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Diana, Princess of Wales, talks with her hairdresser Richard Dalton while their Royal Australian Air Force plane stops to refuel in Fiji before continuing to Australia. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Dalton also wrote in his memoir, "It's All About the Hair," that Diana "used to get very upset" when tabloids suggested Hewitt was Harry's father.
Ingrid Seward, editor-in-chief of Majesty magazine, has written numerous books about the British royal family. (Shutterstock)
For Diana, the regret went beyond revealing her affair. Seward said the princess wanted William and Harry to know that their parents' marriage had once been built on love.

The former Prince Charles, Prince of Wales and Diana, Princess of Wales, attend the Gulf War Victory Parade at Mansion House on June 21, 1991, in London. The couple announced their separation in 1992. (Anwar Hussein/Getty Images)

"That's one of the reasons she wished she hadn't mentioned Hewitt," Seward said. "It was very important to her that the children knew that their father had loved her. In that interview, it didn't seem like Charles loved her at all, which was not what she was trying to put out."
