title: Wayne Newton says today’s politicians are missing one quality Ronald Reagan always had
summary: Wayne Newton recalls Ronald Reagan's unwavering honesty and shares a heartbreaking moment when Nancy Reagan said her husband no longer knew her.
story: The producer shared the lesson he learned from Ronald Reagan that he has tried to apply to his own life.
Danke Schoen, Mr. President.
Wayne Newton says his late friend, former President Ronald Reagan, had one quality that's become a rarity in Washington, at least in the legendary entertainer's eyes: honesty.

The Las Vegas crooner, who was a longtime friend of the Reagans, recorded "This Is America," a song inspired by the biopic "Reagan," starring Dennis Quaid. A new director's cut of the film is available to stream.
‘REAGAN’ FILM SET TO RELEASE DIRECTOR’S CUT AMID ALLEGED ONLINE CENSORSHIP

President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan are seen here with Brooke Shields (left), Wayne Newton, and Kathleen McCrone, date unknown. Newton recorded a song for the biopic "Reagan," A new director's cut is available for streaming. (Credit: Maidun Collection/Alamy Stock Photo)
"I hope that people get to know that if there's one thing our politicians today could be lacking, it's the ability to tell the truth," Newton told Fox News Digital.

"And the one thing that Ronald Reagan always did was tell the truth. No matter where or how that went, that's where he was coming from. And I would like to see that kind of honesty back in people's thoughts today when it comes to politicians."

Ronald Reagan served as the 40th President of the United States for eight years, from Jan. 20, 1981, to Jan. 20, 1989. He served two consecutive terms after winning the presidential elections of 1980 and 1984. (Bettmann Archive)
Newton supported Reagan during his campaign for governor of California, performing at events on his behalf. Reagan served as governor from 1967 to 1975 before winning the presidency in 1980.
WATCH: ‘REAGAN’ PRODUCER SHARES WHAT HE LEARNED FROM RESEARCHING RONALD REAGAN

"I can tell you that the person that you saw was the one you always got," Newton said. "It was a wonderful, wonderful lesson in treating people the right way, telling the truth and always having a great sense of humor about what you were doing and how you were doing it. And he couldn't have been more honest with not only who he was, but what he was."
"It was one of the highlights of my life," Newton added.
From left: Dennis Quaid and Jon Voight attend the Los Angeles Premiere of "Reagan" at TCL Chinese Theatre on Aug. 20, 2024, in Hollywood, California. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

Newton also witnessed a more personal side of Reagan: his enduring love for his wife, Nancy Reagan. Their romance began in Hollywood and lasted more than half a century. The two actors married in 1952, building a partnership that carried them from movie sets to the White House.
Former President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan share a moment in this undated photo. The couple married in 1952. (Getty Images)

Their relationship faced a painful test after Reagan announced his Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in 1994. As the former president's memory faded and his health deteriorated, Nancy became his primary caregiver, protecting her husband's privacy while remaining by his side. She described the experience of watching her husband's health decline as a "long, long goodbye."
Nancy cared for Reagan until his death in 2004 at 93.

Singer Wayne Newton arrives at the funeral service for former President Ronald Reagan at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library. Reagan was buried on the west lawn at the library after a week of memorial services and national mourning. He died on June 5, 2004, at his home in Bel Air, California. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"I would have to say that the memory that comes to mind immediately is not one that brings me pleasure, but it's one that's the truth," Newton said. "I remember talking to Mrs. Reagan as the disease was taking on its worst days with the president. She told me, 'I had the worst day of my life yesterday.' And I said, 'What happened?' She said, 'I walked into the bedroom, and he didn't know who I was.'"

"Every time I think of them, that picture comes to mind," he said. "Love was the gift that they gave each other and it was devastating. Alzheimer's is a cruel disease. He loved his wife with all his heart. She loved him with all her heart. They did everything together. They were always together."
Nancy died in 2016 at 94.
Singer Wayne Newton attends the 69th birthday party for Ronald Reagan on Feb. 3, 1980, at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)
Newton also recalled how traveling with Reagan and connecting with Americans across the country deepened his patriotism and strengthened his commitment to honoring U.S. service members.
A photograph of Wayne Newton and Ronald Reagan is seen in a display case at the museum at Casa de Shenandoah on Sept. 14, 2015, in Las Vegas. (© David Becker via ZUMA Wire)

"I felt like I found somebody who not only shared my love and appreciation for our military personnel, but they were such an important part of his life and certainly, such a large portion of mine. It was special to meet someone who felt the same way, was ready to walk the walk and do what needed to be done. And that was support our men and women in the military."

"Spending time with him simply proved that I was on the right track in life," Newton said. "I felt that hopefully I could wind up with the same appreciation and love and courtesy that he showed everybody. And this was not a job to him. The person that you met was real, he was someone who had a deep love and devotion for the country. You never had the feeling that he would go in a different room, take off his coat and become a different person."
Wayne Newton performs at an inaugural event for Ronald Reagan's second inauguration in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 1984. (Alamy)

Before entering politics, Reagan enjoyed a successful Hollywood career that spanned nearly three decades. He later moved into television, hosting "General Electric Theater" from 1954 to 1962, before pursuing a political career that led him to the California governor's office in 1967.

Newton said Reagan rarely discussed his Hollywood career, preferring to focus on his life outside the spotlight.

"He never did talk about his Hollywood years," Newton said. "He simply talked about who he was, what he was and what he felt. The thing that struck me when I first met him, because we met at a horse show, was his love of horses and ranches. That would always make him light up. He loved the fact that he could go home, get on his horse and go for a ride. And I happen to suffer from the same thing!"

Today, Newton continues entertaining audiences in Las Vegas, where he first performed at age 15. Retirement is simply not in his vocabulary, he said.

"I think what keeps me going is walking out every night and seeing people's smiling faces when I'm doing my show," he explained. "It gives me a reason to wake up every day."

"I remember when I was about four years old, my parents took me to see Hank Williams, Hawkshaw Hawkins and Kitty Wells," Newton said. "We were so far back in the theater because my parents couldn't afford a better seat. I couldn't even see the performers. I could just hear them. title: Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend’s brother describes haunting instant he saw actress ‘purple’ before death
summary: Zach Hickerson recounts the terrifying moment he found Hayden Panettiere purple and unresponsive in a South Carolina Airbnb before his 911 call.
story: Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reports on actress Hayden Panettiere's official cause of death being ruled an accident due to toxic effects of fentanyl and other substances on 'The Story.'

The brother of Hayden Panettiere's on-and-off boyfriend broke his silence on the actress's final moments, detailing the terrifying instant he realized she wasn't breathing inside a South Carolina Airbnb.

In his first on-camera interview since the 36-year-old actress died of an accidental fentanyl-related overdose on Aug. 16, Zach Hickerson, the brother of Panettiere's on-and-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, recounted the frantic moments before his desperate 911 call.

Zach arrived at the Airbnb the two had been staying at to find Panettiere sleeping, or so he thought. When he walked into the living room, Hayden was slumped over on a pullout couch, cross-legged with her hair covering her face.
He initially thought nothing of it, noting she often fell asleep in that position.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S FINAL MOMENTS REVEALED IN FRANTIC 911 CALL FROM BOYFRIEND’S BROTHER
Hayden Panettiere's boyfriend's brother recalled the actress's final moments in his first on-camera interview. (Getty Images)
Expecting Panettiere to wake up at any moment and ask about their plans, Zach sat in a nearby chair while Brian lay down beside her, but he quickly realized something was wrong when she didn't react.

"Brian ultimately pulled her up on his chest to wake her up," Zach recalled in an interview with TMZ. "When he did that, I had a clear view of her face. Her face was pale, her lips were purple ... and I immediately knew something was incredibly wrong. I didn't know necessarily that she was completely unconscious in that moment. I just knew that she was purple.

"That was my reaction to Brian," Zach remembered. "I said, 'Brian, she's purple.' Actually, 'Oh my god, she's purple,' is exactly what I said. And I said, 'I've got to call 911.' He goes, 'Call them.'"

Zach Hickerson walks into a home in South Carolina Aug. 18. (Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital)
Zach and Brian performed CPR on Panettiere until the paramedics arrived. Life-saving measures went on for a long time, according to Zach.

"When they called it, I was kneeling at her feet, almost in front of her, and I just remember them saying, 'We have to call it,' and they named the time," Zach said. "I was crying. I put my hand on her leg and said goodbye."

Panettiere's death was ruled accidental in October, two months after the actress was found unresponsive. The Greenville County Coroner's Office revealed she died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine.
Zach told TMZ his brother Brian had previously revived Panettiere with Narcan before her fatal Aug. 16 overdose, explaining why the life-saving medication was on hand in their South Carolina Airbnb.
Brian Hickerson picks up a plastic bag left on a bench on Aug. 24. (Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital)

"I know that, along the way, Hayden was very clear that she struggled with different things at different times. I know painkillers were part of that along the way," Zach said. "I did not know at the time that that was one of the things that was perhaps part of the struggle in this recent season of her life.

"But I did know — and I've learned or been affirmed after the fact — that Brian had had to Narcan her before," Zach explained. "So, just through my dialogue with him, I know that they traveled with it as a precautionary measure, especially if it was a season where those types of drugs were around.

"I'm glad that he had it. I wish that it would have worked," he added. "I had never seen it and wouldn't have even known how to use it. I'm glad that he did. That's my understanding. They just had it as a precautionary measure, given the fact that he had to do it before."

Zach also fired back at Panettiere’s mother after she publicly accused him and brother Brian of fabricating their account of the "Heroes" star's final hours, warning that her comments are "dangerously close" to crossing a legal line.

"One, the truth is the truth. My statement hasn't wavered. The story that I told to you, to the cops, to the investigators is what happened," Zach insisted. "We didn't need to concoct a story. We didn't need to create a story.

"We didn't need to create a narrative. I don't know why anybody would even think that we would want to do that, or what reason would we have to do that. She was our best buddy. She was part of our family, to an extent."

Panettiere had an on-again, off-again relationship with Brian in the years before her death at 36. title: 'Facts of Life' star Lisa Whelchel, 63, vows she'll never repeat ayahuasca trip after frog venom ordeal
summary: Lisa Whelchel says a Peru ayahuasca retreat left her with burned skin, frog venom and violent illness, an ordeal the "Facts of Life" star won't repeat.
story: Lisa Whelchel dishes on what it was like working with the future "Sexiest Man Alive" and filming the new season of "Collector's Call."

A spiritual retreat in Peru turned into a physical ordeal for "The Facts of Life" star Lisa Whelchel, who endured burned skin, frog venom and violent illness during an ayahuasca trip she says she would never repeat.

"Could you ever imagine Blair Warner drinking ayahuasca and puking her brains out? Or even little miss goody-two-shoes Lisa Whelchel? Well, that’s what I did," she revealed in an Instagram video. "And I’m back with all the gory details."

Whelchel explained she was a part of a group of 19 who traveled into the jungles of Peru for the ayahuasca experience. The 63-year-old actress claimed 17 of those people had a "phenomenal life-changing experience." However, she was not one of them.
TIM ROBBINS TURNS TO AYAHUASCA AFTER FEELING 'CONSUMED BY ANGER' OVER CANCEL CULTURE

The funny parts, the terrifying parts, the vulnerable parts that I didn’t think I would ever share, and the parts that are not flattering at all."
Whelchel broke down those "terrifying" moments in a follow-up post on Substack, recalling a ceremony that involved frog venom and burned skin.

"The venom naturally contains healing properties claimed by its practitioners to have anti-inflammatory effects, regulate blood pressure, eliminate depression, cure addictions, as well as cancer, fertility issues, hepatitis and AIDS," she wrote. "I was told to tolerate the uncomfortable feelings as long as I could handle them and, when I had had enough, let [the guide] know, and he would pour cold water over my head and neck which would cease the flow of venom and its effects."

summary: Craig Morgan reveals how off-the-grid Alaska winters with no neighbors for seven miles transform his family's communication and daily routines.
story: The country singer mainly lives in Tennessee but spends winters in Alaska.
Craig Morgan and his family spend their winters off the grid in Alaska, where their nearest neighbor is seven miles away.

"We go up after Christmas and we like to try to stay till March," the country singer told Fox News Digital. "Now, sometimes we'll leave and come back home, depending if I have something to do — If I have a show or a speaking engagement or anything like that. But generally, we try to stay for a couple months."
Morgan said that their life in Alaska "cannot be explained. It can only be experienced."
JOSH DUHAMEL SAYS HIS HEART RATE DROPS 25% AT OFF-GRID MINNESOTA CABIN
Craig Morgan and his family spend winters at their off-the-grid home in Alaska. (Noam Galai/Getty Images; Jerry Lake Alaska/Instagram)

During a typical day in the winter, the "Redneck Yacht Club" singer said they typically don’t see daylight until 10:30 in the morning.

title: Bob Newhart faced $6M lawsuit threat after trying to quit hit sitcom: book
summary: CBS threatened Bob Newhart with a $6 million lawsuit when he tried to quit "The Bob Newhart Show" before its sixth season, a new biography reveals.
story: Biographer Michael Seth Starr spoke out on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia" about how losing his wife Ginnie and close friend Don Rickles deeply impacted Bob Newhart.
Bob Newhart could make millions laugh, but a $6 million lawsuit was no laughing matter.
The comedy legend once tried to quit his hit CBS sitcom, "The Bob Newhart Show," only to discover the network wasn't ready to let its ratings star walk away.
The contract dispute is detailed in Michael Seth Starr's biography, "Bob Newhart: The Life and Laughter of an American Treasure," which chronicles the comedian's nearly 65-year career.
BOB NEWHART, LEGENDARY COMEDIAN AND SITCOM STAR, DEAD AT 94
Comedy legend Bob Newhart considered walking away from "The Bob Newhart Show" after five seasons, but a contract dispute with CBS complicated his plans. (CBS via Getty Images)
Newhart wasn't exactly in a position to face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit.
"I don't have $6 million," the comedian later admitted. "And my wife wouldn't lend me any of her money."
Although he publicly credited fan support for his decision, Newhart later acknowledged that financial pressure played a major role in his return.
Bob Newhart starred in two beloved CBS sitcoms, "The Bob Newhart Show" and "Newhart," building a television comedy career that spanned decades. (CBS via Getty Images)

"When I said I wanted to quit, the people in the cast and the production crew were all affected, of course and they helped influence me to change my mind. Then there were letters from fans and people I met on the street. But I guess the main reason I decided to come back was that CBS threatened to sue me for $6 million because there was a year left on my contract."
According to Starr's biography, Newhart approached CBS executives Bob Daly and Robert Wussler about leaving "The Bob Newhart Show" before its sixth season.
Bob Newhart's contract negotiations with CBS are chronicled in Michael Seth Starr's biography, "Bob Newhart: The Life and Laughter of an American Treasure." (Kensington Publishing Corp.)
His attorney warned that if a replacement series failed to generate comparable revenue, CBS could seek damages Newhart estimated at "about fifty or sixty million dollars."
The comedian also questioned the show's creative future, with head writers Tom Patchett and Jay Tarses occupied with other projects.

"So, I thought maybe five years was enough. I'd rather go off a year early than a year late," he recalled. He hoped to negotiate television specials instead, saying, "I'd rather do specials, even if it means walking away from a lot of money."

CBS ultimately convinced him to return for a sixth and final season, with Starr describing concessions that included better scripts, flexibility to miss one or two episodes and "a modest bump" in his $30,000-per-episode salary.
'MARY TYLER MOORE' STAR ED ASNER SAYS CAST WAS LIKE A FAMILY: 'WE FORGAVE EACH OTHER'S FAULTS'
Bob Newhart faced a potential multimillion-dollar lawsuit after attempting to leave his hit CBS sitcom, "The Bob Newhart Show," before its final season. (CBS via Getty Images)
CBS executive Robert Wussler later recalled Newhart telling him and Daly, "You can sue me and take me to court."
Wussler recalled their response: "Wait a minute — we don't want to sue you. We just want you back."
Newhart eventually agreed, recalling, "Both ["The Mary Tyler Moore Show"] MTM and CBS were so darned nice to me, I got to thinking: 'Why not go ahead with another year?'"

Bob Newhart became one of America's most celebrated comedians, building a legendary career that spanned more than six decades across stand-up comedy, television and film. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images)
He added, "What’s so tough about it? People were already starting to say I was quitting because I wouldn’t have ["The Mary Tyler Moore Show"] anymore as a lead-in, which was nonsense."
Newhart ultimately returned for the final season, which ended in 1978. He went on to star in another hit CBS sitcom, "Newhart," which ran from 1982 to 1990.

He later won his first competitive Emmy in 2013 for his guest role as Arthur Jeffries on "The Big Bang Theory."
Legendary comedian and sitcom star Bob Newhart died July 18, 2024, at age 94. (Alison Buck/Getty Images for Backstage Creations )
Newhart was married to his wife, Ginnie, for 60 years before she died in April 2023. The couple had four children together.
During an appearance on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," Starr spoke about their relationship and how Ginnie's death affected Newhart.

"He and Ginnie were so close, and I think losing her was just such a big blow. And I mean, he had been slowing down in the last maybe five or six years of his life. I interviewed him maybe about a year and a half or two years before he passed away. And he didn't sound great. He was coughing a lot, and he sounded a little weak, but he was in his 90s."

"I mean, he did live a very long life and very fruitful life," he noted of Newhart. "And we're still talking about him now, and I think people will be talking about him for years and years after this. So he certainly left his mark on the American public and the American consciousness."

title: ‘Charlie Brown’ voice actor received zero residuals for nearly 50 years due to banned ’70s contract
summary: Todd Barbee, the voice of Charlie Brown in "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," says he got no residuals for decades until SAG-AFTRA renegotiated old contracts.
story: Former Charlie Brown voice actor Todd Barbee spoke out on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia" about going decades without "Peanuts" residuals under a 1970s buyout contract.
Good grief — it turns out the voice of Charlie Brown didn't even make peanuts in residuals.

Todd Barbee was just 10 when his father's connection to producer Lee Mendelson landed him the iconic role of Charlie Brown in 1973's "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving." Generations grew up watching his performance on network TV, yet Barbee, now 63, revealed to host Joseph Sibilia on his podcast, "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," that he didn’t receive residual checks until about six years ago.
"Aside from the bountiful residuals I'm sure you've collected for the last 50-plus years, what has been the most rewarding part of being a part of the 'Peanuts' legacy?" Sibilia asked Barbee.
‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS
"A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" premiered on Nov. 20, 1973. Todd Barbee was about 10 years old when he voiced Charlie Brown in the special. (Allstar Picture Library Ltd./Alamy Stock Photo)

"Well, let me correct you on one front," Barbee replied. "We were actually under an old contractual relationship from the '70s that is no longer allowed by Screen Actors Guild and AFTRA, which is American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. The contract was a buyout, and that is not allowed by the unions anymore. I think it was overturned in the '80s."
"So, we did not receive any residuals at all," Barbee noted. "In fact, I didn't receive a single residual until about six years ago."

The initial gig paid "pretty handsomely" at the time "in 1970 dollars." He used his paycheck to help his mother buy the house that she still lives in to this day after his parents divorced. However, he didn't see any residual checks, no matter how massive the special became as a holiday tradition.
WATCH: CHARLIE BROWN VOICE ACTOR TODD BARBEE WENT DECADES WITHOUT ‘PEANUTS’ RESIDUALS

"Peanuts" made its debut on Oct. 2, 1950. The travails of the "little round-headed kid" Charlie Brown and his pals eventually ran in more than 2,600 newspapers, reaching millions of readers in 75 countries.

According to Barbee, everything changed after union renegotiations around streaming rights following Apple TV's acquisition of the "Peanuts" catalog. The streaming service obtained the exclusive rights to the "Peanuts" catalog in 2020, including the widely beloved "A Charlie Brown Christmas."
Charles M. Schulz holds a drawing of Charlie Brown, one of his "Peanuts" characters, on Jan. 1, 1962. (CBS via Getty Images)

"During the big strike, writers' strike and everything that happened about five or six years ago ... Screen Actors Guild renegotiated some of these things," said Barbee. "And they determined Apple TV right now actually has the entire 'Peanuts' catalog. And what Screen Actors did [was say], 'Look, that doesn't have anything to do with these old contracts. That was for broadcast television. You're a streaming service. And as such, you need to pay these people current residuals.'"
The SAG-AFTRA logo is displayed outside the National Headquarters on Wilshire Boulevard during the actors strike in Los Angeles on Oct. 24, 2023. (AFP via Getty Images)
"So now, I do make some money every year off all the specials," said Barbee. "It's not giant amounts of money, but you know, it's significant. And I look forward to getting that check every year."
Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA, Apple and Peanuts Worldwide for comment.
The Charlie Brown balloon is seen during the 90th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 24, 2016, in New York City. (WireImage)

From 1972 to 1974, Barbee voiced several "Peanuts" characters across five different TV specials. Because producers insisted on authentic kids' voices rather than adults imitating children, every young actor received what Barbee called a "Dear John" letter.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
"One of the things that's very interesting about all the characters in 'Peanuts' is you got a 'Dear John' letter the moment your voice changed," he told Sibilia.
Snoopy, Lucy, Charlie Brown and Linus stand in a line in a 1968 drawing from Charles Schulz's comic strip "Peanuts." (Getty Images)

"They were looking for kids whose voices hadn't changed. They really ... had an idea about the intonation and the character of the voice, and it needed to be a kid's voice. And so, there was an audition. They wanted to do a number of specials at the same time, one after the other. They were talking about Thanksgiving and Easter and others."
"I was about 10 then, maybe a little bit more than 10 years old," Barbee reflected. "And the next thing you know, they had me voice for Charlie Brown and they selected me."

After leaving acting behind, Barbee pivoted to graphic, commercial and site design in the San Francisco Bay Area. In a fitting nod to "Peanuts" creator Charles Schulz, an avid hockey fan who built a famous ice arena in Santa Rosa, Barbee's design work includes the site plan for Fisherman's Wharf's observation wheel and its inaugural seasonal outdoor ice-skating rink.

In the 1973 special, Charlie Brown wants to do something special for the gang, but the dinner he arranges becomes a disaster when caterers Snoopy and Woodstock prepare toast and popcorn as the main dish. Humiliated, it will take all of Marcie's persuasive powers to salvage the holiday for Charlie Brown. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
For decades, Barbee kept his "Peanuts" past under wraps.

"People that were in the know knew about it," said Barbee. "But many of the people that I've known throughout the years, I never talked about it. It was just not a big thing for me. It was just kind of a funny insider thing. And if you really got to know me, you either found out, maybe I dropped it or a friend mentioned it."

Peanuts characters appear in a scene from "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," 1973. (Alamy)
Today, Barbee says the greatest reward is knowing his voice still brings holiday cheer into homes across America half a century later.

"I get this fan mail with frequency still to this day," said Barbee. "And that just always puts a smile on my face because I realize how this character has influenced so many people's lives over the course of, you know, half a century. And there's something very, you know, very special about that. So, it's cool to be involved in that."

title: Sylvester Stallone endured broke, lonely days cleaning lion cages before Henry Winkler changed his life
summary: Henry Winkler recalls visiting Sylvester Stallone's blacked-out Lexington Avenue apartment, where the future "Rocky" star wrote scripts before fame.
story: Sylvester Stallone joins Fox & Friends to discuss his new memoir, The Steps, opening up about his difficult upbringing, the lessons it taught him as a father and the personal experiences that inspired Rocky.

Before Sylvester Stallone became a Hollywood heavyweight, he was a broke, lonely actor living in a cramped New York City walk-up apartment with few friends to lean on — until Henry Winkler came along.

In his memoir, "The Steps," the "Rocky" icon recalls crossing paths with the future "Happy Days" star on the set of 1974's "The Lords of Flatbush." Though Stallone joked they were polar opposites — Winkler, a Yale graduate, and Stallone from "the college of what's the matter [with] you" — the two forged an instant bond.

For Winkler, it didn't take long to see Stallone's fierce determination to make it in Hollywood. It was a drive he witnessed firsthand when he visited his co-star's home on Lexington Avenue for the first time.
SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE

Paul Mace, Sylvester Stallone, Henry Winkler and Perry King are seen on the set of "The Lords of Flatbush," directed by Martin Davidson and Stephen Verona. Stallone and Winkler became fast friends on set. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
"He was living there with his first wife and their bull mastiff, who had more slobber than the Atlantic Ocean," Winkler recalled to Fox News Digital.

"He painted his windows black so that he would never be bothered by what time of day it was. He wouldn't be influenced by time. Instead, he just wrote and wrote. And from the minute we met on the set of a movie in which we made no money whatsoever, you could see him. You could see his drive. You could see there was something so special, so funny, so articulate coming out of this, 'I'm going to eat you for breakfast.' And it only continued."
Sylvester Stallone has written a new memoir, "The Steps: A Memoir." (2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLC)

"If you listen to Sly Stallone, you quickly realize he's a philosopher," Winkler shared. "You would never put the two together, but it's true. And he's so open. His upbringing would put any man or woman down. It would put them in a corner shaking for the rest of their life. But his motto is 'keep on punching' and it's true. He kept on punching. And it's been an honor to be his friend."
WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST

In his book, Stallone described how Winkler had to "step over a homeless guy while walking up five flights of stairs" just to see his "shabby place and get a glimpse into my world." Instead of being horrified, Winkler was impressed by the library of tattered books and a shelf holding about 15 screenplays. Stallone had been keeping busy writing.
When Winkler picked up one of Stallone's scripts, he was stunned. Winkler urged Stallone to keep writing.

Sylvester Stallone appears in a scene from "The Lords of Flatbush" (1974) after his character's girlfriend tells him she is pregnant, and he takes her to a jeweler to buy a ring. (FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images)
Stallone told Fox News Digital he never forgot Winkler's kindness and encouragement during a time when hearing "no" was the norm.

"You cannot get two people more different in every aspect," Stallone said with a laugh. "We were, as I wrote, an 'odd couple.' And yet, he gave me such confidence. He's an intellectual, and I didn't think of myself that way. I didn't see myself that way at all. When he saw the writing, he said, 'You wrote all this stuff?' I said, 'It's not good.' He then said, 'That's not the point. You did 15, 15 scripts. It's harder to make it as a writer than an actor. This is impressive.'"
Sylvester Stallone said that despite his differences with Henry Winkler, they became good friends. (Getty Images)

Stallone wrote, "We were an odd couple. He was an intellectual Jewish kid from the Upper West Side who graduated from the Yale School of Drama — the real deal. I had to learn everything the hard way. We were anomalies in each other's lives. To see us together was like watching a zebra hang out with a buffalo. Still, we clicked, because Henry is a genuinely wonderful human being."

"The Steps: A Memoir" by Sylvester Stallone is available now. (William Morrow)

Years later, after scraping by in New York and taking odd jobs like working at a deli, ushering at a movie theater and cleaning lion cages at the Central Park Zoo, Stallone headed west. He and his then-wife, Sasha Czack, made the cross-country trip to California in hopes of finally getting his big acting break. But they knew no one on the West Coast and didn't have a place to live. Stallone wrote, "We had barely $500 left of the $830 we departed New York with."
Sylvester Stallone was so broke when he married his first wife, Sasha Czack, that he wore a movie costume. (Bettmann Archive)
But there was one person Stallone knew he could call: Winkler. By then, the actor had already moved to California and become a star on "Happy Days."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Sylvester Stallone told Fox News Digital Henry Winkler believed in him early on in his career. (Getty Images)

"When I came out to California, he was the only guy I knew," said Stallone. "It was comforting because, again, he was very complimentary and welcoming. He kept saying, 'Working with you on "Lords of Flatbush" helped me with The Fonz, playing a tough guy.' I kept telling him, 'No, man, you did that all on your own.' But he saw something in me, even before ‘Rocky.’ Yes, this was a long time ago, but that's how great of a guy he was. He still is."

"Really, our relationship goes back to 1972," Stallone said with a smile. "It's amazing. Again, we're so different, yet there's a bond there that he actually instigated. I was a loner, no doubt about that. And yet he would insert himself, talk to me, be very outgoing and witty. He wanted to be my friend. And he was from Yale. He didn't have to be my friend. But he genuinely cared. We bonded, and it's terrific."
Henry Winkler won his first Emmy Award in 2018 for his role in the HBO Max show, "Barry." (Neilson Barnard/FilmMagic)

Stallone and Czack eventually settled into a rental in Encino for $300 a month. The house was barely 500 square feet, and there was no grass or air conditioning. Still, Stallone said he was determined to make it big in Hollywood.
Sylvester Stallone wrote "Rocky" and starred as boxer Rocky Balboa. (Getty Images)
In the book, Stallone described first arriving at Hollywood and Vine. He had no idea that the nearby Walk of Fame would one day bear his name.

Henry Winkler appears as Fonzie in "Happy Days." (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
"That I would have a star there less than 10 years later, and only a few blocks away, still boggles my mind," he wrote.

Sylvester Stallone strikes at a punching bag in a boxing ring while his coach, Burgess Meredith (1908-1997), watches during training at a gymnasium in a still from the film "Rocky," directed by John G. Avildsen. (United Artists/Courtesy of Getty Images)

Winkler said he never doubted that one day, his friend’s dreams would become a reality.
Sylvester Stallone is seen here on Jan. 12, 1979. (Getty Images)

Henry Winkler and Sylvester Stallone attend the hand and footprints ceremony for Bob Daly and Terry Semel, co-CEOs of Warner Bros., at Mann's Chinese Theater in Los Angeles, on Sept. 30, 1999. (Getty Images)
"I called him one day and I said, 'You're like a fine wine. You were great, and now you have blossomed.' He just kept punching. Isn't he amazing? He punched his way to the top."

title: French cinema star Gerard Depardieu to face trial in alleged rape of young actress, lawyer says
summary: Gerard Depardieu will stand trial in the alleged 2018 rape of Charlotte Arnould, who says the French actor assaulted her in his Paris home when she was 22.
story: Metropolitan Police release footage of Russell Brand's interviews from 2023, 2024 and 2025 after his conviction on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
French actor Gerard Depardieu will stand trial in the alleged 2018 rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters Thursday.
Arnould accused the 77-year-old Depardieu of raping her in 2018 when she was 22 and he was 70. She claims he assaulted her in his Paris home.
Depardieu, a veritable star of French cinema, has faced numerous sexual assault claims in recent years.
In May 2025, a Paris court found him guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set and ordered that he be added to France's national sex offender registry.
CATE BLANCHETT MOURNS HOW #METOO GOT 'KILLED VERY QUICKLY,' STILL 'SYSTEMIC LAYER OF ABUSE'

French actor Gerard Depardieu and his lawyer Jeremie Assous leave during a suspension of hearing as part of his trial in which he is accused of sexually abusing two women on March 25, 2025, in Paris, France. (Chesnot/Getty Images)
Depardieu initially appealed the ruling, but dropped his appeal in mid-November.
"I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that no longer exists," he said, adding, "I have therefore decided to withdraw my appeal."

Depardieu also apologized and said, "On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did."
Despite appearing to acknowledge his behavior was inappropriate in the 2025 case, Depardieu has denied any wrongdoing in the Arnould case.
GERARD DEPARDIEU SPEAKS OUT, MAINTAINS INNOCENCE AFTER BEING CHARGED FOR RAPE AND SEXUAL ASSAULT
French actress, singer and dancer Charlotte Arnould poses during a photo session in Paris on March 10, 2025. (Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images)
In a 2023 op-ed in French newspaper Le Figaro, Depardieu wrote, "Never, ever have I abused a woman. To harm a woman would be like kicking my own mother in the stomach."

In the essay, he claimed, "A woman came to my house once, walking lightly, going up to my room of her own accord. She now says she was raped there. She returned there a second time. There has never been any coercion, violence, or protest between us."
Arnould, in a social media post shortly after the letter became public, called it "a truly vile message."

"He positions himself as the victim to elicit compassion and sow doubt. To put things in context, when I went to his place, I was 22 years old, I weighed 37 kilos because I suffered from anorexia, and he was a friend of my father's," she told Elle magazine.
Charlotte Arnould, left, leaves the courtroom during the trial of Gerard Depardieu, accused of sexual assault, at the Paris courthouse on Oct. 28, 2024. (Bertrand Guay/AFP via Getty Images)
The young actress and aspiring dancer also added that "at no point did I consent."
Arnould's attorney, Carine Durrieu-Diebolt, also said that she was "shocked and scandalized" at Depardieu's letter.
Delphine Meillet, another attorney representing Depardieu, told The Associated Press that he disputes the ruling to proceed with his case, though he did not specify if he plans to appeal.
Attorneys for Depardieu and Arnould did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.

title: Kelsey Grammer calls American Dream a ‘gift’ he wants to pass down to his 8 children
summary: Kelsey Grammer says the American Dream is a "gift" that he wants to pass down to his eight children as he marks the United States' 250th anniversary with "The America Opus."
story: "Frasier" star Kelsey Grammer reflects on the importance of freedom, opportunity and hard work as he shares the values he hopes to pass down to his children.
Kelsey Grammer believes the American Dream is alive and well, and the "Frasier" star is determined to make sure his eight children understand the freedom and opportunity that come with it.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 71-year-old actor reflected on the values he hopes to instill in his children as the United States of America celebrates its 250th anniversary, and he helps commemorate the nation's history through the collector's book "The America Opus."
"The thing I most want to pass down to them is the understanding that it's your job. Your gift is the American Dream," Grammer said. "What it entails is up to you."
KELSEY GRAMMER WARNS OF CHILLING DANGER FACING AMERICANS WHO FORGET NATION'S FOUNDING HISTORY
Kelsey Grammer shared that the greatest gift he can give his eight children is the understanding that the American Dream belongs to them. (Getty Images)
"Every individual has the same right to figure out what that dream is and to make it happen," he added.
The "Cheers" alum shared his view that the American Dream is not just about achieving personal success, but also about having the opportunity to make a difference.
WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER ON WHAT HE WANTS HIS 8 CHILDREN TO LEARN: 'YOUR GIFT IS THE AMERICAN DREAM'

Grammer pointed to Alexander Graham Bell as an example of someone who made his American Dream a reality while helping others, noting that the inventor's efforts to help deaf children communicate eventually led to the development of the telephone.

"My hat is off to people who end up thinking of something that millions of people need. Why wouldn't we allow those people success? Why wouldn't we praise them? Sort of laud them as being the examples of how wonderful America is," Grammer said.

Kelsey Grammer hosted the Giving A Smile Foundation's 2nd Annual Smile Under the Stars Charity Gala presented by Rifkin Raanan Dentistry and honoring Robert and Linell Shapiro at The Beverly Hilton on Nov. 12, 2026. (Getty Images)
"These people are all American heroes by virtue of the fact that they kept working at their dream," he continued. "Their dream was to help somebody. And it ended up helping millions of people."
When asked how he hopes his children will remember him beyond his Hollywood career, Grammer emphasized the importance of setting an example through hard work and personal responsibility.
THE FOUNDING FATHERS GAVE US AMERICA. 250 YEARS LATER, WE STILL DEPEND ON GOOD DADS

"I hope they look on me as a guy who was incredibly fair. Firm. I have high expectations of people, I expect people to show up," he said. "Because I do. One of my sayings that I say to people is like, if I've got a job being done around the house and I haven't seen the guys for a few weeks, I say, 'You know, if I did my job this way, I wouldn't have this house, I wouldn't have anything else.'

"You gotta show up," Grammer continued. "That's the big thing. Your American Dream actually is in your hands. I mean, and I do say this to a lot of people these days, I say like, 'Anybody tells you the American Dream's over, don't give them your vote because that's what they want. They want it over. Theirs is that it's over.' You know, no thanks."
Grammer shares his oldest child, daughter Spencer, with his first wife, Doreen Alderman. The actor and Spencer appeared on "Today" in November 2022. (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images)

Grammer, who has been married four times, shares his eldest child, daughter Spencer Grammer, 43, with his first wife, Doreen Alderman. He is also father to daughter Greer Grammer, 34, whom he shares with his ex-girlfriend Barrie Buckner.
The "Grand Isle" actor has daughter Mason Olivia, 25, and son Jude Gordon, 22, with his ex-wife Camille Grammer, 54. He married British former flight attendant Kayte Walsh in 2011.
Grammer and Walsh are parents to daughter Faith Evangeline, 14, and sons Kelsey Gabriel, 12, Auden James, 10, and Christopher, 1.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Grammer, who previously indicated that he has considered running for office, said that for now, he had set aside his political ambitions to focus on fatherhood.
"I have put it on the back burner because I've got all these new kids and I really want to be a present dad," he said.
Grammer admitted that he has regrets over not being present enough for his older children earlier in their lives.

"My first couple of kids — I wasn't around for them as much as I would have liked to have been," he said. "And I think they may even still have some sensibilities about that, sensitivity about it, rather, and I'd like to make it up to everybody because you need a dad there."
Grammer went to say that he didn't have an understanding of what fatherhood meant after growing up without his own dad.

The actor's parents, Frank Allen Grammer Jr. and Sally Cranmer Grammer, divorced when he was 2 years old, and he was raised primarily by his mother and maternal grandparents. In 1968, Grammer's father was shot and killed in the U.S. Virgin Islands when the actor was just 13.

"I didn't have a dad, you know, I didn't know what it was to be called a dad till I was one," he said. "I'd never used the word till I became a dad. So it's really important to me, but a good dad, hopefully, would be what you want in office. You want a guy that shows up."

Grammer also explained how he believes he has changed after becoming a father again later in life.

"I've got four kids with my current wife, Kate, and it's such an extraordinary experience," he said. "It's just that — it's so lovely in every way. These surprising young human beings that are in your life and in your care, and you're gonna do your best to not mess them up, but we always do."
"Kind of not really — I mean, look, I'm steady," he continued. "I'm a steady guy. Maybe I wasn't always, but I am now, and I'm proud of that and that they have that to look to."

Grammer recently teamed up with British luxury publisher Opus to create "The America Opus," a large-format illustrated book celebrating the United States' 250th anniversary. "The America Opus" explores pivotal moments in American history, highlighting the people, achievements and challenges that have shaped the country over the past two and a half centuries.

"The America Opus" will be released in two editions, including the Marquee Edition, which is limited to 2,500 copies at $2,500, and a smaller Classic Edition with fewer pages.

"What's nice about the book is we're not actually out to — we have no axe to grind or no political stance to make," Grammer said. "We're actually basically just doing some snapshots of extraordinary moments in the American story."
"Some of them when we were in the ascendancy. Some of them maybe not our best story, not our best foot forward, but you know what, we're pretty open and honest about all that," Grammer continued.

"But there's no reflection other than the fact that this has been an extraordinary experiment, the American experiment," he added. "And the 250 years that we've lived will hopefully point to another 250 that are just as extraordinary."

"The America Opus," which is available for preorder and is expected to begin shipping in December, features an introduction by Grammer and a foreword by President Donald Trump, who also signed it.

title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65; bandmates pay emotional tribute
summary: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, whose playing powered 1980s hit "Rio" and "Hungry Like the Wolf," has died at age 65 of prostate cancer, his family said.
story: His family released a statement calling him "a brilliant guitarist," as well as a wonderful husband, loving father and proud grandfather. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died of prostate cancer at the age of 65, Fox News Digital confirmed.
Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by family on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates.
"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his wife, Tracey, said on behalf of the family.

"He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
DURAN DURAN GUITARIST ANDY TAYLOR IS ‘RADIOACTIVE’ AFTER ‘NUCLEAR’ CANCER TREATMENTS
His family added that the musician "faced the last few years with so much courage and determination," noting "he never gave up" and kept "fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life."
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died at the age of 65. (Michael Putland/Getty Images)

"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful," they added. "Andy knew just how deeply he was loved, and we take great comfort in that. We will miss him every single day."
Members of the band each wrote their own tribute to Taylor on the band's website, with lead singer Simon Le Bon writing, "There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart."
He added that when he thinks of Taylor he remembers "the blond bombshell, firebrand teenager I met in 1980" who had "spikey hair and a spiky personality" and was an extremely talented guitar player.

"I have so many wonderful, hilarious, tragic memories of our time together: on tour, in the studio, in our little flat on Caroline Road, Balsall Heath at 6am," he added. "And through it, & above it all he was in love with his family - most important thing in his life."

"The 'Geordie Genius', 'the live wire from Newcastle': how fortunate we were to have found him," Roger Taylor said.

"The incredible, talented musician and gifted songsmith arrived on a train from Cullercoats to knock us into shape and help us grow into the burgeoning version of Duran Duran that took on the world within a year or two of his arrival.
"The sadness cuts extremely deep, but admiration and respect run even deeper for the Taylor that wasn't related but will forever be my brother. Rest in peace now, Andy."

Duran Duran formed in the late 1970s, releasing their self-titled debut album in 1981 and quickly making a name for themselves as a group ready to push boundaries. They became household names with the release of their second album, "Rio," in 1982, which featured hits like "Hungry Like the Wolf."

Despite their success, the band went on hiatus in the mid-1980s, with two members, including Taylor, pursuing solo projects. He reunited with the band in 2001 but left again in 2006. As a band, they have won two Grammy Awards, have a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music," the band said in a statement.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

title: Brad Pitt, Angelina Jolie settle 4-year French winery lawsuit that sparked plane abuse claims
summary: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie moved Wednesday to dismiss claims against each other in their Château Miraval battle, saying they settled "in the best interests of our family."
story: The former couple settled the case over ownership of their French winery outside of court after four years. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled their four-year legal battle over the sale of their French winery, Château Miraval.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further. Any comments in media stories attributed to ‘sources’ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," representatives for Pitt and Jolie said in a joint statement Wednesday to Fox News Digital after both sides moved to dismiss claims against each other.
Terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

Pitt first sued Jolie in 2022, after she attempted to sell her company, Nouvel, to Tenute del Mondo, a subsidiary of the Stoli Group, in 2021, effectively transferring her 50% ownership interest in Miraval. The actor has fought back against the sale since 2022, claiming it breached an agreement between the two.
Jolie and Pitt settled their legal battle over the sale of their French winery.  (Photo by Mustafa Yalcin/Anadolu via Getty Images)
BRAD PITT WINS COURT RULING FORCING ANGELINA JOLIE TO REVEAL PRIVATE MESSAGES
After Pitt sued Jolie, the actress' company accused the actor of running a "vindictive campaign" to "loot" the profitable business since she first filed for divorce in 2016.

Nouvel accused Pitt of "hijacking" Château Miraval and "wasting" the company's assets on unnecessary renovation projects, including spending $1 million on swimming pool renovations, according to court documents previously obtained by Fox News Digital.

Details of their divorce also became known when she filed her cross-complaint, which claimed it was Pitt who "refused to buy her interest unless he received his newly expanded NDA, enforceable by an $8.5 million holdback specifically designed to force her silence about his abuse and cover-up."
They split following an altercation on a plane in which Jolie claimed he got physical with her. (Getty Images)
The cover-up refers to allegations of an incident that took place on a private plane from France to Los Angeles involving Jolie and her children.

The "Maria" actress also filed a suit against the FBI in April 2022, six years after the bureau launched an investigation into the alleged 2016 altercation. The investigation closed two months after the alleged incident without charges being brought against Pitt.
During the 2016 fight, Pitt allegedly "choked one of the children and struck another in the face" and "grabbed Jolie by the head and shook her."
"Some of the children pleaded with Pitt to stop," according to documents filed in Los Angeles Superior Court. "They were all frightened. Many were crying."
Jolie also filed a lawsuit against the FBI, which she later dropped. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
She later dropped the lawsuit against the FBI.

After Jolie filed the cross-complaint, a source close to Pitt told Fox News Digital called the move a "legal attack" which took "a simple business dispute" and turned it into her team's "the latest example of them harming the entire family by making it personal."
Pitt has denied being abusive. He also spoke about that period of his life while on the "Armchair Expert" podcast in June 2025, noting he had gotten sober since then.

"I was pretty much on my back, you know, or on my knees," Pitt said of his decision to get sober. "I was trying anything and everyone. Anything anyone threw at me. It was a particularly difficult time. I needed rebooting. I needed to wake the f--- up in some areas. And it just meant a lot to me."
A source close to Pitt denied the allegations. (Presley Ann)
"I had taken things as far as I could take it, so I removed my drinking privileges," he added later.
In an interview with Esquire earlier this year, he said he was sober for seven years but had started drinking again "in a more restrained manner."
The couple bought a controlling stake in Château Miraval in 2008, and spent time there together throughout their relationship.

The two were expected to face off in court in 2027, with Pitt and his legal team accusing Jolie of dragging out the dispute in April, after she requested to push the trial start date by nine months to late 2027.
Pitt previously accused Jolie of dragging out the court proceedings. (Getty Images)

"One key witness, Ms. Jolie’s former business manager, Terry Bird, has unfortunately passed away," a joint status report previously obtained by Fox News Digital read. "Plaintiffs understand that another potential key witness, Ms. Jolie’s transactional lawyer, Laurent Schummer, is likely too ill to testify. This is yet another reason that a nine-month delay of the trial date would prejudice Plaintiffs."

Pitt's team added that the ongoing legal issue left him "deprived of the quiet enjoyment of his home in France," and hurt the business, with Jolie's team responding that there is "no evidence anywhere" that Pitt's ability to live in the chateau "has been impacted by this case one iota."
Jolie's team also claimed the request to delay the court proceedings was because of the complexity of the case.

The two actors met in 2004 while filming the movie "Mr. & Mrs. Smith." Pitt and his wife, Jennifer Aniston, later announced they were separating in January 2005, and finalized their divorce later that year. He and Jolie were then spotted in Kenya with her adopted son, Maddox, seemingly confirming their relationship.

title: John F Kennedy Jr search commander says Ted Kennedy made one strict demand after divers found nephew’s body
summary: New book "The Last Flight" details the 1999 search off Martha's Vineyard where John F. Kennedy Jr.'s body was recovered with his wife and her sister.
story: Captain W. Russell Webster and Theresa M. Webster, authors of "The Last Flight," detail the five-day search for John F. Kennedy Jr. and his family's specific recovery requests.

In the agonizing days following the 1999 plane crash that killed John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and her sister Lauren Bessette, Sen. Ted Kennedy issued a strict, emotional mandate to the federal crews racing to recover their bodies: All three would be brought to the surface together.

Retired U.S. Coast Guard Capt. W. Russell Webster, who spearheaded the search efforts, co-wrote "The Last Flight" with his wife, maritime historian Theresa Mitchell Webster. The book chronicles the massive recovery mission after Kennedy's single-engine plane crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Martha's Vineyard.
Navy divers recovered all three bodies on July 21, 1999 — five days after the plane went down off Martha's Vineyard.
LAST PERSON TO SEE JFK JR. ALIVE REVEALS CHILLING PREMONITION ABOUT HIS FATAL FLIGHT THAT NIGHT

John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn Bessette Kennedy (pictured here) and her sister Lauren Bessette died on July 16, 1999, when the small plane Kennedy was piloting crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Martha’s Vineyard. They are the subjects of a new book, "The Last Flight," written by Capt. W. Russell Webster and Theresa M. Webster. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"It became more complicated to ensure that his family's wishes were followed," Webster told Fox News Digital about the senator. "It was complicated because, normally, when bodies are recovered, they're recovered individually. He insisted that his nephew not be recovered as a priority. That was difficult, not only during the later body recovery, but also very early on when John F. Kennedy Jr. was found outside the airplane."
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"The Last Flight: The Untold Story of the Search for JFK Jr. and the Race Against the Atlantic" is available now. (Harper Select)
"There was a sense of urgency, driven primarily by the family doctor to have the divers go back down and retrieve him," said Webster.
John F. Kennedy Jr. and his wife Carolyn walk with their dog on Jan. 1, 1997, in New York City. (Evan Agostini/Liaison/Getty Images)

In the book, Webster wrote, "Senator Kennedy was adamant that Navy divers bring up John, Carolyn and Lauren at the exact same time in a single salvage basket. Even though his staffers initially pushed for JFK Jr. to be raised first because his body was outside the wreckage while the women were trapped inside, the senator insisted they be recovered together, so his nephew would not be perceived as receiving special treatment, even in death."
WATCH: JOHN F. KENNEDY JR. RECOVERY COMMANDER RECOUNTS 5-DAY SEARCH MISSION
Webster wrote that the divers were racing against time. "Walking the Atlantic floor stirs up silt, further compromising low visibility," he wrote.

The divers quickly found Kennedy's Piper Saratoga. There was no roof on the plane, and the windows were missing, "having been blown out from the impact." Kennedy Jr. was on his side on the ocean floor near the wreckage.
Where John Kennedy Jr. kept his Piper Saratoga airplane. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"Senator Kennedy insisted that the bodies be raised together at the same time," Mitchell Webster told Fox News Digital. "So, the Navy on the USS Grasp, has what's called a basket. It's a large metal piece with sides for the divers to hang onto. The platform on which they stood in that basket was large enough for them to put three bodies on it. So, they were raised together, and no preferential treatment was shown to JFK Jr."
A Coast Guard helicopter hovering over the ocean during the search for John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn and her sister Lauren. (Steve Liss/Getty Images)
"His uncle, from what we've been told and from what Russ had observed, was extremely respectful of the process and extremely grateful, as was his family, to the people doing the work."
The Bessette sisters were found together inside the upside-down fuselage, still strapped into their seats.
Carolyn Bessette Kennedy poses for a picture at the Annual Fundraising Gala March 9, 1999, at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City. (Evan Agostini/Liaison/Getty Images)

The book describes Kennedy as a constant, protective presence who remained beside his nephew and the Bessette sisters. Once the remains were transferred onto a 55-foot Coast Guard vessel, Kennedy and his sons boarded with them. During the transit, with a Navy chaplain in attendance, the senator invited the Coast Guard crew to join his family in prayer.

Sen. Ted Kennedy is briefed by Lt. Cmdr. Eric Anderson aboard the USS Grasp, on July 21, 1999, during the recovery of the victims. (US Navy Supervisor of Salvage)

When the boat reached shore, Kennedy overruled an aide who wanted to delay unloading until more relatives arrived. He insisted the caskets be brought straight to the waiting hearses. He stepped in to help carry them.
Ted Kennedy gives his nephew John Kennedy Jr. a piggyback ride down the ski slopes in Stowe, Vermont, one Easter weekend. (Bettmann Archive)

"He obviously never left their sides," said Webster. "After everything was done, he and his wife visited my command at Woods Hole and recognized everybody. He took pictures with everybody, gave out cookies and brownies. It was a very human experience."

A Coast Guard ship, carrying Sen. Ted Kennedy and his son, Congressman Patrick Kennedy, on Gay Head, as they head to the USS Grasp, which recovered the body of John F. Kennedy Jr. (Stephen Jaffe/AFP via Getty Images)

In retrieving the bodies, the crew wasn't just worried about beating the elements. There were also potential looters. Webster said they were driven by a very real fear that "treasure hunters" or commercial fishermen would stumble upon the wreckage first and steal personal items to profit off the tragedy.
"Massachusetts State Police Divers assisting in the Kennedy search had to contend with dive operations in waters recently chummed for a local shark tournament," read the book. (Harper Select)

"I think it certainly was a motivation, the potential for not only treasure hunters, but also for fishermen," said Webster. "This was an active fishing area, and we knew we were driven by the fact, not only by the priority given to us, but also with the knowledge that leaving the wreckage and leaving the victims behind was an unacceptable outcome."
Coast Guard Lt. j.g. Tiffany Drumm, Rear Adm. Richard Larrabee and Navy Cmdr. Jeff Pauls are briefed by Lt. Cmdr. Eric Anderson aboard the USS Grasp on July 21, 1999. (US Navy Supervisor of Salvage)
It was one fisherman in those active waters who unknowingly became a key witness to the tragedy.

A television technician holds up the official handout map of the search and rescue area off Martha's Vineyard, before a press conference. (John Mottern/AFP via Getty Images)

Just before 9:40 p.m. on July 16, 1999, Pittsburgh attorney Victor Pribanic was casting his line for striped bass off Squibnocket Point on the southwestern tip of Martha's Vineyard. A loud, jarring sound echoed across the dark Atlantic. He turned toward the open ocean, saw nothing in the haze and went back to fishing. Pribanic was unaware that he had just heard the final moments of Kennedy's plane.
"It wasn't an explosion. It was a boom," said Webster. "The impact was grave, and it was severe. They likely just went down 116 feet."
A grainy side-scan sonar (SSS) image of John F. Kennedy Jr.'s airplane at a depth of 116 feet in the Atlantic Ocean, 7.25 miles southwest of Martha’s Vineyard. (NOAA)
Looking back, Webster said he was proud of his crew's commitment to duty in retrieving Kennedy's beloved nephew and his family, even as a heavy sadness settled over everyone involved.
John F. Kennedy, Jr. gives his wife Carolyn a kiss on the cheek during the annual White House Correspondents dinner on May 1, 1999, in Washington, D.C. (Tyler Mallory/Liaison/Getty Images)

"I remember feeling exhaustion," said Webster. "I believe I had just laid down for no more than an hour after not sleeping since I got the original call. It was a mixed feeling, a feeling of profound grief and a feeling of profound happiness.

"I worked with a number of families that we could never save their loved ones or find their remains so that they could celebrate their lives in ceremonies. For me, it was a dichotomy of feelings. One was, 'Oh my God, we found them as a team.' And the other was, 'Yes, they're really dead.'"

Ultimately, the National Transportation Safety Board determined the crash was caused by spatial disorientation. Though Kennedy Jr. had recently passed his written instrument exam, he was not yet certified to fly solely using his cockpit instruments. Just weeks before the crash, a certified flight instructor had noted in his record that he was not ready for instrument conditions.
Jackie Kennedy Onassis stands with her son John F. Kennedy Jr., who graduated from Phillips Academy at Andover. Daughter Caroline and Sen. Edward M. Kennedy were also present. (Bettmann Archive)
"What was clear to me was that in those final miles, he had transitioned into an instrument-rated flight that he was not prepared for," Webster said.

John F. Kennedy Jr. pictured while recovering from a broken left ankle, an injury he sustained in a paragliding accident about six weeks before his fatal plane crash. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Even for fully qualified pilots, it can take up to 35 seconds to recover from spatial disorientation, Webster said. It’s a critical window Kennedy Jr. didn't have once the plane began its steep descent.
"He had to have been anguished, confused, just frightened," said Mitchell Webster. "It must have been very difficult."
A Navy diver aboard USS Grasp is assisted with his suit. (US Navy Supervisor of Salvage)
On July 22, 1999, the families scattered the ashes of Kennedy Jr. and the Bessette sisters in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Martha's Vineyard.

title: Christina Ricci admits Cher is 'still mad at me' decades after one mistake ended 'Mermaids' bond
summary: Christina Ricci says Cher still holds a grudge over a voicemail she never returned at 19, decades after they played mother and daughter in "Mermaids."
story: Christina Ricci says her "Mermaids" costar Cher still holds a grudge against her. (Getty Images)

Nearly four decades after playing mother and daughter in the 1990 classic "Mermaids," Christina Ricci revealed that her off-screen relationship with Cher has been rocky — all because of an unreturned voicemail from when Ricci was 19.

During a recent appearance on "Watch What Happens Live," host Andy Cohen asked Ricci if she had stayed in touch with the music icon after filming "Mermaids" and appearing in the video for "The Shoop Shoop Song."

CHRISTINA RICCI WILL NEVER BE 'GIRL NEXT DOOR,' SAYS HAPPY PEOPLE DON'T DO ANYTHING INTERESTING
Winona Ryder, Cher and Christina Ricci pose for a publicity portrait for the film "Mermaids," 1990. (Getty Images)

"She left me a voicemail about how journalists are always trying to get the worst things, and blah blah blah," Ricci recalled. "And she was so sorry, and I was 19, and so I didn't return that message."

That teenage oversight appears to have stuck. Ricci noted that her efforts to reconnect with Cher over the years have been met with "radio silence."
Despite the decades-long silent treatment, Ricci holds no ill will — and even took Cher's side in the standoff, noting how supportive the Oscar winner had been to her as a child actor on set.
