title: ‘Friday Night Lights,’ ‘Mosquito Bowl’ author says America has lost the Greatest Generation's sense of duty
summary: "The Mosquito Bowl" author Buzz Bissinger says America has forgotten the selfless duty of the Greatest Generation, whose college football stars left fame behind to fight in WWII.
story: "Friday Night Lights" and "The Mosquito Bowl" author Buzz Bissinger tells Fox News Digital why modern America must remember the ordinary men who sacrificed everything during World War II.
"Friday Night Lights" author Buzz Bissinger believes modern America has lost touch with the selflessness that once defined the "Greatest Generation."

The 72-year-old Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist penned the 2022 nonfiction book "The Mosquito Bowl," which was adapted into Peter Berg's new Netflix war movie of the same name. "The Mosquito Bowl" tells the true story of elite college football stars who walked away from fame and future wealth to enlist in the Marines and fight in the Pacific Theater during World War II.
While speaking with Fox News Digital at the film's premiere during the AFI Film Festival, Bissinger argued that kind of sacrifice has largely disappeared today.
HOLLYWOOD MARINE VETERAN ROB RIGGLE DOUBTS MODERN STARS WOULD MAKE JIMMY STEWART'S WWII SACRIFICE

"I think we've forgotten," Bissinger said. "I know they're called the Greatest Generation, but we have forgotten what it is like to serve, to have a sense of duty, to do something regardless of whether you're going to come back or not. And these are things we have to remember."

"Friday Night Lights" and "The Mosquito Bowl" author Buzz Bissinger believes that modern America has lost the sense of duty that defined the Greatest Generation.  (Brianna Bryson/FilmMagic; Circa Images/GHI/Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"We were together," he continued. "These men fought. They were never heroes. They never thought of themselves as heroes. They were ordinary men in extraordinary circumstances who felt it was really, really important to serve their country. And many of them didn't come back."
AMERICA'S VETERANS AND MILITARY HEROES DESERVE FAR MORE RECOGNITION THAN THEY GET: YOUTUBE STAR

"And they need to be memorialized," he added. "It helps remind me of the greatness of this country, just how great this country was. There was no division. We were in unison, and these men personified that. And they had great lives ahead of them, but they didn't make it."

Both the book and the movie depict the Mosquito Bowl, a tackle football game played on Christmas Eve in 1944 on Guadalcanal between two Marine regiments whose ranks included some of the country's top former college football players. Months later, 15 of the 65 players were killed fighting in the Battle of Okinawa.
WATCH: 'Friday Night Lights' author Buzz Bissinger says America has 'forgotten' the Greatest Generation's duty
FOX SPORTS TO HONOR MILITARY AHEAD OF VETERANS DAY WITH TWO-DAY SALUTE DURING COLLEGE FOOTBALL, NFL COVERAGE

During his interview with Fox News Digital, Bissinger drew a comparison between modern celebrity sports culture and the dozens of elite college athletes who put their lives on the line in World War II, many of whom had already been drafted by NFL teams.

"I was actually thinking about how many pro football players have served in the military. The answer is virtually none," he said. "To have 65 football players who went to college and are now in the Marine Corps serving, forget it."
KELSEY GRAMMER STILL FEELS 'SENSE OF SMALLNESS' FOR NOT SERVING IN MILITARY: 'I DO MY BEST TO MAKE UP FOR IT'
"It was a whole different era," Bissinger continued. "You gave up your dreams. You had no choice. You had to serve. It was in your heart."
Bissinger said that the Marines who fought in WWII "personified" the country's unity.  (Getty Images)

He cited Dave Schreiner, a celebrated University of Wisconsin two-time All-American football star who turned down an NFL career and non-combat military posts to enlist in the U.S. Marine Corps and serve on the front lines.
Schreiner was mortally wounded during the Battle of Okinawa in June 1945 and died the following day at age 24.
LAST SURVIVING 'ROSIE THE RIVETERS' HONORED BY WWII MUSEUM ON D-DAY ANNIVERSARY: 'WE CAN DO IT'

"All of them could have gotten out, I think, because they were athletes, and athletes are coveted," Bissinger said. "But they didn't. They didn't. It was offered, and they said, ‘No, I have to go. I have to go.’ And that's pretty rare. You will not see that happen today."
The author said the Marines featured in his book were "ordinary men in extraordinary circumstances." (Getty Images)
Bissinger pointed out that many of the football players who fought in WWII could have used their status to get safer stateside opportunities but refused.
THE DAY AFTER MEMORIAL DAY, AMERICA’S DEBT TO THE FALLEN STILL REMAINS

Berg's adaptation of "The Mosquito Bowl" focuses on four real-life college football stars who enlisted in the Marines after Pearl Harbor, including Schreiner, who was played by Broadway star Tom Francis, John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård) and Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson). The screenplay was co-written by Berg and Mark L Smith.
PETER BERG SAYS 'CALL OF DUTY' MOVIE WILL EXPLORE 'THE COST OF WAR' WITH SERIOUS TONE

Bissinger spent five years researching and writing "The Mosquito Bowl" including digging through military records and family archives. While speaking with Fox News Digital, the author compared the process to a "detective story" since many of the first-hand witnesses and people who participated in the real-life Mosquito Bowl had died.
During his research, Bissinger made a personal discovery when he unexpectedly uncovered his own late father's service in the 4th Marine Regiment.
Bissinger spent five years researching and writing "The Mosquito Bowl." (Gamma-Keystone via Getty Images)
"He never talked about it. I didn't know, was he on the line? Was he a rifleman? Was he, you know, a waiter?" Bissinger recalled.
Bissinger, who was born Harry Gerard Bissinger III, explained that he was searching for his own name in the records since he was named after his father.

"So I looked up the roster records, and his name is my name," Bissinger said. "I'm the third, he's the second. And there's his name. But not only that, he is a rifleman, so he's on the lines. And he's in the 4th Regiment, which is one of the regiments that I was writing about, so I'm seeing all these names from the book and, for all I know, he could have been there. He could have been at the game."

"It was mind-blowing, and it put me over the top," he continued. "And what I learned — I'm so proud of him. And I stop because I get worked up. I just wish I could have said that 'I'm really proud of you. I'm really, really proud of you.' But he's been gone for a long time."
However, Bissinger told Fox News Digital that learning about his father's history established a connection that they didn't have when he was alive.
"I've never felt closer to him," Bissinger said.

The Pacific Theater of World War II officially ended on September 2, 1945 (V-J Day), when Japanese representatives signed the formal Instrument of Surrender aboard the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. (Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Berg's late father, Laurence Berg, was also a Marine who served in the Korean War. Bissinger recalled he and the director, who are also second cousins, recently shared a moment in which they wondered how their fathers would have reacted to "The Mosquito Bowl."
"Last week, we were walking out of the Marine Corps Museum, and we both said, ‘What would it be like if our fathers were here?,'" Bissinger said.

"Now, they were kind of critical guys, so the first thing they would do is criticize the film, but then they would hug us, and they would feel such incredible pride, not just for us, but for the family," he continued. "It would have been a great moment, but we'll have to imagine it."
"The Mosquito Bowl" stars Ray Nicholson as Tony Butkovich, Tom Francis as Dave Schreiner, Bill Skarsgård as Bob Baumann, and Nicholas Galitzine as John McLaughry.  (Kane Skennar / Netflix )

Bissinger said that while audiences remain hungry for stories about real-life heroes like his father and the men of the Mosquito Bowl, he believes Hollywood too often waters down the true cost of combat.

"I think what happens is, particularly in war movies, they ultimately get sanitized," he said. "Filmmakers, directors, studios are afraid of showing war as it is because they think people can't handle it. I think that's ridiculous, and I think it's wrong."

"In order for us to see just how tragic and brutal war is, we have to see it," Bissinger continued. "We have to see it. I tried to do that in the book and Pete has certainly done that in the film. People may flinch, people may not be able to handle it, but to me, it doesn't matter. If you want to know what war is like, you have to watch this film and read other books, and maybe, maybe collectively, we'll say, ‘Enough.’"
WATCH: 'Friday Night Lights' author Buzz Bissinger says 'The Mosquito Bowl' cast nailed it 'to a T'
Bissinger told Fox News Digital that he keeps a picture of Schreiner hanging on his wall to remind him of the harsh realities of war and the sacrifices made by the fallen players.

"I still can't quite comprehend that these guys are no longer with us," he said. "Dave Schreiner, beautiful guy, 6'2", perfect, the perfect two-time All-American, great son, great family, and his whole life ahead of him. And he died 12 hours before officials surrendered."

"And I'm just haunted by that," Bissinger continued. "Because he should have — they should have had a life. They didn't waste their lives, but it's still, in a sense, is the waste of a good human being. And that's just hard for me to overcome. So he reminds me, he keeps me going."
Bissinger said he keeps a picture of Schreiner hanging on his wall.  (Kane Skennar / Netflix )
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Bissinger admitted that ahead of watching "The Mosquito Bowl," he was worried about whether the film and its young cast would preserve the integrity of the men they were portraying. However, he told Fox News Digital that he was blown away by their performances.

"They did it to a T," he said. "They're all great. Ray Nicholson will knock your socks off. Bill Skarsgård, Tom Francis, Nick Galitzine — they were phenomenal. And so at a certain point, I'm not looking at them as people they're making a movie about, I am seeing them now as the characters they were, and that was great."

"The Mosquito Bowl" marks a creative reunion for Bissinger and Berg. The director previously adapted Bissinger's 1990 bestselling nonfiction book "Friday Night Lights" into the acclaimed 2004 movie of the same name and later the hit TV series that ran on NBC from 2006 to 2011.
Bissinger praised the young cast, saying, they "did it to a T." (Kane Skennar / Netflix )
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Bissinger also credited Berg, who is known for helming gritty, realistic filmmaking after having helmed "Lone Survivor," "Deepwater Horizon" and "Patriots Day," with refusing to compromise the book's spirit.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"He, to a T, wants to retain authenticity and the integrity of the book and he did that in ‘Friday Night Lights’ and since then we've really become brothers," Bissinger said. "We talk all the time. I pitch projects to him. He says, 'You're out of your mind. I'm not doing that.' But then something hits and it took a while. It took a little while."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"But once he got the thread, which is really about the loss of innocence, he got it," he said. "He's fun to work with. He is a hoot on the set. He has a great character. Hollywood needs more of them, I'll tell you."

title: British police name suspects charged in break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate's home
summary: Two men are charged after a break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate's Anmer Hall on the Sandringham Estate, with police deploying dogs and drones.
story: Royal reporter Kinsey Schofield discusses how two people were able to break into a cottage belonging to the UK’s royal family on ‘Fox News @ Night.’
British police announced on Wednesday two men have been charged following a report of a break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate’s country home on the Sandringham Estate.
The Norfolk Constabulary confirmed that Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were arrested in connection with the incident at Anmer Hall; authorities said the property was unoccupied at the time.
The men have been charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They remain in custody and are due to appear in Norwich Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday.
The suspects were taken into custody near the country house after police received a call about suspicious activity at around 6 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET) on Monday.

British police are seen on Nov. 24, 2026, at the royal family’s Sandringham Estate investigating a burglary at Anmer Hall, a secondary residence of Prince William and Princess Kate. (Martin Pope/Getty Images)
FORMER PRINCE ANDREW ‘SHAKEN’ BY MASKED MAN THREAT, BUT MORE SECURITY WOULD SPARK ‘PUBLIC BACKLASH’: EXPERT

"Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area," police said in a statement to Fox News.

The Sun reported that William, Kate, and their three children — Prince George, Princess Charlotte, and Prince Louis — were staying at their primary residence, Forest Lodge in Windsor, at the time of the incident.
Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom residence on the 20,000-acre Sandringham Estate, was given to William and Kate as a wedding gift by the late Queen Elizabeth II.

Prior to moving in, the couple oversaw a £1.5 million renovation that included major security upgrades, such as rerouting a public road, planting dense tree lines for privacy and establishing a seasonal no-fly zone over the property.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Duke of Rothesay, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, Duchess of Rothsay, with Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis arrive for the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at The Hydro on Aug. 1, 2026 in Glasgow, Scotland. (Jeff J. Mitchell/Getty Images)
RENTALS NOW ALLOWED IN HISTORIC WATER TOWER ON KING CHARLES' SANDRINGHAM ESTATE WHERE ROYALS SPEND CHRISTMAS
The family regularly visits the country estate for weekend getaways and school holidays, and it served as a private sanctuary for Kate during her cancer treatment in 2024.
The break-in raises fresh concerns over royal security, as William and his immediate family receive 24-hour armed protection as working royals.
The incident also marks the latest security scare on royal grounds.
A general view of the front of Anmer Hall on the Sandringham Estate on Jan. 13, 2013 in King's Lynn, England. (Indigo/Getty Images)

title: ‘The Vow’ star Jace Cates recommits to saving himself for marriage despite ‘sex-positive culture’
summary: "Chris Harrison’s: The Vow" star Jace Cates opens up about saving himself for marriage, why faith in relationships matters, and dating in a sex-positive culture.
story: The reality star is committed to waiting until marriage to be intimate with someone again, going against today's "sex-positive culture."
"Chris Harrison's: The Vow" star, Jace Cates, is giving his opinion on modern dating and how the current "sex-positive culture" can complicate things.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 30-year-old reality star said he is committed to saving himself for marriage, noting that while he was in his 20s, "there were times that I absolutely" wasn't in "lockstep with my faith," noting that might be why he was "single at 30."

"I talk about being a fan of Jesus or also being a follower of Jesus. There's a big difference," he said. "So, when you're a follower of Jesus, there is specific beliefs that you have to actually be a follower of Jesus to build that relationship around Jesus and have faith be a part of the relationship. And the next person I'm intimate with, I want that to be my wife. And I think that's important."
Adding: "And I know it's hard, because it's a very sex-positive culture. And it's a sacrifice for sure for people to make. And I think that's something that people have to navigate."
Jace Cates, 30, is searching for his future wife among 10 women on Fox Nation's faith-focused dating series "Chris Harrison's: The Vow." (Fox Nation)
CHRIS HARRISON RETURNS TO REALITY TV WITH 'THE VOW,' FOX NATION'S FIRST-EVER DATING SHOW

"I think we got away from being okay with talking about faith in a relationship and going to church together," he said. "And I think as people are looking intentionally and leading with faith, those are conversations that couples need to have sooner rather than later. That's about intentional dating and I think it's something that people need to discuss."

The new Fox Nation show, "Chris Harrison's: The Vow," follows Cates as he navigates relationships with 10 women seeking lasting commitment and marriage over six episodes.
While on "Chris Harrison’s: The Vow," Cates navigates relationships with 10 women as he tries to find lasting love. (Fox Nation)
His experience on the show ultimately changed his view on dating, as he was left completely unplugged as he "was away from my phone, my laptop [and] couldn't communicate with my family."

"All I could do was be in silence and rely on my relationship with God. And it's something I've tried to take back to my real life," he explained. "One thing I'll say, viewers, when they tune into the show and see what happens, I'm just extremely grateful that I had this experience to show me how important that is more than I even believed before I went on the show."

In addition to the "sex-positive culture," Cates thinks technology is also a problem when it comes to modern dating, as "people have access to people now, more than ever," noting this is when being intentional in the pursuit of love is important.

Cates told Fox News Digital, that the faith aspect of the show separates it from others of its kind, noting everyone who participated was "trying to build something real and people actually looking for love."
Cates said he would like a traditional marriage in which they support one another 100%. (Fox Nation)

When it comes to what he is looking for in a relationship, the Oregon native admitted he is hoping for a more traditional marriage, but not in the way people might think, noting the term has a "negative connotation right now."

"I think for me, traditional marriage means just supporting your person 100 percent in what they are looking to do in life," he said. "And if my future wife wants to be a stay-at-home mom, I want to be a supportive husband and support her 100 percent. If she wants to be a CEO of a company, I will support her 100 percent and we will make it work. I think that is what traditional means to me. And that's just because that's how my parents were in their relationship."

He also feels that the work at home should be split evenly when it comes to raising children, saying when he was growing up, both his mom and dad were very involved in his childhood, adding, "I just want to give that to my kids when I raise them, because it worked so well for me."

"I think men, you understand if you are gonna bring kids into this world, it is one of the most important jobs you're gonna have is to be a great father," he said. "I can only speak for men. You have responsibility, and it's time for you to step up and if you're not ready for it, then maybe that's not for you. title: Thomas Markle, estranged father of Meghan Markle, indicted on child pornography charges
summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan Markle, has been indicted on child pornography charges involving 35mm film negatives of minors under 12.
story: Meghan Markle's estranged father, Thomas Wayne Markle, is deemed mentally competent to stand trial during a federal court hearing. He’s charged with one count of possession of child pornography.
Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan Markle, was indicted on child pornography charges.
Markle, 82, is charged with possessing child sexual abuse material (CSAM), specifically 35 mm film negatives of prepubescent minors and minors who had not yet reached the age of 12 years old.

title: Doctors uncover well-formed fetal skeleton inside 10-year-old boy suffering from stomach pain
summary: Doctors in Pakistan removed a parasitic twin skeleton with a spine and limbs from a 10-year-old boy after an ultrasound and CT scan revealed a rare mass.
story: Dr. Emma Macdonald-Laurs, a pediatric neurologist at Murdoch Children's Research Institute, discusses a groundbreaking AI detector that spots hidden epilepsy lesions with a 94 percent success rate in pediatric test cases. Spiros Kounadis and his 12-year-old son, John Kounadis, share how this technology helped John become completely seizure-free after a successful surgery.

Doctors in Pakistan removed a partially formed fetal skeleton from inside a 10-year-old boy who had been suffering from abdominal pain, a low-grade fever, and unintentional weight loss, according to a newly published medical case report.

The incredibly rare condition — known as "fetus in fetu" — occurs in roughly 1 in 500,000 live births. The case, documented in the journal Case Reports in Pediatrics, was especially unusual because the condition is almost always diagnosed in infancy.
Despite its name, the mass is never a viable fetus. Rather, it is a malformed, parasitic twin that becomes absorbed into its host twin's body during early development in the womb.

In this case study, the boy was admitted to the hospital on June 16 after experiencing symptoms for 10 days. An ultrasound revealed a "mass-like lesion" in his upper left abdomen, just below his ribcage.
FILE - The child was admitted to the hospital on June 16 after experiencing symptoms for 10 days, according to the case study. (Kannika Paison)
TAKING OZEMPIC OR WEGOVY COULD LEAD TO EXTRA CANCER SCREENINGS, NEW STUDY SAYS

A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed that the growth — measuring roughly 4 by 4 by 5.5 inches — contained fat tissue, tooth-like calcifications and a well-formed spine. When surgeons later removed it, the mass also had discernible limbs, as well as hair and nails.

Because the removed tissue wasn't properly preserved before reaching the lab, doctors couldn't run microscopic tests on it and noted that their diagnosis remains presumptive rather than definitive, as a rare, highly developed tumor couldn't be entirely ruled out.

The doctors in the case concluded that fetus in fetu should remain on clinicians' radar when imaging reveals a complex abdominal mass in a child — even well past infancy — particularly alongside symptoms like unexplained stomach pain or abdominal swelling.

The paper didn't reach any conclusions about how long the mass had been inside the boy, but because fetus in fetu is a congenital condition originating in early embryogenesis — one of the earliest phases of pregnancy — the growth had presumably been there since before he was born.
Three ultrasound images included in the paper show the mass growing the boy's abdomen. (Case Reports in Pediatrics)
DOCTORS WARN OF LEAD EXPOSURE HEALTH RISKS AFTER CONTROVERSIAL ARMY DETONATION IN IOWA
The paper noted that the boy was "previously healthy" until 10 days before being admitted to the hospital, so it remains unclear why the mass only began hurting him 10 years into his life.
Because the boy's mother never had a prenatal ultrasound during pregnancy, the condition went undetected before he was born.

The mass was removed from the boy without complications, though he needed one blood transfusion while he was recovering. He was discharged from the hospital 11 days after he was admitted, according to the paper.
FILE - Doctors noted the boy was "previously healthy" until 10 days before being admitted to the hospital. (mihailomilovanovic)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
At his last check-in about 10 weeks later in September, he was completely symptom-free and healing well, the paper's authors reported.
The doctors recommended that the boy return for routine ultrasounds and blood tests over the next five years due to a rare risk of the condition recurring or becoming cancerous.

title: Does ‘man flu’ really exist? Here’s what an emergency room physician says
summary: Dr. Stephanie Widmer confirms the "man flu" is not a real medical diagnosis, though some data suggests men may face worse outcomes than women.
story: Emergency medicine physician Dr. Stephanie Widmer examines the popular concept of the "man flu" and explains why there is no clinical proof that men experience more severe cold symptoms.
When a minor cold knocks a man onto the couch for days, it’s often dismissed as a classic case of the "man flu" — but is there real science behind it?
Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a New York City emergency medicine physician, medical toxicologist and Fox News medical contributor, confirmed that the "man flu" is not a real medical diagnosis.
"It is very interesting that ‘man flu’ is becoming a very commonly used term," she told Fox News Digital.
MEN AND WOMEN WHO SMOKE MARIJUANA MAY EXPERIENCE DIFFERENT EFFECTS, STUDY SUGGESTS
But the question remains: Do men actually get "sicker" or experience more severe symptoms than women when they have a cold or the flu?
A doctor said it has not been proven that men have more severe symptoms or suffer more when sick. (iStock)
While some evidence already points to biological differences in how men's and women’s immune systems respond, the doctor noted that the issue "deserves a little bit more attention" from researchers.

"At the end of the day, there is no evidence ... that men have more severe symptoms, suffer more, or experience more pain or discomfort when it comes to the flu, colds or other respiratory viruses and viral illnesses," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
There is some data, however, suggesting that men may be hospitalized more or may experience worse mortality after a flu infection than women, according to Widmer.
"But again, that doesn't mean they are necessarily experiencing more severe symptoms," she said. "It doesn't prove that the man flu does exist, so to speak."
Some data suggests that men may be hospitalized more or may experience worse mortality after a flu infection than women. (iStock)

While some theorize that women tolerate illness better because the biological capacity for childbirth gives them a naturally higher pain threshold, Widmer noted that this hypothesis has not been scientifically proven.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I'd like to think that's true," she said. "Women have babies. We can endure a lot of pain, but … [it’s not] backed by science."

Research from the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, published by the National Institutes of Health in 2022, found that acute pain tolerance is more consistent over time in women than men, while men showed higher pain tolerance in sporadic sessions.
Research found that acute pain tolerance is more consistent over time in women than men, while men showed higher pain tolerance in sporadic sessions. (iStock)
Another 2022 study, published in the Journal of Psychosomatic Research, debunked the "man flu" theory, titling the paper "Man flu is not a thing."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The research analyzed the symptoms of men and women with sinus infections, finding that there was no difference in initial physical severity. Women felt worse at the start, but recovered faster than men.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Although a certain gender difference was found both in the clinician [and] patient-rated ARS symptoms, the hypothesis of a ‘man flu’ should be disregarded," the authors stated.

title: Low levels of common vitamin could be stealing nearly 30 minutes of your sleep
summary: Low vitamin D blood levels were linked to about 23 minutes less sleep per night in a new study of adults 40 and older that used wearable sensors.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel tells 'The Ingraham Angle' the benefits of 'miracle' Vitamin D and why testing is so important and more.
Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels, according to a new study that tracked sleep with wearable sensors.
The study, led by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the National Institute on Aging, used data collected from 2012 to 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.
The researchers looked at blood tests and sleep data from 460 adults ages 40 and older, averaging 71 years of age.
ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES
After dividing the participants into three groups by vitamin D level, they found that the highest group slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than the group with the lowest levels.
People with lower levels also stayed awake longer after waking up at night — a pattern that held regardless of age, gender or race.
Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels. (iStock)
The connection between vitamin D and sleep was strongest among Black participants, who made up about 22% of the group.

"Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to White adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels," lead author Diefei Chen, a doctoral candidate in epidemiology at the Bloomberg School, said in a press release.
CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA

Most earlier studies on vitamin D and sleep relied on people reporting how well they thought they slept. In this study, researchers used blood draws and actigraphs, which are watch-like motion sensors that measure sleep and wake times.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The team also checked vitamin B12, which previous studies linked to sleep. While higher levels correlated with less nighttime wakefulness in women and more in men, the authors noted the results were statistically inconclusive.

Middle-aged and older adults with low blood levels of vitamin D slept an average of about 23 minutes less per night and stayed awake longer after nighttime awakenings than those with normal levels. (iStock)
The findings were published on Oct. 14 in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.
Poor sleep and vitamin D deficiency are both widespread among older adults, with previous research linking sleep disturbances to higher risks of dementia, heart disease and diabetes.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study had several limitations. Because the researchers looked at snapshots of data rather than testing a treatment in a clinical trial, they could only establish a link between vitamin D and sleep.
The findings did not prove that low levels cause poor sleep or that taking supplements will fix it.
Further research is needed to determine whether higher vitamin D levels actually improve sleep health, and whether the findings apply to younger adults or people with cognitive impairment. (iStock)
Because blood tests can't distinguish between vitamin D from sunlight, food or supplements, the study could not determine whether the source matters.
In addition, the researchers did not track whether changing a person's vitamin D levels over several years leads to changes in their sleep.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Because everyone in the study was 40 or older and had no cognitive impairment, the results may not apply to younger people or adults with memory and thinking problems.

"These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health," senior author Adam Spira, a mental health professor at the Bloomberg School, said in the news release.

title: Supplements in the spotlight as longevity doctor shares his personal daily routine
summary: Dr. Kien Vuu shares his daily supplement stack, from creatine and NMN to glutathione, each supporting muscle health, cellular energy and longevity.
story: Dr. Kien Vuu discusses how targeted supplements work alongside healthy lifestyle choices to support muscle growth, cellular energy and overall performance.

Nearly eight in 10 Americans take at least one dietary supplement for their health, according to a September 2026 Pew Research Center survey — yet clinicians warn that routine supplementation isn't always necessary or safe.
Dr. Kien Vuu, a Los Angeles-based physician specializing in longevity and author of the book "Thrive State," spoke to Fox News Digital about the role supplements play in overall health.

"Supplements are a signal," he told Fox News Digital during an event at Soft Bar + Cafe in Brooklyn, New York. "How we live life are signals. How we eat, how we sleep, how we move, how we connect with people, they're all signals to the body — and supplements can play a very important role."
DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT
Certain supplements can support muscle growth, metabolism and cellular energy, but they work best when they're paired with "lifestyle choices and targeted support," the expert said.
Vuu, a partner with longevity and supplement brand Solaray, shared the supplements he takes on a daily basis.

Certain supplements can support muscle growth, metabolism, cellular energy and overall molecular support, but they work best when they're paired with "lifestyle choices," the longevity expert says. (iStock)
No. 1: Creatine

Creatine, an amino acid-based compound, has become popular among fitness enthusiasts, as it has been shown to aid in boosting energy during exercise. The supplement is "really important" for muscle health and recovery, Vuu said.
COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The supplement has also demonstrated cognitive benefits, assisting with memory and processing speed, according to the National Institutes of Health.

Combining creatine with an MBP (milk basic protein) — a whey protein fraction studied for supporting bone formation and reducing bone breakdown — can support both muscle energy and bone health, according to Vuu.

Combining creatine with an MBP (milk basic protein) — a whey protein fraction studied for supporting bone formation and reducing bone breakdown — can support both muscle energy and bone health. (iStock)
No. 2: NMN
NMN, short for nicotinamide mononucleotide, is a compound the body uses to make NAD+ — a vital coenzyme that helps cells convert food into energy and repair damaged DNA.
ANTI-AGING SUPPLEMENTS TAKEN BY MILLIONS MAY UNDERMINE CANCER TREATMENT, STUDY WARNS

As a basic step in his longevity routine, Vuu said he typically takes NMN to support cellular energy as natural NAD+ levels decline with age — though independent researchers note that clinical evidence in humans is still emerging.
No. 3: Glutathione

Glutathione, a tripeptide antioxidant produced naturally in cells, helps the liver detoxify harmful compounds and protects cells from oxidative damage caused by pollution, stress and aging, according to UCLA Health.

In the body, the compound also plays a vital role in supporting immune and liver function, protecting red blood cells from oxidative damage and facilitating amino acid transport across cell membranes.
Glutathione can help reduce stress by detoxing the body. (iStock)
"When I travel or get super stressed, I like to use glutathione," Vuu said. "I find myself and my nervous system behaving a lot better."
No. 4: Daily supplements
Vuu also takes several staples aimed at filling common nutritional gaps, including vitamin D, magnesium, a multivitamin and fish oil for omega-3 fatty acids.
DR OZ REVEALS 3 FREE WAYS TO BOOST YOUR HEALTH — NO MEDICATION REQUIRED

"What I see very deficient in people these days is vitamin D," he said. "Even if they're out in the sun, our bodies are using so much vitamin D, fighting against some of the stresses we have in life, that it's really low."
The doctor recommends seeing a physician to determine the need for certain supplements. (istock)

Data from the National Institutes of Health shows that roughly one-third of U.S. adults are clinically deficient in vitamin D, and factors like sunscreen, winter sunlight angles, varying skin tones and higher body fat can limit how much the body produces.

"Supplementing with [vitamin D] improves their hormones, it improves their energy, it improves their sex life, improves their immune system," Vuu said — though clinicians note those benefits typically apply to people correcting a true deficiency rather than those whose levels are already normal.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The doctor said he also takes mitochondrial supplements such as ubiquinol — the active antioxidant form of CoQ10 — which supports cellular energy production and helps protect cells from oxidative damage.
The supplement 'sweet spot'

While many people fall short on certain nutrients — or could benefit from targeted supplementation — it is possible to overdo it. Vuu said it's important to know your baseline health and to target your specific needs.
"If you're a person looking to supplement, go work with a physician first," he advised. "See where your labs are, see what symptoms you might be having, and then recognize what your goals are."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The sweet spot is knowing what you need, knowing what the baseline is, and then taking the targeted [approach] to support you … You're not supposed to take everything, and it's going to be different for everyone."
Vuu added that supplements clearly play an important role in how the body functions, noting that "our cells are energetically listening to everything."
The physician recommends connecting with the community as a means of supporting supplement effectiveness. (iStock)
Supplements work best when paired with healthy lifestyle practices, including adequate sleep, regular exercise and social connections, he noted.

Connecting with people and maintaining a sense of community has been shown to be beneficial to health, Vuu said. Pairing a proven supplement like creatine with real-world connection and enjoyment, he said, creates the ultimate "health stack."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Beyond pills and powders, the expert suggested one final daily "supplement" for everyone: vitamin G — which stands for gratitude.
Recognizing life as a gift and feeling fortunate to be alive helps keep fear and anxiety at bay, he said.

"If you can feel gratitude, you're putting your nervous system in a state of calm, which actually improves symptoms and improves your health in the long term."

title: Thanksgiving on Ozempic: Clever tricks to survive the feast without offending the host
summary: Dietitian Patricia Araujo shares tips for Thanksgiving dinner on GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy, from protein picks to portion control.
story: Patricia Araujo, a registered dietitian at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, shared her practical tips for enjoying the holiday meal — without overdoing it or making your host feel slighted.
With roughly 15% of Americans now reporting they have used a GLP-1 medication for weight loss, many Thanksgiving dinner plates may be a little less crowded this year.
Less "food noise" and a smaller appetite can make it tricky for people taking Ozempic, Wegovy or other glucagon-like peptide-1 drugs to navigate the etiquette of a traditionally large feast.
Patricia Araujo, a registered dietitian at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, shared her practical tips for enjoying the holiday meal — without overdoing it or making your host feel slighted.
HOW SKIPPING BREAKFAST TO SAVE ROOM FOR DINNER SHOCKS YOUR BLOOD SUGAR AND METABOLISM
Navigating social dynamics
Handling topics around food and diet can be challenging for patients on a GLP-1, according to Araujo.
With roughly 15% of Americans now reporting they have used a GLP-1 medication for weight loss, many Thanksgiving dinner plates may be a little less crowded this year. (iStock)
While people shouldn’t feel pressured to disclose anything about their personal or medical history, it can be helpful to think ahead of time about how much they want to share, she advised.

If guests question why you aren't eating a certain dish or urge you to take seconds, Araujo recommends having a polite response ready, such as, "That looks delicious. Thank you for offering. I've had enough," or simply, "I'm comfortably full right now."
THE 8 HEALTHIEST BEANS YOU SHOULD BE EATING MORE OFTEN, ACCORDING TO NUTRITION EXPERT
People don’t necessarily have to tell others that they’re taking medication, she noted.

"Sometimes just sharing that they're working on eating smaller portions, or they're making some dietary changes, but still acknowledging that the food is great and that they are happy to be able to share that meal together can be enough," Araujo said.
Foods to prioritize and limit
The dietitian recommends that people on a GLP-1 should get plenty of nutrient-dense foods, with an emphasis on protein, fiber, vitamins and minerals.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Protein is important because it helps us maintain muscle mass when we're taking a GLP-1 and losing weight," she told Fox News Digital.
Handling topics around food and diet can be challenging for patients on a GLP-1, according to the dietitian. (iStock)
At a Thanksgiving table, good sources of protein include roasted turkey without the skin, beans, chickpeas, lentils and tofu, Araujo said.

"Fiber is really important for digestive health and to keep things moving," she said. "Good sources of fiber are fruits, vegetables and whole grains. At Thanksgiving, that can be roasted vegetables, a leafy salad, maybe a baked sweet potato."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Because GLP-1 medications suppress appetite and can trigger side effects like nausea or constipation, rich, high-fat dishes are much harder on the stomach.

Araujo advises being cautious with fried foods, heavy casseroles and sugary desserts — anything loaded with butter, oils or heavy creams — and sticking to "smaller quantities or smaller portion sizes" if you do indulge.
Portion control
People taking Ozempic or similar medications who have a decreased appetite shouldn’t feel obligated to load up their plates or eat to the point of discomfort, the dietitian said.
At a Thanksgiving table, good sources of protein include roasted turkey without the skin, beans, chickpeas, lentils and tofu, the dietitian said. (iStock)
"Giving ourselves permission to eat smaller portions, not feeling pressured to have to finish everything on our plate, will be helpful during Thanksgiving," she told Fox News Digital.
To help manage portion sizes, Araujo recommends taking a look at what's available before putting food on the plate.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Another tip is to use a smaller plate, like a salad plate, if that's available," she suggested, noting that it’s best to eat slowly, take small bites and listen to "satiety cues."
"If you still have food left on the plate, I think asking for a to-go dish is always a good idea," Araujo added.
Advance prep and healthy swaps
For those who are concerned that healthy foods might not be available on Thanksgiving, it’s wise to contact the host ahead of time.
"That looks delicious. Thank you for offering. I've had enough."

"You can ask about food choices, or even offer to bring your own dish," Araujo said. "Use that as an opportunity to bring something that's nutrient-dense that you know you can eat and tolerate and still enjoy the gathering, but feel well."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

When possible, she recommends putting a healthy spin on traditional Thanksgiving dishes. "For example, we can make stuffing healthier by swapping the white bread for a whole-grain, high-fiber bread and adding in some vegetables."

title: Taking Ozempic or Wegovy could lead to extra cancer screenings, new study suggests
summary: A study for the Radiological Society of North America links GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy to higher breast density on mammograms in 62.5% of women.
story: AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Elisa Port, Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Breast Advice,' highlights how AI uncovers hidden tumors and slashes false positive results, especially for women with dense breasts.
Women taking popular weight loss medications may have higher breast density on mammograms and require more follow-up imaging, even when none of those abnormalities turn out to be cancer.
That's according to a new study scheduled for presentation at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, Nov. 29-Dec. 3, 2026, in Chicago.
The study examined 107 women, ages 34 to 79, who took GLP-1 receptor agonists, a class of drugs that includes Ozempic and Wegovy, for weight loss for at least one year.
POPULAR WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES

Participants lost between six and 107 pounds, with an average loss of 40 pounds. Researchers reviewed 214 screening mammograms taken before and after at least a year of treatment, according to the study.
Specialized software showed that breast density rose by at least one category in 62.5% of participants who took GLP-1s. Eight women moved up two density categories.
Radiologists also saw smaller breasts in roughly 58% to 79% of patients, depending on the reviewer, and increased skin thickening in about 9% to 18%.
Women who lost weight on GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy for at least a year saw higher breast density on mammograms. (iStock)
Higher breast density is generally tied to a greater risk of breast cancer and can make tumors harder to spot on X-rays.

However, the pattern seen after weight loss likely reflects a shift in proportions rather than more dense tissue growing, according to lead author Dr. Eva C. Gombos, a diagnostic radiologist at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston.
POPULAR WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
"It was surprising that 62.5% of women had increased BI-RADS breast density despite substantial weight loss, with no decreases observed," Gombos said in a release.
"This may reflect disproportionate loss of breast fat, causing a relative increase in mammographic density even as absolute fibroglandular volume decreases."

When a person loses significant fat from the breast, the remaining milk ducts and supportive tissue — known as fibroglandular tissue — can make up a larger share of what shows up on the image, even if the total amount of that tissue did not grow.
Gombos also noted that losing breast fat and volume can leave extra skin or skin folds, which may help explain why skin and connective tissue strands looked more prominent on some scans.

Researchers emphasized that the imaging changes should not discourage women from taking GLP-1 drugs or getting routine mammograms since any long-term impact on breast cancer risk remains uncertain. (iStock)
Nearly 22.4% of the women were called back for additional imaging after screening, compared with an average U.S. recall rate of about 10%.

Two women had technical recalls to repeat scans due to positioning or imaging issues. Four women were referred for biopsies, and all four came back benign. All other callbacks also turned out to be benign or negative, including three simple cysts.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Gombos emphasized that the findings should not pose a concern for women taking GLP-1 drugs or cause them to skip routine screenings.
Whether these density shifts carry any long-term change in breast cancer risk remains unclear and needs more research.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The study was retrospective and looked back at medical records rather than following patients forward in a controlled trial, the researchers noted.
It did not establish whether the imaging changes affect long-term breast cancer risk.

Because rapid weight loss can alter how breast tissue looks on scans, patients should tell their mammography teams about GLP-1 use and recent weight loss so radiologists can interpret changes accurately. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Gombos recommends that women tell their breast imaging team if they use GLP-1 medications or have recently lost a significant amount of weight because it helps technologists and radiologists more accurately compare new scans to older ones.
Novo Nordisk, maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, emphasized that it continuously monitors the safety profile of its medicines, reviewing emerging data as it becomes available.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Individuals respond to treatment uniquely based on multiple biological and lifestyle factors, which means outcomes can vary from person to person," a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
"We recommend that all patients maintain close contact with their healthcare professional to discuss any questions or concerns about their treatment, and for ongoing guidance and careful monitoring."

title: Doctors warn of lead exposure health risks after controversial Army detonation in Iowa
summary: The Army detonated five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, and FEMA says residents within 20 miles must shelter until the all clear.
story: Officials share the latest details with the public after the U.S. Army detonated the 68 barrels of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

The U.S. Army blew up about five tons of lead azide, a toxic bomb-making chemical, in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, raising concerns over airborne heavy-metal exposure.
The mission was reportedly necessary because the substances were "unstable" and liable to explode if tampered with.

While a Trump administration official reported that the detonation exceeded expectations by achieving maximum mitigation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) warned that residents within 20 miles should continue to shelter in place to avoid inhaling lead dust, and should follow EPA safety guidance "until given the all clear by officials."
IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

"[The] EPA has been on the ground in Iowa BEFORE the controlled detonation, we will be here DURING the detonation, and we will be here for as long as necessary AFTER detonation to ensure communities are safe," the Environmental Protection Agency said prior to the blast.
Barrels of unstable lead azide are stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant ahead of a planned controlled detonation Wednesday. (U.S. Army)
The agency predicted a brief increase in lead in the air above Middletown, as officials in Iowa and Missouri warned of potential exposure to toxic lead dust.
According to Mayo Clinic, even small amounts of lead can cause serious health problems. Long-term buildup of lead in the body can get stored and slowly re-enter the bloodstream over time.
AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY
At very high levels, lead can damage the kidneys and nervous system in both children and adults, leading to complications in the brain, seizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms and unconsciousness.
Children under 6 years old are the most susceptible, as lead poisoning can severely impact development of their bodies and brains.
A plume rises after the U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of lead azide at its Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Austin Johnson)

According to the Iowa Farm Bureau, Iowa leads the nation in producing corn, pigs, eggs, ethanol and biodiesel — commodities that end up in everyday household products." The state also ranks No. 2 in soybean production and cover crops.
One Iowa farmer, Doug Seyb, spoke with PBS about his concern that the detonation could impact his nearby farm, including his cows out at pasture and local ponds that fill the farm's water tank.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The public fears that lead could eventually enter the food supply through crops grown in contaminated soil and livestock raised on contaminated water.
Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician, medical toxicologist and Fox News medical contributor, confirmed that lead being dispersed into the air is "not a small deal."
Children are especially susceptible to lead poisoning, medical experts caution. (iStock)
"Lead has no beneficial role in human physiology," she said. "In fact, lead in the human body can really mess with biology."

People who eat fresh produce already take in trace amounts of heavy metals like lead, which is widespread in soil — but detonating a "tremendous amount" of the toxic metal raises the risk of dangerous exposure, Widmer warned.
AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY
"If there is an enormous amount that is going to be contaminating the food supply, the water, the air that people are breathing in, this is very concerning," she said.
The US Army detonated a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026. (Reuters/Jim Urquhart)
Widmer suggested that Americans near the detonation site should continue to listen to guidance to shelter in place, keep windows closed, and turn on ventilation or air purifying systems.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We know that lead is dangerous for humans, but we don't know how much, or if any, lead they're being exposed to," she said. "It could be none. It could a ton."
The EPA reported no levels of lead in the air 30 minutes after the detonation, but Widmer noted that just because the blow is over doesn't mean there is no lingering impact.

"Lead inhalation is one of the most efficient ways that lead can be dispersed into the human body," she said, adding that even if it's not inhaled, it can be dispersed into the soil. "It can stay in soil, it could stay in water," the doctor said.

"The very concerning thing is that lead can have negative effects on the human body without even showing any symptoms," she said. "There's still going to have to be testing. Follow-up is really key here."
Lead poisoning symptoms
Symptoms in adults can include the following, according to Cleveland Clinic.

Besides breathing in the toxic lead dust dispersed through the air, fallen particles contaminating water and soil can also pose a health risk, experts say.

Those who believe they have been exposed to lead, even without showing symptoms, should visit a healthcare provider for a blood test to check for exposure and lead levels, Widmer advised.
