title: How skipping breakfast to save room for dinner shocks your blood sugar and metabolism
summary: Dietitian Gabrielle Kishner warns that skipping breakfast before Thanksgiving causes blood sugar crashes, carb cravings and overeating at the holiday meal.
story: New York City registered dietitian Gabrielle Kishner says skipping breakfast and lunch on Thanksgiving lowers blood sugar, which can trigger sugar cravings and lead to overeating at dinner.
Fasting all morning to save room for a big holiday feast might seem like a smart strategy, but experts say it can have unwanted health effects, and that there are better ways to prepare.

When people go hours without food, blood sugar levels drop, triggering headaches, nausea and irritability, according to Gabrielle Kishner, a registered dietitian nutritionist and founder in New York City.

"Once we get those uncomfortable symptoms of hunger, we're going to eat really fast when we get into Thanksgiving, because we're starving," Kishner told Fox News Digital. "We're also going to crave more carbs and sugar to get that blood sugar back up."
DOCTORS SETTLE DEBATE OVER DRINKING COFFEE ON AN EMPTY STOMACH AND POTENTIAL HEALTH RISKS
Previous research has found that skipping daytime meals leads to significantly higher post-meal blood glucose spikes at dinner compared with eating regular meals.
Regular breakfast omission has also been linked to disrupted circadian rhythms, impaired insulin sensitivity and a sluggish metabolism, as well as compensatory eating later in the day.
The expert recommends eating a balanced breakfast containing carbohydrates, protein, fiber and healthy fats within two hours of waking. (iStock)
To avoid coming to the dinner table starving, Kishner recommends eating a balanced breakfast within two hours of waking up and avoiding gaps of longer than four to six hours without food.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Combining carbohydrates, protein, fiber and healthy fats like Greek yogurt with berries and chia seeds, or avocado toast topped with hard-boiled eggs, helps stabilize energy and blood sugar, so diners arrive "comfortably hungry," she said.
If the main meal takes place early in the afternoon, a balanced midmorning snack containing two nutrient groups, like vegetables and hummus, can help bridge the gap.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
How diners build that first plate also affects digestion and energy.
Kishner recommends filling half the plate with fiber-rich fruits and vegetables, eating those first to slow digestion and help stabilize fullness.
The second half of the plate should be split evenly between protein, like turkey, and carbohydrates, such as stuffing or mashed potatoes.
The dietitian urges diners not to compensate the next morning by restricting food or skipping breakfast again, which only restarts the cycle of blood sugar crashes and overeating. (iStock)

Once the meal begins, pacing plays a major role in preventing gastrointestinal distress, Kishner said. Eating quickly makes it harder for the stomach to break down poorly chewed food, leading to bloating and discomfort.

It takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes for the stomach to send satiety signals to the brain, meaning fast eaters often consume far more food than they need before realizing they are full, according to Cleveland Clinic.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Kishner recommends pausing midway through the meal to assess hunger levels, and waiting 10 to 20 minutes after finishing a plate before going back for seconds.
Rich, creamy and sugary dishes take longer to digest, so sampling small portions from the dessert table helps to prevent stomachaches without making favorite foods off-limits.
Sip water throughout the day and return to your normal eating routine the following morning rather than restricting food to compensate, the expert advises. (iStock)

For those who do end up overindulging, gentle movement afterward can ease the post-meal slump. Kishner suggests taking a 10- to 15-minute walk with family or friends after the meal to aid digestion and blood sugar regulation.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Blood sugar typically peaks 30 to 90 minutes after a meal, and even brief, light-intensity walking helps blunt glucose spikes and keep insulin levels steady. Drinking water throughout the day also helps to digest food, according to Kishner.
Above all, Kishner urges diners not to compensate the next morning by restricting food or skipping breakfast again, which only restarts the cycle of blood sugar crashes and overeating.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: FDA approves first new breast cancer hormone therapy in over two decades
summary: Genentech says its oral drug Wilserdly reduced recurrence or death risk by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy in the Phase III lidERA breast cancer trial.
story: National Cancer Institute Director Tony Letai joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to discuss an NIH study linking exposure to ‘forever chemicals’ to an increased risk of aggressive breast cancer.
A new early-stage breast cancer therapy has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the first time in more than two decades.

Wilserdly (giredestrant), an oral hormone therapy from San Francisco-based drugmaker Genentech, received the approval after positive trial results in treating adults with early-stage ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.
This subtype is the most common form of the disease in which tumor growth is fueled by the hormone estrogen rather than excess levels of the HER2 protein.
NEW DRUG APPROACH OFFERS HOPE FOR PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT AGGRESSIVE CANCERS

The Phase 3 lidERA study showed that the drug reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy, including generic pharmaceuticals like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, according to a Genentech press release.
Wilserdly by Genentech has been approved by the FDA to treat early-stage and advanced breast cancer. (Genentech)
Patients were also less likely to quit treatment because of side effects like joint pain and hot flashes compared to standard options, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study found a reduction in cancer returning in distant parts of the body, like the bones, liver or lungs.

Aditya Bardia, M.D., global principal investigator of the lidERA breast cancer trial and professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, noted that this finding is "particularly significant" because once breast cancer spreads to distant organs, it is "generally no longer curable."
The phase III lidERA study showed the drug reduced the risk of disease occurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy. (iStock)
The foundational hormone therapies used for early-stage breast cancer have remained "largely unchanged" since the 2000s, Bardia told Fox News Digital.
"These medicines have saved countless lives, but there has been room for improvement, both in terms of effectiveness and tolerability," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Now, for the first time in more than two decades, we have a new foundational hormone treatment that has been shown to be more effective than our existing standard therapies in early-stage breast cancer."
Because most breast cancers are caught early and fall into the hormone receptor-positive subtype, the new therapy has the potential to help a large number of patients, Bardia added.
Genentech plans to continue developing how Wilserdly can serve breast cancer patients. (iStock)

Earlier this year, the FDA also approved Wilserdly combined with everolimus, an oral cancer medication, for the treatment of adults with ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease had recurred during or after completing endocrine-based therapy.
This makes Wilserdly the "first and only" SERD (selective estrogen receptor degrader) that is FDA-approved to treat both early-stage and advanced ER-positive breast cancer.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Levi Garraway, M.D., chief medical officer and head of global product development, commented in a statement that the FDA approval is due to the drug showing "superior efficacy" against other therapies that have long been the standard of care.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, plans to continue investing in "broad development" of Wilserdly, exploring its potential across disease stages and in new treatment combinations, according to Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham.

Bardia encouraged patients to speak with their oncologists about the new treatment option, particularly those whose recent diagnosis is "consistent with the regulatory label and approval of the drug. "
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Popular actor says bladder cancer discovery followed one strange bathroom symptom
summary: Jonathan Frakes says the sight of pink urine led to a cystoscopy and a high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer diagnosis caught in time.
story: Board-certified physician Dr. Janette Nesheiwat joins 'Fox News Live' to break down the American Cancer Society's updated prostate screening protocols for men aged 50 to 69.
For "Star Trek: The Next Generation" star Jonathan Frakes, a life-altering health scare began not with physical pain, but with a strange sighting during a regular trip to Phoenix.
"My pee was pink," Frakes shared during an episode of his podcast, "Dropping Names with Brent and Jonny," alongside his co-star Brent Spiner and urologic surgeon Dr. Ram Narayanan. "I was unnerved."
Searching for an easy explanation, Frakes said he considered blaming his diet. Maybe it was beets, he mused, before realizing he hadn't touched one in six years.
MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS
Frakes ultimately called his doctor, a decision that may have saved his bladder.
According to Narayanan, Frakes experienced what is clinically known as painless gross hematuria, or visible blood in the urine without accompanying pain.
Painless visible blood in the urine can be a medical red flag requiring a trip to the doctor for urological evaluation.
"When it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag," the doctor said on the podcast.

While blood in the urine can stem from benign causes like urinary tract infections or kidney stones, painless visible hematuria is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. It always warrants an immediate urological evaluation, according to both Cleveland Clinic and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
DIAGNOSTIC TEST COULD FLAG WHICH MEN NEED AGGRESSIVE PROSTATE CANCER TREATMENT AND WHICH DON'T

Days after finishing a fan convention, Frakes underwent an in-office cystoscopy, a quick procedure in which a thin camera examines the lining of the bladder. Inside, Narayanan spotted small, fern-like growths.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Three days later, Frakes was in the operating room to undergo a blue light cystoscopy — a specialized exam that uses an imaging dye to make hidden tumors glow — and tumor resection to scrape away the abnormal tissue.
The biopsy confirmed high-grade, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
Jonathan Frakes credited his wife, Genie Francis, for saving his life by encouraging him to act quickly and get evaluated right away. (Getty Images for Hallmark Media)

To illustrate why early timing was so critical, Narayanan compared the bladder to a layer cake — scraping away the surface "icing" removed the tumor before it could invade the deeper muscle wall, which often forces surgeons to remove the entire bladder and fashion a new one from a piece of intestine.
"At the end of it, he says, 'I think we got it all,'" Frakes recalled.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
To prevent the cancer from returning, Frakes underwent six weekly rounds of intravesical therapy, where a liquid medication is placed directly into the bladder.
While immunotherapy is the standard first-line treatment, a nationwide shortage led Narayanan to administer a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and docetaxel.
"At the end of it, he says, ‘I think we got it all.’"
According to medical experts, this dual-agent chemotherapy has proven to be a highly effective alternative during immunotherapy shortages.

While inspecting Frakes’ bladder, Narayanan noticed a secondary issue: an enlarged prostate. As Frakes joked on air, his surgeon told him, "While I was in there, I noticed your prostate is the size of a small town."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The enlarged prostate was forcing Frakes’ bladder muscle to work overtime, a condition called trabeculation, which can eventually lead to bladder failure.
After ruling out prostate cancer via MRI, Narayanan performed a surgery to remove roughly 135 grams of obstructing tissue through a single tiny incision.

The cast of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" poses in California in 1987. Front row, from left: Marina Sirtis (Counselor Deanna Troi), Patrick Stewart (Captain Jean-Luc Picard), and Gates McFadden (Dr. Beverly Crusher). Back row, from left: Jonathan Frakes (Commander William T. Riker), Brent Spiner (Lt. Commander Data), Whoopi Goldberg (Guinan), LeVar Burton (Lt. Commander Geordi La Forge), and Michael Dorn (Lt. Worf). ((Photo by CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images))
As a result, Frakes was able to stop taking his daily prostate medications, and his urinary symptoms vanished.

Other than immediate family, the actor kept his diagnosis private until deciding to share his story during Men’s Health Awareness Month to encourage other men to overcome their reluctance to see a urologist, whom Narayanan affectionately calls "primary care doctors below the belt."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If something happens like [what] happened to you, check it out immediately," the doctor urged listeners. "Don't be shy. Don't be afraid."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
summary: Pennsylvania officials say an unvaccinated Centre County resident died of measles, the ninth death this year, as the state leads the nation in cases.
story: Dr. Marc Siegel warns that dropping measles vaccination rates could cost the U.S. its elimination status. The Fox News senior medical analyst joins hosts Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the rise to over 5,000 cases in 2026. Siegel outlines what is driving the decline and explains how communities can protect public health.

Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.
Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.
The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.
A measles screening sign is posted at the entrance of Geisinger's Hospital for Advanced Medicine in Danville, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 21, 2026. (Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.
Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.
Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.
Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

One-year-old River Jacobs is held by his mother, Caitlin Fuller, while he receives an MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio, at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025, in Lubbock, Texas. (Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)
TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM
The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.
For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.
Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

Josh Shapiro, governor of Pennsylvania, speaks during the Bradford County Democrats Breakfast at the Sayre VFW in Sayre, Pennsylvania, on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. (Photographer: Heather Ainsworth/Bloomberg)
AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’
Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.
When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.
Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an event at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services building on Oct. 5, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.
The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Alzheimer’s risk jumps 53% for millions living with common blood sugar condition
summary: New research suggests people with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, with experts pointing to blood sugar control.
story: Dr. Caghan Kizil, professor of neurological sciences at Columbia University Department of Neurology, discusses new research showing that people living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.
People living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without the condition, a new study suggests.
Researchers from Curtin University's School of Population Health in Australia reviewed 40 observational studies including people with Alzheimer’s disease and type 2 diabetes.

After accounting for other health and lifestyle factors, the researchers found that individuals with this condition have a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. That translates to roughly 4.7 new cases for every 1,000 people tracked over a year.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

"It doesn't add newer experiments or show that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer's disease, but how we should read it is that someone with diabetes has about one and a half times more chance of getting Alzheimer's disease compared to someone without it," Dr. Caghan Kizil, professor of neurological sciences at Columbia University Department of Neurology and recipient of the Catalyst Cure One, Cure Many Award in Neuroinflammation from the American Brain Foundation, told Fox News Digital.
People living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without the condition, a new study suggests. (iStock)
The findings were published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy on Nov. 9.
ALZHEIMER’S BLOOD MARKER COULD PREDICT COGNITIVE DECLINE RISKS, MAYO CLINIC SAYS

Unlike earlier reviews that often combined different forms of diabetes and dementia, the new analysis looked specifically at type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease to calculate the rate of new cases, according to lead study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health.
Researchers found that individuals with type 2 diabetes have a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. (iStock)

"Reporting both relative risk and incidence measures helps explain not only whether risk is higher, but how frequently new cases occur," Adewuyi told Fox News Digital. "What stood out was the fuller picture that emerged when we examined how often Alzheimer’s disease developed alongside how risk compared between groups."
Experts point to a few key ways that poor blood sugar control harms brain cells over time.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES

Excess blood sugar can stiffen and narrow blood vessels in the brain, causing a decrease in blood flow and oxygen to brain cells, according to Dr. Nikhil Palekar, director of Stony Brook Medicine's Center of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease in New York.
"Insulin resistance prevents the brain cells from utilizing glucose, resulting in reduced cellular energy and neuronal functions," Palekar, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
To protect brain health, a doctor advises monitoring blood sugar, getting 150 minutes of weekly moderate aerobic exercise and eating a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet. (iStock)
Maintaining optimal blood sugar levels can reduce the risk for Alzheimer’s, the doctor confirmed.
"GLP-1 agonists have been shown to lower elevated blood sugar levels as well [as] decrease brain inflammation, which is a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease," Palekar said.
Limitations of the analysis
There were some limitations, including extreme variation across the studies.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Because the individual studies reported vastly different rates — ranging from fewer than one to nearly 30 new cases per 1,000 people each year — the researchers could not pinpoint a single, exact risk rate.
Additionally, the analysis relied on real-world observational data rather than controlled clinical trials.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Importantly, these are population-level findings," Adewuyi said. "They cannot predict whether a particular person will develop Alzheimer’s disease."
Variations in where the studies were conducted, how long patients were tracked and which outside health factors were considered all influenced the outcomes.
The early signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s are most often related to becoming more forgetful, according to a doctor. (iStock)
Alzheimer's is one of the most prevalent dementia types, comprising almost 70% of all cases, Kizil noted, which is why the studies are heavily focused on that condition.
However, as diabetes can deprive the brain of essential nutrients, it can contribute to a wide range of neurological diseases beyond just Alzheimer’s.
Lowering the risk
For people who have diabetes along with an increased risk of developing dementia, Kizil recommends undergoing cognitive screenings much earlier, alongside blood sugar control and other measurements.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

People with diabetes or any type of cardiovascular risk factors, including high blood pressure, should work proactively with their doctors on metabolic control and earlier cognitive monitoring, he advised.
Adewuyi emphasized that the study provides no basis for changing medication or adopting tighter blood glucose targets specifically to prevent Alzheimer’s disease.
To support brain health, a doctor recommends following a primary care physician’s guidance to closely monitor blood sugar levels alongside key lifestyle modifications. (iStock)

"If someone notices persistent changes in memory or thinking – particularly if these are affecting medicines, glucose monitoring or daily activities – they should discuss them with their healthcare team," he advised.
The early signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s are most often related to becoming more forgetful, according to Palekar.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Some of those include "short-term memory loss, such as forgetting recent events or conversations, misplacing things routinely, having difficulty managing finances or performing complex daily tasks," the doctor told Fox News Digital.

To support brain health, Palekar recommends following a primary care physician’s guidance to closely monitor blood sugar levels alongside key lifestyle modifications — "specifically, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise 150 minutes a week and a balanced diet, such as the Mediterranean diet."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Who owns your body parts after surgery? Doctors uncover the complicated rules
summary: Surgical patients are asking hospitals to hand over removed organs, teeth and joints as keepsakes, but pathology rules and release forms stand in the way.
story: Dr. Raymond Lynch, director of the Division of Transplantation at HRSA, discusses how updated federal organ donation guidelines seek to protect patients and improve communication with families facing difficult end-of-life decisions.
Most people want to forget their time in the operating room, yet some surgical patients insist on bringing their removed body parts home as souvenirs.

While hospitals usually throw away removed tissue as medical waste, a small number of patients asks doctors to pack up their organs, teeth and worn-out joints after surgery, according to TIME magazine.
Doctors say these patients want keepsakes for many reasons, from marking personal milestones to honoring cultural traditions.
ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

Examples included a patient who kept her removed uterus in a jar after a hysterectomy as a reminder of the pain she survived, and another who dried her removed fallopian tubes to display in a box with flowers, according to the report.
While hospitals typically discard removed tissue as medical waste, some surgical patients ask to bring their organs, teeth or joints home as souvenirs. (iStock)
Other saved items included a pulled wisdom tooth fashioned into a calligraphy pen and a piece of medical tubing saved from a hospital stay and later given to a future spouse, the magazine said.

Dr. Robyn Power, a gynecologic surgeon in South Florida, told TIME that only about five of her patients finished the paperwork to take tissue home over the past year, though more people are asking about it.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
She said patients living with painful conditions like endometriosis sometimes want the removed tissue as physical proof of what disrupted their lives.
"It means something different to everybody," Power said.
Hospital rules and safety

Taking a body part home takes more than asking a surgeon in the recovery room.Dr. Kenneth Perry, an emergency room physician based in South Carolina, told Fox News Digital that rules surrounding who owns removed tissue vary widely.
Before any surgical tissue can be released to a patient, pathologists must examine the specimen for disease. (iStock)

"As odd as it sounds, the ownership of tissue and other things removed from a person’s body is actually not settled law," Perry said. "Each state and each institution will have its own views on how to handle different tissues."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

In the emergency room, Perry said doctors often let patients take home low-risk items like passed kidney stones, salivary gland stones or splinters, as long as the objects are not tied to a police case, like a bullet.
Larger organs or body parts carry more risk because doctors must rule out infection or serious disease before releasing them.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"For instance, if an extremity or an organ has been removed due to infection or bleeding, it is often required that it goes through pathology testing to ensure it is safe," Perry said.

He added that for pregnancy-related tissues, such as a placenta or remains from a miscarriage, hospitals typically have different rules and separate steps involved for families who ask to take them home.
Patients debate the rules online
Some surgical patients have taken to Reddit to share their confusion and experiences with trying to keep removed body parts.
Surgeons say patients request removed tissue for varied reasons, from honoring cultural traditions to keeping physical proof of chronic conditions. (iStock)

"Seeing as the hip bone is coming from my own body, I don't understand why I cannot," one user wrote ahead of a hip replacement in Washington State after a surgeon claimed that state law rejected his request to keep the bone.
"My best friend's son got to keep one of his tonsils to take to school for show and tell," the user added.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Others pushed back, pointing to health hazards and hospital rules.
"It's considered medical waste. Yes, bones can carry risks," one commenter wrote.

"It really depends on the state laws, but most will not allow it," wrote another user who said they worked in pathology. "You can have a funeral home bury it if you like, but probably not take it home."

title: Popular bedroom supplements often fail to deliver, says longevity physician
summary: Dr. Pablo Prichard shares why most sexual enhancement supplements fail and how L-arginine and L-citrulline may help blood flow and erectile dysfunction.
story: Dr. Pablo Prichard, an Arizona-based surgeon who focuses on longevity and preventative health, warns that most over-the-counter sexual enhancement products are ineffective — and some carry health risks.

Pharmacy aisles and social media feeds are crowded with capsules, powders and gummies promising to boost libido and sexual performance. Yet according to physicians and clinical research, most over-the-counter sexual enhancement products are ineffective — and some carry health risks.
It's a mistake to treat all sexual health concerns as a single problem, according to Dr. Pablo Prichard, an Arizona-based surgeon who focuses on longevity and preventative health.
Before reaching for a bottle, patients should understand the difference between low sex drive and physical performance issues like erectile dysfunction or vaginal dryness, he told Fox News Digital.
WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD
"When you're looking at supplements, you have to think, ‘Is this supplement affecting what my problem is individually?’" Prichard said.
"Because if you have a hormonal issue, and you take a supplement that supposedly increases your blood flow, that doesn't necessarily improve your condition."
Hundreds of unregulated "all-natural" supplements have been found by the FDA to contain hidden, undeclared prescription drugs like sildenafil and tadalafil, the doctor said. (iStock)

If performance issues stem from restricted circulation, certain amino acids may offer modest support. Supplements like L-arginine and L-citrulline target the nitric oxide pathway, which helps relax and widen blood vessels, Prichard said.
According to Cleveland Clinic, L-citrulline converts into L-arginine in the body to boost nitric oxide production, and small clinical studies suggest it may help improve mild erectile dysfunction.
VIAGRA COULD DO MORE THAN ADVERTISED AS STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH SUPERPOWER
Still, the clinic notes that overall scientific evidence remains mixed, larger clinical trials are needed, and the supplements are less reliable than prescription treatments.

"If you actually have a blood-flow issue, then taking a supplement like this … that improves your blood flow could actually help," Prichard said. "If you don't have a blood-flow issue, and it's another problem, then taking a supplement like this probably won't help."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While certain herbal extracts, such as Panax ginseng and saffron, have shown potential in small trials to improve erectile function and sexual satisfaction, experts urge caution with unregulated sexual enhancement blends.
"The FDA has repeatedly seen actual Viagra in these 'herbal Viagra' medications," Prichard said.

Mixing hidden prescription ingredients or certain herbs with heart medications, blood pressure drugs or blood thinners can trigger life-threatening drops in blood pressure or elevated bleeding risks. (iStock)

Laboratory testing by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has identified hundreds of over-the-counter products marketed as "all-natural" sexual enhancers that secretly contain prescription drug ingredients — most commonly sildenafil (the active ingredient in Viagra) and tadalafil (found in Cialis).

Because these hidden drugs aren't listed on the label, the agency warns that consumers risk dangerous side effects or severe drops in blood pressure, particularly if they take heart medications containing nitrates.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Taking unknown doses of prescription erectile dysfunction drugs can trigger dangerous side effects.

Prichard warned that combining hidden sildenafil — or even high doses of L-arginine — with heart medications like nitroglycerin or hypertension drugs can cause life-threatening drops in blood pressure. Similarly, mixing herbs like ginkgo biloba with blood thinners can elevate bleeding risks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For both men and women experiencing low desire or dryness tied to shifting hormone levels, consulting with a physician is more effective than guessing at the store, the doctor advised.

Fundamental lifestyle habits such as getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, managing stress and consulting a doctor for underlying medical conditions are far more effective than relying on pills. (iStock)
Any new or worsening changes in sexual function warrant a medical checkup, as they could be a warning sign of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or depression.
"I think a lot of times, people take the easy way out and say, 'Yeah, I have this problem, I'm just going to take this pill ... and that's going to fix my problem,'" Prichard said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Foundational habits like prioritizing sleep, managing stress and getting both aerobic and strength exercise "can have a much bigger influence on your sexual health than just taking a supplement," the doctor added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Common sleep habit linked to 50% higher death risk in heart patients, recent study finds
summary: A PLOS One study of 3,287 US adults with heart disease links sleeping nine or more hours to a 51% higher risk of all-cause mortality over 15 years.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses a new study challenging the traditional eight hour sleep rule on America Reports.

Adults with heart disease who sleep nine or more hours per night could be at a higher risk of death from both heart-related and non-heart-related causes than those who sleep seven to eight hours, according to a recent study.

The cohort study in the journal PLOS One, titled "Sleep duration and cause-specific mortality among US adults with heart disease," analyzed data from 3,287 adults with heart disease from the 2004 National Health Survey linked to the National Death Index running until Dec. 31, 2019.

In the National Health Survey, participants answered whether they had heart disease based on if they had ever been told they had coronary heart disease, a heart attack or a heart condition or disease, according to the study.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

"Sleep affects blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, inflammation, and appetite hormones, and all of these influence cardiovascular risk," Erin Palinksi-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian and Certified Diabetes Care and Education Specialist (CDCES), told Fox News Digital.
Sleeping too much or not enough could be warning signs of various health problems and worth mentioning to a doctor. (iStock)
The study authors adjusted for health factors and lifestyle behaviors such as body mass index (BMI), alcohol consumption, smoking, physical activity, diabetes, hypertension and more.
Sleep per 24 hours was categorized into durations of six hours or less, seven to eight hours and nine or more hours.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Over approximately 15 years of follow-up, 49.4% of participants died.
Out of all participants, 16.7% died from heart-related causes and 32.6% died from non-heart-related causes.
Sleep impacts blood pressure, blood sugar regulation and inflammation, which all influence cardiovascular risk. (iStock)
After adjusting for all lifestyle factors, researchers found that sleeping nine or more hours was linked to a higher mortality risk, compared with sleeping seven to eight hours.
There was a 51% increased risk of all causes of death, a 53% increased risk of heart-related causes of death and a 50% increased risk of non-heart-related mortality.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Sleep duration of six hours or less was significantly associated with non-heart-related death only in the least-adjusted model, and the connection weakened with further adjustment.

"Because the study is observational, it shows an association, not cause and effect. Long sleep may be a symptom of underlying problems like more advanced heart disease, depression, sleep apnea, or medication side effects, and the study couldn't fully account for those," Palinski-Wade said.
It's important to monitor heart health, which includes paying attention to sleep quality and quantity, registered dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade noted. (iStock)
The authors noted that their findings do not invalidate the negative cardiovascular effects of getting too little sleep.

"I'm not aware of a convincing biological mechanism by which extra hours of sleep damage the heart," Antony Chu, MD, a cardiologist and clinical assistant professor at Brown University’s Warren Alpert School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"What I see clinically is that patients sleep longer because something is pulling on their reserve: worsening heart failure, untreated obstructive or central sleep apnea, depression, sedating medications, anemia or frailty," Chu said.

Sleeping too much or too little are both potential red flags, Palinski-Wade noted, so it’s important for people to pay attention to how rested they feel rather than only focusing on the number of hours they slept.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Because the study only tested people with pre-existing heart conditions, it should not be used to suggest that prolonged sleep leads to heart disease in the general population, she added.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Social media users are eating huge amounts of carrots and shrimp for a natural tan
summary: Dr. Navin Arora says the viral carrot tan from eating carrots, tomatoes and shrimp is real but no substitute for sunscreen and basic sun safety.
story: Dermatologist Dr. Jody Levine joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss critical sun safety topics during Wellness Week. Dr. Levine explains why a base tan offers minimal protection and compares different types of sunscreen and the protection they provide.
Some social media users are "carrotmaxxing," "tomatomaxxing" and "shrimpmaxxing," in the hopes of getting a sun-kissed glow that lasts them all winter long.

The trend, which calls for eating large quantities of carrots, tomatoes and shrimp, or taking supplements packed with their compounds, relies on carotenoids, natural pigments found in certain foods, the New York Post recently reported.

The outlet highlighted wellness creators promoting raw carrots as a way to get a "carrot tan," including one who said she no longer gets fake tans, and followed two Atlanta moms who said they take a daily carotenoid supplement for a "healthy glow."
COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY
The supplement they take is a blend of three carotenoid pigments: beta-carotene, lycopene and astaxanthin, the compounds that give carrots, tomatoes, shrimp and salmon their color.
Carrots contain beta-carotene, a pigment that can affect skin tone. (iStock)
Wellness influencer Lee Tilghman Pollis, meanwhile, recently said on Instagram that raw carrots have given her "the best skin of my life and I will die on this hill."

Another influencer went viral on TikTok for her carrot tan, telling followers that she no longer gets fake tans or stays out in the sun and instead eats three to four large carrots a day for several months to build up her tan.
DOCTOR REVEALS 4 HIDDEN HEALTH RISKS OF SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INDOORS
Experts say the skin-color change is real and generally harmless, but it's no substitute for basic sun-safety measures.
Carotenoids in tomatoes, shrimp and salmon can also give foods their yellow, orange or red hues. (iStock)

"Beta-carotene, lycopene and astaxanthin are fat-soluble pigments, and when you eat a lot of them they build up in the outermost layer of the skin," Dr. Navin Arora, a board-certified dermatologist and medical director of Borealis Dermatology in New York, told Fox News Digital.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW WILL RESTRICT SALES OF SOME MUSCLE-BUILDING SUPPLEMENTS TO MINORS
The buildup can create a yellow or orange tint, often first visible on the palms, soles and around the nose.

There is no reliable dose for achieving a cosmetic change, Arora said. Small studies have found visible changes after about six weeks of eating extra servings of fruits and vegetables, though results can vary. The color also fades gradually after a person cuts back, he noted.
Dermatologists warn that a carotenoid glow does not protect skin from UV exposure. (iStock)
That pigment buildup, known as carotenemia, is generally harmless, Arora said, but skin that turns yellow-orange without a dietary change should be evaluated by a health care professional.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The food trick does avoid skin damage caused by UV exposure, which also raises the risk of skin cancer and premature aging.
"The carotenoid glow involves no UV damage at all, but it also gives you no meaningful sun protection," Arora warned. "'Carrot color' is not a substitute for sunscreen."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Dermatologists also caution that carotenoid supplements taken for a tan may carry risks for certain people. (iStock)

Arora cautioned against taking high-dose carotenoid supplements for appearance, though. High-dose beta-carotene supplements have been linked to increased lung cancer risk in people who smoke or used to smoke, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For people seeking a bronzed look, Arora recommends self-tanners, professional spray tans, bronzers or tinted sunscreen. He advises pairing them with broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Eating a colorful, carotenoid-rich diet is great for your overall health," he said. "I’d treat the glow as a bonus, not the goal."
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Iconic MTV star turns 60, shares her no-guilt approach to fitness, food and aging well
summary: Daisy Fuentes shares her 20-minute strength training routine, menopause sleep tips and the guilt-free "anti-hustle era" that keeps her strong at 60.
story: As Daisy Fuentes turns 60, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a low-key wellness routine — built on 20-minute workouts, a "magical" sleep trick and a guilt-free "anti-hustle era."
During her 1990s rise as an MTV icon and supermodel, Daisy Fuentes admitted that "being cute" was her top priority.
Now, as she enters her 60s, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a more grounded approach to health.

Speaking with Fox News Digital, Fuentes, who is primarily based in Los Angeles, opened up about embracing a guilt-free "anti-hustle era" — sharing her 20-minute workouts, a "magical" sleep trick and the surprisingly simple habits that keep her rested and strong.
JENNIFER ANISTON’S SECRET TO STAYING FIT AT 57 STARTS WITH ONE SIMPLE WORKOUT ROUTINE
Fuentes’ health and wellness priorities have shifted a great deal in the decades since she started modeling and appearing on TV in her late teens and 20s, she shared.

"In that era, I was more focused on, how can I look better? How can I lose a few pounds to look better in certain clothes? It was very superficial. And as the years have passed, health and wellness has started to become an inside job," Fuentes said.
As Daisy Fuentes turns 60, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a low-key wellness routine. (Daisy Fuentes Instagram/Celeste Canino)

"When you start realizing that most of your life has already happened, how you want to live your life now … becomes more about being present and being able to enjoy the time that you have left," she added.
LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS
Amid the litany of longevity-focused tips and tricks circulating online, Fuentes said she strives to keep it simple and not be "obsessive" about health and wellness.
"On social media, depending on your algorithm, you can get bombarded and overwhelmed with all the [things] that you're supposed to be doing and not doing," she said.
Model and TV personality Daisy Fuentes poses for portraits around September 1993. (Getty Images)

"Yes, some of those things are smart … I do a lot of the things, but I also realized at a certain point that it's much more important to have fun, to be present, to not obsess, and to leave a little room for the unexpected."
Optimizing sleep
As Fuentes entered her 50s, she started to experience some sleep challenges, which she attributed to fluctuating hormones during menopause.

"Balancing out my hormones [and] going on HRT [hormone replacement therapy] helped tremendously," she said. "It got me feeling back to my old self, where the minute I got in bed, I would do a little scrolling and all of a sudden my eyes would start closing."
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG

Although Fuentes admits that she breaks a few traditional "sleep hygiene" rules — such as scrolling on her phone in bed – she does wear red-light-blocking glasses and strives to keep her social media algorithm strictly positive.
Fuentes said she relies on what she describes as a total "sensory experience" to stay asleep, including wearing a silk eye mask.
Fuentes said she strives to keep it simple and not be "obsessive" about health and wellness. (Celeste Canino)
"Right as I'm going to sleep, I pop that mask on, and it's almost like magic," she said. "It does something to your brain. It relaxes you." She also uses an air purifier that provides white noise.
"Our room is set up for sleep," Fuentes said. "We don't hear anything, we don't see anything and it is a sensory experience … a routine that instantly prepares your mind for what it needs to do."
Moving through life
When it comes to fitness, Fuentes said she strives for consistency, but, above all, listens to her body.

A key component of her routine is strength training, which she does four or five times a week. "That doesn't mean it has to be long … I can do a full-body weight training in 20 minutes, and that's what's important to me right now," she said.
WOMEN WHO START COMMON HORMONE THERAPY IN THEIR 50S MAY HAVE 23% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK
Other mainstays of Fuentes’ fitness regimen include Pilates, walking and staying active outdoors. "That's what keeps me and my mind really feeling better," she said.
A key component of Fuentes' fitness routine is strength training, which she does four or five times a week. (iStock)
"Sometimes I get on a vibration plate with my weights and just do 15 minutes of that, doing a plank, doing some sit-ups on it, some squats — I just try to do whatever I can," Fuentes said.
"Some days I have more energy, some days I don't, and I don't beat myself up about it. I do what I feel like doing and as long as I'm doing something, I'm OK."
Eating for longevity

When it comes to nutrition, Fuentes’ biggest shifts over the last decade were driven by physical changes during menopause. Noticing stubborn weight gain around her midsection in her mid-50s, she said she scaled back to about two meals a day and eliminated mindless snacking.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"I try to make it very protein-based," she said. "I start my day with a coffee that already has 20 grams of protein in it ... And if I'm having a snack in the middle of the afternoon, it's going to be protein-packed yogurt with some nuts and berries."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While Fuentes adopted a vegetarian, plant-based diet in her mid-40s, she emphasized that healthy eating doesn't require an "all-or-nothing" mindset, encouraging others to lean into more whole foods that match their lifestyle and preferences.
Embracing an ‘anti-hustle’ lifestyle
After decades of fast-paced working – both on and off-screen – Fuentes made a conscious decision in her late 40s to embrace a slower pace of life.
Fuentes shared her gratitude for being able to enjoy time with her husband, musician Richard Marx, whom she met in her mid-40s. (Getty Images)

"Ambition that never ends is something that I think needs to be adjusted as we flow through life," she said, adding that she no longer desires to "be out there and be chosen" the way she did in her 30s.

"I started embracing the fact that I am in this era of my life where I don't want to work like when I was 30 … and it's OK to feel proud of myself for what I have accomplished," she said. "I don't want to feel guilty for enjoying the fruits of my labor, for enjoying my life now."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

When it comes to decompressing, Fuentes said she recharges by spending quiet time in the home spaces she loves decorating. Some of her favorite ways to unwind include reading, having tea with a friend, sitting in her backyard or taking an hour-long walk.
"I don't want to feel guilty for enjoying the fruits of my labor, for enjoying my life now."
Fuentes shared her gratitude for being able to enjoy time with her husband, musician Richard Marx, whom she met in her mid-40s.

"Finding love and finding your person later in life made me feel so grateful to have the time to spend with him," she said. "Why would I want to pretend to be busy doing something when what really fills my heart is to be with him, to have fun, to do what I want to do right now?"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Fuentes acknowledged that she is in a "privileged" and fortunate position, she pointed out that she spent decades sacrificing to earn it.
Stepping into her "anti-hustle era" in her 50s and 60s, she said, is about questioning whether you are staying busy out of habit — or are ready to embrace a new, more fulfilling stage of life.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: GOP lawmaker who defied blue wave reveals roadmap to win back Gen Z
summary: Clay Fuller says the GOP lost its ability to reach young voters after Charlie Kirk's assassination, urging economic policies to restore the American dream.
story: Young Voices commentator Maggie Anders discusses the shifting political alignment of Gen Z with host Stuart Varney.
Rep. Clay Fuller, R-Ga., said he knows how to get young voters back into the GOP fold.

"Since Charlie Kirk's assassination, I think our side has kind of completely lost the ability to talk to younger Americans," Fuller, who took over for Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., told Fox News Digital.

"I think when we talk to younger Americans, I want to talk directly to that young man or young woman who only has the ability to live in their parents' home because they can't afford a house. Do you know what the average age of a first-time homebuyer in the United States is? It's 39. And that shouldn't be where we are as a country."

At 45 years old, Fuller skews on the younger end of Congress. He's also one of the relatively few bright spots Republicans have seen since November — Fuller won his first full term on Nov. 3 by nearly 20 points, while the House GOP overall suffered significant losses.
BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT
Rep. Clay Fuller, R-Ga., speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on April 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Fuller first came to Congress in mid-2026 via a special election when Greene abruptly resigned amid a public falling out with President Donald Trump.
FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'
And unlike his predecessor toward the end, Fuller has not created divisions between himself and his fellow Republicans. But he's calling on them to do more for America's youth.

He lamented the "brain drain" plaguing both his northwest Georgia district and other parts of the U.S. far outside major cities. Young people leave after college to seek out urban centers with more opportunity, creating a seemingly neverending cycle that sees economic downturns drain the life out of small American communities.
I'M GEN Z: IF THE GOP WANTS MY VOTE, STOP THE SPEECHES AND FIX THE HOUSING CRISIS

"That's the number one thing that I'm focused on every day, is making sure that we're bringing that American dream back to being a reality," Fuller said. "I want that to be true for young Americans, too. When they look at the town that they grew up in and their ancestors have been buried in, they know that they can stay there and have a career."
Fuller himself built a career in his home state, serving in the military after graduating from college before working as a district attorney in northwest Georgia.

He said Republicans could have the high ground with young Americans if they doubled down on their economic policies, as well as the "larger philosophical outlook about who we are as a country and individual rights."
Republican candidate Clay Fuller, right, kisses his wife, Kate, as election results roll in during an election night watch party on April 7, 2026, in Ringgold, Ga. (Mike Stewart/AP Photo)

"I want to talk to those young Americans to say, 'Look, I know this isn't your first choice of where you want to be. And you're doing everything you can to achieve that American dream. That white picket fence should be a reality to you, and every policy that we should put in place, from immigration to economic policy to national security, should be focused on making sure that dream is more accessible to you than it was a couple of weeks ago,'" Fuller said.

"We just have to double down on supporting those policies and putting them in place and keeping that promise to the American voter, and they'll turn back, especially once they see how crazy some of the people that got elected to the House and Senate are going to be."

Young voters were among the key groups who turned away from the GOP en masse during the last election. Fox News' Power Rankings cited disenchantment with the Iran war and Trump's tariffs as key reasons for many Americans' rejection of the right.
JUSTIN HASKINS: 3 HUGE REASONS REPUBLICANS LOST. HERE’S WHAT THEY NEED TO WIN IN 2028
Fuller argued that the next two years, however, will demonstrate that Democrats' policies are not conducive to bringing the American dream back to reality.

"They know what was available to their great-grandparents and their grandparents. That's all they want to see," Fuller said. "I think we can put those economic policies in place, and those young Americans that felt like a house is too far out of reach ... we can put the economic policies in place that makes that a reality. And I think at that point, yeah, people will support us because they know that socialism and communism, it doesn't work."
Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., leaves the Capitol Hill Club after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on March 25, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

During his lengthy sitdown with Fox News Digital, Fuller maintained a focus on economic and health issues for his district — citing "forever chemical" like PFAS multiple times and his push to combat the high rates of cancer among his constituents — even when asked about his predecessor's penchant for throwing verbal bombs at both Democrats and fellow Republicans.
He said he had no ill will toward Greene and even lauded her dedicated staff.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I certainly had talked to her. There were people in our office who had been long-term staff members of hers and appreciated her opinion on both the district and the staff that we had, especially in our district office," Fuller said when asked if Greene helped him with the transition. "She talked glowingly about everybody that worked there, and we have an incredible in-district team. But otherwise, again, I always know any position that I'm going to add to, I've got my own priorities, I've got my own focus. And from day one, that's what I've been focused on."
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: ICE agent faces six years in prison in case that could open 'floodgates' for prosecutions, lawyers warn
summary: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Gregory Morgan faces two assault charges over a Minnesota highway encounter as his attorneys seek federal court.
story: Fox News correspondent Garrett Tenney reports as ICE agent Christian Jerry Castro pleads not guilty to state charges, including second-degree assault, in connection with a Minnesota shooting.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent faces up to six years in prison on an assault charge following a Minnesota highway encounter in which no one was injured.

Gregory Morgan's attorneys warn the case could have far-reaching consequences, potentially emboldening state and local prosecutors nationwide to bring criminal charges against federal officers carrying out President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
At stake in Morgan's legal fight is the extent to which federal protections shield officers from state and local criminal prosecution for actions taken in their official capacity.

"We are the tip of the spear," Rachel Paulose, a former U.S. attorney and managing attorney at the Upper Midwest Law Center, which is helping Morgan fight to keep his case in federal court, told Fox News Digital. "And so what happens here is going to impact what woke, politically motivated district attorneys around the country are doing to persecute law enforcement agents who are simply doing their job and carrying out the orders of an administration with which they disagree."
Morgan was charged on April 16 with two counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon stemming from a Feb. 5 highway encounter during Operation Metro Surge.
15 ANTIFA RADICALS INDICTED, 12 ARRESTED IN SWEEPING FEDERAL PROBE INTO MINNEAPOLIS ANTI-ICE OPERATIONS

Left: Closeup of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and gear during a protest at the Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis, Minnesota, January 8, 2026, in response to the shooting of a woman by an ICE officer who killed the woman. (Photo by Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Right: Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty speaks during a press conference to lay out the charges against Samit Apurva Patel related to the attack on Mohamed Yusuf over the weekend, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, at the Hennepin County Government Center in downtown Minneapolis, Minn. (Photo by Anthony Souffle Lavinsky/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) (Michael Siluk / UCG / Universal Images Group / Getty Images; Anthony Souffle Lavinsky / The Minnesota Star Tribune / Getty Images)
Morgan's attorneys contend he was returning to base under direct orders after withdrawing from a hostile neighborhood where a protester had threatened to kill him.

Unfamiliar with Minnesota roads, Morgan mistakenly drove along the highway shoulder, according to Paulose. The driver of a Cadillac then allegedly swerved into his path twice, braking sharply the second time and bringing Morgan within inches of a collision, according to defense court filings.
Fearing for his safety and that of his fellow ICE agent, Morgan yelled, "Police, back off," and displayed his firearm in what his attorneys described as a "low-ready" position.
Prosecutors, however, alleged Morgan deliberately drove along the shoulder to bypass rush-hour traffic and pointed his firearm at the Cadillac's occupants after the driver attempted to slow him down.
"The defendant attempts to transform his moment of road rage—committed on a state highway against Minnesotan victims—into a federal enforcement action," prosecutors wrote in a June filing.

In a Nov. 19 filing, Morgan's attorneys accused Hennepin County prosecutors of relying on an outdated legal standard in their push to return the case to state court, arguing that the conduct underlying the charges need to just be related to his federal duties, not be explicitly required by them.
Federal immigration agents tackle and arrest a protester in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on Feb. 3, 2026, during Operation Metro Surge. (Alex Kormann/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)
DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST

Morgan's defense rests in part on a federal law with roots dating back to the War of 1812, which allows federal officers facing state criminal charges to move their cases into federal court if the alleged conduct is sufficiently connected to their official duties and they have a plausible federal defense.
Paulose said the law was intended "to insulate federal officers from vindictive prosecutions by local and state officials who simply disagree with federal policy."

Prosecutors maintained Morgan was no longer actively enforcing immigration law during the encounter, but his attorneys argue his authority to protect himself and his fellow agent did not end when he left an enforcement site.
Morgan's attorneys argued prosecutors are relying on a more restrictive legal standard that Congress abandoned in 2011 when it expanded the scope of the law.
"Nothing in the State’s briefs explains why the federal authority to protect federal officers disappears when the officer is on a highway rather than at a target address," Morgan's attorneys wrote.

Both occupants of the Cadillac invoked their Fifth Amendment rights and did not testify during an evidentiary hearing, according to Morgan's latest filing. Morgan, meanwhile, testified and was subjected to cross-examination.

The defense also challenged prosecutors' assertion that the Cadillac driver was unaware Morgan was an ICE agent, citing the driver's statement to investigators that he "got the ICE vibe from him at first."
The driver also reportedly acknowledged making the "not so bright decision to try to stop" Morgan's vehicle.
While prosecutors maintained any threat had subsided before Morgan displayed his gun, his attorneys argued Morgan had no way of knowing whether the driver would strike again.

Ryan Pacyga, Morgan’s defense attorney, also faulted ICE for deploying agents in ordinary rental vehicles without emergency lights or sirens, arguing Morgan had limited means of identifying himself as a law enforcement officer.
"He didn't want this guy hurt. He didn't want to get hurt. He had his partner in the car with him," Pacyga told Fox News Digital.

Morgan's attorneys have seized on Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty's own rhetoric, pointing to her characterization of Operation Metro Surge as an "occupation," to bolster their argument that his case belongs in federal court
"A prosecutor’s hostility is the most direct form that prejudice can take, because the prosecutor decides whom to charge," Morgan's attorneys wrote.
Paulose also took aim at prosecutors' decision to issue a nationwide arrest warrant for Morgan despite his willingness to surrender peacefully.
"I think it underscores that the purpose of this prosecution is not about justice, it's about political grandstanding," Paulose said.
Pacyga characterized the nationwide warrant as a "stunt," questioning why prosecutors waited 10 weeks to charge Morgan despite subsequently arguing he posed a danger warranting $100,000 bail.
A federal law enforcement agent outside a home during a raid in south Minneapolis, Minnesota, on Tuesday, Jan. 13, 2026. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"If that's the argument, you wouldn't sit on it for two months before you charge it, right?" Pacyga said.

Keeping the case in federal court would not strip Moriarty of her authority to prosecute Morgan but would put his fate in the hands of a federal judge, who could dismiss the charges on constitutional immunity grounds.

Should U.S. District Judge Nancy Brasel keep the prosecution in federal court, Morgan's attorneys intend to seek dismissal under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, which can shield federal officers from state criminal liability for actions authorized by federal law and reasonably necessary to carry out their duties.

Paulose also pointed to the independence of federal judges, who receive lifetime appointments, while Pacyga argued that drawing jurors from a larger swath of Minnesota would help insulate Morgan from local hostility toward ICE.

Pacyga said a federal trial would draw prospective jurors from rural and suburban communities across the southern two-thirds of Minnesota, where he believes attitudes toward immigration enforcement are more balanced.
"I'm a lifelong resident of the Twin Cities, and I will tell you that the majority of people in Hennepin County are anti-ICE," Pacyga said.
But if the case is handed off to state court, Morgan's attorneys are prepared to take the fight to the Eighth Circuit.
Pacyga said the legal battle is already attracting attention beyond Minnesota.
DOJ SENDS GRAND JURY SUBPOENAS TO PHILADELPHIA DA KRASNER AFTER JUDGE'S REFERRAL, SOURCES SAY
"There are a lot of different cases around the nation that are watching this case," Pacyga said. "This literally is at the tip of the spear."
For Paulose, the case raises the question about whether law enforcement officers should bear the consequences of political opposition to the administration they serve.

"Unpopular initiatives can be defeated at the ballot box, unpopular politicians can be voted out by the people, but law enforcement officers who are simply doing their job should not and cannot be targeted, persecuted, and prosecuted under our Constitution," Paulose said.
Even before standing trial, Morgan is feeling the financial repercussions of his prosecution.

The agent, a father who shares custody of his daughter, has already lost tens of thousands of dollars in income after being reassigned to duties that prevent him from working overtime, according to Pacyga.
A felony conviction could cost Morgan his law enforcement career, while consecutive three-year sentences could put him behind bars for six years, Pacyga said.
