"He is caught in the middle of a huge political battle that he has nothing to do with. And it's really disheartening," Pacyga said.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Mamdani eyes 2028 kingmaker role as expert warns socialist movement could gain power even in defeat
summary: Zohran Mamdani is reportedly meeting with labor leaders to build a socialist coalition capable of winning the White House in the 2028 election.
story: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday that a progressive candidate would "absolutely" have a path to the White House in 2028.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's efforts to shape the 2028 Democratic presidential field could help socialists build lasting political influence, even if their preferred candidate ultimately loses the nomination, according to political analysts.

"The 2026 midterm bluenami showed us that the Democrat party is shifting far left, and Mamdani is hoping to capitalize on that momentum," Nicole Huyer, senior research associate for the Heritage Foundation's Institute for Economic Policy Studies, told Fox News Digital.
"What’s really interesting, is that Mamdani seems to be thinking beyond individual candidates for 2028, and more toward building an organized political infrastructure for socialists," she added.

Mamdani, a self-described Democratic socialist, stunned the political establishment in 2025 when he defeated former Gov. Andrew Cuomo in New York City's Democratic mayoral primary before winning the general election, marking a major victory for the socialist movement.

The New York City leader recently held private meetings with top union leaders as part of a broader effort to encourage labor-aligned and leftist candidates to launch White House bids in 2028, Axios reported Nov. 8, citing four anonymous sources.
MAMDANI MAKES BEHIND-THE-SCENES MOVES TO SHAPE 2028 DEMOCRATIC PRESIDENTIAL RACE
Democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani, the Democratic Party's mayor nominee in New York City, speaks to reporters on Aug. 7, 2025. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
Mamdani has argued that progressive Democrats cannot afford to let their midterm gains slip away, according to the report.

"He’s making sure that whoever the candidate is in 2028 will have a strong Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and progressive movement backing them," Huyer continued. "Basically translating all of the victories socialists saw in 2026 into a coalition capable of winning nationally in 2028."

Even if Democratic socialists fail to secure the party's 2028 presidential nomination, the campaign itself could help build a stronger movement for future elections, according to Stu Smith, investigative analyst at City Journal.

"We will see whether DSA and its allies can turn this vision into reality, but even a failed campaign could prove galvanizing," Smith told Fox News Digital. "Many of DSA's current leaders were politicized through Bernie Sanders's presidential campaigns."

"Even if a more moderate Democratic nominee ultimately emerges, it may prove to be a Pyrrhic victory if the effort helps cultivate a new generation of DSA talent that continues to shape left wing politics and public policy in ways that diverge from traditional American political norms," Smith added.
RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY
Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside of a Trump owned building during a May Day rally in New York City in 2019. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
MAMDANI CONFIDENT THERE'S A PATH FOR A PROGRESSIVE CANDIDATE TO THE WHITE HOUSE IN 2028
Huyer went on to say that certain policies favored by some Democratic socialists, such as steep wealth taxes and rent control, could "be devastating" to the U.S. economy.
"Socialism may be gaining ground ideologically and culturally due to messaging success, but the socialist economic agenda remains completely destructive," she said.
The DSA’s "Workers Deserve More" platform proposes enacting "aggressive wealth taxes on the richest individuals and corporations" to spend on public goods and infrastructure projects.
SOCIALISTS LAUNCH RADICAL PLATFORM TO ABOLISH THE US SENATE IN BID TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM AMERICA
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks onstage at CultureCon 2026 on Oct. 3, 2026, in New York City. (John Nacion/Getty Images)

Several DSA chapters across the U.S., including Los Angeles, Atlanta and Chicago, have recently issued "Run AOC Run" resolutions to urge Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to launch a 2028 White House bid, City & State New York reported.

More progressive candidates may potentially shift the 2028 Democratic primary field to the left, but they could also split the vote and create an opportunity for a more moderate candidate to win, the Manhattan Institute's Director of Public Opinion Matthew Shor told Fox News Digital.

"On the one hand, a larger number of progressive candidates could push the field toward policies favored by the party’s most committed activists," Shor stated. "But on the other hand, too many progressives could split the vote in that lane and let a moderate circumvent them en route to the nomination. As much as any faction wants to influence the conversation, they would much rather win the nomination."
The DSA’s platform also calls for abolishing the Electoral College and replacing the U.S. president and Supreme Court "with an executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress."
Several Democratic socialists secured major wins in this year's midterms.

Six DSA-endorsed candidates won their House races in the 2026 midterms: Melat Kiros in Colorado; Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York; Donavan McKinney in Michigan; Angela Gonzales-Torres in California; and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Fox News Digital previously reported.

Still, Democrats embracing far-left candidates in the next election cycle could help the GOP to "regain political momentum" they lost in the 2026 midterms, Wayne Winegarden, senior fellow in business and economics at the Pacific Research Institute, said.
MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WINS NYC HOUSE SEAT AS DSA EXPANDS ITS REACH IN CONGRESS

"While many progressives may run [in 2028], the Democrats have large majorities in Congress because moderate candidates won in places that have voted Republican for years," Winegarden told Fox News Digital. "Democrats have a strong chance to maintain control over Congress and win the Presidency if they demonstrate they are governing effectively from the center and nominate candidates for President who would govern as such."
"Should the Democrats embrace the progressive left, they will create a pathway for Republicans to regain political momentum," he added.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani arrives at the subway station in the Queens borough to go to City Hall in New York, Friday, Jan. 2, 2026. (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/AP Photo)
When reached for comment on Nov. 10, Mamdani’s office referred Fox News Digital to remarks he made at a Nov. 9 press conference.

"And when it comes to these meetings, I [have] sought and continue to meet with labor leaders precisely because they have been on the front lines of delivering for those working people and the importance of ensuring that the crises that affect working people are at the centerpiece of any of the politics that come from now until 2028," Mamdani told reporters.

2028 White House hopefuls should prioritize key issues like the U.S. affordability crisis instead of focusing on securing politicians' endorsements, political strategist Mally Smith told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"All the candidates running, instead of focusing on who might endorse them, need to create a forward-looking vision for how to tackle the two main issues voters care about going into 2028: corruption and affordability," Smith explained. "If you have a strong vision for those two issues, endorsements and votes will follow."

title: Russian-born conservative activist faces criminal charge after 'embarrassing' political foe online: warrant
summary: Liuba Wofford-Keller, a Russian-born activist in North Carolina, says her cyberstalking charge over social media posts is retaliation for political speech.
story: Liuba Wofford-Keller claims that she is the victim of political persecution after her activism against a Democratic congressional candidate and an online back-and-forth with a local Democrat.

A Russian-born conservative activist in North Carolina says she is being targeted for her political speech after she was charged with a crime stemming from online interactions with a local Democratic Party official.
Liuba Wofford-Keller is an outspoken activist for local Republican candidates and has spoken out against Congressman-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., during this year's election cycle.

But Wofford-Keller's online interactions with Lisa Wells, the secretary of the Moore County Democratic Party, led to the Republican activist being charged with cyberstalking under North Carolina law. Wofford-Keller says the charges remind her of the communist regime she left behind in Russia.

Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) speaks with other congressional freshmen of the 120th Congress after a group photograph on the steps of the House of Representatives at the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 12, 2026. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
PROSECUTOR DROPS CASE AGAINST WOMAN ACCUSED OF THREATENING TRUMP ON TIKTOK
Over the course of the year, Wofford-Keller engaged multiple times online with Wells.

Wofford-Keller describes meeting Wells only twice in person, on North Carolina's primary election day in March and on Election Day in November. She says that in between those two dates, the online fight ensued. Wells is also local precinct chair in Moore County.
Those interactions are the basis for a state charge against Wofford-Keller for "embarrassing" Wells online.

"On or about the date of offense shown and in the county named above the defendant unlawfully and willfully did knowingly permit an electronic communication device, SOCIAL MEDIA under the defendant's control to be used for a purpose prohibited by G.S. 14-196.3, REPEATEDLY POSTING FOR THE PURPOSE OF ANNOYING, HARRASSING (sic), EMBARRASSING [the complainant]," a warrant for Wofford-Keller's arrest says.
'MONEY OUT OF POLITICS' BALLOT MEASURE SPARKS FIRST AMENDMENT FIGHT IN BATTLEGROUND STATE
The statute listed in the warrant prohibits repeated communication "with the intent to abuse, annoy, threaten, terrify, harass, or embarrass any person."
But that law offends Wofford-Keller's sensibilities, who says it reminds her of the country she fled.

"Freedom of speech is very important in our society because without the freedom of speech we have a totalitarian regime when the government dictates to you and tells you what you can say, what you cannot say," she told Fox News Digital.

"One of the reasons I moved away from the communist totalitarian regime of the USSR is just to be able to say things, to have the freedom to speech, to have constitutional rights which Russian citizens unfortunately do not have."

A Soviet WWII tank destroyer SU-100 drives through Red Square during a military parade in Moscow, Russia, on June 24, 2020, to commemorate the 75th anniversary of victory in the Great Patriotic War. (Vladimir Trefilov - Host Photo Agency/Getty Images)
She says she never predicted running into such problems in the United States.

"It's very disconcerting to me because coming from a communist country, which I escaped, coming here for freedom in 1992, I would have never imagined that I would be arrested in America for a post that dates March 4th," she said, referring to the time when the post was made compared to when the criminal claim was made.
TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS

Wells told Fox News Digital that she "presented months of documented conduct, including screenshots of electronic communications and social media activity," to a local magistrate judge, who in turn "independently found probable cause and issued criminal process." She added that she is waiting for the local Democratic Party to find a new secretary before she officially leaves the role.

"I fully support free speech, including political criticism," Wells said. "My concern was a prolonged pattern of conduct that went beyond political disagreement and affected my sense of safety at home and in my community."
During the same period of time, however, Wofford-Keller says Wells also posted online to her and about her.

"[I] met the woman twice in my life, both on election days, and we had a heated political debate on social platforms," Wofford-Keller told Fox News Digital. "That's about the quintessence of my knowing the Democrat secretary for Moore County, Lisa Wells."

In a separate application for a protective order, Wells claims that Wofford-Keller frequently mentioned the town where she lived on social media, identified her publicly as a precinct chair in Whispering Pines, North Carolina and said that posts on Facebook made by Wofford-Keller about shooting AK-47s at a gun range, which were not directed at Wells, made her "afraid that her conduct could escalate into physical violence."
Residents of Mecklenburg County in Charlotte, N.C., cast their votes at precinct #2 on Nov. 6, 2018. (Logan Cyrus/AFP via Getty Images)
There has not yet been a hearing on the protective order.
Asked if Wofford-Keller ever directly threatened or doxxed her, Wells steered the conversation back towards the cyberstalking charge.
TPUSA REPORTER SAYS FAMILY CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING HER IS NOW TRYING TO SILENCE HER WITH RESTRAINING ORDERS

"Her behavior and what she did for eight months fit the elements of cyberstalking," she said, noting that the posts felt threatening to her. She declined to share the posts with Fox News Digital, citing advice from her attorney.

Wofford-Keller, who has no criminal record and possesses a clearance for contract work that she does as a language services provider for the Department of War, says Wells has no reason to be afraid or feel threatened by her. She accused Wells of using her pro-gun posts as a way to "craft an image of me of somebody who is unstable, somebody who has threatened her life."
She believes Democrats in the U.S. today are no different than communists in Soviet Russia.

A historical Soviet propaganda poster from 1950 titled "The Great Stalin - banner of the friendship between the peoples of the USSR!" is displayed at the Museum of Socialist Art in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Sept. 27, 2026. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"The people that we have now who call themselves Democrats are full-blown, unhinged communists, and they act in no way different than the Soviet apparatus did when they put people in labor camps," said Wofford-Keller.
But Wells says it's not about party affiliation.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Political disagreement is something I deal with constructively every day," she said. "This was never about anyone's party affiliation. It was about conduct I believed crossed a line, which is why I sought legal advice and, on my attorney's recommendation, went to the magistrate on a Sunday to have the evidence reviewed."
The Moore County Sheriff's Office explained that it was tasked with executing the search warrant by the magistrate, and did not play a role in investigating any potential crime.
The magistrate court did not return a request for comment.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Socialist newcomers’ old words take new turn as they prepare to enter Congress
summary: Zohran Mamdani-backed DSA candidates and Rep. Randy Fine face scrutiny over past comments on policing, ICE, Islamophobia and the 9/11 attacks.
story: Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports Democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier is facing scrutiny over deleted tweets praising Marxism, forcing elite party leaders to duck accountability while modern moderates like Senator John Fetterman demand answers over the party's hard-left turn.

As January approaches and newly elected lawmakers prepare to take their oaths of office, past statements could prove troublesome as they jockey for committee assignments with powerbrokers seeking to protect the image of their respective parties.

The midterm elections sent a new crop of lawmakers affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America to Congress — in a few cases, unexpectedly. While some sought to moderate their image after the primary season, controversial remarks made on the campaign trail or years before their candidacies could follow them to Capitol Hill as they seek committee assignments and influence within the Democratic caucus.
Fox News Digital reviewed some of the most controversial remarks made by the incoming lawmakers — comments that could complicate their efforts to build influence in the new Congress.
Darializa Avila Chevalier: ‘Defund and abolish’

In an early test of his political sway, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani endorsed a duo of DSA-aligned Democrats in primaries for congressional districts encompassing portions of four of the city’s five boroughs.
MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WITH HISTORY OF ANTI-AMERICAN RHETORIC WINS VICIOUS DEM PRIMARY RACE

Darializa Avila Chevalier, U.S. Democratic House candidate for New York, speaks at a Get Out The Vote rally at Kings Theater in Brooklyn, New York, on June 18, 2026, ahead of the state's primary election on June 23. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Darializa Avila Chevalier, a left-wing graduate student at the City University of New York, was one such candidate. She defeated longtime Rep. Adriano Espaillat, chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, by a relatively small margin during a June primary contest. Before and after Chevalier’s primary victory, scores of controversial deleted social media posts made by the socialist hopeful garnered national media attention.

"No. It means ending policing full stop. Period. No more police at all ever," she responded to one user on social media in 2020 who asked her if abolishing the police only entailed getting rid of law enforcement "as we know it."
"F**k you. We’re gonna defund and abolish. You don’t get to water down our movements," she said in another post that year.

Though once in vogue, calls to defund or abolish the police have since become politically toxic, something House Democratic leadership will likely have in mind when determining what to do with Chevalier once she shows up in D.C.
Chevalier has also signaled an affinity for ideas outside the normal range of American political discourse.
JOHNSON WARNS COMMUNISM IS 'ON OUR OWN SHORES' AFTER FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES WIN NEW YORK PRIMARIES

Socialist New York congressional nominees Darializa Avila Chevalier (L), Claire Valdez (C) and Brad Lander. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images; Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Seize the means of production," she wrote in 2019.
"The pyromania associated with anarchism is very intriguing to me," wrote Chevalier about a year later.
The socialist newcomer has also signaled a hostility to the Democratic establishment, an institution that now holds considerable sway over her political future.

"I have no nuance to add. F*ck Kamala Harris," Chevalier wrote in response to the then-vice president telling Central American migrants not to come to the United States illegally in 2021. She also reposted content criticizing the Democratic National Committee and other mainstream liberal institutions from the left.
In response to criticism, Chevalier has stated those posts no longer reflect who she is and that she has grown considerably since writing them.
Melat Kiros: ‘Inevitable’

Elected to represent Colorado’s First Congressional District as a Democrat, Melat Kiros, a socialist, has attracted criticism for her attempts to explain — and, in the telling of critics, justify — terrorist attacks.

In a June interview, speaking on the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Kiros stated that they were "inevitable in the sense that we destabilized a lot of the Middle East." On the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks in Israel, she told Twitch streamer Hasan Piker that they too were "an inevitable consequence of apartheid, of occupation, decades of occupation."
Calling an attack inevitable, however, does not necessarily equate to endorsing the attack itself.
ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ SHRUGS OFF PAST 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS, JOKING 'WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY'

Democratic congressional candidate Melat Kiros speaks to supporters at an election-night watch party after winning the Colorado primary on June 30, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. Kiros defeated incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo., in the Democratic primary. (Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images)

Kiros, who was born in Ethiopia, has also accused Israel of genocide and called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — both hotly debated positions within the Democratic Party.
Chris Rabb: ‘Lock those f***ers up’
Much like Chevalier, Chris Rabb is a DSA member who has railed against law enforcement and endorsed economic ideas considered by some to be radical.
"Would you like to eliminate cash bail and establish a wealth tax?" Fox News host Sean Hannity asked Rabb during an August interview.
"Absolutely," answered Rabb.
"Would you like to abolish prisons and abolish the police?" Hannity followed up.

"Well, what’s interesting about that statement is, long before there was any notion of policing, we had founders that did not even understand that term," Rabb said. "Policing is something that’s evolved over time. Ultimately, what we want is to have communities that are safe. And 99% of what police do [is] not going after the bad guys, all of that can be done in different ways by professionals who are trained to do so."
DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST CALLS SOCIALIST CANDIDATES 'PARASITES' WHO COULD 'SET THE PARTY BACK DECADES'

PA State Rep. Christopher Rabb, D-West Oak Lane, stumps with New York progressives in New York City. Rabb has been uniquely silent, compared to his Democratic Philadelphian and Pennsylvanian compatriots in the wake of virulent anti-Semitic protests in Rittenhouse Square. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)
While Rabb generally supports reducing the number of criminals in prisons, calling America’s high incarceration rate "morally wrong," he makes one notable exception.

"But I will make an exception for all of those f***ers who are lawless MAGA thugs who have destroyed lives and communities," Rabb said on an October episode of Wajahat Ali’s podcast. "Lock all of those f***ers up. I know that seems a little hypocritical of me being on the left and being anti-incarceration, but lock those f***ers up."
Claire Valdez: ‘Militarized terrorist organization’
Elected alongside Chevalier on Mamdani’s New York City DSA congressional slate, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez has her share of controversial comments.
In January, for instance, she called ICE a "militarized terrorist organization that is destroying our country" and endorsed calls to disband the agency.
Valdez has also called for subjecting one of the largest industries in the United States to public ownership.
"We need to, like, nationalize the airline industry, but let’s start by abolishing PreCheck," she said during a May appearance on the B*tchuation Room podcast.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached Chevalier, Kiros, Rabb and Valdez with requests for comment on Tuesday but has received no responses as of publication.

title: Texas attorney general-elect refuses to defend Ten Commandments classroom law
summary: Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson says he won't defend the Ten Commandments law requiring displays in every public school classroom.
story: Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson says he won't defend the state's Ten Commandments classroom law, breaking with outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton ahead of a potential Supreme Court review.

Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson said this week that he won't defend a law requiring public schools across the state to display the Ten Commandments as the U.S. Supreme Court weighs whether to review the case.

In an interview with The Dallas Morning News, Johnson, the first Democrat to be elected Texas attorney general in nearly three decades, called the law "unconstitutional," marking a distinct split with outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who championed the bill.
"My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional," Johnson said.

"The court will have the ultimate say as to what's constitutional and what is not, but I'm the one who says what the state's position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken," he continued.
TEXAS DEM JAMES TALARICO RIPS 'UN-CHRISTIAN' COURT DECISION ON WHAT'S ALLOWED IN CLASSROOMS

Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson said he would not defend a state law requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments, calling it unconstitutional. (Mikala Compton/Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)
Under state law, Senate Bill 10 requires that a "conspicuous" copy of the Ten Commandments be displayed in every classroom in every public school and open-enrollment charter school across Texas.

In April, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the law did not violate the Constitution, a major victory for proponents of the legislation, including religious freedom advocates, who have long argued the biblical text is a crucial component of America's legal, moral and historical heritage.
However, the law may still face legal scrutiny if the Supreme Court opts to review the case.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has defended the state's Ten Commandments classroom law against legal challenges. (Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Johnson's opposition to the law has already become part of Paxton's legal strategy, according to The Dallas Morning News. In a filing with the high court earlier this month, attorneys from Paxton's office cited Johnson's reluctance to back the law as a reason the justices should decline to hear a challenge to it.
In the filing, Paxton argued that Johnson's office might not adequately defend the law, depriving the justices of "an adversary presentation" if they agree to hear the case, the newspaper reported.

The federal appeals court ruling upholding the Ten Commandments law would remain in place if the Supreme Court declines to hear the case, preserving a legal victory for Paxton before he leaves office in January.
Johnson's victory in Texas was part of a series of Democratic electoral victories across the Lone Star State, including wins in the U.S. Senate and gubernatorial races.

title: Why Mamdani’s move to close infamous NYC jail could be 'massive hit' that reverberates for years: expert
summary: Zohran Mamdani's Rikers Island closure plan leaves 4,160 jail beds for a city of nearly 9 million, and one expert warns of overcrowding and violence.
story: Manhattan Institute scholar Rafael Mangual told Fox News Digital that Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan to close Rikers Island by 2032 could leave the city without enough jail beds and threaten public safety.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) announced that Rikers Island would be closed "once and for all" by 2032, a promise one crime expert said doesn't add up and could release violent criminals back onto the streets.

Mamdani pledged to replace the city's largest jail with four smaller ones across different boroughs, while corrections officers and criminal justice scholars have raised concerns that shrinking the population of more than 6,000 inmates could carry lasting consequences.
Rafael Mangual, head of research for policing and public safety at the Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital there won't be enough beds to accommodate a city of nearly 9 million people.
"If New York City gets this wrong, make no mistake, there will be a massive hit to public safety," Mangual said.
MAMDANI IN HOT SEAT OVER POST MOURNING DEATH OF INMATE CHARGED WITH CALLOUS CRIME: 'ABSOLUTELY SHAMEFUL'

A crime expert warned that Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan to close Rikers Island by 2032 could threaten public safety. (Barry Williams / New York Daily News via Getty Images ; Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

The replacement jails in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx will have a capacity of 4,160 beds, with an additional 340 therapeutic beds for inmates with mental illnesses and other medical needs. They will be placed closer to public transit and courthouses.
Mamdani said the decision to push the closure of Rikers back by five years was because of "prior administration delays." The city will also invest $146 million in support services.

The mayor’s office directed Fox News Digital to its Rikers Island closure plan and Mamdani’s remarks at a press conference last week, where he defended his position by saying, "We are making a conscious decision to advance a new model of a criminal legal system in our city, one that takes on that problem head-on."
Mangual maintained the plan could lead to significant overcrowding and trigger more "violence and other kinds of contraband problems."
"You can expect that the jails will continue to operate at 100% of capacity for as long as they exist if that project actually comes to fruition," he said.
He added that the city's jail population dropped below 4,000 in April 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, shootings and homicides spiked.
That year, there were 1,531 shootings, up 97% from 2019, and 462 murders, up from 319 in 2019, according to the New York City Police Department (NYPD).
HOUSE REPORT SAYS NYC PROSECUTORS TAILORED PLEA DEALS TO SHIELD ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FROM DEPORTATION
A corrections bus exits the entrance to the Rikers Island jail complex in Queens, New York, on Nov. 20, 2026. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

"The experiment is not going to be a pretty one and that's the thing that I think people need to be most concerned with," he said, saying that Rikers had between 9,000 and 10,000 inmates during 2017 and 2018, which were some of the city's safest years.
Despite the city seeing record-low murders and shootings so far this year, according to NYPD data, Mangual said other major crimes, like felony assaults, remain high.
"That's a major problem that is only going to get worse," he said.

He said previous efforts to bring down the jail population have posed additional risks to public safety, pointing to the city's bail reform law and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg's limits on low-level prosecutions that have made it easier to avoid jail.
"We certainly haven't been able to get it down to where it is now without compromising public safety," he said.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECTS WITH LENGTHY CRIMINAL RECORDS ARRESTED IN STABBING OF OFF-DUTY NYPD DETECTIVE
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaking with inmates on Rikers Island while they watch a World Cup semifinal soccer match on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

Mangual said repeat offenders like Alexander Florentino could now be put back on the streets. Florentino, a homeless illegal immigrant, was arrested this month on a murder charge in the death of a 62-year-old woman inside her Chinatown apartment one day after a judge released him without bail, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and court records.
Warning that reducing the jail population will only "erode the incapacitation benefits that incarceration provides," Mangual said the city will be left with no other solutions.
"The idea that there's an alternative to incarceration is one of the most misguided notions in criminal justice policy debates," he said.

Rikers has faced years of controversy, with many inmates and activists criticizing harsh conditions, trial delays and limited access to family members and support services. The city’s goal is "to build a safer and more humane jail system," according to a Nov. 20 press release.

But Mangual believes city officials still aren't looking at the full picture, arguing that building multiple jails with the same systems, inmates and guards will not solve the problem and that some criminals are "simply too dangerous to coexist with the rest of society."
"What they ought to have done was invest in refurbishing the jails that already existed, building new ones with adequate space, and then moving the inmate population around as required," he said.
If the plan moves forward, Mangual said the city could see crime surge on a "much larger scale."

"We're already seeing what that could possibly look like when you have individuals who are out walking the streets with 30, 40, 50, 100 prior arrests and they eventually kill somebody or shove somebody in front of a subway train," he said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Bragg's office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

title: Mamdani handed out $95K in staff raises the same day he warned of $12B budget deficit: report
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani approved $850,000 in raises for City Hall aides in his first year, according to payroll records reviewed by the New York Post.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces intense public backlash, and Staten Island crowd members booed him at a recent event. National correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on independent estimates showing Mamdani's free universal child care program could cost $9.3 billion dollars, fifty-five percent more than claimed.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani approved roughly $850,000 in pay raises for dozens of City Hall aides during his first year in office, according to municipal payroll records reviewed by the New York Post.
The records show the raises were distributed to at least 46 staffers since Mamdani took office in January, bringing total compensation increases near $1 million.

The Post counted 21 new hires who received raises totaling $450,000 before their first anniversary on the job, more than twice the combined number of first-year employees who got raises under Eric Adams and Bill de Blasio.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to reporters in front of a painting of Alexander Hamilton about the city's finances during a news conference in New York Feb. 17, 2026. (Seth Wenig/AP Photo)
MAMDANI TURNS ON NEW YORK CITY TEACHERS UNION WITH LAWSUIT BLOCKING PAY RAISES FOR EDUCATORS

On Jan. 28, five City Hall employees were granted salary increases totaling $95,000 on the same day Mamdani announced New York City faced an estimated $12 billion budget deficit, the records show. The mayor’s office later lowered that projected deficit to approximately $5.4 billion.
The mayor’s office on Nov. 12 confirmed the city’s fiscal 2027 budget rose $3.3 billion from the budget adopted in June, reaching $129.2 billion.
MAMDANI'S TAXPAYER-FUNDED INFLUENCER ARMY ACCUSED OF PLOTTING PRESSURE CAMPAIGN AGAINST NYC CEOS
The payroll disclosures detail significant salary adjustments across several executive staff positions.

Julia Simcoe and Jacob Russell each received raises of more than $60,000, bringing their salaries to $148,000 and $145,000, respectively, the Post reported. Three other City Hall staffers received raises ranging from $30,000 to $45,000.

Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, center, and Julie Menin, speaker of the New York City Council, center right, during an announcement of a handshake agreement on the 2027 budget in the rotunda of City Hall in New York June 30, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
MAMDANI’S AFFORDABILITY REVOLUTION STUMBLED AS RENT COSTS SOAR TO RECORD HIGHS
The salary increases come as Mamdani, who took office Jan. 1 as the city's first self-described socialist mayor, faces fiscal constraints and administrative hurdles on core campaign pledges.

Mamdani’s plan to eliminate bus fares across the five boroughs has stalled after pushback from New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who noted the Metropolitan Transportation Authority cannot absorb the loss of revenue from fare boxes. While Mamdani’s campaign estimated the initiative would cost $700 million, the New York City Independent Budget Office (IBO) projected that fully eliminating fares would cost New York State roughly $1.1 billion.
EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL

The administration has also faced capacity limits with its universal childcare initiative. A pilot program aimed at 2-year-olds launched with 2,000 available seats but drew more than 5,700 applicants, leaving roughly 3,700 children on waitlists. The program cost $73 million to launch, and the IBO estimated an expanded citywide version would cost $425 million by 2028.

Meanwhile, Mamdani's plan to establish five city-run grocery stores that sell items 30% below market value has drawn skepticism from retail analysts and economists who question whether the discounts can be sustained without ongoing taxpayer subsidies.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to reporters during a news conference in New York Feb. 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

Fox News Digital asked the mayor's office what civil service guidelines justified the early salary bumps, why raises were authorized the same day Mamdani warned of a $12 billion deficit and how City Hall reconciles the payroll increases with budget constraints on programs like universal childcare and free transit.
A spokesperson for City Hall did not immediately return a request for comment.

title: From turkey shortages to helicopter deliveries: The extraordinary history of Thanksgiving during war
summary: The U.S. military has delivered Thanksgiving dinner to troops from Civil War Union troops to Vietnam's War Zone D, a tradition born in wartime.
story: House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.
In November 1966, 12 American soldiers stationed at an isolated outpost in a Vietnamese war zone were about as far from a traditional Thanksgiving at home as they could get.
Their only means of resupply was by air. But the U.S. military was determined to get them Thanksgiving dinner anyway.

A mess sergeant at Bien Hoa prepared turkey and all the trimmings, packed the meal into insulated containers and sent it by helicopter into War Zone D, where three officers and nine enlisted men of a 5th Special Forces detachment sat down to Thanksgiving dinner, according to Defense Department records preserved by the National Archives.
The delivery was one piece of a massive logistical effort the U.S. military has undertaken during wars spanning generations to get traditional Thanksgiving meals to troops serving in combat zones.
Soldiers are pictured eating Thanksgiving dinner during World War I, in 1918. (National Archives)

From civilians sending tens of thousands of turkeys to Union troops during the Civil War to helicopters carrying hot meals to soldiers in Korea, the holiday has been observed through some of the nation's most consequential conflicts.

Thanksgiving became a national tradition in the midst of war. President Abraham Lincoln issued his 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation as the Civil War entered its third year, calling on Americans to observe the final Thursday of November as a day of "Thanksgiving and Praise."
By the following year, Americans on the home front were mounting a massive effort to get Thanksgiving dinner to Union troops.

Former War Department official Charles A. Dana later recalled the "great turkey movement" of November 1864. In New York alone, organizers reported having 20,000 turkeys ready to send to the front, according to Dana's account. A Philadelphia committee sought transportation for another 4,000 destined for troops serving under Gen. Philip Sheridan.
U.S. service members stationed at an airbase in Norfolk, England, select turkeys for their Thanksgiving dinners at a local farm on Nov. 6, 1943. (National Archives)
By World War II, the effort to put turkey on troops' Thanksgiving tables had grown so large that it affected whether Americans at home could find one for their own.

In August 1943, the War Food Administration restricted most civilian turkey sales as the government sought millions of pounds for the armed forces. An initial goal of at least 10 million pounds for troops overseas was expanded to include military installations at home, and the government ultimately obtained roughly 30 million pounds before the order was lifted in October, according to wartime government records.
A year later, delivering Thanksgiving dinner near the front could carry its own risks.
102-YEAR-OLD NAVY VETERAN STILL CRAVES HOT WINGS AFTER 102 COMBAT MISSIONS IN KOREA: 'I MIGHT MAKE IT TO 115'

Sailors Leo F. DesJarlait, left, Eulice E. Wheeler, center, and G.J. Lindner eat turkey and trimmings at an advanced U.S. Navy base in the Aleutian Islands on Nov. 24, 1944. Lindner gives a "4.0" sign, meaning "perfect," in response to the Thanksgiving meal. (National Archives)

In Germany's Hürtgen Forest, Lt. Paul Boesch of the 121st Infantry Regiment later recalled being told that hot turkey dinners had arrived for his men amid some of the European campaign's most grueling fighting. Boesch protested that sending soldiers to collect the food would expose them to German artillery, but the order to distribute the meal stood.
His fears proved well-founded. As troops gathered to retrieve the food, German artillery struck the area, killing and wounding several men, according to Boesch's account.
Six years later, American troops were again eating Thanksgiving dinner near the front, this time in the bitter cold of North Korea.

On Thanksgiving Day 1950, Marines around the Chosin Reservoir were served turkey and cranberry sauce, candied sweet potatoes, fruitcake and mince pie. In the subzero temperatures, the food quickly began to freeze.
US NAVY RELEASES PHOTOS OF 'FRESH MEALS,' PUSHES BACK ON REPORTS OF FOOD SHORTAGES ON MIDDLE EAST WARSHIPS

The dinner came as U.S. commanders remained optimistic that the war could soon be over. The following day, Gen. Douglas MacArthur launched an offensive that became known as the "Home-by-Christmas" campaign.

Instead, Chinese forces entered the fighting in massive numbers. Within days of Thanksgiving, Marines around Chosin were surrounded and battling through one of the most brutal engagements of the Korean War.

Pfc. John A. Arnett, left, receives a turkey leg from Cpl. Fred Burks during Thanksgiving dinner in Korea on Nov. 22, 1951. The chow line was set up on the back side of a hill roughly 200 yards from the main line of resistance. (National Archives)
More than half a century later, another generation of American troops was spending Thanksgiving at war in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In 2003, President George W. Bush secretly flew into Baghdad to surprise roughly 600 troops gathered for Thanksgiving dinner at Baghdad International Airport. Air Force One approached with its cabin shades drawn and lights dimmed amid tight security surrounding the trip.
"I was just looking for a warm meal somewhere," Bush joked before addressing the troops and helping serve Thanksgiving dinner.
In Afghanistan, getting that dinner to troops stationed far from major bases could require a different kind of operation.
President George H.W. Bush eats Thanksgiving dinner on the hood of a Humvee while visiting U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia during Operation Desert Shield on Nov. 22, 1990. (National Archives)

On Thanksgiving 2007, helicopters carried turkeys and traditional fixings from Bagram Airfield to soldiers at remote firebases in the Tagab Valley, according to a contemporaneous U.S. military account.
It was the first hot meal some of the soldiers had eaten in months. Because the positions still had to be defended, troops rotated between Thanksgiving dinner and standing watch.
"The white meat was magnificent," Pfc. Matt Lorimer of the 82nd Airborne Division said.
President George W. Bush traveled to Iraq in 2003 to meet with troops without the public's knowledge. (Tim Sloan/AFP/Getty Images)
At another remote Afghan outpost two years later, troops spent a month fattening five scrawny turkeys purchased locally for Thanksgiving. But five birds were not enough to feed roughly 150 soldiers.
Additional turkey was flown from the United States to Bagram Airfield and then transported to the outpost. Even that was not the end of the journey.

A handful of soldiers were manning an observation post on a mountain spur roughly 6,900 feet above sea level. Their Thanksgiving dinner was packed up and flown by helicopter up the mountain to them.

title: New California law could keep teens in booster seats until age 16 unless they pass test
summary: Assemblymember Lori Wilson's seat belt fit test bill requires minors to pass five criteria before riding without a booster seat or in the front seat.
story: Why buckling a child into a car seat with heavy winter layers is not recommended.

Beginning in the new year, minors will be required to pass a five-step seat belt fit test before they can ride without a booster seat or sit in the front seat of a vehicle. The bill's author, Assemblymember Lori Wilson, cited figures showing that child injuries and fatalities in crashes have risen since the pandemic, with children ages 8 to 12 disproportionately affected.
"Extending the required age for booster use and implementing straightforward testing can significantly enhance child safety," CalMatters reported.

"So the best thing to do to keep your child safe while riding in a vehicle matches what our law is," Wilson said of the bill in April 2025. "It really is to take into consideration all the varying types of seats that we sit on in the car. This is about safety.
"This is about making sure that if something happens, you are safe, and I think that’s the key thing that we’re trying to drive home is that it is not about treating people like babies."
3 CAR SEAT INSTALLATION MISTAKES YOU NEED TO AVOID
A California law could keep children, including some teenagers, in booster seats until age 16.  (Cars.com)

Previously, children ages 8 and older — or those at least 4 feet, 9 inches tall — could ride without a booster seat. Under the new law, Assembly Bill 435, children ages 8 to 15 may use a regular seat belt without a booster only if they meet all five criteria:

Sit with their back flat against the vehicle's seat.Bend their knees naturally over the edge of the seat.Have the shoulder belt fit snugly across the middle of their chest and shoulder, rather than their neck.Have the lap belt sit low across their hips and touch their upper thighs.Maintain that position throughout the entire trip.
Sit with their back flat against the vehicle's seat.
Bend their knees naturally over the edge of the seat.
Have the shoulder belt fit snugly across the middle of their chest and shoulder, rather than their neck.
Have the lap belt sit low across their hips and touch their upper thighs.
Maintain that position throughout the entire trip.
MELATONIN WARNINGS: NEARLY HALF OF PARENTS GIVE IT TO THEIR KIDS TO HELP THEM SLEEP, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION

Side shot on the seats for children mounted in minivan. A new law in Italy requires child car seats to be equipped with alarm devices to prevent parents from leaving children inside vehicles for hours.  (iStock)
Improper car seat and booster use remains widespread, according to federal and industry studies.
GOT A TIP?
A 2011 National Child Restraint Use Special Study found that 46% of car seats and booster seats had at least one major installation or use error that could reduce their effectiveness in a crash.
Nearly all seats had some form of misuse, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

A 2021 study by AAA and the National Safety Council found that more than half of all car seats brought to child passenger safety technicians for inspection were improperly installed or used, and that only one in five parents and caregivers sought expert help securing their child's seat.

title: Biden book sales lag way behind Obama, Clinton memoirs in first week
summary: President Joe Biden's memoir, "Promise Me, America," sold 21,000 copies in its first week, per Circana, far behind presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton's totals.
story: Fox News' Lara Trump discusses former President Joe Biden's new memoir as he defends his 2024 debate performance with president Donald Trump. Trump details how Democrats allowed for Biden's decline to go on behind the scenes.

Former President Joe Biden's new memoir, "Promise Me, America," sold only 21,000 copies in its first week of publication, falling well short of memoirs by former presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, according to market research firm Circana.
In 2020, Obama's "A Promised Land" sold more than 800,000 copies within the first 24 hours of publication, reaching 1 million copies sold by the end of its first week.
Clinton's "My Life" hit the 1 million copies benchmark within two weeks of its release.
BIDEN MEMOIR DRAWS FIRE FOR ‘DENIAL’ AS CRITICS FLAG GAZA, RACIAL-EQUITY OMISSIONS
Despite its apparently low sales numbers, Biden's book still topped the New York Times Best Sellers list for nonfiction.
The new book, "Promise Me, America," by former U.S. President Joe Biden is displayed at Skylight Books Nov. 17, 2026 in Los Angeles. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
The book's publisher, Little, Brown and Company, said in a statement it was "immensely proud" of the book reaching the top of the chart.
JOE BIDEN ADDRESSES CRITICS WHO SAID HE HID HIS STAGE 4 CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN UPCOMING MEMOIR
Biden's promotion of the book had been limited by his relatively scant appearances to promote it, an effort hampered by the former president's 2025 prostate cancer diagnosis.

"Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won't be able to do as many conversations about my book as I'd hoped. However, I'm hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves," Biden wrote in a Nov. 8 post on X.
The book's diminished sales numbers compared to Biden's Democratic predecessors appear to follow a trend of the public's relative disinterest in the Bidens' bibliography.
JILL BIDEN SAYS FORMER PRESIDENT WILL LIVE WITH STAGE 4 CANCER 'FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE,' HAS SLOWED DOWN

President Joe Biden talks with son Hunter Biden upon arrival at Delaware Air National Guard Base in New Castle, Del., June 11, 2024, as he travels to Wilmington, Delaware.  (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images)

President Joe Biden, former President Barack Obama and former President Bill Clinton during a memorial service for Ethel Kennedy at the Cathedral of St. Matthew the Apostle in Washington, D.C., Oct. 16, 2024. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Former President Joe Biden's post-vice presidential memoir, "Promise Me, Dad," did relatively well compared to the Biden family's other offerings.

title: Powerful NY Democrat Andrea Stewart-Cousins dead at 76, reports say
summary: Andrea Stewart-Cousins, the trailblazing Democratic leader of the New York state Senate since 2019, was found dead at her Yonkers home Friday at age 76.
story: Andrea Stewart-Cousins, the New York State Senate majority leader and the first Black woman to lead the chamber, has died at age 76.
Andrea Stewart-Cousins, the trailblazing majority leader of the New York State Senate, has died at age 76, according to multiple reports.
Stewart-Cousins, the first Black woman to lead the state's upper chamber, was found dead in her Yonkers home on Friday morning, police sources told the New York Post.
Her daughter reportedly tried to get in touch with her on Thursday night before calling for a welfare check.

Stewart-Cousins, a Democrat, was first elected to the state senate in 2007. She then became majority leader in January 2019 after Democrats won a majority in the chamber in the 2018 midterm elections.
NYC MAYOR MAMDANI ANNOUNCES DELAYED PLAN TO CLOSE CITY'S LARGEST JAIL
New York Democratic State Sen. Andrea Stewart-Cousins speaks during a news conference in New Rochelle, N.Y., Feb. 18, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"She was a groundbreaking leader who shattered one of New York’s highest glass ceilings," Mike Murphy, a spokesman for the Democratic majority, said in a statement.
Stewart-Cousins entered a state government marked by a tumultuous Democratic conference amid feuds and power struggles, Politico reported.
In 2018, Democrats eventually won 39 of the state Senate’s 63 seats, giving the party its first stable majority since World War II.
The next year, state lawmakers spent their time addressing progressive pieces of legislation, such as immigration, abortion protections and tenants' rights, according to the report.
NYC SUSPECT IN CHINATOWN FATAL BEATING HAD 5 OPEN CASES AS MAMDANI PUSHES PLAN TO CLOSE RIKERS
The New York state Capitol before Gov. Kathy Hochul delivered her State of the State address in the Assembly Chamber at the state Capitol Jan. 10, 2023, in Albany, N.Y. (AP Photo/Hans Pennink)

The Business Council of New York State issued this statement: "We are deeply saddened to learn of the sudden passing of Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins. As the first woman to lead a conference in the New York State Legislature, she made history and will forever be remembered for her strong leadership and dedication to New Yorkers.

"A partner to The Business Council, Andrea was always willing to listen to employers and work toward common ground on behalf of the business community. We extend our deepest condolences to her family, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time."
U. S. Congressman Ritchie Torres hosts a news conference in support of the re-election of Gov. Kathy Hochul. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y., said he was "saddened" to hear of Stewart-Cousins' death.

"She was a trailblazer whose leadership helped shape New York and opened doors for generations to come," he said. "Her commitment to public service and the people she represented will not be forgotten. My thoughts are with her family and loved ones."

title: Mamdani's top 4 socialist promises met with reality checks as his first year in office nears its end
summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze covers only about 1 million rent-stabilized units, while his city-run grocery pilot faces long lines and shortages.
story: Government-run supermarkets face intense scrutiny, and Joanne Trattoria owner Joe Germanotta criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan to open city-owned grocery stores.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a socialist, has begun delivering on several of his signature campaign promises in his first year leading the largest city in the U.S.
But the limited scope of those efforts raises questions about how much of his far-left agenda he can realistically implement.
Fox News Digital breaks down some of Mamdani's most controversial campaign promises and those he's made a priority in the first of his four years in office.
NYC MAYOR TOUTS ‘SOCIALIST’ WINS IN FIRST 100 DAYS ALONGSIDE BERNIE SANDERS
Rent freezes

On the campaign trail, Mamdani pitched freezing monthly rent costs as a key strategy to lower the cost of housing for New Yorkers. Roughly 67.7% of those who live in the five boroughs of the city are renters, according to the most recent government data released in 2024.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani listens to reporters' questions during a news conference at Athens Square Park Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
"As mayor, I will freeze the rent every year that I’m in office. That’s a guarantee," Mamdani said in a campaign video posted near the beginning of his campaign in 2024.

True to his word, the New York City Rent Guidelines Board announced Mamdani’s promised freeze in June, detailing a 0% increase in one-year leases beginning between October 2026 and October 2027 and a 0% increase for two-year leases beginning in the same window.
Mamdani hailed the announcement as a significant victory for the city, highlighting the longer-lease lock.

"This is a historic victory for New York City tenants. After reviewing the data and hearing from New Yorkers across the city, the independent RGB has delivered a freeze on one-year leases, and the first-ever freeze on two-year leases in our city’s history," Mamdani’s office said in a press release in June.
"This is the relief that working people across our city deserve."

Notably, the freeze does not apply to all rental apartments in New York City, instead covering about 1 million rent-stabilized units. According to the Community Service Society, a nonprofit poverty advocacy group, rent-stabilized apartments make up 41% of the city’s rental units.
A residential apartment building near the Manhattan Bridge in the Brooklyn borough of New York July 3, 2025. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
City-run grocery stores

Although Mamdani’s city-run grocery stores haven’t yet launched in earnest, a pilot test of what they could look like has raised questions about whether the idea will meaningfully address the food scarcity issues Mamdani highlighted on the campaign trail.

"This month we got polling that showed that two-thirds of New Yorkers support city-owned grocery stores, a policy we’ve championed for months and would guarantee cheaper groceries," Mamdani said last year.
Even so, the first version of the city-run grocery store was met with complaints of long lines, shortages and disorganization when it launched in February.
MAMDANI’S AFFORDABILITY REVOLUTION STUMBLED AS RENT COSTS SOAR TO RECORD HIGHS

Groceries sit behind Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, during an announcement on municipal grocery stores at a Campaign for Hunger community food distribution center in Brooklyn, N.Y., July 27, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
In a recent interview, Mamdani said he still has plans to build on the idea.

"What we’re going to do is — in a city of more than a thousand supermarkets — we’re going to create five. … They’re cheaper supermarkets, supermarkets with a discount," the mayor said during a recent interview with The New York Times.
Mamdani has said he hopes to sell products at 30% below the market price.

The proposal has sparked skepticism from economists and commentators over how the city could deliver such steep discounts in an industry known for razor-thin profit margins. With grocery prices up about 33% nationwide since 2019, critics say the plan must explain how prices could undercut private retailers by 30% without significant public subsidies.

"This is completely insane. Also, not possible unless taxpayers are subsidizing all the groceries. Grocery store profits are tiny, a few percentage points a year, at best," Outkick founder Clay Travis wrote.
Universal childcare
Like his grocery store initiative, Mamdani’s plan to implement free universal childcare has struggled to keep pace with demand, falling short of the full promise.

"Since the beginning of this campaign, I’ve championed universal childcare, making a commitment to deliver it to New Yorkers as young as six weeks to five years of age," Mamdani said in a campaign video in 2025.

New York City Mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani interacts with pre-K students at Friends of Crown Heights Education Center Nov. 13, 2025, in the Flatbush neighborhood of the Brooklyn borough in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Mamdani argued that, without expanded childcare, the city would experience billions in lost productivity from workers who couldn’t enter the workforce.
"My administration will address this crisis by providing no-cost childcare to families with children as young as six weeks up until they’re five years of age."
STEVE FORBES: MAMDANI’S SOCIALIST RENT-CONTROL PUTS NEW YORK ON THE ROAD TO HOUSING RUIN

To facilitate the plan, Mamdani said he believed using government spaces, co-locating with the Department of Education, subsidizing commercial rent and relaxing regulatory requirements would help bring down costs.

Mamdani launched his plans back in January, announcing a preliminary version of the plan. The rollout was limited to select areas in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens and only applied to 2-year-old children.
In an August press release, Mamdani said the program had a 2,000-seat capacity and over 5,700 applicants, leaving roughly 3,700 children on waitlists.
In the same release, Mamdani said he expected the city’s capacity to grow sixfold, going from 2,000 to 12,000.
The New York City Independent Budget Office, a government watchdog, confirmed the program’s $73 million cost and estimated that the expanded version would cost roughly $425 million in 2028.
According to the United States Census, there are approximately 489,000 children in New York City under the age of 5.
Fare-free buses

As of early 2026, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has pushed back on Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposal for citywide free buses, arguing the Metropolitan Transportation Authority cannot afford the estimated annual loss in fare revenue. (Nikolas Lanum/Fox News Digital)

Mamdani’s free bus plans have put him at odds with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul over whether the state should shoulder more of the burden for the mayor’s designs, leaving his campaign promises only partially fulfilled amid costs that would exceed his initial estimations.

Early on in his administration, Mamdani was asked when New Yorkers could expect the promise of free fares. Mamdani left the answer open-ended but pledged to fulfill his commitment by the end of his term.
"I have said when we ran this campaign … I’m making buses fast and free. I have said that by the time I am done being mayor, those will have been delivered," Mamdani said in January.

So far, Mamdani has taken steps toward increasing busing efficiency in NYC by developing 50 priority corridors for speed improvements. But discussions about making the buses free have stalled at the state level.

New York’s bus system is run through the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), a state-created public authority. The body is controlled by the governor, who appoints the MTA chair and its board.
The group makes controlling decisions about its fares.
Although she expressed sympathy toward Mamdani’s design, Hochul said she could not remove the sources of revenue from New York City’s public transportation.

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is taking criticism over a bill she signed last week that empowers the state attorney general to investigate and fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive practices against labor union members. (Adam Gray/Pool/Getty Images)

"I cannot set forth a plan right now that takes money out of a system that relies on the fares of the buses and the subways. But can we find a path to make it more affordable for people who need help? Of course we can," Hochul said at a political retreat earlier this year.

Mamdani’s campaign originally estimated the plan would come with a $700 million price tag. However, the New York City Independent Budget Office released an estimate in June, finding that fully eliminating fares would cost New York State roughly $1.1 billion.
Even so, Mamdani said he believes the designs will ultimately be fulfilled.

"I continue to be excited at the work of making the slowest buses in America fast and free. And I appreciate the governor’s continued partnership in delivering on that agenda of affordability," Mamdani said at a news conference earlier this month.

Rama Duwaji, wife of Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, and Jumaane Williams, public advocate of New York, during a City Hall ceremony to celebrate the New York Knicks' NBA Championship (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Mamdani is approaching the end of his first year as mayor. He was elected in November 2025 and was sworn in on Jan. 1, 2026. His term runs through Jan. 1, 2030.
Fox News Digital's Amanda Macias contributed to this report.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: GOP senator shares tragic update about husband's death
summary: Sen. Deb Fischer's office says Bruce Fischer died by suicide, revising the belief he passed peacefully at home as the family asks for understanding.
story: Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., being sworn into office by then-Vice President Mike Pence alongside her husband, Bruce Fischer, who died on Sunday. (Sen. Deb Fischer; Facebook)
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Bruce Fischer, the husband of Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., died by suicide on Sunday, the senator's office said Friday.

"There has been a sad update in the death of Senator Fischer’s husband, Bruce," a spokesperson for Fischer's office said in a statement posted to X. "Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home. Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life."
"The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss and asks for understanding in this time of mourning," the statement continued.
Chair Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., gavels to order the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Legislative Branch hearing on April 15, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
REPUBLICAN SENATOR'S HUSBAND DEAD: 'OUR FAMILY IS HEARTBROKEN'
The spokesperson added that there will be no further comment on the matter, "and no other details will be provided."
The update comes after Fischer announced on Monday that her husband had died the past weekend.

"It is with a heavy heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Bruce," Fischer said in a statement posted on social media at the time. "Bruce was my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family. His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him."
"On November 22, Bruce passed away peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors," the statement continued.
AMERICANS COULD FACE $100 HIKE IN INTERNET BILLS UNDER PLAN EYED BY LAWMAKERS
FILE - Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., speaks during a hearing, March 14, 2023, in Washington.  (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fischer and her husband met as students at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the Lincoln Journal Star reported. The couple married in 1972 and had three sons.
Republican Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen on Monday extended condolences to Fischer and her family.
Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., second from left, stands alongside her husband Bruce, third from left, and then-Vice President Kamala Harris. (Sen. Deb Fischer; Facebook)
"Suzanne and I are keeping Sen. Fischer and her family in our thoughts," Pillen wrote on X. "We share our prayers as she deals with this great personal loss."
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., said Monday in a post on X that he felt "very sad" to hear about Fischer's passing.

"Bruce left his mark on this world through his love for family, his faith, and his ranch," Ricketts added. "Susanne and I send our deepest condolences to Deb, the entire Fischer family, and all their loved ones during this difficult time. The Fischer family is in our prayers."

title: US pilot tells Trump which fighter jet is ‘world’s greatest’ during Thanksgiving phone call
summary: An F-16 pilot told President Donald Trump the jet is the "world's greatest" during a Thanksgiving call, saying "you couldn't pay me to switch airplanes."
story: President Donald Trump, during a Thanksgiving call with Air Force Lieutenant Colonel Brant Smith, asked which fighter jet was the best. Smith told him it was the F-16. Trump made calls to service members of all six U.S. military branches.
President Donald Trump learned what the "world's greatest" fighter jet is, according to an F-16 pilot, during a phone call on Thanksgiving Day.
"So could I ask, before I give my little speech to you — a little quick one — could I ask, so the F-16, you love it, right?" Trump asked U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Brant Smith.
"World's greatest fighter jet, sir," Smith replied.
Trump spoke to Smith from his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida as the president and first lady Melania made calls to service members from all six branches of the U.S. military.
A LOOK AT HOW THE TRUMPS SPEND THEIR THANKSGIVING HOLIDAY THROUGH THE YEARS
First lady Melania Trump makes Thanksgiving calls to U.S. service members next to President Donald Trump from Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on November 26, 2026. (REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque)
Trump asked Smith to compare his F-16 to other fighter jets like the F-22 or F-35, to which Smith replied: "The F-16 all day."
TRUMP SAYS AIR FORCE PILOTS DESCRIBED A ROUND UFO FLYING THREE TIMES FASTER THAN AN F-22 FIGHTER JET
"You couldn't pay me to switch airplanes," Smith added.

"I love flying this airplane. And I think there are very few pilots in this room that would argue with me. Both of those airplanes (F-22 and F-35) are great, and they have their place in the world and in the war. But, this is a lot of fun. We get to do it all, and it does it all very well," Smith said.

A U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jet is seen patrolling the skies above the Middle East as "American forces maintain regional presence and vigilance," according to U.S. Central Command. CENTCOM confirmed late Friday that American forces repelled multiple Iranian drone attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. (CENTCOM)
The president also asked Smith about his service and queried about what he was doing at the time.
"We are pre-installing the air base in Saudi Arabia," Smith replied.
CENTCOM'S THANKSGIVING MESSAGE TO TROOPS 'IS ONE OF DEEP GRATITUDE' FOR THEIR 'EXCEPTIONAL WORK' PROTECTING US

"You have a pretty large crowd of pilots, maintainers and ops support personnel from the 510th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, the Buzzards. We're an F-16 unit. We've been on here since about ten days before Epic Fury kicked off. And we're flying combat operations out in the straits every day," he continued.
Trump complimented Smith on the military's efforts in the Middle East and in the war with Iran.
TRUMP PAUSES TURKEY PARDON TO SALUTE US TROOPS GUARDING STRAIT OF HORMUZ: 'WATCH OVER AND PROTECT'

"And you're seeing some big victories, aren't you? Knocking them out left and right, knocking out the launchers, knocking out the missiles, knocking out left and right. Amazing job you're doing, Brant," Trump said.
"Thank you, sir," the airman responded.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN UNLEASHED MISSILE, DRONE SURGE AFTER MIDTERMS

President Donald Trump participates in a call with U.S. service members from his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Thanksgiving Day on November 27, 2025, in Palm Beach, Florida. (Pete Marovich/Getty Images)
Smith also told the president he believes Iran was "starting to run out of things." Trump concurred.

"Yep. I think they are. I think they are. And that'll continue. And we're getting stronger. We sent an extra aircraft carrier," Trump said, referring to the Nimitz-class USS Theodore Roosevelt, which arrived in the Middle East on Nov. 16 to relieve USS George Washington.
US RACES TO BUILD BUNKERS ACROSS MIDDLE EAST AS IRANIAN STRIKES THREATEN AMERICAN TROOPS
"In my opinion, they're not very smart. They're making big mistakes. They've made a lot of mistakes. Their economy is down the tubes," the president said of Iran.

"Every day the stellar F-16 squadron is conducting missions across the Middle East to defend our interests and our assets. Like few people could ever even think about. This year, you've flown more than 2,000 sorties over more than 12,000 hours across eight different operations, including Operation Epic Fury. And you're getting plenty of time out there, aren't you, Brant?"
