"Yes, sir," Smith said, adding, "Nine months and 10 days."
"And you love it, right?" Trump asked.
"Yeah, we're having fun," Smith said. "This is what we trained for."
"Amazing. The best in the world," Trump replied.

title: From Hollywood mogul to Biden-Harris insiders, Democrats turn to familiar faces to shape their next chapter
summary: Abdul El-Sayed's transition team director previously claimed Zionists were "controlling" U.S. politics, while Tyler Perry co-chairs Georgia's team.
story: National Review columnist Caroline Downey and Democratic strategist Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan. The panel discusses Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's rising influence and the impact on the 2028 Democratic primary.

On the heels of the blue wave in the 2026 U.S. midterms, incoming Democratic leaders are tapping an eclectic mix of political veterans, business executives and entertainment figures to help shape their transitions into power.

From a Hollywood mogul and former Biden administration officials to figures with ties to Republican leaders, the appointments offer an early glimpse into the people Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern — and the experience and connections they hope to bring into their new administrations.

Several incoming Democrats are turning to familiar faces from the Biden administration. In New Mexico, Gov.-elect Deb Haaland tapped former Biden presidential speechwriter Felicia Salazar and former Interior Department official Joan Mooney for her transition team, while California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra selected Arsenio Mataka, who previously served as his senior counselor at the Department of Health and Human Services under Biden, to direct policy for his transition team. In Ohio, Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton tapped Elisabeth Hire, a former aide to then-Vice President Biden, as a transition co-chair.
Haaland's campaign and Becerra's campaign each did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

A sign points to a vote center during the in-person early voting period in California's Proposition 50 special election on Oct. 27, 2025 in West Hollywood, California. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)

The transition teams will help incoming leaders prepare to take office, including identifying potential administration officials, shaping policy priorities and laying the groundwork for their first days in power. The selections also offer a window into the experience, relationships and perspectives newly elected Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., tapped Egyptian-American lawyer Brenda Abdelall as the director of his transition team, Politico Playbook first reported in early November. Abdelall previously claimed that Zionists were "controlling" much of U.S. politics, The Washington Free Beacon reported Nov. 6, though Harris' 2024 presidential campaign said at the time that the remarks did not reflect Abdelall's current views.

"The Zionists have a strong voice in American politics," Abdelall told the New York Sun during a conference for the American Muslim Council in 2002, the Free Beacon reported. "I would say they're controlling a lot of it."

Abdelall previously served as the assistant secretary of partnership and engagement at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. She also directed the Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign's outreach to Arab American voters, Reuters reported.
U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party convention, on August 29, 2026, in Lansing, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS

El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital on Nov. 9 that Abdelall "comes to the role of transition director with decades of experience leading teams at the highest levels of politics, including the Biden-Harris administration."

"While at the Department of Homeland Security, Brenda worked to implement the nation’s first National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism and frequently spearheaded efforts to counter the rise of hate crimes and violence across the country," Richner added. "The transition team is committed to building a team that reflects the great diversity of Michigan and ensuring that the El-Sayed office serves all communities across the state."
El-Sayed is set to assume office on Jan. 3, 2027.
DEMOCRATIC SENATOR-ELECT CALLS TRUMP 'UNSERIOUS FOOL' WHILE DEFENDING COMBATIVE POLITICAL STYLE
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Democratic Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms announced Nov. 6 that filmmaker and actor Tyler Perry would serve as one of 10 co-chairs of her transition team, dubbed "Georgia's Promise," WBAL-TV reported. Perry has long been known for his philanthropic efforts, including supporting underserved communities and charitable causes across Georgia. Bottoms lauded Perry as "an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta," WDSU reported.

Victorious Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, speaks onstage during her election night watch party at the Atlanta Marriott Marquis on Nov. 3, 2026 in Atlanta, Ga. (Megan Varner/Getty Images)
EX-BIDEN OFFICIAL WINS GEORGIA DEM PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR IN BID TO END PARTY'S LOSING STREAK

The news that Perry will serve on Bottoms’ Georgia transition team has sparked some criticism due to the entertainment mogul facing two active lawsuits accusing him of sexual assault and misconduct, allegations his attorneys have denied, Variety reported Nov. 6.
Perry has denied all sexual assault and harassment allegations made against him, People reported on March 3.
Maxscene, a division of Tyler Perry Studios, did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Bottoms previously was an executive producer on Netflix’s "Miss Governor," a 2025 political comedy sitcom produced by Tyler Perry Studios, per online film database IMDb.
Other prominent figures that have been tapped for Bottoms' transition committee include Home Depot co-founder Arthur Blank and former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance Roz Brewer, WBAL-TV reported.
Bottoms’ campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.
Bottoms is set to take office on Jan. 11, 2027.

Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson's transition team includes Mark Penley, a former deputy attorney general who reported outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to the FBI, and Erin Epley, who served as lead attorney in Paxton's impeachment, The Houston Chronicle reported Nov. 16.

Johnson also tapped Amanda Crawford, a former appointee of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, and Thaddeus Cleveland, a Republican sheriff from Terrell County, as part of his transition team, according to the Chronicle.
Johnson's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley is also turning to the world of professional sports, tapping Alex Lasry, a former senior vice president of the NBA's Milwaukee Bucks, to serve on his transition team, Wisconsin Public Radio reported Nov. 11.

Lasry, the son of former Bucks co-owner and billionaire businessman Marc Lasry, helped oversee the franchise's operations during its rise to the 2021 NBA championship and played a key role in developing Milwaukee's Fiserv Forum arena. He also mounted an unsuccessful bid for the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination in 2022.

Crowley's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

title: How to spot real Black Friday savings this holiday season amid the affordability squeeze
summary: A marketing professor warns that Black Friday deals aren't always real discounts, citing shrinkflation and inflation as factors that obscure true savings.
story: University at Buffalo marketing professor Dinesh Gauri shares his tips for scoring the best Black Friday prices, from researching deals ahead of time to taking advantage of online shopping and in-store pickup options.
Black Friday deals are everywhere, but a sale price does not always mean real savings.

With budgets under pressure, amid a persisting affordability crisis and rising fuel prices with the raging Iran conflict, shoppers are looking for ways to stretch their money during the holiday shopping season this year.

The forecasts point to a season of cautious spending. Visa Business and Economics Insights expects holiday sales to increase 4.5% from last year — but after accounting for higher prices, the actual increase in what shoppers buy is projected to be just 1.1%.
That makes it all the more important for shoppers to know what they’re paying for and whether a sale is truly a deal.

"It's still a good time to shop. It's just that you just have to be a little bit more careful," Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, told Fox News Digital when discussing holiday and Black Friday shopping.
7 HOLIDAY SHOPPING SCAMS TO WATCH FOR THIS SEASON

Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, recommends checking price histories and setting a budget before shopping for Black Friday sales. (Irfan Khan/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images)
Gauri revealed that shopping during Black Friday does not always produce the best deal — especially when it comes to essential technology like cell phones.
He advised shoppers to set a budget and research prices before making a purchase, especially for big-ticket items.
"Have a number in mind and do your research before you go about spending the money," he said, recommending price-tracking sites and extra promotions.
Gauri cited higher gas prices compared with last year as a potential pressure point for consumers, particularly those considering larger purchases.

While the average price of a gallon has risen from approximately $3 in November 2025 to $3.64 per gallon this November, according to AAA, the surging price of diesel is what is impacting the cost of nearly all goods for Americans.
GOOGLE'S NEW AI SHOPPING CART TRACKS DEALS ACROSS STORES

Tariffs are another potential source of price pressure. A New York Fed analysis found that about 26% of tariff increases from 2025 had been passed on to consumer prices. Retailers may also respond to higher costs by raising prices or reducing package sizes.
Gauri said some retailers have done both, a practice known as shrinkflation.
"The package size is getting smaller, even though the price might be the same," he said. "You’re shaving off, let’s say, 10% of the product."
Shoppers are expected to use holiday discounts to stock up on essentials as well as gifts, Adobe Analytics projects. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Gauri said Black Friday promotions now often begin during Thanksgiving week and run through Cyber Monday, giving shoppers more time to compare prices online and in stores. The shift from doorbusters that once drew shoppers to stores before dawn the Friday after Thanksgiving means consumers can now research deals, order products and arrange for pickup or delivery.

To make sure a discount is worthwhile, Gauri recommended using price-tracking websites and Amazon’s price-history feature to check what an item has cost in recent months. "Consumers tend to overspend sometimes because they do not remember what an item previously cost," he said.

He also advised shoppers to compare prices across retailers and check each store’s price-matching policy before making a major purchase. Some retailers exclude Black Friday specials from those policies, he said.
Black Friday promotions can offer real savings, but shoppers should compare prices to make sure a markdown is actually a deal. (Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images)
Gauri cautioned that Black Friday is not always the best time to shop.
"For cellphones, Black Friday doesn’t get you anything special," he said, adding that the best deals on phones or plans often come in October, around new product launches and carrier promotions.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Still, shoppers may find Cyber Week discounts useful for stocking up on everyday essentials.

Adobe Analytics projects online sales of clothing basics will run 210% above the September average, while personal hygiene products will be up 150%. Baby products, pet supplies and household cleaning items are also expected to see a boost.
With budgets under pressure, Gauri advised shoppers to set a spending limit before heading into the holiday sales.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Brookings Institution president, dies at 80
summary: Strobe Talbott, the former deputy secretary of state who advised Bill Clinton on Russian affairs and led the Brookings Institution, has died at 80.
story: Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state who once worked at Time magazine, died at age 80.

Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped U.S. foreign policy before he went on to lead the Brookings Institution, died Thursday at the age of 80.
Talbott’s son, Devin Talbott, said his father died peacefully after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, The Associated Press reported.

An Ohio native, Talbott began his journalism career as an intern at Time magazine while studying at Yale and Oxford, where he was roommates with future President Bill Clinton. Clinton later joked that his job in their shared apartment was to make Talbott breakfast every morning.
NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

Strobe Talbott, president of the Brookings Institution, right, and Wolfgang Ischinger, chairman of the Munich Security Conference on Security Policy, left, participate in a news conference in Berlin on July 16, 2008. (AP Photo/Franka Bruns)
While at Time, Talbott was tapped to translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former Soviet leader ousted in 1964, which earned him a full-time role at the magazine.
Over a 21-year career there, he focused on U.S.-Soviet relations, led the Washington bureau, and wrote as a foreign affairs columnist.
In 1994, Talbott joined the Clinton administration as deputy secretary of state, helping guide U.S. relations with Russia and other post-Soviet states.
In a statement, Bill Clinton said no one was better suited to advise him on Russian affairs than Talbott, noting that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton also relied on his counsel.
TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?
Strobe Talbott, president of the Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin on July 16, 2008. (AP Photo/Franka Bruns)

"He was analytical, completely devoted to diplomacy, and on the level," Bill Clinton said. "With his expertise, we made real progress building trust between two former adversaries — moving beyond decades of confrontation to reduce the nuclear dangers future generations would inherit and build a Europe where more people could live in freedom and peace, including through the expansion of NATO and resolving ethnic conflicts in the Balkans. Together we laid the groundwork for greater cooperation while putting Russia on a path to democracy."
"Sadly, its current leader has taken the country in a different direction," Clinton added, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993. (AP Photo/James Finley)
He described Talbott as a "good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," and said, "Hillary and I will miss him very much."
After leaving government, Talbott served as president of the Brookings Institution from 2002 to 2017 and chaired the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
President Bill Clinton during his last State of the Union Address before Congress. (Douglas Graham/Congressional Quarterly/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren. His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009; he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: FLASHBACK: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving surprises for US troops — see the moments
summary: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving trips to war zones, with Donald Trump serving turkey at Bagram Airfield and George W. Bush visiting Iraq.
story: Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and children while their loved ones are deployed across the globe. She expresses deep appreciation for their strength and resilience in keeping their homes full of love.
Under a cloak of secrecy, two American presidents made surprise Thanksgiving visits to war zones, bringing a taste of home to U.S. troops serving thousands of miles from their families.

Sixteen years apart, President George W. Bush celebrated with American troops in Iraq in 2003, while President Donald Trump served Thanksgiving dinner to service members in Afghanistan in 2019. Both visits were carried out under tight secrecy, catching troops by surprise as they spent the holiday far from home.
Trump secretly traveled to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, when he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war.
INSIDE TRUMP’S INTIMATE MEETING WITH NATION’S BRAVEST SOLDIERS DURING WHIRLWIND TEXAS TRIP
President Donald Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to U.S. troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019, in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time, later adding, "And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."
The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.
ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE'
President Donald Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to U.S. troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019, in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.
Less than two years later, President Joe Biden oversaw the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021.
WOUNDED MARINES RELIVE THE HARROWING KABUL AIRPORT ATTACK IN EXPLOSIVE NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY
Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to U.S. troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019, in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)
The withdrawal unfolded as the Taliban rapidly seized control of Afghanistan, culminating in the fall of Kabul and a frantic evacuation at the city's airport.

Sixteen years earlier, Bush pulled off a similar Thanksgiving surprise in Iraq, secretly flying into Baghdad International Airport on Nov. 27, 2003, to celebrate with American troops just eight months after launching the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein's regime.
GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS

President George W. Bush helps serve Thanksgiving dinner at the Bob Hope Dining Facility, Baghdad International Airport, Iraq, during a surprise visit with troops, November 27, 2003. (U.S. National Archives and Presidential Libraries)

Bush stunned hundreds of service members when he appeared at their Thanksgiving dinner, emerging to cheers and applause before helping serve a traditional holiday meal and posing for photos with troops stationed far from home.
"I can't think of a finer group of folks to have Thanksgiving dinner with than you all," Bush told the troops at the time.
"We're proud of you," he added. "Today, Americans are gathering with their loved ones to give thanks for the many blessings in our lives."
News of his trip was not even released until Air Force One had already left Iraq.
US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS

President George W. Bush carries a platter of turkey and fixings as he visits US troops for Thanksgiving in Baghdad, Nov. 27, 2003. Bush made the Thanksgiving visit to troops in Baghdad under the greatest secrecy and security. (ANJA NIEDRINGHAUS/AP POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Bush's visit came as American forces battled a growing insurgency following the fall of Saddam Hussein's government earlier that year. Despite Bush's declaration in May that major combat operations had ended, U.S. troops continued to face deadly attacks as the military worked to stabilize the country.

Just weeks later, U.S. forces captured Saddam Hussein in December 2003.

title: Democrats, Republicans find rare common ground when asked what they're thankful for
summary: Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill may clash on policy, but this Thanksgiving, lawmakers say family is what they're most thankful for.
story: House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

An ocean of ideological differences separates Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill, but they're largely in agreement over one thing this Thanksgiving, and it's usually miles away from Washington, D.C.
"I'm thankful for family," Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo., told Fox News Digital. "It's what drives me to keep going, to keep doing this, keep fighting for the country."

Families across America are gathering for Thanksgiving, kicking off a holiday season that's meant for reflection and refocusing on things that matter most. And members of Congress who spoke with Fox News Digital about that special day are no different.
The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 10, 2026. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"You know, elections can be a bumpy road in many ways, and it's easy to take a shot at somebody who's running — we put ourselves out there. But it's the family, really, and I'm grateful that my wife and my three kids who are in their 20s are so supportive," Rep. John Mannion, D-N.Y., said. "So that's what I'm thankful for."
Reps. Randy Fine, R-Fla., and Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., singled out their children.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
"I'm very grateful to how great my boys are doing despite the challenges of this job, and just my whole family for putting up with all of this and being there for me," Fine said.
Burchett told Fox News Digital he was "more than blessed."
Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo., leaves the Capitol Hill Club after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on March 25, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I've got a beautiful wife and a daughter, and I never thought I was gonna have a family. And I prayed, asked Jesus that I'd have a family, and I got one, dadgum it, and it is wonderful," Burchett said.
Rep. Mike Quigley, D-Ill., said he was grateful for the U.S.'s ability to still come together despite people's many differences.
SOUND OFF: WILL DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS COME TOGETHER FOR THE GOOD OF THE COUNTRY?
"I'm most thankful that this country still reminds itself that there's more that unites us than divides us," Quigley said.
Two more Democrats said they were thankful for their party’s success in the midterm elections.
Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., arrives for the vote on the budget resolution in the U.S. Capitol on April 10, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
"I'm thankful for the excitement of next year, to get things done," said Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill.
Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., said he was thankful for "an opportunity to make a difference in people's lives."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Democrats got a huge majority, and that allows us to help people," Thanedar, who lost his own re-election bid, said.

title: Universities, schools nationwide use Thanksgiving as chance to promote 'Day of Mourning' and decolonization
summary: Campus Thanksgiving events have been reframed as a "National Day of Mourning" for Indigenous remembrance, with Salem State and Pratt citing historical harm.
story: Loudoun County parent Rachel Pisani joins 'Fox & Friends' to express outrage over school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a 'Day of Mourning.' Pisani argues the 'woke' curriculum teaches children to hate their country.

Thanksgiving is a day of celebration and spending time with family for the vast majority of Americans, but for several students on college campuses across the country, the national holiday is a source of anguish that is being expressed in the form of protests and counter-programming events.

On Nov. 18, George Washington University hosted an event called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration" that was described as a chance for students to examine Thanksgiving, Christmas and Independence Day through an intersectional lens, including experiences of "belonging, exclusion, cultural erasure, and historical harm."

"Through facilitated dialogue and shared reflection, students will engage in meaningful conversations about historical memory, social responsibility, and the complexities of celebrating within a diverse society," the student life event description read.

At the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee, the American Indian Student Center & Electa Quinney Institute for American Indian Education hosted a Nov. 17 event called "AlterNative Giving," which was described as "a community gathering that offers a meaningful alternative to the traditional Thanksgiving narrative. Instead of focusing on colonial histories, we come together to honor Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and giving."
TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN ‘MISSES CORE IDEOLOGY' AND MUST TARGET LINGERING DANGER ON CAMPUSES, WATCHDOG WARNS
A modern recreation of the first Thanksgiving in the autumn of 1621 at Plimoth Patuxet Museums (formerly Plimoth Plantation) in Plymouth, Mass. (Courtesy of Kathy Tarantola/Plimoth Patuxet Museums)
Salem State University promoted an event that labeled Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" and told students the land they are being educated on was stolen from Indigenous people.

"The land occupied by Salem State University is part of the traditional and ancestral homeland of the Massachusett tribe," the school’s website posted. "We acknowledge the genocide and forced removal of the Massachusett tribe and their kin from their summer home in Nâmkek."
CALIFORNIA COLLEGE LECTURER REMOVED AFTER ERUPTING AT STUDENT OVER QUESTION ON NATIVE AMERICANS

A review of university calendars found several examples lamenting the downsides of Thanksgiving, including Occidental College, which said the holiday is a "reminder of settler colonialism and its devastating impact on Indigenous individuals, communities and tribes."

The Pratt Institute lists "National Day of Mourning" as an occasion for Indigenous remembrance and reflection, and the University at Albany lists the holiday as "National Day of Mourning/Thanksgiving."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
George Washington University hosted an event on Nov. 18 called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration." (iStock)

The colonial messaging around Thanksgiving isn't limited to universities but is also occurring at elementary and high schools, including in Loudoun County, Virginia, where a parent recently pushed back in an interview with Fox News about school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a "Day of Mourning."

On its website, the San Diego County Office of Education explained that "November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the diversity, history, and living cultures of Native peoples. It is also the month when Thanksgiving is observed in the United States, a holiday that carries very different meanings for different people, including many Native communities."

Oregon’s Bethel School District links to a "Decolonizing Thanksgiving: A Toolkit for Combatting Racism in Schools" on its official Equity, Access & Inclusion webpage. Listed under teaching resources, the toolkit appears alongside material about honoring Native peoples on Thanksgiving.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Trump takes on Somali welfare dependency in Thanksgiving message, lays out who should stay in US
summary: President Donald Trump says only 2% of Minnesota's Somali community should stay, claiming on Truth Social the rest should be thrown out to save the state.
story: President Donald Trump said Rep. Ilhan Omar could be deported or face jail when asked about questions surrounding her age, calling the Minnesota Democrat "a disgrace to our country."

In a lengthy Thanksgiving message on Truth Social Thursday, President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community, saying they should be allowed to remain in the United States, while calling for the immediate removal of those receiving government assistance while unemployed.

The holiday post mixed praise for "AMERICAN PATRIOTS" with criticism of the "Radical Far Left" and Minnesota’s Somali community, which Trump has frequently accused of public assistance fraud in the state.

"I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance," Trump wrote in the post. "These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay."
SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME

President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community in a Thanksgiving message, while calling for the majority to be "thrown out" of the United States. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images; YASUYOSHI CHIBA/AFP via Getty Images)

Ken Martin, chair of the Democratic National Committee, said Trump was spending the holiday "spewing hatred, attacking immigrants and bragging about his ballroom," saying he should instead be reminded that Thanksgiving is about "gratitude, generosity and community, not bigotry and interior decorating."

"As a proud Minnesotan, let me make something abundantly clear: our Somali American neighbors are part of the fabric of our state," Martin wrote on X. "They are small business owners, teachers, healthcare workers, parents, and hardworking Americans. They contribute far more to the spirit of this country than a man who can’t even get through a Thanksgiving greeting without demonizing an entire community."
"In Minnesota, we pull up another chair at the Thanksgiving table," he added. "Trump apparently would rather deport the people sitting around it."
SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS

A demonstrator waves the flag of Somalia as a vehicle passes by a rally in protest against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), amid a reported federal immigration operation targeting the Somali community, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on December 8, 2025. (Tim Evans/Reuters)
Trump’s remarks echo ongoing criticism from some Republicans regarding public benefit usage and fraud cases within the community.

During a House Oversight Committee hearing in January, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, highlighted data on government support programs, noting that 54% of Somali-headed households in Minnesota receive food stamps.
Elsewhere in the post, Trump claimed that "murderers, drug dealers, and criminals" — who he said illegally entered the U.S. from foreign prisons and mental institutions — have largely been deported.
"They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again," he wrote.
TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

"We won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE — but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands," he added. "We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!"
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also shared a holiday message on social media, with a video focused on opportunities provided by the U.S.

"We know how special this country is. It's the place that gave us freedom. It's a place that gave us opportunity. It's a place that's given our parents, our grandparents, and many of you the chance not just to do well in life, but to leave our children better off than ourselves," Rubio said in the video.

In the attached caption, he added, "Being an American is a gift unlike any ever afforded to any other peoples throughout human history — we have so much to be thankful for. Happy Thanksgiving."

title: Politics, money and Thanksgiving dinner: Just two words can help avoid argument
summary: Dr. Joel Davis Brown says swapping "yes, but" for "yes, and" can keep Thanksgiving dinner talk civil as post-midterm politics turn tense at the table.
story: Dr. Joel Brown, a communication expert, shares how replacing one common phrase and asking a simple question can help defuse disagreements and keep holiday gatherings civil.

As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense.

Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil.
"‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation."

Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather, it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions."
FOOD PRICES ARE RISING BEFORE THANKSGIVING. AN ECONOMIST SHARES WAYS TO SAVE

Dr. Joel Brown says the holiday dinner table can quickly become a source of tension when family members disagree, but choosing the right words can make all the difference in preventing heated exchanges. (iStock)
If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that."
The question, he says, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate.

He also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another. Rather than trading facts and figures to win an argument, he said, people may make more headway by sharing personal stories and listening to the experiences behind someone else’s opinion.

"If you’re going into these exchanges as looking to win an argument, maybe change your approach," Brown said. "Maybe instead of trying to win that argument, you try to understand the other person’s perspective."
BLACK FRIDAY DEALS ARE EVERYWHERE. HERE’S HOW TO SPOT REAL SAVINGS
Holiday gatherings can bring family and friends together, but differing opinions and heated conversations can sometimes lead to tension. (iStock)

Brown said it helps to decide in advance what you want from the interaction, whether that’s getting through the meal, building a relationship or persuading someone. That goal can shape how you respond.
Political topics aren't the only ones that can get tense when families come together.

For personal questions about marriage, children or other life choices, Brown recommends setting expectations before the gathering. Talk with family or friends about what would help everyone feel comfortable, and be clear about what you do and do not want to discuss.

Additionally, if a conversation becomes stressful, take a breath, sip water or step away from the table. Brown said people should know their own triggers and remember they are not responsible for managing every interaction.
Making small changes to the way people communicate may help keep holiday celebrations peaceful, enjoyable and focused on togetherness. (iStock)
He encourages approaching disagreements with empathy, which he described as listening to another person’s story without taking on their position.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Family members may not see eye to eye, he said, but the holiday can still be a chance to learn from one another.
"Look at these as learning opportunities," Brown said.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: 2026's biggest political turkeys: Scandals, gaffes and other memorable unfortunate moments from this year
summary: Eric Swalwell's California gubernatorial collapse, Tim Walz's fraud scandal and more: the political figures whose 2026 ended in scandal and defeat.
story: From Eric Swalwell to Tim Walz, several political figures are looking back on 2026 with regret after making the list of biggest political turkeys.

As 2026 comes to a close, several political blunders, missteps, and serious allegations have left prominent politicians and notable figures presumably looking back with regret. Here are the top political turkeys who made headlines for unfortunate reasons this year.

Heading into 2026, Eric Swalwell was a well-known member of Congress and the leading Democratic contender in the race for governor of California. By March, he had become the frontrunner in the race and looked poised to take control of the nation’s largest economy in a state where Democrats rarely lose in statewide general elections.

Shortly after, that all changed when allegations of sexual assault and other misconduct surfaced in April, prompting prominent Democrats to swiftly withdraw their endorsements and call for Swalwell to abandon his gubernatorial bid.
SWALWELL’S FORMER DEM RIVAL UNLOADS ON HIS ‘LIGHTWEIGHT’ CAREER AS SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS EMERGE

Several prominent political figures faced controversy, public missteps and serious allegations throughout 2026, landing them on this year's list of political turkeys. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images; Drew Angerer/Getty Images)

Swalwell denied the sexual assault allegations, but within days he suspended his campaign and resigned from Congress amid bipartisan calls for his ouster, which effectively ended his political career and put him in potential legal jeopardy.

Swalwell faces a federal investigation and separate probes in New York and Los Angeles into sexual assault allegations, which he denies. FBI agents seized his electronic devices and searched his Washington home in August, and in October searched a Beverly Hills mansion where he had stayed. No criminal charges have been filed.
In 2024, Walz was elevated to the top of the national scene when he was chosen by former Vice President Kamala Harris to be her running mate for president.
Since then, Walz’s political fortunes have taken a downward turn after the Harris-Walz ticket lost the presidential election, leading some pundits to criticize the decision to add him to the ticket.

In January 2026, Walz’s political career took another hit when he announced he was dropping his bid for re-election as governor amid a massive fraud scandal that is estimated to have cost the state billions.
Polling in June showed that Walz’s approval rating had dropped to its lowest level since he took office.
ANGER SWELLS AFTER SWALWELL'S 'OPEN SECRET' WITH WOMEN WENT UNREPORTED FOR YEARS

Republicans faced historical headwinds heading into the midterm elections and were dealing with significant voter frustration on issues like gas prices and affordability. While many expected Democrats to have a good night on Nov. 3, the GOP ended up losing control of both chambers of Congress ahead of President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

Additionally, Democrats picked up control of the majority of governorships in the United States as well as control of the majority of state legislatures, giving the party a dominant presence it hasn’t seen in decades.
Axios reported that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship.
TIM WALZ SAYS HE TAKES RESPONSIBILITY FOR MINNESOTA FRAUD BY NOT RUNNING FOR RE-ELECTION

After years as one of the most recognizable and outspoken Democratic members of Congress, Crockett will be out of a job on Capitol Hill in 2027 after opting against House re-election to pursue an unsuccessful Senate bid.

Her decision followed Texas Republicans’ redrawing of the congressional map, which reduced the number of Democratic-leaning seats in the Dallas-Fort Worth area from three to two and scrambled the plans of three Democratic incumbents. Crockett’s redrawn 30th District remained Democratic-leaning, but she chose a statewide campaign rather than seeking another House term.

Crockett lost the Democratic primary to state Rep. James Talarico in March, then reignited tensions by describing the contest as a "racist race" and pushed back against expectations that she would campaign alongside him. "People keep trying to say, ‘Well, Jasmine has to go and hold his hand.’ No, I don’t," she said during a July podcast appearance, arguing that supporting Black candidates further down the ballot would help increase turnout.

Although Crockett and her campaign said she had endorsed Talarico through her post-primary call to support the Democratic ticket, her reluctance to campaign with him and his omission from her political action committee’s endorsements fueled questions about her enthusiasm. Talarico defended her, saying he welcomed her endorsement, while Crockett maintained that elevating lesser-known candidates would benefit Democrats on the ballot.
Talarico ultimately defeated Republican Ken Paxton by about 12 percentage points, becoming the first Texas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat there since Lloyd Bentsen was re-elected in 1988.

The socialist Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate was dominating in the polls heading into the August Democratic primary, but her campaign stumbled in its final days as she struggled to explain past calls to cancel Thanksgiving before narrowly losing to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a candidate who had exited and then returned to the race.
Progressive firebrand Francesca Hong sought to topple the Democratic establishment in a closely watched Wisconsin showdown. (Talia Sprague/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The controversy centered on a resurfaced 2020 social media post in which Hong wrote, "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," and criticized celebrating colonialism. Asked on CNN in August whether she still wanted the holiday canceled, Hong initially emphasized that Thanksgiving was painful for some communities rather than directly rejecting her earlier position. She later reversed course, saying she loved Thanksgiving and did not want to cancel it. After losing the primary, Hong acknowledged that she regretted the CNN interview.
The Republican senator lost her seat in deep-red Mississippi to Democrat Scott Colom after an answer about rising beef prices became damaging campaign fodder.

Asked by WLOX anchor Hugh Keeton about rising beef prices during a local television interview, Hyde-Smith responded, "You know, you have so many proteins to choose from." Colom later used the exchange in a campaign ad featuring voters saying they would rather pick another senator.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Colom ultimately defeated Hyde-Smith by just 8,031 votes, a margin of less than 1 percentage point — close enough that her remark, amplified by her opponent’s advertising, could have made the difference in a race that cost Republicans a seat many believed was safe.

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich singled out the remark while discussing Republican losses with Larry Kudlow on Fox News before the race was called, arguing that suggesting cheaper food failed to address voters’ economic frustrations.
"I mean, it’s not the job of a senator to explain her failure by suggesting a new diet," Gingrich said.

Other honorable mentions include Democratic Fayette County Council candidate Jaime West, who was ridiculed by critics who said she appeared to be drunk and slurred her way through attacks on Republicans during a televised candidate forum; Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, whose controversial ad featuring his opponent’s mother drew fierce blowback before he lost his race; and Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner's fall from grace as he suspended his campaign after being accused of sexual assault.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Trump, NATO chief push Russia to avoid any actions that would 'expand the war' with Ukraine
summary: President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte, who met Wednesday night at Mar-a-Lago, urged Russia to avoid actions that might expand the Ukraine war.
story: Fox News foreign correspondent Jeff Paul joins ‘The Story’ to comment on a study estimating that more than 700,000 Russian troops have been killed since the war in Ukraine began. He also reports on Poland’s accusation that Russia violated its airspace, prompting international concern.
President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte are calling on Russia to avoid making any moves "that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war" against Ukraine.
The declaration came after the pair got together at Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thanksgiving Eve for what was described as an "outstanding meeting."
However, Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, according to the mayor of the Ukrainian capital.

"The meeting was very impactful, with the war between Russia and Ukraine and the conflict in Iran being the primary subjects, as well as all of the record setting achievements that we have made together at the summits in the Hague and at Ankara," Trump and Rutte said in a joint statement.

"We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," the statement added. "Lastly, we talked about the importance of continuing to expand defense spending and investment in our industrial base, both in the United States and across NATO."
PUTIN'S WAR DEATH TOLL REPORTEDLY TOPS 700,000 AS RUSSIA SCRAMBLES FOR RECRUITS
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte meets with President Donald Trump during a visit to Mar-a-Lago in Florida on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. (Reuters)

On Thursday, Trump said on Truth Social that "during my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly."
Trump met with Putin recently at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China.

"I really believe this is a strong possibility — Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH — and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!" Trump added. " It was an Honor meeting with Secretary General of NATO, Mark Rutte, last night at Mar-a-Lago, where many topics were discussed, and in which I updated him on my talks with President Putin."
Rutte also said in a post on X following the meeting, "It’s clearer than ever that American leadership remains essential as we build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO."

The Kremlin on Thursday accused Ukraine of trying to expand the war after Ukraine sank a Russian warship in Libya using drones and attacked a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend, Reuters reported.

"As regards the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine, this appears to refer to attempts by the Kyiv regime to expand the geographical scope of this conflict. We are witnessing terrorist activity by the Kyiv regime in the Mediterranean and the Baltic," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying.
NATO SECRETARY GENERAL MARK RUTTE WARNS ON UKRAINE WAR RISKS AHEAD OF TRUMP MEETING

A fire burns in the Desnianskyi district following a Russian ballistic missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Russian forces attacked the district, causing multiple fires and injuring seven people. (Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA/Reuters)

"This cannot fail to cause concern amongst coastal states, and most likely within the Alliance as a whole — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Of course, nobody would want the conflict to spread geographically, and these are potentially very dangerous actions on the part of the Kyiv regime," Peskov added, according to Reuters.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least seven people were wounded in Russian strikes overnight, hitting a shopping center and other buildings, Reuters also reported.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump shake hands at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Transportation secretary Sean Duffy flies $148K Jetson ONE at NASA
summary: Sean Duffy flew a $148,000 Jetson ONE solo over NASA's Kennedy Space Center, and two days later five eVTOLs flew in formation at a public airshow.
story: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy discusses the importance of congressional funding for America's aviation system, the need to modernize aging infrastructure and the challenges facing air travel on 'Hannity.' Duffy also addresses the urgency of improving aviation technology, strengthening safety measures and ensuring the Federal Aviation Administration has the resources needed to prevent disruptions and maintain the reliability of the nation's air transportation system.

Seeing a $148,000 flying machine lift off at NASA's Kennedy Space Center would be impressive on its own. Now put U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in the pilot's seat. That's exactly what happened recently when Duffy took a Jetson ONE for a solo flight over the Florida spaceport. Two days later, five of these personal electric aircraft were flying in formation during a public airshow.

Jetson says Duffy became the first sitting U.S. transportation secretary to pilot a personal electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as an eVTOL. His flight also raises an interesting question about where personal aviation is heading. After all, we're talking about an aircraft that can fly without its operator needing a pilot's license under certain FAA rules. But before you start clearing space in your garage, let's look at what this aircraft can actually do and where you can legally fly it.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE
A Jetson ONE electric aircraft flies above the grounds of NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida during a recent flight demonstration. (Jetson)
Sean Duffy takes the Jetson ONE for a solo flight

Duffy climbed into the single-seat Jetson ONE during the UP.Summit gathering at Kennedy Space Center. He lifted off vertically and performed flybys using the aircraft's joystick controls. Jetson says its computerized flight system automatically helps stabilize the aircraft, making it easier to maneuver.
After landing, Duffy made his enthusiasm clear. "Personal flight isn't the future anymore, it's here," he said.

For Jetson, having the nation's top transportation official experience the aircraft firsthand was a major moment. However, Duffy's flight did not change any FAA regulations or expand where the Jetson ONE can legally operate.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy prepares to climb into the $148,000 Jetson ONE for his solo flight at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. (Jetson)
Five Jetson ONE aircraft fly together at NASA

Duffy's solo flight was only part of the excitement. During the November MAX POWER airshow, Jetson sent five aircraft into a synchronized formation from Kennedy Space Center's historic Shuttle Landing Facility. The event also featured NASA research aircraft and the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds.

Among the five Jetson aircraft was Astro, the flying police vehicle owned by the Florida Polytechnic University Police Department. We recently covered this $148,000 electric police aircraft, which the university hopes to use for public safety operations.

Astro features police lights and a special registration, N911FP. At Kennedy Space Center, the aircraft took part in the formation flight and appeared on display for attendees. However, its participation in the airshow does not establish that the department has received approval for routine police operations. The university has been pursuing separate FAA authorization.
FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER
Five Jetson ONE aircraft take part in a coordinated flight demonstration at NASA's Kennedy Space Center, including a model operated by Florida Polytechnic University Police. (Jetson)
How fast can the $148,000 Jetson ONE fly?

The Jetson ONE looks like a giant drone with a seat in the middle. Eight electric motors power its propellers, allowing it to take off vertically without a runway. The aircraft also has an open cockpit and a lightweight aluminum frame that folds for storage. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach 63 mph and stay airborne for approximately 20 minutes per charge. It carries one person, with a maximum pilot weight of 210 pounds.

Jetson also highlights several safety features, including a ballistic parachute and radar-assisted automatic landing. The company says the aircraft can remain airborne if one motor fails. Those features sound reassuring, although they cannot eliminate the risks of flying.

Then there's the price. A Jetson ONE currently costs $148,000 before taxes and additional fees. Jetson says its 2026 and 2027 production slots are already sold out, with new orders targeting 2028 delivery. So even if you're ready to spend the money, you won't be taking delivery anytime soon.
Why FAA rules still limit the Jetson ONE

Here's something that might surprise you. Jetson designed the ONE to operate under the FAA's Part 103 ultralight regulations. Qualifying aircraft can be flown recreationally without a pilot's license or an airworthiness certificate.

But the rules come with restrictions. Under FAA Part 103 regulations, ultralights are limited to recreational or sporting purposes. Operators generally must fly during daylight hours and cannot fly over congested cities or outdoor gatherings. Flights in certain controlled airspace also require prior authorization.

Weight is another important factor. Jetson lists the ONE at 253 pounds with batteries. That's just below the 254-pound empty-weight limit for powered ultralights under Part 103. The FAA also applies specific rules to how that weight is calculated. These regulations help explain why the Florida Polytechnic University Police Department needs separate FAA authorization before using Astro for official law enforcement operations.

Jetson previously said the university required approval under Part 91 to integrate the aircraft into police work. That's also why Duffy's flight deserves attention. He oversees the department responsible for the FAA, and he's now experienced this technology himself. Whether that leads to new discussions about personal electric aircraft remains to be seen.
Jetson ONE attracts another major aerospace name

Duffy isn't the only prominent figure showing interest in Jetson. On Nov. 2, the company announced that Sir Peter Beck, founder and CEO of Rocket Lab, had become a Jetson ONE owner after experiencing the aircraft firsthand. According to Jetson's announcement, Beck has already received his Founders Edition aircraft.

The company expects it to fly by Christmas, pending regulatory approvals. Having a rocket company founder purchase one certainly gives Jetson another high-profile supporter. However, we'll learn much more as additional aircraft reach customers and begin flying outside carefully organized demonstrations.
The single-seat Jetson ONE flies above Florida's Space Coast, showcasing a personal electric aircraft capable of reaching speeds up to 63 mph. (Jetson)
What this means to you

You probably won't see a Jetson ONE flying over your neighborhood anytime soon. Its $148,000 price puts it well beyond most people's budgets, and the roughly 20-minute flight time limits how far it can practically travel.

FAA restrictions also prevent recreational ultralights from flying over congested areas. Still, it's exciting to see personal electric aircraft moving into customers' hands. And with police departments exploring the technology, there could eventually be applications beyond recreational flying.

If you're considering buying one, take the training seriously, even though qualifying Part 103 ultralights don't require a pilot's license. You'll also want to understand exactly where you can legally fly before making such a large purchase.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to admit, I'd love to take a Jetson ONE for a spin. The idea of lifting off vertically and flying around in something this compact sounds like an incredible experience. Seeing five of them together at Kennedy Space Center makes me even more curious about where this technology could go. But I also have questions about how we're going to handle more personal aircraft sharing our skies.

Duffy has now experienced one firsthand, and I hope that leads to some serious conversations about safety and how these aircraft should be regulated. I'm especially interested in what happens with Florida Polytechnic's flying police vehicle. That's where we'll start to see whether this technology can deliver something useful beyond recreational flying.
Would you trust yourself to fly a Jetson ONE without a pilot's license, or should the FAA require formal training before anyone takes one into the sky? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: AI bionic eye breakthrough could help restore sight
summary: An AI bionic eye trained on a blind man's brain responses helped UC Santa Barbara researchers produce more predictable phosphenes with less current.
story: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson discusses Elon Musk's Neuralink Blindsight device, which aims to restore visual perception to people who are blind. He explains how the technology works and what regulatory hurdles remain.

At a hospital in Spain, a 27-year-old man who lost his sight after a traumatic brain injury reported seeing flashes of light when researchers stimulated part of his brain. Those flashes were limited, but scientists have now used artificial intelligence to gain more control over the brain activity behind them.

The research could help make future artificial vision systems more reliable. Scientists are developing an AI bionic eye approach that learns how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation. Although the technology remains experimental, it could eventually help people who have lost their sight regain some degree of vision.
So, how does this brain implant work, and what would it take to turn a few flashes of light into useful vision?
MOUTHPAD LETS YOUR TONGUE CONTROL A COMPUTER

Camera-equipped glasses used in bionic vision research show how scientists are exploring technology that could eventually help restore limited sight. (Matt Perko, UC Santa Barbara)
How an AI bionic eye works

When you look at something, your eyes send signals to your brain, which processes what you're seeing. But what happens when those signals can no longer reach the brain? For years, scientists have been developing electronic implants that attempt to restore some vision.

Some stimulate the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Others take a different approach by sending electrical signals directly to the brain. That's what makes this research interesting. Scientists are studying a device called a visual cortical prosthesis, sometimes described as a bionic eye. Despite the nickname, the implant goes into the brain rather than the eye.

It targets the visual cortex, the part of the brain responsible for processing visual information. When researchers stimulate this area with electricity, a person may experience flashes or spots of light known as phosphenes. These sensations can resemble glowing dots or simple shapes. However, getting the brain to produce consistent results has been a major challenge.
A blind man helps researchers test the brain implant

In 2024, researchers from UC Santa Barbara traveled to Spain as part of a collaborative study with ETH Zurich and Miguel Hernández University involving a 27-year-old man who had lost his sight after a traumatic brain injury. At IMED Elche Hospital, the man had received an experimental implant containing 96 electrodes placed in his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain implanted for six months before being removed.

During the study, researchers delivered small electrical currents through the electrodes. The man reported experiencing flashes of light and various shapes. That was encouraging, but the researchers wanted to go further. They needed to understand why certain electrical signals produced particular sensations and whether those responses could become more predictable.
FIRST-EVER GENE THERAPY FOR HEARING LOSS GETS FDA APPROVAL: 'GROUNDBREAKING'
Researchers are using AI to better understand how electrical stimulation affects the visual cortex and predict the flashes of light a blind person experiences. (PeopleImages/Getty Images)
How AI makes the bionic eye more precise

This is where artificial intelligence helped the researchers make progress. Scientists trained a deep learning model to study how the man's brain responded to different electrical stimulation patterns. Instead of relying solely on the settings sent to the electrodes, the AI analyzed the actual brain activity those signals produced. It also considered what the brain was doing immediately before stimulation.
That's important because brain activity can fluctuate over time, which can affect how someone responds to the same electrical signals.

Using this information, researchers identified stimulation patterns more likely to produce particular brain responses. When they tested those AI-designed patterns, the results improved. The researchers achieved greater accuracy in producing their intended patterns of brain activity while using less electrical current. They also discovered something important.

The brain activity recorded after stimulation was a better predictor of what the man reported seeing than the electrical settings alone. In other words, knowing how the brain responded gave researchers a better indication of the man's visual experience.
Michael Beyeler, an associate professor at UC Santa Barbara who helped lead the research, explained the goal.
"Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around," he said.
That approach could help future implants adjust to changes in brain activity rather than depend on the same stimulation settings every time. The research was published in the journal Neuron.
Could an AI bionic eye restore actual vision?

It's an exciting possibility, but there's still a long road ahead. The man in this experiment experienced flashes and shapes of light. He did not regain normal eyesight, and researchers have yet to demonstrate that this AI approach can provide the functional vision someone would need to read or recognize faces. The experiment also involved only one participant. Scientists need additional research to determine how well the approach works in other people.

Still, the findings address a significant challenge. Researchers can stimulate the brain, but predicting exactly what someone will experience has been difficult. AI could help close that gap by learning how each person's brain responds and identifying better ways to deliver electrical signals. We've also covered a tiny retinal implant that helped people with advanced age-related macular degeneration regain some central vision.

That device works with the retina and specialized glasses. The new research takes a different route by targeting the brain directly. It could eventually offer another option for people whose eyes or optic nerves can no longer send visual information effectively, provided their visual cortex can still respond to stimulation.
ROBOT PERFORMS 26 CATARACT SURGERIES WITH SURGEON CONTROL

Researchers used AI to study how electrical stimulation produces brain responses that can lead to flashes and shapes of light, bringing scientists closer to more predictable artificial vision. (iStock)
What needs to happen before bionic eyes become available?

Researchers still have several challenges to overcome before this technology could become a practical treatment. First, they need to demonstrate that the approach works safely and consistently in more people. Scientists must also determine whether the flashes and shapes produced by electrical stimulation can become useful visual information. Another challenge involves keeping the implant responsive as the brain changes.
A stimulation pattern that works during one session may produce different results later.

The AI approach tested in this study offers a possible way to address that problem. However, researchers have yet to demonstrate a complete system that continuously adapts and delivers useful vision during everyday activities. For people dealing with vision loss today, technology already provides other forms of assistance.

Our article on tech tools that make vision loss easier to manage at CyberGuy.com explores features that can help with everyday tasks. As for this new research, the next challenge involves turning more predictable brain responses into visual experiences that could help someone navigate the world.
Kurt's key takeaways

The possibility of helping someone regain their sight through a brain implant is pretty remarkable. What I find especially interesting about this research is how AI could help scientists understand the way each person's brain responds to electrical signals. That could eventually make artificial vision more reliable. But there's still a big difference between seeing flashes of light and being able to recognize what's around you. I'd love to see this technology reach a point where someone who has lost their sight can recognize familiar objects or move around more independently. We're not there yet, and this was only one participant. Still, if researchers can turn these early results into useful vision, it could make an enormous difference in people's lives.

If scientists could someday restore even a small amount of your vision through a brain implant, would you consider the surgery, or would you wait until the technology could provide clearer sight? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
