title: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
summary: A researcher claims Google Gemini pulled private Gmail billing details into chats, and Google confirms some connected-app data may face human review.
story: Cybersecurity threats escalate as Leah Siskind analyzes Google’s warning about hackers using AI to automate cyberattacks against companies. Discussing the battle between defenders and attackers with John Roberts, the FDD AI Research fellow references Anthropic’s release of advanced models months ago. Siskin warns that super advanced AI models now have the dangerous ‘ability to detect vulnerabilities’ in software systems.

Think about everything sitting in your Gmail inbox right now. Maybe there's a conversation with your doctor, a recent bank statement or a personal message you never intended anyone else to read. Your Google Drive may hold years of private documents. You probably don't spend much time thinking about who might see that information beyond the people you share it with. But what happens when you connect those services to Google's Gemini AI assistant?

An independent researcher has raised concerns about how Gemini handles information retrieved from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The findings prompted questions about whether some private content could end up in conversations reviewed by humans.

We contacted Google, and the company confirmed that some information retrieved from connected Gmail and Drive accounts may be seen by human reviewers under certain circumstances. Google stressed that these connections are off by default. Here's what you should know before giving Gemini access to your personal information.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

Google's Gemini assistant can retrieve information from connected Gmail accounts to answer questions, raising concerns about how private emails may be handled. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
Researcher raises concerns about Google Gemini privacy

An independent researcher using the name thisisme6598 published findings on GitHub, raising questions about the way Gemini retrieves information from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The researcher tested Gemini using a personal Google Account with connected apps enabled. According to the published findings, Gemini sometimes retrieved information from emails or files during conversations without someone explicitly asking it to search Gmail or Drive. For example, the researcher described asking Gemini whether an internet service bill seemed too expensive. During some tests, Gemini reportedly retrieved billing information from Gmail, including payment amounts, account details and confirmation numbers.

In certain instances, the researcher reported that Gemini returned several sentences directly from an email and, in some tests, the entire email, including its headers. The researcher argues that this behavior creates a privacy concern because information retrieved into a Gemini conversation may become eligible for human review. However, the published findings do not establish that a human reviewer actually accessed the researcher's emails. Google told CyberGuy that the reported retrieval was standard behavior for someone who had voluntarily connected their apps. The company also emphasized that retrieved files remain visible only to the authenticated account holder and are not exposed publicly through this process.
Can human reviewers see your Gmail and Drive information through Gemini?

Yes, under certain circumstances. Google's own Connected Apps privacy documentation confirms that trained human reviewers, including service providers, may review a subset of information processed through Gemini's connected apps. That information can include summaries or excerpts from relevant Gmail messages and Google Drive documents.

In some cases, Google acknowledges that reviewers may see a complete email or file if it is short or especially relevant to the request. Google also says human reviewers may access some Gmail inbox content when investigating abuse or harm or responding to submitted feedback.
The company uses these reviews to evaluate Gemini's responses and improve its services.

Simply using Gmail or Google Drive does not subject your private content to this review process. The concern involves information retrieved after someone voluntarily connects those services to consumer Gemini. Google says it does not train generative AI models directly on someone's entire Gmail inbox or Drive. However, relevant information processed during Gemini conversations may be used for model improvement, depending on account settings. Google specifically warns against connecting apps containing confidential information someone would be uncomfortable having a reviewer see.
What Google told CyberGuy about Gemini privacy

We contacted Google directly to ask whether human reviewers could access Gmail messages or Drive files processed through the consumer Gemini app. We also asked whether the company had changed its privacy disclosures, notified existing customers and provided ways to prevent human review. A Google spokesperson told CyberGuy:

"Gmail and Google Drive’s core privacy protections remain unchanged, and your private emails and files are not reviewed by humans simply by using Gmail, Drive, or built-in Workspace features. Connecting those apps to the consumer Gemini app is off by default — it’s an optional way to get more personalized, time-saving answers across your Google apps when you want them. Users can disconnect their apps in Gemini settings at any time without losing access to Gemini’s core features."

Google also confirmed that when someone connects their apps to consumer Gemini with activity saving enabled, a small subset of conversations may undergo human review. Those conversations can contain relevant information retrieved from connected services. Before trained service providers review the material, Google says it separates the conversations from the associated Google Account and takes steps to reduce identifying information. The company also disputes the suggestion that the researcher's findings demonstrate public exposure of private files.
Did Google change its Gemini privacy promises?

Another part of the controversy involves changes to Google's public privacy disclosures. In Oct. 2023, Google published a blog post about its approach to generative AI privacy. The company said that content from Gmail, Docs and Drive accessed through Bard's Workspace extensions would not be seen by human reviewers or used to train the Bard model.

On Oct. 16, 2026, Google added an update to that same blog post. The new language explains that Google has introduced additional optional features allowing people to connect Workspace information to other Google services. Google says that when someone enables these newer features, a subset of the information may be used to train generative AI models, depending on their settings. It may also undergo human review in limited circumstances. The researcher argues that the change represents a reversal of Google's earlier privacy commitment.

However, Google's original statement concerned Bard's Workspace extensions, while the updated disclosure addresses newer connected features. The available evidence does not establish that Google quietly changed the underlying handling of information in existing connections. We asked Google whether people who previously connected their accounts were notified about the updated disclosures or asked to provide additional consent. Google's response did not directly address those questions. Instead, the company emphasized that the newer connections are optional and can be disabled. That leaves an important question about how clearly Google communicates changes to its AI privacy practices, particularly as new features gain access to more personal information.
APPLE TIGHTENS MAC SECURITY AS AI AGENTS SEEK YOUR FILES

Google Workspace with Gemini brings AI features to Google's productivity tools, with different data privacy protections for business accounts than for personal Gemini accounts. (Photo by Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
What happens to your information after human review?

Google says it disconnects conversations from the associated Google Account before sending them to trained service providers for routine review. The company also takes steps to reduce personal information. However, removing account identifiers does not necessarily eliminate every sensitive detail contained in an email excerpt or document summary.

Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub explains that conversations reviewed by service providers may be retained for up to three years, even after someone deletes the corresponding activity from their Google Account.

Turning off Gemini's History setting, previously called Keep Activity, prevents future conversations from being used to train generative AI models unless someone submits feedback. However, Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes, including with help from human reviewers.

On Nov. 16, 2026, Google announced changes to its Gemini privacy controls. Under the previous policy, Google retained conversations for up to 72 hours when Keep Activity was turned off. Under the new policy, Google will retain conversations for approximately two months when History is turned off. The company is rolling out these changes globally over several weeks.
How to protect your Gmail and Google Drive privacy
If you use Gemini, it's worth checking which accounts and services you've connected. You may find that you don't need every feature enabled. Here are some settings worth reviewing.
Google groups Gmail and Drive under Google Workspace in its connected-app settings. Here's how to check the connection on a computer.

Go to gemini.google.com and sign in to your personal Google Account.At the bottom of the sidebar, click Settings (which may appear as Settings & help).Select Personal Intelligence.Click Connected Apps.Find Google Workspace, which includes Gmail and Drive.Click More options (the three-dot menu) next to Google Workspace and select Disconnect.Follow any on-screen instructions to complete the change.
Go to gemini.google.com and sign in to your personal Google Account.
At the bottom of the sidebar, click Settings (which may appear as Settings & help).
Select Personal Intelligence.
Click Connected Apps.
Find Google Workspace, which includes Gmail and Drive.
Click More options (the three-dot menu) next to Google Workspace and select Disconnect.
Follow any on-screen instructions to complete the change.

If you see a different menu, look for Connected Apps in Gemini's settings. Google offers different connection controls depending on account eligibility and available features. You can reconnect supported services later if you decide to use them.
If you want to prevent future conversations from being used to train Google's generative AI models, review this setting.

Visit Gemini Apps Activity.Sign in with the Google Account you use for Gemini.Find the History or Keep Activity control near the top of the page.Click On to open the available options.Select Turn off or Turn off and delete history (which may appear as Turn off and delete activity).Follow the confirmation prompts.
Visit Gemini Apps Activity.
Sign in with the Google Account you use for Gemini.
Find the History or Keep Activity control near the top of the page.
Click On to open the available options.
Select Turn off or Turn off and delete history (which may appear as Turn off and delete activity).
Follow the confirmation prompts.

Turning off History stops future chats from being used to train generative AI models unless you choose to submit feedback. Some connected apps, including Google Workspace, become unavailable. Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes. Depending on whether the latest privacy update has reached your account, conversations may be retained for up to 72 hours under the previous policy or approximately two months under the new policy.
WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

Google's Personal Intelligence feature can connect Gemini to Gmail and other Google services, allowing the assistant to provide personalized responses using information from those accounts. (Photo Illustration by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Google is introducing a separate privacy control that lets you keep your Gemini conversation history while opting out of generative AI model training. If the new setting is available on your account, here's how to find it on a computer.

Go to gemini.google.com.Click Settings.Select History.Uncheck the box next to Chat content including text & uploads.Also make sure Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares is unchecked if you see that option.Click Turn off to confirm.
Go to gemini.google.com.
Click Settings.
Select History.
Uncheck the box next to Chat content including text & uploads.
Also make sure Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares is unchecked if you see that option.
Click Turn off to confirm.

Google says future chats will no longer be used to train generative AI models unless you submit feedback. However, human review may still occur for other service improvements and safety purposes. If you want to prevent Gemini from retrieving information from Gmail and Drive, disconnect Google Workspace separately.

Disconnecting an app does not automatically delete information from earlier Gemini conversations. Google says Gemini may still use information from previously saved chats even after you disconnect the original app. That's why it's important to both disconnect the app and delete conversations containing sensitive information.

Open Gemini Apps Activity at myactivity.google.com/product/gemini.Sign in to your Google Account.Click Delete above your activity.Select All time if you want to remove your saved history.Confirm the deletion.
Open Gemini Apps Activity at myactivity.google.com/product/gemini.
Sign in to your Google Account.
Click Delete above your activity.
Select All time if you want to remove your saved history.
Confirm the deletion.
Remember that previously reviewed information may remain subject to Google's separate retention policies, even after you delete your activity.

Think carefully before giving an AI assistant access to confidential documents or personal communications. If you don't need Gemini to retrieve information from Gmail or Drive, leave those connections disabled. Also, remember that uploading a document directly into Gemini creates a separate privacy consideration.

Google says uploaded content may be used to improve its services when History, previously called Keep Activity, is enabled, potentially with help from human reviewers. Whether that content is used to train generative AI models also depends on your training settings and whether you submit feedback.
Does this Gemini privacy concern affect business accounts?

Google says the connected-app disclosures involved in this controversy apply to personal Google Accounts using consumer Gemini. Business, Enterprise and Education accounts covered by Google Workspace commercial terms have different privacy protections. According to Google's response to CyberGuy, customer data governed by those commercial terms is not reviewed by humans or used to train foundational AI models.

If you use Gemini through an employer or school, your organization's settings and agreements determine which features are available and how information is handled. The important point is that the consumer Gemini privacy rules discussed here should not automatically be applied to commercial Workspace accounts.
Kurt's key takeaways

I can understand why someone would want Gemini to search their Gmail or find a document buried in Google Drive. We've all wasted time digging through old emails looking for something we need. Having an AI assistant do that work sounds pretty appealing. But I think Google has a responsibility to make the privacy implications much clearer before someone connects an account. Most people probably don't expect information pulled from their private emails to become part of a conversation that could eventually be reviewed by another human being. I appreciate that Google responded to our questions and explained the safeguards it uses. Still, I would have liked a more direct answer about whether existing customers were notified when the privacy disclosures changed. If you're giving an AI assistant access to years of personal information, you deserve to know exactly how that information might be handled. Personally, I'd leave Gmail and Drive disconnected unless I had a specific reason to use those features.

Would you trust an AI assistant with access to years of your private emails if you knew some of that information could be seen by human reviewers? Or has Google crossed a privacy line, even with your permission? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Housefishing could fool you with AI real estate photos
summary: Housefishing scams use AI real estate photos to fool buyers. Google Lens reverse image search and live video walkthroughs can help expose the fakes.
story: Bilt Rewards founder and CEO Ankur Jain joins 'The Claman Countdown' to discuss how mortgage rates are affecting the housing market. Jain also discusses the launch of a new AI-driven Neighborhood OS platform.

You find a beautiful house online. The driveway looks brand new, and the landscaping could be straight out of a home magazine. You get excited, schedule a showing and start thinking about where your furniture might go. Then you pull up to the address and wonder whether you're looking at the same house.

That's the growing concern behind housefishing, a term for real estate listings that use digitally altered or AI-generated photos to make properties look better than they actually are. A recent report highlighted complaints from homebuyers and renters who described misleading property pictures as "false advertising." With AI tools becoming more convincing, it's getting harder to know whether you're looking at a home's actual condition or a digital makeover. So how can you tell whether a listing photo shows the home you're actually getting, and what should you check before scheduling a tour?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
HIS HOME CHANGED HANDS FOR $5. COULD IT HAPPEN TO YOUR FAMILY?
A real estate agent reviews property information with prospective buyers as concerns grow over AI-altered listing photos that may misrepresent homes. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is housefishing in real estate?

Housefishing happens when property photos create an unrealistic impression of a home. AI can make an outdated property appear freshly renovated without anyone doing the actual work. For instance, two photos can show the same two-story house, but create very different impressions.

The original photo can show a home with a dark asphalt driveway and large shrubs covering much of the front porch. But an AI-enhanced version can show a clean concrete driveway and a newly styled entrance.

This example shows how digital alterations can make a property appear to have undergone an expensive makeover. If those improvements exist only in the edited photo, someone visiting the property could be in for an unpleasant surprise.
When do AI real estate photos become misleading?

Virtual staging has been around for years. Adding digital furniture to an empty living room can help buyers understand how they might use the space. AI simply makes those transformations easier and more realistic. But replacing a worn-out kitchen with an AI-generated renovation is another story. Laurent Cardinal, founder of real estate technology company Planpoint at planpoint.io/, believes agents need to be upfront about what they've changed. "The line is drawn where the intent is," Cardinal explains.

He supports using AI to show what a home could look like after renovations, provided agents clearly disclose the changes. His recommendation is straightforward: Show the original photo alongside the edited version so prospective buyers can compare them. However, digitally hiding property defects or replacing an unattractive view crosses that line. "That's cheating and it's hurtful to everyone in the market," Cardinal says. A misleading listing can waste someone's time and influence important financial decisions. For renters, the consequences can be especially serious if they send a deposit based on photos that fail to reflect the property.
Why AI-generated property photos are getting harder to spot

You might think you'd recognize an AI-generated photo immediately. Maybe the furniture looks strange or a window seems out of place. Unfortunately, today's tools can produce convincing results. Sometimes the changes are subtle enough to escape a close look. Cardinal warns that even people familiar with AI-generated content can struggle to identify it. "But there's no silver bullet here, and anyone can get caught," he says.

Unusually perfect rooms can raise questions, especially when architectural details appear inconsistent between photos. However, traditional real estate photography can also be misleading. Wide-angle lenses make rooms appear larger, while carefully chosen lighting can minimize visible imperfections. AI creates an additional concern because it can alter the features of the property itself. That makes it increasingly difficult to judge a home's condition from listing photos alone.
FAKE VACATION RENTAL SITES USE LIVE CHAT TO STEAL YOUR DATA
Homebuyers review property details with an agent, highlighting the importance of verifying listing photos before making a purchase. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Are agents required to disclose AI-altered real estate photos?

The rules depend on where the property is located and which listing service an agent uses. California has already taken action. Under Assembly Bill 723, which took effect Jan. 1, 2026, real estate professionals must disclose covered digital alterations in advertisements for properties for sale. They must also provide access to the original, unaltered photos. The law covers changes made using traditional editing software or AI. Routine adjustments to lighting or color generally fall outside the requirements when they don't misrepresent the property. California has also approved Assembly Bill 2025. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the state will require disclosures for digitally altered rental advertisements, with access to original photos when existing pictures have been changed.

Meanwhile, New York has warned agents about misleading AI property pictures. In November 2025, the New York Department of State reminded real estate professionals that advertisements must accurately represent properties for sale or rent. Agents who publish deceptive advertisements can face disciplinary action. Multiple listing services have their own restrictions. Stellar MLS, for example, requires disclosure of virtually staged photos and prohibits edits that conceal property defects or alter permanent features. There is currently no single nationwide law requiring every AI-edited real estate photo to carry a disclosure. Still, existing advertising laws and professional rules can apply when pictures mislead prospective buyers.
Can AI help detect housefishing?

Interestingly, the same technology creating misleading property photos may also help identify them. Cardinal's company, Planpoint, connects listing photos to interactive floor plans. That allows prospective buyers to see how rooms fit together instead of relying on individual pictures that may be difficult to interpret. Its Planpoint Visit platform also offers AI photo detection. The technology checks newly uploaded property photos for signs of AI generation and displays a warning when it finds something suspicious. Cardinal says the company achieved a 98% success rate in its internal testing.
A couple browses online listings, where AI-enhanced photos can make it difficult to tell what a home actually looks like. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from housefishing
Before scheduling a showing or putting money down on a property, there are several ways to check whether the listing photos tell the whole story.

If a home looks suspiciously polished, ask the agent whether any pictures have been digitally altered. Request the original photos so you can compare them. Pay particular attention to kitchens and bathrooms, where expensive renovations can significantly affect a home's value. If an agent cannot explain what was changed, ask more questions before moving forward.

Cardinal recommends a simple way to verify a property's appearance. "The easiest way is to request a live video call with the agent or the owner," he says. Ask to see the areas you're most interested in, including anything that looks unusually perfect in the listing. A live walkthrough can reveal details that edited photos might hide. However, it cannot prove that the person showing the home has authority to rent or sell it.

Look carefully at the room dimensions and window locations. Then compare those details with the photos. Cardinal suggests asking, "Do the rooms and angles add up?" If a small bedroom appears enormous in a listing, ask whether the pictures were digitally altered. Remember that wide-angle photography can also exaggerate the apparent size of a room.

Search the property's address in Google Maps and look at the exterior using Street View. Compare the driveway and surrounding homes with what's shown in the listing. You might notice changes that deserve a closer look. However, Street View pictures can be outdated, so differences don't automatically mean an agent used AI.
Reverse-search the property photos

Use Google Lens or another reverse-image search tool to check whether the same property pictures appear elsewhere online. You may find older listings showing the home before it was digitally enhanced. You could also discover that someone copied photos from another property to create a fraudulent rental advertisement. For help getting started, see our guide on how to reverse search an image on your phone.

Never rely solely on listing photos when making a financial commitment. If you're renting, independently verify the identity and authority of the landlord or agent before sending a deposit. For a home purchase, arrange an in-person showing and an independent inspection before committing to buy. A polished listing photo cannot tell you whether the property has hidden problems.

Those example of the two photos of the same house really show how far AI has come. The updated version looks fantastic, and I can see why someone would want to schedule a showing. But what happens when you arrive and discover that the beautiful driveway and landscaping don't actually exist? I think AI can be a great tool for helping buyers see a home's potential, especially if they're considering renovations. The problem starts when agents present those digital upgrades as the real thing. Buying a home is a major investment, and people deserve to know exactly what they're getting before they fall in love with a property online. I'd like to see more transparency from real estate agents, with original photos available alongside any AI-enhanced versions. There's nothing wrong with showing what a house could become, but buyers should never have to guess what it looks like today.

Would you walk away from a home if you discovered the agent had used AI to make it look better than it actually was, or would you consider that acceptable marketing? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Your holiday shopping data needs a cleanup before Black Friday
summary: Data brokers may expose your name, home address and phone number to scammers sending fake USPS delivery texts ahead of the Black Friday shopping rush.
story: University at Buffalo marketing professor Dinesh Gauri shares his tips for scoring the best Black Friday prices, from researching deals ahead of time to taking advantage of online shopping and in-store pickup options.

Your phone buzzes: "USPS: Your package could not be delivered due to an incomplete address. Update your details within 12 hours." You did order something last week. Probably several things. So your thumb hovers over the link. That's the whole trick.

Black Friday lands on Nov. 27 this year, and the holiday delivery rush is already underway. That gives scammers plenty of opportunities to send fake delivery alerts that arrive when you're expecting a package.

Meanwhile, your shopping habits and personal details may be circulating through data brokers. Here's how that information can make scams more convincing and what you can do to clean it up before the holiday shopping rush gets even busier.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Holiday shopping makes fake delivery alerts especially convincing, giving scammers more opportunities to trick people waiting for packages. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How your holiday shopping profile gets built

Every time you shop online, sign up for a discount or share your contact information, you may add to a growing collection of personal data. Some businesses use that information for their own marketing, while others share certain details with advertising partners or data brokers.
Here's where some of that information comes from:

Loyalty signups. That "10% off if you join" offer often means sharing your name, email address, phone number and shopping preferences. Depending on the store's privacy policy, some information may also be shared with marketing partners.Shipping addresses. Sending gifts directly to relatives means retailers and delivery companies may store additional addresses in your account or order records. Those records do not automatically become public, but they add to the information businesses collect.Marketing categories. Shopping activity and online tracking can help companies classify people as frequent online shoppers or likely holiday gift buyers.People-search websites. Data brokers can compile names, phone numbers, home addresses and information about relatives from public records and other sources.

Loyalty signups. That "10% off if you join" offer often means sharing your name, email address, phone number and shopping preferences. Depending on the store's privacy policy, some information may also be shared with marketing partners.

Shipping addresses. Sending gifts directly to relatives means retailers and delivery companies may store additional addresses in your account or order records. Those records do not automatically become public, but they add to the information businesses collect.
Marketing categories. Shopping activity and online tracking can help companies classify people as frequent online shoppers or likely holiday gift buyers.
People-search websites. Data brokers can compile names, phone numbers, home addresses and information about relatives from public records and other sources.

As I've covered before, loyalty programs and store memberships can contribute to the information companies collect about you. Add the personal details available through people-search sites, and someone looking to target you may find more information than you'd expect. The FTC explains that people-search companies collect information from multiple sources and sell reports containing personal details, sometimes including relatives' names and addresses.

You can use the free exposure scanner we recommend at CyberGuy.com to check whether your personal information appears on publicly searchable websites. Keep in mind that a free scan cannot uncover every private data broker database. The results might surprise you.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Online purchases and loyalty programs can contribute to the personal information companies collect and share with marketing partners. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How scammers turn personal information into a delivery scam

A fake delivery text doesn't need to know exactly what you ordered. During the holidays, plenty of people are expecting packages, so a message about a delivery problem can seem believable. Scammers often send these messages to large numbers of phone numbers without knowing anything about the recipients. However, personal information obtained from public sources or data brokers can help make some scams more convincing.
Here's how that information could be misused:

Your real name and street address can make a fake delivery warning look more convincing.Your shopping interests can help someone impersonate a retailer you recognize.Your family's publicly available details can give scammers information to use when posing as delivery companies or other businesses.
Your real name and street address can make a fake delivery warning look more convincing.
Your shopping interests can help someone impersonate a retailer you recognize.
Your family's publicly available details can give scammers information to use when posing as delivery companies or other businesses.

The FTC reported that fake package delivery problems, often involving messages impersonating USPS, were the most commonly reported type of text scam in 2024. The problem extends beyond package deliveries. According to FTC testimony released in March 2026, Americans reported $15.9 billion in fraud losses during 2025 across all scam categories. A typical fake delivery message directs you to a convincing website and asks you to pay a small redelivery fee. That payment request is the trap. The scammer wants your credit card details and may also try to collect other sensitive information. Here's something important to remember: USPS does not charge a fee for redelivery. Its legitimate text tracking service also requires you to request tracking information first, and those tracking messages do not contain links.
Reviewing shopping accounts and privacy settings can help limit how much personal information you share before Black Friday. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why the cleanup should happen before Black Friday

Data removal takes time. Brokers process opt-out requests on different schedules, and personal information can reappear even after it has been removed. Starting now gives you a chance to identify exposed information and begin requesting removals before the busiest shopping days arrive.

There is one important distinction. Removing your information from data brokers can reduce your exposure over time, but it cannot guarantee that scam texts will stop or prevent scammers from contacting you this holiday season. That's why data cleanup should go hand in hand with safer shopping and delivery habits.
Your 15-minute pre-Black Friday cleanup
You can get started in about 15 minutes, although completing data removal requests and having companies process them can take much longer.

Look up your name on people-search websites such as Spokeo, Whitepages or BeenVerified. Check whether your home address, phone number or relatives' information appears. If you find information you want removed, look for the site's opt-out instructions.

Check the privacy settings on the websites and apps you use most frequently. Look for options to limit promotional emails, personalized advertising and sharing with marketing partners. You can also review saved shipping addresses and remove outdated entries you no longer need. Keep in mind that deleting a saved address may not erase information retained in previous order records.

If a message claims there's a delivery problem, open the retailer's or shipping company's official app or website yourself. Check the tracking number and delivery status there. Do not enter payment details through a link in an unsolicited message, even if it includes your name or address.

Instead of spending hours submitting individual opt-out forms, an automated data removal service can send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, depending on the provider and plan you choose. Some services also submit recurring removal requests to help address information that reappears. While no service can erase every piece of information about you online, it can help reduce your exposure. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Talk with your parents and other relatives about fake delivery messages. Make sure everyone knows to verify unexpected payment requests through the carrier's official website or app. For USPS specifically, explain that it does not charge redelivery fees. A message demanding immediate payment to release a package should raise suspicion.

If you receive a suspicious delivery message, don't respond or click the link. You can forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM) and use your phone's reporting feature. For messages impersonating USPS, you can also report them to spam@uspis.gov. If you already entered your credit card information on a suspicious website, contact your card issuer immediately. Ask about blocking the card, disputing fraudulent charges and monitoring your account for unauthorized activity. You can also report the incident at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about these fake delivery texts is how easily they blend into our holiday routines. When you're ordering gifts and waiting for packages, a message about a delivery problem can catch you at exactly the wrong moment. I also think we need to pay more attention to how much personal information is floating around online. Taking a few minutes to search your name, review your shopping accounts and start removing exposed information is worthwhile. But remember, even if you clean up your data, scammers can still reach you. My advice is simple: Never let an unexpected text dictate how you check on a package. Open the official app or website yourself and verify what's actually happening before you share a single detail.

title: Can hackers still read Gmail after a password change?
summary: Remus Stealer malware developers claim Gmail access survives a password change, but Google says the attack targets infected devices, not a Gmail flaw.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You change your Gmail password after noticing something suspicious. You sign out of unfamiliar devices and figure your account should be safe again. But what if someone could still read your Gmail after a password change? That's the unsettling claim behind Remus Stealer, a malware service being marketed to cybercriminals. Its developers claim they can keep accessing Gmail messages even after someone resets their password and revokes existing sessions.

However, security researchers have not independently verified those claims, and Google disputes the suggestion that the malware exploits a Gmail security flaw. The company says this type of attack targets infected devices rather than Gmail itself. Google also warns that changing your password may not solve the problem if malware remains active on your computer. Here's what the investigation uncovered and how to protect your inbox.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED
A screenshot from the Remus malware dashboard shows a Pinterest verification email that criminals claim they can access through a compromised Gmail account. (Hudson Rock)
Hackers claim their malware can keep reading Gmail

Security researchers at Hudson Rock examined promotional materials for Remus Stealer, a type of malware designed to collect sensitive information from infected computers. In a November 9 report, the company described a new feature advertised in version 1.3.9 of the malware. The developers claim it allows criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from their control dashboard. The promotional screenshots show lists of emails and individual messages. There's also a "Mail" option connected to records of infected devices. According to the developers, criminals can retrieve email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

The developers make an even more concerning claim. They say changing a Google password or revoking existing sessions won't necessarily stop someone from accessing the mailbox. They also advertise a way to share mailbox access with other criminals through links. Think about what that could mean if the claims prove true. Someone with access to your Gmail could potentially read private conversations or collect password reset messages for other accounts. However, these claims come from the people selling the malware. Independent researchers have yet to demonstrate that the feature works as advertised.
What security researchers actually discovered

Hudson Rock contacted the malware developer and spoke with someone who claimed to have used the Gmail feature. That person said they could still access an inbox after closing the browser, resetting a session and changing the Google account password. The developer also described a technique involving browser memory but didn't provide enough technical information to verify it. There are important limits to the investigation.

Hudson Rock did not reverse engineer the feature or conduct controlled testing after a complete account recovery. Researchers also couldn't independently verify the customer's claims. Most importantly, the investigation never established that criminals could retrieve newly arriving emails after someone had properly secured their Google account. The screenshots demonstrate that the service advertises a Gmail-reading interface. They don't prove that Remus can defeat Google's protections after a full recovery. There's also no evidence in the report of a previously unknown Gmail security vulnerability.

Researchers also could not rule out other explanations, including incomplete session revocation, previously collected messages or unauthorized access that remained active through another route. Without controlled testing, there's no way to confirm exactly how the advertised feature operates.
NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH
The Remus malware dashboard displays a Gmail inbox, although researchers have not verified claims that access continues after a complete account recovery. (Hudson Rock)
Google responds to the Gmail malware claims

We reached out to Google about the research, and the company rejected the suggestion that the reported activity involved a vulnerability in Gmail. A Google spokesperson said: "Attacks involving infostealer malware that target session tokens on personal devices are not new, and there is no Gmail or Google vulnerability at play here. We routinely upgrade our built-in defenses to protect users against session theft and automatically secure accounts when we detect suspicious activity. Users can invalidate stolen sessions by removing malware from the affected device and revoking active sessions via g.co/mydevices."

Google explained that this kind of attack targets infected personal devices rather than exploiting Gmail itself. The company also highlighted something especially important for anyone recovering from malware. If the infection remains on a computer when someone resets their password, the malware could capture the new login session. That means a fresh password alone may not solve the problem. Google recommends removing the malware before signing back in on the affected device. From a separate, trusted device, you should also change your password, revoke suspicious sessions through Google's device activity page at myaccount.google.com/device-activity and review your account using Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. The infected computer should remain disconnected until the threat has been removed.

The company says it regularly strengthens its defenses against stolen sessions. Those protections include frequent cookie rotation and additional authentication checks when someone attempts sensitive account changes. Google also highlighted Device Bound Session Credentials, a Chrome security technology designed to make stolen session cookies harder to reuse on another device. This protection applies to supported Chrome sessions, with availability depending on the platform and service. These protections help reduce the risk of account theft, although they don't eliminate every possible malware attack.
Why hackers may access Gmail without your password

You probably open Gmail every day without typing your password. That's because your browser remembers that you've already signed in. Behind the scenes, browsers and applications use session cookies or authentication tokens to maintain access to accounts. These digital credentials help keep you signed in without repeatedly entering your password. Unfortunately, criminals know how valuable that information can be. Infostealer malware can target stored authentication data on an infected computer. If an attacker obtains a valid session, they may be able to access an account without entering the password again. That can also undermine the protection you'd normally expect from two-step verification because the legitimate account holder has already completed the sign-in process.

However, a stolen session doesn't automatically give someone unlimited access. Google can invalidate sessions, and some sensitive actions require additional verification. Google's documentation explains that changing a password generally revokes OAuth access and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions, although certain exceptions apply. Google also notes that password changes sign people out of most devices, but some trusted devices and third-party connections may remain signed in. Those exceptions do not prove that Remus uses any of these methods. The concern with an infected computer is that malware may capture fresh authentication information when you sign in again. That's why securing the computer and reviewing account access are essential parts of recovery.
Warning signs someone may be accessing your Gmail

An unfamiliar Google security alert deserves attention, especially if you haven't signed in from a new device. You should also investigate password reset messages you never requested. These can indicate that someone is attempting to access another account connected to your email address, although an unexpected reset message alone doesn't prove an account has been compromised.

Other warning signs include missing messages or people telling you they received strange emails from your address. Check your Sent folder for messages you didn't write. You might also discover forwarding rules or account recovery settings you don't remember changing. If something looks suspicious, open your Google account directly rather than following a link in an unexpected message.
Infostealer malware can steal login session information from an infected computer, potentially allowing hackers to access Gmail without entering a password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to protect your Gmail from malware and hackers

If you suspect that someone has accessed your Gmail, take action promptly. The goal is to secure your account while preventing malware from stealing fresh login information. Google emphasizes that removing the infection and revoking compromised sessions are both essential. You can begin securing your account from a trusted device while keeping the suspected infected computer offline.
If you believe your computer has been infected, disconnect it from the internet. Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing your important accounts.

A criminal who gains access to your Gmail may change settings so incoming messages get forwarded to another email address. That could allow someone to receive copies of new messages even after you change your password. Google requires verification when someone adds a new forwarding address, but you should still check for forwarding that may have been configured without your knowledge.

Passkeys offer stronger sign-in security, but they cannot remove an existing infection or automatically prevent theft of an already authenticated session. Google's Advanced Protection Program adds stricter account safeguards, including tighter restrictions on third-party access.

Remember how many online services use your email address for account recovery. If criminals accessed your mailbox, they may have seen verification messages from other services. Review important accounts for unfamiliar activity. Pay particular attention to unexpected password changes or security alerts.

If you reused your Google password anywhere else, change those passwords too. Use unique credentials for every important account, and consider a password manager to keep track of them. For additional protection, my CyberGuy article on identity thieves who don't need your password explains other ways criminals try to get around traditional account security.
Kurt's key takeaways

For years, changing your password has been one of the first things I've recommended when an online account gets compromised. I still believe that's essential. But this investigation highlights something many people overlook. If malware is running on your computer, it may be able to steal fresh login information after you've changed your password. What concerns me is how much of our digital lives depend on a single Gmail account. Think about the personal messages sitting in your inbox and the accounts that rely on your email for password recovery.

Someone who gains access could potentially create problems well beyond your inbox. Google's response makes an important distinction. This is a threat involving malware on infected devices, not a newly demonstrated vulnerability in Gmail. We should also remember that the most alarming claims about this malware have yet to be independently verified. There's a big difference between what criminals advertise and what security researchers can actually demonstrate.

If you suspect an infection, make sure the malware has been removed before trusting a fresh login. Then change your password from a trusted device and revoke any suspicious sessions. Those extra steps can help prevent someone from regaining access to your account.

title: Tech billionaire plans 1,000-year floating city at sea
summary: Palmer Luckey says SLAB, his floating industrial city, would last 1,000 years, hosting metal processing and oil refining beyond California rules.
story: Palmer Luckey wants to move American industry offshore to escape state and local regulations. His ambitious SLAB project raises big questions about the future of manufacturing in the U.S.

How frustrated would you have to be with government red tape to decide the ocean looks like a better place to build a factory? Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey has an answer. He wants to create a massive floating industrial city where American companies could operate beyond certain state and local restrictions.

The project is called SLAB, and Luckey says it would have a design life of 1,000 years. That's a pretty extraordinary promise for something sitting in the middle of the ocean. However, the reasoning behind the project may be even more surprising than the structure itself. We discussed Luckey's ambitious plans in detail on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast" at cyberguy.com/podcast. So, what exactly is he planning to build, and could moving American industry offshore really solve the problems he's trying to escape?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS
Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries, speaks at Los Angeles Air Force Base in California in August 2026. (Christopher Kim/U.S. Space Force)
What is Palmer Luckey's 1,000-year floating city?

Palmer Luckey, the founder of Oculus and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has revealed plans for a floating industrial platform called SLAB. In a November 18 post on X, Luckey explained that he began developing the project after Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014. He used some of the money from that sale to pursue an idea that has fascinated technology entrepreneurs for years.

The concept is known as seasteading. It involves building permanent structures on the ocean where people can live or operate businesses outside some of the restrictions that apply on land. Luckey's version focuses heavily on American industry. He wants to create a place where companies could conduct activities that face significant regulatory hurdles on the mainland. The illustration accompanying his announcement shows an enormous platform rising above the ocean with buildings and industrial facilities on top.
AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Floating homes made from shipping containers in Copenhagen, Denmark, offer a real-world example of construction on water, although Palmer Luckey's proposed SLAB industrial city would be far larger. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why Palmer Luckey wants to move American industry offshore

Luckey believes government regulations have made it unnecessarily difficult for certain industries to operate in the United States. His proposed solution is to move some of those operations offshore. He specifically mentioned metal processing and oil refining. He also identified desalination and medical research as possible activities for SLAB. In his announcement, Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen American industry by creating a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations."

His argument is that companies could operate more efficiently if they avoided certain state and local restrictions. He also wants the offshore platform to be cheaper than building comparable facilities on land, although he has not publicly demonstrated that the economics would work. There is also a more controversial possibility. In a separate exchange on X, Luckey suggested that offshore facilities could provide access to medical treatments currently prohibited in the United States. That raises difficult questions about patient safety and whether those activities could legally take place offshore.
How much money is behind SLAB?

Luckey says he and several close friends funded SLAB at a $1 billion valuation back in 2017. However, that figure refers to the project's reported valuation at the time. It does not establish that $1 billion has been spent building it. He also says the project has made significant progress, although considerable work remains. So far, he has not publicly disclosed a confirmed construction schedule or a precise location for the proposed platform.

Interestingly, Luckey only decided to discuss SLAB publicly after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He pushed back on that description, saying the project was much older and considerably more ambitious. His comments suggest that data centers could be part of the broader concept, but SLAB was conceived for other industrial activities as well.
Can a floating city really escape U.S. regulations?

This is where Luckey's proposal runs into some complicated legal questions. According to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, most coastal states, including California, have jurisdiction over submerged lands extending approximately three nautical miles offshore. Beyond that boundary, federal authority becomes especially important. The United States has a territorial sea extending 12 nautical miles from its coastal baselines. It also maintains an exclusive economic zone extending up to 200 nautical miles offshore.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains that the federal government retains authority over certain offshore structures and activities within that zone. Consequently, moving a business beyond California's coastal boundary would not automatically eliminate federal oversight. Environmental requirements and maritime regulations could still apply. The legal picture would also depend on whether SLAB floats freely, anchors to the ocean floor or operates under a particular country's registration. Luckey has yet to explain exactly how the platform would navigate those requirements.
Could an ocean city really last 1,000 years?

Building a permanent industrial community offshore presents extraordinary engineering challenges. Saltwater gradually corrodes exposed structures, and powerful storms can place enormous stress on offshore installations. Maintaining a facility for centuries would require substantial engineering and ongoing repairs. Then there is the expense of running an industrial operation at sea. Workers would need transportation to the platform, while supplies and equipment would have to travel across the water.

That makes Luckey's goal of operating more cheaply than comparable land-based facilities particularly ambitious. A 1,000-year design life is also a target rather than a demonstrated lifespan. Until Luckey releases detailed engineering evidence, there is no way to independently verify whether SLAB could meet that goal.
The Marco Polo offshore oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico illustrates the scale of industrial operations at sea and the engineering challenges they face. (GuavaTrain/Wikimedia Commons)
Why this floating city could send a message to California

California has long been associated with technological innovation, yet it also has extensive environmental and land-use regulations. Some businesses argue that permitting requirements make industrial development more expensive and time-consuming. Luckey's proposal brings that debate into focus. Moving industrial activity offshore would be a drastic response to regulatory frustration. However, the idea also raises a question worth asking: Have some regulations become so burdensome that entrepreneurs would rather build at sea than navigate the approval process on land?

Of course, industries involving hazardous chemicals or experimental medical treatments require serious oversight. Those protections help prevent accidents and protect public health. At the same time, regulations can become unnecessarily complicated or outdated. Governments need to examine whether their approval processes encourage responsible innovation or create obstacles that serve little practical purpose. Luckey has not identified the specific California laws he hopes to avoid. For now, his project highlights a broader argument about how America regulates industrial development. Whether SLAB becomes a functioning offshore community remains to be seen.
Kurt's key takeaways

I find the whole idea fascinating, but something about it also strikes me as completely absurd. Have we really reached a point where building a giant industrial platform in the ocean sounds more appealing than dealing with government regulations on land? California, in particular, should be paying attention. This is a state that helped create Silicon Valley, yet we're now talking about taking American industry offshore to escape regulatory headaches. I'm certainly not suggesting we eliminate important environmental or safety protections. But there's a point where excessive regulation can start working against the very innovation we should be encouraging. I'd much rather see American businesses building here, creating jobs and developing new technology without unnecessary roadblocks. Luckey still has a tremendous amount to prove before SLAB becomes reality. But the fact that he's seriously pursuing this idea should give policymakers something to think about. For more on this story and our discussion about the future of American innovation, listen to The CyberGuy Report Podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/.

title: What United Airlines banning AI agents from booking flights means for your travel plans
summary: United Airlines is blocking unauthorized AI travel agents from its booking systems, warning that automated purchases could put MileagePlus miles at risk.
story: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the threat of rogue artificial intelligence agents targeting bank accounts. Knutsson shares safety tips to protect personal finances from unauthorized transactions and addresses AI-enabled romance scams, detailing a case where a woman was defrauded of $10,000 by a scammer posing as Jon Bon Jovi.

Wouldn't it be nice to tell an AI assistant to find the cheapest flight to your destination and book your favorite seat while you do something else? That kind of convenience is getting closer. But United Airlines wants to make sure an unauthorized AI assistant never gets that far.

The airline is restricting third-party AI agents from accessing its booking systems without permission. United says these tools could expose sensitive customer information and make purchases travelers never intended to authorize. The concern also extends to MileagePlus accounts, where an automated mistake could put valuable airline miles at risk.

The decision comes as AI assistants become increasingly capable of taking action on our behalf. While that sounds convenient, United is raising questions about how much control we should give software over our travel plans. Here's where United draws the line and what you need to know before letting AI handle your next flight booking.

FORMER ANTHROPIC SECURITY LEADER WARNS AI AGENTS ARE BECOMING TOO AUTONOMOUS FOR HUMANS TO KEEP THEM IN CHECK
United Airlines is restricting unauthorized AI agents from accessing its booking systems, citing concerns about customer security and unwanted transactions. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
Why United Airlines is blocking AI agents

On Nov. 11, United Airlines published an official news release titled United Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents. The airline explained that protecting customer information and account security prompted the restrictions. According to United, sharing account credentials with personal AI assistants can expose sensitive information. The airline also warned that automated actions might lead to unwanted purchases or changes to existing reservations. Then there's the issue of frequent flyer miles. United specifically mentioned the possibility that an AI assistant could use MileagePlus miles without the traveler intending that redemption.

To address those concerns, United is restricting unauthorized personal AI agents from accessing its digital platforms. The rules also reach travel agencies and booking services that might use automated AI tools to access United's systems. United says it is updating its policies to support these restrictions. The airline also plans to continue evaluating how personal AI assistants interact with its services.
What exactly is an AI travel agent?

You may already use AI to research vacation destinations or figure out which airport is closest to your hotel. An AI travel agent takes that technology further by performing tasks for you. For example, you could ask an AI assistant to find a flight under $400 that arrives before dinner. Instead of simply recommending flights, an AI agent might search booking systems and attempt to complete the reservation. Some agents can also interact with websites using a browser. That means they may be able to enter personal information and complete steps that normally require you to click through a booking process.

The convenience is easy to understand. However, granting an AI assistant access to your airline account can also give it the ability to make changes you never intended. For more on what these assistants can do, see our article on eight seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent.
United says AI agents could create airline safety problems

United's concerns go beyond account security. The airline also warns that automated AI activity could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. Consider what happens when you check in for a flight. Airlines require travelers to acknowledge important safety information, including whether their bags contain prohibited hazardous materials.

United specifically points to the requirement for a person to confirm that baggage contains no banned substances, such as explosives. An AI assistant handling check-in could potentially bypass that acknowledgment. After all, how would an AI assistant know what you actually packed in your suitcase? United has identified this as a potential regulatory concern. The airline has not established that every AI-assisted check-in violates federal law.
Could United cancel a flight booked by an AI agent?

This may be the biggest concern for travelers experimenting with automated booking tools. United revised its Contract of Carriage on Nov. 11. The updated rules prohibit AI agents from making or modifying tickets and purchasing airline products or services.

The contract also identifies reservations made or changed through AI agents as subject to cancellation without advance notice. The definition of an AI agent includes automated tools even when a traveler supervises or approves their actions. However, there is an important exception for existing reservations.

United says bookings made by AI agents before Nov. 11, will not be canceled under the new restriction. The airline recommends reviewing those reservations to confirm that they were properly booked and ticketed. If you previously used an AI assistant to arrange United travel, open the United app or website and verify your itinerary. Check that your ticket was actually issued rather than assuming a booking confirmation means everything is complete. You can review the airline's published rules in its Contract of Carriage at united.com/en/us/fly/contract-of-carriage.html.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
Travelers can still manage flights through United's website and app, but unauthorized third-party AI agents face new restrictions on accessing the airline's systems. (Robert Alexander/Getty Images)
Can you still use AI to plan a United Airlines trip?

Yes, although United has established limits on how outside AI tools can interact with its systems. You can still ask an AI chatbot for general travel advice or help creating an itinerary. United's guidance allows AI-assisted research and trip planning as long as the tool does not access United's website or app. However, an unauthorized AI agent cannot search United's website or app on your behalf. The restriction also covers automated purchasing and reservation management. That means an AI-powered browser feature that automatically searches United's website could fall under the restriction, even if it never buys a ticket.

United says assistive technology for travelers with disabilities remains unaffected. Traditional travel booking services can also continue operating through permitted channels. The restriction specifically addresses unauthorized AI agents, including those used by travel agencies. According to United's published guidance, the airline does not currently work with any third-party AI agents under this policy.
Southwest Airlines is taking a different approach to AI

While United is putting restrictions in place, Southwest Airlines is exploring a different approach. On Oct. 6, Southwest announced a ChatGPT integration. The feature allows you to discover destinations and shop for Southwest flights directly through ChatGPT. However, Southwest's integration still directs you to the airline's website to complete purchases. The company describes the arrangement as an early step toward broader AI-powered booking capabilities.

That approach gives Southwest a way to use AI for flight discovery while maintaining control over the final transaction. United is taking a more restrictive position on outside AI assistants. The airline says it will continue evaluating the technology as it develops.
How to protect your United Airlines bookings and miles

If you normally book flights through United's website or app, you can continue doing so. You can also use permitted travel booking services. However, if you've started experimenting with AI assistants that make purchases or manage accounts on your behalf, United's restrictions deserve your attention. An AI agent with access to your airline account could potentially reach sensitive travel information. Depending on its permissions, it might also make purchases you never intended to authorize. Here are a few ways to protect yourself.

Avoid giving third-party AI assistants your MileagePlus password or other sensitive login information. If you've already shared your credentials with an AI agent, United recommends changing your password immediately. You should also remove any saved login details from the AI service. Consider using a password manager to create and securely store a strong, unique password for your airline account. This can help protect your account if a password you use elsewhere gets exposed in a data breach.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices from malware and malicious links designed to steal login credentials. This is especially important if you use travel booking websites or receive airline confirmation emails. While antivirus protection won't stop an AI assistant from making an unauthorized reservation, it can help prevent cybercriminals from gaining access to your MileagePlus account. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Use United's official website or app, or a booking provider operating under United's rules. United currently does not work with third-party AI agents under this policy. Even if an AI assistant offers to complete a reservation with your approval, that does not necessarily make the transaction permissible.
UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’
United warns that giving AI agents access to customer accounts could expose sensitive information and potentially put valuable MileagePlus miles at risk. (iStock)

Review your MileagePlus balance for unexpected activity. If you notice a redemption or purchase you don't recognize, secure your account immediately. Contact United through its official website or app to report the activity and request assistance.

Check your booking confirmation and make sure United has issued your ticket. If an AI assistant arranged your travel before Nov. 11, verify the reservation directly with the airline. United says those earlier bookings will not be canceled under the new restriction.

AI can still help you plan a trip using general information without accessing United's systems. However, complete your flight purchases and reservation changes yourself through permitted channels. That way, you can review what you're buying without risking a prohibited AI-agent transaction.
Kurt's key takeaways

I can see why United is concerned. I've spent enough time searching for flights to appreciate the idea of handing that job over to AI. Let the assistant find me a great fare and save me the hassle of comparing a dozen options. I'm all for that. But the moment it starts making purchases or accessing my airline miles, I want to know exactly what it's doing.

I recently spoke with travel expert Katy Nastro, who discovered that someone had stolen 50,000 miles from her American Airlines account. Her experience had nothing to do with AI agents, but it reminded me how much value we keep in these loyalty programs. I certainly wouldn't want an automated mistake putting those rewards at risk.

At the same time, I do wonder whether security is the only concern driving United's decision. Airlines have spent years building direct relationships with travelers. AI agents could change how we compare fares and choose which airline gets our business. I would hate to see useful technology held back simply because it gives you more control over the shopping process. United says it will keep evaluating these tools, and I hope that eventually leads to a secure way to book flights using AI. Until then, I'm happy to let AI help find my next trip. I'll take care of the booking myself.
