title: Fugitive football coach fled into woods of small mountain town – year later, hunt for truth faces steep climb
summary: Travis Turner, the fugitive football coach who vanished in Southwest Virginia, remains missing a year later as U.S. Marshals and state police search on.
story: Travis Turner, the missing Union High School football coach, has evaded Virginia State Police and the U.S. Marshals Service for a year. A $5,000 reward remains active.

The search for a star football coach who disappeared amid child abuse allegations continues a year after he fled in the heavily wooded mountains of Southwest Virginia, leaving his belongings behind and his community hunting for answers.

Travis L. Turner, 46, the former head football coach at Union High School in Big Stone Gap, fled his Appalachia home on Nov. 20, 2025, shortly before state police arrived to question him in a child sexual abuse investigation.

Turner, according to his wife, Leslie Caudill Turner, walked into the woods behind their property with a firearm while police were on the way to his home. Authorities sought to question Turner but had not yet obtained an arrest warrant.

Days later, prosecutors charged Turner with five counts each of possessing child sexual abuse material and using a computer to solicit a minor. At the time, Virginia State Police said that "additional charges are pending."
Union High School head football coach Travis Turner disappeared in Virginia. (Leslie Turner/Facebook)
MISSING VIRGINIA COACH TRAVIS TURNER FUELS TENSE SCHOOL BOARD MEETING AS JUDGE SEALS CASE RECORDS: REPORT
Since Turner is considered a fugitive, the U.S. Marshals Service joined the search, alongside VSP.
Brady McCarron, deputy chief of the U.S. Marshals Service Office of Public Affairs, confirmed with Fox News Digital that a reward of up to $5,000 for information leading to Turner remains active.
Mist hangs between mountains in Big Stone Gap, Virginia, May 18, 2018. Travis Turner was a longtime football coach in the community. (REUTERS/Brian Snyder)
"There is not much we can reveal about the search," McCarron said. "We continue to coordinate with all of our partners in the search, as we have throughout the search."
VSP said they continue to receive tips, with hundreds coming in since early 2026.
FUGITIVE HIGH SCHOOL COACH ERASED AS SCHOOL SCRUBS STAFF PROFILE AMID CHILD-PORN CHARGES: REPORT

Travis Turner was leading the Union High School football team through an undefeated season when he disappeared from his family’s home in Appalachia, Virginia on Friday, Nov. 21, 2025. (Facebook/Leslie Caudill Turner)
"The Virginia State Police, along with our federal and local partners, remains committed to finding answers," VSP spokesperson Matthew Demlein told Fox News Digital.
"This is a complex investigation, and we ask for the community’s continued understanding and patience as we work through every layer of the case and pursue every credible lead."
Travis Turner coached at Union High School in Big Stone Gap, Virginia. (Google Maps)
Search challenges
Finding someone deliberately avoiding detection presents a different challenge when compared to searching for someone who is accidentally lost, according to experts.
The initial search for Turner, according to VSP, involved drone, search-and-rescue teams, K-9 units, and help from federal and local agencies.
In a March statement, VSP said authorities followed up on more than 178 leads from seven states, but none resulted in his capture.

Authorities announced that they had obtained 10 warrants to charge Travis Turner with five counts of possession of child pornography and five counts of using a computer to solicit a minor. (Facebook/Leslie Caudill Turner)
Dr. Robert J. Koester, a Virginia search-and-rescue expert and author of "Lost Person Behavior," told Fox News Digital that numerous factors could affect capturing Turner.
MISSING COACH TRAVIS TURNER LEFT WITHOUT ESSENTIALS AS FAMILY URGES HIM TO FACE CHILD PORN CHARGES: ATTORNEY

Search experts should first consider whether someone is likely to stay in a particular area and the difficulties of finding them there. Koester said searchers generally start by assessing the missing person's likely behavior, then use historical data, which helps them determine where to look.
A mountaintop-removal coal mine outside of Appalachia, Virginia, Aug. 13, 2019. Travis Turner vanished in the community he called home. (REUTERS/Charles Mostoller)
He added that experts should also look at the differences between evasive people, fugitives and despondent people who deliberately hide.
"All of these (evasive, fugitive, despondent with hiding) make the probability of detection much more difficult," Koester said in an emailed statement.
Travis Turner disappeared from his family’s home in Appalachia, Virginia on Friday, Nov. 21, 2025. (Facebook/Leslie Caudill Turner)
Searchers should revisit previously-searched areas since someone trying to avoid detection could "move back into a searched area," he added.

Koester said search dogs can help investigators locate people who intentionally hide. He recalled cases involving despondent people in distress who remained hidden until search dogs picked up their scent.
US MARSHALS OFFER REWARD FOR FUGITIVE VIRGINIA FOOTBALL COACH, WARN HE 'MAY BE ARMED' AS FEDS JOIN MANHUNT

Someone's familiarity with the area can typically determine how far they’ll travel and how effectively they can evade being caught. Koester said someone unfamiliar with the landscape will usually travel shorter distances, while someone who knows the area is more likely to travel further while avoiding detection.
Terrain presents another challenge, Koester said.
Union High School head football coach Travis Turner is pictured in a photo released by the Virginia State Police. (Virginia State Police)

"Dense vegetation, rugged terrain, and poor weather makes searching more difficult (lowers probability of detection)," he said. "Dense vegetation and rugged terrain will also alter where and how a subject will travel.
"All of those factors make the search more difficult. Surprisingly, weather doesn't have a major influence on how a subject travels."
Without access to investigative records and search maps, however, Koester said he could not assess Turner's case or speculate about where he is or what happened to him.
VIRGINIA HIGH SCHOOL COACH LABELED 'FUGITIVE' AS LOCAL COMMUNITY ALLEGES LONG-KNOWN ACCUSATIONS: REPORT
However, he explained that the chances of Turner hiding elsewhere and evading police is "possible but [not] probable."

"Is it possible that a meteorite will strike my office in the next 5 minutes? Yes, it is possible," he said. "Professor Nelson says 1:1,600,000 per lifetime so average males lives 76.5 years so that would be 1 in 13,000,000,000,000.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"I would think the subject decided to disappear and start a new life would be better than the meteorite example but still unlikely."
In December 2025, at the recommendation of Wise County Commonwealth's Attorney Brett Hall, a Wise County Circuit Court judge sealed records connected to Turner's criminal case.
Hall said that sealed records protect a victim's privacy, while preventing the release of information that could compromise a future trial.
Travis Turner's disappearance has stunned the Big Stone Gap community. (Virginia State Police)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Nearly a year later, the allegations, evidence and outstanding evidence remain sealed, leaving critical questions about the case unanswered.

Turner's disappearance doesn’t necessarily mean felony charges against him will also vanish. According to the Virginia Supreme Court, "with limited exceptions, there are no statutes of limitations for felony cases."
Travis Turner coached football at Union High School, Virginia, which plays its games at Bullitt Park in Big Stone Gap. (Google Maps)

Under Virginia Code § 19.2-76.1, felony warrants are reviewed after seven years, and the state can ask a court to keep warrants in place while an investigation remains active.
GOT A TIP?
Meanwhile, the family is reportedly cooperating with authorities and have allowed them access to repeated property searches.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Leslie Turner took to social media following her husband's disappearance, urging friends to "please pray." (Leslie Turner/Facebook)
In a December 2025 statement, Leslie Turner's attorney, Adrian Collins, addressed speculation surrounding family members and the ongoing search.

title: 'Flying saucers,' a 1,650 mph radar track and Skinwalker Ranch troops: 10 wild finds in unsealed UFO files
summary: Three unseen military UFO videos from the Middle East and a 1,650 mph radar track over the western United States headline 40 declassified Pentagon files.
story: Astrophysicist Avi Loeb, lead advisor to the new Trump-era UAP Governance Board, discusses why the government previously maintained secrecy regarding unidentified aerial phenomena. Loeb explains that some objects are unidentified and could pose national security risks from adversarial nations. He advocates for transparency, noting his council seeks to collect unclassified data to better understand these UAPs and potentially make groundbreaking discoveries.

Newly declassified Pentagon and CIA records – including three previously unseen military UFO videos from the Middle East and a radar track clocked at roughly 1,650 mph over the western United States – pull back the curtain on decades of government investigations into unexplained aerial encounters.

The trove of 40 documents and three videos, released Nov. 20, includes everything from 1952 CIA "flying saucer" warnings to 2026 military infrared footage of unidentified objects. Alongside a 494-page progress report from defense contractor Bigelow Aerospace detailing a $22 million Pentagon UFO program, the files span more than 70 years of unexplained encounters across land, sea and air.
A War Department official declined to offer any analysis of the release to Fox News Digital "so the American people can make up their own minds regarding the files."
NEW TRUMP UFO FILE DUMP INCLUDES MILITARY FOOTAGE OF MYSTERIOUS STAR-SHAPED OBJECT
From a glowing disc reported over Montana nuclear missile silos to plans for a secret underground Nevada vault, here are 10 wild finds from the newly released files.

A satellite image shows a UFO spaceship at night amid an FBI investigation and alien evidence near Area 51, capturing a flying saucer and galaxy survey of a mysterious object in the sky. (Getty Images Creatives)

The latest release includes three previously unseen military videos from the Middle East, recorded on heat-seeking and night-vision cameras in 2020, 2023 and 2026 and sent by U.S. Central Command to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO).
BURCHETT TELLS ‘RUTHLESS’ MORE UFO VIDEOS TO COME

The shortest clip, a 13-second video from 2023, shows a camera turning to follow a single object – which Pentagon notes call an "area of contrast" – while keeping it near the center of the screen. A 20-second video from 2020 captures another single object entering from the right and moving left as the camera pans and zooms in and out to keep it in view.

The longest and newest clip, a 54-second video from 2026, tracks several objects moving from right to left across the screen. As the camera turns and zooms in several times, it focuses on two of the objects climbing up and to the left before briefly losing sight of them.
FORMER PENTAGON UFO CHIEF DISPUTES FBI BLACK TRIANGLE SIGHTING, SAYS REPORTS LACK EVIDENCE
In notes attached to the videos, officials stressed that the descriptions do not represent a final conclusion on what the cameras captured.

Civilian air-traffic radar over the western U.S. picked up eight unexplained hits in 2023 that stretched 38.5 miles in just 84 seconds at an estimated altitude of 55,000 to 70,000 feet – far above normal commercial airliners.
TRUMP SAYS AIR FORCE PILOTS DESCRIBED A ROUND UFO FLYING THREE TIMES FASTER THAN AN F-22 FIGHTER JET

Pentagon analysts calculated that if one object produced all eight blips, it was moving 1,650 mph – roughly Mach 2.5 – and made a sharp 39-degree turn. Because the radar swept only once every 12 seconds, investigators could not prove a single craft caused the track and left the case unresolved.

A newly declassified Pentagon graphic details an unresolved 2023 radar track over the United States that recorded eight detections spanning roughly 38.5 miles in 84 seconds – an apparent speed of about 1,650 mph, or Mach 2.5. (Department of War)

On Dec. 16, 1953, Lockheed engineer Clarence "Kelly" Johnson – who later designed the U-2 spy plane and the SR-71 Blackbird – spotted a dark, crescent- or wing-shaped object from the ground at his ranch near Agoura, California. Watching through eight-power binoculars, Johnson reported the craft hovered motionless for about three minutes before climbing away to the west toward Point Mugu.
NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS

What stood out in the newly released file is that Johnson was not alone. At the exact same time, a crew flying nearby aboard a Navy WV-2 aircraft spotted the same object from the air and gave matching descriptions of its shape, position and sudden climb out to sea.
Despite the independent accounts from both the air and the ground, the Air Force's Project Blue Book later wrote the sighting off as a lenticular cloud.

During the height of the 1952 UFO wave, CIA analysts tallied roughly 1,500 "flying saucer" reports since 1947 – including a massive surge of 250 sightings in July 1952 alone, the month before the agency's Office of Scientific Intelligence compiled an August briefing on the phenomenon.

To explain the wave, the CIA briefing laid out four leading theories: misidentified weather balloons or aircraft, natural optical illusions and atmospheric effects, secret Soviet or domestic weapons programs and extraterrestrial craft – noting that roughly 10% to 20% of the cases could not be explained away.
EX-PENTAGON OFFICIAL SAYS UAP FILES REVEAL 'TREASURE TROVE' OF INTELLIGENCE DATING BACK TO THE 1940S

In an accompanying memo, CIA Director Walter B. Smith warned the Psychological Strategy Board that the sudden flood of sightings posed national security and "psychological warfare" risks, urging officials to examine how the reports could trigger public panic or be exploited by the Soviet Union.

Military and contractor records document decades of unexplained objects hovering near American atomic sites, led by a massive review called "Project Northern Tier" that tracked hundreds of encounters near Strategic Air Command nuclear missile bases along the U.S.-Canadian border.

Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana stands out across the records for repeated sightings of glowing discs and strange lights directly over its nuclear missile fields – including a March 1967 encounter where 10 Minuteman nuclear missiles suddenly went offline while security guards reported a glowing disc hovering just above the silo gate, as well as a wave of 1975 intrusions over Montana missile sites that repeatedly scrambled Air Force jets.

In a separate historical file from Oct. 13, 1957, two teenagers reported seeing a humming, bell-shaped silver-gray craft near the Enrico Fermi atomic power plant in Monroe County, Michigan – adding to a pattern of sightings around nuclear facilities stretching back to the early Cold War.

A hand-drawn sketch included in a newly declassified 1957 military intelligence file depicts a saucer-shaped object estimated at 120 feet wide, reported by two teenagers near the Enrico Fermi atomic power plant in Monroe County, Michigan. (Department of War)

In an eight-page Air Intelligence Information Report dated Oct. 12, 1957, military investigators documented an encounter reported by a five-person fishing party off the Massachusetts coast, roughly 800 yards from Martha's Vineyard and one to two miles east-southeast of Woods Hole.

The file includes a hand-drawn sketch and witness statement detailing the unidentified object's shape, position and movement over the water as observed from the boat, adding a rare coastal maritime sighting to the Cold War records.

Program logs confirm active-duty military personnel were sent to Utah's infamous 480-acre Skinwalker Ranch under the Pentagon's $22 million Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP). The report notes an earlier six-year study on the property between 1996 and 2002 had logged roughly 70 unexplained incidents – ranging from colored orbs and flying objects to cattle disappearances, disembodied voices and poltergeist-like activity – leading contractors to deploy three military investigators alongside a program adviser to the ranch from June 30 to July 2, 2009.

On the first night, the team walked out on foot near a north-south line of trees and felt a sudden temperature drop of about 5 degrees coming from their left, while the air behind them remained noticeably warmer. One adviser asked if it was a "poltergeist-like effect," and another remarked that the hair was standing up on the back of his neck and his legs felt heavy – a foreboding sensation that vanished as soon as they walked back toward the main homestead.

Later during the trip, using Generation 3 night-vision goggles, the observers spotted a bright, hovering light source – yet when they compared notes, all four trained witnesses reported seeing completely different shapes: a circle, an oval, a rectangle and a diamond.

Inside Bigelow Aerospace's progress report, a proposal called "Project Forum" outlined plans to host public debates at California universities aimed at building mainstream acceptance of unidentified aerial phenomena.

Under the plan, event moderators would treat the existence of UFOs and extraterrestrial visitations as an established fact – explicitly instructing panelists that whether the phenomenon is real was "NOT a subject for any of the debates."

Instead, the proposed sessions were meant to focus on how the government and the public should respond, framing the issue around national security and scientific study while keeping skeptical arguments off the stage. The declassified files contain no evidence that the Pentagon ever approved or held the forums.

Senate Majority Leader Sen. Harry Reid (D-NV) speaks during a news conference October 21, 2009 on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

On June 24, 2009, then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid sent a confidential letter to Deputy Defense Secretary William Lynn III warning that the program had uncovered "highly sensitive, unconventional aerospace-related findings" and asking to lock it behind strict black-budget secrecy limited to just 14 people nationwide.

The Pentagon pushed back hard. On Nov. 13, 2009, Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) Deputy Director Letitia Long formally rejected the request, ruling unclassified scientific research could not legally be hidden under those secrecy rules, and DIA leaders wrote in a December 2010 memo that the contractor's work was of "limited value to DIA."

In May 2009, Bigelow Aerospace drew up architectural plans for a 5,000-square-foot underground concrete vault at its North Las Vegas complex, designed to sit 15 to 20 feet beneath the desert floor with 3-foot-thick walls and heavy steel doors.

story: Omaha police said 21-year-old French national Terry Kanmacher traveled to Nebraska and fatally stab 22-year-old daycare worker Lauren Becker, whom he had gone on one date with in 2023.
A French man is suspected of traveling to the United States to murder a woman he had gone on a date with three years earlier, according to police.

Lauren Becker, 22, was stabbed to death on Tuesday morning as she was walking into her job at an Omaha, Nebraska, daycare center, where her alleged killer waited for 45 minutes before stabbing her, police said during a news conference. The suspect, identified as 21-year-old French national Terry Kanmacher, had been living in France before he arrived in Omaha and allegedly killed Becker.

CALIFORNIA MOM BEGGED FOR HELP BEFORE EX GUNNED HER DOWN IN FRONT OF THEIR 4-YEAR-OLD SON: DA
Lauren Becker, 22, was fatally stabbed outside the Omaha daycare center where she worked on Tuesday morning. (Omaha Police Department)

title: Zeldin touts 'best-case scenario' after massive controlled detonation in Iowa
summary: EPA chief Lee Zeldin says air monitoring after an Iowa Army Ammunition Plant detonation found zero detectable airborne lead, calling it a best-case scenario.
story: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin discusses what it took to ensure there were no harmful materials after the detonation of a lead azide stockpile in Iowa on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin described initial air monitoring results after Wednesday's controlled detonation of a hazardous chemical stockpile in Iowa as a "best-case scenario," with the agency releasing its first laboratory results Friday night.
In its first batch of post-detonation laboratory results, the EPA said the detonation did not result in an increase in lead levels in bodies of water that serve as drinking water sources.

"The first lab results have arrived, indicating that @USArmy’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday DID NOT result in AN ELEVATION of lead in the water bodies that act as drinking water sources," the EPA posted on X. "As of data received Friday night, there was no detection of lead in drinking water sources taken after the detonation."

No lead was detected in 38 water samples collected from public water supplies following the detonation, including samples of treated drinking water and untreated water at intake locations, according to the EPA.
US ARMY TO PROCEED WITH IOWA DETONATION OF DEGRADED BOMB MATERIALS: ‘A CONSENSUS DECISION’
The US Army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Nov. 25, 2026. (Reuters/Jim Urquhart)

Speaking in an interview on Fox News earlier Friday, Zeldin said four air monitoring stations positioned downwind of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant recorded no detectable airborne lead after the controlled detonation.
"We only have measurements of 0.0, sometimes referred to as zero detect, sometimes referred to as non detect," Zeldin said.
"It's not that we just had a small elevation of lead being detected in our air monitoring," Zeldin added. "We had 0.0 readings on our air monitoring, and that's certainly a best-case scenario."

While the air monitoring results have been encouraging, Zeldin emphasized that the agency is continuing its environmental assessment, comparing thousands of samples collected before and after the detonation.
"We are going to make sure we do all of our due diligence," he said.
The EPA administrator said the agency expected to begin releasing the first post-detonation sampling results as early as Friday night.
"Hopefully that confirms what we saw at the air monitor," he said.
The agency's ongoing assessment comes after Wednesday's controlled detonation of the bomb-making chemical in Middletown, Iowa.
DR MARC SIEGEL: IOWA'S CANCER RATE IS RISING; ONE ANSWER MAY BE FOUND IN THE WATER

EPA personnel and contractors collect air, water, soil and dust samples in Middletown, Iowa, to assess potential environmental damage after Wednesday's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. (U.S. EPA Heartland Region via X)
Roughly 5 tons of degraded lead azide were destroyed after being deemed unsafe and unstable amid concerns that a plume of potentially toxic dust could drift toward Missouri in the wake of the blast.
The EPA has collected more than 3,000 air, water, soil and dust samples, including 1,639 before the detonation to establish a baseline and 1,618 afterward to assess potential environmental changes.

In a separate update Friday, the EPA reported that it had completed 88% of post-detonation sampling at homes where samples had also been collected before the blast and was working to complete the remaining assessments.
The agency said air monitoring concluded Thursday afternoon after 30 consecutive hours of no detectable airborne lead.
EPA REPORTS 'ZERO DETECTION OF AIRBORNE LEAD' DAY AFTER IOWA LEAD AZIDE DETONATION

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin attends a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in the Oval Office of the White House March 13, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump also sought to reassure residents Thursday about their safety following the detonation.
"They're 100% safe," he told reporters.
He emphasized that the U.S. Army did a "phenomenal job" with the detonation.

Environmental samples collected by the EPA in Iowa are being analyzed for potential contamination after the controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. (U.S. EPA Heartland Region via X)
Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

title: American Airlines planes clip wings during busy holiday travel weekend at Reagan National in DC
summary: The FAA will investigate after two American Airlines Boeing 737s clipped wings at Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., sending both back to gates.
story: Two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s clipped wings at Reagan National Airport Friday, prompting an FAA investigation. No injuries were reported. (ATC.com; Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Federal authorities are investigating after two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s clipped wings as they taxied for takeoff Friday at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) in Washington, D.C., forcing both aircraft to return to their gates.

The Federal Aviation Administration told Fox News Digital American Airlines Flight 638, bound for Dallas, clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152, headed to Chicago, while waiting in the departure queue at about 5:10 p.m.
Both planes returned to their gates and were checked by Airports Authority Fire and Rescue personnel, according to the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.
The American Airlines incident happened the day after Thanksgiving as travelers returned home after the holiday. (Nathan Howard/Reuters/File)
UPS CARGO PLANE, COPA AIRLINES PASSENGER JET COLLIDE AT MIAMI AIRPORT, LEAVING 2 INJURED

A Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Fire-Rescue aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle passes American Airlines airplanes at Terminal 2 at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport Nov. 7, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images/File)
REAGAN NATIONAL AIRPORT MAKES DRASTIC CHANGE FOLLOWING DEADLY 2025 MIDAIR COLLISION
The MWAA said no other flights were disrupted during the busy holiday weekend, and the airline noted customers from both flights will re-depart Friday evening.
The FAA will investigate the incident.
Rep. Nick LaLota shared a photo from aboard a plane after he said a second plane clipped a wing while on the DCA tarmac in April 2025. (Rep. Nick LaLota/X/File)

Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital at the time that he was on the plane alongside Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., Richie Torres, D-N.Y., and Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y. No injuries were reported.

"Serving in Congress has come with some once in a lifetime experiences… like just now while stationary on the runway at DCA, another plane just bumped into our wing," LaLota wrote in a social media post shortly after the collision.

title: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum protests new DEA tip line for reporting criminals, corrupt officials
summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico filed a formal complaint over the DEA tip line that lets anonymous callers report cartel operatives.
story: Former acting DEA Administrator Derek Maltz joins 'America's Newsroom' to discuss the capture of cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in Mexico during a raid that left at least 11 dead. Maltz explains the significance of the arrest and what is needed to combat Mexican drug cartels.

Mexico has filed a formal complaint with the United States over a new Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) tip line that allows anonymous callers to report corrupt government officials and cartel operatives, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday.

title: DHS accuses California of endangering ICE officers after bodycam shows police telling agents 'good luck'

title: Hackers breach Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, report says
summary: Hackers reportedly breached the U.S. Air Force's Cloud One platform, putting sensitive personnel and logistics data at risk, sources told Reuters.
story: Former White House Chief Information Officer Theresa Payton examines the national security implications of this hack. Payton outlines why seventeen government agencies remain highly vulnerable to sophisticated cyberattacks amid a wider string of high-profile technology outages.
Hackers reportedly breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship Cloud One computing platform, potentially accessing a wide swath of logistic and personnel data, three sources reportedly told Reuters.
The hack, which was discovered within the past month during system updating, may have jeopardized "a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data," according to Reuters.

"The Department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department information, systems, and mission capabilities. Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical warfighting assets remains a top priority," an Air Force spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement.
PENTAGON DATA BREACH EXPOSES SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBERS, PERSONAL INFO OF 2.76M US MILITARY, CIVILIAN PERSONNEL

"The Department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements. Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk-management processes," the statement concluded.
United States Air Force emblem on a circular surface with surrounding trees, sky visible in the background, Walnut Creek, California, April 18, 2023. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
Reuters' sources were not able to identify the identity of the hackers, the extent of their intrusion or the scope of what data they may have been able to collect, if any.
The discovery of the breach has led to disruption across the Cloud One platform, the sources told the outlet.

Cloud One is a proprietary system the Air Force launched in 2017 to combine the capabilities of the four major information technology platforms the department uses: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Google-owner Alphabet.
PENTAGON DATA BREACH EXPOSES RECORDS OF OVER 3M PEOPLE

The Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, a system that coordinates air defense radars, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 global Air Force locations, are part of the Cloud One platform.
"A breach here is a big deal," one source told Reuters.
CIA HIT BY CYBER BREACH THAT EXPOSED UNCLASSIFIED DATA ON INTELLIGENCE ANALYSIS NETWORK: SOURCES

A member of the USAF inspects Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAM) on a trailer in front of a US Air Force (USAF) B-1 Lancer bomber, on the tarmac at RAF Fairford in south-west England on March 11, 2026. (Henry NICHOLLS / AFP via Getty Images))
The reported breach is the latest in a series of recently disclosed hacks on government and military systems.

The FBI's National Crime Information Center has been the victim of hacking twice in the past few months, CNN reported last Friday. The CIA also recently suffered a data breach that exposed unclassified data used by law enforcement across the country, sources told Fox News.
HOMELAND SECURITY DATA LEAK EXPOSES 41K WORKERS

A late October hack on Department of Homeland Security (DHS) systems exposed the personal information of over 41,000 DHS employees, including undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.
A recent cyberattack on the Department of Treasury disabled portions of the department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

Additionally, the National Security Agency (NSA) made headlines when sources reportedly told CNN the agency's internal communication network was suffering from a service outage.

In 2023, Cloud One leadership, in an article on FedScoop.com, touted Cloud One's 100% success rate in combatting adversarial intrusions.
"There is no room for error when it comes to security," Cloud One's leadership wrote.

story: Anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot joins Bill Hemmer to discuss the legal fallout after a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the botched execution of Christa Pike. A Tennessee death row inmate who was convicted of torturing and murdering a 19-year-old classmate in the 1990s and survived a botched execution earlier this year is complaining about her treatment behind bars.

Attorneys for 50-year-old Christa Pike – the only woman on Tennessee's death row – asked a judge Monday to order prison officials to allow private mental health evaluations without a lawyer in the room, according to court records.

Officials also labeled van Eys as a "treating provider" and questioned the purpose of her work, Pike's lawyers alleged.

When Pike’s lawyers later requested access for Porterfield, prison officials said she would also have to be accompanied by a lawyer and "would not be permitted to keep her own notes and evaluation materials," the filing stated.

Pike's attorneys argued that the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) has no legal or policy basis to dictate how they represent her, asserting that the rule requiring a lawyer to personally accompany every expert is "imposed arbitrarily."

Her team also argued that TDOC’s own written policy defines an attorney as "any person working for, on behalf of, or under the direction of an attorney" – a definition they say covers the psychologists – and contains no requirement that a lawyer accompany outside experts.

CHRISTA PIKE'S FIRST WORDS REVEALED AFTER SHE UNEXPECTEDLY WOKE UP WHILE LAWYERS THOUGHT SHE WAS 'BRAIN DEAD'

The new fight comes weeks after Pike complained in a statement dictated to her legal team that she has been kept largely isolated in the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center since surviving the execution attempt.

Convicted killer Christa Gail Pike listens to proceedings on April 2008 in Knox County Criminal Court in a bid for a new trial in the 1995 killing of fellow Job Corps student Colleen Slemmer. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Following the Sept. 30 execution attempt, Pike was rushed to a hospital and remained unconscious for days. Her attorneys at one point believed she was brain-dead and expected her to be taken off life support, before she regained consciousness and was discharged back to prison.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee subsequently halted the state's remaining executions for the year and ordered an independent review of what went wrong, while signaling that Pike's death sentence is unlikely to change.

story: Survivor Skyler Boschen says recent attacks at NYU, Northwestern, Barnard and Stevens will continue unless colleges support survivors and parents act.

At least four young women have been attacked on or near U.S. college campuses in the last month, with one sexual assault survivor warning that these crimes will keep happening unless both universities and families step up.

Licensed therapist Skyler Boschen said colleges must offer better support for survivors, while parents need to teach their children boundaries early and ensure young men have role models who break the cycle of violence at home.
The recent attacks have happened on students attending four major universities – Stevens Institute of Technology, New York University, Northwestern and Ivy League Columbia.

title: Pregnant inmate escapes in New Mexico prison transport SUV during Whataburger stop
summary: Pregnant inmate Rebecca Taylor escaped a New Mexico corrections vehicle during a Whataburger stop in Albuquerque following a prenatal appointment.
story: New Mexico police launched a search for 26-year-old Rebecca Taylor, a pregnant prisoner who escaped custody in Albuquerque, after she allegedly climbed into the driver's seat of a state corrections SUV and drove off while stopped at a Whataburger.
A search is underway for a pregnant inmate who escaped in a New Mexico corrections vehicle during a stop for food at Whataburger, authorities said on Thursday.

Rebecca Taylor, 26, escaped from custody on the way to the Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants following a prenatal appointment on Wednesday morning, according to the New Mexico Corrections Department.
Taylor was incarcerated on multiple theft and burglary charges.
"Please use caution, and do not attempt to approach her. Wanted individuals can be unpredictable and may react unexpectedly if approached or confronted," the corrections department said.
TENNESSEE INMATE CONVICTED OF MURDER ESCAPES FROM PRISON, STEALS PICKUP TRUCK, MANHUNT UNDERWAY: OFFICIALS
Rebecca Taylor was incarcerated on multiple theft and burglary charges. (New Mexico Corrections Department)
She was last seen wearing a prison jumpsuit.
Three officers were transporting Taylor and another incarcerated woman back from their prenatal appointments when the group stopped for food in Albuquerque, officials said, according to KOAT.
At about 11:35 a.m. on Wednesday, they stopped for Whataburger along 98th Street.
Three officers were transporting Rebecca Taylor and another incarcerated woman back from their prenatal appointments when the group stopped for Whataburger in Albuquerque. (Epics/Getty Images)

As the driver stepped out of the vehicle, Taylor unbuckled herself and climbed into the driver’s seat before driving away, the outlet reported. The other inmate was able to jump out of the car and is now back in custody.
Taylor was not restrained during transport because she was pregnant.
It was unclear where the other two officers were after the vehicle stopped for food.
The Dodge Journey SUV was later found in an Albuquerque neighborhood with only Taylor's orange jumpsuit inside the vehicle. She has not been seen since.
MISSOURI STATE HIGHWAY PATROL CAPTURES CONVICTED MURDERER WHO ESCAPED TENNESSEE PRISON
Rebecca Taylor was not restrained during transport because she was pregnant. (iStock)

"The vehicle was later located by GPS in the area of Crestview Drive SW in Albuquerque. Taylor was not inside the vehicle when it was located," the corrections department said.
Officials said it remains an active and ongoing multi-agency search.

title: Trump mourns Florida detective killed by suspected drunk driver on Thanksgiving
summary: President Donald Trump paid tribute to Palm Beach County Detective Alan Smith, a bomb squad expert killed in a wrong-way crash on I-95 on Thanksgiving.
story: President Donald Trump paid tribute to Florida Detective Alan Smith, who was killed in a Thanksgiving morning wrong-way crash involving a suspected drunk driver with three prior DUI arrests.
President Donald Trump paid tribute Thursday to a Florida sheriff's detective killed in a wrong-way crash involving a suspected drunk driver on Thanksgiving morning.
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office identified the fallen officer as Detective Alan Smith, who had served with the department for nearly 20 years.
Smith, who specialized in explosives-related investigations, was fatally struck by a wrong-way driver on Interstate 95 early Thursday morning, according to the sheriff's office.
"It is with profound sadness and heavy hearts that we announce the devastating loss [of] our own, Detective Alan Smith," the department said in a statement.
DRUNK WRONG-WAY DRIVER KILLED MASS TROOPER AFTER 9 DRINKS AT BAR, DA REPORT SAYS
Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Detective Alan Smith was killed in a Thanksgiving morning wrong-way crash after nearly 20 years of service. (Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office)
Speaking Thursday during an event at Mar-a-Lago, Trump paid his respects to the family of the fallen officer, whom he described as "highly respected."
"I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, an expert at bombs and explosives, who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty," Trump said.
Trump described the crash as "horrific," saying the other driver had been traveling in the wrong direction on Interstate 95.
"It was a drunk driver. Really drunk driver," Trump said. "He was going on the opposite side of the highway, if you can believe it. And so it's a terrible thing that happened."
The Florida Highway Patrol arrested Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, Thursday afternoon at St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach.
SUSPECT IN DEADLY PHILADELPHIA POLICE AMBUSH FACES 76 CHARGES, ORDERED HELD WITHOUT BAIL

President Donald Trump speaks next to first lady Melania Trump as he makes Thanksgiving calls to U.S. service members from Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on Nov. 26, 2026. (REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque)
Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Martinez in the same handcuffs carried by Smith.

Martinez is expected to be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail once he is released from the hospital. He faces multiple charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide, aggravated battery, aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer and driving with a suspended or revoked license.
Authorities said Martinez has been arrested three times for DUI and that his driver's license had been revoked for 10 years, according to local outlet CBS12.

"This is a tragedy that shouldn't have happened," Florida Highway Patrol Maj. Kevin Strickland said. "He shouldn't have been driving a car at all, so part of our investigation is gonna determine how he was driving the car he was driving and how he got access to that vehicle."
ALLEGED DRUNKEN DRIVER WAS OVER 3 TIMES THE LIMIT WHEN HE KILLED NEWLY ENGAGED WOMAN DAYS AFTER JAIL RELEASE

Detective Alan Smith specialized in explosives-related investigations and served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. (Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office)
Smith joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in January 2007 before becoming a member of its bomb squad in 2012 and graduating from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013.
He also served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), specializing in explosives-related investigations.
Beyond his law enforcement career, Smith was a college professor and was working toward completing his doctoral degree, according to the sheriff's office.
He is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and their 14-year-old son, Alexander.
"Above all his professional and academic accomplishments, Alan's greatest pride was his family," the sheriff's office said.
THE FBI IS CHANGING HOW IT FIGHTS CRIME AND PROTECTS AMERICANS IN THEIR COMMUNITIES
A wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County, Florida, claimed the life of a sheriff's detective early Thanksgiving morning. (Florida Dept. of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles)
Tributes poured in from across the country, including from FBI Director Kash Patel.

"Detective Smith was one of the FBI's own, having graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013," Patel wrote on X, adding that Smith had "a long decorated career of service to this country."

"This is yet another reminder of the sacrifices our law enforcement make standing their posts even on holidays to keep us safe," he added. "Never forget them and their families. Our prayers are with Detective Smith's wife and 14 year old son, as well as the colleagues he leaves behind."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., Florida's governor-elect, also reacted to Smith's death, calling the news "devastating."
"This is a sober and heartbreaking reminder of the dangers that our brave law enforcement officers face day in and day out as they risk everything to keep us safe," he posted on X.

title: Apple AirTag leads firefighters to cat stuck in narrow gap between cement walls
summary: Firefighters drilled through concrete to free a missing cat tracked by an Apple AirTag in California, reuniting the feline with its owner.
story: A California owner used an AirTag to find their missing cat after it became trapped in a narrow gap between two retaining walls. Riverside County firefighters pulled the feline to safety.
Firefighters in Southern California rescued a missing cat wedged in a narrow gap between two concrete walls after the pet was tracked to the location thanks to an Apple AirTag on its collar.
The orange-and-white feline was stuck in a 4 to 5-inch-wide gap between two 8-foot-tall retaining walls in Indian Wells, the Riverside County Fire Department said on social media.
The owner located the missing cat using an AirTag attached to its collar, and firefighters were then able to free the animal from the tight spot.
TEXAS FIREFIGHTERS RESCUE DISTRESSED RACCOON AFTER ITS HEAD GETS STUCK IN A HOLE IN A TREE
The orange-and-white feline was stuck in a 4- to 5-inch-wide gap between two 8-foot-tall retaining walls. (Riverside County Fire Department)
With help from Riverside County Animal Services, "firefighters used specialized equipment to gain access through the wall and safely extricate the cat," the fire department said.
"Great teamwork by all involved in bringing this furry family member to safety!" the post added.
The cat was then reunited with its owner and transported to an emergency veterinarian for medical treatment.
A MISSING KITTEN RODE UNDER A CAR HOOD. AI BROUGHT HER HOME
Video showed a firefighter drilling into a concrete wall before pulling the cat free and lifting it out of the wall. (Riverside County Fire Department)
Video posted by the fire department showed a firefighter drilling into a concrete wall before pulling the cat free and lifting it out of the wall.
Images also show a firefighter holding the cat after it was rescued from the gap.
It was unclear how the animal managed to get stuck in the narrow gap.
The owner located the missing cat using an AirTag attached to its collar. (Riverside County Fire Department)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While the AirTag was used as a useful tool to rescue the cat, Apple typically does not recommend using the device for tracking pets.
Apple wrote on its website in January, while announcing the release of the new AirTag, that the device is designed "exclusively for tracking objects, and not people or pets."

title: TPUSA mourns Florida high school chapter president killed with family in devastating plane crash
summary: Turning Point USA's student program is mourning Hunter Stokes, 16, who led its Fort Myers chapter, after the Cessna 210 he rode in crashed off Horn Island, Mississippi.
story: Six family members from Fort Myers, Florida, were killed Tuesday when their small plane crashed off the Mississippi coast while returning from a fishing trip in Louisiana. Those killed were Brent Stokes, Hunter Stokes, Michael Knox, Arlyn Knox, Charles Holden Knox and Truett Knox. Brent Stokes was piloting the Cessna 210. Divers found all six victims inside the aircraft, two miles off Horn Island, Mississippi. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

Turning Point USA's student program mourned the death of a Florida high school chapter president this week after the teen and five members of his family died Tuesday in a plane crash off the Mississippi coast.
The organization said it was "heartbroken" over the loss of Hunter Stokes, 16, who led the Fort Myers High School Club America chapter.
"Hunter was a young patriot who loved his country and led by example," TPUSA Students said in a Wednesday post on X.
SIX FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN PLANE CRASH ON WAY HOME FROM FISHING TRIP IDENTIFIED

Turning Point USA remembered Hunter Stokes, 16, a Florida teenager who was president of the TPUSA Fort Myers High School Club America chapter. Stokes was killed, along with his father and other relatives, in a plane crash this week off the Mississippi coast on the way back from a fishing trip. (Facebook; TPUSA Students)

"From attending our Chapter Leadership Summit this summer to helping lead his chapter’s 9/11 Flag Run in honor of the victims of the September 11 attacks, Hunter was dedicated to making a difference in his community," the statement continued. "We are grateful to have had Hunter as part of our TPUSA family. Please join us in lifting his family, friends, and fellow chapter members up in prayer."

Hunter was killed in the crash alongside his father, Brent Stokes, 50; his aunt and uncle, Arlyn and Michael Knox, both 43; and his cousins, Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr.
DOZENS MISSING AFTER PASSENGER FERRY SINKS AS RESCUERS SCOUR SOUTH PACIFIC COASTLINE

The crash killed Brent Stokes, 50, and his son Hunter Stokes, 16, Brent Stokes’ sister Arlyn Knox, 43, her husband Michael Knox, 43, and their sons Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10. (Facebook)
GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS
The group was returning to Florida after a family fishing trip.

"They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family," both families said in a joint statement to The News-Press.
The six were aboard a Cessna 210 piloted by Brent Stokes when the aircraft went down two miles off Horn Island, Mississippi, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
Officials said the plane entered a descent of 10,000 feet per minute prior to the crash.
GOT A TIP?
White sand beaches are seen at Horn Island in the Gulf of Mexico, Mississippi, on June 26, 2010. (James Edward Bates/Biloxi Sun Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
Air traffic controllers advised Stokes of precipitation and adverse weather shortly before losing contact with the aircraft at about 3:45 p.m. local time, the New York Post and the FAA reported.
Brent Stokes was the president and CEO of Stokes Marine Inc., while Arlyn and Michael Knox led Knox Technologies, an IT company based in Fort Myers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
St. Cecilia Catholic Community on Wednesday said Brent and Hunter Stokes were former parishioners.

"Please keep the Stokes and Knox families in your prayers during this time of loss," the community wrote in a Facebook post. "May the Lord grant eternal rest and the promise of the Resurrection. Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Georgia man accused of killing wife after dispute over children's Christmas presents
summary: A Georgia man was charged with murder after police say he fatally shot his wife following an argument over Christmas presents for their four children.
story: Authorities in Georgia have charged 33-year-old Gene McCall Allen with murder after he allegedly killed his wife, Bonnie LaShea Allen, following an argument between the couple over Christmas presents for their four children. (GoFundMe)
A Georgia man was arrested after allegedly shooting and killing his wife following an argument about Christmas presents they purchased for their four children.

Gene McCall Allen, 33, was arrested Friday and charged with the murder of his wife of about eight years, Bonnie LaShea Allen, 32, according to the Walker County Sheriff's Office. He is being held at the Walker County Jail without bond.

Deputies responded to the couple's home in Rossville, south of Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the evening of Nov. 14 following a report of a woman who had been shot, according to an incident report obtained by People. Deputies found Gene Allen performing CPR on his wife, who had been shot in the head.
A deputy also found a gun resting on a closet shelf facing toward the room, according to the report.
MARATHONER ASKED HUSBAND ABOUT ‘POWDERY’ WATER BEFORE FATAL FALL – THEN POLICE FOUND HIS GOOGLE SEARCHES
Gene McCall Allen was arrested on Friday and charged with murder in the death of his wife, Bonnie LaShea Allen. (Walker County Sheriff's Office)

Gene Allen told deputies that the gun was inside the closet when it went off, People reported. He also allegedly told authorities he and his wife argued earlier that day about the Christmas presents they bought for their children, saying she raised concerns about the cost of shipping and the quality of the gifts.
The report also notes Gene Allen said he had four beers that day.
Bonnie Allen's family created a GoFundMe to help the children with their everyday needs, including clothing, according to the fundraising site. Her children are now being cared for by family members.
Bonnie LaShea Allen was remembered as a devoted mother who never missed an opportunity to support her children. (GoFundMe)

"Bonnie LaShae’s children & family [are] heartbroken over the tragic loss of a mother, daughter, sister, aunt and loved one who was taken far too soon. In the blink of an eye, her little children have lost their mother, and their lives have been changed forever," the fundraiser states.
"No family should ever have to experience this kind of heartbreak, especially these little ones who have so much life ahead of them," it added.
The GoFundMe has raised about $12,000 as of Thursday evening.
In her obituary, Bonnie was remembered as "an amazing mother who never missed an opportunity to support her children."
FLORIDA DEPUTY KILLED EX-GIRLFRIEND OVER A TV, THEN HIMSELF, SHERIFF SAYS
Bonnie LaShea Allen's children are now being cared for by family members. (GoFundMe)

"Whether cheering them on at a ball game or encouraging other children, she was always there, proudly showing her love and support. She was her children’s biggest fan, greatest encourager, and strongest supporter," the obituary reads.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"She was a blessing to everyone fortunate enough to know her. Bonnie had a joy that was contagious and a personality that could light up any room. She was fun-loving, full of life, and always brought happiness wherever she went. A strong, natural leader, Bonnie had a way of encouraging others, making people feel welcome, and leaving a lasting impression on everyone she met. She will be remembered for her beautiful spirit, unwavering love for her family, her faith, and the joy she brought into so many lives," it added.

title: EPA reports 'zero detection of airborne lead' day after Iowa lead azide detonation
summary: The EPA reports zero detection of airborne lead after the detonation of five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.
story: FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton discusses the aftermath of the U.S. Army’s successful controlled detonation of nearly 5 tons of lead azide in Iowa on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Thursday that its air monitors continue to report "zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region" after the detonation of a stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

The statement comes as the EPA said it collected more than 1,000 samples following Wednesday's controlled detonation of the bomb-making chemical in Middletown, Iowa. Nearly 1,600 air, water, soil and dust samples were taken beforehand to establish a baseline for measuring any potential environmental changes.

Around five tons of degraded lead azide were destroyed after being deemed unsafe and unstable, and there were concerns that a plume of potentially toxic dust could drift towards Missouri in the wake of the blast.

"Following the controlled detonation, EPA sampled homes, public parks with playgrounds, and every drinking water intake in the pre-detonation plume model. Today, EPA personnel and contractors will be specifically sampling schools, playgrounds, daycares, churches, and more in the region," the EPA said Thursday.
ARMY DETONATES TONS OF LEAD AZIDE IN IOWA AS MAP SHOWS DUST PLUME PROJECTIONS
The U.S. Army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026. (Reuters/Jim Urquhart)

"Partnering with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, EPA has collected samples from nearby farms both before and after the controlled detonation," it also said. "Extensive sampling of water in the Mississippi River watershed has been completed both before and after the controlled detonation."
The EPA added that "air cassettes that sample for lead will be replaced to continue sampling today," and that "soil and dust sampling is expected to conclude today."
ARMY DESTROYS 68 BARRELS OF DEGRADED LEAD AZIDE IN IOWA

"The Trump EPA will continue its presence on the ground for as long as needed to ensure the proper environmental monitoring is taking place following the successful controlled detonation," it concluded.
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said late Wednesday that the controlled detonation "exceeded expectations in a big way."
A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: Has the holiday tradition ever been canceled?
summary: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed by a powerful coastal storm, but the New York City tradition has been canceled only three times.
story: Severe weather delays millions of Thanksgiving travelers as major coastal storms postpone the iconic parade in New York City.

While severe weather forced the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to postpone until Saturday for the first time ever, the holiday tradition has only been canceled three times in its century-long history — a three-year hiatus for World War II.

New York City officials announced Wednesday evening that this year's march would move to Saturday, Nov. 28 at 8:30 a.m. as a powerful coastal storm brings heavy rain and damaging wind gusts between 60 mph and 70 mph to the Northeast and New England, according to FOX Weather. Forecasts projected Thursday morning gusts between 35 mph and 45 mph, exceeding safety limits requiring sustained winds below 23 mph and gusts under 34 mph for balloons to fly.

Even when severe weather threatened past parades, organizers historically kept the march moving on Thanksgiving Day, grounding all the giant balloons only once, in 1971, when heavy rain and high winds kept the inflatables deflated while floats and marching bands continued down the route, according to FOX5 New York. The city's current wind limits were adopted after the 1997 parade, when 40 mph gusts blew the "Cat in the Hat" balloon into a lamppost and injured spectators.
A LOOK AT HOW THE TRUMPS SPEND THEIR THANKSGIVING HOLIDAY THROUGH THE YEARS

People line up along Central Park West at 70th Street to watch Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade when the tradition returned from a three-year hiatus due to World War II on Nov. 22, 1945. (Gordon Rynders/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)
To find the only years the parade was canceled altogether, you have to step back more than eight decades to the World War II home front.

Following the Dec. 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbor, American factories shifted to wartime production, and critical supplies like rubber and helium were needed for the military. For three straight years — 1942, 1943 and 1944 — Macy's canceled the Thanksgiving Day march so its materials could support the war effort.
Rather than issuing a dry corporate notice, Macy’s ran a 1942 newspaper advertisement written from the perspective of its grounded balloons, according to the American Rosie the Riveter Association.

"We Macy balloons have always stood for peace and plenty of fun for all," the advertisement read. "We were a weaving and bobbing symbol of democracy at play. We figured in a parade devoted to laughter and shenanigans. Fear never marched in our ranks."
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade at Times Square in New York City, on Nov. 22, 1945. (Gordon Rynders/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)
"But now we’ve a war to win and we’ve enlisted, to help make the world safe for future parades full of merriment and good will," the ad continued.

On Nov. 13, 1942, Macy's Jack Strauss formally donated the giant balloons to New York City Mayor Fiorello La Guardia and the New York City Salvage Committee, according to Macy's and The New York Times. During a dramatic City Hall ceremony, La Guardia dressed as St. George and symbolically slayed an air-filled, 60-foot dragon balloon with a knife, converting the parade stars into 650 pounds of scrap rubber bound for military tires, life rafts or dirigibles.
CENTCOM'S THANKSGIVING MESSAGE TO TROOPS 'IS ONE OF DEEP GRATITUDE' FOR THEIR 'EXCEPTIONAL WORK' PROTECTING US

Canceling the march also conserved helium, metal cylinders, tires and gasoline while freeing up New York police officers to guard warehouses and docks instead of managing a 2-million-person crowd, Macy's noted at the time. Even with the streets quiet, the department store kept some holiday magic alive with its mechanical window displays designed by Russell Patterson, which opened at 9 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day with a 26-float show titled "The Funny Page Parade."

When the parade finally returned in 1945, the pent-up excitement turned the route down Central Park West from 106th Street to Herald Square into what The New York Times described as a second victory parade. An estimated 2 million spectators lined the streets, including more than 30,000 people packed into Times Square.
"For the generation born during the war it was the opening of a new wonderland," The New York Times reported at the time.

Attendants drag the huge "Bobo the Hobo" balloon down the street as spectators enjoy the sights at the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, Nov. 22, 1945. In the distance in the left-center, more balloons can be seen on their way down the street. (Getty)

Seven bands and 20 floats marched past a large model of the Statue of Liberty in Times Square as NBC broadcast the event on television for the very first time. Helium-filled giants returned to the Manhattan skyline, including a 45-foot "Bobo" holding 6,600 cubic feet of helium, a 40-foot teddy bear, a triple-scoop ice cream cone and a 16-foot aerialist swinging from a 25-foot balloon that required occasional top-offs of helium along the route when its head began to sag.
Since that triumphant 1945 comeback, the march has rolled on through other national crises until this week's storm.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In 2001, following the Sept. 11 terror attacks, Macy's Public Relations Vice President Ronnie Taffet told The New York Times there was no discussion of canceling the event, noting officials "from the mayor on down" felt holding the parade was vital.
In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, there was no audience along the parade route and organizers cut down the march from two blocks to one.

title: Secret Pentagon UFO hunt drew blueprints for hidden Nevada bunker to store ‘exotic’ materials
summary: Declassified Pentagon records reveal Bigelow Aerospace planned a secret underground vault in Nevada to store recovered UAP hardware and samples.
story: Newly released clips from the Pentagon’s eighth UAP batch capture U.S. military sensors tracking unexplained objects in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

Buried beneath 15 to 20 feet of Nevada earth, behind 3-foot-thick reinforced concrete walls, a steel vault door and a heavily guarded access tunnel, a Pentagon contractor drew up plans to build a 5,000-square-foot subterranean fortress.

The bunker was designed to store what was described as acquired "exotic material or tissue" – including recovered hardware and biological samples tied to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), the Pentagon’s broader term for UFOs and other unexplained sightings in the air, space or sea.

The blueprint was not drawn from science fiction. It is detailed inside a 538-page declassified contractor report released by the Department of War as part of the Trump administration's latest batch of UAP records, exposing how close a private firm came to building a secure repository under a $22 million Pentagon program.
EX-PENTAGON OFFICIAL SAYS UAP FILES REVEAL 'TREASURE TROVE' OF INTELLIGENCE DATING BACK TO THE 1940S

The vault plans highlight the ambitions behind the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program – also referred to in Pentagon correspondence as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program.

A section of a July 2009 report by Pentagon contractor Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) details architectural plans for a 5,000-square-foot underground vault in North Las Vegas to store recovered hardware and biological samples. (Department of War)

Launched in 2008 through a $10 million congressional earmark steered by then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., and the late Sen. Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii, the effort was billed as a study of foreign aerospace threats out to 40 years in the future.

Internal Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) briefing notes from May 2009 say Reid was hunting for radical technological "leaps" across 12 areas – ranging from futuristic propulsion and stealth to directed-energy weapons, space-time travel and how advanced craft affect pilots.
Behind closed doors, however, contractor Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) was preparing to acquire and store physical materials.
'NON-HUMAN' BODIES ALLEGEDLY RECOVERED FROM CRASHED UFO, DOCUMENTARY FILMMAKER CLAIMS
When the DIA solicited bids in August 2008, only one company applied: North Las Vegas-based BAASS, founded by longtime Reid supporter Robert Bigelow. The DIA awarded the contract the following month.
Then-Senate Majority Leader Sen. Harry Reid speaks during a news conference on Oct. 21, 2009, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Within weeks, BAASS moved into a nondescript building on South Polaris Avenue in Las Vegas and began turning it into a fortified compound – installing soundproofed offices, electronic deadbolts, tinted windows, security cameras and an 8-foot perimeter fence while stripping all company names and logos from the exterior.

By May 2009, as the firm's payroll swelled to 47 full-time employees – including scientists, engineers and former military and law enforcement investigators – BAASS began shopping for five additional Las Vegas Valley office buildings to house a 5,000-square-foot laboratory, physical evidence storage and a secure conference room.

At the same time, the company's administrator drew up blueprints for the underground bunker at Bigelow Aerospace's North Las Vegas complex, a site protected by razor wire, surveillance cameras and round-the-clock armed guards with military backgrounds.
UAP WHISTLEBLOWER MAKES STUNNING CLAIM ABOUT SECRETS BEHIND GOVERNMENT’S RECOVERED CRAFT

A satellite image shows a UFO spaceship at night amid an FBI investigation and alien evidence near Area 51, capturing a flying saucer and galaxy survey of a mysterious object in the sky. (Getty Images Creatives)

"The need for a highly secure underground vault operated by BAASS became apparent in line with a BAASS priority to pursue and acquire recovered hardware and biological samples from the corporate world and/or from private individuals and groups located elsewhere, including Brazil," the July 2009 10-month report states.
Plans called for multiple security doors along a concrete access tunnel leading into the buried structure, with any protruding surface components "extensively camouflaged," the filing adds.
To shield the program from broader scrutiny, Reid pushed the Pentagon to place the effort behind one of the military's highest secrecy walls.

On June 24, 2009, Reid wrote directly to Deputy Defense Secretary William Lynn III warning that investigators had uncovered "several highly sensitive, unconventional aerospace-related findings" that required "extraordinary protection."

Reid argued that standard classification protocols were not enough, warning that foreign intelligence services would target the program's methods and that public disclosure could scare off private industry partners.
One of Enigma’s most compelling witness accounts involves two unknown, lighted objects being observed underwater from a boat, according to Marine Technology News. (iStock)

He urged Lynn to place portions of the effort inside a Restricted Special Access Program governed by a strict "Bigoted Access List" – a tightly controlled roster limiting knowledge of the program's existence to a handful of pre-approved officials.
PENTAGON’S NEW UFO FILE RELEASE LOGS NEAR-MISS AS ‘SUPER-HEATED’ ORBS APPROACH US HELICOPTER

In an attachment to his letter, Reid proposed a 14-person access list that included himself, Inouye, Lynn, Senate aide Robert T. Herbert, seven government and military personnel and three BAASS contractors.

An attachment to then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid's June 24, 2009, letter to Deputy Defense Secretary William Lynn III proposes a 14-person "Bigoted Access List" of government officials and BAASS contractors for the program. (Department of War)
When DIA officials evaluated the program's actual work, however, they reached a sharply different conclusion.

In its first year, BAASS paid outside scientists to write 26 research papers on sci-fi-sounding concepts – including warp drives, wormholes, antigravity, invisibility cloaking and mind-controlled machines, contract records show.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

While a DIA office initially praised the papers as solid academic surveys – noting several received positive peer reviews, including from researchers at Sandia National Laboratories – the agency's leadership refused to lock the program behind top-secret classification rules.
A witness drawing included in the July 2009 BAASS report illustrates a cigar-shaped object estimated at 100 meters long during Brazil's 1977 Colares UAP wave. (Department of War)
In a Nov. 13, 2009, memo, DIA Deputy Director Letitia A. Long formally rejected Reid's secrecy request.

"All program documents delivered to [the Defense Warning Office] during FY 2009 (the first year of the program) were unclassified because the contractor had not established a secure facility, and program employees were being vetted for clearances," Long wrote.

Long noted that federal regulations prohibit the DIA from classifying basic scientific research unless it clearly relates to national security, adding that the agency was "unaware of any report containing information sufficiently sensitive and vulnerable to require extra protection."

A witness sketch reproduced in the July 2009 BAASS report depicts a cylindrical object and its flight path during Brazil's 1977 "Operation Plate" UAP investigation in Santo Antônio do Tauá. (Department of War)

Later that same month, DIA Director Lt. Gen. Ronald L. Burgess Jr. and Lynn met with Reid in person and told him the contractor's reports were of "limited value to DIA," recommending the project be moved out of the intelligence agency altogether, Burgess later wrote in a December 2010 memo.

Although Congress tacked on another $12 million for the effort in fiscal year 2010 – bringing total funding to $22 million and yielding 12 additional technical reports – the DIA did not continue the contract beyond its second year.

Alongside the paper trail, the Pentagon's eighth UAP release under the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) also included three newly declassified infrared and electro-optical sensor videos submitted by U.S. Central Command to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO).

Recorded aboard U.S. military platforms in 2020, 2023 and 2026, the clips show sensors panning and zooming to track unidentified "areas of contrast" across the frame, including a 54-second 2026 recording in which a sensor tracks two separate objects before intermittently losing contact.

Pentagon officials noted in the release that the video descriptions do not reflect analytical conclusions about the nature or significance of the objects, and said no redactions were made to hide information about UAP encounters under President Donald Trump's transparency directive.

title: CENTCOM's Thanksgiving message to troops 'is one of deep gratitude' for their 'exceptional work' protecting US
summary: CENTCOM spokesman Tim Hawkins told Fox News Digital that the military command is "grateful" for the family members of American forces positioned overseas.
story: U.S. Central Command spokesperson and U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins praises American service members and their families.

U.S. Central Command spokesperson and Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins told Fox News Digital that his message to the more than 50,000 service members stationed across the Middle East this Thanksgiving is "one of deep gratitude for the exceptional work they're doing."

"Right now, they're focused on a variety of missions, including helping protect shipping moving through the Strait of Hormuz, an international waterway. They're also maintaining America's ironclad blockade against Iran. Highly effective," Hawkins said. "And they're also protecting America and Americans from terrorists. So a lot of hard work. We're very grateful for their outstanding focus, commitment, and dedication to the mission."
Hawkins also said CENTCOM is "grateful" this holiday for the families of America's men and women in uniform.

"We have a highly motivated team deployed to the Middle East, but as many of us know in uniform, military service does not come without great personal service, great personal sacrifice, and great personal cost. And that cost isn't just unique to our service members, it is also shared by the family members back at home who are waiting," Hawkins told Fox News Digital.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS

Capt. Dan Keeler, USS Abraham Lincoln's commanding officer, greets his family members after the carrier returned home following an extended deployment in the Middle East, at Naval Base Coronado in San Diego, Calif., on Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters)

"They're praying. They are holding down the home front during a very, very challenging period of time," he added. "So I want all of them watching to know they are in our thoughts, and we are also grateful to them, and we wish them a happy Thanksgiving."
CENTCOM has played a key role in Operation Epic Fury against Iran, which was launched on Feb. 28.

"Of course, a lot of folks focus on Iran, and that has been a primary focus, but we've been doing other things, continuing to ensure that ISIS doesn't reconstitute in order to protect America and Americans," Hawkins said about the Islamic State terrorist group.
US MILITARY COMPLETES WITHDRAWAL OF TROOPS FROM IRAQ AFTER 12-YEAR MISSION
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper shakes hands with soldiers and sailors in Bahrain. (CENTCOM)

CENTCOM said in September, following the departure of U.S. forces and equipment in Iraq, "Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve (CJTF-OIR) remains operational and is now headquartered in Jordan as U.S. forces continue the counter-ISIS mission in Syria alongside Coalition partners and the Syrian government."
Sailor Timothy Nickles greets his daughters after the USS Abraham Lincoln returned home to Naval Base Coronado in San Diego, Calif., on Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters)

"We've also been working shoulder to shoulder with our partners and defending against Iranian aggression," Hawkins told Fox News Digital. "There have been around 10,000 or more projectiles fired at innocent civilians, Gulf neighbors, and our service members have stood shoulder to shoulder with our regional partners and protecting not only our forces, but the civilians around.
A pilot is seen in an Air Force F-35A stealth fighter jet after the aircraft landed at a base in the Middle East, in this photo released by CENTCOM on Nov. 9, 2026. (CENTCOM)

"And of course, as you have seen in the Strait of Hormuz, traffic is flowing through, and that's because of the great commitment of our service members in protecting international shipping," he added.
